A cross-family review pass is still owed before ratification, because the owner allowed no further agent slot tonight. c4 (build profiles) is held until the a0_035 release ends; c7 waits on #6623.

criteria.text: One build function declares jet, the runtime pack, jetpack, the docs site and the release package as targets, so `jet build` builds them concurrently from one graph and the packages suite reuses that jetpack instead of building its own.

Every generated registry table (CoreEnumRows, CoreStructureRows and the rest) comes from `b.generate` over its source registry, so it cannot be stale, and the precommit generator checks for those tables are deleted.

The C compiler and musl are declared with `b.toolchain` and `b.probe`. JET_PACK_MUSL_LIB and the other toolchain environment variables are deleted, and a missing tool fails at once with a registered error.
The self-host stages and the s2 == s3 byte-identical check are build actions; a stage whose inputs are unchanged is reused. The shell steps they replace in Tools/agent/chain are deleted.

Each compiler package (JetFoundation, JetLexer, JetParser, JetSema, JetIR, JetBackend, JetCli and the rest) is its own library target that compiles in parallel, so an edit rebuilds only the packages that depend on it. Depends on #6623.
Build profiles give a fast `dev` profile for targeted testing and a `ship` profile for release stages.
Every build records a core.build graph receipt with per-target wall time. receipt_diff between two commits shows what rebuilt and why, and the per-phase timeline for #6610 is read from it.

The step-output-in-read-folder rule (Graph.jet and Jetpack Validation.jet, spec.md:5050, E3502) compares resolved real folders, not spelled paths. A dependency bound at .jet/deps (or any other alias) that resolves to a folder holding a step output is refused. The project root and each dependency root are threaded into both validators and resolved through the host. A BuildGraphRules #Test covers the alias case.

cards.title: Portable seed: build a working Jet on a machine that has only a C compiler or a WebAssembly runtime
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-11-07: seeding and bootstrapping the compiler is a separate question from transpilation (#6675, D-EXPORT-TARGET1) and is frozen for the future. Transpilation comes first.

Goal: a machine with no Jet binary builds a current Jet from what it already has, so a seed never goes stale and a new platform is never stuck.

Candidate plan from the earlier D-EXPORT-TARGET1 draft, which is not ratified: compile the compiler with the existing WebAssembly writer, then turn that .wasm into C with a committed WebAssembly-to-C translator. A small C host answers the runtime's system calls on POSIX, and compile-time code runs on the IR evaluator instead of an x86-64 child. Every release checks that the seed rebuilds the release's own stage-2 bytes. Once the #6675 C target exists, exporting the compiler to C is the alternative route. Trust limit: a seed built from generated output still trusts the compiler that wrote it; only an independent Jet implementation removes that.

criteria.text: An adversarial design review in Docs/audits tests the seed's claims (durability, onboarding, trust) against existing bootstrap chains: Zig's WebAssembly seed, Nim's generated C, mrustc, and bootstrappable builds. Every gap it finds is on a card or ballot.
A ratified Tower ballot picks the seed route (WebAssembly translated to C, the #6675 C target, or prebuilt binaries only), with same-program alternatives and the trust limits stated.

Exporting the compiler's own source to C (and to Wasm) gives a compiler that, built with only a C compiler (or a Wasm runtime), compiles the same tree to a byte-identical stage-2 compiler: a portable seed for every release, linked with #6186.
Install docs describe building Jet from the exported seed with a stock C compiler, and a fresh machine with no Jet binary follows them to a working jet.

cards.title: The hosted Jetpack engine takes about 3 minutes to build on a quiet host while the whole compiler self-compiles in about 10 s
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-11-07: Pareto speed work for the fresh-clone full profile.

The packages suite builds the hosted Jetpack engine (Jetpack/Bootstrap/Assemble.jet hosted, then `jet build src/jetpack.jet`, in Compiler/test.jet jetpack_prepare). It took 184 s when it started on a quiet host and about 13 minutes on one core under load. The compiler, a larger codebase, self-compiles in about 10 s (#6527). The ratio points at something specific to the Jetpack build path (the assembled single unit, its optimization level, a pathological function, or a phase that grows superlinearly), not at code size.

log.text: Main 2026-11-07: SpeedLead landed 3412bcf62f (jet build cache entries, locks, leases and touches publish unsynced; reads verify digests, so a lost entry is a miss; the rlib cache, runtime pack, objects and LTO keep their syncs). The store publish tail went from 127.3 s/17.0 s to 8.4 s/5.0 s (fresh store, interleaved), with zero fsync calls during the build (strace). It also landed ef8a3f930d (L0534 copied the 12.5 MB engine module once per block: sema.finalize 149 s -> 5.8 s; sema.bodies 97 s -> 2.7 s; tests/ui_lint/map_group_round_trip.jet still prints L0534 at 10:9). Whole hosted engine build: 168 s -> 33.0 s at load 14 (28.6 s on a rerun); a cache hit takes 16.9 s. Proof by Main is pending (batch).

criteria.text: A per-phase profile of the hosted engine build (front end, sema, lowering, optimization, emission, link) names where the time goes, and it is recorded on this card with the commit.
criteria.evidence: Per-phase traces (jet build --trace; wall s / CPU s; 12 CPUs pinned on the busy 32-CPU host) of jet build src/jetpack.jet in the assembled hosted project (618 sources; one 12.5 MB module). dev eaa085b237: total 156.8-243.9 s wall, of which sema.finalize 98-149 s (sema.bodies 48-97 s wall / 547-928 CPU-s) and the store tail 17-127 s (fsync D-state); the front end 5-7 s, lowering 0.7-1.2 s, ir.opt 2.2-3.5 s, emission 0.7-0.9 s, link 0.15 s. Root cause 1: store fsyncs, fixed by 3412bcf62f (no fsync calls in strace). Root cause 2: the L0534 lint (10ce9aab90) copied the whole module bytes per block, fixed by ef8a3f930d. With both fixes: total 32.95 s wall / 49.7 CPU-s; sema.finalize 5.81 s; store tail 11.8 s under writeback throttling; cache hit 16.9 s. The table and the exact commands are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SpeedLead/6684-phases.md.

criteria.text: The root cause is fixed in the compiler or in Jetpack's assembly, and the hosted engine build on a quiet batch host takes at most 30 s, measured and recorded with the commit.
The built engine is byte-for-byte the same program as before the fix, or every packages-suite engine claim still passes.

cards.title: The Jetpack engine unit's claims all run serially because they share process state
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-11-07: card the remaining slow phases.

Compiler/test.jet jetpack_engine_rows runs `jet test src/jetpack.jet --serial` over the assembled engine unit (about 559 claims), because the claims share process state. Every claim waits for the one before it.

log.text: Main 2026-11-07, from SpeedLead measurements (hosted engine unit, after #6684 fixes; host busy, load 12-40): `jet test src/jetpack.jet --serial` took 243 s (compile 55 s, claims about 188 s); without --serial 195 s, with the same 807/22/15 and the same 22 known failures. One clean parallel run is evidence that the claims share no state, not proof; dropping the flag means editing jetpack_engine_rows. Compiling the unit alone at load 7 takes 15.7 s. 715 claims take under 0.1 s each; four take 102 of 225 s: StoreIngestLate.jet:42 "store closure readers are serialized with registration and compaction" 57.8 s, StoreIngestLate.jet:31 18.0 s, Lifecycle.jet:302 14.9 s, NixCache.jet:784 11.5 s. strace of the 57.8 s claim shows it is CPU-bound in the store, with no child processes and temp files on tmpfs: every closure-graph load re-verifies every record (producer and metadata decode, receipt rehash, seal checks), and 70 ingest+load pairs make that quadratic. Under 1 minute needs incremental verification in the store (a trust-design change), plus parallel claims. Ruled out: per-test module-scope copies in sema (5.7 s sema.bodies at low load).

criteria.text: The wall time of the engine unit's compile and its serial claim run are measured on the batch host and recorded with the commit.
Claims that share process state are isolated (each owns its state, or the shared state is per-claim), so the unit runs without --serial and every claim still passes.
The engine unit's claims finish in under 1 minute wall.

cards.title: Plain jet decides by file extension: `jet run x.c`, `jet build x.c` and `jet x.c` compile C (and C++) instead of parsing it as Jet
cards.body: Owner order 2026-11-08: "Yes obviously we should decide behavior based on extension. That needs to be fixed." Probe on seed a0_038: `jet run hello.c`, `jet build hello.c` and `jet hello.c` parse the C file as Jet and print jet.InvalidStatement ("Expected a call... found <"). `jet cc hello.c` took 75 s and then failed with E1275 (C/C++ build sandbox unavailable). Plain jet already compiles C inside Jet programs (c@path deps and #FFI(c) bodies, Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/ForeignLink.jet) through the toolchain C pack or CC; the entry commands must route a C or C++ source through that same one mechanism (I8), not through a second path.

log.text: Owner rulings 2026-11-08. Q7: H1, core.crypto.Hasher really streams (new, update and digest stay; the public data field becomes private native SHA state). Q8: ship bwrap in the C toolchain pack for now, until the sandbox is built properly in Jet; the Jet sandbox is a longer-term card, not now (filed separately so bwrap removal is not lost). Q15: all five behaviors confirmed; no C++ standard library now (maybe a stretch goal).

QuickLead landed 775f3b07ae (28 files; unverified by Main, queued for the batch). c1: jet run, jet build and jet x.c, with .cc, .cpp and .cxx as C++, go through ForeignLink jet_cli_native_c_tools; case run_entry/c_and_cpp_files_run_by_extension (cases run_entry PASS 18, FAIL 0). c2: E2116 UnhandledSourceExtension with a UI snapshot; #! scripts stay Jet. c4: golden Examples/Interop/FFI/PlainC.c PASS on O0, O1 and O2. c3 partial: E1275 now names its reason (Bubblewrap not on PATH) and pkg_sha256_hex is native. fetch-toolchain went from 23.2 s to 15.2 s (hyperfine, 3 runs, host load about 33). But jet run hello.c is still 25 to 28 s with no JET_CC_PACK_ROOT, and jet cc with bwrap takes 80.5 s real (13.0 s user); the rest waits on owner choices H and B. jet build hello.c with the pack takes 29.8 ms. Behavior choices built and pending owner confirmation: O0, O1 and O2 mapping; build output to .jet/build/<stem>; check, doc and dev refuse with E2116; no mixing .jet and .c; no C++ stdlib in the pack.

criteria.text: `jet run x.c`, `jet build x.c` and `jet x.c` (and .cc, .cpp, .cxx for C++) compile the source with the toolchain C path that Jet programs already use for their C, then link and run it; each prints the program output and exit code on this host with no extra flag, case-tested.
A source whose extension jet does not handle gets a registered diagnostic naming the extension and the extensions jet accepts, with what/why/fix text and a UI snapshot (I4), never a Jet parse error.

`jet cc hello.c` and `jet run hello.c` work on this development host: the E1275 sandbox refusal seen on 2026-11-08 is root-caused and fixed, and a fresh C compile finishes in seconds, not 75 s (receipt with times).
An Examples/ entry runs a C file with plain `jet run`, golden-tested (I5).

cards.title: Jet depends on no other language: port every C dependency (musl, libgcc, SQLite, mbedtls) to Jet
cards.body:
Owner order 2026-11-08: "We need to fix the issue blocking build.jet but also need to remove the C dependencies. Start by directly porting the functions being used but we also need full coverage of the libraries that are dependencies. Ensure all are tracked."

Census (Main, dev 9b21994eb3, seed a0_038): jet_runtime_jet.o has 55 undefined symbols, 54 from musl (33 math, 6 pthread, 4 DNS, 11 process, terminal and filesystem calls) plus jet_rt_fault_report. The source has 72 #Import(c) or #FFI(c) sites outside tests, fixtures, binders and examples: JetRuntime CompilerNeededMath.jet 29, RouteSys.jet 8, Thread.jet 6, HostNetResolver.jet 4, RouteTerm.jet 2, and TextFmt, Sync, ProcessSignal, NetRoutes and HostSpawn 1 each; JetDevserver WatchService.jet 7 and WebHost02.jet 4; JetCli Host.jet 2; JetTestKit RequireTool.jet and Assets/no_nix.jet 1 each; Tools/ci/CompiledWorkloadPeerLauncher.jet 1; and Tools/agent-eval/ffi-assurance 2 (a C-interop proof, which stays). The runtime pack links musl libc.a, libgcc.a and libgcc_eh.a (jet-runtime/foreign/platform). Vendored C: Core/Vendor/Sqlite3 (core.db) and Core/Vendor/Mbedtls (core.net TLS), together about 474k lines of C and headers. The clang C toolchain pack serves only users' C interop and `jet cc`, a feature that stays.

Order: first port the functions Jet uses today (math, threads, syscall wrappers, DNS, the compiler's and tools' own C imports), so the runtime pack drops musl and libgcc. Then port the vendored libraries in full: mbedtls, then SQLite. Each library port covers the whole library that the dependency provided, not only today's call sites. #6682 c4's fresh-clone C compiler requirement disappears once the runtime pack and every artifact jet build Compiler makes contain no C.

log.text: Owner ruling 2026-11-08 ~14:10: a new public API does not need a ballot or owner approval for now. Agents follow best practices and idiomatic Jet, using Jet API-building features (typed records with defaults, traits and derives, typed config, Result errors), in the shape of existing Core modules. Other owner gates (syntax, commands, dependencies, invariant exceptions, scope) stay.
Owner Q8 ruling 2026-11-08: bwrap ships in the C toolchain pack as a stopgap; its removal (a Jet sandbox) is tracked on #6697, longer term.

Owner 2026-11-08: track full libc coverage too ("We should already have a lot of what libc covers just need to fill the gaps"), filed as #6696. Owner approved spawning leads for mbedtls (#6694) and SQLite (#6695).

Which artifacts need which C (SpeedLead, nm on the c4-built jet and on seed a0_038): jet links mbedtls (T mbedtls_ssl_setup, T jet_tls_new) through JetCli core.http.client (BuildHTTPTransport.jet, the HTTPS build fetch) and core.http.server tls (BuildWeb.jet), both reaching Core/Net/Tls.jet #Import c.mbedtls. jet links no sqlite (no sqlite3_* symbol, no core.db reached). jetpack links mbedtls and no sqlite. The runtime pack ships both foreign archives, which a user program links only when it reaches c.mbedtls or c.sqlite3 (ForeignLink.jet jet_cli_vendored_c_archive). So after #6693, mbedtls (#6694) is the only C that jet itself needs; SQLite (#6695) is needed only so the pack can serve user programs that use core.db. The fresh-clone criterion therefore needs #6693 and #6694 for jet, and #6695 for the pack.

criteria.text: Every child card is done.
`jet build Compiler` on a fresh clone with no C compiler, no musl and no Nix builds jet, jetpack and the runtime pack (receipt on a clean HOME with PATH holding only the seed jet and coreutils).

jet, jetpack and every runtime pack file contain no object compiled from C: a symbol and section census of each artifact names only Jet-produced objects, and the pack's foreign/platform directory is gone.
No #Import(c) or #FFI(c) remains in Compiler, Core, Jetpack or Tools outside the C-interop feature itself, its tests and its proofs (census command and output in the receipt).

cards.title: No C: port the runtime's 33 libm functions to Jet, then all of math.h
cards.body:
Owner order 2026-11-08: "We need to fix the issue blocking build.jet but also need to remove the C dependencies. Start by directly porting the functions being used but we also need full coverage of the libraries that are dependencies. Ensure all are tracked."

Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/CompilerNeededMath.jet imports acos, acosh, asin, asinh, atan, atan2, atanh, cbrt, ceil, cos, cosh, exp, exp2, expm1, floor, fma, fmod, hypot, log, log10, log1p, log2, pow, round, sin, sinh, sqrt, tan, tanh and trunc from musl. Port them to Jet first; sqrt, floor, ceil, trunc, round and fma may lower to the x86-64 instructions where those give the IEEE result. Then cover every remaining C23 math.h function Core exposes or will expose. Every function returns the same bits as musl's on every tier (I9), web included.

log.text: Owner ruling 2026-11-08 (chat, Q16): A. core.math gains the remaining C23 math.h functions under snake_case names, and every function also takes F32 through the existing F32 builtin dispatch (musl *f.c bits). Option C (C-ABI exports) was not chosen. c3 proceeds on this surface.

G1Lead landed 7639370892 (c4 local libm fixes; runtime pack rc=0; cases core_math 15 pass, 1 known-failing #5454; bits identical to musl on all 5 cells, 4M calls each) and b53d287e41 (c4 paired perf cells and musl-bit goldens). Jet over musl median wall: sin 1.20, cos 1.02 to 1.23, exp 1.41, log 1.59, pow 1.42. c4 stays open; the rest is general O1 codegen, logged on #6414 (owner Q17). Queued for Main batch.

G1Lead landed 71ec4588bb (c1: 29 libm routes in Jet; musl-equivalence corpus 74,409 rows, 0 differ on O0, O1, O2 and web; the m runtime has 25 undefined symbols, none math) and 66879594c0 (c2 part: erf, erfc, lgamma and gamma on musl 1.2.5 algorithms, 2,554 rows, 0 differ). Both queued for Main batch verification; not met until then. c4 is blocked: Jet is slower than musl with identical bits at O1 (sin 1.23x, cos 1.34x, exp 1.82x, log 2.04x, pow 1.74x; O2 similar). G1Lead is finding the root; general codegen roots go to #6414.

G1Lead progress 2026-11-08: all 29 runtime libm routes are ported (trig, exp and log, pow, cbrt, hypot, hyperbolics) and being verified. The libm C imports, the web host math entries and the C platform-libm fixture are gone. Found: erf, erfc, lgamma and tgamma are Abramowitz and Stegun approximations, not musl; Main approved switching them to musl bits under c2. The c3 public surface (about 45 C23 names and F32 forms) is an owner question. Options: A in core.math with F32 overloads; B a separate core.math.f32; C C-ABI exports only.
Assigned 2026-11-08 by Main: G1Lead, after its in-flight #5949 commit.

criteria.text: The 33 functions are Jet, CompilerNeededMath.jet imports nothing from C, and the runtime object asks libc for no math symbol (symbol census receipt).
criteria.evidence: 71ec4588bb. Main 2026-11-08 on 5987d18926 (integration b1 build): ELF undefined-global census of the built runtime object Compiler/JetCli/.jet/build/jet-runtime/jet_runtime_jet.o: undefined 12, C math 0 (a0_039 object: 55 undefined, 30 libm). Compiler/JetRuntime/imports.list carries no libm name.

criteria.text: Each ported function matches musl bit for bit on a committed corpus: special values (signed zeros, infinities, NaNs, subnormals), musl libc-test math vectors and random inputs, on O0, O1, O2 and web.
criteria.evidence: 71ec4588bb and 66879594c0. Main 2026-11-08 with the integration b1 compiler (5987d18926): jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter core_math_matches_musl_bit_for_bit_on_every_tier PASS 1/1; corpus 33 functions, 76,399 rows, 0 differ from musl, asserted on O0, O1, O2 and web.

criteria.text: Full coverage: every C23 math.h function (float and double forms, frexp, ldexp, modf, remquo, nextafter, erf, tgamma, lgamma and the rest) exists in Jet. Functions musl 1.2.5 provides match musl bit for bit on the musl-equivalence corpus (documented musl bugs such as acosh of large negative inputs returning a number instead of NaN are fixed and listed); functions musl lacks (rsqrt, exp10m1, exp2m1, log2p1, log10p1, the pi-trig family, pown, powr, rootn, compoundn) are correctly rounded, matching MPFR bits on a committed corpus that includes the CORE-MATH hard cases; all on O0, O1, O2 and web, with no host libm and no fused operations
A paired perf cell compares each hot function (sin, cos, exp, log, pow) with musl's; Jet is not slower.

cards.title: No C: threads without pthread (Thread.jet, Sync.jet)
cards.body:
Owner order 2026-11-08: "We need to fix the issue blocking build.jet but also need to remove the C dependencies. Start by directly porting the functions being used but we also need full coverage of the libraries that are dependencies. Ensure all are tracked."

Thread.jet imports pthread_create, pthread_join, pthread_detach, pthread_attr_init, pthread_attr_setstacksize and pthread_attr_destroy; Sync.jet imports one more C symbol. Replace them with clone3 or clone, Jet-owned stacks and Jet's own thread control block and thread-local area, with futex join.

log.text: Owner ruling 2026-11-08 (Q9): "lean towards A but need downsides engineered away". Direction: a process-wide C gate. Before building, the design must remove or mitigate each downside of A (serialized parallel TLS handshakes and blocking C calls until mbedtls is ported, user C serialized forever, reentrancy when C calls back into Jet, a blocking C call stalling every other C caller, fork) and pass an adversarial review; the redesign goes back to the owner with each remaining cost named.

SchedLead started 2026-11-08. Scheduler c3 is paused and unlanded; notes are in the lane scratch c3-paused.md. Measured c3 state: w11 task-clock 23.8 to 19.6 ms, clones 20 to 12, RSS 4.3 MB. The Thread.jet THP stack fix folds into this card: Jet-mapped MAP_STACK stacks replace the madvise workaround (w11 RSS 13.7 to 5.5 MB, fib smoke 16.3 to 5.3 MB, measured on the unlanded patch).
Assigned 2026-11-08 by Main: SchedLead, after its in-flight release fix; scheduler c3 pauses.

criteria.text: Thread.jet and Sync.jet import nothing from C, and the runtime object asks libc for no pthread symbol.
Thread spawn, join, detach, stack size, thread-locals, panics in threads and the scheduler's carriers keep their behavior: the thread, task and scheduler cases pass on O0, O1 and O2.
Spawn and join cost is measured against the pthread build, and the Jet build is not slower.

setuid, setgid and setgroups (and initgroups, ported to Jet with /etc/group plus the nscd GETINITGR query) apply to every thread in the process through a Jet synccall over the thread registry, as POSIX and musl define. Today the raw per-thread setuid and setgid in HostProcess.jet change only the calling carrier, a privilege-drop defect. A case drops privileges with tasks on several carriers and checks every /proc/self/task/*/status.

cards.title: No C: direct syscalls for the runtime's process, terminal and filesystem calls
cards.body:
Owner order 2026-11-08: "We need to fix the issue blocking build.jet but also need to remove the C dependencies. Start by directly porting the functions being used but we also need full coverage of the libraries that are dependencies. Ensure all are tracked."

Runtime imports to replace: fork (HostSpawn.jet), getgroups and initgroups, getloadavg, sysconf, times, clock_gettime, mkfifo, realpath, utime, signal, tcgetattr and tcsetattr, inet_pton, __errno_location, and the C imports of RouteSys.jet (8), RouteTerm.jet (2), ProcessSignal.jet, TextFmt.jet and NetRoutes.jet. Use the Linux syscalls directly (clock_gettime through the vDSO, signal through rt_sigaction with a Jet restorer, initgroups and getgroups from /etc/group, getloadavg from /proc/loadavg, sysconf from the auxiliary vector and /proc, realpath with Jet path resolution, tcgetattr and tcsetattr through ioctl).

log.text: Correction to the 1f8f46177e receipt (SchedLead): the objdump line on the restorer resetting rsp was not verified and is withdrawn; the strace facts stand. help_pty is 0 PASS and 13 known-failing. Fork regression, confirmed reachable: core.sys.fork() (Core/Sys/Sys.jet:657) lets the child run any Jet code, which can reach musl calloc (getaddrinfo), getgrouplist (initgroups), pthread_create or vendored C, and the raw syscall-57 fork skips the atfork locks and the tid fix-up that musl fork did. Spawn is unaffected (clone CLONE_VM|CLONE_VFORK, raw syscalls only before execve, HostSpawn.jet:288-461). An older hazard: the Jet allocator lock (Alloc.jet:305) was never held across fork. Main ruling: option B, a runtime fork gate (a shared rwlock around runtime musl calls, taken exclusively by fork with alloc_lock and the stdout lock, then reinitialized in the child), lands right after #6691 with a fork-under-load case. The residual for C threads created by user or vendored C folds into the owner thread question for #6689.

SchedLead landed 1f8f46177e (unverified by Main; queued for the batch). Direct syscalls replace fork, getgroups, getloadavg, sysconf, times, clock_gettime (vDSO), mkfifo, realpath, utime, signal (rt_sigaction with a Jet restorer), tcgetattr and tcsetattr, and inet_pton. Symbol census: jet_runtime_jet.o has 42 undefined symbols, none of the 13 card symbols; left are __errno_location, getaddrinfo, freeaddrinfo, gai_strerror, initgroups, jet_rt_fault_report, 6 pthread and 30 libm. Probe output is byte-identical with the musl build at none, basic and full. Web: canonicalize of / or . now answers without fs, getgroups and utimensat are handled, and the web host place() writes an empty auxv for the vDSO lookup. Focused cases pass at none, basic and full (118 web), apart from one timing flake that passed on rerun and known environment failures. Open: the raw fork skips the musl atfork locks, so a forked child that uses C malloc in a multithreaded C-linking program could deadlock; Main asked SchedLead whether any public path reaches it.

Main 2026-11-08: initgroups and setgroups stay on musl in #6690. They move to Jet with the synccall of #6689, because a per-thread port would regress the process-wide behavior of today. Found by SchedLead: the Jet setuid and setgid (HostProcess.jet) are raw per-thread syscalls that change only the calling carrier; the fix is the new synccall criterion of #6689.
Assigned 2026-11-08 by Main: SchedLead, after #6689.

criteria.text: None of these runtime files imports anything from C, and the runtime object asks libc for none of these symbols (symbol census receipt).
Every Core API built on them keeps its behavior and error kinds: the process, signal, terminal, time, files and net cases pass on O0, O1 and O2.

core.sys.fork() is as safe as it was under musl fork: a runtime fork gate holds the runtime C-call lock, alloc_lock and the stdout lock across the fork syscall and reinitializes them in the child; a case forks while other carriers allocate and resolve, and the child completes.

cards.title: No C: a Jet DNS resolver replaces getaddrinfo
cards.body:
Owner order 2026-11-08: "We need to fix the issue blocking build.jet but also need to remove the C dependencies. Start by directly porting the functions being used but we also need full coverage of the libraries that are dependencies. Ensure all are tracked."

HostNetResolver.jet imports getaddrinfo, freeaddrinfo and gai_strerror. Replace them with a Jet resolver that reads /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf (nameserver, search, ndots, timeout, attempts, rotate) and /etc/nsswitch.conf's hosts line, queries over UDP with TCP fallback on truncation, and orders A and AAAA answers by RFC 6724 the way getaddrinfo does. Go's pure resolver is the reference for scope.

log.text: Owner ruling 2026-11-08 (Q14): Go resolver semantics, not exact musl getaddrinfo. Owner words: "yes, go with go. We want pareto behavior, what is correct and the best method for the majority of situations. more advanced behavior and apis can be built for experts beyond that." c2 reworded.

Main 2026-11-08 correction: musl never reads /etc/nsswitch.conf, so the keep-behavior criterion means the Jet resolver does not read it either. The body text "nsswitch.conf hosts line" was wrong. The resolver matches musl 1.2.6 getaddrinfo exactly: search-list failure aborts with EAI_AGAIN or EAI_NODATA, both A and AAAA must answer, the default nameserver is 127.0.0.1, results are RFC 6724 sorted. A switch to Go-style semantics (continue the search on a candidate failure, keep A answers when AAAA times out) is an owner question.
Assigned 2026-11-08 by Main: SchedLead, after #6690.

criteria.text: HostNetResolver.jet imports nothing from C, and the runtime object asks libc for no resolver symbol.

For localhost, names in /etc/hosts, numeric hosts, a local test DNS server (A, AAAA, CNAME, NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, truncation then TCP, timeout) and search domains, the Jet resolver follows Go pure-resolver semantics (owner ruling 2026-11-08): a failed search candidate (timeout, SERVFAIL, NODATA) moves on to the next candidate, and when A answers but AAAA fails or times out the A answers are returned. Addresses come back in RFC 6724 order with the error kinds core.net already defines; every difference from musl getaddrinfo is listed in the case file and case-tested.
Resolution runs on the scheduler without blocking a carrier.

cards.title: No C: the compiler's and tools' own C imports (JetDevserver, JetCli, JetTestKit, Tools/ci)
cards.body:
Owner order 2026-11-08: "We need to fix the issue blocking build.jet but also need to remove the C dependencies. Start by directly porting the functions being used but we also need full coverage of the libraries that are dependencies. Ensure all are tracked."

WatchService.jet declares close, inotify_add_watch, inotify_init1, pipe, poll, read and write through #FFI(c). WebHost02.jet declares mkdirat, openat, renameat and unlinkat. JetCli Host.jet has 2 C imports, JetTestKit RequireTool.jet and Assets/no_nix.jet 1 each, and Tools/ci/CompiledWorkloadPeerLauncher.jet 1. Replace each with the Core or runtime API that does the same job, adding the missing Core surface (an inotify-backed watch, say) where none exists, through the normal Core review.

log.text: Owner ruling 2026-11-08 (Q23, recommendation): public #Unsafe("reason") process.exit_unmapped(code) -> Never (audited like sys.stop) replaces the compiler and tool runtime exit imports, and public testing.skip(reason: String) marks the running #Test skipped (like Go t.Skip). No toolchain access to Core internal routes.

Reassigned 2026-11-08 by Main (owner raised the agent cap to 10): CFreeLead, starting now. It was queued for QuickLead after #6530 and #6677. Process (owner order 2026-11-08): leads write code and submit patches; Main builds, integrates and tests in batches and returns every failure to its author at once.
Assigned 2026-11-08 by Main: QuickLead, after #6686.

criteria.text: None of these files declares or imports a C function (census receipt).
jet dev's file watching and web host, the CLI paths, the testkit's requires: probes and the peer launcher keep their behavior (their cases pass).

cards.title: No C: the runtime pack and program links drop musl, libgcc and libgcc_eh
cards.body:
Owner order 2026-11-08: "We need to fix the issue blocking build.jet but also need to remove the C dependencies. Start by directly porting the functions being used but we also need full coverage of the libraries that are dependencies. Ensure all are tracked."

Once the math, thread, syscall, DNS and compiler-import cards land, the runtime needs nothing from libc. Remove musl's libc.a, libgcc.a and libgcc_eh.a from Tools/packaging/PrebuildRuntime.jet and from Compiler/build.jet's runtime step (JET_PACK_MUSL_LIB, PLATFORM_ARCHIVES, the nolibc section split in Image/RuntimePack.jet, and jet-runtime/foreign/platform). The runtime pack then builds with no C compiler. Programs with C interop still link their C closure; this card decides nothing about that feature.

log.text: Assigned 2026-11-08 by Main: SpeedLead, once #6688 to #6692 land (it owns PrebuildRuntime and build.jet).

criteria.text: PrebuildRuntime.jet and build.jet's runtime step use no CC, AR or JET_PACK_MUSL_LIB, and the pack's foreign/platform directory is gone.
A pure-Jet hello and the w-cells link with no C archive, start without libc's startup, and their size and startup time are measured before and after.
The full case suite passes on the pack built without musl.

cards.title: No C: port mbedtls to Jet in full (TLS 1.2 and 1.3, X.509, PSA crypto)
cards.body:
Owner order 2026-11-08: "We need to fix the issue blocking build.jet but also need to remove the C dependencies. Start by directly porting the functions being used but we also need full coverage of the libraries that are dependencies. Ensure all are tracked."

Core/Net/Tls.jet uses c.mbedtls (Core/Vendor/Mbedtls, 272 C and header files). Port the whole library the vendored configuration builds: TLS 1.2 and 1.3 client and server, X.509 parsing and verification, and every cipher, hash, MAC, KDF, key exchange and signature it provides (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, SHA-1 and SHA-2, HMAC, HKDF, ECDHE on X25519 and the NIST curves, ECDSA, RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 and PSS). Constant-time code is required where mbedtls is constant-time. Security closure (Docs/spec/contributing/security-closure.md) applies.

log.text: Owner rulings 2026-11-08. Q10 A: public builtin U64.mul_wide(other) -> (U64, U64), lowered to one widening multiply on every tier. Q11 B: public core.net.dtls (DTLS 1.2) over the ported engine. Q12: agree, full functional coverage; mbedtls C plumbing (PSA key store, net_sockets, timing, threading, memory_buffer_alloc, debug strings) maps onto Jet own net, files, alloc and tasks.

S1 landed b53a78981d (TlsLead; precommit passed; queued for the Main batch). One hash engine (priv hashes in Crypto.jet) for SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3, HMAC, HKDF and PBKDF2; old copies in Crypto.jet, Expert.jet and Service.jet deleted; public surface unchanged. Case core_crypto_api/digests_macs_and_kdfs_match_the_mbedtls_and_wycheproof_vectors_on_every_tier passes on jet run, run --release and dev with 0 failures: mbedtls shax 589, md 100, hkdf 3, pkcs5 7; wycheproof hmac_sha256 174, hkdf_sha256 86, pbkdf2 60. Pins in input/vectors/UPSTREAM.md. Cases crypto 44/0, uuid 2/0, service 75/0. Perf against mbedtls 3.6.7 (load about 30, noisy): sha256 5x faster (SHA-NI), pbkdf2 3x faster; sha1 12x, sha512 3.2x and sha3 7.5x slower, and hmac 64 B 2.1 us against 943 ns. c5 is open on those. MD5 and RIPEMD-160 move to R1 (__core_crypto_hash).

TlsLead plan accepted 2026-11-08. Scope from the vendored mbedtls 3.6.7 default config (129,589 C lines in 117 files): every hash, MAC, KDF, cipher and mode, AEAD, DRBG, constant-time bignum, 13 ECC curves, RSA, DHM, LMS, ASN.1, PEM, PK, PKCS#5/7/12, X.509 parse, verify and write, TLS 1.2 and 1.3 client and server with every key exchange and extension built, and DTLS 1.2. Slices: S1 hashes, S2 AES with every mode, S3 AEAD, S4 AES-NI and PCLMULQDQ leaves, S5 ARIA, Camellia, DES and DRBG, S6 bignum, S7 ECC, S8 RSA, DHM and LMS, S9 ASN.1, PEM and PK, S10 X.509, S11 record layer and TLS 1.3 key schedule, S12 TLS 1.3, S13 TLS 1.2, S14 tickets and DTLS, S15 the one-commit cutover. Main rulings: G-a uses private runtime leaves for the wide multiply (a public U64.mul_wide is an owner question); G-c TlsLead owns the X64 crypto forms and JetRuntime crypto leaves; O1 ports full function and maps the C plumbing onto Jet facilities (told the owner); O2 DTLS public API is an owner question; O3 vectors go in-repo with upstream pins and the Apache-2.0 license. Existing Core/Crypto is about 10x off the mbedtls throughput (ChaCha20-Poly1305 51 ms/MiB, SHA-256 18 ms/MiB scalar), so its cores move to fixed inline arrays.
Assigned 2026-11-08 by Main to TlsLead (spawned with owner approval). The brief is in the Main lane scratch, briefs/TlsLead.md.
Assigned 2026-11-08 by Main: unstaffed: needs the owner's permission for another lead.

criteria.text: Core/Net/Tls.jet and every Core caller use the Jet implementation, and Core/Vendor/Mbedtls is deleted.
Every algorithm passes the mbedtls test-suite vectors and the Wycheproof vectors that apply to it.

Handshakes interoperate with OpenSSL and with the old mbedtls build on every supported version, suite and curve (TLS 1.2 and 1.3, client and server, resumption, ALPN, SNI, client certificates), case-tested.
A constant-time check (dudect-style timing test or equivalent) covers every secret-dependent primitive, and a security review records no open finding.
Handshake and bulk throughput are measured against mbedtls, and Jet is not slower.

U64.mul_wide(other) -> (U64, U64) returns the high and low words of the full 128-bit product, lowered to one widening multiply instruction on O0, O1 and O2 and with the same meaning on web; registered in the Prelude with #Tests, an example plus golden, and the bignum leaves use it (owner ruling 2026-11-08, Q10 A).

core.net.dtls exposes DTLS 1.2 client and server over UDP on the ported engine, idiomatic Jet in the core.net.tls shape (typed config, Result errors, Close), with interop cases against the vendored mbedtls DTLS peers and an example plus golden (owner ruling 2026-11-08, Q11 B).

cards.title: No C: port SQLite to Jet in full (core.db)
cards.body:
Owner order 2026-11-08: "We need to fix the issue blocking build.jet but also need to remove the C dependencies. Start by directly porting the functions being used but we also need full coverage of the libraries that are dependencies. Ensure all are tracked."

Core/Db/Db.jet uses c.sqlite3 (Core/Vendor/Sqlite3, the amalgamation). Port the whole library the vendored build provides: the SQL language, the file format (databases written by either build open in the other), the pager and journal and WAL modes, locking and the VFS, and the compiled-in extensions (FTS3, FTS5, JSON1, RTree, DBSTAT, STAT4, SOUNDEX, column metadata), with the flags PrebuildRuntime.jet sets today.

log.text: SqliteLead plan accepted 2026-11-08. Target is SQLite 3.45.0 with the PrebuildRuntime SQLITE_FLAGS: full SQL, VDBE, planner with STAT4, B-tree, pager, rollback journal, WAL with shm, the unix VFS with fcntl locks, memdb, FK on by default, and the FTS3/4, FTS5, JSON1, RTree, DBSTAT, SOUNDEX and column-metadata extensions. load_extension stays refused as today. The engine lives as private core.db parts under Core/Db/Engine/; the public core.db API is unchanged. Slices: S0 scratch-only C oracle, S1 file-format read, S2 B-tree and pager write, S3 minimal SQL end to end, S4 full SQL against sqllogictest slices, S5 WAL, locking and crash recovery, S6 extensions, S7 perf against C (speedtest1 and the db cells), S8 the one-commit cutover deleting Core/Vendor/Sqlite3. Main rulings: SqliteLead owns the new Compiler/JetRuntime/HostDbVfs.jet; shared registry rows go in Core.jet and CoreSourceParts.tsv; existing file leaves are reused and only missing ones added; sqllogictest goes in as a pinned manifest plus runner, with no corpus committed.
Assigned 2026-11-08 by Main to SqliteLead (spawned with owner approval). The brief is in the Main lane scratch, briefs/SqliteLead.md.
Assigned 2026-11-08 by Main: unstaffed: needs the owner's permission for another lead.

criteria.text: Core/Db/Db.jet uses the Jet implementation, and Core/Vendor/Sqlite3 is deleted.
The public sqllogictest corpus passes, along with every Core db case and example.
File-format round trips: databases written by C SQLite open in Jet and the reverse, in rollback-journal and WAL modes, including crash-recovery tests.
Speedtest1 and the db perf cells are measured against C SQLite, and Jet is not slower.

cards.title: No C: full libc coverage in Jet (census libc against Core and the runtime, then fill every gap)
cards.body: Owner, 2026-11-08: "We should already have a lot of what libc covers just need to fill the gaps." Track full coverage of what a C libc provides (POSIX and C23: memory, strings, stdio and files, time and locale, process, signals, threads and sync, networking and name resolution, math, environment, users and groups, terminal, dynamic memory), as Jet-native Core or runtime surface. Step one is a census: every libc function family, with the Core or runtime API that already covers it, and the gaps. Then each gap is filled through normal Core review (new public API needs a ballot). Math is #6688; threads, syscalls and DNS are #6689 to #6691.

log.text: Split 2026-11-08 by Main: CFreeLead owns the non-math gaps; G1Lead keeps the math rows (with #6688 c3) and LibcCensus.jet.

Owner ruling 2026-11-08 (chat, Q18): reach parity coverage. Quote: i dont need to see every api design, just use best practices, idiomatic jet with excellent api, making use of jet s api features appropriately. So the libc gap fill needs no per-API ballot: each gap gets idiomatic Jet surface designed by the lead, using Jet features (effects, Result errors, typed handles, Close) rather than C shapes. New syntax, invariant exceptions and dependencies still go to the owner.
8b040ecdba (G1Lead): the census prints on demand; Docs/audits/libc-census.md is removed, matching the reworded c1. Queued for Main batch verification.

G1Lead landed 6dedd63f5a (Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet plus Docs/audits/libc-census.md): 261 families, 1,482 functions, every POSIX.1-2024 function once plus the C23 additions; 119 covered, 40 partial, 23 language, 79 GAP. The committed generated doc breaks AGENTS.md, and the fault is in the Main criterion. c1 is reworded, and G1Lead is removing the doc and keeping the script on demand. GAP areas: math (rint family, issignaling, Bessel, C23 pi-trig, exp10 and log2p1 family, pown and rootn family, fromfp, fmaximum family, narrowing ops, canonicalize, totalorder, payload); all of fenv; complex elementary functions plus carg and cproj; isblank, isgraph, ispunct, isxdigit, the isw forms, wctype, wctrans and the _l variants; memset_explicit, swab; a64l, l64a; fdopen, fileno, ungetc, setbuf, setvbuf, ctermid; posix_fadvise, fallocate, readv, writev, mknod, statvfs, pathconf; dup family, isatty, ttyname, aio, posix_devctl; mlock and typed memory; posix_spawnattr and sched policy; signal sets and masks, sigwait, sigqueue, sigaltstack, pthread_kill; pthread attributes, mutex and cond attributes, rwlock, spin, once, TLS keys, atfork, semaphores; atomic fences; clock_settime and CPU-time clocks; set-uid and set-gid family, the group database, utmpx, crypt; sendmsg, recvmsg, socketpair, sockatmark, netdb iteration, if_nameindex; mq, shm_open, SysV IPC; tcgetpgrp, tcsetpgrp, pty functions; setlocale, locale_t, nl_langinfo, gettext, catgets, fmtmsg. Which gaps get Jet surface is an owner question (Q18); each new public API needs a ballot.
Assigned to G1Lead 2026-11-08, after #6688 c1 and c2 land: a committed census script listing every C23 and POSIX.1-2024 function family against Jet Core or runtime coverage.

criteria.text: A committed census script (Tools/agent/LibcCensus.jet) lists every libc function family (C23 and POSIX.1-2024) with the Jet Core or runtime API that covers it, or names it as a gap, and checks that every named Jet API exists. It prints its table on demand; no generated census file is committed.
Every gap is either filled with idiomatic Jet surface in the shape of existing Core modules, or carries an owner ruling that Jet does not need it.

cards.title: No C: a Jet Linux sandbox replaces the bwrap binary shipped in the C toolchain pack
cards.body: Owner order 2026-11-08 (Q8): "B4 BUT that is a longer term card I dont want done now. for the time being, ship bwrap until the sandbox is built PROPERLY in jet, make sure this task is not lost so we dont forget to remove bwrap in the future." Context: #6686 found no bwrap on a NixOS host, so jet cc refused with E1275. The stopgap ships bwrap (a C binary) in the C toolchain pack. This card builds the sandbox in Jet (namespaces plus landlock or seccomp, ratified D-PORTABLE1=A: Jet own sandbox) and removes bwrap. Longer term: not to start before the owner says so. Related: #6687 (Jet depends on no other language), #4268 (authority and sandbox boundaries).

criteria.text: Process isolation for jet cc and every other sandboxed launch is done by Jet code (user, mount, pid and network namespaces, landlock rules or a seccomp filter) with the same confinement bwrap gave; a case proves each refused access.
The bwrap binary is gone from the C toolchain pack and from every launch path, with no fallback; the pack is re-pinned without it.
On a host without unprivileged user namespaces, the launch refuses with a registered diagnostic (what/why/fix and a UI snapshot) naming the missing kernel feature.

cards.title: Diagnostics from b.generate modules render against the entry file at generated offsets
cards.body: Found by MetaLead (2026-11-08). A diagnostic in a module produced by b.generate in a build.jet is rendered with the entry file path and source text at the generated module offsets, so the caret and snippet point at unrelated entry-file lines. Repro: $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MetaLead/p9, jet build run.jet (copy the repro into a fixture). Expected: the diagnostic names the generated module (a stable virtual path) and shows its generated text, with the generating build.jet call as a note.
cards.checkSteps: a UI snapshot case: a build.jet that generates a module with a type error renders the error against the generated module path and text, with a note at the b.generate call

cards.title: Correctly rounded Core math: replace the musl ports with CORE-MATH-grade results
cards.body: Owner 2026-11-08: "it needs to be portable and accurate. we want people to use jet for EVERYTHING including mathematics, simulations". G1Lead audit (musl 1.2.5 worst cases reproduced against MPFR 4.2.2): under 1 ulp: exp .51, exp2 .51, pow .52, log .52, log2 .55, cbrt .67, log10 .81, sin/cos .83, atan .86, log1p .90, expm1 .91, acos .93, asin .98; over 1 ulp: tan 1.01, erf 1.02, cosh 1.03, hypot 1.03, atan2 1.55, atanh 1.80, sinh 1.87, asinh 1.91, tanh 2.22, acosh 2.24, erfc 3.72, exp10 4.14, tgamma 15.9, lgamma 4.4e15 near its zeros, Bessel j0/j1/y0/y1 1e14-1e15 near zeros. Plan: port CORE-MATH (MIT) binary64 and binary32 per function family into Jet, worst gaps first (lgamma, tgamma, erfc, tanh, acosh, exp10, atan2, then the rest), each replacing its musl port in one cutover; Bessel needs its own accurate design (no correctly rounded binary64 implementation exists). Estimate about 150 agent-hours serial.
cards.checkSteps: per function: a committed MPFR-generated corpus (CORE-MATH .wc hard cases plus random inputs) shows 0 mismatches against correctly rounded bits on O0, O1, O2 and web; jet test never calls MPFR; the census marks each function CR

decisions.title: Game asset handles
decisions.gist: Choose how game assets are declared, loaded, and diagnosed.
decisions.story: Lena makes a platformer. She wants a typed `player_sprite` handle everywhere and a Jet diagnostic if a PNG is missing or used as a sound.
decisions.inWild: scene.assets.image("assets/player.png")?

options.name: Scene asset registry with typed handles
options.detail: Assets load through `scene.assets`, returning typed handles tied to scene identity.
options.code:
player :: scene.assets.image("assets/player.png")?
jump :: scene.assets.sound("assets/jump.wav")?

options.name: Top-level loaders
options.detail: Flexible, but weakens scene-owned diagnostics and editor identity.
options.code: player :: game.asset.image("assets/player.png")?

options.name: Manifest asset catalog
options.detail: Strong packaging provenance, more ceremony for one-file games.
options.code: targets: { game: { assets: { player: "assets/player.png" } } }

comparisons.note: Resource handles are editor-friendly; Jet should keep them typed and source-owned.

decisions.title: ECS over Scene
decisions.gist: Choose the component and query API that layers over `Scene`.
decisions.story: Omar starts with a simple scene, then adds hundreds of enemies. Components and queries should be another view over the same scene data, not a second engine.
decisions.inWild:
component Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
scene.query(Position, Velocity)

options.name: `component` declarations plus `scene.query`
options.detail: Components are typed declarations; queries are scene methods, preserving one scene identity.
options.code:
component Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
loop item in scene.query(Position, Velocity) { }

options.name: Struct marker components
options.detail: No new declaration form, but component intent is less visible.
options.code:
struct Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
scene.component<Velocity>()

options.name: System functions over query parameters
options.detail: Concise for experts, but puts scheduler vocabulary before the beginner scene story.
options.code: system move(pos: Position mut, vel: Velocity, frame: Frame) { }

comparisons.note: Typed queries are strong; Jet should hide scheduler complexity until needed.

decisions.title: Game input bindings
decisions.gist: Choose how input bindings and per-frame snapshots are named.
decisions.story: Aya wants keyboard today and gamepad later. Replay files should store actions, not raw device quirks, so logic is deterministic across dev, CI, and builds.
decisions.inWild:
scene.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])
frame.input.pressed(.jump)

options.name: Scene bindings plus frame snapshot
options.detail: Bindings live on `scene.input`; frame logic reads deterministic `frame.input` snapshots.
options.code:
scene.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])
frame.input.pressed(.jump)

options.name: Global input map
options.detail: Short, but weak multi-scene/editor isolation.
options.code: game.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])

options.name: Typed action enum
options.detail: Explicit and replay-friendly, more ceremony for tiny games.
options.code:
enum Action { jump }
frame.input<Action>().pressed(Action.jump)

comparisons.note: Action maps are beginner-friendly and replayable.

decisions.comment: Both A & C

decisions.title: Game replay contract
decisions.gist: Choose the replay API, file format, and determinism contract.
decisions.story: Ben gets a physics bug report. The player sends one replay file; Ben runs it under `jet dev` and compiled mode and gets the same frame transcript.
decisions.inWild: game.Replay.record("runs/bug-142.jreplay")

options.name: `game.Replay` API plus `.jreplay` artifact
options.detail: First-party typed artifact contains input actions, seeds, fixed-step timing, backend identity, and budget events.
options.code:
game.run(scene, replay: game.Replay.record("run.jreplay"))
game.Replay.play("run.jreplay", scene)?

options.name: CLI-only replay
options.detail: Keeps source clean, weakens tests that need replay facts.
options.code: jet game record game.jet --out run.jreplay

options.name: User serialization hooks
options.detail: Expert control, but no shared deterministic contract.
options.code: scene.on_snapshot((frame) => writer.write(frame.input))

comparisons.note: Input-stream replay is proven; Jet should type and version the artifact.

decisions.title: Game backend selection
decisions.gist: Choose how renderer, audio, and editor backends are selected.
decisions.story: Sana starts with a no-op CI backend, develops on raylib, and later targets wgpu. Gameplay code should not change when backend changes.
decisions.inWild: game.run(scene, backend: game.Backend { renderer: raylib.renderer() })

options.name: Typed `game.Backend` value
options.detail: Backends are explicit typed values passed to `game.run`; beginners can omit for the default headless/no-op path.
options.code:
game.run(scene)
game.run(scene, backend: game.Backend { renderer: raylib.renderer() })

options.name: Manifest target backend
options.detail: Fits packages, but single-file games need hidden defaults or a second path.
options.code: targets: { game: { backend: { renderer: core.raylib } } }

options.name: CLI-selected backend
options.detail: Useful for CI, harder to audit from source.
options.code: jet run game.jet --game-renderer=core.raylib

comparisons.note: Plugins are flexible; Jet should keep one stable Core scene API above replaceable backend packages.

decisions.title: Game budgets
decisions.gist: Choose how frame, memory, asset, and draw-call budgets attach and report diagnostics.
decisions.story: Nico ships a handheld build with strict frame, memory, and draw-call ceilings. Violations should be Jet diagnostics with replay context.
decisions.inWild: scene.budgets.set(game.Budgets { frame: 16.ms, memory: 96.mb })

options.name: Scene/package budgets, same model
options.detail: Budgets attach to scenes for one-file games and package targets for projects; sema/runtime treat both as one fact model.
options.code: scene.budgets.set(game.Budgets { frame: 16.ms, memory: 96.mb })

options.name: Package-only budgets
options.detail: Clean for CI, but one-file games lose budget diagnostics unless packaged.
options.code: targets: { game: { budgets: { frame: 16.ms } } }

options.name: Runtime watcher API
options.detail: Dynamic control, weaker build/dossier/CI facts.
options.code: budget_watch.attach(scene)

comparisons.note: Budgets work best when CI can fail deterministically.

decisions.comment: Both A & C

decisions.title: jetos Studio launch command

decisions.inWild: jetos studio

options.name: jetos studio (recommended)
options.detail: Studio belongs to the OS engine and keeps package-manager verbs out of OS UX.
options.code: jetos studio

options.name: jet studio --os
options.detail: One Jet umbrella command, but blurs engine boundary.
options.code: jet studio --os

options.name: Editor command only
options.detail: Friendly inside IDEs, weak for docs, CI repro, and support.
options.code: Jetos: Open Studio

comparisons.note: Discoverable but not scriptable; jetos needs both.

decisions.title: jetos Studio default editing view
decisions.gist: Choose Studio's default editing view.
decisions.story: Ren enables Steam and SSH. They want safe toggles first, then the exact module diff before saving.

Studio -> Services -> SSH -> Enable
Diff: module system.laptop { services.ssh.enable: true }

options.code: canvas

comparisons.note: Declarative review is strong; beginner settings UI is weak.

decisions.title: jetos Studio local state boundary
decisions.gist: Decide what Studio may persist outside Jet source.
decisions.story: Priya arranges panels and filters proof logs. She does not want those UI choices to become semantic config or noisy PR diffs.
decisions.inWild:
.jet/studio/cache.json
system/laptop.jet

options.detail: Studio may persist view prefs under .jet, never semantic settings.
options.code: .jet/studio/cache.json

options.name: Committed .studio.jet metadata
options.detail: Reviewable UI metadata, but another source-like artifact.

decisions.title: jetos Studio activation proof gate
decisions.gist: Choose how Studio blocks risky activation.
decisions.story: Mara changes kernel and filesystem settings. Studio must tell them whether VM boot and rollback proof are required before switch.
decisions.inWild:
Risk: boot + filesystem
Required: plan, VM boot, rollback proof
Switch: disabled until proof passes

options.name: Plan-only warning
options.detail: Always allow switch after diff approval. Fast, weaker than D-WD8 proof intent.
options.code: warning only

options.name: Risk-based hard gate (recommended)
options.detail: Boot/kernel/filesystem/service-risk changes require VM and rollback proof; low-risk changes require plan/diff unless policy says more.
options.code: switch disabled until proof passes

options.name: Always VM proof
options.detail: Simple and safe, but over-applies proof to trivial edits.
options.code: VM required for every switch

comparisons.note: Offers VM/build tools but leaves policy to user habit.

decisions.title: jetos Studio plan/proof schema stability
decisions.gist: Decide whether Studio proof/diff artifacts are public schemas in v1.
decisions.story: Owen wants CI to show the same plan, risk, and proof result that Studio shows before activation.
decisions.inWild:
jetos plan @laptop --json > plan.json
jetos prove @laptop --json > proof.json

options.name: Public schemas from first write flow
options.detail: Studio and CI share stable JSON immediately.
options.code: jetos plan --json

options.name: Internal GUI schema first
options.detail: Faster GUI iteration, but CI cannot trust the same artifact.
options.code: internal schema

options.name: Public after read-only Studio (recommended)
options.detail: Stabilize once projection fields prove out, before activation handoff.
options.code: public before switch flows

comparisons.note: Plans are useful because CI and humans inspect the same object.

decisions.title: Declarative containers and microVMs
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos declares containers and microVMs under one proof model.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one proof-backed workload model with explicit isolation backends.
decisions.story: Walter runs Postgres in a container and a risky service in a microVM. Both need network, storage, secrets, health checks, and rollback proof, but they should not become two unrelated config languages.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one proof-backed workload model with explicit isolation backends.

options.name: Hybrid: workload declarations with container/microVM profiles (recommended)
options.detail: One workload.<name> mechanism declares isolated workloads. The backend enum selects Container or MicroVM; shared fields cover image/package, ports, mounts, secrets, health, resources, proof, and rollback. Backend-specific knobs live under nested profiles. Beginners see one concept; experts control isolation depth.

options.name: Separate `containers` and `microvms` trees
options.detail: Matches ecosystem words and keeps backend specifics obvious, but duplicates policy/proof fields.
options.code:
containers.db { image: image.postgres }
microvms.sandbox { memory: 2048.MiB }

options.name: Packages only
options.detail: Treat containers/VMs as packages launched by services. Reuses service machinery, but hides isolation/proof semantics.
options.code: services.db.exec: package.postgres_container.run

comparisons.note: Powerful but split modules; Jet can unify proof concepts.

decisions.title: Hardware profiles and specialisations
decisions.gist: Choose the surface for hardware scans, reusable device profiles, and boot-selectable variants.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: generated local truth, reusable device knowledge, and boot-selectable variants without duplicating hosts.
decisions.story: Earl installs on a laptop with NVIDIA and a desktop with GPU passthrough. He needs hardware facts generated once, community profiles applied explicitly, and specialisations selectable at boot without duplicating a host.
decisions.inWild:
jet os init devhost
// emits what? how do variants compose?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: generated local truth, reusable device knowledge, and boot-selectable variants without duplicating hosts.

options.name: Hybrid: scanned hardware modules plus reusable profiles and specialisations (recommended)
options.detail: Hardware scan emits hardware.<host> source. Systems import that source and can apply first-party/community hardware profile packages. Specialisations are named boot variants over the same host and generation, with option-priority/explain output showing what changed.

options.name: Inline hardware in system
options.detail: All facts live in system.<host>. Fewer modules, but generated hardware and authored policy mix noisily.
options.code: system.devhost { hardware.gpu: .Nvidia }

options.name: Profile packages only
options.detail: Hardware profiles are packages users add. Good sharing, weak for local scan facts and drift reporting.
options.code: packages: [hardware.nixos-hardware.framework-13]

comparisons.note: hardware-configuration.nix + nixos-hardware + specialisations are separate conventions.

decisions.title: Declarative disks and impermanence
decisions.gist: Choose how disk layouts, encryption, filesystems, and persisted paths are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: guided beginner install and expert disko/impermanence power share one storage source truth.
decisions.story: Inez wants btrfs subvolumes, LUKS, an ephemeral root, and a precise persist list. The installer must show exactly what will be destroyed and what survives rollback before touching a disk.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: guided beginner install and expert disko/impermanence power share one storage source truth.

options.name: Hybrid: storage tree consumed by installer and activation (recommended)
options.detail: One storage tree declares disks, partitions, encryption, filesystems, mounts, ephemeral roots, and persistence. The installer uses the same source for destructive actions; activation uses it for mounts and persistence proof. Guided install can draft storage source, never own hidden disk state.

options.name: Separate `disk` and `impermanence` modules
options.detail: Mirrors existing tools. Clear boundaries, but persistence and mount truth can drift.
options.code:
disk.main { ... }
impermanence.persist: ["/var/lib"]

options.name: Installer-generated only
options.detail: Installer records disk facts outside source. Fast first install, but not reproducible or reviewable.
options.code: jet os install --guided

comparisons.note: Community tools solve each half separately; Jet can make one proof-backed source.

decisions.title: Declarative theming
decisions.gist: Choose the source surface for wallpaper, palette, fonts, cursor, and per-app theme projection.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one reusable theme source with exact host/app control and Studio preview over the same facts.
decisions.story: Doris wants one wallpaper and palette to drive GTK, Qt, terminals, editors, and the display manager, with per-app opt-outs and Studio preview. It should be first-party source, not community glue.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one reusable theme source with exact host/app control and Studio preview over the same facts.

options.name: Hybrid: reusable theme profiles with inline host overrides (recommended)
options.detail: theme.<name> modules are reusable theme profiles. A system references one and may override specific targets inline. The theme engine derives/apply palettes across GTK, Qt, terminals, editors, DM, and Studio preview; per-app opt-outs stay explicit.

options.name: Inline system.theme tree
options.detail: Fewer modules, but themes are harder to reuse across hosts/variants.
options.code: system.devhost { theme.wallpaper: file("forest.png") }

options.name: Per-app theming only
options.detail: Each app module owns colors/fonts. Flexible, but no single source of truth.
options.code:
programs.ghostty.theme: ...
programs.helix.theme: ...

comparisons.note: Community module proves the demand; Jet can make it first-party and proof-backed.

decisions.title: Declarative Flatpak and foreign app ecosystems
decisions.gist: Choose how Flatpak remotes, apps, permissions, and reconcile policy are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one Flatpak authority graph, ergonomic per-user app use, and proof-gated reconciliation.
decisions.story: Sam currently has an activation script that adds Flathub, installs desired apps, removes undeclared apps, and updates them. Jetos should plan that change, prove it, and roll it back like everything else.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one Flatpak authority graph, ergonomic per-user app use, and proof-gated reconciliation.

options.name: Hybrid: central Flatpak policy plus user-app projections (recommended)
options.detail: apps.flatpak declares remotes, refs, pins/tracking, reconcile mode, and permission policy. User environment app modules can reference those Flatpak apps for per-user install intent. Activation computes one plan/diff/proof and rollback path.

options.name: User-env app modules
options.detail: Flatpaks are just per-user program modules. Good integration, but remotes/reconcile/permissions become scattered.
options.code: user.user.programs.discord.source: flatpak("com.discordapp.Discord")

options.name: Activation script bridge
options.detail: Keep a generated script. Preserves today’s behavior, but diff/proof semantics stay opaque.
options.code: activation.script("flatpak install ...")

comparisons.note: Community module exists because NixOS lacks first-party Flatpak reconciliation.

decisions.title: Kernel and performance tuning surface
decisions.gist: Choose how kernel profiles, sysctl, zram, sched-ext, initrd, and bootloader tuning are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: friendly profiles for the default path, exact typed knobs for experts.
decisions.story: Hank wants a safe laptop default, a CachyOS performance profile for gaming, zram, one sysctl, sched-ext, and a quieter initrd. These knobs affect boot and performance, so they need typed source and proof.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: friendly profiles for the default path, exact typed knobs for experts.

options.name: Hybrid: safe profiles plus typed expert overrides (recommended)
options.detail: Beginners choose profile enums such as safe/lts/performance. Experts override typed boot/performance families for kernel params, sysctl, zram, sched-ext, initrd, and bootloader. Every override carries risk/proof classification and explain output.
options.code:
performance.profile: .Gaming
boot.kernel.profile: .CachyOSLatest
boot.kernel.params += ["quiet"]
performance.zram.memoryPercent: 50
performance.sysctl.vm.swappiness: 10
performance.scheduler: .Scx("scx_lavd")

options.name: Free-form kernel option map
options.detail: One map for all low-level knobs. Flexible, but loses type checks and explainability.
options.code: boot.options["vm.swappiness"] = "10"

options.name: Profiles only
options.detail: Choose safe/lts/performance profiles; no individual knobs. Great beginner path, insufficient expert control.
options.code: performance.profile: .Gaming

comparisons.note: boot/sysctl/zram/scx are powerful but scattered across modules.

decisions.title: jetos fleet target and authority surface
decisions.gist: How fleet hosts name remote machines and authority.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: tiny label defaults for beginners, explicit reusable authority facts for real fleets.
decisions.story: Mara deploys to web1, web2, and db from CI. The fleet already says which system each host runs, but jetos still needs to know the SSH target, user, privilege boundary, and host identity without hiding authority in shell scripts.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: tiny label defaults for beginners, explicit reusable authority facts for real fleets.

options.name: Hybrid: host target fields with label defaults and reusable target refs (recommended)
options.detail: Each fleet host carries typed target/authority fields beside its system. If omitted, the friendly label can be used as a safe SSH default. Reusable deploy.target refs avoid duplication for bastions/CI. Host key policy, privilege boundary, and identity are proof-visible.

options.name: Host label is SSH name
options.detail: Use `web1` as the SSH target by default, with few knobs. Very small for beginners, but weak for CI, non-DNS labels, alternate users, bastions, host-key policy, and audit output.
options.code:
module fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }
# jet push prod uses ssh web1

options.name: Separate deploy.targets map
options.detail: Fleet topology stays pure and a separate map binds labels to SSH details. Explicit, but splits one host's deploy facts across two places and creates ordering/debug friction.
options.code:
module fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }
deploy.targets.web1: ssh("deploy@web1.example.com")

options.name: External inventory file
options.detail: Read SSH targets from YAML/JSON/SSH config. Familiar to ops teams, but Jet cannot type-check or explain the full authority graph from source alone.
options.code:
module fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }
# targets loaded from inventory.yml

comparisons.note: Node deployment facts live in node config fields such as targetHost and targetUser.
Deploy nodes bind host names to SSH user/host details and profiles.

decisions.title: jetos fleet rollout and rollback policy
decisions.gist: How fleet push sequences hosts and rolls back failures.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: safe magic default plus exact rollout choreography for experts and CI.
decisions.story: Olive pushes a config changing OpenSSH and a service port. She needs jetos to stage hosts safely, prove health on each machine, stop on bad health, and roll back the failed host without leaving a mystery half-deploy.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: safe magic default plus exact rollout choreography for experts and CI.

options.name: Hybrid: staged proof-gated rollout with plan/stage controls (recommended)
options.detail: Default push is staged and proof-gated with rollback-and-stop. Experts can choose batch/canary/dependency order, health timeout, and stage-only/continue flows using the same rollout object. All-at-once is an explicit policy, never the default.
options.code:
rollout: .Staged(
    batch: 1,
    canary: [web1],
    health_timeout: 60s,
    on_failure: .RollbackAndStop
)

$ jet push prod --plan
$ jet push prod --stage
$ jet push prod --continue

options.name: All-at-once with rollback
options.detail: Activate every host concurrently, then roll back failures. Fast for homogeneous fleets, but a bad config can hit every machine before proof catches it.
options.code: rollout: .Parallel(on_failure: .RollbackFailed)

options.name: Plan-only until explicit continue
options.detail: Every push computes and uploads generations, then requires a second command to activate. Very cautious, but beginners lose the magic safe default and CI needs extra orchestration.
options.code:
$ jet push prod --stage
$ jet push prod --continue

options.name: Delegate rollout to external orchestrator
options.detail: jetos builds closures and an external deploy tool decides sequencing. This avoids owning rollout semantics but fails the first-party deploy-rs/colmena parity goal.
options.code:
$ jet push prod --emit-plan deploy.json
$ external-rollout deploy.json

comparisons.note: Supports remote activation with rollback-on-failure profile behavior.
Rolling updates default to staged rollout with health gates and stop/rollback controls.
Can deploy to many nodes but the health/proof model is less language-owned.

decisions.title: Desktop option spellings — the one-line swap surface
decisions.gist: The exact user-typeable spellings for choosing a desktop. Everything else derives from these lines, so they are the most-typed jetos options after packages. Under D-JPK-OSNS1=B full-word namespaces.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: B contradicts ratified namespace law (D-JPK-OSNS1=B / D-JOS-SYSTEMTREE1 place desktop under services) and spends an amendment on saved keystrokes; C's record value has undefined merge semantics — does setting the record reset unset fields? — vagueness that bites the option-priority engine; D's combinatorial enum explodes on every new session type and has no home for displayManager. A wins but leaves `.Auto` derivation and invalid-combo diagnostics unstated, which is where implementers diverge. One flag for the ratifier: the environment enum has no value for the D-JOS-DESKTOP1=A JetOS-owned Wayland session — reconcile when that frozen surface (D-JETOS-FREEZE1) ships natively.
decisions.story: One line must swap the whole desktop; a second may pin the session type; a third may override the display manager. Enum values are teaching surfaces: unknown values list the valid set.
decisions.inWild:
services.desktop.environment: .Gnome
services.desktop.environment: .Kde        // entire desktop swapped
services.desktop.session: .X11             // wayland is the default
services.desktop.displayManager: .Greetd   // else auto-derived

options.label: services.desktop.{environment, session, displayManager}
options.detail: Nested under the existing services.desktop.* namespace next to autoLogin/profile; enums .Gnome/.Kde/.Hyprland/.Niri, .Wayland/.X11, .Auto/.Gdm/.Sddm/.Greetd.

options.label: top-level desktop.* namespace
options.detail: desktop.environment / desktop.session / desktop.displayManager as a new top-level namespace — shortest to type, needs a namespace-list amendment to D-JPK-OSNS1.

options.label: single record option
options.detail: services.desktop: Desktop.{ environment: .Kde, session: .Wayland } — one structured value, one line for the common case, record fields for the rest.

options.label: DE value carries session
options.detail: desktop: .KdeWayland / .KdeX11 / .Gnome / .Hyprland — one enum, zero second line; combinatorial values, no invalid combos possible by construction.

options.name: services.desktop.* with lawful .Auto derivation and typed assertions (hybrid)
options.detail: Spellings are Option A's under the ratified full-word tree (D-JPK-OSNS1=B, D-JOS-SYSTEMTREE1): `services.desktop.environment: .Gnome/.Kde/.Hyprland/.Niri`, `session: .Auto/.Wayland/.X11` defaulting `.Auto`, `displayManager: .Auto/.Gdm/.Sddm/.Greetd` defaulting `.Auto` — one line swaps the desktop; the other two exist only as overrides. `.Auto` derivation is law, not vibes: session resolves to the DE's preferred session, displayManager resolves Gnome->.Gdm, Kde->.Sddm, Hyprland/Niri->.Greetd, and `jet os explain services.desktop.displayManager` prints the derivation and winning priority. Invalid combos fail at eval as typed assertions naming both source lines (`.Niri` supports only `.Wayland`/`.Auto`), and an unknown enum value lists the full valid set with a nearest-match suggestion. Combinatorial DE-x-session values (Option D) are rejected forever: every fact keeps exactly one option home, so adding a session type or DM never renames existing configs.
options.code:
services.desktop.environment: .Kde     // one line, whole desktop swaps
services.desktop.session: .X11          // optional; default .Auto -> wayland
// error: .Niri supports only .Wayland — set at services.desktop.session (line 7)
jet os explain services.desktop.displayManager   # .Sddm, derived from .Kde

decisions.title: Baseline profiles — exact visible contents of terminal and graphical installs
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos ships a lean modern terminal and a complete no-command-line desktop while keeping every installed part visible in config.jet.
decisions.explainer: Recommended D treats baselines as source templates, not runtime imports. The installer materializes every package, service, option, policy, and low-level component into config.jet; the realized closure must trace every installed root back to one of those source entries. The terminal template stays small but modern. The graphical template adds one complete GNOME path and hardware support, with Studio handling settings, packages, updates, generations, proof, and rollback without requiring a terminal. No duplicate app for the same job, no second package system by default, and no unexplained background service. Experts may remove or replace any layer; jetos reports broken obligations and proof failures but never silently restores a baseline choice.
decisions.story: Maya installs jetos on a small server and wants a useful modern terminal without a desktop. Her father installs it on a laptop and expects Wi-Fi, headphones, printing, updates, files, documents, media, and system settings to work without opening a terminal. Later Maya replaces the kernel and network stack. Both need config.jet to show the whole system, with no hidden profile contents or defaults silently returning after an edit.

options.name: Named profile imports
options.detail: config.jet imports baseline.terminal or baseline.graphical. This keeps the file short, but the installed package and service graph is hidden behind the import until the user follows it elsewhere. Baseline updates can also change a machine without an obvious local source diff.

options.name: Fully materialized minimal profiles
options.detail: Both terminal and graphical installs write their complete contents into config.jet, but the graphical set adds only GNOME, a browser, audio, fonts, Bluetooth, and printing. Auditability is strong; the desktop still leaves common beginner jobs and system administration dependent on package discovery or the terminal.
options.code:
packages: [packages.fish, packages.helix, packages.git, packages.ripgrep]
services.desktop.environment: .Gnome
services.audio.pipewire.enable: true
// Files, updates, documents, archives, disks, and media need later setup.

options.name: One universal batteries-included profile
options.detail: Every install writes the complete graphical tool and service set into config.jet, including headless machines. This is maximally consistent and visible, but a server receives desktop packages and services with no baseline job to perform.

options.name: Two fully materialized, purpose-built baselines (recommended)
options.detail: Terminal and graphical are two source templates, expanded directly into config.jet by init/installer; there is no baseline import and no hidden installed default. Terminal contains the boot/kernel/init/filesystem/user/logging/time/locale/certificate/network/firewall/package-management substrate; standard compatibility utilities; fish, Helix, Git, OpenSSH client, curl, rsync; and the curated modern interactive set ripgrep, fd, bat, eza, fzf, zoxide, jq, and btop. No remote server is enabled by default. Graphical contains all terminal entries plus GNOME on Wayland/GDM; NetworkManager UI; PipeWire/WirePlumber; Bluetooth; printing/scanning; firmware and power management; portals, polkit, keyring, fonts, input, automount, and notifications; jetos Studio; Firefox; Nautilus; GNOME Console, Text Editor, Papers, Loupe, Showtime, File Roller, Calculator, Calendar, Clocks, Disks, Snapshot, Settings, and a Jetpack-backed Software view. One app per baseline job; Flatpak and alternate app stores remain explicit opt-ins. Studio exposes install/remove, settings, updates, generations, proof, and rollback through the same config.jet transactions. Baseline evolution arrives as a reviewable source diff and never applies silently. Removing or replacing a low-level entry is authoritative: jetos shows unmet typed obligations and failed proof, but does not heal or reinsert the old choice.

comparisons.note: NixOS offers deep declarative control, but imports and module defaults can make the effective system larger than configuration.nix shows.
