D keeps the declarative graph while materializing the chosen baseline into the user's source and requiring source provenance for every installed root.

Arch makes a minimal system and expert choice straightforward, but the user assembles desktop completeness by hand. D preserves a lean terminal target while giving graphical users a complete, maintained starting source.
comparisons.code:
pacstrap /mnt base linux networkmanager
# User chooses and wires every desktop component afterward.

comparisons.note: Fedora provides a cohesive GNOME experience and modern applications, but image manifests and package layering are not a single user-owned declarative system file. D adopts cohesive desktop curation while keeping the whole machine editable as source.
comparisons.code:
rpm-ostree status
# Strong image provenance; baseline contents are not materialized into one local config.

comparisons.note: Guix can describe a whole system in one program and supports generations, but users still commonly compose imported service sets and package lists. D shares the source-owned system model and adds a no-terminal graphical authoring path over the same source.

decisions.title: Cross-platform executable lease security
decisions.gist: Which existing promise changes so executable packages can work safely on macOS and Windows.
decisions.explainer: Jetpack verifies a package, copies its output into a lease snapshot, and must keep every executable name bound to those verified bytes while a child and its descendants run. Linux does this with a private read-only mount. An unprivileged macOS process has no equivalent immutable named PATH view; Windows file handles can block replacement of files but do not alone protect every descendant name lookup. Today the non-Linux backend returns an error for every lease, even data-only outputs; that empty-output bug is ungated and will be fixed. Executable outputs expose a real conflict among three ratified promises: hostile same-user swaps fail before handoff, Linux/macOS/Windows are tier-1 native, and Jetpack uses no root or daemon. No known design keeps all three. The owner must choose which promise changes.
decisions.story: Mira uses one committed lockfile on Linux, macOS, and Windows. She runs a formatter directly and through jet env. Another same-user process swaps the original package path after verification. Jetpack must execute the verified bytes or refuse; it must never follow the replacement. Beginners need one ceremony-free workflow, while experts need exact audit proof of the native protection used.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
[jet:dev] $ formatter --check src/
checked 18 files

# A same-user process renames the verified output and replaces it with a malicious symlink tree.
# Jetpack must execute the leased bytes or refuse, never follow the replacement.

options.name: Protected native lease service
options.detail: Keep tier-1 usability and the hostile-race guarantee by narrowly amending the no-root/no-daemon law. Linux keeps its unprivileged private mount. This option also ratifies new macOS/Windows distribution-installer behavior: official Jet installers register a root-owned macOS LaunchDaemon or Windows LocalSystem service after one explicit admin approval; no new Jet command is added. The service independently re-verifies the locked digest and copies executables into an OS-protected lease directory the caller cannot rewrite. It authenticates the local caller, then impersonates that caller and launches the child under the caller UID/session/token with no root/SYSTEM privileges or inherited service handles. The child PATH puts protected lease bins first, followed by the caller's approved inherited/system PATH; privilege-sensitive service variables and handles are removed, and package executable names can resolve only through protected lease dirs. A jet env lease lives through the shell and all descendants, then deletes after the process tree exits. The service has no network access, never resolves packages, and fails closed if stopped, mismatched, or unverifiable. Ordinary run/env use remains ceremony-free and offline.
options.code:
# During the new official macOS/Windows installer flow ratified by A:
Install protected executable lease service? [yes/no] yes
installed jet-lease-service 1.0.0

$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
[jet:dev] $ formatter --check src/
checked 18 files
[jet:dev] $ sh -c 'formatter --check tests/'
checked 7 files

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  protected
service            1.0.0, toolchain-matched
request identity   user, authenticated
child identity     user, no service privileges
handles/env        service authority removed
PATH                protected lease bins, then approved caller/system bins
network             denied
handoff             root-protected verified lease
same-user redirect blocked

$ jet env  # service stopped or version mismatched
error E1292: protected executable lease service is unavailable
fix: repair the Jet installation; no child or shell was started

options.name: Relax the hostile same-user guarantee
options.detail: Keep no-root/no-daemon and tier-1 usability, but explicitly weaken the security law on macOS and Windows. Jetpack uses a private snapshot, restrictive native handles where available, and digest validation immediately before launch. This catches corruption and non-racing swaps, but a hostile process running as the same user can race the final validation and a descendant PATH lookup; post-exit detection cannot undo executed code. Doctor and audit output name the weaker guarantee. This option is an intentional safety downgrade, not an equivalent backend.
options.code:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
warning L1292: this host cannot exclude a same-user executable PATH race
why: macos has no unprivileged immutable named PATH view
fix: audit local same-user processes before running executable packages
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
warning L1292: commands in this environment have the weaker macos lease guarantee
[jet:dev] $ sh -c 'formatter --check tests/'
checked 7 files  # a hostile same-user final-lookup race is not excluded

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  guarded, weaker than linux
same-user redirect not excluded

options.name: Fail closed for non-Linux executables
options.detail: Keep no-root/no-daemon and the full hostile-race guarantee. Fix data-only leases on every platform, but reject leases containing executables on macOS and Windows before any child starts. A new registered diagnostic explains that the platform cannot provide the required immutable handoff. This narrows D-JPK-PLATFORM1: macOS and Windows remain native for data libraries and non-executable package operations, but executable packages are Linux-only until an equally safe unprivileged primitive exists.
options.code:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
error E1292: executable leases are unavailable on macos
why: Jetpack cannot create an immutable PATH view without a protected service
fix: run this executable package on Linux; mutable cache paths are never used

$ jet env  # project declares formatter executable
error E1292: this environment needs an executable lease unavailable on macos
no shell was started

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  unavailable
policy             fail closed

$ jetpack build data:unicode-tables
completed  # data-only leases still work

comparisons.note: Nix protects immutable store objects through privileged ownership and a daemon. Option A uses the same concrete authority boundary, but scopes it to verified executable handoff: no resolution, builds, cache networking, or general store ownership.
comparisons.code:
$ nix-store --verify --check-contents
# protected store paths remain outside user write authority

comparisons.note: Linux supplies a private read-only mount view inside an unprivileged user namespace. Jetpack already uses it to map stable PATH names to inherited descriptors.
CreateFile sharing flags can prevent replacement or deletion of opened executables, but a complete PATH solution must also protect directory/name resolution and child handoff.

decisions.title: jetos user-data backup and snapshot declaration
decisions.gist: How a jetos system declares backup/snapshot coverage for /home and other user data — generations (#327) only cover the system store, so there's no restore path for a user's own files today.
decisions.story:
Glossary: a generation is an atomic, versioned record of a full system build/switch (jet os generations, jet os rollback). A snapshot is a captured copy of file data at one point in time. A workload (D-JOS-CONTAINER1) is jetos's existing managed-thing mechanism: pick a backend, get shared image/mounts/secrets/health/resources/proof/rollback fields. Retention is how long old backups are kept before they're pruned.

Alex is editing ~/Documents/report.docx, fat-fingers a find-replace, saves over the good version, and closes the laptop. Ten minutes later Alex wants yesterday's copy back — no git repo, no cloud sync, just "give me my file from before." Priya, on the same jetos machine, wants more: her whole home directory backed up weekly to an offsite bucket, encrypted, in case the laptop is stolen or the disk dies — borgbackup-class protection she already runs on her old distro. Today jetos has no declaration surface for either need.

options.name: Fold backup into the existing generation/rollback engine
options.detail: Backup becomes a scoped extension of the system-generation source: a backup { ... } block inside system.<host> or user.<name>, walked by the same jet os generations / jet os rollback engine already ratified in D-JPK-OSGEN1/D-JOS-USERAPPLY1. No new CLI verb. Rejected: generations were designed for atomic whole-system state transitions triggered by jet os build/switch; backups are periodic captures of mutable data on their own clock. Mixing the two in one history list means a system-config rollback and a file-restore look like the same operation when they aren't — a real safety and long-term-correctness problem, not just an ergonomic one: jet os rollback on a mixed timeline risks reverting unrelated system state when the user only meant to recover a file.
options.code:
# config.jet
system.laptop {
  backup {
    hourly: paths(["~/Documents"])
    weekly_offsite: paths(["~"], encrypted: true, remote: "s3://alex-backup/home")
  }
}

$ jet os build && jet os switch
switched to generation 42 (system, 2026-07-10 14:00)
backup scope armed: hourly(~/Documents), weekly_offsite(~, encrypted)

$ jet os generations
  42  2026-07-10 14:00  system   switch (kernel bump)
  41  2026-07-10 13:00  backup   hourly snapshot (~/Documents)
  40  2026-07-10 12:00  backup   hourly snapshot (~/Documents)
  39  2026-07-09 09:00  backup   weekly_offsite snapshot (~, encrypted)
  ...

$ jet os rollback --path ~/Documents/report.docx --at "3 days ago"
restored ~/Documents/report.docx from generation 17 (2026-07-07 14:00)

options.name: Standalone top-level `backup.<name>` mechanism
options.detail: A new declaration kind, independent of generations and of workload: backup.<name> { source, schedule, backend } with its own backend enum (.LocalSnapshot / .EncryptedRemote) and its own CLI surface (jet os backup snapshot|restore|list|verify|prune). Clean separation of concerns, but it duplicates the exact field spine — secrets, health, proof, rollback, resources — that D-JOS-CONTAINER1 already built for workload. That's a second mechanism doing a job ("declared thing with a backend enum, health checks, and a rollback path") the platform already has one mechanism for, which is the I8 violation the workload precedent exists to prevent: the next managed-thing need after this one faces the same fork (extend workload, or mint backup.<name>-style #3), fragmenting the surface further over time.
options.code:
# config.jet
backup.documents {
  source: paths(["~/Documents"])
  schedule: .Hourly
  backend: .LocalSnapshot
}

backup.home_offsite {
  source: paths(["~"])
  schedule: .Weekly
  backend: .EncryptedRemote {
    remote: "s3://alex-backup/home"
    encryption: .AgeKey(secrets.backup_key)
  }
}

$ jet os backup list documents
  2026-07-10 14:00  snapshot 118
  2026-07-10 13:00  snapshot 117
  2026-07-09 14:03  snapshot  94
  ...

$ jet os backup restore documents --file ~/Documents/report.docx --at "3 days ago"
restored ~/Documents/report.docx from snapshot 94 (2026-07-07 14:03)

options.name: `workload.<name>`-style backend enum, backup as a managed workload
options.detail: Reuses the exact mechanism D-JOS-CONTAINER1 ratified for Container/MicroVM: one workload.<name> declaration, a backend enum that now also includes .Snapshot and .EncryptedRemote, and the same shared fields — mounts (what to capture), secrets (encryption key), health (did the last capture/restore succeed), resources, proof, and rollback. Restore goes through jet os rollback, the exact verb users already know from generations and other workloads — no new CLI surface to learn, and the proof/health machinery already gating container and microVM workloads (partial-write detection, post-action health check) applies to backups automatically instead of needing its own copy. One declaration shape covers 'run a container,' 'run a microVM,' and 'protect this data' — genuinely the same underlying question (what backend manages this, and how do I roll it back) asked three ways.
options.code:
# config.jet
workload.documents_backup {
  backend: .Snapshot
  source: paths(["~/Documents"])
  schedule: .Hourly
  rollback: .Enabled
}

workload.home_offsite {
  backend: .EncryptedRemote
  source: paths(["~"])
  schedule: .Weekly
  secrets: [secrets.backup_key]
  remote: "s3://alex-backup/home"
}

$ jet os build && jet os switch
switched to generation 42
workload documents_backup: healthy (last capture 14:00, 118 snapshots, 3d retention)
workload home_offsite: healthy (last capture 2026-07-09 09:00, encrypted, verified)

$ jet os rollback --workload documents_backup --path ~/Documents/report.docx --at "3 days ago"
restored ~/Documents/report.docx from workload documents_backup capture 94 (2026-07-07 14:03)

comparisons.note: Scheduled local snapshots (rsync/btrfs) with a GUI restore browser — the beginner story this ballot must match: no config, click a date, get the file back.
Encrypted, deduplicated, retention-pruned remote backups — the expert story: borg init --encryption=repokey, borg create, cron schedule, borg prune --keep-weekly=4.
comparisons.code:
# borgbackup: borg create repo::'{hostname}-{now}' ~ ; borg prune --keep-weekly=4
# jetos target: workload.home_offsite { backend: .EncryptedRemote, schedule: .Weekly, secrets: [...] }

decisions.title: jetos options search: dedicated verb, extend jet search/info, or Studio-only
decisions.gist: Whether searching/browsing jetos's typed system.* options (search.nixos.org parity) is a new `jet os options <query>` verb, a type-aware extension of the already-ratified `jet search`/`jet info` verbs, or a GUI-only feature in jetos Studio with no CLI at all.
decisions.explainer: B wins on discoverability (a beginner reaches for the one front door they already learned from package search, D-JPK-DISCOVER1, instead of remembering a second jetos-specific command) and on I8 (options become another typed, tagged result kind in the one 'find a named thing' index rather than a second search implementation to keep in sync). A is the runner-up if the owner wants option results to never carry a type tag. C is ruled out by the kill criteria: it strips a working default (option discovery) from every headless/terminal-baseline host, which is jetos's own first-class target.
decisions.story:
Terms used below — typed option: a `system.*` config field jetos already knows the type, default, and doc string for from the schema itself, not scraped from doc comments like NixOS's option pages; provenance: which `config.jet` line last set a value, and why it won over other declarations that touch the same option; offline index: a precomputed local search index, no network needed; front door: the command a user types first when they don't know the exact name yet.

Priya inherits a coworker's jetos laptop. The login screen shows Gdm; she expected Sddm, because she remembers the previous owner picking KDE. She doesn't know jetos's dotted option names. A NixOS veteran in her position would open search.nixos.org in a browser tab — jetos ships no such site, and card #323 exists to close exactly that gap. She wants to type a rough guess of the setting she's after, see the typed option it resolves to (key, type, default, one-line doc), then jump to why it currently resolves the way it does on this host. That second step, `jet os explain <key>`, already shipped (ratified B-E7-DESKTOPNS1) and prints the derivation and winning priority once she has the exact key. This decision is only about how she finds that key in the first place — it must not re-solve provenance, `jet os explain` already owns that job (I8).
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os explain displayManager
error: unknown option `displayManager`
  did you mean `services.desktop.displayManager`?
  jetos ships ~200 system.* options across desktop, network, boot, users, and
  services trees — nobody memorizes exact dotted paths.

(there is currently no command that finds the exact key from a guess)

options.name: Dedicated verb under jet os
options.detail: A new `options` leaf under the already-ratified `jet os` group (D-JPK-OSVERB1's check|init|plan|proof|build|switch|rollback|generations|lift|import|image list gains one member). It searches only the typed system.* tree, so every result is an option — no result ever needs a tag distinguishing 'package' from 'option'. This is the same shape D-CLI-SURFACE1 (frequency rings, ratified outcome B) already uses elsewhere: a new leaf nested under an existing area word, not a new top-level name.
options.code:
$ jet os options displayManager
2 matches for "displayManager":

  system.services.desktop.displayManager
    type:    .Auto | .Gdm | .Sddm | .Greetd
    default: .Auto  (derived: Gnome->Gdm, Kde->Sddm, Hyprland/Niri->Greetd)
    doc:     "Which login/session manager starts the graphical session."

  system.services.desktop.displayManagerTheme
    type:    string
    default: "adwaita"
    doc:     "GTK theme applied to the login screen."

run `jet os explain <key>` for why an option resolved the way it did on this host

$ jet os options gdm
0 matches for "gdm" in the options tree — did you mean a package?
  run `jet search gdm` to search installable packages instead

options.name: Extend jet search / jet info
options.detail: Extends the already-ratified discovery surface (D-JPK-DISCOVER1: `jet search`/`jet info` + LSP completions) instead of minting a new verb. One query hits the option index and the package index together; each result is tagged `[option]` or `[package]`. `--options`/`--packages` narrow an ambiguous query. D-JPK-DISCOVER1's own LSP completions already span 'package names and typed option fields' through one mechanism — this option extends that same discovery surface to the terminal instead of splitting it.
options.code:
$ jet search displayManager
system.services.desktop.displayManager   [option]
  type:    .Auto | .Gdm | .Sddm | .Greetd
  default: .Auto  (derived: Gnome->Gdm, Kde->Sddm, Hyprland/Niri->Greetd)
  doc:     "Which login/session manager starts the graphical session."

system.services.desktop.displayManagerTheme  [option]
  type: string · default: "adwaita"

run `jet os explain <key>` for why an option resolved the way it did on this host

$ jet search gdm
gdm  [package]  v46.0 — GNOME display manager daemon
system.services.desktop.displayManager = .Gdm   [option]

2 results (1 package, 1 option) — narrow with --packages or --options

$ jet info system.services.desktop.displayManager
system.services.desktop.displayManager  [option]
  type:    .Auto | .Gdm | .Sddm | .Greetd
  default: .Auto
  doc:     "Which login/session manager starts the graphical session."
  set by:  config.jet:42 — run `jet os explain system.services.desktop.displayManager`

options.name: Studio-only, no CLI verb
options.detail: Options search lives only in jetos Studio's browser view (#264 prototype, under D-JOS-FIRSTBOOT1's control-center surface). No `jet os options` and no `jet search --options` exist; a terminal user gets a teaching error pointing at Studio. This is the closest match to search.nixos.org's own shape — a browsable site, not a shell command — but jetos explicitly targets headless/server hosts elsewhere in the spec, and B-E7-BASELINE1's terminal baseline installs no GUI at all. A terminal-baseline host has no path to discover an option name short of reading source.
options.code:
$ jet os options displayManager
error: unknown command `options` under `jet os`
  jetos option search is a Studio feature — run: jetos studio
  (Studio -> Options tab -> type "displayManager")

$ jet search displayManager --options
error: unrecognized flag `--options` — jet search covers installable packages only
  for jetos option search, run: jetos studio

# on a terminal-baseline host (B-E7-BASELINE1, no GUI installed):
$ jetos studio
error: jetos Studio is not installed on this host (terminal baseline ships no GUI)
  no CLI fallback exists for option search on this host

comparisons.note: search.nixos.org is a website; nixpkgs itself ships no CLI equivalent for module options (community `nix search` covers packages only). This is the exact parity gap card #323 names — the comparison rules out 'do nothing' but doesn't settle A vs B vs C.
comparisons.code:
$ nix search nixpkgs firefox
* legacyPackages.x86_64-linux.firefox (140.0)
# NixOS module options have no official CLI search — users open search.nixos.org

comparisons.note: brew search/brew info cover formulae and casks through the same two verbs, tagging results by kind. Direct precedent for option B's one-surface, tagged-result shape.
comparisons.code:
$ brew search git
==> Formulae
git ✔
git-lfs
==> Casks
gitup
$ brew info git
git: stable 2.45.1

comparisons.note: kubectl explain <type>.<field> is a dedicated verb for typed schema fields, separate from kubectl get/describe. Precedent for option A's dedicated leaf under an existing area word.
comparisons.code:
$ kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.image
KIND: Pod
FIELD: image <string>
  Docker image name.

decisions.title: JetOS declarative networking surface (wifi / firewall / VPN / printing / bluetooth)
decisions.gist: Where and how a JetOS host declares its network — wifi, firewall, VPN, printing, bluetooth — so beginners get zero-config day one and experts get reproducible nftables-class control.
decisions.explainer: B keeps one canonical mechanism (I8) and matches every ratified precedent: net.hostname/net.firewall already live inline in system.<name>, and reusable portable pieces already use the name-referenced module convention (user.<name>, theme.<name>, deploy.target). Beginners get the full zero-config day-one experience from an empty net surface — Default-tier NM+DHCP, deny-inbound firewall, CUPS+Avahi discovery, bluetooth all on. Experts get full nftables-class control by dropping the same net.firewall field to a typed Firewall.nftables family and full WireGuard control via reusable vpn.<name> modules — every piece stays typed, merged, proof-rendered, and rollback-able. A is rejected only because it splits a host's identity across two host-keyed roots; D fragments one host's network across four places to look; C is the weakest on the ranked priorities: its raw-passthrough blobs are unverified, unmerged, and unrollback-able, reintroducing the silent-omission hole D-JOS-NIXIMPORT1 and D-JOS-NIXBACKEND1 exist to close.
decisions.story: Priya installs JetOS on a new laptop. Day one she wants exactly what Linux Mint gave her: click the network icon, pick her home wifi "orchard", type the password once, and the shared hall printer prints — no file edited, nothing declared. Six months later she runs a homelab. Now she wants her laptop's whole network state reproducible in source, so a fresh reinstall restores it byte-for-byte: a static-keyed WireGuard tunnel back to her home gateway, a locked-down firewall that only opens SSH, and that same hall printer pinned to a driver. The magic of the first day and the reproducibility of the second have to come from one coherent surface. This ballot decides what she types for the reproducible half without losing the zero-config half — every option below runs the exact same scenario: host `devhost`, wifi `orchard`, one WireGuard tunnel to `home-gw`, one shared network printer.
decisions.inWild:
A homelab laptop repo:

  system.devhost.jet     # the host
  modules/net.jet        # portable, reusable network pieces
  nm/  nft/              # (only if a raw-passthrough model is chosen)

Priya runs `jet os switch devhost` after each edit and expects the report to prove exactly what the firewall, tunnel, and print queue became — with a one-command rollback if it is wrong.

Glossary (terms used below):
  - NetworkManager (NM): the Linux daemon that manages wifi/ethernet connections; what a desktop's network icon drives.
  - nftables: the modern Linux firewall/packet-filter ruleset engine (successor to iptables).
  - WireGuard: a simple, fast VPN; a tunnel is defined by a keypair, an endpoint, and allowed IP ranges.
  - CUPS + Avahi: the Linux printing service and the mDNS discovery that finds shared printers on the LAN automatically.
  - Default tier: JetOS's ratified priority level (D-JOS-PRIORITY1) for a safe out-of-box value an expert may override.

Beginner baseline shared by every option: with NOTHING network declared, the Default tier turns NM on with DHCP, brings up a firewall that denies unsolicited inbound, runs CUPS+Avahi so `HP-LaserJet` in the hall auto-appears, and enables bluetooth. Priya joins `orchard` in the desktop portal and it persists. Declaring things is only for reproducibility and expert control.

options.name: One typed net.<host> block (mirror hardware.<host>)
options.detail: A dedicated host-keyed root, sibling to system.<host>, holds ALL network state in typed sub-fields (wifi/firewall/vpn/printers/bluetooth). The system module imports it. One place to read a host's whole network; matches the hardware.<host> shape exactly. Cost: two host-keyed roots exist for one host — network config lives in net.devhost, everything else in system.devhost, so "where is the host configured" has two answers.
options.code:
// modules/net.jet
module net.devhost {
    hostname: "devhost"
    wifi:     [ Wifi.{ ssid: "orchard", key: secret.wifi_orchard } ]
    firewall: Firewall.{ policy: .DenyInbound, open: [22] }
    vpn:      [ Wireguard.{ name: "home", endpoint: "home-gw.example.net:51820",
                           address: "10.7.0.2/24", key: secret.wg_home,
                           peers: [ Peer.{ pubkey: "kZ3…=", allowed: ["10.7.0.0/24"] } ] } ]
    printers: [ Printer.{ name: "hall", uri: "ipp://hall-hp.local/ipp/print", driver: .DriverlessIpp } ]
    bluetooth: .On
}

// system.devhost.jet
module system.devhost {
    imports: find("./modules")   // picks up net.devhost
}

$ jet os switch devhost
  net.devhost
    hostname   devhost
    wifi       orchard        NM connection · key ← secret.wifi_orchard
    firewall   deny inbound · open 22/tcp          [Default policy + 1 rule]
    vpn        home           wg0 → home-gw.example.net:51820  10.7.0.2/24
    printers   hall           ipp://hall-hp.local  (driverless)
    bluetooth  on             [Default]
  proof: nftables ruleset rendered · wg0 staged · cups queue present
  switch complete · generation 42 · rollback: jet os rollback

options.name: Inline net.* in system.<host> + reusable named tunnels/printers
options.detail: No new host-keyed root. Host-bound network stays where net.hostname/net.firewall already live today — as net.* options inside system.<host>. Portable, reusable pieces (a tunnel, a printer profile) become name-referenced modules (vpn.<name>, printing.<name>), exactly the convention already ratified for user.<name>/theme.<name>/deploy.target, and referenced by bare name from the host. One mechanism, one host root; a tunnel defined once is reused across laptops. Beginner: an empty net surface = every Default-tier service on.

options.name: NetworkManager-delegation + raw passthrough escape hatch
options.detail: JetOS owns only the common typed knobs (NM engine, wifi list) and, for anything it does not model, accepts raw NetworkManager keyfiles and raw nftables files as passthrough sources. Smaller JetOS-owned surface. Cost: raw passthrough files are opaque — JetOS cannot diff, merge, prove, or roll them back the way it does every typed option, so the WireGuard tunnel and any custom rules become unverified blobs in an otherwise typed/proof-checked host. This reintroduces exactly the silent-omission risk D-JOS-NIXIMPORT1/D-JOS-NIXBACKEND1 forbid.
options.code:
// system.devhost.jet
module system.devhost {
    net.manager: .NetworkManager
    net.wifi:    [ Wifi.{ ssid: "orchard", key: secret.wifi_orchard } ]

    // anything JetOS does not model → raw passthrough, opaque to the checker
    net.raw.nm:       [ NmConnection.file("./nm/home-wg.nmconnection") ]
    net.raw.nftables: File("./nft/rules.nft")
}

$ jet os switch devhost
  net.wifi          orchard        NM connection
  net.raw.nm        home-wg.nmconnection    PASSTHROUGH · not merged/proven
  net.raw.nftables  rules.nft               PASSTHROUGH · not merged/proven
  warning: 2 raw passthrough sources — no diff/impact/rollback proof for these
  switch complete · generation 42 · rollback: jet os rollback (NM/nft blobs restored as-is)

options.name: Split typed declarations (firewall.<host> / vpn.<name> / printing.<host> / bluetooth.<host>)
options.detail: Each concern is its own typed module, workload.<name>-style, composed onto a host. Portable concerns (vpn.<name>) are name-keyed and reused across hosts; host-bound concerns (firewall.<host>, printing.<host>, bluetooth.<host>) are host-keyed. Strong separation and reuse. Cost: a single host's network is now spread across three host-keyed modules plus inline wifi — four places to look to answer "what is devhost's network," and three new top-level namespaces to learn.

comparisons.note: The surface JetOS is matching. Everything lives inline under one config attrset; there is no first-class reusable tunnel object, so a WireGuard peer shared across machines is copied or hand-factored with lib functions. Motivates the name-referenced vpn.<name>/printing.<name> module in options B and D.
What option C passes through verbatim. A .nmconnection is an opaque INI blob NM reads directly; JetOS delegating to it cannot type-check, merge, or prove the contents — the tradeoff C accepts.

Precedent JetOS already ratified for reusable, name-referenced profiles (user.<name>, theme.<name>). Options B and D extend that same convention to portable network pieces rather than inventing a new reuse mechanism.
comparisons.code: # a module defined once, referenced by name from many hosts — the shape vpn.<name> copies

decisions.title: jetos beginner app store — pick the UX archetype
decisions.gist: How a beginner browses and installs software on jetos with zero syntax knowledge: an Apps tab inside Studio, a standalone storefront app, a keyboard-first search overlay, or a rich storefront view built into the one Studio shell.
decisions.explainer: D gives the zero-syntax beginner Mint's browse-by-looking discovery (storefront depth, screenshots, categories) without splitting jetos into two GUIs to learn, and makes the reproducibility model legible on demand rather than forcing a diff-review that would undercut the one-click promise — the same rich-default-with-depth-one-key-away resolution the owner already ratified for jet ? (D-FE-HELP1=D). Ranked on beginner discovery and preserved reproducibility, not effort.
decisions.story:
Terms used below — declarative source: your machine's config.jet, the single file that defines what is installed; reproducible: rebuilding from that file always yields the same machine, so a GUI must write the file, never secretly change live state; user profile: the user.<name> block in config.jet that lists a person's apps; generation: one built, switch-in-able version of the system you can roll back to; provider/source: where a package comes from (a local core repo, or nixpkgs).

Priya installed jetos an hour ago. On Linux Mint she opened Software Manager, searched "inkscape", saw a screenshot, clicked Install, and drew. She does not know jetos config exists and should not have to. Today four genuinely different apps could give her that moment: an Apps tab bolted into Studio (the config editor she'll eventually meet), a separate storefront window dedicated to browsing, a keyboard-first search overlay she summons and types into, or a rich storefront that lives as a first-class view inside Studio's one shell. All four must, underneath, add one line to her user.priya profile and rebuild — that is the non-negotiable reproducibility constraint, identical across every option. What differs is only how Priya experiences finding and installing Inkscape.
decisions.detail: HARD CONSTRAINT on all four options: 'Install' writes the declarative-source diff above and rebuilds through the profile/generation engine (D-JOS-USERENV1, D-JOS-USERAPPLY1). No option may mutate live state imperatively -- that would break jetos's reproducibility guarantee. The options differ ONLY in discovery UX, not in what installing does to the machine. This is a new Studio-adjacent view, so it needs a ballot per the D-WD7 guardrail (new view = new ballot) and the DESIGN-BRIEF UX-archetype-first rule. Shared visual system per DESIGN-BRIEF (near-black ground, one accent, system fonts); no theming, mascots, or invented jargon. Non-Nix machines that lack the nixpkgs provider must show the D-JPK-NONIX1 clear-message path on Install; that wiring is an implementation detail identical across all four archetypes.

options.name: Apps tab inside Studio — install lands in the config you already edit
options.detail: Core loop: open Studio, switch to the Apps section, browse a category grid with screenshots, click Install, and the app appears in the same user profile Studio is already editing. One GUI surface: Studio gains an Apps section beside Network/Users/Services/Theme; the install shows up in Studio's existing 'Review changes' diff-and-apply flow, so 'what did I install and why' is answerable in one place. Weakness: Studio is fundamentally a settings/config editor, and browse-to-discover is a different mental mode; a storefront squeezed into a settings sidebar can feel cramped versus Mint's full-window shelf. Reproducibility (constant): Install stages the user.priya.packages diff and applies via Studio's normal switch.
options.code:
jetos Studio                                   devhost . priya
+ Sections ---------+- Apps -----------------------------------+
|  Network          | [ search apps           ]   Graphics v  |
|  Users            | +----------+ +----------+ +----------+  |
|  Services         | | Inkscape | |  GIMP    | |  Krita   |  |
| >Apps             | |[screensh]| |[screensh]| |[screensh]|  |
|  Theme            | | Install  | | Install  | | Install  |  |
|  Review changes . | +----------+ +----------+ +----------+  |
+-------------------+--------------------------------------+
click Install on Inkscape -> Review changes (1):
   user.priya.packages  + apps.inkscape
   [ Apply ]  builds a generation, switches on confirm

options.name: Standalone storefront app — a dedicated Software-Manager window
options.detail: Core loop: launch a separate 'Apps' application (not Studio), browse a rich storefront — featured, categories, big screenshots, ratings — and one-click Install/Remove. This is the straight GNOME-Software / Mint Software Manager transplant: mouse-first, full-window, image-heavy, built purely for discovery. Strength: the best pure browse-by-looking beginner experience, unconstrained by a settings tool's layout. Weakness: jetos now has TWO GUI surfaces (Studio for config, Apps for software); a beginner must learn which window changes what, and both front-ends sit over the same core, so behavior must stay perfectly consistent. Reproducibility (constant): Install writes user.priya.packages and runs the profile switch; the storefront is a view over the profile engine, not an installer of its own.
options.code:
Apps                                           devhost . priya
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
| Featured  Graphics  Office  Games  Developer  Installed       |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
| +- Inkscape ------------------------------+  * 4.7            |
| |         large screenshot                 |  Vector          |
| |                                          |  drawing         |
| |                                          |  [ Install ]     |
| +------------------------------------------+                 |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
click Install -> writes source, runs `jetos user switch priya`
   [ok] Inkscape installed . generation 8 . Undo
(a separate window from Studio)

options.name: Package palette overlay — keyboard-first, extends jet ?
options.detail: Core loop: summon a search overlay (Super+Space, or `jet apps`), type the app name, Enter to stage the install. Reuses the ratified D-FE-HELP1 hybrid-palette pattern extended from commands to packages: empty state offers Featured/categories as a goal list; typing fuzzy-finds across configured providers (#323's data); Tab peeks a screenshot/details inline; Enter follows the palette's prefill-never-run discipline — it shows the exact one-line diff and asks to confirm before anything builds. Strength: instant, keyboard-first, consistent with jet ?, no second heavy GUI. Weakness: weakest for the true zero-knowledge beginner who wants to browse by looking — a finder assumes you can roughly name what you want, so discovery-by-eye (screenshots, wandering a category) is thin. Reproducibility (constant): Enter stages the user.priya.packages diff, applied by the profile engine.
options.code:
devhost > jet apps        (or Super+Space -> Apps)
+- find an app -----------------------------  Graphics ------+
| > inksc                                          3 shown  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
> Inkscape        vector drawing               apps:inkscape
|  Inkscape-dev    development build                        |
|  Inklevel        printer ink monitor                       |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|  enter stage install . tab screenshot/details . Esc close  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
Enter -> shows the exact edit, confirm to apply:
   + user.priya.packages: [core.hello, apps.inkscape]
   [y] apply -> builds + switches a generation

options.name: Hybrid — rich storefront as a first-class view in the one Studio shell
options.detail: Core loop: open Studio's Apps view — a full storefront with featured rows, categories, and screenshot galleries (B's discovery depth) — housed in Studio's single product shell (A's one-surface answer); one-click Install builds and switches the generation, and the exact staged source edit is one click away for anyone who wants it, never forced (D-FE-HELP1's own resolution: rich default, depth one key away). Takes: storefront's mouse-first browse-by-looking as the default, Studio's one shell so there is never a second GUI to learn, and the auditable diff surfaced on demand so the reproducibility model is legible without gating a beginner behind it. Left out: a separate storefront window (rejected — two surfaces), and forcing a diff-review on every install (rejected — undercuts the zero-syntax promise). Reproducibility (constant): one-click Install still stages and applies the user.priya.packages diff through the profile engine; 'View source' just reveals what already happened.
options.code:
jetos Studio > Apps                            devhost . priya
+ Browse --------------------------------------------------------+
| Featured . Graphics . Office . Games . Installed   [ search ] |
| +- Inkscape -------------+  vector drawing          * 4.7     |
| | [  screenshot gallery ]|  [ Install ]   < source >          |
| +-------------------------+                                   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
one-click Install -> app installs (generation builds + switches)
   quiet toast:  Added to user.priya . Undo . View source
click < source > (optional, never forced) -> the exact edit:
   + user.priya.packages: [core.hello, apps.inkscape]
Browse depth of a storefront . install is one click .
the diff is one click away for anyone who wants it . one shell.

comparisons.note: The gap this closes: full-window browse by category with screenshots and one-click Install/Remove, zero syntax knowledge. It mutates live state directly; jetos must deliver the same feel while writing declarative source instead (the hard constraint).
B's model: a dedicated storefront app separate from system settings — rich discovery, but a second GUI surface beside the settings tool.

Today's declarative baseline with NO beginner store: you search search.nixos.org in a browser, then hand-edit configuration.nix and rebuild. D keeps that reproducibility but replaces the hand-edit with a storefront click, source visible on demand.
comparisons.code: web search -> edit configuration.nix by hand -> nixos-rebuild switch

decisions.title: Per-app configuration syntax inside user.<name>
decisions.gist: How a user declares "install and configure app X this way" inside a user.<name> profile — the pattern all ~30 app modules (git, fish, VS Code, ghostty, ...) will follow.
decisions.explainer: One record, one lowercase name per app, types inferred: completion in a single place lists every app, every field of every app is typed and suggested (nothing hidden behind strings), typos reuse the existing construction errors, and all thirty modules are forced into one identical shape (I8). Option C's sharing is not lost — a named apps.* module holding the same record composes on top of B through ordinary module reference whenever a second machine appears, without making profiles mandatory for the single-machine beginner.
decisions.story:
Terms used below: an "app module" is the typed schema plus file projection jetos ships for one application (it knows git's fields and that they land in ~/.config/git/config); "passthrough" is raw config text jetos copies verbatim into the app's generated config file for anything the typed fields don't cover yet.

User is moving his home-manager setup to jetos. His config has thirty-odd apps: git with a signing key, fish with aliases, starship, ghostty, helix, VS Code with pinned extensions and settings, browsers with policies, Discord. In NixOS each app is a pile of repeated lines — programs.git.enable = true; programs.git.userName = "User"; programs.git.signingKey = "..." — and every community module names things differently (extraConfig vs settings vs config). He wants to type an app's name once, get completion for every field that app supports, and have his work laptop share the same app set as his desktop with one host-specific difference: the signing key only exists on the work machine. Whatever shape this ballot picks is the shape every future app module copies, so consistency across all thirty is the whole game.
decisions.inWild:
Today the owner's parity-import fixture spells this as flat option keys -- a placeholder:

    options: [
        apps.program.git.userName: "User",
        apps.program.git.signingKey: "ABC123",
        apps.program.vscode.extensions: ["rust-lang.rust-analyzer", "jet.jet"],
    ]

Every option below replaces this with a typed declaration inside `module user.user { ... }` (D-JOS-USERENV1). All options share the same uniform conventions, so they apply no matter which shape wins:

- Presence means installed and configured. No `enable: true` ceremony; removing the declaration removes the app.
- Every app's config value supports the same three standard fields: `package:` (override which package provides the app; defaults to the module's first-party mapping), `extraConfig:` (passthrough text merged verbatim into the generated config file), and `files:` (extra whole files keyed by path).
- `jetos user plan user` (D-JOS-USERAPPLY1) shows the result before anything is written:

    $ jetos user plan user
    user user -- 4 apps
      git      install git  write ~/.config/git/config          (identity, signing)
      fish     install fish write ~/.config/fish/config.fish    (2 aliases)
      vscode   install code write settings.json, keybindings.json; 2 extensions pinned
      ghostty  install ghostty write ~/.config/ghostty/config   (1 passthrough line)

options.name: Typed app list — the type is the app
options.detail: apps: is a list of typed values; each app module ships a type (Git, Fish, VSCode) and listing a value of that type installs and configures the app. The type name is the app's identity, so nothing is written twice. Community app modules are ordinary types from jetpack packages — publishing one requires no central schema change. Tradeoffs: discoverability starts from type names, so a beginner must guess capitalization (VSCode? VsCode?) before completion helps; the list needs a common app-value kind behind the scenes, and "is git configured?" means scanning a list rather than looking up one field. Duplicate listing is a checked error.

options.name: One apps record — a named field per app
options.detail: apps: is a single typed record with one optional lowercase field per known app; setting the field installs and configures the app. The app's everyday name is the key, the config type is inferred from the field (.{ }, D-DOTCTOR2), so the type name never appears. This is the one obvious place to look: completion inside apps: .{ lists every app available in the environment, and "is git configured?" is one field lookup. Field typos and duplicates fall out of the existing every-field-exactly-once construction rule — no new checking machinery, same errors as any struct. Installing an app-module package from jetpack adds its field to the record; an unknown name is a normal error with a suggestion. Tradeoff: the record's field set is assembled from installed app modules rather than being one fixed type, which the LSP and sema must treat as environment-dependent.

options.name: Reusable app profiles — declare once, attach per user
options.detail: The canonical unit is a named apps.<name> module — a set of app configs declared once, outside any user — and user.<name> attaches profiles by reference, exactly the theme shape (D-JOS-THEME1: reusable profile, inline override where it's composed). Sharing across users and hosts is the default posture: the desktop and the work laptop attach the same apps.dev, and the work host overrides one field inline. Inside a profile, apps are declared with the named-field shape from option B. Tradeoffs: a single-machine beginner must still name a profile before configuring anything — one extra hop between "I want git" and typing git's fields — and a value's origin can be two files away from where it applies. Overrides layer by the ratified priority tiers (D-JOS-PRIORITY1).

options.name: Role groups — shell, editor, terminal as the top level
options.detail: The user profile is organized by what the app is for: shell:, editors:, terminal:, vcs:, tools: groups, each holding the apps that fill that role. A newcomer who doesn't know app names can start from the role ("I want a shell prompt") and discover starship inside shell:. Tradeoffs: thirty real apps don't categorize cleanly — is fzf a shell tool or a search tool, is Logseq an editor? — so every app needs an assigned home the user must learn, misfiled guesses become errors, and two plausible homes for one app is exactly the two-ways-to-say-it problem I8 exists to prevent. Role words are also a vocabulary the user must absorb before their first app.

comparisons.note: The bar to beat. Flat programs.* namespace, enable flag required per app, one line per field, and field names that drifted across thousands of community modules (extraConfig vs settings vs config). Powerful, but repetitive to write and inconsistent to learn.
The opposite extreme: a pure install list with no configuration at all. Trivially discoverable, but every app's actual config still lives in hand-managed dotfiles — the gap the app modules close.

decisions.title: Mobile (iOS/Android): compile target scope and who owns signing + store submission
decisions.gist: Whether Jet compiles real iOS and Android apps as first-class targets, and whether signing and app-store submission are first-party Jet commands or someone else's tools.
decisions.explainer:
Glossary first. **Code signing**: Apple and Google refuse to run an app unless its binary is cryptographically signed with a developer key; unsigned apps do not install on a phone, period. **Provisioning profile**: an Apple file that says which developer, which app id, and which devices a signed iOS build may run on. **Keystore**: the Android equivalent — a local file holding the signing key; lose it and you can never update your app again. **App Store Connect / Play Console**: Apple's and Google's web services where builds are uploaded, reviewed, and released; both expose official REST APIs. **Notarization**: Apple's malware scan for apps distributed *outside* the Mac App Store (macOS-side; iOS App Store review replaces it). **NDK**: Google's toolkit for putting native (non-Java) code in an Android app. **.ipa / .aab**: the upload file formats for the App Store and Play Store.

Scope of this ballot: card #480 gates G1 (target scope) and G2 (signing/store ownership), which are coupled — a compile target you cannot sign is a demo, not a product. G3 (the Android/Kotlin widget-interop transport, the JNI parallel to ratified D-FFI-SWIFT1) and G4 (native hot-reload/preview) are **explicitly deferred to follow-up ballots on this card**; every option below is compatible with any G3/G4 outcome. iOS widget access needs no new gate: D-FFI-SWIFT1 (=A) already ratifies the Swift bridge for macOS/iOS.

Ratified frame this must extend: D-NATIVEUI1=A (thin core library over platform widget APIs via FFI, own renderer later), D-NATIVEUI2=B (all platforms simultaneously, one Backend seam), #134's shipped GTK4 backend (same reactive/view/style/component model on every backend — I8), and D-BUILDTOOLCHAIN1=A (toolchains, SDKs, and signing identities are typed jetpack-provisioned handles). Options A and B continue that family; option C knowingly diverges from it and says so.

One hard external fact shapes everything: Apple licenses the iOS SDK for use on Apple hardware only, so *linking* an iOS app requires a Mac with the Xcode SDK present no matter who owns the rest of the pipeline. Every option below handles that with an honest gated error on other hosts (the D-FFI-SWIFT1 precedent). Android has no such wall: the NDK, the .aab bundler, APK signing, and the Play upload API are all fully driveable first-party from any OS.

Trust-boundary note (this is the real long-term cost, and it is a safety question, not an effort question): Apple and Google change store policy and API details continuously. Whatever owns the pipeline inherits that churn forever. In options A and B the churn is contained in jetpack — a separately versioned tool — so the Jet language, compiler, and runtime never change to satisfy a store policy. In option C the churn lands on the user, inside Xcode and Android Studio projects Jet does not see.
decisions.story: Priya built a notes app in Jet. It runs on her Linux desktop today through the GTK4 backend from the same reactive code, and `jet build --target=web` gives her a web version. Her users keep asking for it on their phones. In Swift she would open Xcode, sign in with her Apple account, let Xcode manage certificates, and press Archive → Distribute. In Jet, right now, there is nothing — `--target=ios` does not exist. She wants to know: can she stay in Jet from `notes.jet` all the way to a build her mother can install from the App Store, or does Jet hand her off to Xcode and Android Studio at the finish line? Where that handoff happens (never / at signing / at the whole UI layer / this epoch at all) is exactly this decision.

options.name: Tier-1 mobile targets; Jet owns signing and store submission end to end
options.detail: Core loop: `jet build --target=ios|android` compiles the same reactive app natively, and one first-party command signs it with locally held keys and uploads it to the store — no Apple or Google tool is ever run. iOS/Android become real compile targets through the existing rustc backend (aarch64-apple-ios, aarch64-linux-android via a jetpack-pinned NDK), rendering native widgets per D-NATIVEUI1=A — UIKit via the ratified D-FFI-SWIFT1 bridge, Android views via the G3 follow-up ballot. Signing is implemented first-party (the Ed25519 signing tier D-PKGSIGN1 set this precedent; pure-Rust Apple codesigning is proven ground — see the rcodesign comparison). Submission talks directly to the App Store Connect API and Play Developer API. Users type `jet ship`; jetpack is the engine behind the seam, same dispatch shape as `jet os` — so store-API churn lives in a separately updateable tool, never in the compiler, and signing keys never leave the user's machine (contrast Expo, which holds them in the cloud). Honest gate: iOS builds still require a Mac with the Xcode SDK installed (Apple's license), but Xcode is never opened; Android works from any OS, fully offline until upload. This is the only option under which "no reason to reach for another language" is literally true for mobile.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=android
   toolchain  android-ndk r27 (jetpack, pinned)
   compiled   notes.jet -> aarch64-linux-android
   built      target/android/notes.aab

$ jet ship android
   no signing key found -> created ./release.keystore (BACK THIS FILE UP:
   Google will not let you update the app without it)
   signed     notes.aab
   uploaded   Play Console -> internal testing track (build 1)

$ jet ship ios            # on her Mac
   signed in to App Store Connect (team: Priya Rao)
   created signing certificate + provisioning profile (stored locally;
   keys never leave this machine)
   signed     Notes.ipa (Apple Distribution: Priya Rao)
   uploaded   App Store Connect -> TestFlight build 1

$ jet build --target=ios  # on her Linux desktop
error: building for iOS requires the Apple SDK, which Apple licenses
       only on Apple hardware
  what: the iOS target links against Apple's UIKit frameworks
  fix:  run this on a Mac (or a macOS CI runner) with Xcode installed —
        Jet uses its SDK, you never open it. `--target=android` works here.

options.name: Tier-1 mobile targets; jetpack orchestrates Apple/Google tools for signing and submission
options.detail: Core loop: Jet compiles natively exactly as in A, but `jet ship` drives Apple's and Google's own command-line tools (codesign, Transporter, apksigner, bundletool) under the hood instead of reimplementing them — the fastlane/Tauri shape. The user types the same commands as A and jetpack provisions and hash-pins the vendor tools as toolchain deps (D-BUILDTOOLCHAIN1=A), laundering their errors into Jet diagnostics in the I2 spirit — raw xcodebuild output never reaches the user. What changes versus A is the trust and failure surface: the pipeline is only as correct, as offline-capable, and as scriptable as Apple's and Google's tools of the week; a vendor tool update can break `jet ship` in ways Jet can report but not fix, and iOS signing additionally requires the full Xcode command-line surface installed, not just the SDK. Keys still stay local. The compile-target half of this option is identical to A, so a later verdict could move B→A signing without touching the language.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=android
   built      target/android/notes.aab      # identical to option A

$ jet ship android
   tool       apksigner 35.0 (jetpack, pinned)
   signed     notes.aab (./release.keystore)
   uploaded   Play Console -> internal testing track (build 1)

$ jet ship ios
   tool       Xcode command line tools 17.2
   signed     Notes.ipa (via codesign)
   uploaded   App Store Connect (via Transporter)

$ jet ship ios            # Xcode CLT missing
error: shipping to the App Store needs Apple's command-line tools,
       which Apple does not allow Jet to bundle
  what: signing and upload run Apple's codesign and Transporter
  fix:  xcode-select --install, then rerun `jet ship ios`

options.name: Jet compiles the logic core; UI shells are hand-written in Xcode / Android Studio
options.detail: Core loop: `jet build --lib --target=ios|android` emits the app's state and logic as a static library with generated Swift and Kotlin bindings (the D-FFI-SWIFT1 bridge run in reverse), and the developer writes the screens twice — SwiftUI in Xcode, Compose in Android Studio — with Apple and Google owning signing and submission entirely. This is Kotlin Multiplatform's shape. Be clear about what it breaks: the one reactive/view/style/component model that D-NATIVEUI2=B and #134 built — the same `NotesView` that renders on GTK4, web, and TUI would NOT render on phones; only the data layer crosses. Two UI codebases per app, drifting independently, reviewed in tools Jet does not check — a permanent I8 exception on the two platforms with the most users. KMP itself is the cautionary tale: JetBrains spent years building Compose Multiplatform to escape exactly this split. Included because it is the honest industry-standard fallback shape, not because it fits Jet's frame.

options.name: Ratify deferral: mobile lands in Epoch 4, desktop/web/TUI finish first
options.detail: Core loop: this epoch ships no mobile target, and that becomes a recorded decree with a named landing slot instead of a silent gap. Grounding is sequencing, not effort: the universal-language plan's own dependency order says UL9 native/mobile comes after UL2 + UL3 + UL6, #134's macOS/Windows desktop backends are still open, and native hot-reload (G4) is web-only — mobile shipped now would be the first backend without a complete dev loop behind it. The decree pins three things so the gap cannot silently rot: (1) `--target=ios|android` produce an honest error naming this decision and the epoch, not a parse error; (2) mobile, when it lands, follows D-NATIVEUI1/2 (same widget-FFI pattern, same one UI model — option A or B of this ballot re-raised then); (3) no interim semi-official path (no option-C shells) that would create a second way to mean it before the first exists. Cost: for at least an epoch, "Jet replaces Swift" is claimably false, and the two largest consumer platforms stay dark while Flutter and RN keep shipping there.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=ios
error: iOS is not a supported target in this epoch
  what: mobile targets are scheduled for Epoch 4 (decision D-NATIVEUI3=D,
        after the desktop backends and native hot-reload land)
  fix:  `--target=web` produces an installable PWA your phone can run today

# Board effect: #480 closes as decreed-deferred; #134 proceeds with
# macOS/Windows desktop + native hot-reload unblocked and unsplit.

comparisons.note: Proves the option-A compile half: Dart AOT-compiles to real arm64 on both platforms, no interpreter. But it never owned the ship half — `flutter build ipa` wraps xcodebuild, signing stays Xcode-managed, and submission is delegated to fastlane or Xcode. That seam is where Flutter's one-language story ends and users file toolchain bugs.
comparisons.code:
$ flutter build ipa            # wraps xcodebuild under the hood
$ open build/ios/archive/Runner.xcarchive   # ...and you're in Xcode anyway
$ fastlane pilot upload        # third-party tool for the last mile

comparisons.note: Shows the demand for one-command shipping — and the trust cost of renting it. Bare RN hands you Xcode/Android Studio projects (option C's ergonomics). Expo's answer, `eas build` / `eas submit`, is one command, but builds run on Expo's servers and Expo can hold your signing credentials in its cloud. Option A is that ergonomic loop with keys kept local.
comparisons.code:
$ eas build --platform ios     # builds on Expo's servers
$ eas submit --platform ios    # Expo-managed credentials, cloud-side

comparisons.note: Option C's shape, from its strongest proponent: shared Kotlin logic core, UI written twice in SwiftUI and Compose, Apple/Google tools own everything past the library boundary. JetBrains' own trajectory — years building Compose Multiplatform to render one UI on iOS too — is the evidence that the split-UI compromise does not hold.

The feasibility evidence for option A's ship half: fastlane drives the App Store Connect and Play upload APIs from plain Ruby with no Xcode GUI, and rcodesign (pure Rust, no Apple code) signs and notarizes Mach-O binaries from Linux. First-party signing and submission is proven ground, not speculation — what no language toolchain has done is make it a built-in.
comparisons.code:
$ rcodesign sign --p12-file dist.p12 Notes.app    # pure Rust, runs on Linux
$ fastlane deliver                                # App Store Connect API, no Xcode GUI

comparisons.note: Option B's shape in the wild: `tauri ios build` / `tauri android build` orchestrate xcodebuild and gradle under one CLI. Works, but users must install and maintain both vendor toolchains, and Tauri's issue tracker absorbs every xcodebuild/gradle regression as its own bug — the orchestrator owns the churn without owning the fix.
comparisons.code:
$ npm run tauri ios build      # requires full Xcode installed
$ npm run tauri android build  # requires Android Studio SDK + gradle

decisions.title: Attach option priority without colliding with real option keys
decisions.gist: Choose the typed source form that attaches Default, Force, or Priority(n) to one option contribution without reserving ordinary dotted keys such as filesystem.swap.fast.priority.
decisions.story: Two reusable modules choose different display managers. The baseline should be overridable, the site policy should normally win, and an emergency module may force a value. Separately, a swap device legitimately has an option named priority. Jet must distinguish precedence metadata from that real setting, show every contender in explain output, and never silently reinterpret a user's option key.

options.name: Typed contribution record
options.detail: An ordinary value remains the beginner path. An expert wraps only the contribution that needs precedence in OptionValue.{ value, priority }, where priority is .Default, .Force, or .Priority(n). The record is structurally distinct from dotted option keys, so filesystem.swap.fast.priority remains ordinary data. Explain output projects the wrapper fields but the option consumer receives only value.
options.code:
options: [
  services.displayManager: OptionValue.{ value: "sddm", priority: .Default },
  filesystem.swap.fast.priority: 5,
  services.audio.enable: true,
]

options.name: Priority value wrapper
options.detail: Default(value), Force(value), and Priority(n, value) wrap one contribution directly. This is compact and unambiguous, but the named tiers look like general calls and mix policy with value construction. Every supported value type must pass through the wrapper unchanged.
options.code:
options: [
  services.displayManager: Default("sddm"),
  filesystem.swap.fast.priority: 5,
  services.audio.enable: Force(true),
  kernel.package: Priority(2500, packages.cachyos),
]

options.name: Contribution attributes
options.detail: Attributes attach policy before one option entry. The relationship is visually clear and does not consume dotted keys, but it creates new attribute vocabulary and makes list-entry formatting carry semantic state outside the value expression.
options.code:
options: [
  #[Default] services.displayManager: "sddm",
  filesystem.swap.fast.priority: 5,
  #[Force] services.audio.enable: true,
  #[Priority(2500)] kernel.package: packages.cachyos,
]

comparisons.note: Nix wraps a value with mkDefault, mkForce, or mkOverride. The wrapper is unambiguous, but Jet can keep its expert form typed instead of relying on dynamically interpreted functions.
CSS attaches !important to one declaration, not to a separate property named priority. This preserves unrelated property names but provides only one override tier.

decisions.lesson:
A declarative system builds one final configuration by combining contributions from many modules. Two modules can set the same option, so the system needs a precedence rule: which contribution wins, and why? A default is a weak suggestion meant to lose to ordinary configuration. A normal value is the usual choice. A forced value is an explicit override meant to beat ordinary choices. Numeric priority adds finer ordering when three tiers are not enough.

This priority is metadata about a contribution, not part of the configured value itself. For example, the value may be the text gdm while the metadata says this is only a default. The final service receives gdm, not a wrapper or priority number. Explain output should still retain every contender and its source so a user can understand the winner.

The naming collision matters because real configuration paths may themselves end in priority, such as a swap device priority. Jet must distinguish that ordinary option key from merge metadata without guessing from its spelling. This ballot chooses the source form that makes that distinction explicit while keeping simple values simple.

decisions.title: Android native-widget and Kotlin interop transport
decisions.gist: How Jet's Android backend reaches native widgets and existing Kotlin libraries without creating a second UI model.
decisions.lesson:
Android applications normally contain Java or Kotlin code running on Android Runtime, plus optional native machine code. The Java Native Interface, or JNI, is Android's standard bridge between those worlds. Jet can compile its application logic to native code, then use JNI to create Android View widgets and receive lifecycle or input callbacks.

Jetpack Compose is Google's newer Kotlin UI toolkit. Compose builds screens from Kotlin functions instead of directly assembling classic View objects. A Compose bridge would generate Kotlin adapters that translate Jet's View tree into Compose calls. That translation must not become a second Jet component model.

The transport matters at two boundaries. Jet's own renderer needs predictable widget creation, updates, events, ownership, and errors. Experts also need access to existing Android libraries whose public APIs are Kotlin or Java. Jet already ratified one `java.*` binder over JNI. This decision chooses whether the Android UI backend uses that common binder directly, adds a Compose-specific adapter, or exposes both behind one backend contract.

For example, a Jet Button remains one Jet Button on every platform. On Android, the chosen transport decides whether its backend creates `android.widget.Button`, calls generated Compose code, or selects either implementation behind the same backend interface. User application code and reactive state remain unchanged.
decisions.story: Mina moves a Jet inventory app from Linux to Android. Its shared screen contains a search field, list, and camera button. She wants standard Android accessibility and lifecycle behavior. Her company also has a Kotlin barcode-scanner library. Mina should keep one Jet screen while still calling that library through a typed, inspectable boundary.

options.name: Direct JNI View backend
options.detail: Jet's Android backend uses generated JNI bindings to Android's classic View toolkit. The same java.* binder projects third-party Kotlin and Java libraries. Every callback crosses one typed boundary with checked ownership and Jet diagnostics. Experts can inspect generated bindings and override provisioned SDK or NDK handles. Compose-only libraries need an explicit Kotlin adapter package.
options.technical: Package a native shared library inside a minimal Android application shell. Generated JNI entrypoints attach to the existing Android Runtime, retain Java objects as opaque owned handles, and lower exceptions to JavaError. UI operations implement the existing JetBackend seam. No second embedded JVM is started on Android.
options.code:
$ jet inspect bind java android.widget.Button
+projected  android.widget.Button -> java.android.widget.Button
+transport  existing Android Runtime via JNI
+
+$ jet build --target=android
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+backend    android-view / JNI
+
+error: Compose-only type `CameraPreview` has no Android View entrypoint
+  fix: add a Kotlin adapter that exposes a View, or choose the Compose-capable transport

options.name: Generated Kotlin Compose bridge
options.detail: Jet generates a Kotlin layer that renders its View tree through Compose. Existing Compose libraries fit naturally, and Android previews see generated Kotlin components. Classic View libraries require Compose interop wrappers. Experts can inspect and pin generated Kotlin, Gradle, compiler-plugin, and SDK inputs. The generated layer adds a platform-specific translation between Jet and native widgets.
options.technical: Jet emits Kotlin composables plus JNI calls into the native Jet state engine. State identity remains owned by Jet; Compose observes snapshots and returns events. Generated Kotlin is derived output, never an editable source of truth.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=android --android-backend=compose
+generated  target/android/generated/JetInventory.kt
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+backend    compose / generated Kotlin bridge
+
+$ jet inspect generated android
+JetInventory.kt  hash:7ad2...  source:InventoryView

options.name: One Android backend protocol with View default and Compose adapter
options.detail: Jet keeps one Android backend contract. Its ceremony-free default uses direct JNI Views. A project may select the first-party Compose adapter without changing Jet components, state, events, or accessibility semantics. The same java.* binder handles ordinary Kotlin and Java libraries in both modes. Experts control the backend, generated adapters, toolchain, cache, and audit output through package policy.
options.technical: Define one AndroidBackend implementation contract under JetBackend. AndroidViewBackend is the default. AndroidComposeBackend consumes the identical checked UI tree and event protocol. Conformance tests require matching tree semantics, state identity, lifecycle restoration, accessibility facts, and diagnostics. Backend selection is build policy, not new language syntax.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=android
+backend    android-view (default)
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+
+$ jet build --target=android --android-backend=compose
+backend    android-compose (same checked View tree)
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+
+$ jet inspect android --audit
+ui-model   core.ui/View
+transport  JNI + generated Compose adapter
+toolchain  android-ndk r27, Kotlin 2.2, hashes recorded

comparisons.note: Flutter keeps one Dart widget model while platform channels reach Kotlin APIs. Its default renderer owns pixels, unlike Jet's ratified native-widget direction.
comparisons.code:
const channel = MethodChannel('scanner');
+final code = await channel.invokeMethod('scan');

comparisons.note: React Native maps one component model to Android views and also permits native modules. Its generated architecture shows why UI transport and library interop should share typed metadata.

recommendation.why: C preserves the ratified native-widget default while letting Compose ecosystems participate through a conforming adapter. One checked View tree and one java.* binder serve beginners and experts.

whyNot.reason: A makes Compose-only libraries require bespoke wrappers even though a reusable conforming adapter can preserve Jet semantics.
B makes a generated Compose translation mandatory and weakens the direct platform-widget default ratified by D-NATIVEUI1.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two backend implementations require parity enforcement. Shared conformance tests and one checked tree make that duplication an implementation detail, not a second user model.

hybrid.synthesis: C keeps A's direct JNI View path as the default and adds B's Compose access as a selectable adapter over the identical backend protocol. Library calls use the ratified java.* binder in either mode.

harvest.aspect: Direct native View access with one typed JNI boundary.
harvest.use: Use it as the default Android backend and common Kotlin or Java interop transport.

harvest.aspect: Natural access to Compose-only widgets and libraries.
harvest.use: Provide it as a first-party conforming adapter whose generated Kotlin remains derived and auditable.

harvest.aspect: One public UI model across transport choices.
harvest.use: Make backend conformance and identical Jet source the binding rule.

decisions.title: Native UI hot reload and component preview model
decisions.gist: How `jet dev` updates running native apps and previews components while preserving one runtime model.
decisions.lesson:
A native hot reload loop changes a running application after source is saved. A plain restart rebuilds and launches again, losing temporary state. A hot swap replaces checked executable units inside a resident process, then reconciles the existing widget tree with the new View tree.

State identity decides what survives. Jet already ratified `@Persist`: a marked module binding survives `jet dev` reload when its module path, name, and compatible value shape still match. Ordinary local state may reset. Widget identity also needs stable source-derived keys so a changed label updates the existing native widget instead of opening another window.

A component preview renders one component with chosen sample inputs, device size, theme, locale, and accessibility settings. It can run inside a separate preview host or inside the same resident runtime used by the full app. A shared host gives previews the same layout, event, lifecycle, and backend behavior as the application.

This choice controls trust as well as speed. Reloaded code must pass the normal parser, semantic checks, and executable TIR pipeline before entering the process. A failed change leaves the last good app running and shows a Jet diagnostic. No native linker or platform-tool error should leak to the user.
decisions.story: Luis adjusts a checkout screen while it runs on an Android phone and an iPhone simulator. He has already filled a long form. Saving a color change should keep the form values, update both native widget trees, and show the same component under large text. A bad edit should leave the last good screen usable.

options.name: Full-app state-preserving hot reload
options.detail: `jet dev --target=ios|android` runs the complete app in a resident native host. Each valid save swaps changed checked modules and reconciles native widgets. `@Persist` state survives by its ratified identity rules. Beginners use one command. Experts inspect swap units, state migration, backend calls, hashes, timing, and fallback reasons. Component previews are ordinary small applications.
options.technical: Reuse checked TIR and the resident JIT or platform dynamic-loading boundary. Compute a module dependency closure, validate ABI and value layouts before activation, apply the swap atomically, then diff the View tree. Unsupported native changes trigger a diagnosed controlled restart, never partial mutation.
options.code:
$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=android
+ready    Pixel 10 / android-view
+changed  CheckoutView
+checked  18 ms
+swapped  7 ms; widgets reused: 12; created: 1
+state    persisted: cart
+
+error E2204: this edit changes a native boundary
+  what: Scanner.scan now returns a different type
+  fix:  Jet kept the last good app running; press `r` for a controlled restart

options.name: Isolated component preview host
options.detail: `jet preview` runs selected components in a dedicated native host with sample inputs and device traits. Changes reload only the preview graph. This makes themes, sizes, locales, focus, and accessibility states explicit. Full applications still rebuild and restart, so navigation, lifecycle, restoration, and cross-component behavior are not exercised in the fast loop.
options.technical: The preview host loads checked component entrypoints and fixture values. It uses the production backend and renderer, but substitutes lifecycle, navigation, storage, and external effects with declared preview capabilities.
options.code:
$ jet preview checkout.jet CheckoutView --target=ios
+preview  iPhone 17 Pro, light, en-US
+
+keys: d device  t theme  l locale  a accessibility  q quit
+saved    component reloaded; app navigation not running
+
+$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=ios
+note: native full-app changes rebuild and restart

options.name: One resident native dev host for apps and previews
options.detail: `jet dev` owns one resident runtime and checked swap protocol. Full-app mode is the ceremony-free default. A preview selector narrows the root component and adds device, theme, locale, lifecycle, and accessibility controls. Both modes use production backends, identical state identity, and the same diagnostics. Experts control swap policy, restart boundaries, devices, capabilities, scheduling, caches, and audit receipts.
options.technical: Model app and preview as root configurations for one NativeDevHost. Every edit passes parser, sema, TIR validation, ABI checks, atomic activation, View reconciliation, and state migration. Preview capabilities are explicit inputs, not mocks hidden in component code. Device and simulator transports carry signed swap bundles and receipts.
options.code:
$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=android
+mode     app; device: Pixel 10
+saved    swapped 2 modules; persisted: cart
+
+$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=ios --preview=CheckoutView
+mode     preview; device: iPhone 17 Pro; theme: light; locale: en-US
+keys     d device  t theme  l locale  a accessibility
+saved    same swap protocol; widgets reused: 12
+
+$ jet inspect dev --audit
+source  CheckoutView@9f31...
+tir     checked@31aa...
+device  simulator-4A2D
+swap    atomic; fallback:none

comparisons.note: Flutter combines stateful full-app hot reload with widget-focused development. Its resident VM shows the value of preserving state while rebuilding the UI tree.
comparisons.code:
$ flutter run
r Hot reload.
R Hot restart.

comparisons.note: Both provide component previews with device and environment controls. Their previews can differ from full application lifecycle behavior, which argues for one Jet host and protocol.

recommendation.why: C gives beginners one real application loop and gives experts precise preview controls without inventing a second renderer or runtime. It directly fulfills D-PERSIST1 through one checked swap protocol.

whyNot.reason: A preserves real application behavior but treats focused previews as disposable mini-apps without first-class environment controls.
B improves component iteration while leaving the full native application loop restart-only and unable to prove lifecycle parity.
