recommendation.tradeoff: The resident host becomes a security and correctness boundary. Mandatory semantic checks, atomic activation, signed device transport, and last-good rollback keep that boundary explicit and auditable.

hybrid.synthesis: C uses A's real full-app resident loop and B's focused environment controls as two root configurations of the same checked native host. Production backends and state rules remain identical.

harvest.aspect: State-preserving edits inside the actual application.
harvest.use: Make full-app hot reload the default `jet dev` mode.

harvest.aspect: Fast component isolation across device and accessibility environments.
harvest.use: Add preview roots and explicit environment inputs to the same host.

harvest.aspect: One swap protocol and one production renderer.
harvest.use: Require app and preview modes to share validation, activation, reconciliation, and audit receipts.

decisions.title: Mobile platform work deferred
decisions.outcome: Defer mobile-native platform work; current burndown focuses the Jet language and Linux support.
decisions.comment: Defer mobile-native platform work; current burndown focuses the Jet language and Linux support.

decisions.title: jetos first-boot welcome: where the driver and codec offer appears
decisions.gist: Where the jetos first-boot driver and codec offer appears: a dedicated Studio welcome view, an inline state on the existing control center, or a terminal flow.
decisions.lesson: The detect-and-apply backend is ungated and ships now. It reads the scanned `hardware.<host>` facts, lists driver and codec candidates, and writes accepted offers as a reviewable `config.jet` diff through the existing declarative-apply path. D-JOS-FIRSTBOOT1=D already ratified that first boot opens Studio as the control center. This ballot decides only where the beginner driver and codec offer is surfaced.
decisions.story: Priya installs jetos on a laptop with an Nvidia GPU and needs the proprietary driver plus media codecs. She boots for the first time and has never seen jetos before. The question is what greets her, and where she accepts the driver and codec offers.
decisions.inWild: The hardware scan (card #326) finds `nvidia` and reports missing codecs. Accepting an offer writes a reviewable diff into the host `config.jet`. A second boot with unchanged hardware shows nothing new.

options.name: Dedicated first-boot welcome view
options.detail: A new Studio view appears once at first boot. It steps through each detected driver and codec offer, then a Finish action deep-links into the normal control-center settings. It never renders again after the offers are resolved.
options.code:
First boot: Studio opens the Welcome view (shown once):

  Welcome to jetos
  Detected hardware needs setup:

  [1/2] Nvidia GPU
        Proprietary driver available.   [ Install ]  [ Skip ]
  [2/2] Media codecs
        H.264 / AAC not installed.      [ Install ]  [ Skip ]

  Finish -> opens the control center.

After Finish, the Welcome view never appears again.

options.name: Inline state on the control center
options.detail: No new view. The ratified control center renders a dismissible offer panel at the top of its normal host/generation/proof home until the offers are accepted or dismissed. This is the same surface a returning user already sees.
options.code:
First boot: Studio opens the control center (the normal home):

  Host: laptop   Generation 1   Source: config.jet   Proof: ok

  +-- Detected hardware (dismiss) ----------------------+
  | Nvidia GPU: proprietary driver     [ Install ]      |
  | Media codecs: H.264 / AAC missing  [ Install ]      |
  +----------------------------------------------------+

  (rest of the control center below)

Once installed or dismissed, the panel is gone. A second boot
with unchanged hardware shows no panel.

options.name: Terminal welcome flow
options.detail: The offer runs as a terminal flow. A first-boot notice on the control center points to `jetos welcome`. The Studio control center renders its ratified home unchanged, with no driver-offer element. A GUI offer can follow in a later ballot.
options.code:
First boot: Studio control center opens unchanged.
A one-line notice: "Run `jetos welcome` to set up detected hardware."

$ jetos welcome
Detected hardware:
  Nvidia GPU     proprietary driver available
  Media codecs   H.264 / AAC not installed

Install proprietary Nvidia driver? [y/N] y
Install media codecs? [y/N] y
Writing config.jet diff... review with `jetos diff`, apply staged.

comparisons.note: Mint ships a separate Welcome app and a standalone Driver Manager window. That is two surfaces for one first-run job, and users miss the Driver Manager because it is not on the path they already walk.
comparisons.code:
Welcome app  ->  (user closes it)
Driver Manager  ->  separate window, often never opened

recommendation.why: B puts the offer on the control center that D-JOS-FIRSTBOOT1=D already opens at first boot. Priya sees driver and codec offers on the surface she lands on, accepts with one click, and learns no second view.

whyNot.reason: Adds a Studio view that renders only at first boot and never again. It is a permanent surface for a one-time event, and it splits driver settings between the wizard and the control center.
Hides the beginner offer behind a terminal command. A first-time GUI user may never learn the proprietary driver or codecs are available, which misses the out-of-box goal.

recommendation.tradeoff: B shows offers inline on the home, so a laptop with several detected devices shows a longer home until Priya acts or dismisses. The panel must collapse cleanly once resolved.

decisions.title: Name the NixOS comparison migration command
decisions.gist: Choose the explicit `jet os` command that may reach the migration-only NixOS backend.
decisions.lesson:
`jet os import` translates existing NixOS source into Jet configuration. The migration comparison backend has a different job: after import, it builds a clearly labeled NixOS guest and captures boot proof for comparison. `jet os proof` remains native-jetos proof; comparison artifacts live only under the migration output.

Only `jet os migrate compare-nixos` may enter `nixos_backend`. Native plan, build, switch, image, and proof dispatch must reject that backend before work. Existing `--out` and `--json` controls remain canonical. Offline mode succeeds only with every locked input present. The choice below decides whether successful comparison always includes boot proof or may stop after building.
decisions.story: Mara imports a laptop configuration, builds native jetos, then creates one NixOS comparison guest. She reads its separate receipt and boot proof without mistaking it for a native generation.
decisions.inWild:
jet os import ~/nixos --host laptop --write --out ./migrated
jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare --json

options.name: Build and boot-prove every comparison
options.detail: The command builds the NixOS guest, boots it, verifies guest identity, and then publishes artifacts. There is no successful unproved comparison state.
options.technical: Success atomically publishes `<out>/nixos/laptop/system.qcow2`, `proof.json`, and `receipt.json`, prints all three paths, and exits 0. Missing locked offline input prints `migration comparison unavailable offline: <input>` and exits 2. Any native command attempting this backend prints `NixOS backend is migration-only; use jet os migrate compare-nixos` and exits 2.
options.code:
$ jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare
built NixOS comparison: ./compare/nixos/laptop/system.qcow2
boot proof: ./compare/nixos/laptop/proof.json
receipt: ./compare/nixos/laptop/receipt.json
$ echo $?
0

options.name: Build by default, prove with --proof
options.detail: The command publishes a labeled comparison guest after building. `--proof` boots it and adds proof before success.
options.technical: Build-only success publishes the image and receipt with `proofState: not-run`. `--proof` publishes all three A artifacts. Offline and forbidden-backend errors match A.
options.code:
jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare
jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare --proof --json

options.name: Plan by default, build with --write
options.detail: The default prints the comparison plan. `--write` builds and automatically boot-proves before publication.
options.technical: Plan exits 0 without artifact paths. `--write` has A success and error behavior.
options.code:
jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare
jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare --write --json

comparisons.note: Legacy comparison is named explicitly and stored apart from production verification.

recommendation.why: A comparison guest is useful only when it actually boots and proves its NixOS identity. Automatic proof prevents a built file from being mistaken for verified comparison evidence.

whyNot.reason: A successful unproved image creates a weaker state that users can mistake for comparison evidence.
The dedicated compare command already states intent; an additional write gate duplicates the existing migration boundary.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every successful comparison includes a guest boot. That is acceptable because boot behavior is the fact this oracle exists to compare.

decisions.title: Fix the `jet os image --format` values
decisions.gist: Add `--format` to `jet os image` and choose its stable native-image value vocabulary.
decisions.lesson:
`jet os image` currently has no public `--format` selector. This decision adds one for native operating-system artifacts. D-JPK-IMAGE1 remains separate: `jet image` builds OCI layouts and does not gain these values.

Each format packages one already-built system generation. Bare `jet os image <host>` keeps ISO as the default. A successful command atomically changes an artifact from `staged` to `built` only after format validation and proof. Cross-architecture requests must produce matching kernel, initrd, firmware, and boot metadata or fail before staging. No aliases or hidden normalization are included in any option.
decisions.story: Inez uses one router generation for an installer ISO, a VM disk, an SD card, and a netboot tree. Each artifact has the same source and closure identity.
decisions.inWild: jet os image router --format sd --arch aarch64 --out ./images

options.name: iso | qcow | raw | sd | netboot
options.detail: Short stable media names cover installer, VM, disk, card, and network boot. Bare image defaults to `iso`. No other spelling is accepted.
options.technical: Success prints artifact and proof paths and exits 0. Proof JSON records `state: built`, canonical format, architecture, source, generation, closure, tools, hash, and boot result. An incomplete directory remains `state: staged`, is not published, and exits 1. Unsupported architecture prints `image format <format> cannot build <arch>: missing matching <asset>` and exits 2.
options.code:
$ jet os image router --format sd --arch aarch64 --out ./images
built sd image: ./images/jetos-router-sd.img
proof: ./images/jetos-router-sd.proof.json
$ echo $?
0

options.name: iso | qcow2 | raw | sdcard | pxe
options.detail: Use ecosystem-specific names. The values are longer and mix file-format, medium, and protocol vocabulary.
options.technical: Default, state transition, architecture errors, artifacts, proof, and exits match A. Only these exact values parse.
options.code:
jet os image router --format sdcard
jet os image router --format pxe

options.name: installer | vm | disk | card | network
options.detail: Use purpose names instead of artifact names. This reads naturally but hides whether the VM artifact is QCOW or another format.
options.technical: `vm` fixes QCOW and `disk` fixes raw. All proof and error behavior matches A.
options.code:
jet os image router --format card
jet os image router --format network

comparisons.note: The file format is commonly called qcow2, while a short CLI value can remain canonical if diagnostics teach it.

recommendation.why: The values are compact, technically exact, and stable across local and automated use. They map directly to artifact and proof identities without aliases.

whyNot.reason: The vocabulary mixes implementation names and delivery concepts while making common values longer.
Purpose names conceal the actual artifact format that automation must consume.

recommendation.tradeoff: `qcow` is shorter than the common file extension `qcow2`. That is acceptable because help and artifact paths show the exact output while the public value stays concise.

decisions.title: Set generation retention and automatic-upgrade policy
decisions.gist: Choose exact lifecycle fields and whether automatic upgrades are enabled by default.
decisions.lesson:
`packages.generations.*` selects protected system-generation roots. E7 plans and explains those roots; the shared E4 Hangar collector deletes only unprotected objects. `deploy.autoUpgrade.*` schedules the existing native sequence: `jet os build`, `jet os proof`, then `jet os switch`. This ballot does not add an update command.

An enabled schedule persists while the user is logged out through the platform user scheduler. No Jet privileged daemon remains resident. Build and proof run without privilege; switch requests one-shot activation authority. Privilege failure leaves the built candidate current-proof intact and the live generation unchanged. Offline input gaps, stale proof, failed health, and rollback each produce explicit receipts and terminal output.
decisions.story: Sam keeps ten rollback generations on a laptop. An operator uses the same fields for a weekly proved update window, without installing a privileged updater daemon.

options.name: Visible retention, automatic upgrade off
options.detail: Init writes all fields into the system module with `enable: false`. Experts turn on the same schedule; it continues while logged out.
options.technical: Plan output lists every kept and collectible generation with reason, scheduled next run, offline input state, candidate, proof fingerprint, activation authority, health window, and rollback target. Missing offline input prints `auto-upgrade: no change; locked input unavailable offline: <input>` and exits 0 with a no-change receipt. Privilege denial exits 2 and retains the candidate. Stale proof refuses switch with exit 2. Failed health rolls back, prints both generation names, writes rollback receipt, and exits 1.

options.name: Security scope enabled weekly
options.detail: Init enables a logged-out weekly security schedule. All other fields and failure behavior match A.
options.technical: `deploy.autoUpgrade.scope: .Security` requires locked provider security classification. Unknown classification becomes offline-style no-change, never a broad upgrade.

options.name: Retention fields only
options.detail: The system module owns retention, but scheduling remains external. Operators invoke existing build, proof, and switch commands.
options.technical: Generation plan and Hangar behavior match A. No `deploy.autoUpgrade.*` fields or scheduler receipts exist.

comparisons.note: A user timer starts a short-lived job and does not require a resident privileged service.

recommendation.why: Retention and update intent stay fully visible, while unattended system mutation remains opt-in. The same fields give experts schedules, offline behavior, proof, health, and rollback control.

whyNot.reason: Default unattended activation changes a machine without the owner first choosing that policy.
Removing source scheduling forces durable system intent into external automation.

recommendation.tradeoff: Beginners must enable automatic updates themselves. That is acceptable because init and Studio can present the choice without silently activating it.

decisions.title: Name the native service journal command
decisions.gist: Choose whether runtime journals use `jet os logs` or a nested service command.
decisions.lesson:
Native service journals differ from `jet dev` output and Jetpack build logs. One JetOS journal backend owns storage, permission checks, generation identity, unit normalization, time filtering, follow mode, remote transport, and JSON rows.

A bare unit like `web` normalizes to `web.service`; an explicit suffix such as `backup.timer` remains unchanged. Without `--host`, the selected local `system.<host>` is used. `--host prod-1` must resolve a declared fleet host and its ratified local authority binding before transport. Remote rows use the same schema as local rows. The examples below are product-copy requirements, not invented diagnostic codes. Card #329 must allocate any missing registered codes in `diagnostics.md` and add UI snapshots before implementation.
decisions.story: Noah sees a failed web-service health check, reads its current-generation journal, follows the restart, then exports identical rows from a remote host as JSON.
decisions.inWild:
jet os logs web --since 10m
jet os logs web --host prod-1 --generation current --follow --json

options.name: jet os logs <unit>
options.detail: The unit is positional and normalizes to a systemd unit. Expert filters extend the same local or authorized remote query.
options.technical: Each JSON line is `{"host":String,"generation":String,"unit":String,"at":String,"cursor":String,"stream":String,"level":String,"message":String}`. Normal completion exits 0. Unknown unit, denied journal access, unknown host, and stale generation exit 2. Remote connection failure or follow disconnect prints the last cursor and exits 1. Card #329 owns code registration plus diagnostics.md and UI snapshots for any message lacking an exact existing code.
options.code:
$ jet os logs web --generation g42
jet os logs: unknown unit `web`; resolved `web.service` is not present in generation `g42`

$ jet os logs web --host prod-1
jet os logs: access denied for `web.service` on host `prod-1`; check the local host authority binding

$ jet os logs web --host prod-1 --follow
jet os logs: host `prod-1` became unavailable; resume with cursor `s=42`

options.name: jet os service logs <unit>
options.detail: A service namespace owns the same normalization, authority, schema, errors, resume cursor, and exits.
options.technical: Behavior and exact product copy are identical to A after dispatch. Card #329 owns missing diagnostic registration and snapshots.
options.code: jet os service logs web --host prod-1 --follow --json

options.name: jet os logs --unit <name>
options.detail: The unit is explicit as a flag. Omitting it queries every authorized unit in the selected generation.
options.technical: Schema, authority, normalization, exact product copy, cursor, and exits match A. Whole-generation access uses the same permission boundary.
options.code:
jet os logs --unit web --since 10m
jet os logs --generation current --json

comparisons.note: `journalctl -u` queries the same journal by unit; Jet can make the unit positional for its common path.

recommendation.why: The canonical `jet os` boundary distinguishes runtime journals, and the positional unit keeps the beginner path direct. Expert filters remain on one backend and schema.

whyNot.reason: A service namespace adds ceremony before any other service subcommands are ratified.
A required flag burdens the dominant one-unit query and invites accidental whole-journal reads.

recommendation.tradeoff: The command reserves `jet os logs` for service journals rather than all OS logs. That is acceptable because boot and proof facts already have `jet os proof`.

decisions.title: Protect live system accounts during declarative removal
decisions.gist: Choose how `users.<name>` absence revokes login while preserving or deliberately disposing of home data.
decisions.lesson:
`users.<name>` describes a live system account. It is distinct from portable `user.<name>` profiles. When a live account disappears from merged configuration, JetOS may revoke login and preserve the home automatically. Any archive or destruction intent lives in the separate `users.removals` tombstone collection; the removed `users.sam` declaration does not coexist with a nested removal field.

A tombstone binds name, expected user ID, expected home, action, reason, source revision, and live fingerprint. It remains in source until an action receipt exists. The generation ledger retains UID reservation and home disposition after source cleanup. Repeated switches are idempotent. Noninteractive activation cannot invent confirmation. Archive and destruction require current backup proof; stale identity, missing proof, or changed home refuses action.
decisions.story: Ari removes a contractor from the system. Login stops on the next switch, but the home remains until an explicit reviewed archive or destruction action completes.

options.name: Absence locks and preserves; tombstones govern disposal
options.detail: Removing `users.sam` locks login and preserves its home and UID reservation. `users.removals["sam"]` is needed only to preserve explicitly, archive, or destroy with audit facts.
options.technical: `.PreserveHome` needs identity facts and reason. `.Archive` additionally needs destination and current backup proof. `.DestroyHome` needs current backup proof and reason. Plan prints account, UID, home, action, backup proof, repeat state, and rollback limit. Stale identity or backup exits 2. Archive/destruction failure exits 1 with live data unchanged. Success writes action and UID-tombstone receipts; repeated switch exits 0 no-change.

options.name: A tombstone is required before declaration removal
options.detail: Removing `users.sam` without a matching `users.removals` row is a plan error. The row chooses preserve, archive, or destroy.
options.technical: Lifetime, UID reservation, stale checks, backup proof, repeat behavior, receipts, and exits match A.
options.code: users.removals: ["sam": [expectedUid: 1004, expectedHome: "/home/sam", action: .PreserveHome, reason: "contract ended"]]

options.name: Absence locks and creates an archive-required tombstone
options.detail: Removing the declaration locks login immediately and creates a pending durable tombstone. Later noninteractive switches refuse until source supplies archive proof.
options.technical: The generated pending state cannot archive or destroy. Source must adopt it with exact identity and backup fields.
options.code:
plan: lock sam; preserve /home/sam; create pending removal receipt
fix: add users.removals["sam"] with archive proof

comparisons.note: Locking an account and deleting its home are separate operations because their recovery properties differ.

recommendation.why: Login authority is revoked immediately while data and UID ownership remain safe. A separate source tombstone provides one audited path for preserve, archive, or destruction without reviving the removed account declaration.

whyNot.reason: Requiring a source tombstone before absence delays immediate login revocation when the owner removes a user declaration.
A generated pending tombstone creates split truth: source says the account is gone while durable semantic removal intent exists only in generated state.

recommendation.tradeoff: Preserved homes and UID reservations remain until an explicit tombstone action is reviewed. That is acceptable because storage and later cleanup are recoverable, while premature identity reuse or deletion is not.

decisions.title: Place and govern declared `/etc` files
decisions.gist: Choose the exact source home and managed-by-default law for `/etc` entries.
decisions.lesson:
No ratified source namespace currently owns arbitrary `/etc` entries, so this ballot chooses one. Entries live inside a complete `module system.<host>` options map. Each entry has a relative path, ownership, mode as a decimal integer, and exactly one content input: inline `contents`, project `source`, or mutable `seed`.

Managed entries use contents or source and are backed by the immutable generation. `/etc/<path>` is a JetOS-owned symlink to that backing file. Mutable entries use seed, are copied once to `/var/lib/jetos/etc/<entry>`, and `/etc/<path>` links there.

Managed and mutable paths cannot overlap by equality or ancestry. Removing a managed entry deletes only its owned link. Removing a mutable entry preserves backing data unless a later decision governs deletion. The samples require exact product copy. Card #401 must allocate missing diagnostic codes, register them in `diagnostics.md`, and add UI snapshots.
decisions.story: Lee manages SSH configuration exactly from source, while one upstream daemon must retain a live-edited state file under `/etc`.

options.name: filesystem.etc map
options.detail: Named entries live under the full-word filesystem family. Managed is default; mutable requires `mutable: true` and seed.
options.technical: `contents`, `source`, and `seed` are mutually exclusive. Seed requires mutable; contents/source reject mutable. Absolute, parent, NUL, duplicate, symlink-escape, file-directory overlap, managed-mutable ancestry overlap, unknown user/group, invalid mode, and stale mutable fingerprints fail during plan. Plan prints backing path, link target, action, ownership, seed fingerprint, drift, and rollback. Card #401 owns missing diagnostic registration and snapshots.
options.code:
module system.laptop {
  options: [
    filesystem.etc: [
      sshd: [path: "ssh/sshd_config", source: ./sshd_config, mode: 384, user: "root", group: "root"],
    ],
  ]
}

jet os plan: `/etc/ssh` overlaps `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`
  `filesystem.etc.sshDir` owns the directory path
  `filesystem.etc.sshd` owns the file path
fix: keep one owner or move one path

jet os plan: mutable `/etc/database/state` changed since this plan
  expected seed fingerprint: sha256:old
  live fingerprint: sha256:new
fix: review the live file and run `jet os plan` again

options.name: system.files.etc map
options.detail: The identical entry law lives under a system-files family. The path repeats both files and etc.
options.technical: All exclusivity, backing, link, deletion, exact product copy, diagnostics, plan, drift, and rollback behavior matches A.
options.code: module system.laptop { options: [system.files.etc: [sshd: [path: "ssh/sshd_config", source: ./sshd_config, mode: 384, user: "root", group: "root"]]] }

options.name: etc map
options.detail: A short top-level map owns the identical law. It adds a new root beside full-word system namespaces.
options.technical: All behavior and diagnostic discipline matches A.
options.code: module system.laptop { options: [etc: [sshd: [path: "ssh/sshd_config", source: ./sshd_config, mode: 384, user: "root", group: "root"]]] }

comparisons.note: Declared `/etc` entries are generation-managed by default; mutable service state normally lives elsewhere.

recommendation.why: The full-word filesystem family states the domain clearly and keeps managed files reproducible. Explicit mutable entries retain expert compatibility with complete drift evidence.

whyNot.reason: The repeated `files.etc` path adds words without adding a semantic boundary.
A new short root conflicts with the established full-word namespace direction.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each entry needs a semantic name and a path. That is acceptable because stable names improve merge provenance while paths remain exact filesystem facts.

decisions.title: Where the C compiler behind jet cc comes from
decisions.gist: Whether jet cc ships a C compiler inside Jet, fetches one through Jet's package store, borrows the host's, or is not built.
decisions.lesson:
A C toolchain is the compiler, linker, and standard C library headers needed to turn C source into a program. Cross-compiling means building on one machine for a different kind of machine. The set of target headers and libraries is called a sysroot.

Zig proved a language can win users through its toolchain before its syntax. The zig cc command is a full C compiler that behaves the same on every machine and targets any platform out of the box. Teams adopt it just to build their existing C code, and meet the language later.

Jet today uses whatever clang and cc the host machine happens to have. That works, but every machine behaves differently, and cross-compiling depends on what the user installed. A jet cc that always works identically would be Jet's front door into every C and C++ estate.

This ballot picks how jet cc obtains its compiler. The choice sets the first-run experience, the install size everyone pays, whether two machines produce identical builds, and whether the wedge exists at all.
decisions.story: Marcus maintains a C codebase with a Makefile that predates him. His CI cross-builds four platforms with four fragile container images. He hears one tool can replace all four with CC=jet cc. If the first try works identically on his laptop and in CI, Jet has a champion inside his company.
decisions.inWild:
# unmodified upstream project, cross-built from an x86 Linux laptop:
$ CC="jet cc -target aarch64-linux-gnu" make
$ CC="jet cc -target x86_64-windows-gnu" make

# CI runs the same two lines and produces byte-identical artifacts.

options.name: Bundle clang, lld, and sysroots inside the Jet install
options.detail: Every Jet install carries a complete C compiler and target sysroots, the way Zig does. jet cc works instantly and offline on a fresh machine. Every user pays the download and disk weight even if they never compile C, and the C toolchain can only update when Jet itself ships a release.
options.code:
$ curl -L jet.dev/install | sh   # one large download, everything inside
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello         # works offline immediately

options.name: Jetpack store provisions a pinned toolchain on first use
options.detail: jet cc looks and behaves exactly like option A, but the compiler and sysroots arrive through Jet's own package store the first time they are needed. Every machine gets the identical pinned toolchain, so builds reproduce everywhere. Air-gapped sites preload it with the store's offline bundles. The base Jet install stays small.
options.technical: Toolchain and per-target sysroots become ordinary content-addressed store packages, riding the same provisioning that already fetches nixpkgs C dependencies (CFFI.rs). Offline staging uses the #957 bundle lanes. Keeps compiler seams dependency-free (I6) and one provisioning mechanism (I8).
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello
  fetching toolchain clang-19.1 (pinned)...   # first use only
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello                     # instant from then on

options.name: Wrap the host toolchain only
options.detail: jet cc translates flags and shells out to whatever clang or gcc the machine has. Nothing to download. Two machines can produce different binaries from the same source, cross-compiling works only if the host happens to have the right pieces, and works-on-my-machine failures return.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello
  # uses /usr/bin/cc — whatever version this machine has
$ ssh ci 'jet cc hello.c -o hello'
  # different cc, different binary, maybe different bugs

options.name: No jet cc
options.detail: C compilation stays internal to Jet's FFI bridges. C estates get call-in interop but no reason to adopt Jet's toolchain first. The adoption wedge this program exists for is abandoned.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c
  error: unknown command "cc"

comparisons.note: Bundles clang, lld, and multiple libcs in one tarball; instant and offline, at the cost of a large install for everyone.
Store-provisioned pinned toolchains; byte-reproducible builds, first use fetches from a cache.
comparisons.code: $ nix develop  # brings the exact pinned gcc/clang

comparisons.note: Downloads toolchains and targets on demand; small base install, per-target additions.

recommendation.why: The experience matches the Zig model from the second invocation onward, and the first invocation is one visible, pinned fetch. Every machine gets bit-identical toolchains — the reproducibility story enterprises audit for. The base install stays small for users who never compile C, and toolchain updates ship on their own schedule. It reuses the store that already provisions C dependencies, keeping one mechanism and the compiler seam dependency-free.

whyNot.reason: Every Jet user pays hundreds of megabytes for a C compiler most never invoke, and a clang security fix must wait for a Jet release.
Host toolchains differ per machine, so the one promise that wins C estates — identical builds everywhere — is broken on day one.
Forfeits the toolchain-first adoption path entirely; C teams get nothing to adopt before the language.

recommendation.tradeoff: The very first jet cc on a fresh machine needs the network or a preloaded offline bundle. Fully air-gapped sites must stage the toolchain bundle in advance.

decisions.title: Migration tier map: which languages get source importers
decisions.gist: Which foreign languages get automatic source conversion into Jet, and which get an explicit call-in-only verdict.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has three ways to meet a foreign codebase. A binder lets Jet call the foreign code where it stands. An overlay replaces one foreign library with a Jet package that must prove identical behavior first. An importer converts foreign source files into editable Jet source with TODO markers, so the team maintains Jet from then on.

The importer contract is already ratified (D-MIGRATE-SRC1): jet import must produce honest, editable Jet, verified by differential tests against the original. Python is the first proof. No other language has a ruling yet.

Conversion quality depends on the source language. Managed languages such as Java or TypeScript have garbage collection and no pointer arithmetic, so their meaning maps cleanly onto Jet's safe surface. C++ has templates, preprocessor macros, and undefined behavior. Faithful conversion of C++ tends to produce machine-shaped output no human wants to maintain.

This ballot decides the wave: which languages get importers, and which get a stated binder-or-overlay-only verdict. Enterprise teams then know the transition story for every pile of code they own.
decisions.story: Elena is an engineering director with 2.3 million lines of Java and 400k lines of C++. Her board approved a five-year modernization. She will only pick Jet if she can show a credible, named path for both piles — even if the two paths differ.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet import java services/pricing/src/main/java
  wrote 214 files under pricing-jet/ (37 TODO markers)
  differential: 1,892/1,892 behavior tests match

$ jet import cpp engine/
  error: C++ has no source importer.
  fix: call it in place instead — use cpp.engine

options.name: Importers for Java, C#, TypeScript/JavaScript, Go, Python; binder-plus-overlay verdict for C and C++
options.detail: The five importer languages cover most enterprise line counts, and each converts into Jet a human would keep. C and C++ get an honest, documented verdict: coexist through the binder, replace module by module by hand, with overlays proving each replacement. No language is left without a named story.
options.code:
$ jet import java src/     # editable Jet + TODOs
$ jet import csharp src/   # editable Jet + TODOs
$ jet import cpp src/
  error: C++ has no source importer.
  fix: use cpp.engine — coexist, then replace by module

options.name: Importers only for scripting languages (TypeScript/JavaScript, Python)
options.detail: Dynamic scripting code converts most cleanly, so only those importers ship. Java, C#, Go, and C++ teams get binders only. The largest enterprise estates — Java and C# — have no conversion story, so a director like Elena cannot present a full modernization plan built on Jet.
options.code:
$ jet import ts web/       # works
$ jet import java src/
  error: Java has no source importer.

options.name: Importers for everything, including a C++ subset
options.detail: Every language gets an importer, with C++ limited to a defined subset. The C++ output would be machine-shaped where templates, macros, or undefined behavior appear, breaking the ratified promise that imported code is editable Jet a team can own. First impressions in the hardest estates would be of generated sludge.

options.name: Stop at Python; every other language is binder-only
options.detail: Only the already-planned Python importer ships. All other languages coexist through binders indefinitely. One scripting importer cannot carry an enterprise migration story; it reads as a demo, not a path, and the tier map this program promises never exists.
options.code:
$ jet import py scripts/   # works
$ jet import java src/
  error: Java has no source importer.

comparisons.note: Won the Java world with a one-click Java-to-Kotlin converter producing idiomatic, editable output — conversion quality drove adoption.
comparisons.code: // IntelliJ: Code > Convert Java File to Kotlin File

comparisons.note: Won JavaScript by making every .js file already-valid input — migration was per-file and gradual.
Transpiles C to Rust but the output is unsafe, machine-shaped Rust that teams struggle to own — the cautionary case for option C.

recommendation.why: It gives every enterprise estate a named, truthful story. The five importer languages convert into Jet a human would keep, which is what makes conversion feel magical rather than burdensome. C++ gets honesty instead of silence: coexist through the binder, replace by hand behind overlay proof. Elena can put the whole plan on one slide.

whyNot.reason: Java and C# are the largest enterprise estates; leaving them binder-only concedes exactly the market this program targets.
A C++ importer would emit unreadable machine-shaped Jet, violating the ratified editable-output contract and poisoning first impressions in the hardest estates.
One scripting importer cannot carry an enterprise migration story; it reads as a demo, not a path.

recommendation.tradeoff: C++ teams are told plainly that conversion is manual behind the binder, and the five importer tracks land over time rather than all at once — some estates wait for theirs.

decisions.title: Command spelling for Jet's C compiler front end
decisions.gist: What the user types to invoke Jet's C compiler: a jet subcommand, a single-word program, both as one mechanism, or a namespaced command.
decisions.lesson:
Jet will ship a built-in C compiler front end (ratified D-ADOPT-CC1=B). Build systems find a C compiler through the CC variable or an explicit compiler path. Whatever spelling Jet picks becomes the string pasted into Makefiles, CMake caches, and CI files across every estate the wedge targets.

There is one practical trap. CC usually holds a single program name. A value with a space, like "jet cc", works in plain make but confuses some tools. Those tools treat the whole string as one file name, cannot find a program by that name, and abort. Zig users hit exactly this with CC="zig cc" and work around it with tiny wrapper scripts in every affected repository.

The spelling therefore decides the first five minutes of adoption on legacy build systems. This ballot picks it.
decisions.story: Marcus, from the toolchain card, pastes CC="jet cc" into his CMake invocation. CMake stores it as a single compiler path, finds no program literally named "jet cc", and aborts. His first five minutes with Jet become a workaround hunt instead of a build.
decisions.inWild:
$ CC="jet cc" make
  # works — make splits the words

$ cmake -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER="jet cc" ..
  CMake Error: Could not find compiler "jet cc"
  # the space is treated as part of one program name

options.name: jet cc / jet c++ subcommands plus jet-cc / jet-c++ alias binaries
options.detail: One mechanism with two spellings. Humans and docs use the subcommand, matching the zig habit and keeping one front door under jet help. Tools that require a bare program name get the installed single-word alias, so CC=jet-cc pastes safely into every build system on the first try. The alias simply re-enters the subcommand — same code path, same behavior, forever.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello        # humans, docs, muscle memory
$ CC=jet-cc cmake ..              # single word — every tool accepts it
# jet-cc re-executes 'jet cc' — one mechanism, two spellings

options.name: Subcommands only: jet cc / jet c++
options.detail: The cleanest single spelling and the exact zig shape. Every space-hostile tool then needs a user-written wrapper script, so the worst first-run experience lands on precisely the legacy build systems this wedge exists to win.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello
$ cat > cc-wrap.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
exec jet cc "$@"
EOF
# every affected repo re-invents this wrapper

options.name: Standalone binaries only: jetcc / jetc++
options.detail: A single word everywhere, so CC always pastes safely. But the compiler leaves Jet's front door. jet help does not list it, typing jet cc gets an error, and the product surface splits into a second command family.
options.code:
$ jetcc hello.c -o hello
$ jet cc hello.c
  error: unknown command "cc"   # muscle memory from zig breaks

options.name: Namespaced: jet toolchain cc
options.detail: Explicit and greppable, and it groups future toolchain verbs under one noun. Three words in CC fail in even more tools than two, and the ceremony reads as policy jargon to the beginner pass. Drop-in adoption is defeated at the paste.
options.code:
$ CC="jet toolchain cc" make
  # breaks wherever two words already broke, plus more

comparisons.note: Subcommand only; CC="zig cc" breakage is a recurring community issue solved per-project with wrapper scripts.
comparisons.code: $ CC="zig cc" cmake ..   # fails in tools that want one word

comparisons.note: A standalone single-word binary designed to be dropped into CC — the paste-safe pattern option A's alias copies.
Everything is a go subcommand; go tool namespaces the long tail — precedent for option D's grouping.

recommendation.why: Drop-in adoption is the entire point of jet cc, so the spelling must survive every legacy tool's CC handling on the first paste. The subcommand keeps one front door and matches zig muscle memory; the single-word alias makes CC=jet-cc safe everywhere. Both spell one mechanism, which I8 permits as flexible spelling of a single canonical path.

whyNot.reason: Space-hostile tools greet exactly the target audience with a failure, and every affected repo hand-writes the wrapper Jet declined to ship.
The compiler leaves the jet front door: jet help discovery and zig-trained muscle memory both miss it, splitting the product surface.
Three words in CC fail in more tools than two, and the ceremony burdens the beginner paste for no safety gain.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two spellings of one tool must stay behavior-identical forever, and installers must manage the extra alias binaries on PATH.

decisions.title: In-place adoption: can jetos convert a running Linux install, and must it be reversible?
decisions.gist: Whether jetos can take over an existing Linux system in place, and whether that conversion must be undoable.
decisions.lesson: Bedrock Linux wins users by installing onto the system they already run. No reinstall, no spare disk. But its conversion is one way: the installer makes the user type "Not reversible!". jetos already has generations, activation proof, and rollback. Those tools could make an in-place conversion safe to undo. Today jetos installs only from ISO media, plus a config importer for NixOS systems.
decisions.story: Maya runs Ubuntu on her only laptop. She wants jetos, but she cannot risk a working machine or spend a weekend reinstalling. She would switch tonight if one command converted her system and one command promised to give Ubuntu back.
decisions.inWild:
# Bedrock Linux today: adoption by hijack, one way
$ sh bedrock-linux-0.7.30-x86_64.sh --hijack
* Please type "Not reversible!" to confirm: Not reversible!
* Hijack complete. Reboot to finish.

# The question for jetos: same on-ramp, but with a way back?
$ jet os takeover laptop
plan: capture current Ubuntu as generation 0, prove, then switch
$ jet os rollback 0
restored: the exact Ubuntu install from before takeover

options.name: Reversible takeover
options.detail: jetos converts the running system in place. The current install is captured as generation 0. The switch happens only after the normal activation proof passes. One rollback command restores the original system exactly. Gain: the easiest adoption path any OS offers, and safer than Bedrock's. Loss: the original system stays on disk until the user deletes it, so disk use roughly doubles at first.
options.technical: Capture: the host root becomes a preserved, bootable generation-0 entry (own kernel, initrd, and boot entry) under hangar management. Refusal: hosts whose disk layout cannot hold two bootable roots get a diagnostic, not a best-effort attempt. Proof: the same activation-proof gate as jet os switch. Rollback: restores the generation-0 boot entry and root as the default.
options.code:
$ jet os takeover laptop
checking host: disk ok, bootloader ok, space ok
capturing current system as generation 0 ("ubuntu-2026-08-04")
building jetos system for host laptop
proof: activation plan verified
switch complete — reboot into jetos, or `jet os rollback 0` any time

$ jet os rollback 0
default boot restored: generation 0 ("ubuntu-2026-08-04")

options.name: Media install and importer only (today's path)
options.detail: No in-place conversion. Users install jetos from ISO media onto a disk they choose. The importer converts an existing NixOS config for them. Gain: jetos never touches a running system, so there is no destructive surface at all. Loss: anyone whose only machine runs another distro must back up, wipe, and reinstall — the biggest group of potential users keeps the highest barrier.
options.technical: Status quo. Install surface stays the hybrid ISO installer with GPT/ESP/ext4/Limine. Migration stays config-level via the semantic importer (#415).
options.code:
$ jet os image build laptop --iso
wrote jetos-laptop.iso
# user writes USB media, backs up /home, reboots, wipes the disk,
# installs, then restores files by hand

options.name: One-way takeover (Bedrock's shape)
options.detail: Convert in place without capturing the old system. Smallest disk cost and the fastest conversion. Loss: the machine has no way back. A failed or regretted conversion means a reinstall from media. This is the exact flaw Bedrock documents about itself.
options.technical: Host root is rewritten into the jetos layout directly. No generation-0 entry exists; rollback history starts at the first jetos generation.
options.code:
$ jet os takeover laptop --no-capture
WARNING: this conversion cannot be undone
type "not reversible" to continue: not reversible
switch complete

options.name: Preview double, then media install
options.detail: jetos never converts the live disk. Instead it builds a virtual machine image of "this machine as jetos" from the imported config, so the user can try their converted system safely. Gain: zero risk to the host. Loss: the journey still ends in a full media reinstall, and a virtual preview can hide real hardware problems like Wi-Fi and graphics drivers.
options.technical: Reuses the importer plus the existing QEMU proof harness to boot a preview guest from the user's captured facts. The live disk is never written.
options.code:
$ jet os preview laptop --from-host
built preview VM from this machine's imported config
booting QEMU guest... (your apps, users, and services, as jetos)
# to adopt for real: jet os image build laptop --iso, then reinstall

comparisons.note: The hijack installer converts the running distro in place and is permanently one way. It is the project's main adoption path and its most criticized risk.
comparisons.code:
$ sh bedrock-installer.sh --hijack
* Please type "Not reversible!" to confirm:

comparisons.note: Has no official in-place conversion. The community nixos-infect script overwrites a cloud host one way, with no capture and no rollback to the old distro.
comparisons.code:
$ curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/elitak/nixos-infect/... | bash
# old distro is destroyed; recovery is a provider reimage

recommendation.why: A reversible takeover turns machinery jetos already owns — generations, activation proof, rollback — into the safest adoption path in the field. It reaches people on their only machine, which is most people, and it keeps the rollback promise that defines jetos.

whyNot.reason: Media-only keeps the highest barrier for the largest group: people with one machine and no spare disk stay locked out.
A one-way conversion breaks the rollback promise and risks a working machine, repeating the exact flaw Bedrock documents about itself.
A preview still ends in a wipe-and-reinstall, so the adoption barrier it was meant to remove stays in place.

recommendation.tradeoff: Generation 0 keeps the old system on disk, roughly doubling use until the user deletes it. Hosts with layouts that cannot hold two bootable roots are refused and must use media install.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared reversible takeover, media-only, one-way takeover, and a virtual preview. It recommended reversible takeover because it opens the largest adoption path without breaking the rollback promise.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested dual-boot side-install, a container trial, and a persistent live-USB trial. All three fold into media install or the preview option because none converts the running system.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined preview with takeover: the takeover flow can boot a preview guest from the same generation-0 capture before switching. This strengthened option A instead of adding a fifth option.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened media-only with the importer story and gave one-way takeover an explicit consent gate. Media-only still excludes single-machine users; one-way still cannot restore the host.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the capture with encrypted disks, unusual bootloaders, low disk space, and secrets inside the preserved root. Option A now refuses unsupported layouts with a diagnostic and documents what generation 0 contains, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Runtime provenance: how a user asks what put a file, command, or process on their system
decisions.gist: Which surface answers "what package, source, and generation put this file, command, or process here?"
decisions.lesson: On Bedrock Linux every file and process has an owner the user can query with one command, brl which. Reviewers single it out as what makes a mixed system understandable. jetos builds systems from two package universes — native hangar packages and imported Nix package closures — across generations. Studio already shows where a config value came from. Nothing yet answers the runtime side: who put this binary here, from which package, in which generation.
decisions.story: Ravi finds an unfamiliar binary on his PATH after a desktop swap. On Debian he would run dpkg -S. On jetos he wants one command that names the package, the universe it came from, and the generation that introduced it — before he decides whether to worry.
decisions.inWild:
$ which weird-tool
/run/current-system/sw/bin/weird-tool

# the question this ballot decides the spelling of:
$ <surface> /run/current-system/sw/bin/weird-tool
weird-tool 1.4.2 — package tools.weird-tool (hangar, native)
introduced: generation 41 ("desktop swap to niri", 2026-08-01)
declared by: system.laptop -> services.desktop.extras

options.name: Extend jet info
options.detail: jet info already answers "what is this?" for packages, and the owner ratified extending jet search and jet info for options search rather than minting a new verb. Teach jet info to accept files, commands, paths, and process IDs too. Gain: one question surface for everything, in the terminal and in scripts. Loss: jet info's help must stay simple while it learns three new target kinds.
options.technical: One provenance resolver maps artifact -> package -> universe (native or compat root) -> generation -> declaring option path. jet info and Studio both render that resolver's answer. Unowned targets (user files, runtime-created files) answer "not owned by any package" honestly.
options.code:
$ jet info weird-tool
$ jet info /run/current-system/sw/bin/weird-tool
$ jet info --pid 4312
weird-tool 1.4.2 — package tools.weird-tool (hangar, native)
introduced: generation 41 ("desktop swap to niri")
declared by: system.laptop -> services.desktop.extras

$ jet info ~/notes.txt
not owned by any package (user file in /home)

options.name: New verb: jet os which
options.detail: Mirror Bedrock's brl which as a dedicated jetos verb. Gain: a short, discoverable command whose name states the question. Loss: it mints a second lookup surface beside jet info, so users must learn which verb answers which kind of "what is this?" question.
options.technical: Same resolver as option A behind a separate verb under jet os. jet info keeps its package-only scope.
options.code:
$ jet os which weird-tool
tools.weird-tool (hangar, native), generation 41
$ jet os which --pid 4312
tools.weird-tool via service desktop-extras.service
$ jet info tools.weird-tool   # still needed for the full package view

options.name: Studio-only drill-down
options.detail: Provenance stays a Studio feature: click any installed file, app, or service to see its package, universe, and generation. No terminal surface. Gain: no new command-line spelling to ratify or document. Loss: scripts, remote shells, and terminal-first users get no answer at all, and the beginner in a broken graphical session loses the tool exactly when they need it.
options.technical: The resolver ships inside Studio's projection layer only. The CLI exposes nothing.
options.code:
# terminal user today, under option C:
$ jet info /run/current-system/sw/bin/weird-tool
error: jet info takes a package name
# answer exists only inside the Studio app

comparisons.note: brl which answers for a command, file, path, or process ID with one spelling. It is the model for the question, though Bedrock only names the providing stratum.
comparisons.code:
$ brl which apk
tut-alpine
$ brl which 1
debian

comparisons.note: dpkg -S and pacman -Qo map a file to its owning package, but say nothing about when it arrived or what configuration asked for it.
comparisons.code:
$ dpkg -S /usr/bin/vim
vim: /usr/bin/vim
$ pacman -Qo /usr/bin/vim
/usr/bin/vim is owned by vim 9.1-1

comparisons.note: Provenance exists but is expert-only: chained store queries that beginners never find.

recommendation.why: One question surface keeps the beginner story simple: point jet info at anything — a name, a file, a process — and it answers with package, universe, generation, and the declaring option. It follows the pattern the owner already ratified for options search (D-JOS-OPTIONSVERB1=B): extend jet search and jet info instead of minting verbs.

whyNot.reason: A second lookup verb splits one question across two spellings and contradicts the ratified extend-don't-mint pattern.
Studio-only leaves terminals, scripts, and remote sessions blind, and fails the user whose graphical session is the thing that broke.

recommendation.tradeoff: jet info grows file, path, and process targets, so its help text and docs must keep the plain name-lookup case front and center.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft mirrored the ratified options-search menu: extend jet info, mint a dedicated verb, or keep it Studio-only. It recommended extending jet info to keep one question surface.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested filesystem-level answers (ownership attributes on installed files) and a shell hook printing provenance on command-not-found. Both folded in as possible backends of the same surface, not separate owner choices.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review confirmed Studio and the command line should share one provenance resolver so both render identical facts. The ballot now names that shared resolver in every option's technical notes.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the dedicated verb with Bedrock's exact ergonomics and Studio-only with click-through from the app library. Each still narrows or splits the question surface.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked coverage with user files, runtime-created files, and files inside imported Nix closures. The surface now answers "not owned by any package" honestly and reports closure membership with its generation, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Post-switch health proof for jet deploy
decisions.gist: What must pass after a host switch before jet deploy treats that host as healthy.
decisions.lesson: A bad switch can lock you out of a remote machine. D-JOS-FLEETROLLOUT1 already requires health checks and rollback on fail. This choice defines the default health bar after switch, including whether Jet must prove it can still reach the host.
decisions.story: Olive deploys a change that breaks SSH. Without a strong default check, the host stays on the bad generation and she cannot fix it from her laptop.

options.name: Control reach plus declared health
options.detail: After switch, Jet must reconnect from the controller and run the host health checks you declared. Both must pass. Experts can turn off reconnect for planned SSH or network changes on the same rollout object. Gain: lockouts roll back by default. Loss: network changes need an explicit opt-out.
options.technical: Amends D-JOS-FLEETROLLOUT1 health meaning. Default health gate is controller reconnect confirm within timeout AND declared host health probes. Expert field e.g. rollout.controlPlaneConfirm: false or per-host override. Failed reconnect triggers the same rollback-and-stop path. Intentional SSH/IP/port changes require the opt-out in source and appear in proof.

options.name: Declared host health only
options.detail: After switch, only the host health checks you declared must pass. Jet does not require a fresh controller reconnect. Gain: SSH and IP changes are easier. Loss: a host can pass local checks while you can no longer reach it.
options.technical: Health gate is declared probes only (services, files, scripts). No mandatory post-switch controller reconnect. Rollback still runs when declared health fails.

options.name: Reconnect only
options.detail: After switch, Jet only proves it can reconnect. Declared service health is optional. Gain: strong lockout defense with a tiny default. Loss: a reachable host can still run a broken app until you add checks.
options.technical: Default gate is controller reconnect confirm only. Declared health probes remain available but are not required for success.

options.name: Opt-in reconnect confirm
options.detail: Default is declared host health only. Reconnect confirm is an expert flag you turn on. Gain: beginners face less friction on network edits. Loss: the safe lockout defense is off until someone remembers the flag.
options.technical: Default matches option B. Experts set rollout.controlPlaneConfirm: true (or magicRollback: true) to require reconnect.

comparisons.note: Magic rollback confirms the machine is still reachable after activation. You must disable it to change SSH, IP, or port on purpose.
comparisons.code:
# deploy-rs README
# magicRollback confirms post-activation connectivity
# disable for intentional SSH/IP/port changes

comparisons.note: Generated fleet scripts treat a remote health file as enough. That is weaker than reconnect proof and is not product closeout.

recommendation.why: Lockout is the costly failure for remote deploy. Reconnect plus declared health matches the safe default people expect from deploy-rs, and keeps expert opt-out on the same rollout object.

whyNot.reason: Local health can pass while the controller cannot reach the host, so Olive stays locked out.
A reachable host can still run a broken service if app health is optional by default.
The safe lockout defense stays off until someone turns a flag on, which fails the beginner magic bar.

recommendation.tradeoff: Planned SSH or network changes need an explicit opt-out in source. Accepted: that friction is cheaper than a silent lockout, and proof shows the opt-out.

reviewPasses.base: Compared reconnect-plus-health, health-only, reconnect-only, and opt-in reconnect. Recommended reconnect plus declared health with expert opt-out.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Also tested no post-switch gate and external watchdog only. Folded those into B and D because they drop first-party lockout defense.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Kept reconnect and declared health together as option A instead of a third hybrid row. Opt-out stays on the same rollout object.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B for network edits and D for explicit control. Both still leave lockout protection off by default.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked false reconnect success on a stale bastion path. Proof must bind controller identity and target host so a wrong hop cannot clear the gate.

decisions.title: Connect identity versus activation privilege
decisions.gist: How jet deploy separates the login used to reach a host from the privilege used to activate a generation.
decisions.lesson: D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1 already requires typed target and authority fields. Remote tools often log in as a normal admin user and activate as root. This choice sets the default split beginners get, and what must show in proof.
decisions.story: Kai deploys from CI to three servers. He wants SSH keys on a wheel user, not root login, and he still needs root to activate the system generation.

options.name: Split connect and activate by default
options.detail: Each target has a connect user and an activate user. The beginner default connects as a normal wheel user and activates as root. Root for both stays allowed when written. Gain: safer SSH defaults with clear proof. Loss: first setup must grant keys and passwordless privilege before the first deploy.
options.technical: Amends D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1 authority fields. Typed connectUser and activateUser (names may match existing surface). Default when omitted: connectUser=wheel-class deploy user policy, activateUser=root for system profiles. User-env profiles may activate as the owning user. Proof records both identities. Preflight fails closed if keys or privilege path are missing.

options.name: One user for both roles
options.detail: One user field covers SSH and activation. Beginners use root for both. Gain: fewer fields. Loss: root SSH becomes the easy path and weaker hosts are common.
options.technical: Single user field on deploy.target. Activation uses the same account as SSH. No first-class connect/activate split in the default surface.

options.name: Forbid root SSH
options.detail: Connect user must be non-root. Activation is always root for system profiles. Gain: strong SSH policy. Loss: labs and recovery hosts that need root SSH become second-class or blocked.
options.technical: Sema rejects connectUser == root. System activation always escalate to root through a declared privilege path.

options.name: SSH config owns identity
options.detail: Jet stores only the host label. OpenSSH config picks the user. Activation privilege stays implicit. Gain: familiar for operators. Loss: Jet cannot type-check or prove the full authority graph from source.
options.technical: Conflicts with D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1 proof-visible authority. Would reintroduce inventory outside Jet source.
options.code:
# ~/.ssh/config
Host web1
  User deploy

# Jet source has no connect/activate users
fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }

comparisons.note: Profiles set user for activation and sshUser for the SSH login. Docs recommend a wheel user for SSH and root for activation.
D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1 already requires typed target and privilege facts in source and proof. This ballot picks the beginner default shape.
comparisons.code:
# from D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1=A
# host target/authority fields are proof-visible

recommendation.why: Split identities match real remote deploy practice and keep root SSH optional. Beginners get a safer default while experts can still write root for both.

whyNot.reason: One user field pushes beginners toward root SSH and hides the privilege boundary.
A hard ban on root SSH blocks valid lab and recovery setups that Jet should still allow explicitly.
Authority outside Jet source breaks typed proof and conflicts with D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1.

recommendation.tradeoff: First deploy needs keys and a privilege path on the host. Accepted: that setup cost is the price of a safe default, and preflight names the missing piece.

reviewPasses.base: Compared split users, one user, forbid-root SSH, and SSH-config identity. Recommended split connect and activate with wheel-plus-root defaults.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Also tested sudo-only without typed activate user and agent-forwarding only. Folded those into A and D as incomplete authority graphs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Kept optional root-for-both inside A instead of a separate hybrid row, so one mechanism covers beginner and expert.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B for tiny fleets and C for hard policy shops. B still weakens SSH defaults; C over-blocks recovery hosts.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked missing NOPASSWD or key setup as silent hangs. Preflight must fail closed with a clear diagnostic before switch.

decisions.title: JetOS install trust without App Store gatekeeping
decisions.gist: How jetos stops malware while still letting people install and run software they choose or build.
decisions.lesson: Apple treats central review and signing locks as security. Those locks also block owner-built apps, peer share, plugins, and fast local tools. jetos already has generations, Flatpak policy, hangar hashes, and Studio risk gates. This choice sets the default trust law for installs. It must protect beginners and keep owner freedom. The same law covers any future jetos device class unless a later ballot changes it.
decisions.story: Maya builds a small drawing app on her jetos laptop and wants her friend to try it tonight. She also wants her parents' laptop to resist random malware from a download. She needs one system that allows her share and still protects the family machine.
decisions.inWild:
# Maya shares a local package with a friend (must work without Jet review):
$ jet pack ./doodle
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
# friend sees capability prompt, not a rejection

# Studio Apps install from catalog:
# Install "Music Player" -> sandboxed; Photos access needs an explicit grant

# After a bad install:
$ jet os generations rollback
# previous generation returns; provenance still names the package

options.name: Capability-first freedom
options.detail: Anyone may install software they choose or build. Third-party and foreign apps start with almost no power. The user grants files, network, devices, or agents later. Hangar hashes and optional publisher signatures feed trust UI. They never block an owner-built local install. Generations and rollback repair bad installs. There is no central review and no category ban.
options.technical: Default runtime policy for user apps and Flatpak refs is deny-by-default capabilities with explicit grants in Studio or Jet config. System hangar closures keep supply-chain integrity (hash, sign/verify, locks). Owner-local packages and jet run paths skip notarization. Catalog ranking may prefer signed publishers; ranking is not a hard gate. Family or enterprise lock modules may tighten policy as expert opt-in.
options.code:
# config.jet — beginner default stays free to install, tight to run
apps.flatpak.permissions.default: .Deny

# friend installs Maya's package
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
grant needed: Documents (read)
# after grant, app runs; no Jet notary step

options.name: Notarization gate
options.detail: Only packages signed by Jet-approved keys or a central notary may run. Unsigned code is blocked unless a hard developer mode is on. That blocks many casual malware installs. Owner-built and peer-shared software become second-class. This repeats the App Store shape jetos is trying not to copy.
options.technical: Hard gate at activation: signature required against a Jet trust root. Local unsigned installs fail closed outside developer mode. Catalog and peer share both hit the same gate.
options.code:
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
error: package is not notarized by Jet
hint: enable developer mode, or submit for review

options.name: Warn-only open install
options.detail: People may install and run anything with full host power. Unknown publishers only show warnings. Maximum freedom and simple plumbing. One hostile package can own the machine. Beginners get alerts instead of real limits.
options.technical: No default capability jail for GUI apps. Trust UI is advisory. Generations still roll back if the user notices damage in time.
options.code:
$ jet install ./free-game.jetpkg
warning: unknown publisher
# proceeds with full user powers

options.name: Curated beginners, free experts
options.detail: The default profile installs only from a curated catalog under sandbox rules. An expert profile unlocks free install. Safer default story. It teaches that real power lives in another mode. Beginners may never learn grants. The catalog risks becoming a soft App Store.
options.technical: Two named profiles in config. Beginner profile rejects non-catalog refs. Expert profile matches option A or C. Mode switch is explicit.
options.code:
profile: .Beginner
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
error: beginner profile allows catalog apps only
hint: switch profile to .Expert

options.name: Disposable VM per app
options.detail: Every GUI app runs in a disposable microVM with gated portals. Strong isolation for hostile binaries. High cost in battery, memory, and desktop fit. Terminal tools and light apps pay a heavy tax. Portal grants are still required, so this does not replace a capability model.
options.technical: App launch always goes through a microVM or equivalent strong boundary. Portals mediate files and devices. Native hangar system services stay outside this path.
options.code:
$ jet install music-player
# launches inside app-vm; Documents access via portal prompt

comparisons.note: Central review and signing locks block whole categories. Security and rent seeking stay hard to separate.
comparisons.code: # no peer install path without Apple approval

comparisons.note: Apps can ship widely. Permissions start tight. Users grant more later. Closest open model to option A.
Hardened Android with stronger sandbox defaults and user control. Still a phone OS with store pressure around it.
comparisons.code: # install unknown apps allowed; sandbox remains

comparisons.note: Bad system changes roll back. Provenance and immutability help recovery. They do not replace app capability grants.

recommendation.why: Capability-first freedom matches jetos goals. Beginners get real limits by default. Owners can build and share without Jet review. Hangar identity, Studio risk gates, and generations already cover supply chain and recovery. The store stays a discovery surface, not a notary.

whyNot.reason: A notarization gate recreates App Store lock-in and blocks the kid-builds-and-shares story.
Warnings without capability limits leave beginners open to full-host malware.
A beginner-only catalog becomes a soft store and hides grants behind an expert mode.
Always-on microVMs add heavy cost and still need the same grant model for portals.

recommendation.tradeoff: Users can approve too many grants. Studio risk classes and clear prompts must keep that rare. Expert family locks can tighten later without changing the default.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared capability defaults, notarization, warn-only installs, split beginner profiles, and per-app VMs. It recommended capability-first freedom.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested mandatory antivirus scanning and web-of-trust-only installs. Those folded into identity signals and expert policy under option A, not separate defaults.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept option A and added catalog ranking by signatures, generation rollback, and optional family locks. Those stay helpers, not hard gates.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened notarization with fast local developer mode and strengthened curated beginners with one-click expert escape. Each still blocks or hides owner freedom.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested peer-share malware, users who grant everything, and signed-but-hostile publishers. Sandbox defaults, rollback, provenance, and honest trust UI repair those cases, so option A remains.

decisions.title: One text for the jetos boot default: the record and the code disagree
decisions.gist: Which bootloader and kernel a fresh jetos machine starts with.
decisions.lesson: One ratified decision now has two texts. The board record for D-JOS-BOOTKERNEL1=A reads systemd-boot with a Linux long-term kernel. The syntax record, the jetos plan, and the shipped code all read Limine with the CachyOS kernel. A second ratified decision from the same day, D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A, carries a first-party CachyOS kernel package, which the long-term kernel text does not allow. Three boot cards are queued against the Limine text. One owner line ends the split.
decisions.story: Sam installs jetos on a spare laptop. The machine must boot, roll back to the last generation, and show a menu that names each one. Sam does not choose a bootloader. Jet does, once, and every later card builds on that answer.

options.name: systemd-boot with the long-term kernel
options.detail: The default boot path is systemd-boot and the kernel is the Linux long-term release. This is what the ratified board record says today. It is the quiet, conservative answer, and it matches what most declarative Linux systems ship. The cost is that three queued cards, the syntax record, the jetos plan and the shipped code all say something else, so all of them change.
options.technical: Keeps the D-JOS-BOOTKERNEL1=A record as stored. Requires amending docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:4501, docs/plans/epoch-7/native-jetos.md, and the shipped jetos boot code, and reworking cards #909, #409 and #910. D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A must also be reopened, because it ratifies a first-party CachyOS kernel package.

options.name: Limine with the CachyOS kernel
options.detail: The default boot path is Limine and the kernel is the CachyOS package. This is what the syntax record, the plan and the code already say, and it is what the sibling kernel decision from the same day ratifies. It also gives jetos a faster desktop kernel by default. The cost is that the stored decision text is wrong today and must be corrected so one text exists.
options.technical: Amends the D-JOS-BOOTKERNEL1 record to match its own rendered form at docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:4501. Agrees with D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A, the first-party CachyOS kernel package with exact source, config, patches and hashes. Cards #909, #409 and #910 proceed as written. Expert override of the kernel package and boot entry fields is unchanged either way.

comparisons.note: Ships systemd-boot as the modern default and a long-term kernel, with GRUB still available.
Ships Limine as an option beside its own tuned kernel, which is the pairing option B names.
Uses GRUB2 with boot loader specification entries, so menu entries are files rather than a generated script.

recommendation.why: It is the answer already written into the syntax record, the plan and the shipped code, and the only one that agrees with D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A from the same day. Choosing it corrects one stored sentence. Choosing the other rewrites four places and reopens a second ratified decision.

whyNot.reason: It contradicts D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A, which ratifies a first-party CachyOS kernel package on the same day and the same card. It also forces a rewrite of the spec, the plan, the code and three queued cards.

recommendation.tradeoff: A tuned desktop kernel carries more patches than a long-term release, so jetos owns more upstream tracking. That is accepted because the kernel package is first-party and already ratified with exact source and hashes.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft set the stored decision text against the rendered spec text and recommended the rendered form, because the code and the sibling kernel decision both agree with it.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a third answer, GRUB, and a fourth, no default with an install-time prompt. Both were dropped: no card, plan or line of code asks for either, and a prompt moves a settled choice onto the beginner.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review asked whether the loader and the kernel can be decided apart. They can, but nothing on the board wants that split, so the menu stays two coherent pairings.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review made the conservative answer as strong as it can be. A long-term kernel with systemd-boot is the least surprising pairing for a declarative system, and NixOS ships it.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked whether the stored record is right and the spec is the error. It could be, which is exactly why this needs an owner line rather than an agent judgement, and the ballot names both texts.

decisions.title: wasm32-wasi as a user-facing server target
decisions.gist: Whether `jet build` gains a server-side WebAssembly target.
decisions.lesson: WebAssembly (wasm) is a portable binary format. WASI is the system interface that lets a wasm program run outside a browser. Some hosting platforms run only wasm, because it starts fast and the host can sandbox it. Today `jet build --target=wasm32-wasip1` fails with E3302, because Jet ships no standard library for that target. Jet's browser target (`--target=web`) is separate and stays. This choice decides whether Jet promises a server wasm target, records a no, or routes wasm work through plugins.
decisions.story: Priya runs a platform team. Her company hosts tenant code on a wasmtime fleet, where every handler is one wasm module. She likes Jet and wants tenants to write handlers in it. She copies the build command from her platform docs and gets E3302. She must now tell her tenants whether Jet will ever build for this platform.
decisions.inWild:
# Priya follows her platform's docs:
$ jet build handler.jet --target=wasm32-wasip1
Error E3302: Target `wasm32-wasip1` is not available.
 Why: rustc doesn't have the standard library for this target compiled in, or the target triple is not recognised.
 Fix: Run `jet self doctor --target=wasm32-wasip1` to see what's missing, or `rustup target add wasm32-wasip1` to install it.

# She retries with a space instead of `=` (open defect, card #1899):
$ jet build handler.jet --target wasm32-wasip1
built: build/handler        # native binary — the flag was silently ignored

# Her wasm host then rejects build/handler: not a wasm module.

options.name: Full supported server target (wasm32-wasip2)
options.detail: Jet ships wasm32-wasip2 as a real server target: stdlib port, CI lane, and full tier parity (I9). Preview 2 carries wasi-sockets, so a Jet server can actually listen and serve, which preview 1 could not. The gain is every platform that deploys wasm server-side becomes a Jet platform. The cost is a stdlib port and a permanent CI lane, paid up front.
