### Read the names, indexes and noncopyable boundary

`T.reflect()` asks for T's compile-time type description.

Under A/C, the proposed `.cases` projection adds its complete case rows.

A row's `.name` is its declared case name.

A payload `Type` descriptor's `.name` is its displayed type label: the worked types here are exactly String, Int and Bool.

`Value.type_name()` returns that captured value's type label as a String; `Value.display()` returns its displayed value.

Thus a String payload holding hello contributes `value:String=hello`; 7 contributes `value:Int=7`; Flag(true) contributes `value:Bool=true`.

Names are display labels, not a substitute for checking type identity.

This explains the operations already used by these workloads, not a second type-name API.

Indexes start at zero: `[0]` selects the first item.

In the private-data witness, Outer's Item case has one field containing Inner.

Its first projection gives `inner`.

Inner's Data case has one field containing Payload; its first projection gives `payload`.

Payload's first struct field is `text`, whose saved value displays secret.

In the mutation witness, State's first field is `inner`; Inner's first field is `texts`.

The two `.fields()[0].value()` steps therefore reach the saved list.

`state.inner.texts[0]` addresses the first element of the original list, not that saved list.

The last witness's first Text field is the saved or newly captured string.

These fixed-shape examples do not replace the generic inspector's loops.

A callback supplies a concrete noncopyable part, separate from Shared's aliasing issue:

```jet
use core.reflect as reflect
enum CallbackMessage {
    Idle
    Work(fn(Int) Int)
    impl Display { fn display(self) String -> "CallbackMessage" }
}
fn visit(message: ^CallbackMessage) Int -> if message == {
    .Idle -> 0
    .Work(callback) -> callback(7)
}
fn refused(message: CallbackMessage) {
    saved :: reflect.of(message)
}
fn run() {
    for_visit :: CallbackMessage.Work((n: Int) -> (n + 1))
    print(visit(^for_visit))
    for_capture :: CallbackMessage.Work((n: Int) -> (n + 1))
    refused(for_capture)
}
```

Expected under A: source checking refuses `reflect.of(message)`; the complete program runs nothing.

NOT RUN.

The root has Display, but Work contains a function value.

Ordinary copying requires duplicable parts, and a function value is not duplicable.

Even Idle cannot bypass this static type-graph check.

The move marker ^ gives the visitor ownership; if message == inspects that owned case and binds its callback without copying it.

The caller must not reuse for_visit.

A separate for_capture value isolates the refused capture.

Remove refused and its call to run only the ordinary visitor; its intended result is 8 under every option.

Replacing Work's callback with an ordinary Int, and adjusting construction and the visitor to that Int, removes this noncopyable part.

A user-defined Clone that invents a replacement callback would not prove an ordinary value copy of the captured callback; the same static eligibility check still applies.

Source grounding, not a new execution: `tests/ui/copy_verb_not_cloneable.jet` uses the same `(n: Int) -> (n + 1)` callback and refuses `~f`; its retained E0211 snapshot explains duplicable parts. `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Reflect.rs` defines Value.type_name and Value.display. decisions.title: Shared lifecycle operations without a universal runtime
decisions.gist: Should lifecycle integrations reuse existing operations instead of defining another general runtime?
decisions.lesson: A lifecycle says how work starts, survives an update, and stops. The captured interpreter backend repeats registration work in run, hot_swap and restart. Sharing that setup does not make a task durable or a job merely local. The example shows the distinction between preserving compatible live state and starting a new process; both options must retain it.
decisions.story: Kai adds a long-running integration. Cancellation, waiting, failure reporting, and identity should reuse existing machinery rather than introduce another scheduler or supervisor.
decisions.inWild:
import asyncio
async def work():
    return 42
async def main():
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:
        task = group.create_task(work())
    print(task.result())
asyncio.run(main())
Source-composed TaskGroup example. Python documents waiting for child tasks at context exit. This does not prove persistent jobs or Jet runtime parity. https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html#task-groups
decisions.detail:
No new type, public method, executor, resource category or I9 exception is authorized. Domain-specific event loops and foreign runtime adapters may remain necessary; reuse means common semantic operations, not pretending all hosts have the same execution model. Durability, cancellation, retry, acknowledgment and capability authority must remain observable. No exactly-once external side-effect guarantee is implied.

Run/hot-swap/restart retention and reset transitions.
Cancellation, child failure, teardown and repeated initialization without stale registrations.

Contribution or failure trial (proposed acceptance, not an observed run):

A: Contributor trial: add one required interpreter host binding. Shared setup installs it for run, hot-swap and restart. The existing per-mode reset/retention rules remain separate.

decisions.title: Require explicit executable entries in ordinary files
decisions.gist: Should ordinary files require an explicit run entry?
decisions.lesson: An entry is the function that starts a program. Jet currently wraps loose file statements in an implicit run function. This choice removes that file shortcut. Interactive cells still receive a wrapper, and libraries still need no entry.
decisions.story: Mira moves a small script into an application. She wants to see where execution starts without discovering hidden startup work.
decisions.detail:
Owner-selected contract awaiting formal Tower ratification. Related historical work: #1627 and #3122. No compiler work or runtime verification was performed during preparation.

Beginner review prompted explicit file-role, initializer, safe-fix, typed-entry, and export explanations. No runtime result is claimed from those illustrative examples. Entry source forms are grounded in examples/features/cli/typed_entry_args.jet and examples/features/comptime/comptime_block.jet.

Fresh review findings were retained. The author resolved each through the contract and linked card criteria. Review metadata describes that sequence; it does not claim an independent rerun or runtime proof.

options.name: Explicit files, implicit interactive cells
options.detail:
Ordinary application targets declare an existing explicit application entry. Existing build/dev/test override-only sources retain their own entry roles. Library compilation, imports, and test discovery do not require an entry. Loose statements in any ordinary source are errors, not ignored code. A runtime top-level initializer is rejected; the author must move its work into a function.

REPL submissions and notebook cells remain interactive inputs, not ordinary files. Their host supplies the entry internally. An ordinary-source executable export needs a legal explicit entry. Refuse unsafe wrapping or a mixed-entry export rather than guessing. Declaration-only exports need no wrapper.
options.technical:
The interview selects this amendment. Amend D-ENTRY-SCRIPT1, D-ENTRY-ORDER1, and run-specific D-CMDOVERRIDE1 wording. Existing explicit entry forms keep their signature, visibility, multiplicity, and binding rules. Basic forms are fn run() and fn run(args: T), where T is a #CLI type. Do not invent a second entry or change typed argument parsing.

A selected application target needs its resolved source-declared application entry. A declaration-only library can be compiled or imported without one. Test discovery runs tests without a dummy application entry. Trying to execute a library as an application requires an entry; the filename alone does not change its role.

Compile-time work finishes while the compiler builds the program, before launch. Existing explicit compile-time definitions remain valid:

```jet
@answer :: 1 + 1
fn run() { print(@answer) }
```

Runtime initialization cannot remain hidden at file scope. This is rejected rather than silently moved:

```jet
use core.testing as testing
root :: testing.temp_dir("demo")
fn run() { print(root) }
```

The author can move that initialization into run when only run uses it. If another function refers to root, blindly moving the binding would break its scope. The automatic fix must refuse that relocation and explain that the value must be passed explicitly or initialized inside a suitable function.

For the simple loose hello program, jet fix hello.jet offers the existing source-edit workflow and produces the fn run() example shown in option A. Preserve statement order, declarations, comments, captures, return behavior, and source locations. Register exact what/why/fix diagnostics and snapshots. Never convert a backend rejection into a user error.

A cell containing print("hello") still runs directly. The host creates its entry internally; users do not edit that wrapper. Exporting executable ordinary source writes fn run() { print("hello") }. Exporting only declarations writes those declarations without a dummy entry. No notebook visual or teaching-path redesign is included.

Remove ordinary-file script lowering and use the canonical explicit-entry path internally. Migrate all callers, examples, generated fixtures, tests, format/LSP projections, and live explanations. Ahead-of-time binaries, run/dev, the interpreter, and applicable web execution preserve the same meaning. These examples isolate entry behavior; effect permission remains a separate requirement.

Command roles remain distinct. jet run and a stock application-launch path require an explicit application entry: fn run or an existing checked metadata-selected callable. jet build compiles its selected output or invokes its existing explicit build override. Libraries need no run. Override-only @build.jet remains valid.

jet dev invokes its selected explicit dev override; override-only @dev.jet needs no dummy run. Otherwise stock dev launches the explicit application entry. jet test invokes its explicit test override or stock test discovery; neither requires a dummy run. Preserve absent-override defaults. Only fn build with its existing BuildContext signature is build-only.

Wrapping fixes inspect checked command and import roles. Never synthesize an entry in library, imported, or test-only sources if that changes selection or multiplicity. If app.jet imports loose helper.jet, do not add a second fn run to the helper. Refuse that automatic edit and explain how to use an explicitly called function.

Interactive execution preserves existing persistent session scope. A host entry must not turn cross-cell bindings into discarded function locals. Prove a binding created in one submission and mutated in the next, imported/declaration visibility, move/borrow state, failures, and reruns. Reuse existing session storage and checked semantics, not a second runtime model.

Declaration-only export preserves existing explicit entries. Executable export without a conflicting entry emits one legal wrapper when meaning is preserved. A notebook mixing an existing run and separately executed cells refuses automatic ordinary-source export rather than guessing a merge. It changes no output file and explains how to consolidate one entry first. Never silently produce a lossy export.

Tier proof observes actual execution identity. Exercise AOT output, normal run/dev, forced interpreter, and existing run_jit_once/dev_iteration JIT paths. Require Cranelift evidence where applicable; interpreter fallback cannot pass a JIT row. Keep applicable web proof separately identified.

options.detail: Keep D-ENTRY-SCRIPT1 and D-ENTRY-ORDER1 unchanged. Loose file statements execute in source order within the generated run body. An explicit run conflicts with that body. Improve teaching without changing the boundary. This is the rejected comparison option, not the selected contract.
options.technical: This is the existing alternative, not the owner recommendation. Imported scripts retain their current restrictions and explicit run remains optional for scripts.

decisions.title: Use project policy automatically and trust one launch explicitly
decisions.gist: How should project policy and trusted launches approve effects?
decisions.lesson: Effects are actions such as waiting or reading files. Metadata is project information in package {} or package.jet. Its policy lists allowed and denied effects. Apply that policy automatically. --trust and -T trust only this launch. Trust once means the same. Explicit denies and language safety still win.
decisions.story: Mira wrote a local script and wants it to run without repeated questions. Her team still needs checked project policy and an audit trail.
decisions.inWild:
deno run --allow-read=./data main.ts
deno run --allow-all main.ts
# Jet does not copy the safety bypass.
# Deno has scoped grants and an allow-all escape. Jet keeps explicit denies binding. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/
decisions.detail:
Owner-selected amendment to D-RIGHTS-CLI1 and application prompting, not an I1 safety exception. Current evidence: Source/main.rs, Source/CmdCompile.rs:1264-1290, crates/jet-cli/src/CLI.rs. Keep the exact owner clarification on the linked card. No provider safety checks are autoapproved by this design. Formal Tower ratification remains open.

Beginner review prompted the worked policy edit, explicit alias, separate trusted/untrusted timelines, cancellation outcome, and safety glossary. The owner’s metadata-free prompt requirement wins: named --allow alone is not an exemption. Source examples use the existing package authority form and core.time sleep syntax.

Fresh review findings were retained. The author resolved each through the contract and linked card criteria. Review metadata describes that sequence; it does not claim an independent rerun or runtime proof.

options.name: Automatic policy, explicit invocation trust
options.detail:
Use --trust or its exact short alias -T with run, dev, and test. Trust once means exactly the same thing. All three approve otherwise approvable effects for this invocation, including new effects after dev edits. They never write policy.

Apply existing project grants and denies automatically. Metadata presence does not approve unlisted rights. A metadata-free effectful launch asks before execution unless trusted; an effect-free program, such as fn run() {}, does not ask. Named --allow alone does not bypass this metadata-free prompt rule.
options.technical:
The owner selected --trust AND -T, replacing earlier candidate names. Before --, these flags belong to Jet; after --, they are application arguments. Trust once and both flags approve the whole invocation, not only the first displayed gap. No invocation trust is persisted or reused by a later independent launch.

Apply declared project policy without a confirmation to use it. A missing right is not an explicit deny: an untrusted gap can be approved, but an explicit project/CLI deny is refused. Keep the existing named --allow/--deny conflict and root/leaf precedence rules. Without metadata, --allow does not replace --trust/-T or Trust once. It does not skip approval. Explicit denies refuse before any prompt. With metadata, named grants retain their existing right-resolution meaning.

For an untrusted gap, show exactly these choices: [1] Trust once, [2] Update project policy, [3] Exit (default), and [m] Arrow menu. The menu selects the same three actions. Exit, Enter on the default, Escape, EOF, unavailable consent, and unrecognized input cancel before execution with the existing non-success refusal status. They write neither a grant nor a deny.

Metadata means the program’s package facts. Inline facts live in package {} in the source. Separate facts live in the selected canonical package.jet. They are alternative existing forms, not two policies to merge. Editing permission changes authority.holds.allow in that selected source, preserving existing denies and other facts.

Worked source before approval, in app.jet:

```jet
package {
    name: "wait-demo"
    version: "0.1.0"
    authority: { holds: { allow: [Mem.Alloc] } }
}
use core.time as time
fn run() { time.sleep(1ms) }
```

For its uncovered Time.Wait effect, choosing Update shows app.jet and this exact proposed field change:

```text
before: authority: { holds: { allow: [Mem.Alloc] } }
after:  authority: { holds: { allow: [Mem.Alloc, Time.Wait] } }
```

Only accepting that displayed edit writes it. The next covered launch uses it without a prompt. If app.jet has no package metadata, offer the minimal inline block and its complete diff before writing. If package.jet already owns the policy, edit that file instead. Do not create a competing manifest or overwrite an explicit deny.

Read-only, virtual, malformed, changed-since-check, or unsafe paths disable the update with a cause-specific action. A transactional snapshot check must protect the exact approved file and bytes. Persist the approved edit and mandatory authority record before using its grant. Do not ask again after the exact edit has already been approved.

Required authority records identify checked source, policy identity, decision origin, effect scope, and actual outcome through the existing typed audit path. The trigger matrix below distinguishes grants from refusals. Once/flags record invocation trust; they do not pretend a project edit occurred. Required audit persistence failure refuses execution. Its protected storage is not disposable history.

Language memory/type checks and user-written Unsafe regions remain enforced. OS, sandbox, enterprise, delegation, and dependency restrictions still bind. Sensitive recording can contain secrets, so its separate consent remains required. Trust never approves unsigned artifacts, package trust changes, unrelated confirmations, or provider safety checks.

Existing --trust appears in environment/toolchain forwarding. Separate that trust domain from application effects during the cutover. Do not forward an application trust bit as permission for unsigned packages or unrelated operations. Noninteractive --trust/-T works; an untrusted uncovered gap without interactive consent fails with actionable policy/flag guidance.

After the policy diff, show [1] Apply displayed edit and [2] Exit (default). Only 1, or Enter on an explicitly selected Apply row, accepts. Bare Enter, Escape, EOF, unavailable consent, and unknown input cancel without writing or launching. No third confirmation follows successful explicit acceptance.

For missing metadata, insert inline facts only into the unique checked source selected by canonical entry identity. Never select an imported helper arbitrarily. A multi-target test/package invocation without one unique policy-owning source disables Update. Explain the ambiguity: select one source or author canonical package policy explicitly.

Before each checked revision’s first effect, automatic project grants, applicable named grants, flags, and Once require a durable authorization-use record. Record actual source/policy identity, right scope, invocation identity, and decision origin. Existing required delegation records remain required. A pure revision needs no authorization-use receipt.

Explicit deny, cancellation, invalid input, and noninteractive missing consent execute no effect and return the refusal status. They produce the typed diagnostic, not a new mandatory persistent event. Honor an enclosing audit policy that already requires recording refusals. Logging failure never changes refusal into approval.

A trusted dev edit does not prompt again for approvable effects. Before its new checked revision performs effects, persist a new authorization-use record linked to the original invocation decision. Record new source/policy hashes and effective rights. A previous revision’s receipt cannot authorize new source. Required write failure refuses the revision’s effects.

Policy edits use the existing authority transaction with explicit phases. Persist an approved-but-not-applied record containing old/new policy hashes and the accepted edit. Atomically replace the checked source, then persist a committed marker. No effect uses the edit before both policy and marker are durable.

A missing commit marker means attempted or uncertain, never completed approval. Every partial transaction refuses execution. Recovery checks old/new hashes under the same lock, then completes or rejects without overwriting unrelated edits. If storage prevents a failure marker, the durable uncommitted record remains uncertain. Never claim rollback or successful persistence without evidence.

Environment preparation has a separate explicit workflow:

```sh
jet env
# Review environment-only approval in its existing interface.
# Inside the prepared project shell:
jet run -T app.jet
```

Application trust is never forwarded as environment trust. An unprepared noninteractive run refuses with the registered environment diagnostic. Its correction points to jet env and then retrying. Explicitly invoked environment/package trust commands keep their own domains. No new generic trust flag is invented. The -T alias is application-only.

Existing persistent service trust remains explicit, for example jet trust grant "acme/web@github:postgres.service" --scope repo. It is separate from the one-session workflow above. Never create that persistent grant automatically, broaden its subject, or waive signature checks.

The prompt trigger is not merely a nonempty uncovered set. Without metadata, any effectful untrusted revision asks even when --allow covers its rights. Show the checked requested effects honestly, not an empty gap. With metadata, show only uncovered approvable effects. A project edit grants only the exact displayed rights, never the universal scope of Once.
options.code:
jet run --trust app.jet  # no prompt for approvable effects
jet dev -T app.jet       # same trust, including later edits
jet test -T app.jet      # same invocation-only trust
jet run app.jet         # untrusted launch below
# Covered policy: no prompt. Only uncovered rights prompt.
# [1] Trust once [2] Update project policy [3] Exit (default)
# [m] Arrow menu
# Once equals --trust. Explicit deny still refuses execution.
# Without metadata, --allow alone still requires approval.

options.detail: Keep --allow and --deny without a universal invocation-trust mode. An interactive once grant covers only the displayed missing set. Keep the existing policy prompt workflow. This is the rejected comparison option, not the selected contract.
options.technical: This retains the existing approval model. It does not fulfill the owner’s universal Once or --trust/-T request. No broad flag may silently reuse package/toolchain trust.

# Next uncovered right needs another approval.
# Once covers the displayed gap only.

whyNot.reason: B preserves the approval ceremony and narrow Once behavior the owner rejected.

recommendation.tradeoff: Trust reduces repeated decisions but authorizes more actions during that invocation.

decisions.title: One top-level .jet directory for project-generated files
decisions.gist: Should all project-generated files live in one top-level .jet directory?
decisions.lesson: One .jet directory can hold build outputs, generated source, caches, and saved records without scattering top-level folders. Jet currently uses build/, .jet-build/, .jet/, and an external run cache. Generated does not mean disposable: saved claims, required evidence, and reproducibility metadata need protection. Neither option permits blanket deletion. Shared downloads and explicit exports are separate from default project outputs.
decisions.story: Mira builds app.jet and keeps a replay as a regression check. She wants one generated directory, not build products scattered beside source. She must still be able to clean rebuildable files without losing that saved check.
decisions.inWild:
# With UseArtifactsOutput enabled; not run here.
dotnet build
# artifacts/bin/MyApp/debug/
# artifacts/obj/MyApp/debug/
# artifacts/publish/MyApp/release_linux-x64/
decisions.detail:
## Answer to the owner question

The earlier ballot framed a single local directory as clutter. That was the wrong comparison for your request. Other tools commonly collect outputs in a project directory. Cargo uses target/. Dart shares .dart_tool/ for project tool caches. Gradle separates .gradle/ from build/. .NET offers one opt-in artifacts/ root. No surveyed source establishes one universal layout.

Recommend the expanded B: one top-level .jet/ that includes build/, not merely the earlier cache-only sketch. A keeps its existing shared-cache meaning; B keeps its local-root meaning. Existing letters are retained so the recorded question remains understandable. The previous recommendation and claim that you selected shared caching no longer apply. Your question is not ratification.

## Evidence and limits

Official sources were read on 2026-09-15. The comparison trees adapt documented layouts; no peer build or performance experiment was run. .NET explains that a common root lets tools predict output paths. Dart explains that a shared tool directory avoids additional ignore entries, but warns against copying its caches between machines. These are documented benefits and limitations, not adoption counts or a user-sentiment survey.

Current Jet source: Source/CmdCompile.rs:9787-9826 places binaries under build/. Source/RunCache.rs:74-84 defaults to ~/.cache/jet/run. Source/RecordIndex.rs:439-459 places the index under project .jet/records. The card retains the existing storage inventory. New Jet storage behavior has not been implemented or exercised.

## Rules shared by both options

Keep the ratified data ownership and trust rules. D-RECORD1 keeps one record index and identity. D-RECORD-SPELL1 keeps saved claims protected. D-HISTORY-LIFECYCLE2 keeps optional history best effort, with a 256 MiB byte-only FIFO budget per canonical project. Saved, required audit, and sensitive protected roots stay outside that quota. This ballot does not change these rules or grant deletion authority.

Classify every owned output before migration. Preserve protected data, references, permissions, and provenance. A path or cache hit never grants trust; D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1 still applies. Migrate all readers, writers, scaffolds, examples, and cleanup paths together. Do not retain compatibility readers or remove unrelated files. Unknown .jet contents are not disposable by name.

Explicit output destinations remain explicit. User-authored source, manifests, application data, credentials, and existing mandatory external audit destinations are not silently moved. Shared downloaded packages and installed toolchains remain in their existing user stores. No new dependency, storage flag, or language syntax is proposed.

options.technical:
All default disposable project build products, generated source, intermediates, run/test caches, and optional records use the platform user-cache root. Keep saved records and required project metadata in project-owned .jet storage. This would require an explicit location amendment for currently ratified .jet/generated paths, without changing generated bytes or reproducibility checks.

Separate canonical project, input, output, target, profile, and toolchain identities. Read-only sources can build when all required output destinations are writable. Protected project writes still require their existing authority. Do not relocate mandatory evidence merely because a cache is writable.

options.name: One top-level .jet directory
options.detail: Put all default project-generated files under .jet/, including build outputs.
options.technical:
One default .jet root belongs to the enclosing declared workspace; otherwise use the enclosing repository, package root, or standalone entry's parent, in that order. Use the closest applicable root. Do not cross into another workspace or imported dependency's authority. Workspace members and entries in nested source folders share that root, with separate identities below it. Unrelated standalone files in one directory share its root, not one .jet directory per filename.

Move default build/ and .jet-build/ products under .jet/build/. Put the project-specific warm run cache under .jet/cache/run/. Keep generated source under .jet/generated/. Retain established .jet record, receipt, report, and lock paths where their ownership is already correct. Other tool-owned project outputs also stay under this one root. The diagram shows examples, not a reason to create unused directories.

Separate members, entry paths, outputs, platforms, profiles, and compiler/toolchain identities below the root. Equal file basenames must not collide. Symlink aliases must resolve consistently. Concurrent commands must not overwrite each other's work. A moved checkout must not reuse invalid machine-specific cache entries.

Ignore only disposable subtrees in version control. Do not teach users to delete or ignore all of .jet: saved claims can belong in version control, and protected evidence has its own rules. Cleanup must select eligible records and rebuildable outputs rather than remove the whole root. User deletion can still destroy saved work; this policy does not make raw filesystem deletion safe.

On a read-only project, optional run-cache or history failure follows existing best-effort rules. A required local build output needs a writable copy or an existing explicit destination that covers the command's writes. Report an unwritable required destination; do not silently create a second output tree or relocate protected evidence. Existing explicit per-command destination controls remain available. No new relocation flag is introduced.
options.code:

  app.jet
  .jet/
    build/                 # Binaries and build intermediates
    cache/                 # Rebuildable caches
    generated/             # Generated source
    records/               # Includes protected saved/ claims
    receipts/              # Retain required evidence
    reports/               # Reports keep their retention rules
    lock                   # Preserve reproducibility metadata
# No default top-level build/ or .jet-build/.

This keeps output separate from source, but uses two project directories. Source checked 2026-09-15: https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/directory_layout.html

.NET 8+ offers an opt-in common artifacts/ root for every project. It separates binaries, intermediates, published apps, and packages. The root is configurable. This is strong precedent for one root, not the universal default. Source checked 2026-09-15: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/sdk/artifacts-output

decisions.title: Where should write and take marks go on method calls?
decisions.gist: Where should a method call show permission to change or take its receiver?
decisions.lesson: A function performs an operation. A method is called through a value, its receiver. & permits temporary exclusive changes; ^ transfers ownership and ends later use of a named value. The permission must mark one exact call. Plain . keeps read calls unmarked. Existing &place windows keep their checked lifetimes.
decisions.explainer:
## Read the example
`struct Buffer` defines a value with one named part, `text`. `impl Buffer` groups methods. `self` names the receiver inside a method.

`buf := Buffer{text: "hello"}` creates a changeable value. `chunk: String` names incoming text. `=` replaces the field, while `{self.text}` and `{chunk}` insert their text inside the quoted result. `append` changes the Buffer. `seal` takes it and prints its text. Every option prints `hello world` once. The caller may use `buf` after `append`, but not after `seal`.

Ordinary functions already use `edit(&values)` and `consume(^text)`. Their declarations use `fn edit(values: &[Int])` and `fn consume(text: ^String)`. Read calls stay unmarked. Static calls through a type have no value receiver and stay unmarked.

## Existing law
D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A defines `&place` as an exclusive write window. A place is a named value followed by fields, indexes, or ranges. A window may be bound and passed under its checked lifetime. This choice does not remove or reinterpret those windows.

Option A writes `buf.&append(...)` and `buf.^seal()`. The mark sits after the ordinary dot and before the method name. It replaces prefix-window calls such as `&values[0..1].sort()` with `values[0..1].&sort()`.

Option B writes `&buf.append(...)` and `^buf.seal()`. It keeps the current prefix-window call and extends that position to taking calls. Prefix scope makes nested calls and mixed chains need grouping. A fresh write receiver is not a place, so B must name it first.

Option C writes `buf&.append(...)` and `buf^.seal()`. The adjacent `&.` or `^.` is one call separator. Plain `.` means a read call. `&.` means write through the receiver for that call. `^.` means take the receiver for that call.

Under C, the composite separators are valid only before a method name followed by call parentheses. They do not access fields, create a window, or move a value by themselves. `?.` keeps its existing optional-access meaning. Ordinary bitwise `&` and power `^` remain separate operators; only adjacent `&.` and `^.` form receiver-call separators.

## Holding a write window
All options keep the window construction:
```jet
values := [2, 1, 3]
window := &values[0..1] // Selects values 2 and 1.
```
A calls `window.&sort()`. B calls `&window.sort()`. C calls `window&.sort()`. Each call sorts the selected values and leaves `[1,2,3]`. A read such as `print(values[0])` is rejected before a later window use. After the sort is the window's final use, that read is accepted and prints `1`.

## The same mixed chain
Assume `duplicate` reads a Buffer and returns another Buffer. Assume `grow` changes its receiver and returns another Buffer. `seal` takes its receiver.

A writes `buf.duplicate().&grow().^seal()`. B writes `next := buf.duplicate()` and then `^(&next.grow()).seal()`. The inner prefix permits `grow`; the outer prefix takes its returned Buffer into `seal`. C writes `buf.duplicate()&.grow()^.seal()`. Under C, each separator marks exactly the following method call.

## Calls inside ordinary arguments
A writes `inspect_buffer(buf.&grow())` and `print(buf.^finish())`. B needs `inspect_buffer((&buf.grow()))` and `print((^buf.finish()))`. C writes `inspect_buffer(buf&.grow())` and `print(buf^.finish())`.

C does not change argument prefixes. `inspect_buffer(&buf.grow())` still marks the outer argument, not the nested receiver. The call-only separator removes that scope question for the marked receiver.

## Exact boundary cases
For a changeable list of Buffer values, C writes `items[i]&.append("!")`. The index is evaluated once. A uses `items[i].&append("!")`; B uses `&items[i].append("!")`.

For a read-only list parameter, every option rejects taking `items[0]`. A mark states requested permission; it never creates ownership the receiver does not have.

`make_buffer()` creates `Buffer{text: "hello"}`. A fresh owned receiver may be taken under C with `make_buffer()^.seal()`. B writes `^(make_buffer()).seal()` because the computed receiver needs grouping.

A fresh C write may use `make_buffer()&.append("!")`; A supports its equivalent inline spelling. These two append examples only prove the permitted call form. `append` returns no value, so the changed temporary is then discarded. B needs a named place for a fresh write call.

Receiver marks do not change access timing. Every user or trait method declared with `&self` reserves write access, evaluates allowed arguments, then activates exclusive access. C's `values&.push(values.len())` uses the same two-phase timing for the builtin `push`, so it reads the length before activation.

Some helper-backed builtins require eager write access. The compiler's builtin registry names them; this ballot adds no source marker or user choice. List examples include `remove`, `sort_by`, `sort_desc`, `sort_by_desc`, `update_first`, and `edit_disjoint`. Therefore `values&.remove(values.len() - 1)` is rejected because the argument reads `values` after eager access begins. A and B preserve the same timing with their spellings.

A newly created ordinary argument may omit ^ under current law. `consume("hello")` is accepted for `fn consume(text: ^String)`. A named argument still needs `consume(^text)`. Receiver calls deliberately require the selected receiver mark, including on a fresh receiver.

No option clones a receiver, changes method lookup, changes evaluation order, creates a raw reference, or weakens use-after-take checks. Missing, extra, or mismatched marks are compile errors with a direct fix.

## Trade-offs
A scopes the mark to one method, but `.&name` and `.^name` make the method name look decorated. It also places receiver marks differently from argument and window marks.

B keeps value prefixes, but the prefix can cover more syntax than the intended call. Nested calls and mixed chains need grouping. Fresh write receivers need temporary names.

C scopes the mark to one method while keeping the receiver before the separator and the method after it. It adds two composite separators. Ruby uses `&.` for optional navigation, so Ruby users may first misread C. Jet already uses `?.` for optional access, which keeps Jet's own punctuation family distinct.

## Delivery
The examples are source-derived design examples, not execution receipts. Ratification selects one canonical receiver-call form. Migrate every caller, example, test, formatter case, editor grammar, completion, diagnostic suggestion, and affected explanation. Keep no compatibility receiver spelling.

Sema checks the written separator against the resolved receiver convention for user methods, traits, and builtins. AOT, default run, forced interpreter, and applicable web execution must preserve one meaning. Generated Rust cannot discover a user error.
decisions.story: Maya appends text to a buffer, then consumes it while printing the result. She wants every call to expose its write or take permission without breaking ordinary chains or changing existing write windows.
decisions.inWild: Rust declares write receivers with &mut self and taking receivers with self, but ordinary dot calls hide those permissions. Ruby uses &. for optional navigation. Jet already uses ?. for optional access. Option C instead uses &. and ^. as explicit write and take method separators. These comparisons explain likely expectations; they do not prove adoption or implementation.

options.name: Mark after the dot
options.detail: Write `buf.&append(...)` and `buf.^seal()`. Each call exposes its receiver permission beside the method. Fresh receivers and mixed chains stay inline. Existing &place windows keep their independent meaning.
options.technical: Add receiver-call marks between the dot and method name. Keep method lookup, receiver evaluation, and borrow classification unchanged. Require a matching mark even when the receiver is an existing write window. Amend D-SHAPE-PLACE1 only where a bare-prefix window call previously supplied sufficient method permission. Migrate that form; do not remove or reinterpret write-window expressions.

options.name: Keep value-prefix receiver marks
options.detail: Write `&buf.append(...)` and `^buf.seal()`. Keep the current write-window receiver spelling and extend prefix marking to take receivers. Write receivers must be places, so name fresh values before calling write methods.
options.technical:
Preserve &place construction and maximal-place binding. Each write/take call must have its own receiver mark; a mark on an earlier chain step does not cover later steps. Add ^ in method-receiver position with explicit grouping for computed receivers. Do not add standalone ^value expressions. Preserve builtin two-phase timing for immediate write receivers and existing exclusive lifetimes for stored windows.

Inside an ordinary argument, preserve argument-prefix precedence. Use `inspect_buffer((&buf.grow()))` or `print((^buf.finish()))` to mark the nested receiver. Without that grouping, the leading mark belongs to the outer argument and the receiver remains unmarked.

options.name: Use capability dots
options.detail: Write `buf&.append(...)` and `buf^.seal()`. The separator states how the receiver enters exactly one method call. Plain `.` remains read. Existing `&place` windows and ordinary argument prefixes keep their current meaning.
options.technical: Lex adjacent `&.` and `^.` as call-only postfix separators. They must be followed by a method name and call parentheses. Record Write or Move on the method receiver, then use the existing resolver and CallBinder path. Do not permit these separators for field access, static calls, or standalone expressions. Keep `?.` optional access, bitwise `&`, power `^`, argument conventions, lookup, evaluation order, and two-phase receiver timing unchanged.

options.name: Mark the value, not the call
options.detail: Write `&buf.append(...)` and `^buf.seal()`. The mark sits on the named value that changes or ends, just like `edit(&buf)`. New temporary values need no mark. Chains stay plain after the first named value.
options.technical: A `&` or `^` mark binds the maximal place after it: one name plus fields, indexes, or ranges. It never binds a call result. Sema checks the mark against the one call that receives that place, as receiver or argument. A fresh receiver takes no mark, matching the existing fresh-argument rule. At line start, `&` or `^` directly followed by a name begins a new statement. A continued bitwise-and or power line keeps a space after its operator. Copy `~` grouping is unchanged. Existing `&place` windows and their checked lifetimes are unchanged.

comparisons.note: Official method-call reference, read 2026-09-16: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/method-call-expr.html#r-expr.method.autoref-deref . Rust inserts receiver borrows and documents lookup surprises. This demonstrates a design contrast, not popularity or performance evidence.

Ruby uses `&.` as its safe-navigation operator. Jet already uses `?.` for optional access, so C deliberately assigns `&.` a different meaning. Official syntax: https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/3.4/syntax/calling_methods_rdoc.html#label-Safe+Navigation+Operator
comparisons.code: user&.name  # Ruby: call only when user is not nil.

recommendation.why: D marks the named value that changes or ends, as arguments already do. Temporaries stay unmarked.

whyNot.reason: A adds a second mark position and decorates method names.
B marks temporaries and needs extra names and grouping.
C adds two separators and marks temporaries in chains.

recommendation.tradeoff: Choose one value-side mark position and a line-start rule over new call separators.

decisions.title: Const generics: a compile-time Int as a type parameter
decisions.gist: May a compile-time number be a type parameter, and how is it spelled?
decisions.lesson: A generic type takes a type parameter: `Pair<T>`. Some types need a number: a 64-byte packet, a 3x3 matrix. Today a constant can size an array field, but `Packet<64>` cannot be written, so each size is a separate struct. A slice does not help: the size must live in the type so a 64-byte frame cannot pass as a 32-byte one. This ballot asks whether a compile-time `Int` may be a type parameter (option D: no) and how to spell it. Running code never builds a type.
decisions.story: Omar writes firmware. His radio frames come in 32, 64, and 128 bytes. He wants one `Packet` type and one `checksum` function. Today he copies the struct three times. With `Packet<@N: Int>` he writes it once, and passing a `Packet<64>` where a `Packet<32>` is expected is a compile error at the call.

options.name: Compile-time sigil: struct Packet<@N: Int>
options.detail:
A value parameter is written with the `@` that S57 gives compile-time names: `struct Packet<@N: Int> { data: [U8#@N] }`, used as `Packet<64>` or `Packet<@lanes>`. Type parameters like `T` are also compile-time, so here `@` marks 'value, not type'; that widens the sigil's meaning. It cannot be misread as a trait bound (`<T: Add>`, which constrains T to implement Add). Inside the body `@N` shadows any outer `@N` constant.

Only `Int` for now; the `: Int` is written so later kinds (`Bool`, `U32`) fit the same slot. Any Int is legal; a negative or zero size fails only where it sizes an array, as `[U8#0]` does today. A bare argument is a literal or `@name`; anything else takes parentheses, `Packet<(@lanes * 16)>`, like `[Float#(@lanes * 2)]`. Inside a generic body arguments are a bare `@N` or fully closed; `Packet<(@N * 2)>` is rejected, so type equality never needs algebra.

`Packet<64>` and `Packet<(@lanes * 16)>` are the same type. One compiled copy per distinct value, like `<T>`. At a call site the value is inferred from the argument, or written explicitly (D-GENERIC-CALL1=A). Value and type parameters mix in declaration order with optional defaults: `Matrix<T, @R: Int, @C: Int = @R>`. `impl<@N: Int> Wire for Packet<@N>` and `impl Wire for Packet<64>` overlap; the existing coherence rule rejects that.

Narrow amendment to S26: a compile-time Int may parameterize an existing type constructor. `Meta.Const` (D-META-GATE1) governs declaring `<@N: Int>`; instantiating a dependency's `Packet<64>` is always allowed.
options.technical: Generic parameter list accepts `@name: Int`. Arguments: literal, `@const`, or a parenthesized comptime Int expression; a bound value parameter may appear only bare. Sema instantiates per distinct value; `[T#@N]` sizes resolve after instantiation and reject non-positive sizes there. A runtime value in the slot is a teaching diagnostic.

options.name: Plain name: struct Packet<N: Int>
options.detail: Rust and Swift shape without a keyword; uniform with the unsigiled `T`. `<N: Int>` looks exactly like a trait bound `<T: Add>` until the reader knows `Int` is not a trait, and the body writes `N`, unlike every other compile-time constant in Jet. The parser cannot tell the kind without name resolution, which Jet's parser does not do today.
options.technical: Disambiguate by resolving the bound: if it names a type rather than a trait, the parameter is a value. Requires name resolution before the parameter kind is known.
options.code:
struct Packet<N: Int> { data: [U8#N] }     // reads like a trait bound <T: Add>
p :: Packet<64>{data: [U8#64]{}}

options.name: Keyword: struct Packet<const N: Int>
options.detail: Rust's spelling, recognized at once by Rust readers, and the body stays unsigiled like `T`. It reserves `const` for one position (I7 has no contextual keywords) when `@` already carries the meaning.
options.technical: Reserve `const` (I7). Parameter kind is known at the parser without name resolution.
options.code:
struct Packet<const N: Int> { data: [U8#N] }   // new reserved word
p :: Packet<64>{data: [U8#64]{}}

options.name: No const generics: keep per-size types
options.detail: Keep S26 as written. Sizes stay array facts (`[U8#64]`); one struct per size by hand, or a generated sibling file per size from `fn build`. Zero grammar change and no monomorphization by value. Cost: `checksum` is written once per size, and a shared field or method cannot be generic over the count.
options.technical: Status quo. Alternatives considered and refused here. A trait with an associated constant (`struct Packet<S: Size>`, typenum style) needs one marker type per size and cannot infer from a literal. A `#N` size parameter reuses the array-size marker but keys the whole feature to arrays.

comparisons.note: A keyword marks a value parameter; only integers, bool, char today.
comparisons.code: struct Packet<const N: usize> { data: [u8; N] }

comparisons.note: Types are values; a function takes a comptime size and returns a struct type. Jet refuses this route.
comparisons.code: fn Packet(comptime n: usize) type { return struct { data: [n]u8 }; }

comparisons.note: Non-type template parameters have existed since the start; the type is written before the name.
comparisons.code: template <std::size_t N> struct Packet { std::array<uint8_t, N> data; };

comparisons.note: Value generics use a plain `let N: Int` marker; only Int today.

recommendation.why: `@` already marks a compile-time name in Jet, so `<@N: Int>` needs no new word and cannot be read as a trait bound; the sigil's meaning widens to 'value, not type'. Inside the body `@N` looks like every other constant. The amendment to S26 stays narrow: a number parameterizes an existing type, no type is computed, and arithmetic over bound parameters is refused so equality stays by value.

whyNot.reason: It reads as a trait bound until the reader knows Int is not a trait, and the parser needs name resolution to know the parameter kind.
Familiar to Rust readers, but it reserves a word for one position when `@` already carries the meaning.
One function per size forever; generated sibling files hide the count in a build step instead of the type.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet takes on monomorphization by value and a second kind of generic parameter. Only Int is allowed, which covers sizes and counts and keeps the type checker away from arbitrary values.

losses.loss: A second kind of generic parameter to learn.
losses.mitigation: A number and a type cannot share one parameter kind without types-as-values.

losses.loss: Only Int values for now.
losses.mitigation: A scope choice: sizes and counts are the shipped need; `Bool` or `U32` can follow in the same slot.

losses.loss: No arithmetic over a bound parameter in a type argument.
losses.mitigation: Deciding `Packet<(@N * 2)>` equals `Packet<(2 * @N)>` needs symbolic algebra.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: completion-beginner-constgen1. Skill: rli5. A stateless fresh reader flagged the unexplained `[U8#@N]`, the trait-bound comparison, and call-site inference; all repaired in option A.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: Anthropic. Fresh agent: completion-adversarial-constgen1. decisions.detail:
## Shared publication contract

D-BUILD-GENVALUE1 already selects Generated item values and b.generate(name, value). This decision adds the shared-preparation entry point, not another template engine. The example assumes make_commands returns that existing Generated type.

Publication returns the normal checked result or a source diagnostic. A generated value is inert until published. Returning it from a helper neither publishes declarations nor executes their runtime bodies.

Names identify generated modules within the current package and input snapshot. Duplicate names, conflicting declarations, illegal target scopes and dependency cycles fail explicitly. Every published declaration retains template, capture and publication provenance.

Standard publication is additive. It cannot replace an existing body, signature or type. Advanced changes require the separate opt-in and transformation contract. Generated source still follows normal visibility, effect and safety checks.

Typed template holes retain their selected meaning only inside templates. An ordinary prepared value is referenced normally outside a template. The advanced control ballot distinguishes captured syntax from compiler metadata queries.

Materialization uses #3421's canonical generated root. Source navigation must work whether physical materialization is requested or a virtual generated document is used. Materialized output is drift-checked rather than treated as independent handwritten source.

Both examples add the same commands module. Its function runs only when the application calls it. Cold and warm preparation publish the same logical declarations with the same effects. The target program cannot change through an imported module's ambient state.

options.name: Program publisher
options.detail: Name the current program before publishing. The receiving program is visible. The common operation needs a receiver lookup.
options.technical: compiler.program() returns the current preparation program handle. Its generate method has the same name, Generated input and failure rules.

decisions.detail:
## What this vote changes

This vote chooses the prep boundary grammar and @PHASE() query spelling. The phase, Runtime, effect, generation and artifact rules below preserve prior owner selections. They are stated to make the complete behavior visible, not to reopen those selections.

## Shared contract

Both choices run ordinary Jet functions, conditions and loops during shared preparation. AOT, default run and interpreter receive the same prepared meaning. Web participates when the program reaches web. A saved AOT artifact does not prepare again when launched.

Prepared values use ordinary names. Compiler-owned metadata remains under callable @ roots. Metadata roots use uppercase names and lowercase members. No extra @ appears merely because a value was prepared.

Generation remains explicit. Evaluating or returning a Generated value does not publish it or execute its generated body. D-BUILD-GENVALUE1 remains the typed item-template contract. Build remains AOT artifact production, not a second shared-preparation meaning.

Runtime barriers use #Runtime(.NoEager) and #Runtime(.Only) on functions, methods or explicit blocks. Neither has a bare shorthand or module-wide default. NoEager prevents automatic eager evaluation but allows an explicit prep call. Only rejects calls during preparation or AOT build execution. Both permit ordinary runtime optimization. These are phase boundaries, not optimizer barriers.

## Failure and effect rules

Preparation may call ordinary helpers under their inferred effects and approved host policy. Invalid phase crossings get source diagnostics before code generation. A pure-result cache cannot suppress observable effects. Each logical invocation observes effects once and in order, even when its pure computation is reused.

Compiler scheduling may wait for declared inputs. It must diagnose dependency cycles rather than guess a result. Preparation of an ordinary application cannot acquire advanced privileges by importing a module.

## Examples and acceptance

calculate_lanes returns 8 in both examples. The program prints 8 on each applicable execution mode. Launching the emitted AOT binary prints 8 without repeating preparation IO. Replacing the call with an ordinary loop remains legal inside braces.

The implementation registers every selected spelling in Syntax.rs. It migrates parser, formatter, editor, diagnostics, examples and current explanations together. Historical ballots are not rewritten. New public grammar outside this decision remains owner-gated.

The compiler-owned @PHASE() query reports Preparation, Build or Runtime at its evaluation site. The result follows language phases, never optimizer decisions. A phase-only branch is checked according to the selected phase and cannot smuggle runtime state into preparation.

## Reader key and direct proof owners

The binding operator :: gives the calculated value a name. A block without a value expression yields Unit, meaning no value. Under B, prep f() + 1 prepares the entire sum. Use (prep f()) + runtime_value to put only f inside preparation.

#3521 proves legal explicit NoEager calls and rejected Only calls, source diagnostics and saved-artifact startup. #3525 proves cycle rejection. #3506 and #3532 prove effects occur once in order on cold and warm runs. @PHASE() returns Preparation, Build or Runtime as defined above.

## Ordinary prepared values in generic uses

The latest owner selection supersedes repeated sigils on ordinary prepared values. Keep Packet<@N: Int> for the selected compile-time binder. Use N in [U8#N] and lanes in Packet<lanes>. This is one ordinary-value naming rule, not a new generic mechanism. #3505 owns the clean parser, checker, formatter and example cutover. D-CONSTGEN1 remains immutable history; typed template holes retain their separately scoped meaning.

decisions.title: Complete reflection contract and callable record shape
decisions.gist: Which record shape should Jet’s complete reflection contract use?
decisions.lesson: Both options approve complete typed facts for types, callables, programs, source, packages, local state and runtime values. Queries use ordinary typed Result errors; missing facts never become empty lists. Runtime retention is explicit. The choice is whether callable facts share one signature record or repeat its fields. The complete field schema appears below.
decisions.explainer: Both options approve complete typed facts for types, callables, programs, source, packages, local state and runtime values. Queries use ordinary typed Result errors; missing facts never become empty lists. Runtime retention is explicit. The choice is whether callable facts share one signature record or repeat its fields. The complete field schema appears below.
decisions.story: A tool author compares one function, method and closure signature. They need typed parameters and honest missing-fact errors. A runtime inspector separately requests retained metadata.

decisions.detail:
## Complete fact contract

This decision approves complete checked reflection, not only a signature cleanup. @TYPE(T), @FUNCTION(f), @METHOD(T, name) and @CLOSURE(value) are callable queries. @PROGRAM(), @PACKAGE() and @SOURCE() expose the corresponding checked snapshot. Ordinary prepared values do not acquire metadata sigils.

The existing selected callable-root convention is fixed. This ballot does not reopen dot-of spelling. Function overloads require an unambiguous selected callable or an explicit typed selection; a bare ambiguous name is an error.

CallableSignature contains ordered params, return_type, effects, calling_convention and generic_bindings. Each parameter exposes name, label, type, default, zone, mutability and source. Defaults distinguish absent, available checked expression and unavailable evaluation. They never execute merely because metadata is read.

Callable records also expose stable identity, visibility, captures, attributes, source, documentation and checked body availability. Closure captures expose binding identity, type, capture mode and lifetime constraints. Compile-time metadata can inspect structure without retaining runtime closure values.

Type metadata covers every compiler Type variant. It includes generics, constraints, traits, methods, fields, enum cases, aliases, numeric dimensions, representation and target layout. Type identity is not a formatted name. Recursive graphs use stable references, not infinite expansion.

Program metadata covers declarations, references, calls, typed expressions, scopes, locals, control flow, effects, obligations and memory facts. Package metadata includes resolved imports, dependencies, settings, contributions and provenance. Source metadata includes exact snapshot identity, spans, comments, documentation and expansion origins.

Use the canonical checked semantic index for program facts. No second ownership analysis or mutable private store is exposed. #3175 supplies bounded local obligations. #3199 and #3202 own facade and diagnostic-origin consistency. #3181 owns the versioned schema cutover.

## Availability, privacy and runtime

A query returns a typed fact or an explicit unavailable, unsupported, stale, invalid, denied or truncated result. Empty collections mean checked emptiness only. Target-dependent facts name their target. Phase-dependent facts name their checked phase and source version.

Preparation can read complete facts within its approved workspace and visibility authority. Reflection does not grant foreign-file or private-dependency access. Opted-in transformations can operate only on explicitly registered targets.

Runtime exposes type and value facts retained for requested roots. It does not ship the complete compiler heap. Runtime type tables name their retention scope and completeness. Erased values preserve actual type identity and lawful access. Dead-code elimination must retain explicitly requested metadata without retaining unrelated metadata by default.

D-ENUM-CASEMETA1 remains binding. Exported reflection captures intentionally disclose the complete lawful captured graph. Ordinary copies preserve captured contents. Shared mutable and noncopyable graphs are refused as specified, not silently approximated.

## Same-program result

Both options report advance's ordered parameter types, defaults and return type identically. Only the member path differs. A method and closure with equivalent callable contracts produce equivalent signature facts. A program without runtime reflection receives no new runtime table allocation.

Every field family receives a named delivery owner and behavioral witness under #3509. Current source models define implementation reuse, not permission to omit requested facts. The contract card implements the owner-visible schema below in the executable registry before consumers implement it. It cannot silently choose different public shapes.

## Reader key and failure witnesses

:: binds a value. @FUNCTION asks for compiler metadata; a dot reads one typed member. An effect describes an operation such as filesystem access. Calling convention describes how a function passes arguments across its selected ABI. The example is pure and has no world-touching effect.

#3523 and #3199 own these query/result witnesses: unavailable before its checked phase; unsupported for a named unimplemented fact; stale after source edits. They also cover invalid checked input, denied private scope and explicitly truncated bounded output. No such result is accepted as complete feature delivery. #3524 proves requested retention and absence of unrelated runtime metadata.

@PROGRAM() means the current authorized checked program snapshot. @PACKAGE() means its lexical package. @SOURCE() means the lexical source snapshot, not an implicit caller capture. Querying another scope requires an explicit authorized handle. These queries do not add host file access.

## Closed query and error schema

These are proposed public types, not claims about current CallableSignatureFact fields. The existing producer currently has string types/defaults and lacks return-type and calling-convention members. #3522 extends the same checked source instead of creating a parallel analysis.

Every fact-query root listed below returns its success type with the ordinary Jet failure carrier: T !MetadataError. This is the existing Result mechanism, not a new wrapper or implicit empty result. An ordinary call may propagate that typed error; ? makes propagation explicit in the examples. Querying an invalid source cannot publish recovered facts as success.

MetadataError is an error record with kind: MetadataFailure, query: String and source: ?SourceSpan. MetadataFailure has exactly six cases: Unavailable, Unsupported, Stale, Invalid, Denied and Truncated. Each case has the following typed payload, not an arbitrary string map.

- Unavailable: required_stage: CompilerStage; reason: String.
- Unsupported: capability: String.
- Stale: requested: SnapshotId; current: SnapshotId.
- Invalid: diagnostics: [CompilerDiagnostic].
- Denied: scope: ScopeId; reason: String.
- Truncated: limit: Int; observed: Int.

Truncated contains no partial fact payload and is never a successful complete result. A bounded query may be retried with an explicit larger limit. An empty successful list means the compiler proved there were no rows. Optional fields mean known absence, not missing analysis. Error text must not disclose denied private content.

CompilerStage is Parsed, Resolved, Typed, Prepared or Emitted. It describes fact availability within compilation, not a new user execution phase. @PHASE() remains Preparation, Build or Runtime. SnapshotId, TypeId, DeclarationHandle, ScopeId, NodeId and ValueHandle are opaque compiler-issued identities. They cannot be constructed by user casts or strings.

The roots and success types are @TYPE(T): TypeInfo, @FUNCTION(f): FunctionInfo, @METHOD(T, name): MethodInfo and @CLOSURE(value): ClosureInfo. @PROGRAM(): ProgramInfo, @PACKAGE(): PackageInfo and @SOURCE(): SourceInfo use the current authorized lexical snapshot. @VALUE(value): ValueInfo and @TYPES(): TypeCatalog provide runtime value and retained-table inspection. Explicit authorized handles select other snapshots through the same root's handle overload.

@METHOD accepts an unambiguous typed method handle as its second argument when a name selects several overloads. A query never guesses the first overload. @VALUE can inspect an erased value without replacing its actual TypeId with the static container type.

## Record notation and cardinality

The following schema uses [T] for an ordered list and ?T for known optionality. The ordinary T !MetadataError carrier marks a field that needs a later checked stage or unretained fact. These are exact field names and types. Records are immutable value projections; references resolve only through the same checked snapshot or a retained captured graph.

SourceSpan has source: SourceId, start: Int and end: Int, using half-open byte offsets. SourceId contains package: PackageId, path: ?String and digest: String. PackageId contains name: String, version: String and digest: String. Digests identify checked content, not the current contents of a mutable file path.

CallableSignature has params: [ParameterInfo], return_type: ?TypeId, effects: [EffectInfo], errors: [TypeId], failure: FailureInfo, calling_convention: CallingConvention and generic_bindings: [GenericBinding]. It also has returned_views: [ViewProvenanceFact] and policies: [PolicyFact]. An absent return_type means no returned value, not an unknown inferred type.

ParameterInfo has name: String, label: String, type: TypeId, default: ?DefaultInfo, zone: ParamZone, access: AccessConvention, variadic: Bool and source: SourceSpan. DefaultInfo has expression: CodeRef, value: PreparedValue !MetadataError and source: SourceSpan. Reading a default never executes it; its value can be unavailable while its checked expression is present.

FunctionInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, name: String, signature: CallableSignature, visibility: Visibility, attributes: [AttributeInfo], source: SourceSpan and documentation: [CommentInfo]. It also has body: CodeRef !MetadataError. MethodInfo adds receiver: ParameterInfo and owner: TypeId. ClosureInfo adds captures: [CaptureInfo].

CaptureInfo has binding: DeclarationHandle, name: String, type: TypeId, mode: CaptureMode, source: SourceSpan and constraints: [ObligationFact]. CaptureMode uses the existing checked capture modes rather than inferring capture from a name. Under option B, CallableSignature's fields appear directly on each callable record; all their types and meanings remain identical.

EffectInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, name: String and source: ?SourceSpan. FailureInfo has carrier: TypeId, source: FailureSource and errors: [TypeId]. GenericBinding has parameter: DeclarationHandle and argument: GenericArgument. GenericArgument is Type(TypeId), Value(PreparedValue) or Measure(MeasureInfo). PreparedValue uses the existing typed compile-time value algebra, never pre-stringified data.

ParamZone, AccessConvention, Visibility, CallingConvention, FailureSource and CaptureMode project their existing checker enums exactly. Their canonical declarations and public case spellings are included in the generated schema. No string catch-all or unchecked extension case is permitted. A new enum case requires the normal public-contract review.

## Type, field and layout records

TypeInfo has identity: TypeId, name: String, form: TypeForm, source: ?SourceSpan and attributes: [AttributeInfo]. It has fields: [FieldInfo], cases: [CaseInfo], methods: [MethodInfo], traits: [TraitInfo], generic_bindings: [GenericBinding] and layout: LayoutInfo !MetadataError. These lists are complete for the requested retained type graph or the root query fails. A scalar's empty fields list is genuinely empty.

TypeForm mirrors every checked type form: Int, Float, Bool, String, Char, List, Map, Shared, Option, Result, Function, Named, Apply and TraitObject. It also includes Tuple, FixedList, IntN, InlineRange, Float32, Tagged, Union, Quantity and Measure. These cases project the exact algebra in crates/jet-foundation/src/AST/types.rs, not a reduced string taxonomy.

Child types in that algebra become TypeId references. Named and applied declarations become DeclarationHandles plus ordered GenericArguments. Fixed lengths use MeasureInfo; dimensions use the existing canonical dimension algebra. Tagged facts separate identity-bearing tags from non-identity annotations. Function forms reference CallableSignature. Type identity follows existing sema equality, including callable labels and zones.

FieldInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, name: String, type: TypeId, visibility: Visibility, default: ?DefaultInfo, attributes: [AttributeInfo], source: SourceSpan and offset: Int !MetadataError. CaseInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, name: String, payload: [FieldInfo], discriminant: PreparedValue !MetadataError and source: SourceSpan. Active-case inspection and captured payloads preserve D-ENUM-CASEMETA1's ratified access and copy rules.

TraitInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, parameters: [GenericBinding], required_methods: [MethodInfo], associated_types: [TypeId] and constraints: [ObligationFact]. LayoutInfo has target: TargetId, size: Int, alignment: Int and abi: AbiInfo. Layout values describe the selected target, never the compiler host by accident. Runtime variants retain the selected target identity.

## Program, source, package and local facts

ProgramInfo has snapshot: SnapshotId, stage: CompilerStage, declarations: [SymbolDef], scopes: [ScopeInfo], references: [ReferenceFact] and calls: [CallFact]. It also has typed_nodes: [CheckedNode] !MetadataError, state_graphs: [StateGraph] !MetadataError, fact_registry: [FactDefinition] and derivations: [DerivationFact] !MetadataError.

SymbolDef, ReferenceFact, CallFact, StateGraph, FactDefinition and DerivationFact are the existing canonical semantic-index record families. Export their complete checked fields and nested cardinalities through one versioned schema, not a second thinner facade. #3199 and #3181 own the exact typed/JSON agreement and version identity. Existing ratified fields stay mandatory; unavailable producer phases use the specified failure carrier.

ScopeInfo has identity: ScopeId, parent: ?ScopeId, declarations: [DeclarationHandle] and source: SourceSpan. CheckedNode has identity: NodeId, kind: CheckedNodeKind, type: ?TypeId, source: SourceSpan, children: [NodeId] and facts: [ObligationFact]. CheckedNodeKind is the closed typed expression/statement/item algebra exported from the existing checked semantic representation. It never exposes mutable Rust nodes.

ObligationFact uses the complete #3175 checked-local schema, including source version, expression point, binding/place identity and before/after state. All approved initialization, move, view, lifetime, cleanup, narrowing, sendability and typestate variants are preserved. A fact points to its checker derivation; no renderer synthesizes a proof.

SourceInfo has identity: SourceId, text: String, comments: [CommentInfo], documentation: [CommentInfo] and expansions: [ExpansionInfo]. CommentInfo has text: String, span: SourceSpan and kind: CommentKind. CommentKind is Line, Block or Documentation. ExpansionInfo has generated: SourceSpan, template: ?SourceSpan, caller: ?SourceSpan, captures: [SourceSpan] and publisher: ?SourceSpan.

AttributeInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, arguments: [PreparedValue], source: SourceSpan and origin: AttributeOrigin. AttributeOrigin is Written or Expanded with its ExpansionInfo. Reading expanded attributes never claims they were directly written by the user.

PackageInfo has identity: PackageId, root: SourceId, dependencies: [DependencyInfo], imports: [ImportInfo], settings: [SettingInfo], profiles: [ProfileInfo] and targets: [TargetInfo]. DependencyInfo, ImportInfo, ProfileInfo and TargetInfo extend the existing canonical package-model records without dropping existing fields. #3523 owns their complete checked projection.

SettingInfo has name: String, type: TypeId, default: PreparedValue, selected: PreparedValue and contributions: [ContributionInfo]. ContributionInfo has value: PreparedValue, source: SourceSpan, kind: ContributionKind and selected: Bool. ContributionKind is Declaration, Profile or CommandLine. Build inputs and outputs retain existing typed BuildPlan records and their source/package provenance.

## Runtime values and retention

ValueInfo has type: TypeId, active_case: ?DeclarationHandle, fields: [ValueFieldInfo] and value: ValueHandle. ValueFieldInfo has field: DeclarationHandle, type: TypeId and value: ValueHandle. ValueHandle follows the existing lawful typed-access, capture and copy rules. It is not a raw address or a way to access arbitrary memory.

TypeCatalog has snapshot: SnapshotId, target: TargetId, roots: [TypeId], types: [TypeInfo] and scope: RetentionScope. RetentionScope is RequestedRoots or WholeProgram. A successful catalog is complete for its declared scope; it cannot imply that unretained program types do not exist.

Explicit runtime query use requests its statically known type/value roots. compiler.metadata.retain(types, facts) additionally retains named roots. compiler.metadata.retain_program(facts) requests the whole checked program catalog. Both run during preparation and preserve normal visibility and host authority. They are read-only retention requests, not advanced transformation grants.

The facts argument is a list of MetadataFamily values: Types, Callables, Program, Source, Packages, LocalState or All. Retaining LocalState preserves static checked facts, not live runtime variable contents. Retaining Source intentionally includes source text and comments within approved scope. The compiler refuses denied content rather than silently stripping a supposedly complete capture.

Runtime queries for an unretained family return Unavailable with the required stage and a retention reason. They do not reopen source files or start a compiler. A program that makes no runtime query and no retention request gets no metadata table allocation.

## Concrete unavailable access

This uses Jet's existing Result deconstruction. program is a ProgramInfo from a Parsed compiler event. Its typed_nodes field is unavailable until type checking completes. Both callable-layout options behave identically.

```jet
if program.typed_nodes == {
    .Ok(nodes) -> print(nodes.len())
    .Err(error) -> print(error.kind)
}
// Prints MetadataFailure.Unavailable, not 0.
```

The query/result types above are part of this ballot's shared contract, not an implementation choice left for #3520. Canonical existing record algebras remain in their executable homes. That reuse is not permission to invent new public fields without an owner decision.


Bounded root queries accept the optional named limit argument as ?Int. Absence requests all rows in the authorized scope. A reached policy or explicit bound returns Truncated; observed counts rows actually observed, not an invented total. Retrying cannot widen visibility or host authority.

@PHASE() is a total compiler-known Phase value, not a fallible fact query. It retains the exact Preparation, Build and Runtime cases from D-PREP-SURFACE2.

options.name: Shared signature
options.detail: Give every callable one typed signature member. All callable kinds share one schema. Parameter access adds one member hop.
options.technical: FunctionInfo, MethodInfo and ClosureInfo reference CallableSignature. The record contains ordered typed parameters, return type, effects, calling convention and generic bindings.

options.name: Flat callable records
options.detail: Repeat signature fields on each callable record. Common parameter access is shorter. Equivalent fields need coordinated definitions.
options.technical: Each callable record directly contains the same typed fields. A generated schema must enforce equivalence across functions, methods and closures.

comparisons.note: The compiler separates a signature from its definition. This is compiler-internal practice, not a stable Rust reflection API. https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_type_ir/ty_kind/struct.FnSig.html

recommendation.why: Extend the existing CallableSignatureFact producer into one complete typed public signature. Reuse its semantic facts without pretending its current string fields are complete.
gains: All callable kinds share one schema.

losses.loss: Parameter access adds one member hop.
losses.mitigation: A named shared record requires a member access; flattening duplicates its public fields.

whyNot.reason: B shortens access but spreads one contract across several records.

recommendation.tradeoff: A named shared record requires a member access; flattening duplicates its public fields.

decisions.title: Complete advanced API with checked change sets or editors
decisions.gist: Should the complete advanced API publish change sets or scoped edits?
decisions.lesson: Both options approve type construction, code parsing, caller capture, insertion, specialization, compiler workspaces and build control. Existing code and signatures may change. Authorization comes from D-META-OPTIN2; host permissions stay separate. This choice assembles edits explicitly or in a private draft. Both recheck affected callers before accepting anything.
