decisions.title: How Jet's core library talks to each operating system
decisions.situation: Every program asks the operating system for real work: printing, opening files, reading the clock, starting threads and getting memory. Today most Jet programs make those requests through the Rust runtime and each system's C library, so building for another system first downloads that system's C files. The owner wants Zig-style builds: any computer builds for every target, and the result is as fast as possible. You are deciding which door Jet's own core library uses on each system: the C library everywhere, raw kernel calls everywhere, or each system's officially supported door. We recommend the supported door per system: direct kernel calls on Linux, Apple's libSystem on macOS, and the Windows system libraries, such as kernel32, on Windows. Jet's own linker joins them using small stub files bundled with Jet. Programs that link C code, or look up computer names on Linux, still use the C library, as ratified law requires.
decisions.gist: Which door should Jet's core library use to reach each operating system: the C library, raw kernel calls, or each system's supported door?
decisions.lesson: The kernel is the core of an operating system; a system call asks it for work. A C library such as glibc wraps those calls for C programs. A stub file lists a library's function names so a linker can build against it without the real system present. A picks each system's supported door: kernel calls on Linux, libSystem on macOS, the Windows system libraries on Windows. B uses the C library everywhere. C makes raw kernel calls everywhere.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. The operating system's kernel does the real work: files, clocks, threads and memory. A program asks it through a system call, a numbered request.

A C library, such as glibc on Linux, is a big collection of ready-made functions for C programs. Most of them end in a system call. Rust, Go, Zig and Jet programs may use it or skip it.

A linker is the tool that joins compiled pieces into one runnable file. To use a library it needs that library's list of names. A stub file is that list without the code: a .tbd file for Apple's libSystem, an import library for Windows DLLs.

Cross compiling means building on one computer for another, for example a Windows file on a Linux laptop. Zig does it from any host because it bundles stub files and its own linker.

A target name says what to build for: CPU, maker, system and C library flavour. x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu means a 64-bit Intel or AMD chip running Linux. aarch64-apple-darwin means an Apple-chip Mac. x86_64-pc-windows-msvc means 64-bit Windows.

Each system promises a different door. Linux promises that its system call numbers never change. Apple promises only libSystem; its kernel calls may change in any update. Windows supports its system libraries, chiefly kernel32. Zig and Go also call ntdll, whose functions are mostly undocumented but have stayed stable in practice. Windows kernel call numbers change between Windows builds.

Today most Jet programs reach the system through the Rust runtime and the C library. Jet's new Linux backend already makes direct kernel calls in Compiler/JetBackend/Source/OS/Linux.jet.
decisions.story: Lena writes a small command-line tool on her Linux laptop. Her users run Linux, macOS and Windows. Today she needs each system's C files before Jet can build for it, and her Linux file only runs on distributions with a new enough C library.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. Compiler/JetBackend/Source/OS/Linux.jet:38-71 has os_syscall, one raw Linux x86-64 system call written as #FFI(asm) under #Unsafe. Owner ruling 2026-10-01 (#4015) made that file the one audited OS layer for the Jet-written runtime. Its header (lines 15-16) notes that runtime symbols still resolve through the C library while the runtime is the compiled Rust runtime. Image/Runtime.jet already builds small static x86-64 images over raw Linux calls with no C library.

The Jet backend generates x86-64 code only (Source/X64) and writes ELF images only (Image/ELF.jet). The repository has no Mach-O writer, no PE writer and no code signing. AOT programs link the Rust runtime and its global allocator through rustc. jet build --target=<triple> passes the target to rustc. Cross builds need the target's toolchain and C library files (cards #758, #1058, #1060), provisioned by Jetpack under D-ADOPT-CC1=B. Known targets include aarch64 Windows and WASI (crates/jet-foundation/src/Layout.rs:712-717).

Ratified law that constrains every option. D-EFF-LINK1=A: a Linux program that needs only Linux calls ships no separate support library or loader, and real host needs choose their startup at build time. D-NETDNS2=A: ordinary name lookups delegate to the platform resolver and honour hosts files, search domains and VPN policy. It rejected the option where Jet reads the resolver settings and sends DNS itself. D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1=A names the program allocator in package.jet; the allocator default is a separate ballot, D-ALLOC-DEFAULT1.

Other systems. No BSD is a Jet target today. When one is added, A's rule picks libc on OpenBSD, which accepts system calls only from its own C library, and decides FreeBSD from its compatibility promise at that time. WASI keeps its own supported door, the WASI imports. Web and no-OS targets are unchanged.

What is the same in every option. Jet code never changes, Core APIs stay the same, and #FFI(c) programs still link real C libraries.

options.name: Each system's supported door
options.detail:
On Linux, Jet's core library makes system calls directly from Jet, one small audited layer per CPU family. A program that needs only Linux calls becomes one static file with no C library and no loader, as D-EFF-LINK1=A requires.

On macOS it calls Apple's libSystem. On Windows it calls the Windows system libraries: kernel32 and ntdll, plus ws2_32 for networking. Jet bundles their stub files and links with its own linker, so any host builds a pure-Jet program for any of the three with no download.

The C library returns only when a program really needs it. A program that links C code gets the system C library, because C code expects it; cross building it still needs the C toolchain Jetpack fetches (D-ADOPT-CC1=B).

A Linux program that looks up computer names, such as example.com, also gets it. D-NETDNS2=A requires ordinary lookups to use the platform resolver. On Linux that resolver lives in the C library and follows its name-service settings, company directories and VPN rules. Numeric addresses and the expert DnsResolver.at path need no C library. Beginners see none of this; the build report names the path that shipped, and experts may choose the C library on Linux with one package.jet line.
options.technical:
Linux needs system call tables for x86-64, aarch64 and riscv64, with errno taken from the -4095..-1 return range. Threads use clone3 or clone with futex, and the startup code sets thread-local storage. Signals use rt_sigaction with a restorer, and the fast clock reads the vDSO found through auxv. Jet states one minimum kernel per release and probes newer calls at run time with a fallback. Static files are static-PIE, so address randomisation still applies.

On the C-library path, threads and thread-local storage go through the C library's pthreads, because glibc owns each thread's control block; Jet's own clone path runs only without the C library. Name lookup on that path calls getaddrinfo. The in-process jet run tier already runs inside a process that has the C library, so it uses the C-library path.

Jet bundles glibc symbol stubs and builds against a stated minimum glibc, as Zig does, so the C-library path also cross builds from any host. In a target name, the -gnu or -musl suffix chooses the C library for the C-library path only; a pure-Jet Linux file uses neither.

macOS: libSystem through bundled .tbd stubs. Jet needs a Mach-O writer that adds the ad-hoc code signature arm64 requires. Files given to other users also need a Developer ID signature and Apple notarization. Those need Apple credentials and Apple's online notary service; tools such as rcodesign do both from Linux.

Windows: system DLLs through import data generated from redistributable symbol lists, such as mingw-w64's .def files, never copied from an SDK. Jet needs a PE writer with import and TLS tables for x86-64 and aarch64 Windows. Proposed expert fact in package.jet: system_library: .c on Linux.

options.name: The C library everywhere
options.detail:
Jet's core library calls the C library on every system: glibc on Linux, libSystem on macOS and the Universal C Runtime (UCRT) on Windows. Cross builds still work if Jet bundles the C library stubs for every target, as Zig does for glibc versions, or builds musl, a small static Linux C library.

This is one model with less Jet code to maintain: one startup, thread and signal path per system. Name lookups, locales and loading C libraries work exactly as C programs expect.

The costs: a Linux file built against a newer glibc will not start on an older one, unless it uses static musl, whose name lookup and locales behave differently from glibc's. Every system call goes through a C wrapper function, and through the dynamic linker's tables when glibc is shared. Every Linux file carries a C library, even hello, and the core library never becomes Jet all the way down.
options.technical: Linux targets pick glibc with version stubs or static musl. Startup uses the C library's crt files. Signal and thread setup go through pthreads. D-EFF-LINK1=A is met only with static musl, because glibc implies its dynamic loader.

options.name: Raw kernel calls everywhere
options.detail:
Jet makes raw system calls on macOS and Windows too, skipping libSystem, kernel32 and ntdll. Every system would be Jet all the way down, with no stub files at all.

Apple and Microsoft do not support this. Windows changes its system call numbers between builds, and Apple changes its kernel calls without notice. In 2016 macOS 10.12 changed kernel calls that Go made directly, and Go programs built before Go 1.7 did not work correctly on it until rebuilt. Go then moved to libSystem in Go 1.11. Shipped Jet programs could break after an ordinary OS update.
options.technical: Would need per-OS-build syscall tables for Windows and per-release tables for macOS, re-verified for every update. Apple states that it does not support statically linked binaries on macOS, because the kernel call interface is private (Technical Q&A QA1118). Go 1.7 release notes: https://go.dev/doc/go1.7.

comparisons.note: Zig makes direct Linux system calls unless C is linked, uses libSystem stubs on macOS, and kernel32/ntdll import libraries on Windows.
Go calls the Linux kernel directly. Since Go 1.11 it calls libSystem on macOS instead of the kernel.

recommendation.why: A gives Zig-style cross builds from any host for pure-Jet programs, with nothing to download. Linux files without C code or name lookups run on any distribution with no loader. On macOS and Windows it uses only the doors those vendors keep stable, and programs that need the C library keep it, as D-EFF-LINK1=A and D-NETDNS2=A require.
gains: Any host builds pure-Jet Linux, macOS and Windows files with no extra download.
Linux files without C code or name lookups are single static files that start on any distribution, with no loader at start-up.
Linux system calls need no C wrapper, so the core library is Jet down to the kernel.

losses.loss: Jet maintains its own Linux layer per CPU family: system call tables, threads, signals, thread-local storage and the fast clock.
losses.mitigation: The x86-64 call already exists in OS/Linux.jet, Zig and Go maintain the same tables, and each family is tested against the C library's results.

losses.loss: A Linux program that looks up computer names links the system C library and its loader, so it is not a single static file and needs a minimum glibc.
losses.mitigation: Jet bundles glibc stubs and builds against an old stated glibc, so the file still cross builds from any host and starts on current distributions. Numeric addresses and DnsResolver.at stay static.

losses.loss: Programs on the C-library path use its startup, threads and thread-local storage, so Linux has two startup and thread paths.
losses.mitigation: The build picks the path from checked facts, as D-EFF-LINK1=A already requires, and the build report shows which one shipped. One test suite must give identical output on both paths and on every tier (I9).

losses.loss: Much of A does not exist yet: an aarch64 code generator, Mach-O and PE writers, code signing and the Jet-written runtime. Today the Jet backend writes x86-64 ELF only, and AOT builds still go through rustc.
losses.mitigation: These are the D-EXEC1 steps that retire rustc, and B or C need the same writers unless they link with the Jetpack toolchain. Until a target's pieces land, it keeps today's rustc build.

losses.loss: A macOS file built on Linux runs with an ad-hoc signature, but files handed to other users also need a Developer ID signature and Apple notarization.
losses.mitigation: Those need Apple credentials under every option. Tools such as rcodesign sign and notarize from Linux, and the build report says when a file is signed for local use only.

losses.loss: Bundled stub files must be legal to redistribute.
losses.mitigation: Jet generates them from redistributable symbol lists, such as mingw-w64's .def files, as Zig does, and never copies SDK files.

whyNot.reason: B puts a C library in every Linux file, even hello, with either the glibc version trap or musl's different name lookup. Every system call also goes through a C wrapper.
C depends on kernel calls Apple and Microsoft change without notice, so shipped programs can break after an ordinary update.

recommendation.tradeoff: A asks Jet to maintain a Linux system call layer per CPU family, two Linux startup paths and its own Mach-O and PE writers. In return pure-Jet programs get dependency-free Linux files and cross builds from any host.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BallotOutcomes. Skill: rli5. Author-run beginner pass under Main's instruction; it found kernel, stub file, linker and cross compiling undefined and Option A's C-library return unclear, so the explainer and A were rewritten to teach them.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude. Adversarial model family: claude. Fresh agent: NewBallotReview. The review rechecked every code fact, decision and Go claim, finding that A's Linux lookup repeated D-NETDNS2's rejected option and that no Mach-O, PE, aarch64 or signing code exists yet. It added notarization, stub-licence, thread-path, Windows ARM64, WASI and BSD edges, and fixed an overstated ntdll promise and an unfair musl-allocator point against B.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Cross build the same hello, file, thread, clock and name-lookup programs from Linux, macOS and Windows hosts. Targets are x86-64 and aarch64 Linux, aarch64 and x86-64 macOS, and x86-64 and aarch64 Windows. Run each on real or emulated targets and compare output with a C-library build.

On Linux, check that a pure-Jet file is static-PIE with no interpreter and no needed libraries. Check errno mapping, EINTR retries, signals, threads and the vDSO clock against glibc results. Check that a name-lookup program selects the C-library path, calls getaddrinfo, starts on the stated minimum glibc and follows /etc/nsswitch.conf exactly as a C program does.

Check that a program linking C code selects the C-library startup and pthreads, and that the build report names the path. The shared test suite must give identical output on both paths and on the in-process jet run tier. Check that macOS arm64 files carry a valid ad-hoc signature, that Windows files import only Windows system DLLs and never the UCRT, and that every bundled stub records a redistributable source.

surface.gist: Which door should Jet's core library use to reach each operating system?
surface.lesson: Programs ask the operating system for work through a door. Linux keeps its kernel call numbers stable forever. Apple keeps only libSystem stable, and Windows keeps its system libraries, such as kernel32, stable. A uses each stable door, with bundled stub files and Jet's own linker, so any computer builds pure-Jet programs for every target. B uses the C library everywhere. C makes raw kernel calls everywhere.

current.note: Today most programs reach the system through the Rust runtime and C library.

wild.note: Zig cross builds from any host with bundled stubs.

options.name: Each system's supported door
options.gist: Kernel calls on Linux; libSystem on macOS; system libraries such as kernel32 on Windows.
gains: Any host builds pure-Jet programs for every target with no download.
Linux files without C code or name lookups are static.
losses: Jet maintains a Linux call layer per CPU family, plus Mach-O and PE writers.
Linux name lookups and C code bring back the C library.

options.name: The C library everywhere
options.gist: glibc or musl on Linux, libSystem on macOS, UCRT on Windows.
gains: One model; C-style name lookup and locales everywhere.
losses: Every Linux file carries a C library and a glibc version floor.
System calls stay behind C wrapper functions.

options.name: Raw kernel calls everywhere
options.gist: Skip libSystem, kernel32 and ntdll; call every kernel directly.
gains: Jet all the way down on every system.
losses: Apple and Microsoft change these calls without notice.
Shipped programs can break after an OS update.

recommendation.why: A gives cross builds from any host with nothing to download for pure-Jet programs, and dependency-free Linux files. It uses only the doors each vendor keeps stable, and keeps the C library where ratified law needs it.
gains: Cross builds from any host, Zig style.
Static Linux files with no C wrapper or loader.
Only vendor-supported doors on macOS and Windows.

losses.loss: Jet maintains Linux call tables and must build aarch64, Mach-O and PE support.
losses.mitigation: x86-64 calls already exist; tests compare every call with C-library results.

losses.loss: Linux programs that look up names link the C library.
losses.mitigation: bundled glibc stubs keep them cross-buildable from any host.

whyNot.reason: B puts a C library, and the glibc version trap, in every Linux file.
C relies on calls Apple and Microsoft change without notice.

recommendation.tradeoff: A Linux call layer to maintain buys dependency-free Linux files and cross builds from any host.

decisions.title: Which allocator hands out memory in every Jet program
decisions.situation: Every list, text and map a program makes needs a piece of memory, and the allocator is the part of the program that hands those pieces out and takes them back. Today Jet programs use each system's own allocator, called malloc, so speed and memory use change from Linux to macOS to Windows. If Linux builds stop using the C library, they also lose malloc. You are deciding what mem.Heap, the default allocator, means once Jet's core library is written in Jet. We recommend a Jet-written allocator that behaves the same on every system, switched on for a system only after it strictly beats that system's malloc in measurements. Jet's own August measurement found glibc's malloc hard to beat, so that gate is real. The system's malloc stays one package.jet line away as mem.System.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's default allocator be a Jet-written allocator that is the same everywhere, each system's malloc, or a bundled C allocator?
decisions.lesson: An allocator hands out pieces of memory and takes them back. It buys big blocks, called pages, from the operating system and cuts them into small pieces, because asking the system each time is slow. mem.Heap is Jet's default allocator. A makes mem.Heap a Jet-written allocator, the same on every system, after a measured speed check. B keeps each system's malloc. C bundles mimalloc, a fast allocator written in C.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. Memory is the computer's short-term storage. A program needs a piece of it for every list, text or map it builds, and gives the piece back when done.

The operating system hands out memory only in big blocks called pages, usually 4096 bytes, and each request is slow. So every program has an allocator. It is like a shop clerk who buys paper in big rolls and cuts off the length each customer needs. When a piece comes back, the clerk keeps it for the next customer.

malloc is the name of the allocator inside each system's C library. Linux's glibc, macOS and Windows each have their own, with different speed and memory use. Rust programs, and Jet programs today, use it by default.

A thread is one line of work that runs at the same time as others in the same program. A size-class allocator keeps separate shelves for pieces of the same size, such as 16, 32 or 48 bytes. Handing out a small piece is then a quick shelf lookup. Each thread gets its own shelves, so threads rarely wait for each other.

To inline code means the compiler copies a short piece of code straight into the place that uses it, skipping the cost of a call.

mimalloc is a well-known size-class allocator from Microsoft Research, written in C.

Jet already lets a package name its allocator in package.jet (D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1=A). Arenas and pools for special cases already exist and do not change.
decisions.story: Omar's Jet web service keeps millions of small texts. Its memory use differs between his Linux and macOS servers, because each system's malloc keeps and returns memory differently. He wants the same behaviour on every server without tuning each system.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/ProgramAllocator.rs:1-8 and :42-45 make JetProgramAllocator the one program allocator: the Rust global allocator of AOT programs and of the jet process, shared with the in-process tiers. Its hidden default is System mode, Rust's system allocator, which is malloc on Linux and macOS and HeapAlloc on Windows.

package.jet accepts allocator: mem.Heap or allocator: mem.Counting.over(mem.Heap, cap: 2.gb) (crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Package/Blocks.rs:233-241, Examples/features/memory/program_allocator/package.jet:3). mem.Heap is today's malloc. Arena, Bump, Pool and Fixed allocators and #Context(allocator:) live in Prelude/Mem.rs; their API is unaffected, though their blocks come from mem.Heap.

Card #2061 measured Jet itself (docs/research/allocator-impact-2026-08-20.md, in git at 5be9a9560^). On glibc 2.42, preloaded mimalloc was 3.2% and 9.4% faster on two loops and 1.4% to 20.4% slower on five workloads. Three of those five are startup-dominated controls. mimalloc used 23% to 93% more memory everywhere. The card closed with no change to the default.

This ballot depends on D-OS-FLOOR1. If Linux builds skip the C library, B means linking the C library just for malloc, and A's allocator is those files' only heap from day one. A Jet-written allocator needs the atomic words approved in D-RT-NATIVE-CAP1=A.

C code linked into a Jet program keeps calling its own malloc in every option. Under D-FFI-CAP1=A, a value passed to C with ^ is freed by C, so it must live in malloc memory.

options.name: Jet's own allocator, the same everywhere
options.detail:
mem.Heap becomes a Jet-written size-class allocator. It gets pages from the system with mmap on Linux and macOS, and VirtualAlloc on Windows. Each thread has its own shelves, a piece freed by another thread goes back safely, and empty pages return to the system.

It behaves the same on every system, so memory use and speed stop depending on which malloc a system ships. Its small-piece path is Jet code the compiler may inline; the measured gate must show whether that helps.

It becomes a system's default only after a measured gate: on Jet's benchmark set it must strictly beat that system's malloc in time and peak memory. Until then mem.Heap stays malloc there. Beginners write nothing. Experts write allocator: mem.System in package.jet to use the system's malloc.
options.technical:
Design follows free-list sharding as in mimalloc (Leijen, Zorn, de Moura, 2019): per-thread pages per size class, a local free list, and an atomic deferred free list for frees from other threads. A thread that exits hands its pages to the others. Large pieces map whole pages. Empty pages return with madvise or VirtualFree. Huge pages stay under the system's own policy; the allocator never asks for them by default.

It is audited #Unsafe Jet over core.mem.native atomics and D-RAWPTR2 storage. Dev sentries (D-MEM-SENTRY1) and the hardened profile (D-MEM-HARDEN1) add quarantine, guard pages and encoded free-list links. mem.System is a proposed name for the platform malloc; mem.Counting wraps either.

One meaning on every tier (I9): the Jet allocator must also be the Rust global allocator of every AOT program and of the jet process itself. Today ProgramAllocator.rs:4-5 and :42-45 already share one allocator between AOT programs and the in-process tiers. Otherwise memory made by the Rust runtime would be freed by a different allocator.

options.name: Each system's malloc
options.detail:
mem.Heap stays each system's malloc, as today. Jet writes no general-purpose allocator. Jet's own measurement (card #2061) found glibc's malloc ahead of mimalloc on five of seven Jet workloads and leaner in memory on all seven. Behaviour keeps differing by system.

If D-OS-FLOOR1 lets Linux files skip the C library, those files must link it again just for malloc. Programs that want a different allocator wrap or replace mem.Heap themselves. Debugging tools such as ASan, Valgrind and heaptrack keep working, because they watch malloc.
options.technical: No allocator work. Linux files without the C library would need either a C-library link for malloc or a second, minimal page allocator.

options.name: Bundle mimalloc, written in C
options.detail:
Jet compiles mimalloc's C source into its shipped runtime, once per target, and makes it mem.Heap. It is widely used and the same on every system from day one.

The costs: Jet's own measurement (card #2061) found mimalloc slower than glibc's malloc on five of seven Jet workloads, using 23% to 93% more memory. It is an outside dependency that Core's dependency rules must approve. Building the runtime for a new target needs a C compiler, and the allocator stays C that Jet cannot inline or check.
options.technical: Vendored mimalloc source, built per target into the shipped runtime by jet cc with a pinned toolchain (D-ADOPT-CC1=B); licence MIT. User builds need no C compiler when the target's runtime is prebuilt. Cross-language inlining needs whole-program LTO across C and Jet, which the Jet backend does not plan.

comparisons.note: Zig ships general-purpose allocators written in Zig and passes the chosen one explicitly.
Rust uses the system malloc by default; a program swaps the whole-program allocator with one attribute.

recommendation.why: A makes memory behave the same on every system and works without the C library. The strict measured gate means it never becomes a system's default unless it beats that system's malloc.
gains: The same speed and memory behaviour on Linux, macOS and Windows, once each passes the gate.
Works in Linux files that skip the C library.
The allocator is Jet code that Jet's own checks and sentries cover.

losses.loss: Jet owns an allocator, where a bug corrupts memory for the whole program.
losses.mitigation: It is audited #Unsafe code with dev sentries, a hardened profile, fuzzing and differential tests against malloc.

losses.loss: The gate may not pass. In card #2061 a mimalloc-style allocator lost to glibc on most Jet workloads and used more memory.
losses.mitigation: mem.Heap stays malloc on any system where the gate fails, so programs never get slower. Only Linux files without the C library have no malloc to fall back on.

losses.loss: Memory that C code will free must come from malloc, so a ^ hand-over to C needs one copy into malloc memory.
losses.mitigation: D-FFI-CAP1=A already marks such hand-overs with ^, so the binding knows where to copy. Values built with mem.System need no copy.

losses.loss: ASan, Valgrind and heaptrack watch malloc, so they do not see mem.Heap allocations.
losses.mitigation: allocator: mem.System in package.jet restores them, and Jet's dev sentries check the Jet allocator itself.

whyNot.reason: B keeps behaviour different on every system and forces Linux files to link the C library just for malloc. Its speed is real, which is why A must beat it.
C adds an outside C dependency that Jet's own measurement found slower than glibc on most workloads, and Jet cannot inline or check it.

recommendation.tradeoff: A asks Jet to build and audit an allocator that must strictly beat each system's malloc before it ships. In return memory behaves the same everywhere, with no C library and no C compiler needed.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BallotOutcomes. Skill: rli5. Author-run beginner pass under Main's instruction, for an owner who asked what an allocator is. It found page, malloc and size class undefined, so the lesson and explainer now teach them with a shop-clerk picture.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude. Adversarial model family: claude. Fresh agent: NewBallotReview. The review rechecked every code fact and found card #2061's own allocator measurement, which the ballot had called missing, plus a match-or-beat gate weaker than AGENTS.md's strict rule. It added I9 tier, C hand-over copy, debugger, huge-page and thread-exit costs, and fixed C's unfair every-build compiler claim.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Build the allocator benchmark set: many small texts, mixed sizes, producer and consumer threads, a long-lived server, a short command, and card #2061's seven workloads. Each is a paired two-program cell, identical except allocator: mem.Heap or allocator: mem.System, recorded in the canonical manifest. Run it on Linux, macOS and Windows and record time and peak memory. The Jet allocator becomes a system's default only where it strictly beats malloc on every cell and both metrics (AGENTS.md performance gate).

Check frees from another thread, thread exit, returning empty pages, allocation failure through the try_ family, and Counting over both allocators. Measure peak memory with transparent huge pages set to always and to madvise. Run dev sentries and the hardened profile over the allocator tests, and fuzz random allocate, free and resize sequences against malloc.

Check that the same program reports the same Counting facts on every tier. Check that memory handed to C with ^ is freed by C without error, and that allocator: mem.System lets ASan and Valgrind see every allocation.

surface.gist: Should Jet's default allocator be Jet-written and the same everywhere, each system's malloc, or bundled C?
surface.lesson: An allocator hands out pieces of memory and takes them back. It buys big pages from the system and cuts them up, because asking the system each time is slow. mem.Heap is Jet's default allocator. A makes it Jet-written and the same everywhere, after a speed check. B keeps each system's malloc. C bundles mimalloc, written in C.

current.note: Today mem.Heap is each system's malloc.

wild.note: Zig ships its own general-purpose allocator.

options.name: Jet's own allocator, the same everywhere
options.gist: mem.Heap becomes Jet-written on each system where it measurably beats malloc.
gains: Same behaviour on every system that passes.
Works without the C library.
losses: Jet must build and audit an allocator that beats glibc.
Hand-overs to C cost a copy; malloc debuggers see less.

options.name: Each system's malloc
options.gist: mem.Heap stays the system's malloc, as today.
gains: No allocator work, and glibc won most of Jet's own measurements.
losses: Speed and memory differ by system.
C-free Linux files must link C for malloc.

options.name: Bundle mimalloc, written in C
options.gist: mem.Heap is mimalloc compiled into Jet's runtime for each target.
gains: Widely used and the same on every system.
losses: Slower than glibc on most of Jet's own workloads.
An outside C dependency Jet cannot inline or check.

recommendation.why: A gives the same memory behaviour everywhere without the C library. A strict speed and memory gate decides each system's switch.
gains: Same behaviour on Linux, macOS and Windows.
No C library or C compiler needed.
The allocator is checked Jet code.

losses.loss: An allocator bug corrupts the whole program.
losses.mitigation: audited code, dev sentries, hardened profile and fuzzing against malloc.

losses.loss: The gate may never pass against glibc.
losses.mitigation: mem.Heap stays malloc wherever the gate fails.

losses.loss: Hand-overs to C cost one copy.
losses.mitigation: the ^ marker already tells the binding where.

whyNot.reason: B keeps per-system differences and needs the C library for malloc.
C adds an outside C allocator that measured slower than glibc.

recommendation.tradeoff: Building one allocator that must beat malloc buys the same memory behaviour everywhere with no C dependency.

decisions.title: How a program starts another copy of itself
decisions.situation: Some programs start a fresh copy of themselves, for example to test crash cleanup in a separate process. Jet's example does this by running os.executable() with one extra argument. After jet build, os.executable() names the program file, so that works. Under jet run, the program runs inside the jet tool, so os.executable() names jet itself. Each child then runs a command like `jet return`, which fails, and the example quietly prints the wrong output. You are deciding how a program reliably relaunches itself in both modes. We recommend a new process.self_cmd(args) call that always reruns this same program, while os.executable() keeps naming the real file of the running process.
decisions.gist: How should a Jet program start another copy of itself so it works the same under jet run and jet build?
decisions.lesson: A process is one running program. os.executable() returns the file the operating system started. After jet build that is your program. Under jet run it is the jet tool, which runs your program inside itself. A adds process.self_cmd(args), which always reruns this program. B makes jet run hand out a small launcher file instead. C only documents the difference and leaves relaunching to each author.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. A process is one running program, with its own memory and its own exit code. A child process is a process another program starts.

Jet has two ways to run code. jet build makes a native program file you can start directly. jet run compiles your program and runs it inside the jet tool's own process. Jet's law says both must behave the same.

os.executable() asks the operating system which file started the current process. After jet build that file is your program. Under jet run it is the jet tool.

process.cmd(argv) builds a description of a child process from a list: the program file first, then its arguments. process.run_spec runs that description and returns a receipt with the exit code and output.

The example cleanup_matrix starts itself six times, each with a case name, to watch cleanup happen in a separate process. Under jet run each child becomes `jet return` or `jet error`. jet does not know those commands, so every child exits with an error.

Relaunch means starting a new copy of the same program. The question is which call names that copy correctly in both modes.
decisions.story: Omar writes a test harness that starts his program again in a child process for each crash scenario. It works after jet build. Under jet run every child prints a jet usage error, and his harness reports success with empty traces.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. Core/sys/sys.jet:53 declares executable() -[Env]> String. The native leaf in crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/OsExtra.rs:18-22 returns std::env::current_exe(). Under jet run the program runs inside the jet process, so that path is the jet binary. Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:1499 only says executable() returns process and operating-system facts. Examples/features/io/sys_executable.jet:1-2 already states that meaning: the jet host under jet run, the built binary after jet build.

process.argv() is already made the same in both modes. jet run hands the program its own argument list through one shared carrier (crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Interpreter.rs:663-690, crates/jet-jit/src/Collections.rs:2286-2289). os.executable() has no such carrier.

Examples/features/io/cleanup_matrix.jet:86-95 relaunches itself with process.cmd([os.executable(), path]). Card #4346 records that under jet run every child ran `jet return` and similar, exited 2, and the example still exited 0. process.cmd takes the full argument list, program first (core-library.md:1574). jet run takes program arguments after `--` (Docs/spec/reference/cli.md:27), and --allow, --deny, --profile and similar flags shape the run (cli.md:127-130).

Other examples relaunch the same way. They are Examples/features/foundations/distributed/run.jet:65-72, foundations/storage/run.jet:20 and io/watcher.jet:91. Jetpack does too, in Jetpack/Store/Tests/Broker.jet:386 and Jetpack/Services/Source/Supervisor/Lifecycle.jet:60. The test helper tests/dev_parts/support.rs:3463-3470 works around the watcher case by pointing argv at the AOT binary.

Other Jetpack code reads os.executable() to find files beside the running binary. Examples are Jetpack/Foundation/Source/SourceRoot.jet:13 and Jetpack/Store/Source/ArtifactStore/NativeRuntimeCache.jet:244.

Ratified law. D-VERDICT-1254-1 requires that nothing works under jet build and fails under default jet run. D-VERDICT-687-1 makes jet run and jet build two views over one compiler. D-EFF-BUILD-REUSE1=B reuses checked work across fresh compiler processes, so a relaunched jet run child does not recheck from nothing.

No Core call today returns the entry file or the jet run flags, so a program cannot build a correct relaunch list by itself under jet run.

options.name: process.self_cmd(args) reruns this program
options.detail:
A new call, process.self_cmd(args: [String]) -> ProcessSpec, builds a child that runs this same program with these arguments. After jet build the list is the program file followed by args. Under jet run it is jet, run, the same absolute entry and every flag that shaped the parent run, then `--` and args. The child therefore runs the same way as its parent.

os.executable() keeps its plain meaning, the file of the running process, which is jet under jet run. The checker warns when os.executable() is the program element of process.cmd, and names self_cmd as the fix. All in-repo self-relaunches move to self_cmd([...]) in the same change, and the support.rs workaround is deleted. The returned value is an ordinary ProcessSpec, so streams, limits and authority work as usual, and .plan() shows the real list.
options.technical:
The run driver records the entry path, project root and the program-shaping flags it applied in the process-start facts. Those flags are rights, profile, preset, fixtures, locked and offline, and they travel through the carrier that already feeds process.argv(). self_cmd reads those facts; an AOT program records its own path instead. Under jet test the child reruns jet test on the same file, and the caller selects a test through its own arguments or environment, as Broker.jet:386-387 does.

The call carries the same -[Exec] effect as process.cmd. One registry row, one Core declaration, one leaf per back end, one registered warning, a spec row beside executable() and goldens for every migrated example on both modes land together.

options.name: jet run hands out a launcher file
options.detail:
Under jet run, os.executable() returns the path of a small launcher file that jet writes before the program starts. Starting that file runs jet run on the same entry with the same flags. Existing code like cleanup_matrix works unchanged.

The cost is that os.executable() no longer names the running file under jet run. Code that hashes its own file, reads files beside it, or reports its path gets the launcher instead; Jetpack's SourceRoot.jet:13 and NativeRuntimeCache.jet:244 do that today. jet must write and mark executable a launcher per entry and flag set, with a .cmd or .exe form on Windows.
options.technical: jet run writes the launcher under the project's .jet directory keyed by entry and flags, reused across runs. The leaf returns that path on the run path and current_exe after jet build. Launcher creation failure must be reported, not silently fall back to the jet path.

options.name: Document the difference only
options.detail:
os.executable() is documented as the running file: jet under jet run, the program after jet build. No new call is added. A program that wants to relaunch must detect the mode and build the jet run command itself.

Today no Core call gives the entry file or the run flags, so this needs at least a mode check and an entry-path fact. The same source still has two meanings, which the parity law forbids.
options.technical: Adds documentation and, to be usable, two facts: whether the program runs under jet run, and its entry path. cleanup_matrix branches on the mode.

comparisons.note: Node keeps process.execPath as the real node binary and offers child_process.fork(file) to rerun a script in a new process.
Python keeps sys.executable as the interpreter, so a script relaunches with the interpreter plus its own path.

recommendation.why: A gives relaunching one call that means the same thing in both modes, which the parity law requires. os.executable() keeps telling the truth about the running file, so code that inspects its own file keeps working.
gains: Self-relaunch works the same under jet run and after jet build.
os.executable() keeps one honest meaning: the file the system started.
The child is an ordinary ProcessSpec, so plans, limits and authority still apply.

losses.loss: Code that relaunches with os.executable() must move to the new call, and code outside the repository that keeps the old pattern still fails under jet run.
losses.mitigation: The in-repo examples and Jetpack callers migrate with the call. The registered warning on os.executable() as process.cmd's program points every other caller at self_cmd.

losses.loss: A relaunched child under jet run starts the jet tool again, which is slower than starting a built program.
losses.mitigation: D-EFF-BUILD-REUSE1=B reuses checked work across fresh compiler processes, and jet build removes the cost entirely.

whyNot.reason: Under jet run, B makes os.executable() name a file that is not the running process. That breaks code that finds files beside its binary, and it adds a launcher file per entry and flag set.
C leaves one source with two meanings and makes every author rebuild the jet run command by hand.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one process call. In return relaunching works in both modes and os.executable() stays truthful.

decisions.title: How you limit the compiler to N threads or one
decisions.situation: Jet's compiler will soon spread its work over every processor core, so large programs build much faster. People also need a way to cap it, for example one thread for a timing test, or two on a laptop that runs hot. Most build tools call this control --jobs, but in Jet the word jobs already means your project's named tasks, run with jet jobs. You are deciding the flag's name and whether a shell setting may also set it; we recommend --threads N and no shell setting.
decisions.gist: What should the flag that caps the Jet compiler's threads be called, and may a shell setting set it too?
decisions.lesson: A thread is one line of work a program runs alongside others; more threads keep more processor cores busy. With no flag, the compiler picks a safe thread count by itself. A names the cap --threads N. B uses the --jobs N and -j N spelling from Cargo and Make. C is A plus a JET_THREADS shell setting.
decisions.explainer:
A processor core is one part of the chip that runs instructions; most computers have 4 to 64. A thread is one line of work inside a program, and 8 threads can keep 8 cores busy.

The compiler will split its work into small pieces that run on separate threads and are merged in a fixed order. The output is byte-for-byte the same with one thread or thirty-two. With no flag, it starts extra threads only when there is useful work and enough free memory, so small programs stay on one thread.

A flag is an option typed after a command, such as --release. A shell setting, also called an environment variable, is a named value the shell hands to every program it starts, such as PATH.

In Jet, jet jobs already lists and runs a project's named tasks, such as a database migration or a release script.
decisions.story: Ana builds a large Jet project during a video call, and her laptop gets hot and slow. She wants jet build to use only two cores. Her teammate wants a one-thread build in CI to compare timings with the parallel one.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. Card #4310 records the owner direction of 2026-10-02: use every core when it is reliable and safe, and keep an explicit single-threaded mode. Its plan names --jobs 1 and --jobs N only as a working spelling. The speed plan (SPEED-PLAN.md:356 and 448-457) marks the command spelling, default and environment variable as this owner ballot.

The word jobs is taken. Docs/spec/reference/cli.md:51 lists jet jobs for named project jobs, and ratified D-JOB-SUBCMD1, D-DX-JOBS-UX1, D-JOB-ARGV1 and D-JOB-ENV1 define that surface. A search of Compiler/, crates/ and Docs/ on 2026-10-04 found no existing --jobs or --threads flag.

Hidden controls already exist. The Rust checker reads an undocumented JET_CHECK_THREADS variable and caps itself at 8 workers (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Bundle/Parallel.rs:6-31). The loader caps front-end workers at 8 (crates/jet-driver/src/Loader.rs:25 and 414-418). The JIT's define batch uses every reported core (crates/jet-jit/src/jit/define_batch.rs:207-209). Separately, JET_SCHEDULER_THREADS sets the running program's scheduler workers (Docs/spec/reference/environment.md:42).

The default is already ratified. D-EFF-JOB-ADMISSION1=A admits work only when useful work and memory permit, never starts one large worker per core blindly, and lets existing expert caps reduce admission. The core count comes from the operating system's available-parallelism answer, which already backs os.cpu_count() (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/OsExtra.rs:10-14).

This ballot covers compiler work only. How many tests jet test runs at once is a separate question.

options.name: --threads N, no shell setting
options.detail:
Every command that compiles accepts --threads N: jet build, run, check, test, dev and inspect. --threads 1 runs the whole compiler on one thread. With no flag, the compiler uses as many threads as memory-aware admission allows, up to the cores the system reports. N must be a whole number of at least 1; 0 or a non-number is a usage error naming the flag. Typing --jobs or -j gets a usage error that suggests --threads.

The name says what is limited and does not collide with jet jobs. It caps the compiler only, never the threads of the program that jet run, test or dev starts. Help text and the build report both call it compiler threads, so jet run --threads 2 is not read as the program's own thread count. No environment variable reads it, so the cap is always visible on the command line.
options.technical: The flag joins the shared compile options in the CLI pack, so every compiling command parses it once. The value caps the admission pool from D-EFF-JOB-ADMISSION1=A; admission may still run fewer. Clean cutover: JET_CHECK_THREADS is deleted, and the loader, checker and JIT pools all draw from that one capped pool. Output bytes and diagnostics are identical for every value, proven by the determinism gate in card #4310. No short form is added.
options.code:
$ jet build                # automatic
$ jet build --threads 2    # at most two threads
$ jet build --threads 1    # one thread
$ jet build -j 2
error: unknown flag -j; did you mean --threads 2?

options.name: --jobs N and -j N, like Cargo and Make
options.detail:
Every compiling command accepts --jobs N and the short -j N, matching Cargo, Make, Ninja and Bazel. --jobs 1 is single-threaded and the default is automatic, as in A. JET_CHECK_THREADS is deleted as in A.

The spelling is familiar to anyone from those tools. In Jet it reads like project jobs. jet build --jobs 4 can be taken to run four of the project's named jobs. Help text that lists jobs as a command would sit next to --jobs as a flag.
options.technical: Same mechanism as A under a different name, plus a one-letter alias. Help text and the jobs reference must explain both meanings of the word.
options.code:
$ jet build -j 2            # at most two compiler workers
$ jet jobs migrate          # a project job, a different thing

options.name: --threads N plus a JET_THREADS environment variable
options.detail:
The flag works as in A. In addition, JET_THREADS=N sets the cap for every Jet command in that shell or CI job, and the flag overrides it. JET_THREADS replaces today's undocumented JET_CHECK_THREADS.

This helps a CI system that wants one setting for all steps. It also means a build can change speed and memory use because of a setting missing from its command line. JET_THREADS would also sit beside JET_SCHEDULER_THREADS, which caps the running program, not the compiler.
options.technical: The CLI reads JET_THREADS once at start, validates it like the flag, and the build report records which source set the cap.
options.code:
$ export JET_THREADS=2
$ jet build                 # at most two threads
$ jet build --threads 8     # the flag wins: eight

comparisons.note: Cargo uses --jobs and -j, plus a CARGO_BUILD_JOBS environment variable; jobs has no other meaning in Cargo.
rustc names its parallel front-end control threads, because it limits threads inside one compiler process.

recommendation.why: A names the control after what it limits, so it never reads as project jobs. With no flag the compiler already picks a safe count, so the flag is rarely needed, and every cap stays visible on the command line.
gains: No confusion with jet jobs and project tasks.
One flag on every compiling command, with --threads 1 for one thread.
The thread cap always appears on the command line and in the build report.

losses.loss: People used to Cargo or Make will type --jobs or -j first.
losses.mitigation: Both answer with a usage error that suggests --threads N, so the habit costs one retry.

losses.loss: A CI system must add the flag to each command instead of setting it once.
losses.mitigation: The automatic default already keeps builds within memory, so most CI needs no flag; a shell setting can be balloted later if real CI asks.

whyNot.reason: B gives jobs two meanings in one tool, so jet build --jobs 4 reads like running four project jobs.
C lets a setting missing from the command line change build speed and memory use, and it would sit beside an existing setting that caps the running program's threads.

recommendation.tradeoff: A gives up the familiar --jobs spelling. In return the flag says what it limits and never collides with project jobs.

decisions.title: One Color value that every Core library uses
decisions.situation: Jet's terminal, game and user-interface libraries each describe a color in their own way today. A color picked for a game cannot be handed to the terminal library without copying its numbers by hand, and the interface library only takes a color as text. On 2026-10-01 the owner chose one Core color value that all three libraries use. This record writes that ruling down.
decisions.gist: Should Core define one Color value that the terminal, game and interface libraries all use?
decisions.lesson: A color is usually four numbers: red, green, blue and transparency, each from 0 to 255. Option A makes this one Core value with conversions to hex text, to HSL and to linear light. The terminal, game and interface libraries take that one value, and their own color types go away.
decisions.story: Ana picks a brand orange for her game's menu and wants the same orange in her terminal tool. Today she copies three numbers into a second color type and types a third spelling as text. Under option A she writes the color once and passes it to both.
decisions.detail:
Owner answer, 2026-10-01 chat (ask question s3288): "One core.color.Color". The question asked, verbatim:

"#3288: tui, game and ui each define their own color struct today. Should Core define one `core.color.Color` (sRGB 8-bit + alpha, with linear/HSL/hex conversions) that all of them use?"

The owner picked the first offered option, which was also the recommended one.

Today Core/tui/tui.jet has TuiColor with Rgb(red, green, blue) as Int. Core/game/raylib.jet:19-35 has RaylibColor{r,g,b,a} clamped by clamp8. Core/ui/ui.jet:123 node_color takes the color as a String. No Core hex, HSL or linear conversion exists. The plan on #3288 lists the module, the provider migration and the golden ui/color_conversions.

decisions.title: New results come back as returns
decisions.situation: Jet lets a function change a value supplied by its caller, which is useful for editing existing data. The same permission can hide a newly calculated answer among the inputs, making callers create a dummy value first. We recommend requiring returns for new results in Jet's public APIs, while keeping real edits and streams. This vote chooses that API rule, not a new keyword or a ban on changing values.
decisions.gist: Must public Jet APIs return new results, rather than fill dummy input values?
decisions.lesson: An output parameter is a supplied value used only to receive an answer. A return sends the answer back from the call. Jet already supports both returns and changes marked with &. Both choices keep real edits, file writes, and foreign calls; neither adds syntax.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: call split(17, 5), then read the returned quotient and remainder. A quotient is the number of whole divisions; a remainder is what is left. Here they are 3 and 2. A struct groups named values; Parts groups these two answers. :: binds a value for reading. := makes a changeable local. An & before an argument permits the function to change that caller-owned value. /% divides whole numbers, and % gives the remainder. A quoted {expression} inserts its value into text.

Expert path: keep & for operations whose purpose is to edit existing data or send pieces to a live destination. An encoder that needs reusable storage can take ownership of that storage with ^ and return it with the result, rather than use a blank output argument. Borrowing, moving, error handling, and caller-selected fixed storage retain their existing rules. This ballot adds no allocation guarantee.

The same tiny program is used throughout: divide 17 by 5 and print 3 2. All displayed Jet programs are source-derived illustrations, not newly executed results. Option A changes which public API shape is accepted in review; option B leaves that shape to the author. The compiler grammar accepts both shapes in either option.
decisions.story: Ana divides a byte count into full blocks and leftover bytes. She wants both answers without creating a fake answer first.
decisions.detail:
Background: CHAT-TASKS.md:125 and 127 identify items 88 and 90, both from owner prompt 2603. In history.db row 2603 the owner asked for a binary size display builtin. The same row says: 'i also dont love the paradigm of c++ where you include an output parameter as an input parameter, i think is should basically be an output. Open to further discussion on this point to see what is truly best of all worlds approach'. The owner expresses a preference, not approval of a compiler prohibition.

Existing-decision check: Tower decision list and decision show on 2026-10-04 confirm D-FMT-BYTES1=A already settles item 88. No general output-parameter policy appears in the decision list. D-EFF-FORMAT-WRITER1=A, ratified 2026-10-03, specifically keeps String-returning Display and compiler-hidden destinations; it does not ban general write parameters. This ballot does not reopen that Display contract.

Grounding: Docs/spec/spec.md:895-908 specifies read T, write &T, and take ^T. Docs/spec/spec.md:914-920 demonstrates an ordinary write parameter. Core/crypto/crypto.jet:91-93 has a genuine state update and a returned digest. Core/encoding/binary.jet:342-345 already returns two named answers. D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D keeps value-side marks. D-FREESTAND-ALLOCAPI1=A preserves fixed values, views, and caller-owned storage in no-heap Core; this ballot must not erase those contracts. D-DENY-COST1=A provides expert cost ceilings; it does not make every returning call allocation-free.

Owner-only scope: choose a required public API design rule versus guidance alone. Enforcement is API review, not a speculative read-before-write detector or a new lint. 'Public' means Jet-authored exported functions, methods, traits, and callback contracts, including Core and published packages. Private helpers follow the recommended return convention but are not a new compiler rejection. Required shared work is updating teaching and checking API contracts against the selected rule; costs common to both options are not listed as option losses.

options.name: Require returned results
options.detail:
A public Jet API returns a newly calculated answer. Multiple answers use one existing tuple or struct return. An output-only parameter is caller-supplied storage whose prior value is not part of the operation and whose purpose is to receive that answer. Such a parameter is not accepted in public API review. The Parts return below is accepted; the blank Parts argument shown in B is not.

Keep & for genuine edits, stateful handles, accumulation, and stream destinations. Examples are sorting an existing list, appending to an existing buffer, updating a hasher, and writing pieces to a file. A buffer's capacity can be a real input even when its previous bytes are not; existing checked byte-reader and fixed-storage contracts stay valid. Do not classify an API solely by whether it reads old bytes. A function named fill is not automatically exempt: the contract must describe the existing state, capacity, or stream being operated on.

Beginner path: receive Parts directly and read its fields. Expert path: use the existing write/take model for real state or storage; return counts and status as ordinary results. No new output marker, second overload, or implicit public destination is added. Display continues to return String.
options.technical:
This is a public API policy, not a syntax or type-system change. Both snippets remain grammatically valid; the B signature fails the selected review rule, not compilation. Apply the rule to exported functions, methods, trait requirements, and callback contracts, so moving the same output argument into a callback does not bypass it. Private helpers and compiler-generated machine calling conventions may use internal destinations.

Cutover: inventory affected public Jet APIs; migrate every output-only contract, implementation, and caller to one return shape, then remove obsolete signatures, aliases, examples, and teaching. Do not rename genuine mutable APIs or create return/output pairs. Do not claim this inventory has already been performed.

Failure and absence use existing return outcomes; a failed calculation produces no success Parts.

Existing mutation or stream failures retain their documented state/partial-write semantics; no new rollback guarantee is imposed. If partial calculation results are useful, put them explicitly in the returned error/result type. 

Preserve move-only results, caller-provided capacity, and no-heap fixed results using existing ownership and storage mechanisms. Ordinary returns may use hidden caller destination storage at the machine boundary; that is not a public output parameter. Raw foreign signatures remain faithful to the foreign contract behind the existing boundary, while Jet-authored public adapters return their new results. A foreign function with unsupported parameter metadata is not guessed or silently adapted.

Example domain: n >= 0 and d > 0; outside that domain existing arithmetic behavior applies. This is an API-shape example, not a new checked-division operation. Both alternatives compute the same quotient and remainder.

options.name: Teach returns; let authors choose
options.detail:
Teach returns as the usual way to obtain new answers, but permit output-only & parameters in public APIs. Ana may call split with a blank Parts value. The author may choose that shape for explicit caller storage or a foreign-style interface without failing API review. Existing String-returning Display remains unchanged.

Beginner path: learn returns first, then recognize that & can mean either editing an input or filling a result. Expert path: keep direct caller-storage APIs with documented initialization, capacity, and failure behavior. No separate out keyword or compiler analysis is added.
options.technical:
Preserve the existing T, &T, and ^T contracts unchanged. An output-only & argument is initialized before the call and still obeys exclusivity, lifetime, and alias rules; this is not uninitialized memory. The example overwrites the complete Parts and reads no old field. It returns Unit and prints the same 3 2 as A. D-EFF-FORMAT-WRITER1 remains authoritative for Display. Real edits, streams, no-heap storage, raw foreign contracts, and arithmetic domain are identical to A.

The return recommendation is teaching, not a rejection or warning. Require documentation of whether each mutable argument is input/output or output-only and what remains valid on failure. An author may retain caller-capacity operations but must not claim that & alone proves lower allocation or fewer copies. Returned results remain available without imposing two parallel spellings for every operation.

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#Rf-out and #Rf-out-multi. F.20 recommends returning outputs because a reference can mean either in/out or out-only. F.21 prefers a struct for multiple outputs. F.20 also preserves reusable capacity and expensive-to-move storage exceptions. This supports distinguishing new answers from real storage inputs rather than banning every mutable parameter. No adoption count or benchmark was obtained.

recommendation.why: A makes new answers visible as returns, without removing real edits or streams. Beginners need no dummy answer; experts keep storage control.
gains: New answers have one public shape.
Multiple answers keep their field names.
Real mutable inputs and stream destinations remain available.

losses.loss: Some existing public output-only APIs need changed callers.
losses.mitigation: Return one tuple or struct, migrate all callers together, and remove the old signature.

whyNot.reason: B keeps dummy answers and lets the same & mark mean either editing input or receiving a new result.

recommendation.tradeoff: A requires source migration for output-only public contracts; real state, capacity, streams, and foreign boundaries keep their existing rules.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Before posting, Main links this draft to its owner-choice card and runs Tower's ballot validator. This is a short policy ballot with no new syntax or invariant exception; independent full-profile reviews are not claimed. No compiler programs, tests, validators, or performance checks were run by the drafter.

Owner acceptance: confirm the scope is exported Jet APIs and API review, not a compiler ban on all & parameters. Confirm that true mutable state, reusable capacity, streams, and raw foreign boundaries remain supported. Confirm whether the strict return policy or guidance-only policy is desired.

After ratification and the bootstrap gate, inventory and migrate every affected contract, implementation, caller, and example. Run the two same-program examples with the then-current compiler and require 3 2. For A, review rejects B's exported output-only shape while the private grammar remains valid. Exercise multiple returned values, move-only results, no-heap fixed outputs, storage reuse, stateful updates, streaming and partial-write errors, foreign adapters, and Display's ratified String return. Exercise failure/absence without a fake success result. Use the existing cost checks and paired programs before claiming an allocation or copying improvement.

surface.gist: Must public Jet APIs return new results, rather than fill dummy input values?
surface.lesson: An output parameter is a supplied value used only to receive an answer. A return sends the answer back. & permits changes. Real edits, streams, and foreign calls remain supported.

current.note: Jet permits this shape. The example is source-derived, not executed.

wild.note: Modern C++ guidance also prefers returns for new answers.

options.gist: Public APIs return new answers; review enforces this, not a compiler ban.
gains: No dummy answer.
Real edits and streams stay available.
losses: Existing output-only APIs need migration; move all callers together.

options.name: Teach returns; let authors choose
options.gist: Returns are recommended; public output arguments remain allowed.
gains: Authors choose caller-storage interfaces.
losses: Dummy answers remain; documentation must explain every mutable argument's role.

recommendation.why: A makes new answers visible as returns. Beginners need no dummy answer; experts keep real edits, storage control, and streams.
gains: One public shape for new answers.

losses.loss: Some existing APIs need changed callers.
losses.mitigation: Return one tuple or struct and migrate every caller together.

designAway.loss: A blanket mutable-parameter ban would remove sorting, state updates, and streams.
attempts: Ban every & parameter; rejected because it removes real inputs.
Distinguish new answers from existing state, capacity, and live destinations; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: genuine mutable inputs and stream contracts retain their existing shapes.

designAway.loss: Returning large or fixed results could be mistaken for forced allocation or copying.
attempts: Promise every return is allocation-free; rejected as unsupported.
Keep existing fixed storage, move ownership, hidden machine destinations, and expert cost ceilings; kept.
designAway.result: No new storage restriction is imposed; any performance claim still needs its own exercised proof.

designAway.loss: Automatic read-before-write classification could reject legitimate capacity reuse or miss intent.
attempts: Infer output-only intent from body reads; rejected because contract intent is not equivalent to data flow.
Enforce the public API rule in contract review; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: no new compiler heuristic, warning, or rejection is introduced.

designAway.loss: Existing output-only public APIs need changed callers.
attempts: Keep compatibility aliases; rejected because they preserve two output shapes.
Migrate all contracts and callers together to one tuple or struct result; kept.
