decisions.title: Where chip knowledge lives, so new hardware can arrive as a library change
decisions.situation: Jet's built-in library is moving into ordinary Jet source files, and the compiler will read only the parts a program uses. Today, teaching Jet a new chip instruction, graphics card or operating system means changing the compiler itself and shipping a whole new release. You asked for hardware support to arrive as a library pull request instead, without giving up speed. This vote decides where knowledge about chips lives, and we recommend typed instruction entries in the library, each with a plain Jet meaning.
decisions.gist: Where should knowledge about chips live, so new hardware support can arrive as a library change?
decisions.lesson: An instruction is one operation a chip can run, such as taking sixteen square roots at once. A library change ships in Jet's built-in library, separately from the compiler program. A plain meaning is ordinary Jet code that gives the same answer more slowly; tests compare it with the chip. Jet's own code generator makes fast-start and default builds; release builds use LLVM, an outside code generator.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: nothing new to learn. Built-in operations such as list sums get faster when the library learns a chip, and every program keeps the same answers.

Expert path: import the chip module, mark a function with the chip levels to build copies for, and test a chip feature at build time. That path is already approved; this vote only decides where the instructions it uses come from.

Shared by every option: the built-in library ships as its own signed bundle. The compiler reads only the parts a program uses. Small built-in operations, such as whole-number math and list indexing, are expanded inline at every build level. Larger library code is compiled once and shared, as already approved.

The options differ in one thing. A library pull request can teach Jet a new instruction at full speed on every build level in A, only in release builds in B, and not at all in C.
decisions.story: Mia's new laptop chip takes sixteen square roots in one step. She wants Jet to use it without waiting for a new compiler.
decisions.detail:
Owner request, 2026-10-04, card #4565: hardware support should arrive by pull request rather than a full compiler release. Performance must stay flawless, Core must be well structured in Core/*.jet, and Core must load only when used. Research: Docs/research/compiler-corelib-boundary-2026-10-04.md.

Settled, not balloted. D-CORE-SOURCE-AUTHORITY1=A already makes Core behavior ordinary Jet source over a small audited kernel. The owner's 2026-09-28 direction on #3690 phases out Rust-native Core. D-EFF-CORE-INIT1=A starts Core services only on use.

Also settled: D-EXEC1=A compiles Core once and shares it across levels. Lazy loading through memory-mapped interface records is implementation work under speed plan SP12 and card #2517. Layering follows D-RINGLAYER1=A and D-FREESTAND-PRELUDE1=A.

Open, and decided here: where chip knowledge lives, and whether Core ships as its own signed bundle. The second point changes D-EXEC1's wording from 'for each Jet version' to 'for each Core bundle'.

Today the compiler crate embeds 222,864 lines of Rust runtime under crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude. The jet-sema crate embeds all 110 Core source texts with include_str! (crates/jet-sema/src/CoreSourceTexts.rs). Any Core edit therefore rebuilds the compiler binary.

Core/*.jet has 40,628 lines in 115 files. Prelude/Core.jet holds 1,757 dispatcher rows that bind Core names to Rust symbols; 599 also carry a separate JIT symbol. TBuiltinOp has 220 compiler operations, about 180 of them library algorithms such as sets and deques.

Hardware today: SIMD kernels are Rust in Prelude/Core/SimdLanes.rs and check the chip on each operation (lines 814-1191). GPU kernels are PTX and SPIR-V string constants in CoreLib/Top/Compute.rs (lines 1160 and 2200). OSTarget.rs is a closed enum of three systems. #Multiversion and core.arch are ratified but absent from code.

Card #3983 is the Jet compiler catching up with a split design. Core is half rows the compiler interprets and half source it re-checks, so both compilers re-implement both halves. With interface records, both compilers read one checked Core instead.

Peers keep a closed kernel of primitive operations: Julia has 92 intrinsic rows, Zig about 121 builtins, Rust 205 compiler intrinsics, Swift 264 builtin rows and Odin 266 intrinsics. Mojo, Swift and Carbon define Int itself in the library.

Hardware without a compiler release uses library declarations mapped to backend operations. Mojo's mulhi calls llvm_intrinsic with a plain fallback. Julia's CUDA.jl adds PTX instructions inside the package through llvmcall. Odin writes its AVX-512 file as library code over portable lane operations.

Rust's trap: stdarch's avx512f.rs binds 369 LLVM intrinsics in the library, but feature names live in rustc_target. Stable AVX-512 features still waited for the Rust 1.89 release on 2025-08-07. Option A keeps feature and level rows beside the instructions.

Under D-EXEC1, Jet's own code generator makes the fast-start and default levels, and LLVM makes only release builds. An LLVM-only door, option B, gives new instructions full speed only in release builds. Terra's documentation warns that its intrinsic set is 'not under Terra's control'.

Performance: kernel operations such as exact-Int arithmetic, checked indexing, atomics and lane math expand inline at every level, as operators do today. Today each Int operation is an out-of-line call, root cause 2 in Docs/audits/compile-cost-hello-2026-10-02.md.

Core methods bound to a kernel operation have no Jet body, the way Carbon binds int.convert_checked. A Core function made only of kernel operations, with no loops and under the inliner's limit, expands at the call site from record MIR. Every other Core body is compiled once.

Loading: rustc 1.97.1 type-checked hello against about 80 MB of memory-mapped standard-library metadata in 0.04 s, measured here on 2026-10-04. Jet's Jet-written compiler spends about 18 s and 11 GB restoring its whole image for hello. SP12 sets a 30 ms startup budget.

Shared work for every option: the signed Core bundle with per-module records and prebuilt runtime objects, the kernel table and roles, the layer rules, #3983 parity, and then the #3690 port. These costs are said once here and are not listed as option losses.

Option A reuses five approved pieces. D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A gives chip-level copies and generated core.arch names. D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A gives the result law and forced-level tests. D-RT-NATIVE-CAP1=A keeps native tools private, D-BUILD-PREBUILT1=D signs objects, and D-FREESTAND-ARTIFACT1=C keeps source as the authority.

options.name: Typed instruction entries in the library
options.detail:
Core gains typed instruction entries. Each entry is a Jet function whose body is the plain meaning. It is marked with the chip feature it needs, its encoding for Jet's own code generator, and the matching LLVM operation.

When the library bundle is built, the compiler checks every entry against the register kinds and encoding forms it knows. It then runs tests that compare the chip with the plain body. Users never receive an entry that fails.

Inside a function copy built for a chip level that has the feature, every build level emits the real instruction. Elsewhere the plain body runs. Using an entry outside such a copy is a build error.

A library pull request can add instructions, chip features, chip levels, operating-system adapters, allocators and graphics-card libraries. A compiler change is still needed for a new kind of register, a new target, a new calling convention, or a new kernel operation.

Beginner path: nothing to learn; built-in operations get faster when the library learns a chip. Expert path: import core.arch.x86, mark a function with chip levels, and test the chip feature at build time, as already approved.

Edge cases: entries that read or write memory stay behind an audited unsafe block at each use. Entries are private to the built-in library and owner-admitted providers. An entry that needs an unknown register kind is refused at bundle build with a named diagnostic.
options.technical:
New marker #Instruction(needs:, encode:, llvm:), registered under I7; the spelling is illustrative until its marker row lands. Rows are generated from vendor tables, the way D-SIMD-NATIVE1 says core.arch names are generated. During Rust emission a row also names its core::arch function.

The kernel is a closed, numbered operation table generated from a declared Prelude twin (D-OPENTABLE1). A Core bundle names the kernel number it needs, and a compiler implements exactly one. There are no ranges and no shims, per the greenfield rule.

The compiler links its own pinned Core copy, so a Core-only release never changes stage-2 bootstrap inputs. A kernel change ships a compiler and a matching bundle together, as every release does today.

I9: every level runs either the instruction or the identical body. D-SIMD-NATIVE1's result law applies: no FMA, approximate or reordering instructions unless the effect row admits non-reproducible results.

An AVX-512 VNNI pull request contains generated rows in Core/arch/x86, a feature row and an x86_64_v4 level change. It also contains Core kernels using the rows in #Multiversion copies, generated forced-level tests, and a paired performance cell.

First AVX-512 support, RISC-V vectors and a new graphics-card target each need one compiler change. That change covers register kinds, the target, or device output. Their instructions, kernels and libraries ride in Core.

Today's x86-64 encoder (Compiler/JetBackend/Source/X64/Encoder.jet) is 392 lines covering integers and control flow. Making vector encoding table-driven from the start costs no rework.

The example names a real LLVM intrinsic (stdarch avx512f.rs:44191), whose rounding operand the row fixes. The encoding text is the EVEX form of VSQRTPS. Lanes<F32, 16> follows D-LANES1's spelling.

options.name: Open door to LLVM operations
options.detail:
Core and owner-admitted providers may name any LLVM operation or LLVM type inside an audited unsafe declaration. Each use also needs a plain Jet body that defines the meaning.

Release builds emit the named LLVM operation. Fast-start and default builds run the plain body until Jet's own code generator learns the instruction, which takes a compiler change.

Gain: anything LLVM supports works in release builds with no compiler change, including new register kinds and graphics-card operations. Cost: new hardware stays slow in everyday builds, and the library depends on LLVM's names.

Beginner path is unchanged. The expert path uses the same import and chip-level marking as A.
options.technical:
New marker #Backend(llvm:), registered under I7. It is allowed only inside #Unsafe declarations in bundled Core and admitted providers (D-RT-NATIVE-CAP1, D-UNSAFE-DEPS1).

Names are validated at bundle build against LLVM's intrinsic table, as Swift's getLLVMIntrinsicID does. A misspelled name therefore never reaches users as a backend rejection (I2).

I9 holds through forced-level tests of the plain body, but speed differs by level. An LLVM upgrade can change which names exist, as Terra's documentation warns. This touches I6's dependency rule.

This is Mojo's model: llvm_intrinsic and __mlir_op in its standard library. Mojo specializes library code per program from .mojoc packages, which D-EXEC1's compile-once rule does not allow for Core.

options.name: Chip knowledge stays in the compiler
options.detail:
Library behavior still moves into Jet source, as already ruled. The instruction tables, chip features, chip levels, operating-system list and target menus stay compiler tables generated from vendor data.

Each new instruction, chip or system is a compiler pull request and ships in the next full Jet release. Every build level gets native code at once.

Beginner and expert paths are the same as in A; only the delivery path differs.
options.technical:
This is today's design for hardware: SimdLanes.rs and the closed lane family in the compiler, plus the closed OSTarget.rs and TargetMachine.rs enums.

It matches Zig, Go and stable Rust, where feature names are compiler tables. It does not meet the owner's request to ship hardware support without a compiler release.

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: github.com/modular/modular at 24f4ceb2ff, Mojo/stdlib/std/_gpu/intrinsics.mojo:348-376. Library code names an LLVM operation for one GPU and keeps a plain fallback. This is the pattern of options A and B. Feature queries such as has_avx512f are library code too (std/sys/info.mojo:412-725).

Primary sources read 2026-10-04: stdarch crates/core_arch/src/x86/avx512f.rs binds 369 LLVM intrinsics in the library. The feature name lives in rustc_target/src/target_features.rs:471, so stable AVX-512 waited for the Rust 1.89 release (blog.rust-lang.org, 2025-08-07).
Primary source read 2026-10-04: cuda.juliagpu.org/stable/hacking/exposing_new_intrinsics. A package adds a new PTX instruction with no Julia release.
comparisons.code:
fma_rp(x::Float64, y::Float64, z::Float64) =
    ccall("llvm.nvvm.fma.rp.d", llvmcall, Cdouble, (Cdouble, Cdouble, Cdouble), x, y, z)

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: odin-lang/Odin core/simd/x86/avx512f.odin:10-15 at 16de4f5103. AVX-512 is library code over portable lane operations, with a per-function feature attribute.

Primary source read 2026-10-04: carbon-language/carbon-lang core/prelude/types/int.carbon:15-36 at d31a8b67d3. The library declares Int and binds its operations to named compiler builtins, like A's kernel-bound declarations.

recommendation.why: A lets a library pull request give new instructions full speed on every build level, while a plain Jet body keeps one checked meaning. It reuses approved chip-level copies, typed instructions, private native tools and signed runtime objects.
gains: Instructions, chip levels, system adapters and allocators arrive by library pull request.
Default, fast-start and release builds all get the real instruction.
Each instruction has one plain Jet meaning, checked against the chip by tests.

losses.loss: A new kind of register or a new chip family still needs one compiler change.
losses.mitigation: Keep that compiler part a small table-driven target description. The instructions, chip levels and libraries for the family still arrive in the library pull request, and later additions need no compiler change.

losses.loss: Each entry carries an encoding and a plain body, not only a name.
losses.mitigation: Generate entries and their chip-versus-body tests from the chip makers' published tables, which the approved typed-instruction plan already requires.

whyNot.reason: B leaves default and fast-start builds slow on new hardware, and ties the library to an outside project's operation names.
C keeps every hardware change behind a full compiler release, which is what you asked to end.

recommendation.tradeoff: A needs one compiler change per new register kind or chip family; every other hardware change becomes a library change at full speed.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Before posting, Main confirms this draft is linked to card #4565 (c0gac1l5) and runs Tower's ballot validator. The drafter ran the store's ballotGaps check offline only. This is a short ballot with at most three options; independent full-profile reviews are not claimed. No Jet compiler, test or performance run was made for this draft.

Owner acceptance has four points. Confirm that the built-in library ships as its own signed bundle versioned against one kernel number, which changes D-EXEC1's 'for each Jet version' wording. Confirm that kernel-only Core functions expand at the call site while other Core bodies stay compiled once. Confirm the new marker under I7, with its spelling settled when its row lands. Confirm that one compiler change per new register kind or chip family is acceptable.

After ratification, Main plans cards in the order the research gives. First comes #3983 parity, then the kernel table and roles, then the #3690 port. After that come the Core bundle with records and prebuilt objects, the instruction catalog, and targets and systems as Core data.

Proofs: generated forced-level bit tests for every row on each chip level. A paired performance cell for each instruction family against the plain body. SP12's 30 ms startup receipt with the bundle. The hello compile cells on #4308. Identical goldens on every level.

gains: Hardware support arrives by library pull request.
Full speed in every kind of build.

losses.mitigation: That compiler part stays a small target table.

attempts: Inline any library body; rejected because it copies library algorithms into every program, against the compile-once rule.
Keep small operations as compiler-known kernel operations expanded inline, and expand only kernel-only library functions at the call site; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: hot operations are inline on every level, and larger library code stays compiled once.

designAway.loss: A library pull request could still need a compiler release for the feature vocabulary, as Rust's AVX-512 did.
attempts: Keep feature and chip-level names in the compiler; rejected because it repeats Rust's 1.89 wait.
Put feature, level and instruction rows together in the library; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: features, levels and instructions arrive together.

designAway.loss: A new register kind or chip family needs a compiler change.
attempts: Let the library declare register kinds through LLVM (option B); rejected because everyday builds would stay slow.
Keep a small table-driven target description in the compiler; kept.

designAway.loss: Writing encodings and plain bodies by hand would be slow and error-prone.

decisions.title: One private door for compiler-provided operations, named jet_builtins
decisions.situation: Jet's built-in library needs a few operations that only the compiler can provide, such as one machine addition or a raw memory read. Today the library reaches them through about 1,700 hidden routing entries and a secret name, so a reader cannot see where compiler magic happens. You asked for one clearly named place, called jet_builtins, like the marker Rust uses for its compiler operations. This vote decides its shape, and we recommend one module written in Jet that only the built-in library may import.
decisions.gist: How should Jet's built-in library declare and call the operations only the compiler can provide?
decisions.lesson: A compiler-provided operation is something Jet source cannot express, such as one machine addition or a raw memory read. The built-in library wraps each one in an ordinary function that users call. A plain meaning is ordinary Jet code that gives the same answer; tests compare it with the compiled operation.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: nothing changes. Programs call the same library functions and get the same answers.

Expert path: reading the built-in library shows builtin. at every spot where the compiler acts. One command lists every compiler operation with its plain meaning, or says it has none.

Shared by every option: the built-in library becomes ordinary Jet, as already approved. Small operations such as whole-number math stay inline at every build level. The options differ only in how the library names and declares the operations the compiler supplies.
decisions.story: Ana reads the library code for adding two U32 values to learn how it works. She finds a call that leads to a hidden table, written in another language, inside the compiler.
decisions.detail:
Owner request, 2026-10-04, card #4570: a marker like Rust's compiler-operation marker, called jet_builtins, so the compiler and Core read as conventional Jet. Research: Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, sections 3 and 4.

Settled, not balloted. D-CORE-SOURCE-AUTHORITY1=A keeps only unexpressible operations in a small audited kernel. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A makes the kernel a closed numbered table and expands kernel-only Core functions inline at every level. D-RT-NATIVE-CAP1=A keeps native tools private to bundled Core and owner-admitted providers.

Today, crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.jet holds 1,757 dispatcher rows whose payload is Rust source, for example line 255. Core makes 620 calls of the form core.x.y(...) inside Core. Core/mem/mem.jet:42-46 calls core.mem.volatile_read from a function of that same name.

Core/mem/mem.jet:20-31 declares five empty structs as compiler-owned shells. Syntax.rs:60 registers __core_intrinsic as a compiler-only namespace.

Peers use two shapes. One module: Rust core::intrinsics, Swift's Builtin module and Odin's documentation-only intrinsics package. A marker on each public declaration: Nim's magic pragma and Carbon's = "int.add" binding. Rust's fallback bodies may be marked as the specification (intrinsics/mod.rs:13-27).

options.name: One module, jet_builtins
options.detail:
Every operation, storage type and marker that only the compiler can provide is declared once, in Jet, in the module jet_builtins. A declaration has a typed signature. When its meaning can be written in Jet, it carries that body, and tests compare the body with the compiled operation on every build level.

Only the built-in library and owner-admitted providers may import the module; any other package gets a clear error. Library code writes builtin. before each use, so a reader sees exactly where the compiler acts. Raw memory operations stay behind a reasoned unsafe block.
options.technical:
Module jet_builtins ships in the Core bundle (D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A). It holds three item kinds: numbered kernel operations, storage types such as Bits<n> and Vector<T, n>, and compiler markers such as Role and Instruction. A function without a body is legal only in this module.

Import admission reuses the D-RT-NATIVE-CAP1 provider registry. core.mem.native becomes Core Jet over the module and keeps its ratified name, so there is still one gate. Raw-memory builtins are #Unsafe functions, so callers still need a reasoned block (D-UNSAFE-EFFECT).

Retires the dispatcher rows during the #3690 port, the __core_intrinsic namespace and the empty shells in core.mem. Compiler markers are written qualified, #builtin.Role, per D-MARKER-MODULE1. I7 rows: the module root and its markers.

New diagnostics with snapshots: unadmitted import, bodyless function outside the module, compiler marker outside Core.

options.name: A marker on each declaration
options.detail:
Any function in the built-in library may carry a builtin marker that names a compiler operation, and then it has no body. There is no separate module; the public function is the compiler operation.

Reading one function shows its binding directly. Finding every compiler operation means searching the whole library, and the functions carry no plain meaning to test against.
options.technical: New language marker #Builtin(op), registered under I7 and legal only in bundled Core. This is the Carbon and Nim shape. Without fallback bodies, I9 tests can compare build levels only with each other.

options.name: Keep routing tables
options.detail: The built-in library keeps calling compiler operations through routing tables, generated from one declared list as already approved. Library calls keep names that look like ordinary library functions, and the table entries keep their other-language payloads until the runtime port replaces them.
options.technical: Today's dispatcher_row and __core_intrinsic model, generated under D-OPENTABLE1=D.
options.code:
// Built-in library: core.math.fabs is a hidden table entry
pub fn abs_float(n: Float) -> Float Never! { core.math.fabs(n) }

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: library/core/src/intrinsics/mod.rs:13-27 and 3673-3679. Compiler operations live in one module; an optional fallback body may be marked as the specification. This is option A's shape.
Primary source read 2026-10-04: stdlib/public/core/IntegerTypes.swift.gyb:95 and 229. The Builtin module is visible only to the standard library, which wraps it in ordinary types.
Primary source read 2026-10-04: lib/system/arithmetics.nim:77. A pragma on each public declaration binds a compiler operation. This is option B's shape.
Primary source read 2026-10-04: base/intrinsics/intrinsics.odin:1-3 and 21. A documentation-only package declares every compiler operation without a body.

recommendation.why: A gives one readable place for everything only the compiler can do. It gives each operation a checked plain meaning, and it makes compiler magic visible wherever the library uses it.
gains: One module lists every compiler-provided operation, storage type and marker.
Each operation can carry a plain Jet meaning that tests check on every build level.
The builtin. prefix marks every spot where the compiler acts.

losses.loss: Library functions add one call around each compiler operation.
losses.mitigation: Wrappers made only of builtin calls expand inline on every build level, as already approved, so the extra call costs nothing at run time.

losses.loss: Outside libraries cannot add their own compiler operations.
losses.mitigation: Owner-admitted providers use the existing admission list, and new chip instructions arrive as library entries without a compiler change.

whyNot.reason: B scatters compiler operations across the library and gives them no plain meaning to test.
C keeps compiler magic hidden behind names that look like ordinary library calls.

recommendation.tradeoff: One extra declaration per compiler operation buys one auditable place and a tested meaning for each.

decisions.title: How built-in library types take on language meaning, such as what + calls
decisions.situation: Some library declarations have a special job in the language: what + calls, what type a plain number becomes, what a loop walks, and what ? unwraps. Today the compiler knows them only by hard-coded names, and the standard traits such as Equatable and Numeric have no Jet declaration at all. A reader of the library cannot see which declaration gives + its meaning. This vote decides how the library marks those jobs, and we recommend one builtin marker written on the declaration itself.
decisions.gist: How should the built-in library mark which declaration gives +, literals, loops and ? their meaning?
decisions.lesson: A role is a job the language gives one library declaration, such as "the trait that + calls" or "the type a whole-number literal becomes". Each role is filled exactly once. Users never write roles; only the built-in library does.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: nothing changes. + still adds, loops still walk lists, and errors now point at real library code.

Expert path: reading a standard trait shows its role at the top. One command prints every role and the declaration that fills it.

Shared by every option: the standard traits become ordinary Jet declarations in the built-in library, as already approved. The options differ only in where the role is written.
decisions.story: Kai wants to know what + does for his own Money type. He searches the library for the trait that + calls and finds nothing, because the compiler keeps that name inside itself.
decisions.detail:
Owner request, 2026-10-04, card #4570. Research: Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, section 5. Depends on D-CORE-BUILTINS1, which provides the builtin. prefix for compiler markers.

Today the standard trait names are Rust constants in crates/jet-foundation/src/Generics.rs:9-43 and again in Syntax/effects_surface.rs:236-262. Numeric's supertraits and static members are Rust arrays at effects_surface.rs:261-262. Policy.rs:1933-1937 lists the derivable traits a third time.

The Type enum has 23 built-in variants and RESERVED_TYPES reserves 42 names, per the boundary report. A search of Core, Prelude and both compilers finds no Jet declaration of Equatable, Comparable or Numeric.

Rust's lang items are 'pluggable operations' marked #[lang = "..."] and loaded lazily (Rust Unstable Book, lang_items). Swift ties literal syntax to protocol conformance. Both put the role at the declaration.

Optimizer knowledge follows from the vote. The optimizer may rely on kernel operation meanings and on role contracts written in Core. It never relies on string tags such as Swift's @_semantics.

options.name: Mark the declaration
options.detail:
The built-in library writes #builtin.Role(.Add) on the trait that + calls, and likewise for literals, loops, ? and the other jobs. The role list is closed and lives in the compiler-provided module.

Each role is filled exactly once; a missing or duplicate role stops the library build. A command prints one page listing every role and its declaration, generated from the markers.
options.technical:
Role is a closed enum and Role(role:) a compiler marker, both declared in jet_builtins (D-CORE-BUILTINS1=A). Only bundled Core may write it. The role table enters the interface record (SP12) and is read by ID.

Retires the trait-name constants in Generics.rs and effects_surface.rs and the Policy.rs list. [INFERENCE] About 25 roles: literal targets, operator traits, equality, order, hashing, iteration, the two carriers, display, close, index and range.

jet inspect roles renders the page. Diagnostics: missing role, duplicate role, role marker outside Core.

options.name: One list in the compiler-provided module
options.detail:
The compiler-provided module holds one list that names, for each role, the library declaration that fills it. The declarations themselves carry no mark.

All roles are visible on one page, but reading the Add trait does not tell you that + calls it.
options.technical: A typed prep table in jet_builtins, roles :: prep { Roles{ add: core.ops.Add, ... } }. Same checks and interface-record storage as A.

options.name: Keep compiler-known names
options.detail: The compiler keeps recognizing roles by fixed names, as today. The traits gain Jet declarations, but nothing in the library says which one + calls.
options.technical: Today's name constants, kept as the one Rust home under D-OPENTABLE1's guard.

comparisons.note: Rust Unstable Book, lang_items, read 2026-10-04: lang items are 'pluggable operations' marked at the declaration, loaded lazily, and most may be defined only once. This is option A's shape.
Primary source read 2026-10-04: stdlib/public/core/IntegerTypes.swift.gyb:89-99. Literal syntax binds through a protocol conformance written on the type.

recommendation.why: A puts each role where a reader looks, on the declaration. The one-page overview is generated from those marks, so the fact is written once.
gains: Reading a standard trait shows which syntax uses it.
One generated page lists every role.
Errors about +, loops or literals point at real library code.

losses.loss: Roles are spread across many library files.
losses.mitigation: A command prints every role on one page, and a missing or duplicate role stops the library build.

whyNot.reason: B hides each role from a reader of the declaration that fills it.
C keeps the language's hooks invisible in the library.

recommendation.tradeoff: One short marker on about 25 library declarations makes every language hook visible.

decisions.title: One generic definition per number family instead of one hand-written type per size
decisions.situation: Jet has whole-number types of fixed sizes, such as U8 and I32, and decimal types such as F32. Each size is hand-written into the compiler in hundreds of places, so the approved 16-bit decimals and 128-bit whole numbers still do not exist. You suggested one definition that builds whichever sizes Jet needs. We recommend one generic library type per family, with the familiar names kept and only the standard sizes allowed.
decisions.gist: Should Jet define each number family once, generically, and keep U8, I32 and F32 as names for its sizes?
decisions.lesson: A number family is a set of types that differ only in size, such as U8, U16, U32 and U64. A generic type takes the size as a build-time number, as in Unsigned<8>. An alias gives one size a short name, so U8 means Unsigned<8>.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: nothing changes. Int stays exact and unlimited. U8{300} is still an error, and errors still say U8.

Expert path: every size behaves the same way because one definition serves them all. The approved overflow policy, conversions and lane types work for every size.

Shared by every option: the approved number rules stay. They cover exact Int by default, checked fixed sizes, lossless widening, the overflow policy and destination-named conversions. The options differ in how the sizes are defined and which sizes exist.
decisions.story: Lena trains a small model and needs 16-bit decimals. Jet approved them months ago, but adding a size means editing hundreds of places in the compiler, so they are still missing.
decisions.detail:
Owner request, 2026-10-04, card #4570: one type with a build-time program that builds whichever sizes Jet needs, instead of ten classes. Research: Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, section 6. Depends on D-CORE-BUILTINS1 for storage and D-CORE-ROLE1 for literal and operator roles.

Settled, not balloted. D-TYPE2-NUM1=A says a sized width is Int plus a proven range and a layout. D-INTBIG1=A keeps exact Int as the default. D-WRAP-SCOPE1=A selects overflow behaviour lexically, D-SHAPE-CONVERT1=A keeps from_<source> names, and D-FOUND-LITERAL1=A routes literals through a capability. D-LOWFLOAT1=A adds F16, BF16 and two 8-bit storage formats, and D-LANES1=A defines Lanes<T, N>.

Today: types.rs:1100-1125 parses only 8, 16 and 32 bits, plus 64 unsigned and the name I64. BuiltinStatics.jet:210-238 lists nine widths and thirteen conversion sources by hand. Rust code matches Type::IntN at 310 sites and Type::Float32 at 204. F16 and BF16 appear nowhere in crates, Compiler or Core.

Peers: Zig builds any width with std.meta.Int. Carbon declares one generic class Int(N). Rust expands one int_impl! macro per width, Swift one template per width, and Julia generates methods with @eval loops.

Compile time: instances are built when the Core bundle is built and stored in the interface record. A user build adds no compile-time evaluation for numbers, against the speed plan's 0.10 s comptime budget for 300k lines.

options.name: One family, standard sizes
options.detail:
The library defines Signed<bits>, Unsigned<bits> and IEEE<exponent, fraction> once each. U8, I32, I128, F16, BF16, F32 and F64 become one-line aliases. Methods, operators, conversions and literal checks are written once per family.

Only the standard sizes exist: 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 bits for whole numbers, and the four standard decimal formats. A value set between sizes, such as 0 to 127, uses the range types Jet already has.

Errors, hovers and documents always show the alias name, such as U8.
options.technical:
Families wrap builtin.Bits<bits> and builtin.Float<e, f> (D-CORE-BUILTINS1=A). The #Arithmetic policy picks add_checked, add_wrap or add_saturate. One prep loop generates the from_<source> methods, and widening becomes one rule over bits and sign.

Type::IntN and Type::Float32 collapse into ordinary generic application. The remaining width-aware sites are layout, ABI and kernel lowering. numeric_type_from_name and the BuiltinStatics tables are deleted. Instances live in the interface record (SP12).

Odd widths stay ranges because D-TYPE2-NUM1 already models a width as Int plus range plus layout. A second spelling such as Unsigned<7> would violate I8.

options.name: One family, any size
options.detail:
The same generic families, but any whole-number size from 1 to 128 bits is allowed, such as Unsigned<24> or Signed<7>. Standard sizes keep their short names.

Bit-packed formats and odd hardware registers get a native type. A value set such as 0 to 127 can then be written two ways: as a range or as Unsigned<7>.
options.technical: Same as A, plus every width in 1..128 for Bits<n> in the kernel and back ends. LLVM supports arbitrary iN; Jet's own code generator would need widening and masking for odd widths. Two spellings for one value set conflicts with I8 and D-TYPE2-NUM1's grid.
options.code:
alias U8 :: Unsigned<8>
sample :: Unsigned<24>{0x7FFFFF}    // native 24-bit value
small :: Unsigned<7>{100}           // same values as Int(0..127)

options.name: One hand-written type per size, in the library
options.detail: Each size keeps its own type, now written in library source instead of the compiler. A shared template or copy keeps the sizes alike. Adding a size means adding a file and teaching the compiler its name.
options.technical: Rust int_impl! and Swift gyb shape. The compiler keeps per-width knowledge in its type enum and name parser.

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: lib/std/meta.zig:942-955 at 0.14.0. One function builds an integer type of any width at build time. This is option B's reach.
Primary source read 2026-10-04: core/prelude/types/int.carbon:15-19. One generic class defines every integer size over a builtin. This is option A's shape.
Primary source read 2026-10-04: library/core/src/num/mod.rs:382-405. One macro call per width generates each type's methods. This is option C's shape.
Primary sources read 2026-10-04: base/boot.jl:280-288 and base/int.jl:87. Each width is a declared primitive type; arithmetic is written once for every bit integer.
comparisons.code:
primitive type Int8    <: Signed   8 end
(+)(x::T, y::T) where {T<:BitInteger} = add_int(x, y)

recommendation.why: A defines each family once, so new sizes are one line and every size behaves alike. Keeping only standard sizes leaves one way to write each value set.
gains: F16, BF16, I128 and U128 arrive as one alias line each.
Every size shares one tested definition of each operation.
User code and error messages keep the familiar names.

losses.loss: Odd sizes such as 24 bits have no native type.
losses.mitigation: A range type with an explicit packed layout covers them; a future battery that needs native odd sizes can reopen this.

losses.loss: Error messages could show Unsigned<8> instead of U8.
losses.mitigation: The alias is the display name in every error, hover and document, and snapshot tests prove it.

whyNot.reason: B gives odd value sets two spellings and adds odd-width work to every code generator.
C keeps eleven near-copies and a compiler change for every new size.

recommendation.tradeoff: Standard sizes only, in exchange for one definition per family and one spelling per value set.

decisions.title: Keep markers independent; make their derivation link explicit
decisions.situation: Jet writes routine code, such as field-by-field equality, for eligible types without asking beginners to add labels. Today a marker and a trait are linked by sharing a name, which hides why they belong together. Markers and traits otherwise do different jobs, so putting one inside the other teaches the wrong relationship. This vote chooses where to write the link; we recommend naming the trait on a separate marker declaration.
decisions.gist: Where should a marker say which trait it implements?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a compile-time label at a code site: a rule records a fact, a code-writing marker adds code, a gate permits a checked exception, and a group names fixed markers. A trait is a type contract: functions a type promises. Neither contains the other. They meet only in derivation, when a code-writing marker writes a trait implementation.
decisions.story: Omar follows #Equatable to its declaration and wants to see which contract its generated code fulfills, without treating every marker as a trait.
decisions.detail:
Owner direction, 2026-10-05: implicit beginner magic, explicit expert control; marker names are PascalCase. Markers and traits are independent, neither a subset of the other. They overlap only where a code-writing marker implements a trait. The nested-marker recommendation is withdrawn. This remains D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 on card #4570, c0s7shwh.

Settled: D-MARKER-LAW1=A merges providers into marker bodies, allows package markers to read/add/reject, and reserves checking changes to trusted built-ins. D-META-BODY1=A supplies a member-list body for an implementation. D-META-NAME1=A requires marker as the declaring word. D-META-FORM1=A and D-MARKER-SITES1=B supply typed parameters and $ facts. D-MARKER-GROUP1=A supplies fixed groups and exclusions; D-MARKER-MODULE1=A supplies pub and qualified library uses. D-CORE-BUILTINS1=A, ratified 2026-10-05, puts compiler-provided markers in jet_builtins and restricts imports. D-CORE-ROLE1=A puts Role(role:) there and restricts its use to Core.

Read-only Tower checks: D-META-AUTO1=A is ratified, automatically derives every structurally eligible trait, and silently leaves ineligible traits absent. D-AUTODERIVE-SYNTAX1=D is ratified: policy: .{ auto_derive: false } disables package defaults; #Equatable requests and #!Equatable refuses automatic generation. A hand-written impl wins over policy and either sign. D-META-AUTO1 also preserves project-wide selection of disabled traits. This ballot neither narrows defaults to four nor adds $auto: false nor changes package controls.

The choice is not settled: D-MARKER-NAME-HYGIENE1=A and D-MARKER-LAW1=A use shared marker/trait names for derivation, without mandating nesting or explicit linkage. B retains that convention; A replaces it with a marker-side clause; C puts selection on the trait. All three keep separate top-level declarations, which can share a file.

Source facts read this session: crates/jet-foundation/src/Generics.rs:9-13 lists standard trait-name constants. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:79-100 lists request rows, including Equatable at 92. Prelude/Derives.jet:13-53 supplies equality for enums, records and numeric bases. Markers.jet:28 supplies Unsafe's signature; :42 supplies Inline independently of traits. Role's declaring signature is grounded in D-CORE-ROLE1; full metadata stays governed by that law. These remnants explain migration, not a reason to retain the old split.

The complete marker-authoring catalog appears once in explainer. Each option shows the same Equatable contract, field-equality body, Point and equal_origin function. Only the link changes.

options.name: Marker names the trait
options.detail: Every marker is an independent top-level marker declaration. A code-writing marker that implements a trait writes derives Trait on its own header. The trait remains only its function contract. Both declarations may sit together in one file, but neither is nested in the other. The explicit link, not a matching name, identifies the generated implementation.
options.technical:
New surface: pub marker Equatable($sites: [.Type]) derives Equatable { member-list }. derives resolves a trait; Self is the marked type. It supplies the association and implied impl header under D-META-BODY1=A. Ordinary code-writing markers without derives retain their ordinary added-item bodies. A marker can use a different name from its trait. Trait references use ordinary resolution; library marker uses follow D-MARKER-MODULE1=A.

One deriving marker names one trait; existing groups combine derivations. Matching names without derives do not invent a link. The explicit clause replaces inferred registration, leaving eligibility, automatic defaults, signed requests/refusals and hand-written precedence unchanged. The marker declaration is the sole registry row, never a row generated from the trait.

Amends name-inferred derivation pairing in D-MARKER-NAME-HYGIENE1 and makes the member-body trait context explicit under D-MARKER-LAW1. Unrelated naming, marker kinds and tiers stay settled. derives is a linking clause, not the removed derive-provider form. Migrate every provider body and redundant request row together, preserving enum and numeric behavior. Diagnostics identify an unknown/non-trait derives target, invalid site or generated members failing the contract, with declaration and use locations.

options.name: Shared name beside the trait
options.detail: Keep today's approved name-pairing law. Declare the pure trait and a separate marker beside it in the same file. The marker is linked to the trait solely because both are named Equatable; there is no link clause. Readers see the code together and write no new linking word, but must know the name-pairing rule.
options.technical: Retains D-MARKER-LAW1=A and the derivation name-pairing convention in D-MARKER-NAME-HYGIENE1=A. The matched trait name supplies the implied implementation context for the D-META-BODY1=A member list; Self is the marked type. Colocation helps reading, but no nesting, trait-owned marker or extra derives/derive clause is introduced. Other marker kinds, the registry, eligibility and automatic/refusal/manual precedence are the shared laws. A rename must keep the pair's spellings synchronized.

options.name: Trait names the marker
options.detail: The trait header writes derive #Equatable to select a separately declared marker. That marker still has its own top-level marker declaration and code-writing body; no hidden marker is created. Readers discover the generator from the contract, while the contract now includes a generation choice beyond the functions it promises.
options.technical:
New header: pub trait Equatable derive #Equatable { contract-members }. Resolve one separately declared code-writing marker, using normal library qualification. The association supplies the D-META-BODY1=A implementation context; Self is the marked type. The trait body contains only contract members. No nested marker, implied declaration or old provider body is introduced. Explicit linkage replaces name-inferred pairing; renaming updates the reference.

The selected marker must accept type sites and generate members satisfying the contract. Resolve declarations independently of file order. The marker declaration remains the sole registry row; the trait reference supplies only the association. Eligibility, signed uses, defaults, manual precedence, origin restrictions and groups stay unchanged. Diagnostics name an unknown/non-code-writing marker or generated members failing the contract.

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-05: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html, proc_macro_derive section. A named derive macro is declared separately, receives the marked type and appends items. This demonstrates independent code generation, not Jet's proposed derives syntax or its automatic defaults.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(PartialEq)]
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

recommendation.why: A writes the relationship where the generated code is built, while keeping traits pure and markers independent. Beginners keep automatic code; experts can read and control the link.
gains: The generating marker explicitly names its contract.
Traits stay pure contracts, not marker containers.
Every marker has a visible top-level declaration.

losses.loss: Deriving marker headers gain one short clause.
losses.mitigation: Write it only when authoring a generator; automatic derivation and existing request/refusal sites stay unchanged.

whyNot.reason: B is familiar and concise, but the link remains an unwritten name-pairing convention.
C makes the generator discoverable from the trait, but mixes generation choice into its contract.

recommendation.tradeoff: A short generator-side clause buys an explicit link without nesting either concept.

The validator mutates only a detached in-memory snapshot. No Tower writes or commits are authorized. Compiler, test and performance runs are outside this rewrite.

B retains same-file name pairing; C writes derive #Equatable on a trait with the marker still separate. All panes show the same six-line Point/equal_origin program. surface.lesson: A marker is a compile-time label at a code site: a rule records facts, a code-writing marker adds code. A gate permits a checked exception; a group names fixed markers. A trait is a type contract: promised functions. Neither contains the other. Their link is derivation: a code-writing marker implements a trait.

gains: Pure trait; explicit link.
losses: One clause when authoring a generator.

gains: Keep today's convention.
losses: The relationship is implicit.

gains: Find the generator from the contract.
losses: The contract includes generation choice.

recommendation.why: A keeps contracts pure and writes the link on the generator. Beginners still get every eligible derivable trait automatically unless refused.
gains: Independent concepts; explicit derivation.

losses.loss: One generator-header clause.
losses.mitigation: Only generator authors write it; automatic code, #Equatable and #!Equatable keep their behavior.

whyNot.reason: B is concise, but relies on matching names.
C is discoverable, but adds generation choice to the contract.

recommendation.tradeoff: One written link; no nesting.

attempts: Use a nested marker to colocate code; rejected by the owner's independent-concepts direction.
Keep separate top-level declarations beside each other, with an explicit marker-side link; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: locality needs no nesting.

designAway.loss: Implicit marker creation would hide where a marker is built.
attempts: Create a marker from a trait's derive block; rejected because no marker declaration is visible.
Require the ordinary marker declaring word for every kind, including deriving and compiler-provided markers; kept.

decisions.title: One way to choose who implements a library service, in builds, scopes and tests
decisions.situation: Library services such as the clock, files, network and memory need an implementation, and sometimes a program wants a different one. Today there are four ways to pick it: a board's build profile, a scope marker with a fixed menu, a test marker for injected failures, and separate fake-maker functions. All four answer one question in four different shapes. This vote decides whether they become one mechanism, and we recommend one interface per service that all four places use.
decisions.gist: Should board profiles, scoped replacements and tests all pick a service implementation the same way?
decisions.lesson: A service is something the library does for you through the system, such as telling the time or writing files. A provider is the code that implements it. A test can install a fake provider, and a small board can install its own hardware provider.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: nothing changes. Programs use the real clock and files; tests stay short.

Expert path: each service has one interface in the library, such as Clock. A board profile, a #Context block and a test all name a value of that interface. Writing a fake for tests and a driver for a board is the same work.

Shared by every option: effects keep saying what a function may use, and providers say which code does it. The approved scope marker and board profile keep their names.
decisions.story: Dev writes a fake clock for his tests, then needs a hardware clock for a small board. Today the test fake, the board clock and the scoped replacement each use a different shape.
decisions.detail:
Owner request, 2026-10-04, card #4570: one uniform way to mark effects, abilities, requirements and features where meanings coincide. Research: Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, sections 7.1 and 8.

Today: target profiles name providers per fact (D-FREESTAND-FACTS1=A; Prelude/Facts.jet:54-67). #Context replaces a Core service per scope (D-EFFECT-HANDLE1=A). Its registry row still lists only allocator, logger and deadline (Prelude/Markers.jet:177).

Tests inject failures with #Test(faults: [Effect]) (D-TESTFAULT1=A; Markers.jet:187). Fakes are separate calls such as testing.fake_clock and testing.fake_rng (Prelude/Core.jet:415-417).

The four answer one question, which implementation runs, so I8 asks for one mechanism. Effects stay separate: an effect is permission, a provider is implementation. D-FREESTAND-FACTS1 keeps machine provision apart from permission planes, and so does this proposal.

options.name: One interface per service; short test faults stay
options.detail:
Each replaceable service is one library trait, such as Clock, Files, Transport, Allocator or LogSink. A board profile, a #Context block and a test all name a value of that trait, with the same key names in each place.

The fake makers become ordinary provider types, such as testing.FixedClock. #Test(faults: [.FS]) stays as the short way to inject failures and is defined as a failing provider over the same trait.
options.technical:
One generated list of service keys feeds both the target-profile fact keys and the #Context marker signature (D-OPENTABLE1). The Markers.jet row's fixed allocator, logger and deadline menu is replaced by that list.

testing.fake_clock and testing.fake_rng dispatcher rows retire into provider types. #Test(faults:) keeps its D-TESTFAULT1 spelling and lowers to a Failing provider. Target-profile providers bind at link time; scope providers reuse D-EFFECT-HANDLE1's context read.

options.name: One interface per service; test faults retire
options.detail: The same single interface per service as A, but #Test(faults:) retires. A test that injects failures installs a failing provider with #Context, the same way as any other replacement. There is exactly one spelling, at the cost of longer tests.
options.technical: As A, plus retirement of D-TESTFAULT1's faults parameter with a teaching diagnostic pointing at #Context(fs: testing.Failing(...)).

options.name: Keep four ways
options.detail: Board profiles, #Context, test faults and fake makers stay separate mechanisms with their own names and shapes.
options.technical: Status quo; implement D-EFFECT-HANDLE1's providers in #Context without sharing them with target profiles or tests.

comparisons.note: D-EFFECT-HANDLE1=A, read 2026-10-04: Core defines one trait per replaceable service, and #Context replaces it for a scope. Option A extends the same trait to board profiles and tests.
[INFERENCE, not re-read this session] Odin's implicit context carries the allocator and logger, which a scope may replace for the code it calls.
comparisons.code:
context.allocator = my_arena_allocator()
process_input()   // allocations inside use the arena

recommendation.why: A gives every service one interface that boards, scopes and tests share, while keeping the short test spelling programmers already use.
gains: A fake for tests and a driver for a board are the same kind of code.
The scope marker accepts every service, not a fixed three.
Fake makers become ordinary library types.

losses.loss: Test faults keep a second, shorter spelling.
losses.mitigation: It is defined as a failing provider over the same interface, so there is one mechanism with a short form.

whyNot.reason: B makes the common failure test longer for no gain in meaning.
C keeps four shapes for one question.

recommendation.tradeoff: One interface per service, with the short test-fault form kept as a spelling over it.

decisions.title: Chip features: automatic by default, explicit control for experts
decisions.situation: Some fast code uses instructions that only newer processors have, such as the wide math of recent Intel chips. Today such code must sit inside a copy built for that chip level, so a helper deep inside a library can stop a beginner's build. You asked why the safe choice is not automatic, with explicit control for experts. This vote decides that, and we recommend that Jet builds the chip copies itself, picks one when the program starts, and keeps the existing marks for experts.
decisions.gist: Should Jet handle chip-specific instructions automatically, with marks only for experts who want control?
decisions.lesson: A chip feature is a group of instructions only some processors have, such as AVX-512 wide math. A chip copy is a version of a function Jet builds for one processor generation. Jet checks the processor once at start and uses the best copy. Every instruction also has a plain version that gives the same answer on any chip.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write nothing. When code uses a chip feature, directly or through a library, Jet builds a fast copy and a plain copy, checks the chip once at start, and runs the best one. Answers are identical on every chip.

Expert path: #Multiversion picks the chip levels and where the switch sits. prep if $build.cpu.has(.AVX512F) writes a branch by hand. jet build --cpu fixes the chip for the whole program. #!Multiversion on a function refuses automatic copies, so its callers must supply the feature.

Shared by every option: chip copies, the start-up chip check, build-time feature tests and instructions with plain meanings are already approved. Nothing here rebuilds code while the program runs; that stays the separate opt-in optimizer.
decisions.story: Mia calls a package's dot function, which uses AVX-512 inside a small helper. Her laptop lacks AVX-512 and her server has it. She should get a correct program on both, and the fast path on the server, without learning any of this.
decisions.detail:
Owner question, 2026-10-05, on this ballot: "why not implicit magic default, explicit expert option." Owner direction the same night: implicit beginner magic, explicit expert control. Card #4570. Research: Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, sections 7.2 and 8.

Settled, not balloted. D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A builds #Multiversion copies and binds the best one at start. D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A already dispatches Core's measured kernels automatically, even in a portable build, and gives forced-level tests and JET_CPU_MAX. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A gives every instruction entry a plain Jet body that tests compare with the chip.

What A changes. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A and D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A make an entry used outside a matching copy a build error. A narrows that error to the two cases where an expert's explicit mark conflicts, listed in option A. Everywhere else Jet adds the copies itself, extending D-SIMD-NATIVE1's Core-kernel default to all code.

Not adaptive. Copies are built ahead of time and chosen by the existing start-up probe. D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1=B, which rebuilds code inside a running program, stays opt-in as the owner ruled. Features stay a separate plane from effects: an effect is permission, a feature is machine provision (D-FREESTAND-FACTS1=A).

options.name: Automatic copies, with expert marks to steer or refuse
options.detail:
Jet works out which chip features each function needs, across calls, as it does for effects. Where code that needs a feature is reached from code that lacks it, Jet adds the switch itself. It builds a copy for the chip level that adds the feature and a plain copy, and the start-up check picks one. Hover, documents and jet inspect show every automatic switch and its copies.

Experts take control with marks Jet already has. #Multiversion(levels) sets the switch point and levels. prep if $build.cpu.has(.X) branches by hand. jet build --cpu or --features fixes the chip for the whole program, so no copies are needed. #!Multiversion refuses an automatic switch on one function.

The build stops only where explicit intent conflicts. One case is an instruction written directly in a #Multiversion copy whose level lacks it, outside a feature check. The other is a #!Multiversion function called where no copy, check or --cpu supplies its feature. Both errors name the call chain.
options.technical:
Feature needs are an inferred plane solved over the existing per-function summaries, separate from the effect row. An automatic switch goes on the outermost needing function in the module where the need arises: the first function on the chain called from another module or from code without the need. Calls inside the copies stay direct and inlinable, under D-CPU-DISPATCH1's same-level rule.

The copy set is the baseline plus the lowest target level that adds each needed feature, such as x86_64_v4 for AVX512F. On a target with no such level, the one copy uses the plain bodies. Plain bodies are tested bit-equal to the instruction (D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A), and D-SIMD-NATIVE1's result law binds every copy, so no FMA or approximate instruction is introduced. The interpreter and JIT run the baseline copy (I9). JET_CPU_MAX caps the choice.

An exported function with an automatic switch records it in the package interface, so callers see no unmet need. A #!Multiversion function exports its need instead. #!Multiversion reuses the ratified refusal sign (D-AUTODERIVE-SYNTAX1=D) on the existing marker: one registry change under I7. Cost: one bit set per function in the summary solve, inside the speed plan's 0.05 s budget, plus one copy per extra level of each switched function.

options.name: Inferred, but an unmet need is a build error
options.detail: Jet works out each function's needs the same way and shows them, but builds no copies on its own. Calling code that needs a feature from code without it is a build error that names the chain. The fix is to add #Multiversion or a feature check. Nothing is built that the author did not ask for.
options.technical: Same inferred plane as A, with no automatic switch. Exported needs are recorded in the package interface. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A's error stands as ratified and extends to helpers.

options.name: Written on every function in the chain
options.detail: A function that uses a feature says so with a marker, #Requires(.AVX512F), and so does every caller up to a chip copy. Needs are visible in source, and nothing happens automatically.
options.technical: New marker #Requires(features...), registered under I7. This is the shape of Rust's target_feature and Odin's enable_target_feature.

comparisons.note: Primary sources read 2026-10-04: base/intrinsics/intrinsics.odin:386-391 and 410-411. A feature is required by an attribute on each procedure and tested with has_target_feature. This is option C's shape.
comparisons.code:
@(require_target_feature="atomics")
wasm_memory_atomic_wait32 :: proc(ptr: ^u32, expected: u32, timeout_ns: i64) -> u32 ---

comparisons.note: D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A, read 2026-10-05: Core's measured kernels already use the best chip level the running chip has, with no user mark. Option A extends that default to all code.
comparisons.code:
values :: [F64]{1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0}
print(values.sum())   // Core's kernel may use AVX2 here; same answer everywhere

recommendation.why: A gives beginners fast, correct code on every chip with nothing to write. Experts keep exact control through marks Jet already has, plus one refusal.
gains: A library's chip-specific speedups need no marks and never break a beginner's build.
Answers are identical on every chip, checked by the existing forced-level tests.
Experts steer with #Multiversion, feature checks or --cpu, or refuse with #!Multiversion.

losses.loss: Automatic copies make the program larger.
losses.mitigation: Copies are made only for code that uses a feature, one per extra chip level. jet inspect lists every switch and its size.

losses.loss: A call into a switched function costs one indirect jump.
losses.mitigation: Calls inside a copy stay direct and inlinable. An expert moves the switch outward with #Multiversion.

whyNot.reason: B stops a beginner's build over a chip detail that a library chose.
C repeats the same mark on every function in a chain and is never automatic.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet adds chip copies by itself, in exchange for no chip marks and no chip errors on the beginner path.
