After ratification, one card: the need plane in the summary solve, automatic switch placement, the refusal row, and interface records, once #Multiversion lands (#4167, #4168). Proofs: forced-level bit tests per level on an automatically switched function, UI snapshots for both conflict diagnostics, and a size report for one switched Core kernel.

surface.gist: Should Jet handle chip-specific instructions automatically, with marks only for experts who want control?
surface.lesson: A chip feature is a group of instructions only some processors have. A chip copy is a version of a function built for one processor generation. Jet checks the processor once at start and runs the best copy.

current.note: Today a helper that uses AVX-512 has no rule, and a direct use outside a chip copy stops the build.
current.code:
pub fn dot(a: [F32], b: [F32]) -> F32 { dot16(a, b) }

fn dot16(a: [F32], b: [F32]) -> F32 { ... }   // uses AVX-512: no rule today

wild.note: Odin writes the needed feature on each procedure by hand.
wild.code:
@(enable_target_feature="avx512f,evex512")
_mm512_srlv_epi32 :: proc "c" (a: __m512i, count: __m512i) -> __m512i { ... }

options.name: Automatic, with expert marks
options.gist: Jet builds fast and plain copies itself; experts steer or refuse with marks.
gains: Beginners write nothing and never hit chip errors.
Experts keep full control with existing marks.
losses: Programs grow by one copy per extra chip level.

options.name: Inferred, errors when unmet
options.gist: Jet works out each need but builds nothing on its own.
gains: Nothing is built that the author did not ask for.
losses: A library helper can stop a beginner's build.

options.name: Written on every function
options.gist: Each function in the chain carries a marker naming its features.
gains: Needs are visible in source.
losses: Every function in a chain repeats the mark.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners fast, correct code on every chip with nothing to write, and experts keep exact control.
gains: No chip marks or chip errors for beginners.
Same answers on every chip.
Experts steer or refuse with marks.

losses.loss: Programs grow by automatic copies.
losses.mitigation: Copies exist only for code that uses a feature, and an inspect command lists each one with its size.

losses.loss: A switched call costs one indirect jump.
losses.mitigation: Calls inside a copy stay direct, and experts can move the switch outward.

whyNot.reason: B stops beginners' builds over a library's chip choice.
C repeats marks along every chain and is never automatic.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet adds copies by itself, for no chip marks or errors on the beginner path.

designAway.loss: Automatic copies could grow programs without the author knowing.
attempts: Copy the whole program per chip level; rejected because size doubles for code that never uses a feature.
Copy only switched functions and their same-module callees, one extra level each, listed by jet inspect; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation.

designAway.loss: A switch placed at the innermost helper would put an indirect call inside hot loops.
attempts: Switch at the function that uses the instruction; rejected for that reason.
Switch at the outermost needing function of the module, so loops inside stay direct, and let experts move it with #Multiversion; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation.

designAway.loss: Automatic copies could change answers between chips.
attempts: Trust each instruction's documentation; rejected.
Use only instructions whose plain body is tested bit-equal, under the existing result law; kept.
designAway.result: Removed.

decisions.title: Learning from real runs: rebuild with a record, and optionally re-optimize while running
decisions.situation: A built Jet program is fully compiled before it ships, so it never learns how it is really used. Java, C# and JavaScript engines watch a running program and rebuild its busiest code, which helps long-running servers. This vote decides whether Jet uses recorded runs when building, also lets long-running programs re-optimize themselves, or stays fully static.
decisions.gist: Should Jet use recorded runs to build faster programs, and may a long-running program re-optimize itself?
decisions.lesson: A record is a file listing what a run used most: busy functions, which way decisions usually went, and which functions a call usually reached. Building with a record changes speed only, never results. An in-program optimizer is a part of the program that recompiles its busiest functions while it runs, using Jet's own code generator. Phones, game consoles and browsers forbid programs from making new machine code while running.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: nothing new to learn. If a package contains a record, release builds use it and say which record they used. Without one, builds work as today.

Expert path: record a real workload with Jet's existing performance tools, keep the record with the source, and rebuild. Under option B, add one build flag to a long-running server to let it keep improving while it runs.

Shared by every option: chip-level copies, build-time code and Jet's own code generator stay as already approved. Recording already follows approved rules: it samples by default and counts exactly on request. Nothing is ever sent off the machine.

The options differ in one thing. A uses recorded runs when building. B does that and also lets long-running programs re-optimize themselves. C uses neither.
decisions.story: Lena runs a Jet web service for months. Her traffic changes with the seasons, and she wants every bit of speed without hand-tuning.
decisions.inWild:
# Go profile-guided optimization (go.dev/doc/pgo)
$ curl -o cpu.pprof "http://localhost:8080/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30"
$ mv cpu.pprof default.pgo     # in the main package directory, committed with the source
$ go build                     # -pgo=auto uses default.pgo; Go 1.22 measured about 2-14% faster
decisions.detail:
Owner questions, 2026-10-04, card #4571. Can a JIT beat AOT? Does a hybrid JIT help when every scenario must be as fast as possible? Could a JIT report hot paths to an AOT build, or could an AOT binary carry an onboard optimizer? Research: Docs/research/adaptive-runtime-specialization-2026-10-04.md.

Settled, not balloted. The Cranelift jet-jit crate is not ported (D-EXEC1=A, ruling of 2026-10-04). Recording is local and never sent (D-TELEMETRY1=A, Docs/spec/reference/network-policy.md:3-4). The record is the existing .jettrace artifact (D-PERFSESSION1=D, D-ARTIFACT-EXT1=A, Docs/spec/observability.md:23,36-52). Sampling by default with explicit counting (D-PROFILE-METHOD1=A), and source records with function totals (D-PROFILE-DETAIL1=A), are law. The compiler never adds CPU copies on its own, because D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A rejected compiler-chosen clones (its option D).

Evidence that runtime tiers beat AOT, and by how much.
- The big factors compare a JIT with an interpreter of a dynamic language: TurboFan 4.35x on JetStream (v8.dev/blog/maglev) and PyPy about 4x CPython 3.11 (pypy.org).
- Jet's static types already capture most of that.
- Over compiled code, gains are 2-20%: .NET dynamic PGO up to 20% (Announcing .NET 8) and JEP 515 training profiles 19% faster warm-up.

JEP 544 (JDK 28) says profile-guided static code "can even be competitive with HotSpot". It keeps a JIT for three reasons: workload change, exact hardware and dynamic loading. .NET documents that ReadyToRun code "is not as highly optimized as code produced by the JIT", so tiering replaces hot methods.

Evidence for recorded runs into AOT.
- Go PGO is about 2-14% faster and recommends committing default.pgo for reproducible builds.
- AutoFDO reaches a 10.5% geomean, which is 85% of instrumented FDO (CGO 2016).
- BOLT adds up to 8.0% on top of PGO and LTO for data-center services, and 20.4% for GCC and Clang (arXiv:1807.06735).
- Propeller adds 1.1-8% beyond PGO and ThinLTO (ASPLOS 2023).
- Android Baseline Profiles make code about 30% faster from the first launch.

Evidence for AOT and against always-on JITs.
- JEP 544 cuts startup 65-80% with AOT code.
- Julia 1.9 cut CSV.jl's time to first run from 11.66 s to 0.08 s.
- About 45% of V8 CVEs since 2019 were JIT bugs, and the JIT kept CET and ACG off (Edge security blog).
- iOS guideline 2.5.2 forbids running new code.
- V8 names iOS, smart TVs and consoles as platforms that forbid writable executable memory, and macOS needs the allow-jit entitlement.

Jet pieces reused.
- One lowering and one runtime (D-TIER-ONEIR1=A, D-TIER-FORM1=A, D-EXEC1=A).
- Slot-table recompilation is already designed: Docs/research/jet-backend-design-2026-10-01.md:513-541, with x64_rebind_slot exercised on an import slot.
- The W^X loader is at :346-352.
- #Multiversion's bit-identical result law (D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A).

Gaps today.
- .jettrace profile rows attribute only to fn run, with no stack samples (observability.md:50-52).
- Release builds still go through rustc (Docs/spec/reference/cli.md:166).
- The word --profile already names build profiles (cli.md:166, D-BUILDPROFILE1), so the record flag needs another word.

Performance law: AGENTS.md:165-168 requires a paired two-program cell. A surface's ratification waits until it strictly beats the plain form. This ballot sets the direction, and the measurement plan in the research report section 4.6 gates each surface.

options.name: Learn from recorded runs
options.detail:
A release build reads a record of real runs and uses it to lay out busy code together and put likely branches first. It also inlines calls the record shows are common, guards and calls the usual target of a closure or trait call directly, and presizes buffers where the record shows typical sizes.

A record kept in the package is used automatically. An explicit flag picks another record or turns recording off. The build receipt names the record and how much of it still matched the code.

Records come from Jet's existing performance tools. You can attach to a live server, which samples it, or run a representative workload with exact counting. Results never change; only speed does.

The same source, the same record and the same toolchain always give a byte-identical program. A record from older code still applies to the functions that did not change, and the rest are skipped.
options.technical:
The record is a canonical profile record inside .jettrace. It is keyed by stable function symbol plus MIR body digest, sorted, and its counts are quantized to log2 buckets of the run total, so re-recording noise gives the same bytes.

The record is a hashed build input in the action key (D-BUILDCACHE1=A). It never reaches comptime, prep if or $build facts. Counts are taken on MIR blocks, the one lowering, so a counting run at O0 equals one at O2.

O1, the Jet backend, uses the record in four ways. Branch weights drive LIR block layout and hot/cold splitting. A hotness-weighted inline budget and guarded devirtualization run inside the bounded O1 passes (#4135, SP20). Value-specialization clones get entry guards. The in-process linker orders functions by hotness (SP19), the Propeller relink approach with no binary rewriting.

O2: when O2 emits LLVM IR, the record becomes !prof branch weights, function entry counts and VP metadata. The rustc bridge is not fed -Cprofile-use, because the emitter retires and its symbols churn. O0 ignores the record.

CPU level: the record reports which level ran, and jet explain suggests a #Multiversion level instead of adding copies on its own.

Needed first: a real PC and stack sampler in the shared runtime, plus function identity and body digest in the source map. Proofs come in three parts. Artifacts with a record are byte-identical at 1 job and N jobs. Goldens are identical with and without a record. A paired run-time cell is measured on a workload different from the recorded one.

options.name: Recorded runs, plus an opt-in in-program optimizer
options.detail:
Everything in A, and one more build flag for long-running programs such as servers. With it, the program starts on its normal prebuilt code. After warm-up it watches itself at a low rate and recompiles its busiest functions in memory.

It does so in three cases. Traffic has moved away from the build's record. A value fixed after startup, such as a route table or a setting, can be built into the code. Or the machine's chip allows more than the build assumed, under the same exact-result rule.

The new code comes from the same program description, through the same Jet code generator, calling the same runtime, so answers are identical. When the program exits it writes a record, so the next build learns too.

The optimizer is off unless you ask for it. It has caps on CPU share and code memory. The build refuses the flag for phones, consoles, browsers and bare-metal targets, and names the reason. On macOS the package must declare the permission to make code. A switch at launch turns the optimizer off, and the program then runs the identical prebuilt code.
options.technical:
Under --adaptive (spelling illustrative), eligible functions call through the slot table: the record's hot functions, or all non-inlined functions if there is no record. Today static images keep rel32 (jet-backend-design:541). The binary carries a compact MIR slice for those functions (D-TIER-FORM1, no second IR). It also carries the Jet O1 pipeline and x86-64 code generator, linked as a library from the same Jet source, plus a sampler thread and Image/Loader.jet.

Compiles run on one background thread. They map RW, copy, mprotect to RX and rebind the slot (:528-533). Thresholds rise as the code cap fills, as JSC does.

Specializations guard at function entry only, and a failed guard calls the kept prebuilt copy. There is no on-stack replacement and there are no frame-state maps; running frames finish in the old body. Jet's immutability facts make folding run-time constants safe with an identity guard only.

I9: a forced test mode compiles every eligible function immediately with synthetic profiles and guards taken both ways, and it runs the goldens (the HotSpot -Xcomp analogue). D-CPU-DISPATCH1's bit-identical rule binds every runtime copy.

Platforms: the build refuses iOS, consoles, wasm and freestanding targets. It checks the macOS allow-jit entitlement and adds a MAP_JIT loader. Windows needs a VirtualProtect loader. Today the OS layer is Linux only.

This is not the Cranelift engine, has no interpreter, and adds no user API. It extends D-EXEC1: shipped binaries may carry the O1 generator, but only under this flag.

Shipping gate: a long-running service whose traffic mix shifts mid-run, plus one run-time-constant workload, must strictly beat A's prebuilt binary, with warm-up and steady state reported separately. Peers are HotSpot with JEP 544 and .NET with ReadyToRun plus dynamic PGO.

options.name: Fully static
options.detail:
Builds never read records, and programs never re-optimize while running. Speed comes from what is known when building: chip-level copies chosen at start, build-time code, and the code generator's own guesses about which branches are likely.

The performance tools still record runs for people to read, but builds ignore those records.
options.technical: No change beyond the ratified #Multiversion and comptime. This gives up the measured profile gains: Go 2-14%, AutoFDO 10.5% geomean, BOLT and Propeller 1-8% on large binaries. It also gives up any response to workload drift or run-time constants. It matches what a Rust user gets without the manual -Cprofile-generate and -Cprofile-use steps.

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: go.dev/doc/pgo. A committed CPU profile named default.pgo is used automatically, and Go 1.22 measured about 2-14%. Option A follows this shape.
comparisons.code:
$ mv cpu.pprof default.pgo     # main package directory
$ go build                     # -pgo=auto
$ go build -pgo=off            # opt out

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: openjdk.org/jeps/544. A training run stores AOT code and profiles. Production starts on them, and the JIT re-optimizes if the workload changes. This is the hybrid of option B; startup falls 65-80%.
comparisons.code:
$ java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp app.jar com.example.App ...   # training run
$ java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar com.example.App ...         # production

comparisons.note: Primary sources read 2026-10-04: learn.microsoft.com ready-to-run and runtime-config/compilation, and the .NET 8 announcement. Prebuilt ReadyToRun code starts fast. The tiered JIT with dynamic PGO replaces hot methods, which helps by up to 20%.
comparisons.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <PublishReadyToRun>true</PublishReadyToRun>  <!-- prebuilt code at start -->
  <TieredPGO>true</TieredPGO>                  <!-- hot methods re-JITted with live profiles -->
</PropertyGroup>

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: clang.llvm.org/docs/UsersManual.html. An instrumented build is run, the profile is merged, and the program is rebuilt. Instrumented counts are reproducible; sampling has very low overhead.
comparisons.code:
$ clang++ -O2 -fprofile-instr-generate code.cc -o code
$ ./code typical-input
$ llvm-profdata merge -output=code.profdata default.profraw
$ clang++ -O2 -fprofile-instr-use=code.profdata code.cc -o code

comparisons.note: Primary source read 2026-10-04: developer.android.com/topic/performance/baselineprofiles/overview. A recorded user journey is compiled ahead of time at install, making it about 30% faster from the first launch.

recommendation.why: B gives every release build the measured speed-up of recorded runs, and lets long-running programs keep improving where the platform allows it. It uses Jet's one code generator, one runtime and the function-swap mechanism already designed, so answers stay identical.
gains: Every release build can use recorded runs, typically 2-20% faster in peers' measurements.
Long-running servers can follow traffic changes and settings fixed at startup, as Java and .NET do.
No second engine: the same program description, code generator and runtime serve every path.

losses.loss: A program built with the optimizer is bigger and spends some CPU and memory while warming up.
losses.mitigation: It is off unless a build asks for it, with fixed caps on CPU share and code memory. It ships only after a paired benchmark shows it beating A's prebuilt program on a long-running workload.

losses.loss: It makes new machine code while running, which phones, consoles and browsers forbid and some security reviews reject.
losses.mitigation: The build refuses the flag for those targets and names the reason. Elsewhere, memory is never writable and runnable at once, and a launch switch runs the identical prebuilt code.

whyNot.reason: A cannot follow traffic that changes after the build or use settings fixed at startup, which is what you asked a runtime tier for.
C leaves measured 2-20% speed-ups unused, against your goal of maximum speed in every scenario.

recommendation.tradeoff: An opt-in, bigger program for long-running servers buys the speed only a running program can find; every other build gets recorded-run speed at no cost while running.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Before posting, Main confirms that this draft is linked to card #4571 (c0nxupyn). Main then runs Tower's ballot validator. The drafter ran the store's ballotGaps check offline only. This is a short ballot with three options; independent full-profile reviews are not claimed. No Jet compiler, test or performance run was made for this draft. Every number is cited from primary sources in the research report.

Owner acceptance has five points.
1. A record kept in the package is used by release builds automatically, Go-style, with an explicit override and opt-out. The flag spelling settles when its CLI row lands; it cannot be --profile, which names build profiles.
2. The in-program optimizer is opt-in for long-running programs and refused for targets that forbid run-time code. This extends D-EXEC1: shipped binaries may carry the O1 code generator, but only under that flag.

3. Under AGENTS.md:165-168, each surface's ratification waits for its paired cell. This ballot decides the direction and the order of work.
4. The in-program optimizer is the one Jet backend linked as a library, never the retired Cranelift engine.
5. A forced-compile test mode joins the I9 differential matrix.

After ratification, Main plans cards in this order.
1. A runtime PC and stack sampler, with function identity and MIR body digest in source maps.
2. The canonical profile record in .jettrace, and O1 consumption: layout, hot/cold splitting, the inline budget, guarded devirtualization, value clones and linker ordering.
3. Counting mode.
4. O2 metadata once O2 emits LLVM IR.

5. A's paired cells.
6. For B: slot calls in static images, the MIR slice, the backend as a runtime library, the sampler policy and caps, the macOS and Windows loaders, and the forced test mode.
7. B's paired cell against A and against HotSpot JEP 544 and .NET ReadyToRun plus dynamic PGO.

Proofs come in four parts. Artifacts with a record are byte-identical at 1 job and N jobs. Goldens are identical with and without a record and under the forced adaptive mode. Forbidding targets get refusal diagnostics. An strace shows no mapping that is writable and executable at once.

surface.gist: Should Jet use recorded runs to build faster programs, and may a long-running program re-optimize itself?
surface.lesson: A record lists what a run used most: busy functions, usual branch directions and usual call targets. Building with it changes speed, never results. An in-program optimizer recompiles a running program's busiest functions with Jet's own code generator. Phones, consoles and browsers forbid making new machine code while running.

current.note: Today Jet can record where a run spent time, but builds never use the record.
current.code:
$ jet perf run server.jet --out server.jettrace   # records where time went
$ jet perf view server.jettrace                     # you can read it...
$ jet build --release server.jet                    # ...but the build never uses it

wild.note: Go builds automatically use a committed CPU record from production, for about 2-14% more speed.
wild.code:
$ curl -o cpu.pprof "http://localhost:8080/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30"
$ mv cpu.pprof default.pgo     # main package directory
$ go build                     # uses default.pgo automatically

options.name: Learn from recorded runs
options.gist: Record what real work used most; the next build uses it.
gains: Typically 2-14% faster in Go's measurements, at no cost while running.
The same source and record always give the same program.
losses: Someone must record real work and refresh it.
Cannot follow traffic that changes after the build.

options.name: Recorded runs, plus an opt-in in-program optimizer
options.gist: A, and long-running programs may recompile their busiest functions while running.
gains: Follows traffic changes without rebuilding.
Can build settings fixed at startup into the code.
losses: A bigger program that uses some CPU and memory while warming up.
Not allowed on phones, consoles or browsers.

options.name: Fully static
options.gist: No records and no optimizer while running; only what is known when building.
gains: Nothing to record, refresh or ship.
losses: Leaves the measured 2-20% gains of recorded runs unused.
No response to changing traffic.

recommendation.why: Every release build gains from recorded runs, and long-running programs keep improving where allowed, with one code generator and identical answers.
gains: Recorded-run speed for every release build.
Long-running servers follow changing traffic.

losses.loss: With the optimizer, the program is bigger and warms up in the background.
losses.mitigation: Off unless asked for, capped, and shipped only after a benchmark beats A.

losses.loss: It makes new machine code while running, which some platforms forbid.
losses.mitigation: The build refuses it there; elsewhere a launch switch runs identical prebuilt code.

whyNot.reason: A cannot follow traffic that changes after the build.
C leaves measured speed-ups unused.

recommendation.tradeoff: An opt-in, bigger program for long-running servers; every other build gets recorded-run speed for free.

designAway.loss: A record could make builds unreproducible.
attempts: Pick up the latest record from a cache or the environment automatically; rejected because the output would depend on hidden machine state.
Make the record an explicit hashed build input, in a canonical sorted form with counts quantized so noise does not change bytes; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: the same source, record and toolchain give a byte-identical program.

designAway.loss: An old record could slow or break a build after the code changes.
attempts: Require a fresh record for every build; rejected as too much ceremony.
Match records by function name and body fingerprint, skip mismatches, and report the matched share; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: stale parts are ignored, and the build says how much still matched.

designAway.loss: A record could change what a program computes.
attempts: Let recorded values feed build-time code; rejected.
Let the record only choose among lowerings the compiler already proves equal, keep it away from build-time code, and test goldens with and without it; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: the record changes speed only.

designAway.loss: Recorded values could capture private data.
attempts: Record any argument value; rejected.
Record counts, call targets and opt-in small scalar values only, never text or collections, and keep the file local; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: records hold no user text and never leave the machine.

designAway.loss: An in-program optimizer could be a second engine that disagrees with the normal build.
attempts: Port the retired Cranelift engine; rejected by the 2026-10-04 ruling.
Link the one Jet code generator as a library, compile from the same program description, call the same runtime, and run all goldens in a forced-compile test mode; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: one code generator and one runtime serve every path.

designAway.loss: Undoing a wrong guess in the middle of a running function is complex and error-prone.
attempts: Copy JavaScript engines' mid-function bail-out with saved frame maps; rejected.
Guard only at function entry, keep the prebuilt copy for every miss, and let running calls finish in the old code; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: no mid-function bail-out exists.

designAway.loss: The optimizer makes programs bigger and uses CPU and memory while warming up.
attempts: Turn it on for every build; rejected.
Make it opt-in with CPU and code-memory caps, and ship it only after a paired benchmark beats the prebuilt program; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation: only programs that ask for it pay.

designAway.loss: Some platforms forbid making machine code while running, and it widens what an attacker can target.
attempts: Turn it off silently at run time on such platforms; rejected because the program would behave unexpectedly.

Refuse the flag at build time with a named reason, never map memory writable and runnable at once, compile only the program's own checked code, and offer a launch switch to run the prebuilt code; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation: forbidden targets fail early and clearly.

designAway.loss: The natural flag word, profile, already names build profiles.
attempts: Reuse --profile; rejected because it collides with --profile release.
Use a different word, settled when the command-line row lands; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: no meaning collision.

decisions.title: Jet's user files: disposable cache and protected identity
decisions.situation: Jet spreads downloaded packages, settings, signing keys and remembered trust across two user folders. You asked to keep only the cache folders, but deleting a cache must not also destroy your identity. This vote decides what moves and where the irreplaceable files stay. No files are moved or deleted by this vote.
decisions.gist: Where should Jet keep files that a cache cleanup must not erase?
decisions.lesson: A cache holds replaceable downloaded or built files. A signing key identifies you; a decrypting key unlocks secrets. Trust records remember which projects and publishers you allowed. Those files and your settings need backup, not cache cleanup.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: keep running the same Jet and Jetpack commands; the default locations change, not project syntax. Expert path: use the existing explicit store and key-folder overrides and standard Linux directory settings; no new override or migration command is proposed.

Both options preserve keys, settings, trust, installed-tool declarations and retention records. Retention records say which package objects an installed tool, project or running process still needs. Project-local .jet files are a separate matter and do not move. Developer scratch remains separate from product files.
decisions.story: Ana wants to reclaim downloaded package space without losing her ability to decrypt a project's secrets or changing which publishers she trusts.
decisions.inWild:
# Linux separates settings from disposable cache.
~/.config/app/
~/.cache/app/
decisions.detail:
Source: $JET_STATE_ROOT/burndown/JET-HOME-QUESTION.md:3-5 records owner prompt 2782 asking about ~/.jet. Item 101/SEED 7 says only ~/.cache/jet and $JET_STATE_ROOT may remain. Its inventory reports ~/.jet at 819 MB and ~/.local/share/jet at 7.0 GB. These are supplied sizes, not fresh measurements.

The inventory lists keys, trust, store, tools, registry content and Git downloads in ~/.jet. The data home contains hangar, leases, lease-service, config, source-kinds and locks. Folder names do not prove every byte is disposable.

The decision list has no general user-home consolidation ballot. Archived D-ECO-HANGARPATH1=A specifies native per-user data paths. Linux uses $XDG_DATA_HOME/jet/hangar or ~/.local/share/jet/hangar. macOS uses Application Support; Windows uses LOCALAPPDATA. Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Store/HangarRoots.jet:111-146 cites that rule and resolves JETPACK_ROOT or platform data. Only absolute XDG_DATA_HOME values are honored. Archival is not a contrary ruling. D-GENERATED-STORAGE2 concerns project files, not user-global homes.

D-CORE-SECRETSTORE1=A places secrets.identity at ~/.jet/keys with mode 0600. JET_KEYS_DIR overrides its folder. Jetpack/Trust/Source/Secrets/RepoSecrets.jet:51-61 does the same. crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:14-18 documents ~/.jet/trust. Jetpack/Nix/Source/Index/IndexClient.jet:50-63 reads public-key and endpoint configuration under the Hangar root. Jetpack/Store/Source/ArtifactStore/StoreConfig.jet:103-105 already uses ~/.cache/jet/store for artifacts. Consolidation changes public default paths, not just leftover folders. Migrate these readers and writers together.

A requests a narrow protected-identity exception to the owner's cache-only instruction. It amends the Linux path in D-ECO-HANGARPATH1 and identity default in D-CORE-SECRETSTORE1. B revises the instruction by preserving the data home and consolidating identity there. Neither elevates the older ruling over the newer owner instruction.

Neither option puts private keys in disposable cache. Moving everything into ~/.cache/jet is not offered as a safe third choice. External cache cleanup can erase it regardless of Jet's own rules.

Scope: Linux default user-global homes only. macOS/Windows defaults and administrator-owned shared stores stay unchanged. Existing JETPACK_ROOT and JET_KEYS_DIR remain expert controls; their owners choose the locations. Honor absolute, nonempty XDG_CONFIG_HOME and XDG_CACHE_HOME, plus XDG_DATA_HOME under B. Otherwise use standard Linux fallbacks. Empty or relative values do not select another home. $JET_STATE_ROOT remains developer-only scratch/proofs, never product keys or settings.

Migration: inventory actual contents before deleting anything. Preserve key bytes and restrictive permissions, public trust roots, trust decisions and user configuration. Preserve native recipes/source registrations, installed-tool declarations, registry identity and retention/lease metadata. Only replaceable package/artifact payloads and fetched Git/index content are cache. Do not assume local or unreproducible objects can be fetched again. Preserve irreplaceable objects and exact receipts before relocation or cleanup.

Stop relevant processes before relocating live leases or sockets. Recreate transient sockets and locks rather than copy stale ones. Verify the complete destination first. Detect conflicting identities/settings instead of overwriting. Remove only accounted-for old contents after successful cutover. Unknown files block removal of their folder and get reported. This ballot task deletes no user files.

After cutover, one resolver serves all affected readers and writers. No persistent old-path fallback, symlink home, dual writes or migration alias remains. Update commands, examples, tests and documentation together. Keys must decrypt the same ciphertext; trust must authorize exactly the same identities. A path change grants no new trust. Cache removal may require reacquisition or a confirmed rebuild, but never regeneration of signing identity. Existing retention rules protect live objects. This vote does not authorize blanket automatic deletion.

options.name: Separate disposable files from identity
options.detail: Move replaceable package and build payloads to the cache home. Keep keys, trust, settings, tool declarations and durable retention metadata in one protected configuration home. Remove the old hidden home and old data home after the verified migration. Ordinary commands need no change; experts keep existing path overrides.
options.technical:
Cache root: $XDG_CACHE_HOME/jet, falling back to ~/.cache/jet. Hangar payloads use <cache>/hangar; artifacts retain <cache>/store. Protected root: $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/jet, falling back to ~/.config/jet. The identity becomes <config>/keys/secrets.identity; trust becomes <config>/trust.

Move public publisher keys, catalog/cache settings, user settings, native recipes/source registrations and tool/retention records under the protected root. Preserve existing relative names where unambiguous. Recreate process sockets/locks on restart beside their owning storage. Durable lease/root facts must survive cache cleanup.

Introduce no public spelling. Amend the cited default-path contracts explicitly. Remove ~/.jet and ~/.local/share/jet only after accounting for every old file. Preserve nonreplaceable store payloads; never delete them automatically. Linux expert overrides remain unchanged.

# After: the same commands use these Linux defaults.
~/.config/jet/keys/secrets.identity  # keep and back up
~/.config/jet/trust                  # keep
~/.cache/jet/hangar/                 # package payloads
$JET_STATE_ROOT/                    # developer scratch only

options.name: One backed-up user-data home
options.detail: Consolidate keys, trust, settings, package storage and durable retention metadata in the established user-data home. Remove the old hidden home. Existing build cache and developer scratch remain caches. Beginners have one product-data folder to back up; experts keep the current data-home and explicit overrides.
options.technical:
Durable root: $XDG_DATA_HOME/jet, falling back to ~/.local/share/jet. Preserve <data>/hangar under D-ECO-HANGARPATH1. Move keys to <data>/keys and trust to <data>/trust. Move user configuration/declarations under this root with unambiguous existing names. Amend D-CORE-SECRETSTORE1's identity default and explicitly revise the owner's cache-only instruction.

Keep ~/.cache/jet build/artifact cache and $JET_STATE_ROOT scratch separate. Do not move all caches into durable data or claim the 7 GB disappears. Existing Hangar retention/cleanup reclaims unneeded objects but excludes identities/settings. Remove ~/.jet after verified cutover, without old-path fallback.

# After: the same commands use one Linux data home.
~/.local/share/jet/keys/secrets.identity  # back up
~/.local/share/jet/trust                  # keep
~/.local/share/jet/hangar/                # package payloads
~/.cache/jet/                            # build cache stays

comparisons.note: Configuration and user data are not disposable cache. Existing Jet code already uses XDG_DATA_HOME; this ballot chooses the Linux classification of Jet's own files, not a new cross-platform directory standard.

recommendation.why: A removes both old homes while keeping identity and trust out of disposable cache. The only exception is one small protected folder.
gains: Cache cleanup cannot erase identity or trust.
Both old default homes disappear after safe migration.

losses.loss: One protected folder remains beyond the requested cache folders.
losses.mitigation: Limit it to identity, settings and durable declarations; put replaceable large payloads in cache and document exactly what needs backup.

whyNot.reason: B is safe and simpler to back up, but keeps the large user-data home you asked to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: Make one explicit protected-data exception rather than risk losing secrets during cache cleanup.

decisions.title: Rule tests written inside a trait, run against every type that implements it
decisions.situation: A trait such as Equatable comes with rules every implementation should keep, such as "a value equals itself". Today nothing writes those rules down, so a wrong == on your own type is found only when something else breaks. Jet already has property tests: a test that takes parameters runs on about 200 generated inputs. This vote decides whether a trait may carry such rule tests, run automatically for every type that implements it.
decisions.gist: Should a trait carry rule tests that jet test runs, without being asked, for every type that implements it?
decisions.lesson: A law is a rule every implementation of a trait must keep, such as "a == a" for Equatable. A property test is a test with parameters; jet test fills them with many generated values and shrinks a failure to the smallest example.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write nothing. When your type implements Equatable or Comparable, by hand or automatically, jet test also checks the trait's laws on generated values of your type and names the smallest value that breaks one.

Expert path: write laws in your own traits as #Test functions inside the trait body. A type that breaks a law on purpose says so with #Waive and a reason, and team policy can forbid waivers.

Shared by every option: the standard traits get Jet declarations in the built-in library, as already approved. The options differ only in whether laws are written, and whether they run.
decisions.story: Mia's Fraction type compares by cross-multiplying, so 1/2 and 2/4 sort as equal, but her equal compares the fields, so they are not equal. Removing duplicates from a sorted list of fractions gives wrong answers weeks later, and nothing pointed at the mismatch.
decisions.inWild:
-- Scala Cats with Discipline: law tests are run per type, by hand
checkAll("Int", MonoidTests[Int].monoid)

-- Haskell base: Monoid laws are written only in the documentation
-- x <> mempty = x
decisions.detail:
Owner request, 2026-10-04, card #4570 (comprehensive ballots for the Core-foundations catalogue). Research: Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, catalogue row 29. Owner direction relayed 2026-10-05: implicit beginner magic, explicit expert control; markers are PascalCase.

Investigation 2026-10-05. Property tests exist (D-TEST1, syntax-decisions.md:3317-3319): a parameterized #Test fn runs about 200 generated cases with shrinking (Examples/features/tooling/property_tests.jet:17-24). Generators cover only Int, Float, Bool, String, Char, sized integers, and lists or optionals of those. Any other parameter type is E0613 (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Bundle/Validation/BodyCheck.rs:1021-1039).

So law tests over user structs need values built from a type's fields; option A adds that rule. D-CLAIM1=C already reports a claim that cannot be generated as "not generated, with the reason" (syntax-decisions.md:8644-8654); A reuses that report.

No trait in Core, Prelude or either compiler states a law today. The standard traits gain Jet declarations under D-CORE-ROLE1=A (ratified 2026-10-05). Float's == is IEEE: NaN is not equal to itself, so Float knowingly breaks reflexivity and needs the waiver path.

Tests are evidence, not proof: the optimizer never assumes a law because a law test passed. It relies only on kernel operation meanings and role contracts (D-CORE-ROLE1).

options.name: Laws run automatically
options.detail:
A trait may hold #Test functions in its body; each is a law. jet test runs every law against every type in the package that implements the trait, on generated values. A struct or enum gets generated values automatically when all its fields can be generated. A type that cannot be generated, such as an open file, is listed as not checked, with the reason.

A type that breaks a law on purpose writes #Waive(law, "reason") on its impl. Core's Float ships the one waiver it needs, so beginners never write one.
options.technical:
A #Test fn inside a trait body takes Self-typed parameters. For each implementing type T in the package under test, jet test runs it with Self = T. It uses the D-TEST1 runner; case count, JET_PROP_SEED and shrinking are unchanged. Generation extends D-TEST1: a struct or enum is generatable when every field or payload is; the runner's size parameter bounds recursion. Ungeneratable types report through D-CLAIM1=C's not-generated record.

#Waive(law: Ident, reason: String) is a new impl marker registered under I7. It is also a new gate kind under D-GATE-LAW1=A, so policy can forbid it and the audit list shows it. Laws run only under jet test, never in builds. New diagnostics: unknown law name in #Waive, #Waive without a reason.

options.name: Laws run when a type asks
options.detail: Laws are written inside the trait the same way, but jet test runs them for a type only when its impl carries #CheckLaws. Nothing runs by default, so nobody meets a law failure they did not ask for.
options.technical: Same law form and generation rule as A. #CheckLaws is a new impl marker under I7. No waiver marker is needed, because an unmarked type is never checked.

options.name: Laws as documentation only
options.detail: Each standard trait lists its laws in its doc comment, and hover and generated docs show them. Nothing runs them.
options.technical: Doc-comment convention only; no runner, marker or generation change.

comparisons.note: [INFERENCE] from memory, not re-read this session: law suites live beside the type class and a test file runs them per type by hand. This is option B's shape.
[INFERENCE] from memory, not re-read this session: base states the Monoid and Functor laws in Haddock comments only. This is option C's shape.

recommendation.why: A catches a wrong == or compare on the beginner's own type with no setup, and the expert keeps explicit control through laws in their own traits and reasoned waivers.
gains: A wrong equal or compare is caught by jet test with the smallest failing value.
Each trait states its rules once, where readers look.
Users write laws for their own traits in the test form they already know.

losses.loss: jet test runs more cases: each law runs for each implementing type.
losses.mitigation: Laws run only under jet test, never in builds, and use the existing property-test case count and seed.

losses.loss: A type that knowingly breaks a law, such as Float with NaN, needs a written waiver.
losses.mitigation: Core ships Float's waiver; a waiver carries its reason and shows in the audit list, where policy can forbid it.

whyNot.reason: B checks nothing until a type asks, so the beginner who writes the wrong equal is never told.
C writes the rules down but never checks them.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little more jet test time buys automatic checks of every trait implementation.

After ratification: law form in both checkers, field-built generation in the D-TEST1 runner, #Waive row and gate kind, laws on Equatable, Comparable, Hashable and the operator traits in Core, Float's waiver. Proofs: UI snapshots for the two new diagnostics; a corpus test where a wrong equal fails with a shrunk value; a not-generated report for a type holding a file.

designAway.result: Removed for ordinary data types; types holding files or handles are listed, not silently skipped.

designAway.loss: Float's == breaks reflexivity for NaN, so an automatic law would fail on a standard type.
attempts: Drop the reflexivity law; rejected because it is the law that catches most wrong equal methods.
Let an impl waive one law with a reason, as a gate kind policy can forbid; Core ships Float's waiver; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation: one reasoned waiver in Core.

designAway.loss: Readers or the optimizer might treat a passed law test as a guarantee.
attempts: Let the optimizer rely on tested laws; rejected because tests are evidence, not proof.
State that the optimizer never assumes a law; kept.

decisions.title: Packages under one root state their shared version, edition and license once
decisions.situation: Each of the 54 areas of Jet's built-in library starts with a header that repeats the same version, edition and license. Any project split into several packages under one root has the same repetition. Changing the version means editing every copy, and a missed copy goes unnoticed. This vote decides how packages under one root state shared facts once.
decisions.gist: How should packages under one root share their version, edition and license without repeating them?
decisions.lesson: A package header is the block at the top of a package that names it and states facts such as its version and license. A root is the package that lists other packages as its members, as in a project with several packages in one folder tree.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: put version, edition and license once in the root. Member headers state only their name and what differs, and every member uses the root's values automatically.

Expert path: a member that releases on its own schedule writes its own version, which wins. Hover on a header, or one inspect command, shows each resolved value and where it came from.

Shared by every option: the built-in library is one root with its areas as members, and ships as one versioned bundle, as already approved. The options differ only in how a member gets the shared values.
decisions.story: Ana bumps her company's monorepo to version 2.0. She edits nine member headers, misses the tenth, and publishes one package still claiming 1.4.
decisions.inWild:
# Cargo: the root states the value; each member opts in field by field
[workspace.package]
version = "1.0.0"

# member Cargo.toml
[package]
version.workspace = true
decisions.detail:
Owner request, 2026-10-04, card #4570 (comprehensive ballots for the Core-foundations catalogue). Research: Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, catalogue row 23. Owner direction relayed 2026-10-05: implicit beginner magic, explicit expert control.

Evidence 2026-10-05: 54 Core files carry an inline package block (D-ECO-INLINEPACKAGE1=A), and all 54 state version "0.0.1", edition "2026" and license "MIT" (Core/math/math.jet:1-10 is typical). No Core root package.jet exists.

D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A (ratified 2026-10-05) ships Core as one signed bundle versioned against one kernel number. So 54 per-area version strings restate one fact. D-ONCE-LAW1=A asks for one home per fact. D-ECO-MEMBERS1=A makes members independent packages listed by a root, depth one; nothing today lets a member take a value from its root.

The catalogue first filed this row as an implementation detail. It is balloted because option A changes the package model for every monorepo, not only Core.

options.name: Members take shared values from the root
options.detail:
The root states version, edition and license once. A member that leaves one of these out uses the root's value. A member that writes its own value keeps it. Name, dependencies and outputs are never shared.

The built-in library gets one root header, and each area header keeps only its name, description and layer.
options.technical:
Inheritable fields: version, edition, license. Resolution happens when the Package model is built; the member's Package record and lock entry store resolved values, so a member fetched alone from a remote monorepo carries them. The index-first fetch already reads the root.

Amends D-ECO-MEMBERS1's wording: members stay independent packages; only unstated inheritable fields fill from the root. Hover and jet inspect package show each value's source. A member outside any root must state all three, as today.

options.name: Members opt in field by field
options.detail: The root states the shared values. Each member writes, per field, that it takes the root's value. Nothing is shared unless the member says so, as in Cargo.
options.technical: New field value .Root accepted for version, edition and license in a member header; resolution and storage as in A.

options.name: Keep full headers, check they agree
options.detail: Every header keeps all its fields. A check fails the build of the built-in library when its areas disagree on version, edition or license. User monorepos are unchanged.
options.technical: A bundle-build guard over Core headers; no package-model change.

comparisons.note: [INFERENCE] from memory, not re-read this session: since Cargo 1.64, [workspace.package] holds shared values and each member opts in per field with field.workspace = true. This is option B's shape.

recommendation.why: A states each shared fact once with nothing to write in members, and an expert still overrides any value by writing it.
gains: Version, edition and license are written once per root.
A version bump is one edit and cannot miss a member.
The built-in library's 54 headers shrink to name, description and layer.

losses.loss: A member header read alone does not show its version.
losses.mitigation: Hover on the header and jet inspect package show each resolved value and where it came from.

losses.loss: A root version change moves every member that did not state its own.
losses.mitigation: That is the intent for one release train; a member on its own schedule writes its version, and the lock records resolved values so the change shows in review.

whyNot.reason: B still repeats one line per field in every member.
C keeps 54 copies of the same facts and helps no user monorepo.

recommendation.tradeoff: Members show fewer facts in their own file, in exchange for one home per shared fact.

Owner acceptance: confirm that version, edition and license are the only shared fields, and that a member's own value always wins.

After ratification, one cutover: resolution in the Package model and lock, and value sources in hover and jet inspect package. Core gains a root package.jet, and its 54 headers keep only name, description and layer. Proofs: a monorepo fixture with an inherited and an overriding member; a remote sparse fetch of one member that carries resolved values; identical Core bundle identity before and after.

surface.lesson: A package header names a package and states facts such as its version and license. A root lists other packages as its members.

current.note: Today every one of the 54 built-in library areas repeats the same facts.

wild.note: Cargo shares values from the root, but each member opts in per field.

version.workspace = true

gains: Each shared fact is written once.

losses: A member file alone does not show its version.

options.gist: Each member says, per field, that it takes the root's value.
gains: Every member file says where each value comes from.
losses: One line per field is still repeated in every member.

options.name: Keep full headers

gains: No package-model change.

gains: A version bump is one edit.
The built-in library's headers shrink to what differs.

losses.mitigation: A member on its own schedule writes its version; the lock shows the change in review.

Store resolved values in the member's record and lock, and show the source on hover and in jet inspect package; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation: resolved values are visible and recorded.

designAway.loss: Sharing too many fields would couple independent packages.

Share only version, edition and license, and let a member's own value win; kept.
designAway.result: Removed.

attempts: Give only the built-in bundle a shared header; rejected because the built-in library should be ordinary Jet.
Use one rule for every root, and let the built-in library use it like any monorepo; kept.

decisions.title: One DataTree contract for parsing and decoding
decisions.situation: DataTree holds parsed data before a program reads it as particular types. Two implementations disagree on repeated keys, number spelling, text-to-number conversion and binary bytes, so the same input can change meaning or fail on a different path. The owner chose strict duplicate handling and typed decoding, exact number text and a byte case. This records those four choices for one public data tree.
decisions.gist: Should one data tree reject duplicate keys, preserve number text, decode strictly and represent bytes?
decisions.lesson: Parsing reads a document into a tree. Decoding then reads that tree as a type such as Int. A Number case keeps the original numeric spelling until decoding. A Bytes case keeps raw byte values. Strict decoding rejects quoted text where a number is required instead of converting it silently.
decisions.explainer: Beginner path: ordinary JSON parsing rejects repeated keys, and quoted text stays text when decoding an Int. Expert path: explicitly use parse_allow_duplicates to retain the later value, decode Number into a checked numeric type, and preserve CBOR byte strings as Bytes. CBOR is a binary document format. Shared work: reconcile one public carrier, format adapters, error messages, tests and reference documentation. The four row choices are independent, not a blanket endorsement of either old implementation.
decisions.story: Lee reads a configuration file and needs repeated settings, exact numbers and quoted text to have predictable meanings.
decisions.detail:
Owner chat on 2026-10-05 selected these four rules for card #4602. Evidence: $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/Idiom-Runtime3/DATATREE-DIFF.md:11-16 covers duplicates, :18-28 numbers, :30-35 strict text and :37-41 bytes. Its :3 explicitly limits the evidence to code reading. Object insertion order is already shared behavior (:9); this ballot does not change it.

Offered duplicate policies: reject repeated keys, keep both, or keep last by default. Offered number policies: preserve exact Number text or normalize numeric values. Offered decoding policies: reject quoted text as Int or convert it leniently. Offered byte policies: preserve CBOR byte strings as Bytes or return an error.

A records the chosen combination. B illustrates the old runtime-like duplicate behavior. C illustrates the map/normalized alternative with lenient decoding as an offered choice. The diff does not establish lenient decoding as an observed built-in output; it describes that policy conditionally. No execution claim is made.

The reference already documents lexical numbers, typed text and bytes, but contradicts itself on CBOR bytes according to :37-41. This record resolves the requested public behaviors, not internal number tagging or runtime-only views. Preserve format-specific textual-cell contracts rather than inferring that CSV, environment or INI text must be decoded like quoted JSON.

options.name: Strict keys and types; exact numbers and bytes
options.detail: Reject duplicate keys by default; an explicit permissive parser keeps the later value. Keep number spelling exactly, reject quoted text when decoding Int, and represent binary byte strings as Bytes. Beginners get errors for ambiguous data; experts opt in to duplicate replacement.
options.technical:
JSON input {"x":1,"x":2} is a parse error. parse_allow_duplicates keeps x:2 at the first x position. Do not retain both pairs in the ordinary object. Number stores the exact numeric text: 1.50 re-encodes as 1.50; 1e2 as 1e2. Values such as 1e400 and integers beyond Int survive parsing exactly; range errors occur when decoding into Int or Float.

Strict typed decoding: JSON {"n":"42"} into a record with n: Int is an error, not n:42. Quoted JSON text must remain distinguishable for that contract; this ballot does not choose the internal representation used to do so. CBOR bytes 0x42 01 FF decode to Bytes([1,255]), not a representation error. Bytes re-encode as a CBOR byte string, not an ordinary numeric array. Reconcile the public carrier and adapters in one cutover without a duplicate runtime DataTree.

The strict rule concerns quoted JSON text being read as Int; do not silently remove existing textual-cell parsing for other formats. Error wording may identify the appropriate kind, but this record does not invent new exact messages.

options.name: Keep both keys; retain exact typed values
options.detail: Keep duplicate key pairs, with lookup returning the first. Retain exact Number text, strict quoted-text decoding and Bytes as on the runtime side. Experts can inspect every repeated pair, but ordinary lookup and permissive replacement no longer agree.
options.technical: For {"x":1,"x":2}, retain [x:1,x:2]; field("x") returns 1 and rendering preserves both pairs. The runtime comparison also reports multiset equality for objects. Number("1.50") preserves spelling; quoted JSON "42" into Int is rejected; CBOR 0x42 01 FF becomes Bytes([1,255]). These rows describe source evidence, not a current runtime test. Only duplicate handling differs from A in this comparison set.

options.name: Keep last; normalize and convert leniently
options.detail: Keep the last duplicate value by default, normalize numbers, permit quoted text to become Int, and reject binary byte strings. This is a forgiving text-input policy with fewer value kinds, but it loses spelling and cannot preserve binary bytes.
options.technical:
Offered alternative rows: {"x":1,"x":2} parses as x:2 without a special parser. Normalize 1.50 to 1.5 and 1e2 to 100.0; numbers beyond the numeric carrier's range may fail during parsing. Permit JSON {"n":"42"} to decode as n:42. Reject CBOR 0x42 01 FF because no Bytes case exists.

This combination is a comparison of offered policies, not an observed implementation bundle. The evidence reports normalized numbers and missing Bytes in the built-in. It reports duplicate rejection there, not ordinary keep-last. Its lenient JSON decode result is conditional on adopting the Text conversion rule. A rejects those alternative policies explicitly.

comparisons.note: JSON.parse illustrates keep-last and normalized number values; not executed or proposed as Jet's contract.

recommendation.why: Record the owner's choices: reject ambiguity, retain exact source numbers and preserve binary bytes.
gains: No silent duplicate replacement.
Lossless number and byte representation.

losses.loss: Loose JSON inputs need an explicit choice or correction.
losses.mitigation: Use parse_allow_duplicates for replacement and fix quoted numeric fields before typed decoding.

losses.loss: Pattern matches must account for Number and Bytes.
losses.mitigation: Update every carrier match and teach checked decoding beside the new cases.

whyNot.reason: Keeping both keys leaves ordinary lookup dependent on which repeated value it returns.
Silent replacement, number normalization and text conversion discard distinctions the owner chose to retain.

recommendation.tradeoff: Explicit handling and lossless values instead of silent cleanup.

decisions.title: Which field cleans up first?
decisions.situation: A struct groups values into fields, and owning fields hold resources that need cleanup. Today whole-value cleanup visits fields from first to last, while local variables clean up in reverse order. Jet does not promise which field goes first, so visible cleanup can change when a compiler changes. This vote chooses the rule for grouped values and leftover fields; I recommend reverse order throughout.
decisions.gist: Should grouped values clean up last field first, first field first, or in no promised order?
decisions.lesson: Owning means being responsible for a value's cleanup. Dropping means ending that ownership and cleaning up. Destructuring moves selected fields into new local names. R below prints its label when cleaned. Call whole(), then partial(); .. leaves second unbound.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: learn one reverse direction for cleanup, including fields inside a value. Expert path: rely on structural order, not physical storage layout. Apply the chosen order recursively to each group of fields still owned at a cleanup point. A moved field belongs to its new owner and is excluded from its former group's cleanup.

The examples are six-line illustrations, not executed receipts. Call whole(), then partial(). Each option uses identical Jet code; only the whole-value output guarantee changes. The candidate destructure fix retains omitted second at the original owner's scope-cleanup position. Newly bound first is a later local, so it cleans first; second follows at the same scope exit. One omitted field cannot demonstrate internal remainder order; the three-field case below can.

Shared work: preserve exactly-once cleanup and existing lifetime, borrowing, error and cancellation rules. This vote does not move cleanup earlier or later, permit new partial moves, add a destructor hook, or change initializer evaluation order. It also leaves the ordering between deferred closes, automatic locals, scope guards and process handlers unchanged. No allocation or speed claim is made.
decisions.story: Sam owns two resources in one record and wants their cleanup messages to have a dependable order.
decisions.detail:
Decision-needed check: S63 / D-SHAPE-RESOURCE1=A / D-SHAPE-RESOURCE2=A in Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2525-2540 ratify scope-end cleanup on success, error, panic and cancellation, and reverse deferred closes. Docs/spec/spec.md:843-847 and Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:1671-1677 order deferred closes, scope guards and atexit handlers. They exclude host kill/abort guarantees.

Examples/features/memory/scope_close_safety_net.jet:1-6 describes reverse automatic-local cleanup and ownership transfer. Docs/proposals/greenfield-memory-system-2026-10-02.md:293-295 describes reverse scope cleanup; it is a proposal, not independent ratified authority. None of these passages chooses field order inside one aggregate. This observable gap needs an OPEN owner vote. Attach it to active card #4566 because aggregate optimizations must preserve observable cleanup. No Tower write is part of this assignment.

The assignment reports today's aggregate cleanup as declaration order. This ballot uses that baseline without claiming new all-backend execution evidence. PerfValues9 reports its candidate fix as uncommitted and unproven. Inspection of .agent-worktrees/perfvalues9/crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/mir.rs:7550-7554 captures the original cleanup position; :7569,7580 registers omitted fields in reverse. Lines 7584-7591 put that group at the original owner's position. Lines 6994-7001 run automatic actions LIFO, giving the omitted fields declaration-order cleanup at scope exit, after later kept bindings.

The corresponding .agent-worktrees/perfvalues9/Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Codegen/Bindings.jet:61-68 captures the original position; :73,84,91 registers omitted fields and :97-101 removes the original owner. These are inspected candidate sources, not a successful compiler receipt. Rust enum lowering at crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/MIRRust.rs:17538-17583 selects moved payload bindings and leaves other fields under Rust cleanup via .. . Do not infer all execution paths from one emitter.

Primary Rust reference: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/destructors.html#destructors-operation specifies declaration-order struct and active enum fields, tuple order, and first-to-last arrays/owned slices. Its drop-scopes section specifies reverse locals. Its introduction excludes uninitialized fields after a partial move.

Primary C++ references: https://eel.is/c++draft/class.dtor#13 specifies reverse construction-completion order for members and reverse construction order for built-in array elements. https://eel.is/c++draft/class.base.init#15.3 specifies declaration-order member initialization. Thus ordinary C++ non-static members clean in REVERSE declaration order, unlike Rust. Do not extend this claim to std::tuple or vector destruction contracts.

Syntax note: Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:780-787 still shows dotted record patterns and requires .. for partial struct patterns. The current owner record $JET_STATE_ROOT/ballots/READY/OWNER-2026-10-05/D-TUPLE-DESTRUCT1.json:12,18 corrects record patterns to dotless braces under D-LIT-DOT1. These examples use { first, .. }. Cleanup order is independent of tuple binding-by-name, positional eligibility, canonical storage sorting and physical layout.

options.name: Last field first
options.gist: Guarantee reverse declaration order, matching reverse local cleanup.
options.detail: Clean a struct's last declared owning field first, then work backwards. Apply the same reverse rule to tuple members, active enum payload fields and current list positions. A beginner learns one reverse cleanup direction; an expert can predict exact side effects.
options.technical:
Ratify reverse source declaration order for structs, named tuples and active enum payloads. Lists clean from highest live logical index to lowest. Restrict that ordering to omitted or remaining fields without changing their cleanup point. Ignore layout, pattern order, initializer spelling and alphabetical storage order.

This changes today's reported aggregate order and resembles ordinary C++ member destruction, not Rust field destruction. Teach 'last position, first cleanup'. 'Last built' is only a mnemonic when construction follows declaration order; no acquisition history is tracked. Preserve all common edge cases above.

options.name: First field first
options.gist: Guarantee today's declaration order; choosing this changes nothing today.
options.detail: Clean owning fields from first declared to last. Do the same for tuple members, active enum payloads and lists from first element to last. This follows the type's reading order and Rust's field rule; it deliberately differs from Jet's reverse local cleanup.
options.technical:
Ratify source declaration order for structs, named tuples and active enum payloads. Lists clean from lowest live logical index to highest. Restrict that ordering to omitted or remaining fields without changing their cleanup point.

Choosing B changes nothing in today's reported declaration-order implementation or PerfValues9 fix. It makes that baseline portable. All execution paths still need coverage and semantic source-order preservation. This matches Rust field/array destruction, not C++ member destruction. Its advantages are top-to-bottom reading and no migration; its cost is two cleanup directions. Preserve all common edge cases above.

options.name: No promised field order
options.gist: Clean every owned field once, but let implementations choose their order.
options.detail: Guarantee cleanup without guaranteeing the relative order of fields in one group. Implementations can retain declaration order or use a different order. Programs that need an order must use explicit consuming closes rather than depending on automatic field cleanup.
options.technical:
Leave relative aggregate field/list cleanup order unspecified, including omitted fields. Declaration, reverse or other orders are allowed. Exactly-once cleanup at the existing point remains mandatory, subject to existing panic/abort boundaries. Unspecified is not undefined behavior: cleanup may print, but an order-specific result is nonportable.

Compilers, execution paths or releases may choose differently. This does not authorize parallel cleanup, changed lifetimes, dropping moved-out fields, or weakened reverse local/defer order. Tests assert membership and counts, not field ordering. Order-sensitive protocols use explicit consuming closes where existing ownership rules permit them.

comparisons.note: Struct fields clean first-to-last; local variables clean last-to-first. Illustration, not executed.
comparisons.code:
struct Pair { first: P, second: P }
fn whole() { let p = pair(); } // first, second

comparisons.note: Ordinary members clean in reverse declaration order. Built-in arrays reverse construction order. Illustration, not executed.
comparisons.code:
struct Pair { P first; P second; };
void whole() { Pair p; } // second, first

recommendation.why: One reverse direction is easier to teach, and a guaranteed order keeps cleanup side effects predictable across compilers.
gains: One direction for locals and fields.
A portable order for visible cleanup.

losses.loss: Existing field-order-dependent programs change behavior.
losses.mitigation: Audit cleanup-sensitive callers and update their expected traces; use explicit consuming closes when a protocol needs another order.

whyNot.reason: Readable and unchanged today, but beginners must learn opposite directions for locals and fields.
Implementation freedom is real, but visible cleanup becomes harder to predict and debug.

recommendation.tradeoff: Change today's field order once to get one predictable cleanup direction.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Before posting, run the read-only READY ballot validator and require exit zero. This OPEN proposal does not authorize compiler changes before the owner votes. No example execution or performance verification is claimed. After ratification, update the specification, resource documentation, changelog, affected execution paths and cleanup-sensitive callers together. Remove obsolete contracts rather than keeping compatibility modes.

Call whole() then partial() and check the chosen trace. Add three owning fields with the middle retained to distinguish remainder ordering. Cover nested structs, named tuples with nonalphabetical source order, reordered initializer expressions, unit/single/multiple-field enum variants, empty/single/multiple-element lists, fixed-size lists, and lists after insertion/removal.

Cover legal partial moves, reinitialization, interrupted construction, immediate discard, fallthrough, early return, failure propagation, loop exit, panic unwind, cancellation and existing explicit-stop cleanup. Check exactly-once cleanup, moved-out exclusions and unchanged local/deferred-close ordering on every execution path. Do not assert complete cleanup after kill, abort or an aborting cleanup panic. Under C, assert field membership and counts, never relative field order.

surface.lesson: Owning means responsibility for cleanup. Dropping ends ownership. Destructuring gives selected fields new names. R prints its label during cleanup. Call whole(), then partial(); .. omits second.

current.note: Today: whole prints first, second. Candidate partial cleanup prints first, second at exit; not an execution receipt.

wild.note: Rust cleans fields first-to-last; C++ cleans ordinary members last-to-first.

options.gist: Reverse field order, like local cleanup.
gains: One cleanup direction.
losses: Changes today's field order; audit callers and expected traces.

options.name: First field first
options.gist: Promise today's order; choosing this changes nothing today.
gains: Top-to-bottom reading; no behavior migration.
losses: Two cleanup directions to learn.

options.gist: Every field cleans once; implementations choose their order.
gains: Compilers retain ordering freedom.

gains: Portable cleanup order.

losses.loss: Existing order-sensitive programs change behavior.
losses.mitigation: Audit callers and expected traces; use explicit consuming closes for another protocol order.

whyNot.reason: Readable and unchanged, but teaches two directions.
Flexible, but visible cleanup is not predictable across compilers.
