decisions.detail:
YOUR QUESTION (q9favyoy, 2026-10-05)

You asked what the best practice and industry standard are for web development, networking and servers. You also asked which choice gives the best cohesive out-of-the-box experience for the most common domains. You added that Jet is primarily module-based, not file- or path-based, and asked the ballot to account for that.

Module-based first. In Jet a package is one namespace, and its files see each other's names with no import (D-MOD-CYCLE1=A, spec.md:1715). project.X resolves by declared module names, not file names. A file name is consulted at one point only: when use app.httpClient or module httpClient; must locate the file that holds that module. So this ballot does not choose a path style for users. It chooses the one rule that links a module name to its file.

Answer: A. Module-first languages fix that link with one rule and never let the host disk decide. Rust maps mod foo to foo.rs or foo/mod.rs. Rails' Zeitwerk maps constants to files through one inflector with an acronym table. Python requires exact case even on case-insensitive disks (PEP 235). TypeScript added forceConsistentCasingInFileNames because macOS and Windows hid casing bugs that broke Linux builds. Go case-encodes module paths in its proxy for the same reason.

WHAT GIVES THE MOST VALUE OUT OF THE BOX

Web projects name files in kebab-case, such as order-items. Python and Rust use snake_case, while C#, Java and Jet's repository use PascalCase. A accepts every one of those spellings for the same module with no setting. It gives the same answer on Linux, macOS and Windows, and turns any ambiguity into an error naming both files.

B keeps exact-only matching in user projects, so copied Jet files break; C finds only two spellings. The tool files package.jet and run.jet keep one fixed lowercase name, so tools and scaffolds never guess.

DECISION BOUNDARY

Owner answer on D-ROUTE-FILES1, Tower question q3nq4q4w, 2026-10-05: "capitalized is how I want the jet repo managed, but don't want to explicitly require PascalCase file names everywhere for all users right now."

This ballot amends the scope of D-PATH-CASE1=A, ratified 2026-10-05 on card #4613 (c0itvqcw). Ratified history is immutable, so the amendment is a new decision. The companion D-ROUTE-FILES2 settles page addresses separately. Both belong to the casing ballot set in Docs/proposals/casing-2026-10-05.md: D-CASE-LAW2 (the source law), D-WIRE-CASE1 and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1 (outside names). This ballot applies that set's rule R1, words are the identity, to file names.

REVISION BY BallotSync, 2026-10-05

The section above, the situation and the recommendation now answer owner question q9favyoy in the ballot itself: the module-first framing, the industry rule, and the out-of-the-box value. The mechanism and options are unchanged.

REVISION BY OpenQuestions, 2026-10-05

After the owner's web-first direction, D-CASE-LAW2 recommends camelCase values, so import examples now read use app.httpClient. The word key is internal and identical under either value style. Option B and C now compare against the import's exact spelling, httpClient.jet. Under camelCase imports, C's exact file and canonical file differ only by capitals, so the collision check rejects that pair. C's remaining loss is that underscore and hyphen file names are never found.

REVISION BY CasingProposal, 2026-10-05

BallotPathScope2 drafted this ballot. Three changes make it match the casing set.

Hyphens are word boundaries, so order-items.jet keys order_items, matching S84's dashed package and module names. Reserved tool files, package.jet and run.jet, are exact lowercase everywhere, including the repository, so a file copied between Jet and a project never changes name.

Scaffolds write Jet's house style, PascalCase, for the code files they create beyond the reserved files; users stay free to rename. The original draft is kept at $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/casing/D-PATH-CASE2.BallotPathScope2.orig.json.

WHAT CHANGES IN D-PATH-CASE1=A

Scope: PascalCase with capital acronyms applies to the Jet repository's own Jet source: Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Examples and tests. It is required by a repository check, not by the compiler, and it is not required for user projects or published packages.

Reserved files: package.jet (D-ECO-FILEROOT1=A) and run.jet (DEFAULT_ENTRY_FILE) keep their exact lowercase names everywhere, including the repository. D-PATH-CASE1=A's Package.jet and Run.jet renames are withdrawn. Rule: a file a tool looks up by a fixed name follows the tool's spelling; a file a person names follows the case law.

D-PATH-CASE1=A said not to scan case-insensitively for another file. Option A replaces that sentence with one word-key comparison that can never choose silently. Its portability rule, rejecting case-only collisions on every host, is kept and extended.

UNCHANGED LAW

Module paths and aliases follow the source value style: snake_case under D-CASE-LAW1=A, camelCase under D-CASE-LAW2=A. D-ONCE-CASE1=A, D-ACRO-CASE1=A and D-ACRO-LEX1=A supply the one naming lexicon and acronym table. D-NEW-TEMPLATE1=A fixes jet new's template names. D-MARKER-CASE1=A already capitalizes marker qualifiers.

OBSERVED BASE STATE, 2026-10-05

crates/jet-driver/src/Loader.rs:5672-5708 finds a module by scanning the project root for a file named exactly name.jet, or a folder name holding run.jet. Matching compares strings, not filesystem lookups, so it is already host-independent.

Loader.rs:5631-5669 reports E0603 for no match and E0606 for several. On base a dotted user name such as tools.util never matches a path. Loader.rs:4658-4697 then reinterprets it as a member import when tools is a module.

Loader.rs:4849-4904 resolves module name; declarations to name.jet or name/module.jet beside the declaring file. Loader.rs:5517-5546 resolves project.X by declared module names, not file names. Loader.rs:5713-5719 derives a file import's default alias by sanitizing the raw stem.

crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/jetpack_config.rs:404 fixes PACKAGE_FILE as package.jet. Syntax/package_files.rs:34 fixes DEFAULT_ENTRY_FILE as run.jet. Source/CmdCompile.rs:5733-5835 makes jet new write package.jet, run.jet and .gitignore, plus optional command homes.

IN-FLIGHT STATE

Branch feat/path-case at 68a1ed4f1 renames repository paths to PascalCase. Its crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/acronyms.rs:38-68 adds module_source_path, the forward lexicon mapping. The branch first renamed user-facing role files too; that is being reverted.

Main approved an interim on 2026-10-05: exact base spelling first everywhere, then canonical PascalCase only for sources under the Jet repository root. All of it lives inside one mapping function, so this ballot's outcome changes one place. Option B makes that interim permanent.

RESEARCH: PROVEN RIGHT WAYS

Python PEP 235 (https://peps.python.org/pep-0235/) makes import require the exact case even on case-insensitive disks. PYTHONCASEOK is the explicit opt-out. Lesson: never let the operating system decide which file a name means.

TypeScript's forceConsistentCasingInFileNames (https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#forceConsistentCasingInFileNames) rejects one file imported with two casings. The webpack case-sensitive-paths plugin (https://github.com/Urthen/case-sensitive-paths-webpack-plugin) exists because macOS builds passed while Linux CI failed.

Go's module proxy protocol (https://go.dev/ref/mod#goproxy-protocol) case-encodes capitals as an exclamation mark plus the lowercase letter. It does so because cache directories may live on case-insensitive filesystems. Deterministic encoding beats trusting the host.

Rails' Zeitwerk loader (https://github.com/fxn/zeitwerk) maps snake_case files to capitalized constants through one inflector with an acronym table. Its migration guide (https://guides.rubyonrails.org/classic_to_zeitwerk_howto.html) records why the older guessing autoloader was replaced. One explicit mapping wins over guessing.

Rust (https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/modules.html) maps mod foo to foo.rs or foo/mod.rs, with an explicit path attribute as the escape. Java's JLS 7.6 (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-7.html#jls-7.6) lets hosts require Foo.java for public class Foo. Both pick one spelling per language.

PROVEN WRONG WAYS

Next.js documents incorrect import casing that works locally and fails on Linux CI: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/module-not-found. That is the cost of letting the filesystem decide.

The logrus organization's change from Sirupsen to sirupsen broke Go builds with case-insensitive import collisions. Its README records the fallout: https://github.com/sirupsen/logrus#case-sensitivity. Two spellings of one name must be an error, not a coin flip.

A 2003 Win32 C code base included headers with the wrong letter case. It compiled on Windows and failed on Linux. Source: mining attachment AT5, video DaJWWePhRsM at 32:20.

Git's core.ignoreCase documentation (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config) shows case-only renames are fragile on default macOS and Windows checkouts. Tooling should prevent case-only twins rather than repair them later.

Plain ASCII case-insensitive matching is not an option. It cannot connect http_client to HTTPClient, because the underscore differs, not only the letters. Jet's lexicon already defines the word split.

SYNTHESIS

Python, TypeScript and Go show the failure: the host's filesystem silently decides. Zeitwerk and Rust show the right shape: one mapping between code names and file names. Option A compares names by their words, using Jet's one lexicon, never asks the filesystem, and errors on any ambiguity.

A differs from Python's exact-only rule deliberately. Jet must already connect imports to capitalized repository files. Exact-only matching would force every user project to choose Jet's spelling, which the owner declined.

Evidence limits: no controlled productivity measurements were found. The recommendation rests on documented mechanisms and recorded breakages.

options.name: Match by words, refuse twins
options.detail: Jet reads each file and folder name as words: http_client, HTTPClient, HttpClient and http-client all read as http client. An import finds the one file whose words match. Two files whose names read the same are an error everywhere. package.jet and run.jet keep their exact lowercase names everywhere, including Jet's repository. Scaffolds write capitalized code files, Jet's house style; you may rename them freely.
options.technical:
Word key: drop .jet. Split at underscores, hyphens, lowercase-to-capital changes, and acronym boundaries from the shared lexicon (rule R1 of the casing set). Digits stay attached, so UTF8 reads utf8. Lowercase the words and join them with underscores. HTTPClient, http_client, HttpClient, httpClient and http-client key http_client; HTTP_APIClient keys http_api_client. Names with other characters, such as spaces or brackets, have no key; literal path imports still reach them. The key is internal, so it does not depend on the source value style.

Owning root: core. selects the Core root. A dependency or realized library name selects its source root, dropping that first segment. Otherwise the project root applies. project.X keeps resolving declared module names unchanged.

Match: candidates are source files whose trailing folders and stem key-match the remaining segments. A folder whose key matches the last segment also matches through its entry file, run.jet. One candidate resolves. A single segment therefore keeps today's whole-project search; a longer dotted name narrows it. module name; declarations use the same key, beside the declaring file.

The member-import fallback for use alpha.value keeps running only after no module matches. File imports derive their default alias from the stem's words in the source value style, so use "App/HTTPClient.jet" binds httpClient.

Reserved names: package.jet and run.jet match only those exact spellings, in user projects and in Jet's repository. Any other casing, such as Package.jet or Run.jet, is rejected with a rename fix, per D-ECO-FILEROOT1=A. Command homes such as @run.jet are reserved the same way.

Collisions: before reading a package, reject two entries in one source folder that fold equal or share a key, on every host. Zero matches report E0603; several report E0606. No candidate order, host lookup or fallback spelling exists.

Repository: a repository check, run by the Jet commit and CI gates, rejects repository source names, other than reserved names, that differ from the canonical PascalCase spelling of their key. It reuses module_source_path from the in-flight branch. The compiler has no repository-root special case. Both compiler halves share one implementation.

Scaffolds: jet new, its templates and jet new route write package.jet and run.jet, and write every other code file in canonical PascalCase, for example Routes/Index.jet. Repository-owned generators under Tools do the same. Users may rename any non-reserved file; the word key keeps imports working.

Diagnostics: E0603 shows the import and example spellings, such as http_client.jet or HTTPClient.jet. E0606 names every matching file and suggests a longer dotted name. The collision error names both files and says they spell one module. The reserved-name error shows the exact rename.

Every root tries name.jet, then module_source_path(name), in that order. No repository-root special case exists. The first hit wins; a second spelling is not reported unless the portability collision check catches a case-only twin.

decisions.title: A page file's words become its web address
decisions.situation: Jet turns each page file in a web app's routes folder into a web address, and today it copies the name letter for letter, so OrderItems.jet answers /OrderItems. You first asked that the address come straight from the file name, without forcing capitals on anyone. You then asked for web best practice: Google and Microsoft recommend lowercase words joined by hyphens, and Next.js, Nuxt and SvelteKit projects name their files that way. We recommend reading the file name's words and writing them lowercase with hyphens, which matches your rule for every lowercase-hyphen file and gives the standard address for any other spelling.
decisions.gist: Should a page file's web address use its name's words in lowercase, or copy the name letter for letter?
decisions.lesson: A route connects a web address to the page that answers it. A name's words are the parts it is built from: OrderItems, order_items and order-items all have the words order and items. A file part written [id] captures one address part as :id. A marker is a tag before a function; #Server.Get("/path") names an exact address.
decisions.explainer: Every option serves the same tiny shop: home at /, items at /order-items, one order at /orders/:id, and purchases at /purchases. GET means reading a page. Examples are file-to-address maps plus one tag line, not complete source files. Each mapped file contains its page function. Shared work: parse page declarations instead of scanning text lines, keep one checked route list, and update scaffolds, documentation and fixtures together.
decisions.story: Maya copies Jet's shop example, whose page files are capitalized like the rest of Jet. She expects the addresses customers type, such as /order-items, not /OrderItems.
decisions.detail:
YOUR QUESTIONS

q3nq4q4w, on D-ROUTE-FILES1: keep capitals for Jet's repository only, take addresses from the file name directly, and spell the marker #Server.Get. Option B is that rule exactly. A gives the same address for every lowercase-hyphen file name, and every option uses #Server.Get.

q8465r4k, 2026-10-05: you asked what the best practice and industry standard are for web development, networking and servers. You also asked which choice gives the best cohesive out-of-the-box experience for the most common domains.

Answer: A. The web standard for public addresses is lowercase words joined by hyphens. Google Search Central recommends hyphens between words and warns that capitals make different addresses. Microsoft's REST guidelines ask for kebab-case path segments. ASP.NET Razor Pages, the major framework whose page files are capitalized like Jet's repository, turns them into lowercase-hyphen addresses, exactly as A does.

Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit and Astro copy file names literally, as B does. They reach the same addresses only because their projects already name route files in kebab-case. So the address standard is the same everywhere; only the file habits differ.

WHAT GIVES THE MOST VALUE OUT OF THE BOX

With A, any file spelling gives the address that search engines, REST guidelines and users expect. That covers Jet's PascalCase examples, kebab-case files from web projects and snake_case files from Python projects, with no tag and no repository exception. B reaches that result only when every file is already lowercase-hyphen, so Jet's own examples would teach /OrderItems. C costs one hand-written line per page, the ceremony file routing exists to remove. #Server.Get("/exact") keeps any legacy or brand address under every option.

DECISION BOUNDARY

Owner answer on D-ROUTE-FILES1, Tower question q3nq4q4w, 2026-10-05: "capitalized is how I want the jet repo managed, but don't want to explicitly require PascalCase file names everywhere for all users right now. let's just use the file name directly for paths. also, #server.Get() should be #Server.Get() in pascal case."

This ballot supersedes the open D-ROUTE-FILES1 on card #4613 (c0itvqcw). Main retires D-ROUTE-FILES1 when posting this ballot. It belongs to the casing ballot set in Docs/proposals/casing-2026-10-05.md, with D-CASE-LAW1, D-PATH-CASE2, D-WIRE-CASE1 and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1.

WHY THE RECOMMENDATION DIFFERS FROM THE OWNER'S STATED DIRECTION

The owner's direction is option B, written down exactly. The recommendation is A, and the proposal argues for it with evidence. For every file already named in lowercase with hyphens, A and B give the same address, so users keep the freedom the owner asked for.

They differ only for capitalized or underscored names. Jet's own examples are capitalized under the owner's repository rule. Under B they would publish /OrderItems and /Index, teaching beginners addresses that common web guidance advises against. Avoiding that under B needs a route-folder exception in the repository, which the owner did not want.

A also drops D-ROUTE-FILES1's By-prefix parameter rule. Brackets stay, so the only new idea is reading a name as words.

REVISION HISTORY

BallotPathScope2 drafted this ballot with the literal rule as A and the D-ROUTE-FILES1 transform as B. CasingProposal revised it to fit the casing set: the word reading is now A, without the By prefix, and the literal rule is B. The original draft is kept at $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/casing/D-ROUTE-FILES2.BallotPathScope2.orig.json.

BallotSync revised it on 2026-10-05 so the ballot itself answers owner question q8465r4k: the section above, the situation and the recommendation now state the web standard and the out-of-the-box value. The mechanism and options are unchanged.

ALREADY SETTLED, NOT RE-DECIDED

D-MARKER-CASE1=A, ratified 2026-10-05, capitalizes every marker part after #. With use core.http.server as server, the marker is #Server.Get. Every option uses it.

D-HTTP-ROUTE-EXPOSE1=A keeps marked struct methods behind explicit mux.mount. D-WEBAUTHOR1 supplies .routes(from:) and the leading-underscore opt-out. D-DX-ROUTER1=A requires one checked App route graph; file routes feed that graph rather than a second table.

OBSERVED JET STATE, 2026-10-05

crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/App.rs:1794-1880 expands only .routes(from:) roots. It skips leading-underscore files, requires fn page, and records each route through record_route. Duplicate and overlapping paths already fail with E2807 at :925-973 and routes_overlap at :1003.

convention_path at :1902-1923 omits a terminal stem only when it is exactly lowercase index or page. It turns [name] into :name and copies every other component literally. So Index.jet becomes /Index, and OrderItems.jet becomes /OrderItems.

convention_has_page at :1930-1941 detects pages by text-line prefixes, not parsed declarations. A commented-out fn page would therefore count.

Source/CmdBackendScaffold.rs:1842-1885 maps jet new route --path back to a file. A *rest segment fails with E2456. route_source at :1936-1939 also writes a // route: comment that the scanner ignores. The self-hosted compiler carries MIRAppRoutesFrom in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/MIR/MIR.jet:3512. The expansion law must be identical in both compiler halves.

The word reading already exists: crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/acronyms.rs:91-158 splits names into words with the acronym list. D-PATH-CASE2 option A uses the same reading to find files for imports.

RESEARCH: PROVEN RIGHT WAYS

Razor's PageRouteTransformerConvention turns /Pages/SubscriptionManagement/ViewAll.cshtml into /subscription-management/view-all. It never changes addresses written with @page. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/razor-pages/razor-pages-conventions. That is option A's model.

Google recommends hyphens over underscores between words, and treats /APPLE and /apple as different addresses. Source: https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/url-structure. Microsoft's REST guidelines say to use kebab-casing for path segments and to return 404 for the wrong case. Source: https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines.

RFC 3986 section 6.2.2.1 makes paths case-sensitive. Windows and macOS file systems are case-insensitive by default; see https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/case-sensitivity. A rule that copies letter case makes a public address depend on a spelling those systems treat as equal.

Jet mining evidence, $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/mine/drafts/cpp-craft/route-files-evidence.card.json: hyphens are the common separator for web files, and lowercase is the common server convention.

Next.js, SvelteKit, Astro and Nuxt copy file names literally; their documentation writes lowercase-hyphen names. Sources: nextjs.org, svelte.dev/docs/kit/routing, docs.astro.build/en/guides/routing, nuxt.com/docs/getting-started/routing. That is option B's model.

Nuxt's definePageMeta path and Razor's @page replace a page's address locally. A page-local override is the proven escape hatch, and every option keeps it.

Rails, Phoenix and Django write every pattern explicitly. That is option C's model.

PROVEN WRONG WAYS

Next.js issue https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/21498 reports Windows URL casing inconsistencies and an infinite /About to /about redirect loop. Lesson: never lowercase incoming requests or add implicit case redirects. A derives lowercase addresses once, at build time, and matches requests exactly.

Evidence limits: no controlled productivity or ranking measurements were found. The recommendation rests on documented mechanisms, official guidance and one failure report.

Scope: only App .routes(from:) roots contribute pages. Builder routes and mounted HTTP structs are unchanged. Detect pages from the parsed fn page declaration, not text-line prefixes. Leading-underscore files stay non-routed helpers (D-WEBAUTHOR1).

Mapping: drop .jet. Split each component into words with the shared splitter: underscores, hyphens, lowercase-to-capital changes and acronym ends from the lexicon. Roots: a terminal stem whose words are exactly index or page is omitted. Index or Page folders stay ordinary segments.

Parameters: a component written [Name] becomes :name, where name is the snake_case word key, so [ID] and [id] give :id and [UserID] gives :user_id. It binds the handler parameter of that name. Other bracket forms are rejected with a fix naming #Server.Get.

Override: extend core.http.server.Get's permitted sites to the fn page of a file under a .routes(from:) root. #Server.Get("/purchases") replaces that file's derived address; it is not an alias. The written address is used exactly, in any case. More than one Get on one page is an error.

Collisions: every final address passes the existing E2807 duplicate and overlap checks. Two files with the same words give the same address, so E2807 names both. Request matching stays exact and case-sensitive, with no lowercasing or redirects.

decisions.title: One way Jet names become outside names
decisions.situation: A Jet field such as avatarURL also appears outside Jet: as a JSON key, an environment variable, a command-line flag, a database column or a web header. You asked what web best practice is and what works best out of the box, and the answer is each place's own published standard. That means camelCase JSON as Google, Microsoft and GraphQL APIs write it, lowercase snake_case SQL, kebab-case flags, capitalized environment names matched exactly, and lowercase headers. We recommend that Jet computes each of those spellings itself, with one optional package setting for snake_case partners such as Stripe, instead of today's mark on every type.
decisions.gist: How should Jet spell its names in JSON, environment variables, flags and SQL?
decisions.lesson: The wire is any place data leaves the program: JSON text, environment variables, command-line flags, database columns. camelCase joins words with capitals after the first: avatarUrl. snake_case joins lowercase words with underscores: avatar_url. kebab-case uses hyphens: avatar-url. A rename gives a field a different outside name.
decisions.explainer: Every option uses the same web service: a UserProfile record with userID, avatarURL and a plan. A browser front end reads it as camelCase JSON, and one partner service expects snake_case JSON. The examples show what the author writes and what each side receives. Shared work: one naming module in the compiler, the same rules in both compiler halves, and jet inspect shapes showing every outside name.
decisions.story: Priya builds an API with forty record types for a TypeScript front end, and one billing package that talks to a snake_case payment service. She wants each package's JSON style set once, not on forty types, and her settings should still come from APP_ environment variables.
decisions.detail:
YOUR QUESTION (q7oo2ws2, 2026-10-05)

You asked what the best practice and industry standard are for web development, networking and servers. You also asked which choice gives the best cohesive out-of-the-box experience for the most common domains.

Answer: A. Every outside place already has a published standard, and the best out-of-the-box experience follows each one automatically. JSON keys are camelCase on the web: Google's JSON style guide, Microsoft's REST guidelines and Graph, JSON:API, GraphQL schemas, the Protocol Buffers JSON mapping and TypeScript clients. snake_case JSON is a large minority, used by Stripe, GitHub's REST API and Slack, so it gets one package setting rather than a mark on every type.

SQL names are lowercase snake_case, because PostgreSQL folds unquoted names to lowercase and camelCase would force quotes everywhere. Environment names are capitals with underscores, the form POSIX uses, and they match exactly because POSIX keeps their case. Flags are lowercase kebab-case long options, as in GNU tools. HTTP header names compare without case (RFC 9110) and are sent lowercase, which HTTP/2 requires (RFC 9113 section 8.2). HTML attributes and CSS names are lowercase with hyphens.

WHAT GIVES THE MOST VALUE OUT OF THE BOX

With A, one Jet record needs nothing written to give each consumer its native spelling. That covers a TypeScript or GraphQL front end, a PostgreSQL table, a container's environment, a shell user and an HTTP/2 peer. The only common case that needs a line is a snake_case partner API, and that costs one line per package. B charges that partner one mark per type, and C lets one type ship two shapes, which breaks generated API documents and TypeScript clients.

DECISION BOUNDARY

Owner request, 2026-10-05, card #4613 (c0itvqcw): one consistent rule for every name, including wire keys, environment variables, URLs, SQL and C names. They should be mapped by one mechanism rather than ad-hoc renames. Owner direction later that day: prefer pragmatic defaults and lean toward web development. Full proposal: Docs/proposals/casing-2026-10-05.md, sections 3.3, 3.4 and 5.1.

This ballot builds on D-CASE-LAW2, which fixes names inside Jet source. Examples assume D-CASE-LAW2=A: camelCase fields with full-capital acronyms. Under D-CASE-LAW2=B the mechanism is identical and data keys default to snake_case words instead. D-WIRE-ACRONYM1 decides how acronyms look in camelCase keys. D-ROUTE-FILES2 decides web addresses from files. D-PATH-CASE2 decides file names.

REVISION, 2026-10-05

Revised by OpenQuestions after the owner's web-first direction. The mechanism and recommendation are unchanged. Data keys now default to the Jet value case, which is camelCase under the recommended law, so a web service writes nothing. The package setting now serves the minority of services that speak snake_case.

Revised again by BallotSync, 2026-10-05, so the ballot itself answers owner question q7oo2ws2: the section above, the situation and the recommendation now state each place's standard and the out-of-the-box value. The mechanism and options are unchanged.

RATIFIED LAW THIS EXTENDS

D-SHAPE-ONE1=A: one shape fact per type; every format reads the same field facts. D-RENAME-CASE1=A: #Rename(.Camel) on a type sets a naming style, and #Rename("name", json: …) on a field sets an exact name per format. A field's own name beats the type style. D-CODABLE-OPTIONS1=A keeps #Rename separate from #Codable. D-SHAPE-CASE2=A keeps foreign names verbatim inside binding modules.

OBSERVED CODE, master 3e5349196

crates/jet-foundation/src/Shape.rs:305-340 holds ShapeFieldNames, one slot per format. Its defaults copy the field name for text formats, derive kebab for args and SCREAMING for env at :946-952. That record is the natural single home.

decisions.title: Acronyms in camelCase and PascalCase data keys
decisions.situation: Under the recommended web-style naming, a Jet field is written userID or avatarURL, and this vote decides whether its JSON key keeps those capitals or reads userId. You asked what the web industry does and what works best out of the box. Google, Microsoft, Protocol Buffers, GitHub's GraphQL API and Apple's automatic converter all write userId, so copying userID would need a hand-written rename on every acronym field to read their data. We recommend writing userId in data keys while Jet code keeps userID.
decisions.gist: In camelCase JSON keys, should Jet write userId or userID?
decisions.lesson: An acronym is a word made of initials, such as ID or URL. camelCase joins words with a capital at each new word after the first: userId. Inside Jet code acronyms are fully capitalized, as in userID; this vote is only about keys in data such as JSON.
decisions.explainer: Every option uses the same record, UserProfile with userID and avatarURL, sent as camelCase JSON. The examples show the JSON Jet writes and what it accepts when reading. Shared work: one conversion in the naming module from D-WIRE-CASE1, used by both compiler halves.
decisions.story: Lena's Jet service reads user records from a Google API and a protobuf service. Both send userId and avatarUrl, and she does not want to rename each acronym field by hand.
decisions.detail:
YOUR QUESTION (q6ebqsdy, 2026-10-05)

You asked what the best practice and industry standard are for web development, networking and servers. You also asked which choice gives the best cohesive out-of-the-box experience for the most common domains.

Answer: A, userId. The industry practice is to write an acronym in a camelCase key like any other word. Google's JSON style guide and API Improvement Proposal AIP-140 do so. The Protocol Buffers JSON mapping turns user_id into userId.

Microsoft's REST guidelines and Microsoft Graph send id and webUrl, and the .NET naming guidelines spell Id, not ID. GitHub's GraphQL API sends avatarUrl and databaseId. Apple's convertFromSnakeCase turns base_uri into baseUri. Full-capital keys such as userID come mainly from hand-tagged Go and Swift code, a minority of public APIs.

WHAT GIVES THE MOST VALUE OUT OF THE BOX

Browser and mobile clients whose fields follow TypeScript, Kotlin or .NET conventions, such as userId, read A's keys with no renames; B needs a rename on every acronym field. Google, Microsoft and gRPC services that publish protobuf JSON match A exactly.

snake_case APIs such as Stripe, GitHub REST and Slack send user_id, and both options read them the same way, because snake_case has no acronym capitals. A partner that really sends userID needs one #Rename("userID") on that field under A, the same per-field cost that B charges for every common API. So A serves the largest share of real traffic with nothing written.

DECISION BOUNDARY

Owner request, 2026-10-05, card #4613 (c0itvqcw): one casing rule for every name, with outside conventions mapped by one mechanism. Owner direction later that day: prefer pragmatic defaults and lean toward web development. Full proposal: Docs/proposals/casing-2026-10-05.md, sections 3.3 and 5.1.

This ballot depends on D-CASE-LAW2 and D-WIRE-CASE1. Examples assume D-CASE-LAW2=A, where fields are camelCase with full-capital acronyms (userID). Under D-CASE-LAW2=B, fields stay user_id and this ballot still decides how the .Camel and .Pascal styles spell acronyms. D-ACRO-CASE1=A keeps userID and HTTPClient in Jet source either way. snake_case, kebab-case and SCREAMING keys are unaffected, because their acronyms are already one case.

REVISION, 2026-10-05

Revised by OpenQuestions after the owner's web-first direction. The question and recommendation are unchanged; examples now use camelCase source names. Under the web-style law, option B would make JSON keys equal the source spelling exactly. The recommendation still holds, because reading other services' data matters more than matching 2 in 100 field spellings.

Revised again by BallotSync, 2026-10-05, so the ballot itself answers owner question q6ebqsdy: the section above, the situation and the recommendation now state the industry practice and the out-of-the-box value. The mechanism and options are unchanged.

The unit test at acronyms.rs:228-229 checks httpHeader, where the acronym is the first word and is lowercased anyway. Seven .jet files use a #Rename case style today. Census: 1.9% of 13,571 field declarations contain an acronym.

EVIDENCE FOR userId

Protocol Buffers maps lower_snake_case fields to lowerCamelCase JSON keys, so user_id becomes userId (protobuf.dev JSON mapping). Google's Java style guide, section 5.3, gives newCustomerId and XmlHttpRequest. The .NET guidelines list Id, not ID. Microsoft Graph sends id and webUrl.

Apple's JSONDecoder documentation says convertFromSnakeCase turns base_uri into baseUri. It notes the strategy cannot infer acronym capitals. Pydantic's to_camel capitalizes each word. JSON:API recommends camel-cased member names.

EVIDENCE FOR userID

Go's review guide writes appID and ServeHTTP, and Swift's guidelines write userSMTPServer. Hand-written Go and Swift JSON keys may follow them. Browser APIs are mixed: getElementById beside innerHTML.

ROUND TRIP

Both spellings round-trip inside Jet. Reading userId splits into user and id. Reading userID splits through the acronym list into the same words. The question is only which spelling Jet writes and requires.

options.technical:
The .Camel style lowercases every word, capitalizes the first letter of each word after the first, and joins them. The .Pascal style capitalizes the first letter of every word. Acronyms get no special case. Words come from the shared splitter, so userID, user_id and userId all have the words user and id.

Enum cases follow the same rule: HTTPError under .Camel is httpError, and under .Pascal is HttpError. Decoding requires the written spelling exactly. A near miss such as userID gets the D-WIRE-CASE1 error naming userId.

decisions.title: A kept link to a list item when the list may grow
decisions.situation: A link lets two names reach the same value without copying it. When a link points at one item inside a list, growing that list can move every item to new memory. Jet must say what a long-lived link to a list item means. This vote picks that rule; I recommend that long-lived links point at whole objects.
decisions.gist: What should happen when a list may grow while a stored link points at one of its items?
decisions.lesson: A link, written `@`, reaches a value without copying it. A list keeps its items side by side, so growing it may move all of them. A short-lived link can simply stop the list from growing until the link is done. A link stored in a field may live much longer than that.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write `[@Node]` when other parts of the program must keep pointing at items. The error message names that change, and `jet fix` applies it. Expert path: keep `[Node]` for flat, fast storage and use short-lived item links, indexes, or `Pool` IDs; `jet inspect choices` shows which links are short-lived.

Shared work under every option: a short-lived link into a list item stops the list from growing or shrinking while it is used. That matches Rust today and needs no runtime cost. Only links the compiler cannot bound to a short scope are decided here.
decisions.story: Mia builds a level editor. Her scene keeps a list of nodes and a link to the selected node. Adding a lamp to the scene must not break the selection.
decisions.detail:
Why this needs a vote. Ratified D-MEMREF1=A lets `@p` link to "a named place, or to a field or item of one". Ratified D-MEMREF-LIFE1=A keeps a target alive in counted memory when its owner may die first. That works for a whole variable.

For a list item it does not. Keeping the old buffer alive does not stop `push` from moving the items. The link would then see stale data, as in Go, or dangle. Applied literally, LIFE1 would box every item of such a list, which is option B. No ratified text chooses among these.

Evidence. Corpus case C03 ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/scratch/memcorpus/cases/03_view_then_push.jet) shows today's rule for brief windows: E0212 on `push`, like Rust E0502. Ante allows shared mutable references only into shape-stable storage. It requires an exclusive reference for vector elements and union payloads (antelang.org/blog/safe_shared_mutability, 2024).

Swift arrays of class instances, and Java or Python lists, store each item as its own object. That is what `[@Node]` spells. Go keeps the old array after `append`, so a pointer into it silently diverges (go.dev/blog/slices-intro). Rust code that keeps item references uses indexes, slotmap keys, or `Vec<Rc<RefCell<T>>>`.

Proposal context: Docs/proposals/memory-model-2026-10-05.md sections 5.3 and 6.

options.name: Kept links point at objects
options.gist: Short item links pause growth; stored ones need `[@Node]` items.
options.detail: A link used only briefly may point at a list item; the list cannot grow until the link is done, as in Rust. A link stored for longer must point at an object. Write the list as `[@Node]` so each item is its own object. The compiler rejects a stored link into `[Node]` and names that change.
options.technical: No runtime cost on `[T]`. `[@T]` items are counted objects under D-MEMREF-LIFE1. The fix is a structured edit applied by `jet fix`.

options.name: The compiler boxes linked items
options.gist: Any list whose items get stored links keeps each item in a box.
options.detail: Write `[Node]` everywhere. When a stored link points into a list, the compiler stores that list's items in separate boxes so they never move. `jet inspect choices` reports the change.
options.technical: Representation chosen per list type or per allocation site. Generic code over `[T]` must handle both layouts. `#Layout(c)` and foreign calls see a different layout.

options.name: Growth stops at run time
options.gist: The list counts stored links; growing while any exist stops the program.
options.detail: Write `[Node]` and link to any item. The list keeps a count of stored links into it. Growing or shrinking the list while that count is above zero stops the program with both source locations.
options.technical: One counter per list header and one test per shape write. No layout change.

comparisons.note: Short borrows block growth; long-lived item references use indexes or Rc. Illustration, not executed.
Shared mutable references cannot point into vector elements; those need an exclusive reference. Source: antelang.org/blog/safe_shared_mutability.

losses.mitigation: The error names the change and `jet fix` applies it.

whyNot.reason: One line elsewhere silently changes a list's layout and slows every item.

recommendation.tradeoff: One visible type change replaces a hidden layout switch or a run-time stop.

decisions.title: Calling a method that changes one field while you hold another
decisions.situation: A method often changes just one field of a record, such as a log or a counter. Today, holding a link to a different field blocks that call, even when the two never touch. Rust has the same limit and has not fixed it. This vote decides whether Jet tracks which fields each method uses; I recommend that it does.
decisions.gist: May you call a method that changes one field while holding a link to another field?
decisions.lesson: A record groups fields. A method marked `&self` may change the record. Today Jet treats every such call as touching all fields. The compiler can read the method and list the fields it really reads or changes. That list is the method's footprint.
decisions.explainer: Beginner path: write ordinary methods; calls that touch different fields just work. Expert path: a public method may state its footprint in the receiver, such as `&self.log` or `&self.[log, hits]`, to promise callers room for future changes. Shared work under every option: direct field access, such as `world.hits += 1`, already works beside a link to another field.
decisions.story: Ravi writes a game loop. He walks `world.bodies` and calls `&world.log_hit()`, which only adds to `world.log`. The checker refuses the call.
decisions.detail:
Evidence in Jet. Corpus case C08 ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/scratch/memcorpus/cases/08_field_borrow_then_self_method.jet) holds `a :: &s.xs` and calls `&s.bump()`. `bump` only changes `count`. Jet reports E0220 and E0212 today, matching Rust's E0499. Case C07 shows the working direct form: one call taking `b.names` and `&b.notes`.

Evidence elsewhere. Niko Matsakis proposed view types in 2021, written `&{golden_tickets} self` (smallcultfollowing.com/babysteps/blog/2021/11/05/view-types). Rust checks one function at a time. A caller cannot see which fields a callee uses unless the signature says so. Rust has not shipped the feature.

Why Jet can do better. Jet already infers a hidden relation for returned views from each body and publishes it in API snapshots (D-MEMPROVENANCE2=A). It lets experts declare that relation with `from` (D-MEMPROVENANCE3=A). Footprints follow the same pattern: inferred by default, published, and optionally declared.

Spelling. A declared footprint reuses the ratified member spread `prefix.[a, b]` (D-SPREAD1=A) on the receiver. No new sigil or keyword is added.

options.name: Inferred footprints, published
options.gist: The compiler learns each method's fields; experts may state them.
options.detail: The compiler reads each method and records which fields it uses. A call that does not touch your linked field is accepted. Public methods publish their footprint, so a change to it is a visible API change. An expert can state the footprint in the receiver to reserve room.
options.technical: Same shape as provenance: inferred, published, optionally declared. Receiver spelling reuses the member spread `self.[a, b]`.

options.name: Stated footprints only
options.gist: Calls are accepted only when the method states its fields.
options.detail: A method that wants this benefit states its footprint in the receiver. Methods without a statement still count as touching every field. This is Rust's view-types proposal in Jet spelling.
options.technical: No inference across bodies. The statement is checked against the body.

options.name: Keep the whole-record rule
options.gist: A `&self` call always touches every field, as today.
options.detail: No change. Programs split the record's fields into separate parameters, or call a free function that takes only the needed field.
options.technical: Matches Rust today. No new facts or API digest entries.

comparisons.note: Rejects the call; the 2021 view-types idea is not shipped. Illustration, not executed.
A mutating method accesses the whole struct, so overlapping accesses conflict. Source: swift.org/blog/swift-5-exclusivity.

recommendation.why: Correct code that touches different fields compiles with no annotation, while library authors still control their promises.
gains: Removes a top Rust borrow complaint.
No new syntax for beginners.

losses.loss: A public method that starts using another field changes its API.
losses.mitigation: The API check names the field; stating a wider footprint up front reserves room.

whyNot.reason: Beginners never write footprints, so they keep hitting the error.
Forces correct code to pass fields by hand.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more published fact per public method buys calls that just work.

decisions.title: A record that keeps text and links into that same text
decisions.situation: A parser often owns its input text and wants to point at pieces of it without copying them. Today a record, a value with named fields, cannot hold such links into its own text, so programs copy every piece or keep start and end positions. Rust, a language with similar safety rules, cannot do this safely without extra libraries. This vote decides whether Jet allows it; I recommend yes, with the compiler finding the text field by itself and no new keyword.
decisions.gist: May a record hold a piece of text and links into that same text?
decisions.lesson: A record, written `struct`, groups named fields. A link, written `@`, reaches a value without copying it. A string keeps its letters in separate memory that stays put when the record moves, meaning it is handed to another name or returned. So links into a record's own text stay valid, as long as that text never changes while links into it exist.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. [@String] is a list of links, each reaching a string or part of one, so a key can be one line of a longer text. text.line_views(input) splits input into links to its lines; text there is Jet's core text module, not the record's field. A parameter written move String takes ownership of the string it is given.

Beginner path: write the record as usual. When only one field can hold what the links point at, the compiler ties the links to that field and freezes it: it cannot change while any link into it lives. To change it, build a new record. Expert path: when two fields could hold it, write the marker #Within(text) before the link field; with one field it is optional and locks the tie.

A marker is a #Name(...) note, like #Doc, not a keyword, though #Within is a new built-in marker with its own rule. Hover and jet inspect types show every tie.

Which fields qualify. Links of type @String can point into a String field, and links to a Node can point into a [Node] list. Only fields of such a type count, and only constructions that build the links from that field create a tie.

Shared work under every option: parsers that do not keep their input work unchanged. Nothing here has run yet: links are not built, so every example states the proposed contract.
decisions.story: Lena writes a config loader. Each `Config` owns the file text and a list of keys found in it. Copying every key can nearly double the memory for large files.
decisions.detail:
Revision by OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07, then repaired by SuiteRepair1 after the SuiteBeginner2 and SuiteAdversary2 passes. The posted B stored start and end positions, and the posted C copied each piece. Both meant no new rule: voting either one changed nothing in the language, and both workarounds stay available under A too. They are now one option B, keep today's workarounds.

The proposed code now uses the ratified copy and move spellings of D-COPY-MOVE-SPELL1=A (2026-10-07). A parameter that takes ownership is `move String`, a last use moves with nothing written, and a copy is `l.copy()`. The current pane keeps today's `^text`, which that vote retires.

Revision (owner question q5w0guta, 2026-10-05). The owner asked whether the `from` keyword is needed. It is not, so this revision drops the first draft's `keys: [@String] from text` clause. The compiler infers the source field when exactly one sibling field owns storage the link can point into. When two or more fit, the record states the source with the marker form `#Within(text)`.

Markers are not keywords. `#Within` uses the existing `#Name(args)` rule form, like the field markers `#Doc` and `#Memo`, but it is a new built-in marker with a new rule to learn. Jet's built-in markers may change checking (D-MARKER-LAW1=A). A marker that locks an automatic choice is the ratified pattern (D-AUTOPIN1=A).

Evidence in Jet. Corpus case C30 ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/scratch/memcorpus/cases/30_self_reference.jet) builds `Doc{text: ^text, head: head}` where `head` is a window into `text`. Jet reports E2307 today and asks for a copy. The compiler already sees that `head` comes from `text`; that is the fact this ballot keeps instead of rejecting.

Evidence elsewhere. Rust's ordinary safe references cannot express a field borrowing a sibling field: moving the struct would invalidate the borrow in Rust's model, even when the data lives on the heap. Rust users reach for helper crates, self_cell and ouroboros, which offer a safe interface over unsafe code behind macros, and both make the user name the owner field.

Niko Matsakis calls these interior references the most notable pattern Rust cannot express (smallcultfollowing.com/babysteps/blog/2024/03/04/borrow-checking-without-lifetimes).

Why it is safe in Jet. A `String` or list keeps its contents in heap memory. Moving the record moves only the header, so a link into the contents stays valid. What can break it is a write to the source: growing, shrinking or replacing the text, or writing a list item that a copy shares. The tie freezes the source, in shape and in value, while any link into it lives.

This builds on the shape rule of the memory-model proposal, section 5.3, and is stricter for tied lists, so copies can share them safely.

Why inference, and why a marker when two fields fit. Eligibility is read from the declaration, and a tie is created by constructions in the record's own module; A's technical note gives the closed rule. With one candidate, the declaration shows which field would be frozen. With two, it would not, so the record names the field. The tie is published, so an edit that adds, removes or moves a tie shows as an API change, and a written marker turns it into a build error.

Ratified law this narrows and amends. D-MEMPROVENANCE3=A left self-referential values out of scope, routing them to `Pin` (D-PIN1=A) and Pool/ID. This ballot narrows that line to links into a sibling field's heap contents; `Pin` stays for values whose own address matters.

D-LINK-ITEM1=A rejects a stored link into a `[Node]` item because growth moves items. This ballot amends it with exactly one exception: a stored link into an item of a tied, frozen sibling list. Every other stored item link keeps its error, and a list of separate objects stays the general alternative.

Ratified law this keeps. The tie adds no owner parameter to the type, so D-MEMPROVENANCE3's rule that type definitions carry none still holds. D-METHOD-FOOTPRINT1=A applies unchanged: a method that changes only other fields may run while `keys` is held. D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A applies to copies: they share storage until the first write, and a frozen source never gets one.

How other files see the tie. Jet already publishes inferred link sources and method footprints (D-MEMPROVENANCE2=A, D-METHOD-FOOTPRINT1=A); the tie is published the same way. Editor hover on `keys` shows `points into text (inferred)`. `jet inspect types` (D-CLI-ONE1=A) lists `Config.keys [@String] within text (inferred)`.

Costs, stated by workload. Under A a tied record keeps the whole input alive while any link lives. Under B, copying K bytes of pieces adds about K bytes plus a header per piece; that is doubling only when the pieces cover the whole input. Positions add two numbers per piece and a slice per use. No measurement was run, and the ballot skill requires a paired parser cell before ratification.

Drift to fix at cutover. Docs/proposals/memory-model-2026-10-05.md lines 397 and 724 still describe the `from` field clause and must move to the inferred form with the same change. The `from` on line 638 is D-MEMPROVENANCE3's result clause and stays.

Suite pass repairs (SuiteBeginner2 and SuiteAdversary2, 2026-10-07). Tied sources are frozen in value as well as shape, so copies can share them under D-COPY-DEFAULT1. The freeze lasts while any link lives, escaping links are counted, and taking a record apart is defined. Eligibility and tie creation have a closed rule covering mixed, empty, outside and generic cases.

D-LINK-ITEM1 is amended by name. B's costs and strengths are stated fairly, the Rust claim is narrowed to ordinary safe references, the decoder limit is explained, and the notation is glossed.

options.name: Inferred tie, marker only when two fields fit
options.gist: The compiler ties the links to the one field they point into and keeps that field fixed.
options.detail:
Write the record with no extra words. A link field such as keys: [@String], a list of links each pointing at part of a string, can be tied to one sibling field that holds what it points at. When exactly one field can, the compiler finds it; when two could, write `#Within(text)` before the link field. With one, the marker is optional and locks the tie.

The tied field is frozen while any link into it lives: tied text cannot change at all, and a tied list can neither change shape nor have its items written. The record can be moved, returned and copied; a copy shares the frozen source and adds one count. Other fields stay writable.

What a user must learn: which fields qualify and that constructions must take the links from the tied field. Also that the freeze lasts while links live, and that a tied record has no derived decoder.
options.technical:
Eligibility, decided on the declaration. A link field of type @T or [@T] has as candidates the sibling fields of type T or [T]. For @String, a String field also qualifies, since @String reaches a string or part of one (memory-model proposal 5.5). A field whose type is a type parameter counts as a candidate, so a generic record's tie never changes with its instantiation. One candidate: the tie is inferred. Two or more: #Within(field) is required. None: no tie.

When a record is tied. A record is tied when a construction in its own module stores links taken from the candidate. From then on every construction and every later assignment to the link field, anywhere, must take links from that field; an empty list is fine. A construction that stores outside links, or might on some path, is an error naming the constructor. If no construction in the module takes links from the candidate, the record is untied and its links follow today's stored-link rules.

Adding a second candidate field later turns an inferred tie into the two-candidate error until #Within names one; writing #Within up front locks the tie against that. The tie is published like inferred link sources (D-MEMPROVENANCE2=A), so any change shows as an API change.

Freeze and lifetime. The source is frozen in shape and value while any link into it lives, not only while the record lives. Links inside the record are plain pointers. A link that leaves the record, such as a returned key, is a kept link holding a count on the source (memory-model proposal 5.4). So the source outlives it and stays frozen until it is gone.

Taking a record apart by move hands back both fields. The text stays frozen while the keys or any link from them lives, and is an ordinary string afterwards.

Copies. Copying a tied record shares its frozen source with one count and copies the other fields by their usual rules (D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A). Nothing can write the source, so the first-write copy never happens and both copies' links stay correct. Allowing item writes in a tied list would need copies to detach and retarget every link; that was rejected as costlier and harder to explain.

Decoders. A derived decoder (#Decode, #Codable) builds each field from saved data on its own, so it cannot know that keys point into text; it is rejected with an error naming the tie. #Encode still saves the fields. The durable form is the text: a loader decodes the text and reruns the parser, so keys are rebuilt, not loaded.

options.name: Keep today's workarounds: copy each piece, or store positions
options.gist: No new rule; records copy each piece or store start and end positions.
options.detail:
No new rule. A record either copies each piece into its own string when it is built, or stores each piece as a start and end position. With positions, code slices the text whenever it needs the piece. Both are what programs do today, and both stay available under A.

B's case: no new marker or rule to learn. Copied pieces are ordinary independent values: they decode with a derived decoder, survive after the input is dropped, and let the rest of the input go. Positions are compact and exact while the text is unchanged.

B's costs depend on the workload. Copying K bytes of pieces adds about K bytes plus a header per piece, which is doubling only when the pieces cover the whole input. An edit that keeps a position in range makes it silently stale, while one that pushes it out of range stops with a bounds error.
options.technical: No change. Copying costs one allocation and copy per piece. Positions cost a bounds-checked slice per use, and nothing ties them to the text, so keeping the text unchanged is the programmer's job.

comparisons.note: Needs a crate with unsafe code inside, such as self_cell, and the user names the owner field. Illustration, not executed.
comparisons.code: self_cell!(struct Doc { owner: String, #[covariant] dependent: Words, });

comparisons.note: Substrings share storage by keeping the whole string alive with a count. Source: Swift String documentation.

recommendation.why: Parsers keep pieces of their input with no copies and no positions, and the common record needs no extra words. Rust's ordinary references cannot express this, so Rust users reach for helper crates with unsafe insides.
gains: Zero-copy parsers that can be returned.
No unsafe code or helper crates; one built-in marker, only when needed.
Records whose links fit only one field need no extra words.

losses.loss: The tied field is frozen while links into it live.
losses.mitigation: Build a new record, or take it apart by move; the text is free once its links are gone.

losses.loss: A record with two text fields must name one with a marker.
losses.mitigation: The error offers the exact `#Within(text)` line, naming the field the constructors used.

losses.loss: A tied record cannot get a derived decoder (`#Decode` or `#Codable`).
losses.mitigation: `#Encode` saves the text; a loader decodes it and reruns the parser, so keys are rebuilt, not loaded.

whyNot.reason: B is safe and simple: copied pieces are independent and decode normally, and positions over unchanged text are exact. But copies cost an allocation per piece, and positions cost a slice per use with nothing stopping an edit from making them stale.

recommendation.tradeoff: One frozen field, and a marker only when two fields fit, buy zero-copy records that move freely.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: SuiteBeginner2. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass tested the complete ballot. Repaired: link-list notation, which fields qualify, what frozen means, the Page constructor and taking a record apart are taught.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude-opus. Adversarial model family: openai. Fresh agent: SuiteAdversary2. The adversarial review attacked the recommendation. Repaired: frozen sources make copies safe, escaping links are counted, inference has a closed rule, D-LINK-ITEM1 is amended by name, and B is credited fairly.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Before posting, run the read-only READY ballot validator and require exit zero. This revision answers owner question q5w0guta: no `from` clause, inferred source, `#Within(field)` marker required only when two fields fit. Links are not built yet (card #3645); no example here was executed, and every outcome below is a proposed contract.

Before ratification, the ballot skill requires a paired cell for a performance-motivated surface. Here a parser cell in the gauntlet matrix compares a tied record with copied pieces and with positions on the same input. This ballot makes no measured performance claim.

After ratification, open one build card linked to #3645. It covers the tie inference in sema and the freeze rule in the ownership checker. decisions.title: Read or create a map entry with one lookup
decisions.situation: Counting words is one of the most common jobs for a map. Today Jet needs two or three lookups to add one to a count, and `counts[w] += 1` is refused because a missing key has no starting value. This vote picks a one-lookup spelling for reading or creating an entry; I recommend giving the starting value inside the brackets.
decisions.gist: How should a program read or create a map entry with one lookup?
decisions.lesson: A map stores values by key. Changing a stored value needs the key's slot. When the key is missing, the program must say what value to start from. Today that takes a separate check and a second lookup.
decisions.explainer: Beginner path: write the starting value next to the key, once. Expert path: the starting value runs only when the key is missing, so a costly default is never built for existing keys. Shared work under every option: `m[k]` without a starting value keeps its ratified meaning, and a missing key still stops the program loudly.
decisions.story: Tom counts words in log files. His loop looks each word up twice and builds an empty list for every key it groups, even keys that already exist.
decisions.detail:
Evidence in Jet. Corpus case C16 ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/scratch/memcorpus/cases/16_entry_or_insert.jet) is rejected with E0165. The working idiom, case C16b, uses `counts.get(w) ?? 0` then a store, which is two lookups. The grouped list needs `has_key`, `add`, and an index, which is three. Case C17 shows `counts["a"] += 1` is E0164 by ratified law.

Why E0164 exists. A compound update on `m[k]` hides a question: what if the key is missing? The ratified teaching text for E0164 names that question. This ballot answers it where it is asked.

Ratified context. D-MEM-INDEXMUT1=B makes `m[k].push(v)` change the stored value in place, and a missing key stops loudly. D-ONCE-VERB1=A keeps `add` for upsert. Neither gives a one-lookup get-or-create.

Performance. This surface is partly motivated by speed, one hash instead of two or three. A paired candidate and plain cell must exist before ratification, per the performance gate.

options.name: Starting value in the brackets
options.gist: `counts[w, or: 0] += 1` finds or creates the entry once.
options.detail: Indexing already names a map slot. Adding `or:` with a starting value makes the slot exist. The starting value runs only when the key is missing.
options.technical: One hash probe; lazy default; a place expression like `m[k]`.

options.name: A slot method

decisions.title: One spelling per command-line flag: which spelling stays
decisions.situation: A few jet command flags have two names that do exactly the same thing, such as --path and --route when you create a new web route. Two names for one switch make help pages longer and scripts inconsistent, and the owner rule is one spelling per name. Removing a spelling is the owner's call. This vote picks which spelling of each pair stays, using one rule for all of them.
decisions.gist: Which spelling stays for each duplicated jet flag: the short one that reads right, or the longer one?
decisions.lesson: A flag is an option after a command, such as --release. An alias is a second name for the same flag. A teaching error is a refusal that names the right spelling. Every option keeps the feature; only spellings change.
decisions.explainer:
Four pairs do the same thing today. jet new accepts --path or --route for a route's address, and --up or --sql for a migration's forward SQL. jet package accepts --cook or --cook-mode for the asset mode, and --clean or --force-clean to wipe its cache.

Under A, the kept spelling is the short one that reads right in the full command and matches its partner flag. A removed spelling is refused with a teaching error that names the kept one. There is no silent alias.

Beginner path: help shows one name per switch. Expert path: scripts get one exact error with the fix, and jet fix can rewrite a script's flags.

Shared work: the same rule applies to any other duplicate an implementer finds during the cutover, such as --scripts-only beside --cook scripts-only.
decisions.story: Omar copies two deploy scripts from teammates. One uses jet new route orders --route /orders, the other --path /orders. He wonders whether they differ and reads the source to find out they do not.
decisions.inWild:
# git: --staged is a synonym of --cached for git diff, a long-standing
# source of confusion. Source: git-scm.com/docs/git-diff
git diff --cached
git diff --staged    # same thing, second name
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05.

Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CLICommands.jet:786-787 registers --path with help Route or output path, and --route as an alias for --path. Lines 941-942 register --cook as an alias for --cook-mode. Lines 951-952 register --force-clean as an alias for --clean. Line 953 adds --scripts-only, which duplicates the cook mode scripts-only.

The Rust CLI parses the same pairs. Source/CmdBackendScaffold.rs:258 maps --path and --route to one field, and :260 maps --up and --sql to one field. crates/jet-cli/src/CLI.rs:717-718 mirrors the help rows.

The elegance audit (card #4021, 2026-10-01) found the first three pairs. It noted that --no-color/--force-color are opposites and --out/--output differ by scope, so they are not aliases. Owner question q00mjarf (1) asks which spelling stays. The owner rule of 2026-10-01 says only the owner removes features.

Retired spellings already have a teaching path. The Jet-written front end teaches retired and moved spellings before E2101 (D-JET-VERBS1 detail, Front.jet).

Research. clig.dev, the Command Line Interface Guidelines, advises one clear full-length name per flag and consistent naming across commands. git diff keeps --staged as a synonym of --cached; readers regularly ask whether they differ. Cargo and the Go tool use one long spelling per flag.

Why the short spelling under A. jet new route orders --route /orders says route twice; --path reads naturally. --up pairs with --down. --cook fast already names a mode, so -mode adds nothing. --clean is the action; force adds no meaning, since there is no unforced clean.

options.name: Keep the short spelling that reads right
options.detail: Keep --path, --up, --cook and --clean. Remove --route, --sql, --cook-mode and --force-clean. A removed spelling gets a teaching error naming the kept one. Apply the same rule to any further duplicate found in the cutover.
options.technical: Delete the alias rows from CLICommands.jet and the matching arms in the Rust parsers. Add the four removed spellings to the retired-spelling table, so each produces E2102 with a Fix line naming the kept flag. Update help, docs, examples and tests in one cutover. No alias period.
options.code:
$ jet new route orders --path /orders   # works
$ jet new route orders --route /orders
Error [E2102]: --route was renamed; use --path
// proposed output; not run

options.name: Keep the longer spelling
options.detail: Keep --route, --sql, --cook-mode and --force-clean. Remove --path, --up, --cook and --clean, with teaching errors.
options.technical: Same cutover with the other row of each pair removed. --up loses its pairing with --down.

options.name: Keep both spellings
options.detail: Leave every pair as it is and document both names in help.
options.technical: No change; the one-spelling rule gets a written exception for CLI flags.
options.code:
$ jet package --cook fast
$ jet package --cook-mode fast   # same thing

comparisons.note: One long spelling per flag; a short letter form is the only extra name.

recommendation.why: One rule picks every survivor: the short name that reads right beside its command and partner flags. Removed names teach the kept one, so no script fails silently.
gains: Help lists one name per switch.
Scripts and docs agree on one spelling.
Flags read naturally: --up beside --down.

losses.loss: Scripts using a removed spelling stop working.
losses.mitigation: Each removed spelling prints the kept one, and jet fix rewrites scripts.

whyNot.reason: Longer names repeat the command's own word and break the --up/--down pair.
It keeps two names for one switch, against the one-spelling rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: A one-time script update in exchange for one name per switch.

decisions.title: Remove the unused #wire field marker instead of renaming it
decisions.situation: Jet accepts a marker spelled #wire on struct fields, but nothing in the compiler reads it, so writing it changes nothing. It is one of two lowercase markers left, and the owner directed that markers be capitalized. Renaming it would keep a marker that silently does nothing. This vote decides whether #wire is removed, or kept as #Wire with or without a job.
decisions.gist: Should the do-nothing #wire field marker be removed, or kept as #Wire?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a # tag on code, such as #Skip on a field. Jet's registry lists every marker. The data-format markers already exist: #Rename sets a field's outside name per format, and #Skip leaves a field out.
decisions.explainer:
Today #wire is accepted on any field and ignored. No decision defines it and no program uses it. Its only other mention is a zero-use triage entry in a test.

The jobs a wire marker might do already have markers. #Rename("user_id", json: "userId") names a field for each format. #Skip leaves a field out. #Encode, #Decode and #Codable request the codecs. The open casing ballot for outside names builds on #Rename.

Under A, #wire is deleted. Writing it gets the normal unknown-marker error with a did-you-mean, which suggests #Rename or #Skip.

Beginner path: no change, since nobody writes it. Expert path: the existing format markers.
decisions.story: Ana sees #wire in the marker list and puts it on a field she wants sent as JSON. Nothing changes in her output, and nothing tells her why.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05 on the dev worktree.

crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:213 declares marker wire($sites: [.Field]). The same file declares Rename at :126, with per-format names for json, cbor, csv, toml, yaml, xml, args, env, db and layout. It declares Skip at :128, and Encode, Decode and Codable at :79-86.

tests/truthfulness.rs:609 lists wire in the zero-use triage, citing card #1830, which is done. The Core-foundations catalogue (Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, row 31) found no source use, no defining decision and no arguments. The row entered in commit 413ac90b6 without a ruling.

D-MARKER-CASE1=A (2026-10-05) says #allow and the unused #wire get capitals. Owner question q00mjarf (2), from 2026-10-01, asks whether #wire is renamed, given a meaning, or something else. The owner rule of 2026-10-01 says only the owner removes features, hence this ballot.

Open ballot D-WIRE-CASE1 maps Jet names to outside names through #Rename and a package naming key. A second field marker for the same job would give two spellings for one meaning, which I8 forbids.

Research. serde (Rust), System.Text.Json (.NET) and Go's encoding/json each have one per-field rename and one skip mechanism. None ships a marker that is accepted and ignored. Silent acceptance of a no-op tag is the wrong way: users believe it works.

options.name: Remove #wire
options.detail: Delete the marker row, its test entries and its triage line. Writing #wire gets the unknown-marker error, whose did-you-mean suggests #Rename or #Skip.
options.technical: Remove marker wire from Prelude/Markers.jet and the truthfulness zero-use entry. Add wire to the retired-marker teaching table, pointing to #Rename and #Skip. Both compiler halves read the one registry (I9). The #allow to #Allow rename under D-MARKER-CASE1 is unaffected.

options.name: Rename to #Wire, no job
options.detail: Capitalize it as directed and keep it accepted on fields. It still does nothing.
options.technical: Rename the row to Wire. Keep the zero-use triage entry. Writing it compiles and has no effect.

options.name: Give #Wire the outside-name job
options.detail: Make #Wire("userId") set a field's outside name, beside or instead of #Rename.
options.technical: Either a second spelling of #Rename, or a migration of every #Rename use and of the open D-WIRE-CASE1 design to the new word.

comparisons.note: One struct tag per format sets the outside name; a dash skips the field (pkg.go.dev/encoding/json).

recommendation.why: A marker that compiles and does nothing misleads people. Its possible jobs already belong to #Rename and #Skip, so removing it loses nothing and completes the PascalCase cleanup.
gains: No marker silently does nothing.
One way to name and skip fields.
The marker list is fully capitalized.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a marker that compiles and does nothing, which misleads anyone who writes it.
It duplicates #Rename, giving two spellings for one job.

recommendation.tradeoff: Removing an unused name rather than renaming a no-op.
