print(answer)   // others keep running, but 42 waits for slow_count

options.name: Keep waits only, and warn
options.gist: The rule stays; a warning asks authors to yield by hand inside long loops.
gains: No runtime cost at all.
losses: Every author and library must remember to yield.
The warning cannot see loops inside libraries.

recommendation.why: A makes deadlines, races, cancellation and fair sharing work for busy code with no new syntax, using the check Jet already runs for plugins.
gains: Runaway handlers stop at their deadline.
Races return when the winner finishes.
One heavy request cannot stall the server.

losses.loss: One cheap check in loops that never wait.
losses.mitigation: Counted loops check once per block, and it ships only after the speed gate shows no slowdown.

losses.loss: Cancellation may land between two loop turns.
losses.mitigation: Only at a whole-turn boundary where panics already unwind; cleanup runs and #Shield still protects.

whyNot.reason: B ends starvation but deadlines, races and shutdown still wait for busy code.
C relies on every author remembering, and cannot see library loops.

recommendation.tradeoff: Building a gated loop check buys deadlines, cancellation and fair turns that reach every task.

decisions.title: Moving between game screens
decisions.situation: Most games have several screens, such as a title menu, the play screen and a game-over screen, each with its own pictures, controls and frame logic. Jet's game library runs exactly one scene, so today a game crams every screen into one frame function and loads every picture at startup. You decide how a Jet game moves between screens and what happens to each screen's pictures. We recommend naming screens in an enum, building each on entry, freeing it on exit, and keeping shared things in one always-on scene.
decisions.gist: How should a Jet game switch between a menu, the game, and other screens?
decisions.lesson: A scene holds a screen's pictures, sounds, controls and frame logic. An enum is a closed list of named choices, so a misspelled screen name fails to compile. Today `game.run` runs one scene for the whole game. Whichever option wins, replays and the live game controls in jet dev must record screen changes.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: declare `enum Screen { Menu Play }`, write one function that builds the scene for a screen, and call `game.run(^shared, start: Screen.Menu, screens: screen)`. Inside a frame function, `f.go(Screen.Play)` asks to change screens. The change happens after the current frame ends. Pictures loaded into a screen's scene are freed when that screen ends. Pictures and controls that every screen needs go into the shared scene, which runs for the whole game. A single-screen game keeps writing `game.run(scene)`.

Expert path: each screen is a scene, so the existing per-scene budget scope gives each screen its own frame-time and memory limits. Replays record each screen change with its frame number. A recorded run therefore replays the same screens in the same order. Anything that must survive a return to a screen lives in the shared scene.
decisions.story: Mia's game has a title menu and a play screen. The ship picture should load only while playing, and the logo should stay on both screens. Today she loads everything at startup and writes one frame function that checks which screen is active.
decisions.detail:
Source: The Cherno reviews the raylib game Spectrum (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eopps3YF6aE, 07:07-17:39 and 23:55-25:40). Evidence is caption text with no frame capture. The game registers its main menu, game scene and death screen by type. It separates assets kept for the whole application from assets loaded per scene. The reviewer praises that split and recommends typed asset kinds over strings.

Jet state on 2026-10-05: checkout master 3e5349196, dev 91a438ce4, Tower revision 74829. The digest was marked inconsistent because the tree was dirty. Core/game/game.jet:19-48 has only Scene, Replay and Backend. Game.rs:542-829 in the Prelude runs exactly one scene. No decision, open ballot, card or spec text mentions switching scenes or assets shared across scenes.

That search covered the decision list, card titles and bodies, Docs/spec and Docs/research. Related law: D-GAME-ASSET1=A keeps asset registries on scenes and rejected top-level loaders. D-GAME3=C made the API scene-first with frame hooks. D-GAME-INPUT1=A (+C) fixes typed actions such as `.start`. D-GAME-BUDGET1 scopes budgets per scene. D-GAME-REPLAY1 requires deterministic replays.

D-DX-GAMELOOP1 owns pause and frame advance in jet dev. D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D puts `&` on the named value a method changes. The examples follow that rule, although shipped game examples still omit it pending #3452.

Research: primary docs were retrieved on 2026-10-05 into legwork/cpp-craft/resources/rule9. Bevy defines world states as a typed enum. It queues changes in NextState and applies them in a transition step with OnEnter and OnExit (01, 02). Entities marked DespawnOnExit are removed when their state ends (05).

Godot's change_scene removes the outgoing scene at once and frees it at frame end. Until the new scene is added, current_scene is null (06). Godot's Autoload guide says scenes have no place for data shared by several scenes. It also says a master scene that loads children stops scenes from running individually. Its answer is always-loaded singleton nodes (07).

Unity's LoadScene in Single mode closes all scenes, loads on the next frame and unloads unused assets. Scene names are case-insensitive strings, and duplicate names need a full path (08, 09). DontDestroyOnLoad keeps chosen objects across loads (11). Additive mode keeps several scenes loaded together (10).

raylib's screen-manager example uses an enum and a switch inside one loop. Its comments say to load all data at startup and unload it at the end (12). What worked: typed states, freeing outgoing scene content at a frame boundary, and one explicit home for shared things. What cost users: string scene names, global singletons, the master-scene workaround and loading everything up front.

No adoption counts, failure rates or performance measurements were obtained. That is an evidence gap, and the ballot makes no performance claim. Owner-only scope: this adds public API to core.game, namely `game.run(shared, start:, screens:)` and `frame.go`. It does not change single-scene games, the asset registry law or the input law.

Fresh review reconciliation, 2026-10-05. D-GAME-ENTITY1 is now open on #238 and owns checked entity handles and changes queued during systems. Option A releases a screen's entities through that same queued-removal path at the frame boundary. A handle to a released entity then reads as gone, exactly as after any queued removal. The two ballots are independent votes; the build lands entities first.

options.name: Typed screens, built on entry, freed on exit
options.detail:
Screens are cases of the game's own enum. `game.run(^shared, start: Screen.Menu, screens: screen)` calls the builder function each time a screen starts. `f.go(Screen.Play)` asks for a change. The change applies after the current frame, so two screens never run in the same frame. When a screen ends, its pictures, sounds, entities and frame functions are released.

The shared scene runs every frame for the whole game. It holds the logo, music and controls every screen uses. Returning to a screen builds it again, so that screen's own state starts fresh. State that must survive lives in the shared scene. A misspelled screen is a compile error, and the builder's arm table must cover every case.
options.technical:
Signature sketch: `game.run(shared: ^game.Scene, start: S, screens: fn(S) -> game.Scene)`, where S is a user enum. `frame.go(S)` does not change the frame value. It records one pending request on the runner, and the last request in a frame wins.

At the frame boundary the runner releases the outgoing screen. Release covers asset handles, components, frame callbacks and input bindings registered on that scene. The runner then calls `screens(next)`. A failed build reports the error with the screen name and keeps the outgoing screen.

Replay records each change as a frame number and screen case. A replay of the same tape reaches the same screens. Budgets use `.Scene(name)` with the built scene's name. The shared scene's frame functions run before the current screen's. No global singleton or top-level loader is added.

options.name: All scenes built at start, switched by handle
options.detail: Every screen is a scene built before the game starts. Frame functions switch with a scene handle taken earlier. Scenes stay loaded for the whole game, so a screen keeps its state when the player returns. Every picture of every screen is loaded at startup and stays in memory. A shared scene still holds things every screen uses.
options.technical: Signature sketch: `game.run(shared: ^game.Scene, scenes: [^game.Scene], start: game.SceneId)`; `scene.id` is a copyable handle read before frame functions capture it. `frame.go(id)` applies at the frame boundary. A handle that names no scene in the list fails when the change is requested at run time, because the list is a run-time value. Replay records `(frame, scene id)`.
options.code:
fn run() {
    shared := game.Scene.new("shared")
    _ := &shared.assets.image("ui/logo.png")?
    &shared.input.bind(.start, keys: [.enter])
    menu := game.Scene.new("menu")
    play := game.Scene.new("play")
    _ := &play.assets.image("play/ship.png")?         // loaded at start, kept all run
    to_menu :: menu.id
    to_play :: play.id
    &menu.on_frame(f -> { if f.input.pressed(.start) -> f.go(to_play) })
    &play.on_frame(f -> { if f.input.pressed(.start) -> f.go(to_menu) })
    game.run(^shared, scenes: [^menu, ^play], start: to_menu)
}

options.name: Keep one scene; the game tracks its own screen
options.detail: No new API. The game keeps a screen value in its frame function and branches on it, like raylib's screen-manager example. Every picture loads at startup and stays loaded. Controls and frame logic for all screens share one scene, so a screen's controls cannot be switched off by leaving it.
options.technical: Uses today's `game.run(scene)`. The escaping frame closure owns and updates its copy of `screen` (S47). Freeing a screen's pictures early is not possible because the scene's asset registry lives for the whole run.

comparisons.note: Typed enum states; changes are queued in NextState and applied in a transition step with OnEnter/OnExit; DespawnOnExit removes marked entities when a state ends (docs.rs/bevy_state, retrieved 2026-10-05). Persistence is the default and scoping is opt-in per entity.

change_scene_to_file removes the outgoing scene at once, frees it at frame end, then adds the new one; current_scene is null in between. Data needed by several scenes goes in Autoload singletons; the guide says a master-scene workaround stops scenes from running individually (docs.godotengine.org, retrieved 2026-10-05).

LoadScene (Single) closes all scenes, loads next frame and unloads unused assets; names are case-insensitive strings and duplicate names need full paths. DontDestroyOnLoad keeps chosen objects across loads (docs.unity3d.com, retrieved 2026-10-05).
core_basic_screen_manager.c: an enum and a switch in one loop; all data is loaded at startup and unloaded at the end (retrieved 2026-10-05).
comparisons.code:
typedef enum GameScreen { LOGO = 0, TITLE, GAMEPLAY, ENDING } GameScreen;
switch (currentScreen) { case TITLE: if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_ENTER)) currentScreen = GAMEPLAY; break; }

recommendation.why: A checks screen names at compile time, loads a screen's pictures only while it runs, and keeps shared things in one explicit scene instead of a global.
gains: A misspelled or unhandled screen fails to compile.
A screen's pictures and controls exist only while that screen runs.
Shared pictures and controls live in one visible scene, not a hidden global.

losses.loss: Returning to a screen builds it again, so its own state starts fresh.
losses.mitigation: Keep anything that must survive, such as the score, in the shared scene.

losses.loss: A pause menu over the game is not a separate screen.
losses.mitigation: Draw the pause menu from the Play screen or the shared scene while play is paused.

whyNot.reason: B loads every screen's pictures at startup and keeps them, and a wrong handle fails only while playing.
C loads everything for the whole game and mixes every screen's controls and logic in one frame function.

recommendation.tradeoff: A rebuilds a screen on each visit; state that must survive moves to the shared scene.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Before posting, Main links this draft to #238 and runs the ballot validator. A fresh-context reviewer must review it first, as the mining skill requires. The drafter ran no Jet program, test or performance check. Every example is derived from source.

Owner acceptance: confirm that screens are user enum cases. Confirm each screen is built on entry and released at the frame boundary after a change request. Confirm the shared scene is the one home for cross-screen assets and controls. Confirm single-scene `game.run(scene)` stays unchanged.

After ratification, implement in Core/game Jet source under #238's retarget criteria. Exercise Menu to Play to Menu, with the ship image released on exit and the logo kept. A misspelled case must fail to compile. A failing builder must keep the previous screen and name the screen.

Two go requests in one frame must apply only the last. A replay must reach the same screens on every execution level. Per-screen budgets must report under the built scene name. Pause and frame advance in jet dev must work across a change. Migrate examples that fake several screens inside one scene.

decisions.title: What a backward range like 10..1 does in a loop
decisions.situation: A range such as 10..1 counts from a bigger number to a smaller one. Today a loop over it runs zero times and nothing warns, so a countdown that forgot its step silently does nothing. A beginner course shows the trap, and the instructor says she makes it often. You decide what it means; we recommend a check error when both ends are written numbers, and an empty loop when the ends are computed.
decisions.gist: When a range's start is bigger than its end, should Jet refuse it, count down, or run zero times?
decisions.lesson: A range names the numbers a loop visits, such as 0..9. A step is the optional third part, as in 0..10, 2. Counting down needs a minus step: 10..1, -1. Today 10..1 without that step quietly visits nothing. A makes that a check error when both ends are written numbers, keeps computed ranges like 0..n-1 empty when n is zero, and writes down what a minus step means. B counts down automatically. C keeps today's silence with an advisory warning.
decisions.explainer:
A range is the list of numbers a loop walks through. In Jet, 0..9 visits 0 through 9, and 0..<10 stops before 10. A third part, the step, says how far each move goes: 0..10, 2 visits the even numbers.

Today a range whose start is bigger than its end, such as 10..1, visits nothing. Nothing reports it. A step of -1 does count down: 10..1, -1 visits 10 through 1. The written rules only describe positive steps, so the minus step works without being stated anywhere.

Option A splits the case by what the compiler can see. When both ends are written numbers, a backward range with no minus step is a mistake. The check reports it and offers the minus step. When the ends are computed, a backward range stays empty, so the common 0..n-1 loop stays correct for an empty list.

A also writes down the minus-step rule. A minus step counts down from the start and includes the end when it lands on it. A step that points away from the end is a check error.

Option B makes every backward range count down. Option C keeps today's empty loop and adds a warning that shows only in the check.
decisions.story: Maya writes a rocket countdown: loop i in 10..1 { print(i) }. The program prints nothing, the check is clean, and she spends ten minutes looking for a bug in print. The fix was one missing step: 10..1, -1.
decisions.detail:
Observed on dev-05ea86f65 on 2026-10-05 (probe p17 and the v3-P2 re-mine). Both loop i in 10..1 and loop j in 0..1, -1 print nothing, and jet check reports no problems. loop i in 10..1, -1 counts down. S19 specifies strides only as a positive source stride and makes a dynamic nonpositive stride E0123. D-RANGE-EXCL1=C says only that a half-open a..<b is empty when a >= b (syntax-decisions.md:574, 590-591).

Inclusive a..b with a > b has no written meaning. Card #4629 currently plans an advisory lint plus a written stride law, which would choose the meaning without a vote.

Sources: Python course 4M87qBgpafk (Boot.dev), the countdown exercise where the instructor says she has made this mistake many times (claims v3-P2:PYB-3, PYB-61, PYB-2; learning-compilers:PY81).

Proven approaches. Python, Rust (10..=1), Kotlin (10..1; downTo counts down), Ruby ((10..1).to_a) and Haskell ([10..1]) all make a backward range empty, silently. Swift's closed range traps at run time when lowerBound > upperBound. That catches the constant mistake but would also crash 0...n-1 for an empty list.

Clippy's reversed_empty_ranges lint (correctness group, deny by default) flags constant backward ranges, because the empty loop is almost always a bug. It does not touch computed ranges. Option A takes the Clippy rule as a check error, Swift's insistence that direction is written, and Python's empty result for computed bounds.

options.name: Written backward ranges are an error; computed ones are empty
options.detail: When both ends are written numbers and the start is bigger, a range with no minus step is a check error that offers the minus step. A step whose sign points away from the end is also a check error. When either end is computed, a backward range is empty, as today. A minus step counts down from the start and includes the end when it lands on it.
options.technical: Sema folds both endpoints and the stride when they are constants. Constant start > end with no stride, or with a positive stride, reports a registered error at the range with a fix edit inserting `, -1`. Constant start < end with a negative stride reports the same error with the reverse fix. S19 gains the negative-stride rule: visit start, start+step, ... while the value stays >= end, inclusive. Runtime ranges are unchanged. One rule for loops, ranges stored as values (D-RANGE-VALUE1) and slices on every tier and in the compile-time evaluator.

options.name: Backward ranges count down by themselves
options.detail: A range whose start is bigger than its end visits its numbers in reverse with no step written. This holds for computed ends too.
options.technical: Range iteration picks the direction from the endpoints at run time. Computed ranges such as 0..n-1 visit 0 and -1 when n is 0, so every index loop over a possibly empty list needs a guard.
options.code:
loop i in 10..1 { print(i) }   // 10, 9, ... 1

loop i in 0..n - 1 { }   // n == 0: visits 0 and -1

options.name: Keep the empty loop, add a warning
options.detail: Backward ranges stay empty everywhere. A new advisory warning marks written backward ranges in the check and the editor. Warnings do not show on jet run.
options.technical: Adds one advisory lint over constant endpoints and writes the negative-stride rule into S19. Runtime behavior is unchanged.

comparisons.note: A backward range is empty; counting down needs a negative step.
A backward closed range stops the program when it is built.
A backward range is empty; Clippy denies written backward ranges by default.

recommendation.why: A catches the written mistake before the program runs, where it is always a bug, and keeps computed loops like 0..n-1 safe for empty lists. Counting down stays one visible step, and the rule for minus steps is finally written.
recommendation.tradeoff: A program that wrote a backward constant range on purpose to skip a loop must delete the loop instead.
gains: A forgotten countdown step is reported before running.
Empty-list loops such as 0..n-1 keep working.
Minus steps get a written meaning.

losses.loss: A deliberately empty constant range no longer checks.
losses.mitigation: Nobody needs a loop that can never run; the error's fix offers the minus step, and deleting the loop says the same thing more clearly.

whyNot.reason: B makes 0..n-1 visit 0 and -1 for an empty list, turning a silent skip into a wrong index.
C keeps the silent empty loop, and its warning is hidden on jet run, where beginners work.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check that loop i in 10..1 is a registered check error with a fix edit inserting `, -1`. Check that 0..10, -1 and 10..0, 2 are errors with the reverse fix.

Check that 10..1, -1 visits 10 through 1 and that 10..0, -3 visits 10, 7, 4, 1. Check that 0..n - 1 runs zero times for n == 0 on every tier and in the compile-time evaluator.

Check the same rule for stored Range values and list slices. Write the negative-stride rule into S19 and close the reversed-range lint plan on #4629.

surface.gist: When a range's start is bigger than its end, should Jet refuse it, count down, or run zero times?
surface.lesson: A step is the third part of a range, as in 10..1, -1. Without it, 10..1 visits nothing today. A makes a written backward range a check error and keeps computed ones empty. B counts down by itself. C keeps the silence with a warning.

current.note: The loop runs zero times and the check is clean.
current.code:
loop i in 10..1 { print(i) }
// prints nothing, no message

wild.note: Clippy denies a written backward range by default.

options.name: Error when written, empty when computed
options.gist: Written backward ranges fail the check; computed ones stay empty.
gains: A forgotten countdown step is caught.
Empty-list loops keep working.
losses: A deliberately empty constant range fails the check.

options.name: Count down by itself
options.gist: Backward ranges visit numbers in reverse.
gains: No step needed to count down.
losses: 0..n-1 visits 0 and -1 for an empty list.

options.name: Empty with a warning
options.gist: Today's empty loop stays; the check warns.
gains: No program changes behavior.
losses: jet run still prints nothing and says nothing.

proposed.code:
loop i in 10..1 { }
// warning (check only): never runs

recommendation.why: A written backward range is always a mistake, so A reports it with the fix. Computed ranges stay empty, so loops over empty lists stay correct.
gains: Countdown slips are caught before running.
Minus steps get a written rule.

losses.loss: A deliberately empty constant range fails the check.
losses.mitigation: Delete the loop; the fix offers the minus step otherwise.

whyNot.reason: B turns empty-list loops into wrong indexes.
C stays silent on jet run.

recommendation.tradeoff: Intentionally empty constant ranges must be deleted.

designAway.loss: A deliberately empty constant range no longer checks.
attempts: Make every backward range an error, including computed ones. Rejected: index loops over empty lists would stop the program.
Limit the error to constants. Kept: only written numbers can be backward by mistake at check time, and they never need to be.

decisions.title: Slices that run to the end of a list, or start at its beginning
decisions.situation: A slice copies part of a list, such as xs[1..3]. Jet slices must name both ends today, so "everything after the first two" needs a method call, and writing xs[2..] gives a confusing parse error. A beginner course uses open-ended slices in nearly every list lesson, and Go, Rust and Swift all allow them. You decide whether a slice may leave one end open; we recommend yes inside index brackets, while steps stay the step_by method.
decisions.gist: Should Jet let a list slice leave out its start or end, as in xs[2..] and xs[..<3]?
decisions.lesson: A slice names the positions to copy, such as xs[1..3] for positions 1 through 3. Today both ends must be written. A lets a slice leave one end open inside the brackets: xs[2..] runs to the end and xs[..<3] starts at the beginning. Steps stay the step_by method. B also adds a step inside slices, xs[0..8, 2]. C adds no syntax and teaches the methods.
decisions.explainer:
A slice copies a run of positions out of a list. Jet writes the run as a range inside the brackets: xs[1..3] copies positions 1, 2 and 3, and xs[1..<3] stops before 3. Today both ends must be written, so the common jobs "from position 2 to the end" and "the first three" need skip(2), take(3) or a length calculation.

Option A allows one open end, only inside index brackets, where the list's length supplies the missing end. xs[2..] runs from position 2 through the last item. xs[..<3] runs from the start and stops before 3, and xs[..3] includes 3. Open ranges stay invalid in loops, because a loop has no length to stop at.

A keeps steps as the step_by method that already exists, so a slice has one meaning: a contiguous run. The parse error for a Python step slice teaches step_by.

Option B adds the loop's step clause inside slices too, so xs[0..8, 2] copies every second item. Option C adds no syntax and makes the errors point at skip, take, drop_last and step_by.
decisions.story: Ravi ports a Python exercise that drops the first two log lines with logs[2:]. In Jet he tries logs[2..] and gets "Expected a value, found ]" with a hint to write a number. He finally finds skip(2) in the reference.
decisions.detail:
Current state on dev-05ea86f65: xs[2..] is E0003 "Expected a value, found ]" with the fix "e.g. x, 42, 3.5" (probe p7); xs[0..4, 2] is E0003 "Expected ] after an index, found ," (p7b); xs[0:2] and xs[::-1] get the same generic reports (APICompPython u03, u04). Range slices copy (D-RANGE-VALUE1=A: one Range type carrying its exclusivity). The jobs exist as skip, take, drop_last and step_by (core-library.md:313, 608). Loops accept a comma stride, loop i in 0..10, 2 (S22).

The 2026-10-05 synthesis set open-ended and stepped slices aside as "only the teaching target is in scope" without a vote. This ballot asks that question.

Sources: the Python beginner course 4M87qBgpafk, where xs[2:], xs[:-2] and xs[::2] carry the list exercises (claims v3-P2:PYB-46 to PYB-50; learning-compilers:PY95, PY101).

Proven approaches. Go, Rust, Swift, Kotlin ranges and Python all allow an open slice end. Rust and Swift do it with open range values inside the index, which is the model A follows. Only Python puts a step inside slice syntax. Rust, Go and Swift use a method or loop for steps. Negative positions counting from the end are left out on purpose, because they turn an off-by-one into a silent wrong item.

options.name: Open ends inside index brackets; steps stay a method
options.detail: Inside index brackets, a range may leave out its start or its end. xs[2..] runs to the last item, xs[..<3] starts at position 0, and xs[..3] includes position 3. The length fills the open end, and bounds are checked as today. Open ranges outside index brackets are an error. Steps stay xs.step_by(n), and a Python step slice teaches it.
options.technical: The parser accepts a missing range endpoint only in index position. Sema lowers it to the existing Range with start 0 or end len - 1 on the indexed value, so slicing code and bounds stops are unchanged. Teaching diagnostics for colon and step slices name the Jet spelling. Same rule on lists, fixed arrays, text views and every tier.
options.code:
logs :: ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
rest :: logs[2..]     // ["c", "d"]
first :: logs[..<3]   // ["a", "b", "c"]
odd :: logs.step_by(2)

options.name: Open ends and a step inside slices
options.detail: Everything in A, plus the loop's step clause inside index brackets: xs[0..8, 2] copies every second item, and a minus step copies backward. step_by stays for iterators, so lists gain a second way to take every second item.
options.technical: Index position accepts the full loop range grammar, including stride. Slicing copies with a stride. Two spellings exist for a stepped copy of a list.
options.code:
rest :: logs[2..]
evens :: logs[0..3, 2]   // ["a", "c"]
back :: logs[3..0, -1]

options.name: No new syntax; teach the methods
options.detail: Slices keep both ends. The errors for xs[2..], xs[:3] and xs[::2] name skip, take, drop_last and step_by with a machine fix.
options.technical: Diagnostic changes only.

comparisons.note: Open ranges inside the index; steps are a method.
One-sided ranges inside the subscript.
comparisons.code:
let rest = logs[2...]
let first = logs[..<3]

comparisons.note: Open ends, negative positions and a step all inside the slice.

recommendation.why: A covers the slices people write most, with the open-range form Rust and Swift proved, and keeps one meaning for a slice. Steps already have a method, so a second step spelling would add a mechanism without a new job.
recommendation.tradeoff: Python users writing a step slice get a teaching fix instead.
gains: "From here to the end" and "the first n" need no method or length math.
Open ends cannot appear where no length exists.
Slices keep one meaning: a contiguous run.

losses.loss: xs[::2] and xs[0..8, 2] stay errors.
losses.mitigation: The error names xs.step_by(2) with a machine fix; the loop step clause still covers counted steps.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second way to take every n-th item, against the one-mechanism rule.
C keeps the most common slice jobs behind method names and length math.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check that xs[2..], xs[..<3] and xs[..3] copy the right items on lists, fixed arrays and text views on every tier. Check that out-of-range starts stop with the existing bounds report.

Check that 0.. in a loop or a binding is an error naming index position. Check that xs[0:2], xs[::2] and xs[0..8, 2] each teach the Jet spelling with a machine fix, using APICompPython probes u03 and u04.

surface.lesson: A slice copies a run of positions, such as xs[1..3]. Today both ends must be written. A allows one open end inside the brackets and keeps steps as step_by. B also allows a step in slices. C teaches methods only.

current.note: An open end is a confusing parse error.

wild.note: An open range inside the index.
wild.code: let rest = &logs[2..];

options.gist: xs[2..] and xs[..<3] work inside brackets.
gains: Common slices need no methods.
One meaning for a slice.
losses: Step slices get a teaching fix.

proposed.code:

first :: logs[..<3]
odd :: logs.step_by(2)

options.gist: Slices also take a step clause.
gains: Python step slices port directly.
losses: Two ways to take every n-th item.

gains: No grammar change.
losses: Common jobs stay method calls.

recommendation.why: A covers the slices people write most, in the form Rust and Swift proved. Steps already have a method.
gains: No length math for common slices.
One meaning for a slice.

losses.loss: Step slices stay errors.
losses.mitigation: The error offers step_by as a machine fix.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second step mechanism.
C keeps common slices behind methods.

recommendation.tradeoff: Step slices get a teaching fix.

Teach step_by with a machine fix at the exact slice. Kept.

decisions.title: Whether + joins two lists
decisions.situation: Joining two lists into a new one is a daily job. Python, Kotlin, Swift and Ruby write it as a + b. Jet writes it as a spread list, [...a, ...b], or a.concat(b), and a + b gets a generic "can't combine" error. Jet already refuses + on text and teaches interpolation instead. You decide whether + joins lists; we recommend keeping + for numbers only and making the error teach the spread list.
decisions.gist: Should a + b join two lists in Jet, or should + stay for numbers and point to the spread list?
decisions.lesson: Joining makes one new list from two. Jet spells it [...a, ...b], with the spread mark ... placing each list's items in order. Today a + b on lists is a generic error. A keeps + for numbers and teaches the spread list with a fix. B lets + join lists and += append. C lets + join lists and removes concat.
decisions.explainer:
Joining two lists makes one new list with the items of the first, then the items of the second. Jet already has a literal for it: [...weapons, ...armor]. The spread mark ... means "put this list's items here", and the literal can mix lists and single items, as in [...weapons, shield, ...armor]. Jet also has a.concat(b), and &a.extend(b) to add to an existing list in place.

Jet refuses + on text, because interpolation is the one way to build text. Lists are in the same position: the spread literal is the one way to build a list from parts. Today a + b on lists gets a generic error that names no Jet spelling.

Option A keeps + for numbers and makes the list error teach the spread literal, with a machine fix. Option B lets + join lists into a new list, and += append in place, as Python and Kotlin do. Option C does B and removes concat so that + is the one method-free spelling.
decisions.story: Mei ports a Python inventory script with all_items = weapons + armor. Jet answers that + can't combine [Item] and [Item] and suggests "a supported operand pair". She searches the reference before finding the spread list.
decisions.detail:
Current state on dev-05ea86f65: a + b on two lists is E0109 "`+` can't compare or combine [Int] and [Int]" (probe p8). Its fix is generic: "Use an operation supported by [Int], or call a named method". a.concat(b) builds a fresh list, the spread literal [...a, ...b] works (D-VARIADIC1), and &a.extend(b) appends in place (claim v3-P2:PYB-51). S8 removes + on text and teaches interpolation (syntax-decisions.md:1372). D-CORE-ONE-NAME1 requires one name per operation with foreign spellings taught. D-FOUND-OPMIX1 covers operators between different types.

Sources: the Python beginner course 4M87qBgpafk, where + concatenation builds a new list in order (claims v3-P2:PYB-51; learning-compilers:PY96).

Proven approaches. Python, Ruby, Kotlin and Swift overload + for sequences. Python's += then mutates the list in place while + makes a copy, a well-known aliasing surprise. Rust and Go have no + on sequences and use concat, extend or append with a spread.

The cost of + is quadratic copying in loops, total = total + chunk, which Python and Java style guides warn about. Option A reuses the literal Jet already has, removes the generic error, and avoids a second spelling beside the spread.

options.name: Keep + for numbers; teach the spread list
options.detail: a + b on lists stays an error, now a teaching error that shows [...a, ...b] with a machine fix, and &a.extend(b) when the left side is a changeable binding. concat follows the one-name rule and is taught as a foreign name pointing at the spread literal.
options.technical: E0109 gains a list-specific teaching branch with fix edits. concat retires through the D-ONCE-RETIRE1 path. No operator change; the spread literal is the one list-building form, mirroring S8 for text.

options.name: + joins lists, += appends
options.detail: a + b makes a new list with the items of a then b. xs += ys appends ys to xs in place on a changeable binding. concat and the spread literal stay.
options.technical: Lists implement the Add hook. += lowers to extend. Three spellings for a joined copy remain: +, concat and the spread literal.
options.code:
all_items :: weapons + armor
bag := ["rope"]
bag += ["torch"]

options.technical: As B, plus concat retires through the D-ONCE-RETIRE1 path.
options.code:
all_items :: weapons + armor
// weapons.concat(armor): teaching error, use +

comparisons.note: + copies; += mutates the same list, which surprises code holding another reference.
No + on Vec; concat and extend name the job.
append with a spread joins slices.

recommendation.why: A gives lists the same rule text already has: one building form, and operators stay arithmetic. The spread literal already joins lists and mixes in single items, so + would only add a second spelling and Python's += aliasing trap.
recommendation.tradeoff: Python and Kotlin users type + first and get one teaching fix.
gains: The generic error becomes a fix that shows the Jet spelling.
One way to build a list from parts.
No hidden quadratic copying from + in loops.

losses.loss: Users from Python, Kotlin and Swift cannot write a + b.
losses.mitigation: The error carries a machine fix to [...a, ...b] and to &a.extend(b) for in-place growth, the same route Jet already uses for + on text.

whyNot.reason: B leaves three spellings for one job and imports Python's += aliasing surprise.
C still keeps two spellings and gives + a second meaning beside arithmetic.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check that a + b on two lists reports the list teaching branch of E0109 with a machine fix to [...a, ...b], and to &a.extend(b) for a changeable left binding. Check that concat reports a teaching diagnostic pointing at the spread literal.

Check that the spread literal joins lists, fixed arrays and single items in order on every tier. Migrate the corpus's concat calls with jet fmt simplify.

A real fix in the error.
losses: Python users get one teaching fix.

options.name: + joins, += appends
options.gist: Lists gain + and +=.

gains: Familiar operator.
losses: + gets a second meaning.

losses.mitigation: Machine fix to [...a, ...b] or extend.

decisions.title: One word for asking whether a collection holds something
decisions.situation: Asking whether a collection holds an item is one of the first things a learner writes. Jet spells it four ways today: contains on lists and queues, has on sets, has_key on maps, and contains_value for map values. Its own error messages disagree, telling a learner to write contains on a set and then calling contains a foreign word. You decide the one word; we recommend has everywhere, with has_value for a map's values.
decisions.gist: Which single word should every Jet collection use to ask whether it holds an item: has or contains?
decisions.lesson: A membership test asks whether an item is in a collection. Jet's rule says one job gets one word, but four words do this job today. A uses has on every collection, with has_value for map values. B uses contains everywhere, with contains_key and contains_value on maps. C keeps today's words and only fixes the error messages.
decisions.explainer:
Membership is the question "is this item in here?" Every collection answers it. Jet's ratified rule says each job gets one name across List, Map and Set, and foreign names are taught by a diagnostic instead of being accepted.

Today the job has four names. Lists and queues use contains. Sets, ordered sets, tallies and bit sets use has. Maps use has_key for keys and contains_value for values. The in-operator error tells a learner to write contains, even on a set, and then the set reports contains as a foreign name and suggests has.

Option A picks has. Every element collection uses has(item). A map uses has(key), because a map's members are its keys, and has_value(value) for the rarer value search. contains becomes a taught foreign name that points at has.

Option B picks contains, the word Rust, Java, Kotlin and Swift use. Maps use contains_key and contains_value. Option C keeps the four words and only makes the error messages agree.
decisions.story: Lia writes 2 in seen, as in Python, and Jet says write seen.contains(2). She does, and Jet says contains is another language's word and suggests has. Two messages from the same compiler sent her in a circle.
decisions.detail:
Current state on dev-05ea86f65 (APICompPython u06, v01): List.contains (Collections.jet:400), Queue.contains (:342), Set.has (:270), Map.has_key (:368), Map.contains_value. `2 in s` on a Set gives E0384 "Write xs.contains(x)", and s.contains(2) then gives E0311 "Did you mean has?". For a Map, E0384 says .contains with no follow-up.

Ratified law: D-ONCE-VERB1 (one verb per job across List, Map and Set) and D-CORE-ONE-NAME1 (one name per Core operation; foreign names are taught). D-LOOP-IN1 says the in-operator diagnostic points at .has(x). The D-ONCE-VERB1 verb table lists no List membership row, although [T].contains ships (claim v3-P2:PYB-34). So the law requires one word but never chose it.

Sources: the Python beginner course (4M87qBgpafk 4:22:00 and 6:04:00), where in on a dict checks keys only and surprises learners (claims v3-P2:PYB-33, PYB-34, PYB-84; learning-compilers:PY116).

Proven approaches. Rust, Java, Kotlin, Swift and C# use contains, with containsKey or contains_key on maps. JavaScript uses has on Set and Map and includes on arrays, which programmers often cite as an inconsistency. Ruby uses include? with key? on hashes.

Jet already ratified has for sets and for the in-operator teaching, so A changes the fewest ratified texts. A also removes Python's keys-only surprise by naming value search separately.

decisions.title: When printed text leaves the program
decisions.situation: When a program prints, the text can go straight to the screen or file, or wait in a small holding area and leave in larger batches. Today Jet sends every print immediately, even into a file or pipe, so printing a million lines makes a million system calls and stdout.flush() does nothing. You decide when printed text leaves the program; we recommend sending it at each line on a terminal and in batches into files and pipes.
decisions.gist: Should printed text leave the program at every print, at every line, or in batches when it goes to a file?
decisions.lesson: A buffer is a holding area for output. Writing it out is called flushing. Today every print flushes at once, even into a file. A flushes each line on a terminal and batches output into files and pipes, and it always flushes before the program waits, reads input, starts a child or exits. B flushes every line everywhere. C keeps today's flush on every print.
decisions.explainer:
Programs print a little at a time. Sending each piece to the operating system costs a system call, which is slow compared with copying text into memory. Most languages keep a small buffer and send it in batches, then flush it at sensible moments.

Today Jet flushes after every print on every stream. On a terminal that is harmless. Into a file or a pipe it multiplies system calls, and the stream's flush method has no work left to do.

Option A follows the rule C and Python have used for decades. On a terminal, text leaves at each line ending, so a person sees whole lines at once. Into a file or pipe, text leaves in batches.

A also flushes before every moment where waiting text could confuse anyone. That includes before the program reads input, sleeps or waits on the network, starts a child process, writes to stderr, stops with an error, or exits. stderr itself keeps flushing on every write, so error text is never held back.

Option B flushes at every line everywhere, as Rust does. Option C keeps today's rule and documents flush as having nothing to do.
decisions.story: Dev writes a log converter that prints two million lines into a file with jet run convert.jet > out.txt. It takes far longer than the same loop in Python or C. The time goes to two million separate writes, and calling stdout.flush() at the end changes nothing.
decisions.inWild:
/* C: stdout is line buffered on a terminal and fully buffered otherwise.
   https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/stdin.html */
for (int i = 0; i < 2000000; i++) printf("%d\n", i);   // few write calls into a file

# Python: the same rule; stderr is line buffered (3.9+)
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.stdout
decisions.detail:
Current state: every non-empty stdout and stderr write flushes, even into files and pipes. The flush flag passed down is dead, so stdout.flush() is a no-op in practice (cpp-craft F3b; Term.rs:152-177; FSIoEnvOsTesting.rs:279-326). The native image runtime also prints text and newline as two writes (card #4013). D-COREIO1=A gives core.io ownership of the standard streams and flush, and says nothing about the default policy.

Card #4634 asks to measure, then fix. The measurement belongs to that card. The default itself is an owner choice because every program observes it in output order, crash output and speed.

Sources: The Cherno, 31 nooby C++ habits (i_wDa2AS_8w 00:43), where std::endl flushing every line is the first habit to drop (claims cpp-craft:I02, R02).

Proven approaches. C stdio buffers stdout by line on a terminal and fully otherwise, and leaves stderr unbuffered (POSIX stdin(3)). Python uses the same split, and since 3.9 makes stderr line buffered. Rust's stdout is a LineWriter everywhere, so output into pipes still pays one write per line unless the program wraps it in a BufWriter. Go's os.Stdout is unbuffered, so heavy output needs bufio by hand.

Known failure of plain buffering: a prompt without a newline stays hidden before input, and buffered output can be lost when a program aborts. Option A removes both. It flushes before input and blocking waits, and the stop path flushes before printing its report.

options.name: Lines on a terminal, batches into files and pipes
options.detail: On a terminal, stdout flushes at each line ending. Into a file or pipe it flushes when its buffer fills. Every stream also flushes before the program reads input, sleeps or waits, starts a child process, writes to stderr, stops with an error, or exits. stderr flushes every write. stdout.flush() forces a flush at any time.
options.technical: core.io keeps one buffer per standard stream in the shared runtime, chosen once from the TTY fact (D-CORE-TERMSTDIN1). The scheduler's blocking points, process spawn, the stop and panic report path and process exit call one flush hook. Every tier shares the rule through the one-runtime law (D-EXEC1). The image runtime's two-write print becomes one buffered write.

options.name: Flush at every line everywhere
options.detail: stdout flushes at each line ending on a terminal and into files and pipes. stderr flushes every write. Output that prints many short lines still makes one system call per line.
options.technical: One line-buffered writer for stdout on every target, as Rust's LineWriter. No TTY check. Large line-oriented output into files keeps most of today's system-call count.
options.code:
loop i in 0..1_999_999 { print(i) }
// jet run convert.jet > out.txt: one write per line

options.name: Keep flushing every print
options.detail: Today's rule stays. Every write leaves at once on every stream. stdout.flush() is documented as having nothing to do. Programs that need speed wrap the stream in their own buffer.
options.technical: No runtime change. Documentation records flush as a no-op for the standard streams.

comparisons.note: stdout is line buffered on a terminal and fully buffered into files and pipes; stderr is unbuffered.
The same terminal versus file split; stderr is line buffered since 3.9.
comparisons.code:
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.stdout
print(i)                  # batched into a file
print(i, flush=True)      # force

comparisons.note: stdout is line buffered everywhere, which keeps one write per line into pipes.

recommendation.why: A gives people whole lines on a terminal and gives files and pipes batched writes, the split C and Python proved over decades. Flushing before every wait, child, error report and exit removes the classic hidden-prompt and lost-output failures.
recommendation.tradeoff: Two programs writing into the same pipe may see their lines grouped differently than today.
gains: Large output into files stops paying one system call per print.
stdout.flush() does real work again.
Prompts and crash reports still appear in order.

losses.loss: Output written into a shared pipe by a parent and a child can group differently than today.
losses.mitigation: Every stream flushes before a child process starts and before waiting on it, so parent output written before the spawn always comes first.

whyNot.reason: B keeps one system call per line into files, which is most of today's cost for line-oriented output.
C keeps the cost and leaves a flush method that never does anything.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Measure on card #4634 first: system-call counts with strace and matched timings for one and two million printed lines into a file, a pipe and a terminal.

Check that a prompt written without a newline appears before read_line returns. Check that output printed before a stop, a panic, a child spawn and exit appears in order in a captured pipe, on every tier.

Check that stderr writes are never delayed. Check that stdout.flush() empties the buffer, and that the image runtime prints one write per print call.

surface.gist: Should printed text leave the program at every print, at every line, or in batches when it goes to a file?
surface.lesson: Flushing sends held output to the screen or file. Today every print flushes at once, even into a file. A flushes per line on a terminal and in batches into files, and always before waiting, input or exit. B flushes every line everywhere. C keeps today's rule.

Flush at every point where another process or person could observe order: before spawn, wait, input, stderr writes, stops and exit. Kept.

Flush whenever the program blocks waiting for time, input or the network. Kept: an idle program has flushed everything it printed.

decisions.title: Whether Jet's web server sends the Date header
decisions.situation: Every web response can carry a Date line saying when the server answered. The web standard requires it from any server with a clock, and caches and clients use it. Jet's server never sends it today, although Jet already formats that exact date style for other headers. You decide whether responses carry Date by default; we recommend yes, read from the program's clock so tests with a fake clock stay exact.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's web server add a Date header to every response by default?
decisions.lesson: A response header is a named line sent before the page. Date says when the response was made. The web standard says a server with a clock must send it. A adds Date to every response from the program's clock, so a test clock gives a fixed value. B keeps today's rule: handlers add it by hand. C adds it only outside tests.
decisions.explainer:
A web response starts with header lines, such as Content-Type, then the body. Date is one header. It records when the server produced the response, in one fixed format called IMF-fixdate.

The standard that defines HTTP says an origin server with a reasonably accurate clock must send Date on its normal responses. Caches use it to compute how old a stored response is. Clients use it to notice clock skew.

Jet's server writes every other framing header itself, but never Date. Jet already formats IMF dates for Last-Modified on static files, so nothing new is needed to produce it.

Option A adds Date to every response the server writes. The time comes from the program's clock, which tests already replace with a fake clock. So a test sees one fixed, predictable Date, while a real server sends the real time. A handler that sets Date itself keeps its own value.

Option B keeps today's behavior and documents that handlers add Date by hand. Option C adds Date only when the server runs outside tests.
decisions.story: Lena puts a small Jet API behind a shared cache. Responses arrive with no Date, so the cache cannot work out their age and stores them by its own guess. Her Go service on the same cache never had this problem, because Go's server adds Date itself.
decisions.detail:
Current state: the server serializer never writes Date. An IMF-fixdate formatter exists and is used only for Last-Modified (claim v3-H2:FknTw9bJsXM-B33). The serializer already owns Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, Trailer and Connection (v3-H2:FknTw9bJsXM-B29). Card #4635 owns the server serve paths.

RFC 9110 section 6.6.1 says an origin server with a clock must generate Date for 2xx, 3xx and 4xx responses, and may for 1xx and 5xx. A recipient cache with no Date must add one on receipt.

Source: ThePrimeagen's From TCP to HTTP course (FknTw9bJsXM), which lists Date among the common response headers used for caching (claims v3-H2:FknTw9bJsXM-B33; web-data-net:C76).

Proven approaches. Go's net/http adds Date unless the handler sets the header to nil. Node's http sets response.sendDate true by default. Rust's hyper adds Date by default and caches the formatted string, refreshing it once a second, so the header costs almost nothing per response. nginx always sends Date.

The known trap is test output that changes every second. Jet removes it the same way it handles all time: the header reads the program's clock service. Test fakes and D-EFFECT-HANDLE1 scoped replacement already control that clock.

options.name: Always send Date from the program's clock
options.detail: The server adds Date to every response it writes, unless the handler already set one. The value comes from the program's clock, so a test with a fake clock sees a fixed date. A real server sends the real time.
options.technical: The serializer reads the clock service once per second at most and reuses the formatted IMF-fixdate text, as hyper does. A handler-set Date passes through. The rule covers the supervised server, the lambda serve path and serve_once, so tests see the same header shape as production.

options.name: Handlers add Date by hand
options.detail: Today's rule stays. The server never adds Date. A handler that needs it formats the time and sets the header itself, and the documentation says so.
options.technical: No serializer change. A public IMF-fixdate helper is documented for handlers.

options.name: Send Date outside tests only
options.detail: The server adds Date when it runs for real and leaves it out under jet test, so test output never contains a time.
options.technical: The serializer checks whether the process runs under the test harness. Production and test responses differ in shape.

comparisons.note: net/http adds Date automatically; a handler can suppress it explicitly.
response.sendDate defaults to true.
Date is added by default and cached once per second.
comparisons.code:
// hyper/src/common/date.rs: cached HTTP date, updated each second
Response::new(body)   // Date added by the server

recommendation.why: A makes Jet's server follow the standard every major server already follows, at almost no cost per response. Reading the program's clock keeps tests exact, which removes the one reason servers ever leave Date out.
recommendation.tradeoff: Raw response bytes in tests now include a Date line set by the test clock.
gains: Caches and clients get the header the standard requires.
Handlers never repeat a date line.
Tests see the same header shape as production.

losses.loss: Existing tests that compare raw response bytes gain one Date line.
losses.mitigation: Under a fake clock the line is fixed, so each expected output is updated once and stays stable; a one-time fixture update covers the corpus.

whyNot.reason: B breaks the standard by default and makes every handler repeat the same line.
C makes test responses differ from real ones, so no test can catch a missing Date.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check that every 2xx, 3xx and 4xx response from the supervised server, the lambda serve path and serve_once carries one Date line in IMF-fixdate form. Check that a handler-set Date passes through unchanged.

Check that a fake test clock produces a fixed Date, and that the formatted value is reused within one second. Update raw-response fixtures in the corpus once.

surface.gist: Should Jet's web server add a Date header to every response by default?
surface.lesson: Date is a response header saying when the server answered; the web standard requires it from a server with a clock. A adds it from the program's clock, so test clocks keep it fixed. B leaves it to handlers. C sends it only outside tests.

current.note: No response ever carries Date.

wild.note: net/http adds Date by itself.
wild.code:
w.Write(body)
// Date: Mon, 05 Oct 2026 18:00:00 GMT

options.name: Always, from the program's clock
options.gist: Every response gets Date; test clocks make it fixed.
gains: Follows the standard.
Tests match production.
losses: Raw-response test fixtures gain one line.

options.name: By hand in handlers
options.gist: Nothing changes; handlers add Date themselves.
gains: No output changes.
losses: Breaks the standard by default.
Every handler repeats a line.

    |> http.with_header("Date", time.now().imf())

options.gist: Real runs send Date; tests never see it.
gains: Test output has no time in it.
losses: No test can check Date is sent.

// jet test: Date absent

recommendation.why: A follows the standard like Go, Node, hyper and nginx do, and the program's clock keeps tests exact.
gains: Standard responses with no handler code.
Predictable tests.

losses.loss: Raw-response test fixtures gain one line.
losses.mitigation: The fake clock makes it fixed; update fixtures once.

whyNot.reason: B breaks the standard and repeats code.
C makes tests differ from production.

recommendation.tradeoff: One-time fixture update.

designAway.loss: Existing tests that compare raw response bytes gain one Date line.
attempts: Leave Date out under tests. Rejected as option C: tests would stop matching production.
Read the clock service the tests already control. Kept: the line becomes fixed and predictable in every test.

decisions.title: A memory limit for each web request
decisions.situation: A web server handles many requests at once. If one request builds a huge list, today it can use all the machine's memory and take every other request down with it. Jet already gives each request a time limit, but not a memory limit. You decide whether each request gets its own memory budget; we recommend a generous default per request, adjustable per route, that ends only the request that goes over.
decisions.gist: Should each web request get its own memory budget, so one runaway request fails alone instead of taking down the server?
decisions.lesson: A budget is a limit on how much memory one request may use. A gives every request a generous default budget, adjustable per route. A request that goes over ends with a server error, and the others keep running. B adds the same budget but leaves it off unless a server sets it. C adds no per-request limit and relies on whole-process limits.
decisions.explainer:
A Jet web server runs each request as its own task. Jet already bounds request time: a deadline cancels a slow request. Memory has no such bound while the program runs. One request that builds a huge value can grow until the operating system kills the whole process, ending every request in flight.

Jet does have a static memory rule, which lets a function promise it allocates at most a fixed number of bytes. That is checked at build time and cannot know how big a user's request will be.

Option A gives every request a running memory budget. Memory the request's task allocates counts against it, and memory it frees counts back. Going over ends that request with a 500 server error and a log record naming the line that crossed the limit. Other requests keep running.

The default is generous, 128 MiB per request, which only runaway requests reach. A route that really needs more, such as an export, sets its own budget. Option B adds the same budget but leaves it off by default. Option C adds nothing and relies on limits for the whole process.
decisions.story: Jun's report endpoint builds the whole year's data in memory when a user picks a wide date range. One such request grows until the operating system kills the server, and 200 other users lose their pages mid-request.
decisions.detail:
Current state: bind and serve take (addr, mux, tls, deadline) and no memory budget (core-library.md:997-998). Request bodies have a shared size limit (core-library.md:984-986; D-CORE-HTTPBODYLIMIT1). D-FOUND-LIFECYCLE1 makes request deadlines a cancellation. D-AUTHORITY-MEM2=A gives a static Mem.Alloc(above: N) denial checked at build time, and D-STACKBOUND1 reports worst-case stack and heap per entry point. Card #4635 owns the serve paths. The v3 A2-langs re-read confirmed the gap (note 2).

Source: Richard Feldman on Roc's NIA platform (DzhIprQan68 17:13-18:33). It gives each request a bounded bump arena, frees everything after the response, and answers 500 when a request exceeds its cap (claims languages-a:R12, R13).

The 2026-10-05 synthesis held this as an evidence gap pending research on response-body escape, streaming and cancellation. This ballot answers those points in the technical text of option A.

Proven approaches. Erlang's max_heap_size kills only the offending process, the model for failing one request alone. Cloudflare Workers and AWS Lambda give each worker or invocation a fixed memory limit. Go and Node have no per-request limit, so one request can exhaust the process.

The known risks are false failures for legitimately large requests and memory that escapes the request. A handles the first with per-route budgets and the second by counting only the request task's live allocations.

options.name: A generous default budget per request, set per route
options.detail: Every request runs with a memory budget, 128 MiB by default. Live memory the request's task allocates counts against it. Going over ends that request with a 500 and a log record naming the allocation site. A route sets its own budget, or .Unbounded. Response bodies being streamed and data handed to shared state stop counting once ownership leaves the request.
options.technical: The request task carries an allocation account in the program allocator (D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1); child tasks inherit it. Crossing the budget raises the existing cancellation on that task, like a deadline, so cleanup runs. The serializer then writes 500 if no response has started, or closes the connection if one has. bind and serve gain limits: .{ request_memory: Bytes }, and mux routes accept memory:.

options.name: The same budget, off unless set
options.detail: The per-request budget exists, but servers have no limit until they set request_memory. Existing servers behave as today.

decisions.title: Log spans that close when their block ends
decisions.situation: A log span is a named stretch of work, such as one frame or one request, that logs and profiles can measure. Today a Jet program opens a span, enters it, and must close it by hand on every way out of the function. A forgotten close gets no warning, so the span silently stays open. You decide how spans end; we recommend that a span closes when its block ends, like files and locks already do.
decisions.gist: Should a log span close by itself when its block ends, or keep needing a written close?
decisions.lesson: A span marks the start and end of a piece of work in logs and profiles. Today you call span, enter and close, and forgetting close is silent. A makes opening a span also enter it, and the block's end closes it, the rule Jet's files and locks already follow. B keeps written closes and adds a warning for a missing one. C adds a block form that takes the work as a function.
decisions.explainer:
A span is a pair of marks around some work, a start and an end, with a name. Logs nest records inside it, and profiles measure the time between its marks. Spans only work if every start has its end.

Today core.log has three calls. log.span(name) makes a span, log.enter(span) starts it and log.close(span) ends it. If a function returns early, throws a failure, or the author forgets, the span stays open. The check is clean and the run prints nothing about it.

Jet already has a rule for this shape. Readers, writers, temporary resources and locks own what they hold until their block ends, or until an explicit close takes them. Option A puts spans under that same rule. Opening a span enters it, and the end of the block closes it on every path. An explicit close still ends it early.

Option B keeps the three calls and adds a warning when a path can leave without closing. Option C adds a block form, log.in_span(name, work), that runs a function inside the span.
decisions.story: Omar wraps each game frame in a span to find a slow frame. One early return skips his close call. The profile shows every later frame nested inside the first one, and nothing told him why.
decisions.detail:
Current state: core.log exposes span(name) -> LogSpan, enter(span) and close(span) (core-library.md:2587-2588; Core/log/log.jet:75-79). Readers, writers, temporary resources and locks own their provider resource until lexical scope exit or an explicit close(^handle) (core-library.md:756-757). Card #4632 lists scoped spans as part of proving jet perf on a game frame.

Probe f_span.jet (APICompSystems, 2026-10-05): s :: log.span("frame"); log.enter(s) with no close checks clean, and jet run --allow=Log prints its work with no warning.

Sources: Jonathan Blow reviving 2003 C profiler code (DaJWWePhRsM 13:00-15:00 and 108:00-110:00), where unbalanced Prof_begin and Prof_end pairs crash or slow down. Also Unreal Fest 2024, Optimizing the Game Thread (KxREK-DYu70 12:00-13:00), on scoped cycle counters. Claims: systems-perf:SP2-DaJWWePhRsM-46, SP2-KxREK-DYu70-15; v3-S1:DAJ-12; systems-perf-deep:SD-DA-06, SD-KX-12.

Proven approaches. Rust's tracing returns a guard from span.enter() that exits the span when dropped, and also offers in_scope(closure). C++ Tracy's ZoneScoped and Unreal's SCOPE_CYCLE_COUNTER are scoped objects. Python OpenTelemetry uses a with block.

Go's OpenTelemetry needs defer span.End(), and forgetting it is common enough that the spancheck linter exists. Option A takes the scoped rule Jet already uses for resources, so no new lifetime concept is added.

options.name: A span closes when its block ends
options.detail: log.span(name) opens and enters the span and returns a handle owned by the current block. The block's end closes it on every path, including early returns and failures. log.close(^span) ends it early and consumes the handle, so it cannot be closed twice. log.enter goes away.
options.technical: LogSpan joins the owned-resource rule at core-library.md:756-757. Sema already inserts scope-exit release for owned resources on every path; LogSpan gains the same release. The separate enter call is removed with a teaching diagnostic. Every tier shares the one runtime, so jet perf traces see balanced spans.

options.name: Keep written closes, warn when one is missing
options.detail: The three calls stay. A new warning marks an entered span that some path can leave without closing. defer log.close(s) is the suggested fix.
options.technical: Adds one advisory path lint over LogSpan values. Runtime behavior is unchanged; the warning shows in the check and editor, not on jet run.
options.code:
s :: log.span("frame")
log.enter(s)
defer log.close(s)
// warning without the defer line

options.name: Add a block form that takes the work
options.detail: log.in_span(name, work) runs a function inside the span and closes it afterwards. The three manual calls stay for code that cannot be wrapped.
options.technical: Adds one Core function taking a callback. The manual calls keep their silent-forget risk, and a callback cannot return early from the caller.

comparisons.note: The entered guard exits the span when it goes out of scope; a closure form also exists.
The span must be ended by hand; a linter exists because people forget.
A with block opens and closes the span.

recommendation.why: A removes the forgotten-close bug instead of warning about it, and it uses the scope rule Jet's files and locks already follow. Early returns and failures close spans correctly with no extra code.
recommendation.tradeoff: Code that kept a span open across several functions must pass the handle or reopen a span.
gains: Spans can no longer stay open by mistake.
One fewer call to open a span.
Spans follow the same rule as other owned resources.

losses.loss: A span that should outlive its block must be returned or stored, as an open file must.
losses.mitigation: Returning or storing the handle moves ownership, exactly as for files, so a long span is still one line; the compiler explains the move.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the manual bookkeeping and only warns in the check, not on jet run.
C adds a second way to make spans and keeps the silent forget in the first way.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check that a span opened in a block closes at the block's end on normal exit, early return, failure propagation and a stop, on every tier. Check that log.close(^s) ends it early and that a second close is a use-after-move error.

Check that log.enter reports a teaching diagnostic pointing at the new rule. Rerun probe f_span.jet: the trace must show the span closed. Check that jet perf frame traces show balanced spans.

surface.gist: Should a log span close by itself when its block ends, or keep needing a written close?
surface.lesson: A span marks the start and end of some work. Today you open, enter and close it by hand, and a forgotten close is silent. A closes it when its block ends, like files. B warns about a missing close. C adds a block form.

current.note: A forgotten close checks clean and runs silently.
current.code:
s :: log.span("frame")
log.enter(s)
if paused -> return   // span never closes
log.close(s)

wild.note: The span's guard ends it at scope end.
