decisions.title: Which compiler and tool moments packages may hook, as ordinary Jet metaprogramming
decisions.situation: Packages want to add their own checks, generated code and editor actions at moments such as after a file is parsed or a program is checked. Jet's metaprogramming already lets a marker body read checked facts, reject code and add items while a program builds. A compiler hook is the same compile-time Jet, attached to a compiler moment instead of a written #Name. Today's only compiler hook is a separate plugin outside Jet, chosen by an environment variable, and both options delete it. This vote decides how many moments to publish now. We recommend the full stage table, with every hook following the rules marker bodies already follow.
decisions.gist: Which compiler and tool moments may packages hook with compile-time Jet, and how many should Jet publish now?
decisions.lesson: A hook is package code Jet runs at a named moment, such as after checking a program. Both options use ordinary compile-time Jet and the same runner as marker bodies. A stage determines the read-only input and allowed results: B can return findings and proposed edits only; A also has an additive generation point. Neither silently rewrites source, and the compiler alone decides validity.
decisions.explainer:
Words: the root package is the one being built. Findings are located lint warnings; editor actions are fixes offered for acceptance. Digests/fingerprints are content-derived change identities, not timings.

Markers run where #Name is written; hooks run on each item at a moment. Both use the ordinary compile-time runner, fact views and Meta policy. Powers depend on stages. A's declared point adds items through compiler.generate's checking/provenance path. B's checked point supplies findings and proposed edits only.

Edits apply through jet fix/editor acceptance. Advanced root-opted-in change sets remain D-META-RECONCILE1's contract; vote that first.

A lifecycle: parse -> resolve declarations/signatures/direct named calls -> declared hooks -> check original/added items -> checked -> emitted. Parsed knows syntax, not types; declared knows resolved names, not validated bodies. Checked includes validated added items, which never re-enter declared hooks. Build points view the single fn build graph; fmt/lsp/test/doc are tool views. B begins at checked.

Layout: lint_rules/package.jet identifies the package; lint_rules/no_print.jet is a source module. Included modules supply discovered #On functions without another registration list. Hook modules/imports compile first. Hooks cannot inspect themselves or their support dependency closure; cycles error.

The import use core.compiler supplies payload/result types. Attachment #On selects a typed point. A function returning [compiler.Finding] returns warnings; return [] means none. B's filter selects declarations and map produces one finding per match.

Level 0 is pure computation; level 1 is declared deterministic inputs recorded in .jet/lock. Existing embed_file/embed_bytes/find snapshot inputs. The expression rules :: embed_file("rules.txt") reads a declared package-relative input, not arbitrary fs.read. Hook level 1 excludes network, including pinned fetch. This is explicitly narrower than general metaprogramming.

Steps are deterministic metaprogram evaluator operations under D-PREP-FUEL1. Package maximum and #StepLimit raises retain that contract; no new limit spelling is added. Ambient clock/random/files/network and #Impure are forbidden. Meta.Generate denial blocks additive output.

Jet's own sandbox uses the shared runner. Powers require granted handles; native compile-time machine code is checked before execution. No separate engine/carrier/protocol remains.

Dependencies hold until the root grants their printed jet trust identity. Source/dependency/stage/power/input-authority changes re-prompt with a diff. Compiler-only upgrades rebuild code/cache, not approval. Root hooks run directly within identical ceilings. CI fails with the exact missing grant, not omits checks.

Cache identity includes code, read inputs, full bodies/spans, payload/compiler identity and grants. Trust precedes reuse; revoked/stale grants cannot replay results. Per-item reuse requires unchanged inputs; whole-program hooks rerun when snapshots change. Actual cost appears in jet build --timings; sample figures are illustrative.

Stage-local identities govern merging, not priority. Identical values deduplicate; contradictions/overlapping edits error naming contributors. Presentation follows priority/package/declaration order. Authors still learn stage types, results and trust, but no separate plugin system.
decisions.story: Mia's team bans print in library code. Today she must build a separate compiled plugin outside Jet and set an environment variable on every developer machine and CI job. She wants to write the rule in Jet, next to her other metaprograms.
decisions.detail:
Owner question q47892zx asks for hooks integrated with metaprogramming and Jet's own sandbox. Both alternatives answer unconditionally: ordinary #On Jet functions use the same compile-time runner as markers/prep, with no external plugin engine. The old post-check plugin and JET_COMPILER_EXTENSION retire. Execution architecture independently supplies the baseline runner and native-code isolation check; hooks do not retain a fallback engine while that cutover is voted.

The choice is breadth, not execution technology: A publishes the whole typed table; B publishes only compiler.checked. D-HOOK-ONE1/A already chooses typed #On attachments. This ballot changes the old D-DX5-HOOK1 carrier, not its read-only/checker-authority intent. D-META-USER1, D-MARKER-LAW1, D-META-PUBLISH2 and D-META-GATE1 govern fact reads, additive publication, provenance and denied powers. D-META-CONTROL2/OPTIN2 change-set reconciliation remains D-META-RECONCILE1; directive 23 allows that reconciliation and forbids new AST-report proposals. None are adopted here.

A's CompilerStage mapping is explicit: compiler.parsed -> Parsed; compiler.declared -> Resolved; added-item checking/ordinary preparation passes through Typed/Prepared; compiler.checked is the validated post-Prepared snapshot; compiler.emitted -> Emitted. Hook modules are compiled first without self/closure inspection; cycles error rather than using an incomplete hook. The stage table determines which facts are available, and no stage promises future facts.

Merge rules in the technical table specify all public results. Step exhaustion is E0952, assertion failure E0953, malformed or cap-exceeding output E1402 naming the hook, package, cap and actual count. Per invocation at most 256 findings and 64 proposed edits; the 257th finding or 65th edit rejects the invocation, not truncates it. Failed invocations produce no accepted partial results and are never cached. Findings are L1401 under the package-qualified hook/lint identity; policy deny converts them to E1293.

Grant identity includes source/dependency closure, stage, result powers and declared-input authority; compiler versions invalidate compiled code, not human approval. Cache identity separately includes compiler/payload schema identity and actual granted scope. Revocation disables both execution and cached results. Declared file contents invalidate results without silently adding file-read authority. Package-owned hooks obey effect/sandbox rules even when no dependency prompt applies.

Asset requests enter the one BuildPlan graph and use its dependency/cycle validation. Asset hooks inspect original graph assets once; returned replacements/additions are not recursively fed to the same hook pipeline. Formatter output is for declared non-Jet kinds; it cannot rewrite Jet source through a formatting side door. Editor edits require selection. Added docs and hovers remain presentation outputs, not compiler validity powers.

Attack on A: one runner does not make a broad public stage surface free. B is genuinely easier to stabilize, and evidence from Kotlin KSP supports stable APIs, not publishing every moment. A remains recommended because the owner wants compiler/tool integration and the typed table supplies per-item checks, additive generation and tool moments without a second mechanism. Payloads can evolve independently only when their dependencies permit; there is no promise of version immunity. Publishing all of A commits to every named point now, not a deferred subset.

options.name: Named stages, run as compile-time Jet
options.detail: Publish every typed point in the table, attached with #On and run by the marker/prep runner. Hook modules are discovered in package sources and listed by jet inspect hooks; self/support-closure inspection and cycles are forbidden. Root hooks run directly within the common ceilings; dependency hooks need grants. A commits to more payloads, cache invalidation sites and debugging surfaces. Separate typed payloads localize changes only where dependencies permit, not guarantee isolation from every future API change.
options.technical:
Compiler stage table, payload -> output. compiler.parsed(File): syntax -> findings. compiler.declared(Declaration): resolved signature/body/direct named calls/spans -> findings and added items. compiler.checked(CheckedProgram): validated program -> findings and proposed edits. compiler.emitted(Artifact): read-only artifact -> findings.

Build/tool table. build.planned(BuildPlan): graph -> findings and asset requests. build.asset(Asset): original asset -> replacement or added assets. fmt.file(File): declared non-Jet kind -> formatted text. lsp.code_actions(ActionRequest) -> editor actions; lsp.hover(HoverRequest) -> notes. test.finished(TestReport) -> findings; doc.page(DocPage) -> sections. Types belong to core.compiler. Formatter-kind ownership is declared with attachment; different results conflict.

Merge identity: items by module/name, assets by normalized path, findings by package-qualified lint/span, edits by source revision/span. Overlapping edits conflict. Docs key by page/section ID, hovers by request/location/note ID, actions by request/action ID, formatted text by file/revision/kind.

Distinct IDs coexist in deterministic order. Identical values deduplicate; different values at one identity error naming contributors. Invalid combined generated code reports publication provenance, not selects one hook.

Stages run once. Added items pass ordinary checking/publication, appear in checked, and never return to declared. Edits never apply during builds. Graph outputs use existing cycle/provenance rules. Advanced changes stay outside this contract awaiting D-META-RECONCILE1.

Runner: marker/prep runner, levels 0/file-only 1, existing prep limits and Meta policy. Deterministic-input APIs snapshot declared files and record locks. No external engine/carrier. Atomic caps are in detail. Code caches include compiler version. Result caches include payload/compiler identity, code, bodies/spans/files and grants. Trust precedes replay.

options.name: One checked stage now, more by later votes
options.detail:
Only the shared work: the existing post-check moment becomes the typed point compiler.checked, attached with #On and run as compile-time Jet like any marker body. The environment variable and the plugin protocol retire, as under A. Grants, inputs, limits, merging and caching follow the same rules as A for this one stage. Every further stage needs its own ballot.

B's case: the smallest payload surface to keep stable, the lesson of Kotlin's move from compiler plugins to KSP, with fewer invalidation sites and one place to debug. Its cost: the only moment is the whole checked program, so a per-declaration rule reruns on every program edit, and generators, asset hooks and editor hooks wait.
options.technical: Publishes one point, compiler.checked(CheckedProgram), with findings and proposed edits, carrying D-DX5-HOOK1's read capabilities as its payload. Registration is #On in source. Runner, limits, grants, declared inputs, failure handling, merge identity and the whole-snapshot cache key follow A's technical note. JET_COMPILER_EXTENSION becomes an error whose fix names the #On form. Any other compiler stage name is an error naming the ballot that would add it.
options.code:
// lint_rules/no_print.jet: the same rule over the whole checked program
use core.compiler

#On(compiler.checked)
fn no_print_in_lib(p: compiler.CheckedProgram) -> [compiler.Finding] {
    p.declarations
        .filter(d -> (d.module == "lib" || d.module.starts_with("lib.")) && d.calls.contains("print"))
        .map(d -> compiler.finding(d, "print in library code"))
}

// grant as under A: jet check names the jet trust grant
$ jet check
Warning [L1401] (no_print_in_lib): print in library code
  --> lib/report.jet:12:5
$ jet build --timings
hooks: no_print_in_lib 41 ms (whole program; reruns on any edit)   // illustrative figures

comparisons.note: A stable symbol API replaced internal compiler plugins (kotlinlang.org/docs/ksp-overview.html).
A compile-time program in the same language receives compiler messages for each phase. [INFERENCE: recalled from the Jai beta material, not re-read this session.]

recommendation.why: A publishes the requested compiler and tool moments as one typed metaprogramming surface, allowing per-item checks and additive generation without a second plugin system. Authors still learn stage types and trust; B's smaller stability commitment remains a real alternative.
gains: Lint rules and generators in plain Jet, at the moment they need.
One metaprogramming system: hooks follow the rules marker bodies follow.
No dependency hook runs unasked.

losses.loss: A whole-program hook reruns on any program edit.
losses.mitigation: Per-file and per-declaration points cache per item, and --timings shows each hook's cost.

losses.loss: More hook stages to keep stable across releases.
losses.mitigation: Separate typed payloads localize change where dependencies permit; they do not guarantee that another stage or its consumers can never be affected.

whyNot.reason: B is the smaller, easier-to-stabilize surface, with the same runner and rules for one stage. But per-declaration caching, generators and tool hooks each wait for another vote, and whole-program reruns are the only choice meanwhile.

recommendation.tradeoff: A larger hook surface in exchange for rules that run at the right moment and cache per item.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: QsBeginner. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass tested the complete ballot. Repaired: stage-dependent generation, lib/liberty parity, lifecycle/discovery, trust glossary, all merge identities and cap errors; B's stability case retained.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude-opus. Adversarial model family: gpt. Fresh agent: QsAdversary. The adversarial review attacked the recommendation. Repaired: no retired-engine references, revocation-safe schema/grant cache keys, hook dependency cycles, asset feedback ceiling and atomic caps; A retained.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Reader evidence and disposition are in D-HOOK-STAGES1's three review files: QsBeginner, QsAdversary and repairs. Docs only; no Tower writes. Vote D-META-RECONCILE1 first.

Shared acceptance: #On uses the marker/prep runner and Jet's own sandbox. Pure/declared-file work obeys step limits/Meta policy. Retire carrier/protocol/variable; JET_COMPILER_EXTENSION errors naming #On. Dependencies hold pending trust. Source/dependency/stage/power/input-authority changes re-prompt; compiler-only upgrades do not. Revocation blocks replay. E0952/E0953 stops are uncached. Malformed/257-findings/65-edits produce atomic E1402, not partial output.

A publishes every table point. No-print matches lib/lib.* but not liberty, through direct resolved calls only; function-value calls are outside this detector. Deny gives E1293. Isolated body edits rerun their declaration when no other read fingerprint changes. Any whole-snapshot change reruns checked hooks. Cached/uncached results agree per tier; backend bytes may differ.

Test support cycles, generation visibility/no feedback, asset graph cycles/no repeated processing and every merge identity. Include identical dedup, contradictory doc/hover IDs, overlapping edits, atomic caps, denied powers and revoked-cache replay. Edits never apply at build. B accepts only checked results and rejects generation/absent stages. Implement the entire option, not a subset.

surface.gist: Which compiler and tool moments may packages hook with compile-time Jet, and how many should Jet publish now?
surface.lesson: A hook is package code run at a typed moment by the same compile-time runner as markers. Both options allow findings/proposed edits at checked; only A adds the declared-stage generation point and tool/build moments. No hook silently rewrites source or gets an external plugin engine.

current.note: Today's only compiler hook is an externally built post-check plugin selected by an environment variable. Both options replace it with ordinary Jet.

wild.note: One plugin hook interface for dev and build (vite.dev/guide/api-plugin).

options.name: Named stages
options.gist: Parsed, declared, checked, emitted, build and tool points, all compile-time Jet.
gains: Lint rules and generators in plain Jet.
Same rules as marker bodies; cached per item.
Dependency hooks never run unasked.
losses: Whole-program hooks rerun on any edit.
More hook stages to keep stable.

options.name: One checked stage now
options.gist: Only the post-check moment, as compile-time Jet; each new stage gets its own vote.
gains: Smallest surface to keep stable, as Kotlin's KSP learned.
Same rules; the plugin and its variable still retire.
losses: Per-declaration rules rerun on every program edit.
Generators and tool hooks wait for later votes.

recommendation.why: Packages asked for hooks across the compiler and tools. A publishes them as compile-time Jet under one stage table and per-item caching.
gains: Lint rules and generators in plain Jet.
One metaprogramming system.

losses.loss: A whole-program hook reruns on any program edit.
losses.mitigation: Per-file and per-declaration points cache per item; --timings shows each hook's cost.

losses.loss: More hook stages to keep stable across releases.
losses.mitigation: Separate typed payloads localize changes where dependencies permit; they do not guarantee immunity for other stages or consumers.

whyNot.reason: Smaller and stable, but per-item caching, generators and tool hooks each wait for another vote.

recommendation.tradeoff: A larger hook surface in exchange for rules that run at the right moment and cache per item.

designAway.loss: Dependency hooks are a supply-chain risk.
attempts: Root package grant through jet trust, digest-bound, like package build hooks.
Hooks get only their snapshot, effect levels 0 and 1, and the step limit, under Jet's own sandbox rules.
designAway.result: Reduced: nothing unrequested runs; an approved hook is bounded by its stage powers, checked outputs and limits, and jet trust revoke removes it.

designAway.loss: Two packages may produce clashing results.
attempts: Order-free merge keyed by span, name, asset path and lint; two different results for one key are an error naming both packages.
Combined results that fail checking name each contributing hook.
designAway.result: Removed as a silent failure: no last-writer-wins, and every clash names its packages.

designAway.loss: Hooks would be a second plugin system beside metaprogramming.
attempts: Run hooks as checked bundles in a separate plugin sandbox; rejected, because it keeps a carrier, protocol and budget set that marker bodies do not use.
Run hooks as compile-time Jet in the runner every marker body uses, under Jet's own sandbox rules; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: one metaprogramming mechanism, the shared runner and Jet's own sandbox, without a separate plugin engine.

designAway.loss: A hook must be built before the code it reads.
attempts: A hook lives in its own module that the build compiles first, as a marker declared in a library is compiled before it is used. A hook cannot attach to its own module.
designAway.result: Negligible: one rule, checked by the compiler.

decisions.title: Where Core keeps mutable state shared by every task
decisions.situation: Jet's built-in library, Core, needs one table that every running task shares, such as the in-memory storage behind web storage in a desktop app. Jet refuses to create such a table at the top of a module today. Keeping the table in Rust instead breaks your rule that Rust leaves Jet entirely. The vote picks its home: the existing marker for state kept across code reloads, a new marker that empties on reload, or a table the host program owns. We recommend the existing marker, #Persist, so Jet owns the table, its locking and its updates with nothing new to learn.
decisions.gist: Should Core's shared tables use extended #Persist, a new #Global marker, or host keyed storage?
decisions.lesson: A process is one running program; its tasks are separate pieces of work. A shared table protects each update with a lock. #Persist already keeps changing state through development reloads. Jet rejects a shared table initializer today. Every option must remove Rust and keep isolated tests from changing the real application's storage.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: application code keeps calling Core storage functions. It never declares a global table or manages a lock. The example starts two tasks, writes different keys, waits for both, and prints dark light. A missing key returns None, not an empty string. This vote concerns Core internals; it adds no requirement to ordinary storage callers. Native storage here means an in-memory table for the current process, not saving to disk between launches. Browser storage retains its existing origin and tab rules.

Expert path: a library declares #Persist STORE :: shared Storage{items: [String: String]{}}. Storage is a record with an items field of type [String: String], a table from text keys to text values. shared creates a Shared<Storage> cell. :: keeps the cell's identity fixed; it does not prevent changing the protected contents. Each statement touching the contents is one locked step. #Transact groups several steps into one indivisible commit. An initializer is the expression that creates the starting value; lazy means it runs on first access rather than at startup.

Reading the examples: fn defines a function; every declaration is public by default. -> names the result type. String? means text or None. [String: String]{} is an empty table. m[k] = v stores v under k, and m.get(k) reads an optional value. task { ... } starts a task; join waits for it. ?? panic(...) stops this example if a task failed. print shows the result. Words after // are comments. #Persist means keep this binding through a compatible development reload; #Global is the proposed alternative, not an existing marker.

Names and copies in the examples. A module-level :: binding is written in capitals, STORE, as Jet's naming rule requires. shared is Jet's word for building a shared cell. v.copy() stores a copy of the caller's text, because the table must own its entries.

A guard is an owned lock token for expert manual access. Existing Shared guards and Condition remain available. No read/edit closures are reintroduced. Plain Shared statements and #Transact are the ratified access forms. Shared handle copies refer to the same cell, not independent tables. A whole-module binding replacement or move-out is not an allowed update of the new shared global.

An execution world is a test scope with its own effect providers and child tasks. A process-global binding is not automatically a test-local binding. Core storage must choose the world's own storage provider inside a controlled world, and the process table outside it. A user library needing isolation passes its own state or uses an existing world provider; it must not claim that a bare #Persist binding is isolated.
decisions.story: Mina implements native web storage in Jet. Two tasks must see one table without losing updates, and parallel tests must not overwrite an application's preferences. She needs to know where that table lives and whether editing her code keeps its contents.
decisions.detail:
Correction, 2026-10-07, answering the owner's question on whether shared is valid Jet (q3tr3c3g). It is. shared is a registered contextual keyword, KW_SHARED in crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs:501, from ratified D-CONC-SHARE1=A. Both parsers read it and the formatter prints it. Examples/features/memory/shared_config.jet:25 builds a cell with shared AppConfig{…}, and a probe of shared Storage{…} inside a function checks and runs.

The same probes found four other errors in the examples, now fixed. [:] is not Jet: it fails with E0003, and the empty table is [String: String]{}. A semicolon between statements is E0373, so task bodies use line breaks. A module-level :: binding must be capitals, E0357, so store became STORE. Storing a borrowed parameter in the table is E0120, so the setter stores value.copy(), the ratified copy spelling (D-COPY-MOVE-SPELL1=A).

With those fixes, today's checker reports exactly one error for A's declaration: E0622, a module binding's value must be a literal. That is the gap this vote closes. Options, letters, recommendation and losses are unchanged.

Implementation finding, not a ballot change. On the dev candidate, writing a table entry through a shared cell is silently lost. After store.items["a"] = "dark" on a local shared Storage, store.items.get("a") is None and len() is 0, also inside #Transact. Plain fields work: c.hits += 1 through a shared cell counts correctly. Every option's acceptance must include an indexed write through a shared cell.

Suite revision by BallotSuite1, 2026-10-07. Examples now follow owner directive 21: no pub, and every declaration is public. They also use today's shared construction syntax, shared Storage{…}, as in Examples/features/memory/shared_config.jet:25. The earlier draft wrote Storage.{…}. The situation was rewritten in plain words. Options, recommendation and losses are unchanged. This vote unblocks the Core state work on card #4717; vote it first.

Owner-only choice, not an implementation detail: D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1 makes #Persist the one writable module binding for reload-pinned state. It does not admit a typed shared initializer or establish process-wide initialization across tasks. This ballot extends that contract rather than assuming the extension is already law. Its source question is $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/CorelibCompiler/HANDOFF.md:57-72. Owner directive #19 in $JET_STATE_ROOT/OWNER-DIRECTIVES.md:69-73 requires complete Rust removal, including provider leaves. Card #4717 records that directive.

Read first using Tower decision show: D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1=A, D-SHAREDGUARD1=A, D-HOTSWAP1=A, D-MARK-REG1=A, then D-CALLSITE-MARK1 for the field structure. Three are imported records; their source spans need reconciliation with the current spec. Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:7554-7567 states the writable #Persist rule; :5913-5914 states compatible swaps and layout restarts.

The old D-PERSIST1 paragraph at :2891-2895 is not authority for silently reinitializing a changed live type. The later D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A rule at :8735-8740 permits declared migration for a published schema, otherwise an announced restart. This ballot preserves that later exception rather than replacing it.

Important correction to the handoff: D-CONC-SHARE1=A, read from Tower, deletes Shared.read/edit closures and constructs cells with shared expr. Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2445-2453 confirms statement locking. D-CONC-STM1=A at :2645-2649 keeps one-run ordered transaction commit. A and B therefore use shared Storage{items: [String: String]{}} and ordinary protected field access. They do not revive Shared<T>{...}, Shared.new, or edit lambdas. D-SHAREDGUARD1's expert guards and Condition survive that amendment. D-MARK-REG1 requires a registry row for B; A adds no marker.

Current source evidence, not a fresh compiler probe: crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Registration/Items.rs:1591-1608 reports E0622, 'a module binding's value must be a literal', for unsupported mutable/#Persist globals. Its note limits their initializers to scalar literals. The handoff additionally reports separate take/set locking for scalar persist storage, including a possible uninitialized read. This ballot does not bless that path for concurrent table updates or claim to repair every scalar operation.

New shared globals keep the handle present and update its protected contents without a take/set gap. Core/web/storage/local.jet and session.jet still forward storage calls, while storage.jet:15-25 defines namespaces. These are moving implementation surfaces, not evidence of completed Jet-owned storage.

Same workload in every option: two tasks independently set keys a and b in the native local namespace, then read their own keys. After both join, the expected output is dark light. Distinct keys make that output independent of task order. A separate acceptance case uses concurrent read-modify-write and a two-key invariant; the basic example alone does not prove either property. All proposed examples are future contracts, not executed results.

World isolation is shared work, not a fourth storage-lifetime option. Ratified D-TEST-WORLD1=A supplies isolated effect providers and task context, and requires parallel worlds to remain independent. A global table cannot become isolated merely by taking a lock. Under all options, Core's controlled storage provider supplies a fresh table per isolated world; descendants inherit it, and the scope accounts for them before releasing it.

Outside controlled worlds, storage uses the process default. A and B can also use an explicitly passed local Shared cell. C needs separate host namespace identities per world, with cleanup at world exit. No process-wide 'clear before each test' workaround is allowed.

Research checked on 2026-10-06. Rust's official OnceLock documentation guarantees one successful initialization under contention, identifies reentrant initialization as an error, and says initializer panic leaves the cell uninitialized. Its Mutex documentation requires guarded access and warns that poisoning is advisory, not a soundness guarantee. Go's official maps article says maps are not safe for concurrent reads and writes; sync.Mutex's source documents lock/unlock ordering and forbids copying a used mutex.

Swift's official book describes one-task actor access and warns that interruption at await can expose inconsistent multi-step state. Its Properties chapter says global constants and variables initialize lazily. Zig's language reference says namespace variables have global lifetime and comptime initialization; lazily analyzed does not mean lazy runtime construction.

Rust sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.OnceLock.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html .

Go sources: https://go.dev/blog/maps and https://go.dev/src/sync/mutex.go .

Swift sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swiftlang/swift-book/main/TSPL.docc/LanguageGuide/Concurrency.md and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swiftlang/swift-book/main/TSPL.docc/LanguageGuide/Properties.md .

Zig source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Namespace-Level-Variables . These are design contracts and documented failure modes, not adoption counts or measured performance. No comparative runtime benchmark or user study was run.

What to borrow: Rust's separation of once-only construction and protected mutation, Go's explicit synchronization of maps, Swift's protected task access, and Zig's clear lifetime. What to avoid: a map without locking, a published half-initialized cell, relying on panic poisoning for memory safety, or treating two individually safe calls as one transaction. A combines safe construction with Jet's existing Shared access and reload identity. C remains credible for a host with its own storage service, but is not permission to retain Rust.

Profile: short is Tower's default for one mechanism with three options. A extends initializer admission using existing marker, binding, shared, and transaction grammar; it requests no invariant carve-out. B uses the existing marker grammar but needs new marker registration. There is no proposed parser grammar change. The full CALLSITE JSON field structure is retained where applicable, with reviewPasses null for the short profile. The assignment requested one self fresh-reader check and prohibited spawning; checkInstructions records that self-check honestly, not independent full-profile reviews.

options.name: Extend pinned Jet state
options.detail:
Admit a #Persist module binding whose initializer creates Shared<T>. Use existing shared expression syntax and an immutable handle binding. Build one cell on first access per process; simultaneous callers wait for the same initialized cell. All tasks outside controlled worlds use that cell. Change contents through existing Shared statement locking, #Transact, or expert guards, never by replacing or removing the module handle. Existing scalar #Persist declarations remain governed by their existing rules.

A compatible jet dev reload retains this cell by resolved module identity plus binding name. The identity must distinguish package instances; equal leaf names in different modules do not collide. Changing initializer text alone does not reset a live cell. Changing module identity or binding name starts fresh state with an announced reset. A new process also starts fresh; this is not disk persistence. Caches whose meaning changes must invalidate entries in Jet or use explicitly scoped state.

A layout change follows the ratified announced restart unless an existing published-schema migration covers it. The unannotated Storage example therefore restarts. In controlled tests, Core selects the world's separate provider table rather than reading this default table. The marker itself does not promise test isolation.
options.technical:
Proposed compiler law: sema admits a shared initializer for #Persist, checks T under existing Shared crossing rules, and records stable binding identity and type/layout facts. The new branch requires :: so the module handle cannot be reassigned, moved out, or transiently absent.

The initializer must be a closed, non-suspending, infallible state-construction expression: literal data and checked pure construction, no task/world capture, external effects, or access to other lazy globals. Cyclic global initialization is rejected, not allowed to hang. The example creates only an empty typed map inside Storage. Allocation remains subject to existing allocation behavior; no new retry policy is introduced.

All execution modes implement identical once-only publication. State is inaccessible until initialization finishes. Ordinary statements use the existing Shared lock/cleanup law, not scalar persist take/set. Transactions and guards remain unchanged; this ballot adds no new atomicity mechanism. A failed or cancelled ordinary update releases locks under existing Shared rules; this ballot does not promise rollback outside #Transact.

Reload never runs the initializer again for a retained cell. Layout/migration checks complete at the existing reload boundary before new code uses old storage. The process default and each test-world provider are implemented in Jet. Vetted #Unsafe FFI/syscalls may supply host synchronization, but no Rust implementation is retained.

options.name: Separate global Jet state
options.detail:
Add #Global for lazily built Shared<T> state with the same immutable handle, initialization checks, statement locking, transactions, and guard access as A. Its lifetime is one process outside development reload. Unlike #Persist, it discards contents when its declaring module reloads, even if the type stays the same. It does not silently change #Persist's purpose. Experts can choose reload-pinned #Persist or reset-on-reload #Global.

When the module reloads, the existing safe reload boundary invalidates the default contents. The next access initializes fresh contents once. Previously copied Shared handles must see the same reset, not keep an orphaned old table. Reset is ordered with protected accesses and reported to the developer. Layout changes still restart under the ratified rule and migration exception. Controlled-world tables remain separate, as in A. No global resetting substitutes for per-world isolation.
options.technical:
New mechanism: add the #Global registry row required by D-MARK-REG1, scoped to immutable module bindings with Shared<T> initializers. It does not allow bare mutable module bindings or reassignable global handles. This explicitly extends the module mutation contract for protected #Global contents; it does not grant arbitrary module mutation. Ordinary marker grammar is reused.

The implementation needs reset-on-reload semantics for one cell identity, including outstanding handle aliases. Reset occurs under existing safe reload and Shared synchronization; no caller sees half-reset contents. Construction restrictions, package-qualified identity, cleanup, execution-mode parity, and Jet-only ownership match A. There is no reset caused by a reload of an unrelated module.

options.name: Use a host keyed store
options.detail:
Do not extend module storage. Core uses a generic host keyed-store family for get, set, remove, and keys. The namespace separates local from session and each controlled world from the process default. Each individual leaf call is synchronized by the host. Storage values are text or bytes, not arbitrary Jet types. Jet owns namespace selection and higher-level policy; the host owns the table and its lock.

This can fit a browser or embedding host that already provides storage. On native, it is acceptable only through an actual non-Rust host service reached by Jet FFI/syscalls. Keeping Rust runtime leaves, even without policy, violates the standing owner directive. There is no invented fallback to a Rust map. If a native host lacks this service, C owes a real non-Rust provider before native support is complete.

A compatible reload keeps the process namespace; process restart resets this in-memory workload. Core/world namespaces are not tied to a reloadable Jet record layout. Layout changes elsewhere still follow the ordinary restart law. Separate get/set calls cannot express an atomic read-modify-write or two-key transaction. Adding a host transaction API would be another mechanism outside C, not an assumed fix.
options.technical:
Proposed private Core leaf signatures: __state_get(ns: String, key: String) -> String?; __state_set(ns: String, key: String, value: String); __state_remove(ns: String, key: String); __state_keys(ns: String) -> [String]. These are contracts, not existing Jet entry points. The shown namespace is the process default.

Controlled-world dispatch selects a distinct host namespace using existing world context, and tears it down when the world ends. Host calls must preserve current storage missing-key and error contracts on each supported target. These four signatures do not add cross-call locking, compare-and-set, arbitrary typed tables, or #Transact participation. No retained Rust is authorized.

comparisons.note: A static OnceLock initializes one Mutex-protected map lazily; the mutex guard scopes updates. An immutable static handle can still protect mutable contents. Returned text is cloned before the guard ends. Initialization recursion and advisory poisoning need care. Rust is a comparison only, not an allowed retained implementation.

Package variables have process lifetime. A package map needs sync.Mutex or another synchronization design for concurrent access. The package initializer runs before use; sync.Once can defer construction. Locking two separate calls does not make their combination atomic. Both tasks below may safely use these helpers.

A global let can hold an actor whose contents change while the global name stays fixed. Actor methods serialize access; callers await them. A let holding an ordinary mutable class is not enough. Two calls remain two operations, and suspension inside a multi-step actor method can admit other work.

Namespace variables have global lifetime and comptime initializers. Lazy analysis is not lazy runtime initialization. A shared mutable map needs explicit synchronization and an allocator chosen by the program. This declaration fragment illustrates lifetime only; it is not a concurrent map implementation.

recommendation.why: A gives Core typed, protected state in Jet using existing shared access and pinned identity. It avoids another marker and a host-owned table while preserving safe reload and isolated-world contracts.
gains: Core owns typed state and update policy entirely in Jet.
One initializer and one stable cell serve every task in the process default.
Existing statement locks, transactions, guards, and reload identity remain the access rules.

losses.loss: Compatible reloads keep old contents even when initializer text changes.
losses.mitigation: Restart development to rerun initialization; caches invalidate versioned entries in Jet. The reload line reports retained state.

losses.loss: The #Persist name must teach process lifetime as well as development retention.
losses.mitigation: Document first-access construction, reload retention, and fresh state after process restart together beside the declaration.

whyNot.reason: B distinguishes reset-on-reload state clearly, but adds a second global mechanism and discards storage values on ordinary module edits.
C suits existing host storage but cannot provide typed Jet tables or atomic updates across calls. Native support still needs a non-Rust host provider.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep state deliberately through compatible reloads; restart to rerun its initializer and use scoped state when retention is unwanted.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Evidence labels: decision records, source admission checks, and official comparison documents were read. On 2026-10-07 BallotQs1 probed the syntax with the installed jet: A's declaration, with the fixes in the detail, reports only E0622, and the shared-cell examples parse. Predicted outputs of the proposed programs were not run, because the declaration is not yet legal. The ballot validator is the only executable verification requested for this drafting assignment; its receipt is reported separately. No Tower writes, implementation, commits, compiler builds, or runtime probes are authorized.

Self fresh-reader exercise requested by the assignment, performed by BallotState using the complete draft and the rli5 skill. This is an author self-check, not an independent fresh-agent beginner or adversarial receipt. The short profile needs no reviewPasses.

Explain: the vote chooses who owns a table used by every task and what a code reload does to it. A and B put the table in Jet; C puts it in a non-Rust host. A keeps contents through compatible reloads, B resets them, C retains its host namespace.

Predict: all three two-task examples produce dark light after the joins because each task writes a different key before reading it. Rerunning the initializer text during a compatible reload is forbidden for A, required on next access for B's reloaded module, and irrelevant to C's host table. A fresh process starts empty in this in-memory workload.

Modify: replace dark with blue in task a, leaving task b unchanged. The expected result becomes blue light in every option. Removing task a's set makes its get return missing only when its key was not already present; A or C can retain that key across reload. This distinguishes a fresh run from a retained session.

Derive: the lesson defines process and tasks; the explainer defines shared locking and immutable handles. Since two tasks reach one protected default table, they share contents but not an unprotected mutable reference. Since the world paragraph selects a separate provider, test isolation follows from that provider choice, not from #Persist. Since each statement is one step, two updates need #Transact for one commit.

Self-check friction table, with task failures and repairs:
| Location | Failed derivation | Severity | Repair |
| Initializer | :: seemed to forbid mutation. | Main | Distinguish handle from contents. |
| Reload | Persist seemed disk-backed. | Main | Define process restart. |
| Tests | Lock seemed to isolate worlds. | Main | Define provider selection. |
| Output | Different keys explain output. | keep | Retain same workload. |
| Layout | Restart seemed unconditional. | Edge | Preserve published-schema migration. |
| Symbols | None and join were unexplained. | Main | Add definitions. |

These are simulated beginner reactions, not user-study observations. The failed chains became derivable after repair. No external reader identity or model provenance is claimed.

Owner acceptance after ratification, not proof already exercised:

1. A's declaration passes sema in every applicable execution mode. An equivalent unmarked mutable module table remains rejected. Reassignment or moving the global Shared handle is rejected.

2. Simultaneous first access constructs exactly one cell with no partially published value. Initializers with global cycles, suspension, world capture, or foreign effects are rejected at sema.

3. The same two-task workload prints dark light on fresh runs. A stress case performs a counter read-modify-write in one protected statement and loses no updates. No reader observes a missing handle during another task's edit.

4. A two-key invariant changed under #Transact is never observed halfway through. Separate statements are demonstrated as separate steps, with no claim of automatic grouping. Existing expert guards release on cancellation and panic.

5. A compatible body-only reload keeps values. An initializer-only edit keeps old values and the reload report says so. Renaming the binding/module reports a fresh identity. Process restart initializes empty state again.

6. Changing unannotated Storage's layout announces a restart before incompatible access. A published-schema case follows an existing covering migration; without one it restarts. No silent decode fallback is added.

7. Two simultaneous controlled worlds use separate storage tables, including child tasks and local/session namespace separation. Neither touches the process default, and world exit accounts for descendants before cleanup.

8. Browser origin/tab scope and missing-key behavior stay unchanged. Native in-memory storage is not represented as durable browser storage.

9. The admitted implementation and its lock/once state are Jet-owned with no Rust dependencies. Host primitives use only vetted Jet FFI/syscalls. Update the existing spec, marker metadata if B wins, diagnostics, examples, and both compiler paths after the owner's vote.

decisions.title: Where the row policy check and display live
decisions.situation: A row policy is a database rule such as "a user may only see tickets they own". Jet builds that rule with the database library. The only way to test one rule against a user, or to print it, sits in the sync library. That copy shares a type name with an unrelated permission list and is being removed, so programs lose both abilities. The vote picks their new home; we recommend two small functions beside the existing database policy function.
decisions.gist: Where should code check a database row policy against a user and print it?
decisions.lesson: A row policy is a database rule that hides rows a user may not see. The database library already builds one with db.policy. Checking a single row by hand and printing the rule are only possible through a sync library copy that is being removed. Whichever option wins, queries keep enforcing the policy automatically.
decisions.story: Priya writes a help-desk app where each user sees only their own tickets. She builds the rule with db.policy and wants a quick test that alice cannot read bob's ticket, plus a readable print of the rule in her logs.
decisions.inWild:
CREATE POLICY own ON tickets USING (owner = current_user);
-- https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html
decisions.detail:
D-DBPOLICY1=A puts per-row access rules in core.db. There, db.policy compiles a checked RowPolicy, and every query, mutation and live path satisfies it or gets a generated filter.

The core library reference documents the core.sync RowPolicy as a closed allow/deny action policy. The runtime leaves (Prelude/Sync.rs) and the tooling/sync_crdt example instead use an owner == user row policy through core.sync.

Restoring the documented core.sync surface removes that row-policy copy. Then core.db has only policy and policy_audit. GoldenW2b and GoldenFix13 found this on 2026-10-07.

options.name: Two database functions
options.detail: Add core.db.policy_allows(policy, user:, owner:) -> Bool and core.db.policy_show(policy) -> String with the same meaning and output as the current runtime leaves. core.sync keeps only its documented action policy.
options.technical: Move the existing Prelude leaves from core.sync rows to core.db rows; the sync_crdt example imports core.db for the policy lines.
options.code:
print(db.policy_show(policy))
print(db.policy_allows(policy, user: "alice", owner: "bob"))

options.name: Methods on the policy
options.detail: RowPolicy gains a Display form and an allows method.
options.technical: Display impl plus a method row on RowPolicy in both compiler halves.
options.code:
print("{policy}")
print(policy.allows(user: "alice", owner: "bob"))

options.name: Queries only
options.detail: No direct check or display; examples observe policies through scoped queries and policy_audit, and the sync example's expected output changes.
options.technical: Delete the runtime leaves; migrate the example.
options.code: print(db.policy_audit(scope))

comparisons.note: Row policies live with the database; their text is readable from the catalog. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html

recommendation.why: It keeps every row policy ability in the database library, matches its existing function style, and preserves today's behavior and output exactly.
gains: One library owns building, checking and printing a row policy.

losses.loss: Two new public function names.
losses.mitigation: They replace the removed sync copies one for one, so the total surface does not grow.

whyNot.reason: B mixes method and free-function styles in one library and hides printing inside interpolation.
C removes a simple check people use in tests and forces a database scope for every rule test.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two new names in the database library; the same two names leave the sync library.

decisions.title: How a module re-exports a name once pub is gone
decisions.situation: A module can pass on a name it imported, so its users find everything in one place; this is called a re-export. Jet is removing `pub` so that every declaration is public, and today's re-export, `pub use`, is the one form still undecided. If every import were public unless marked, a shapes library that forgets the mark on a file helper would offer `shapes.files`, and dropping that import later would break its users. The vote picks how a module re-exports; we recommend keeping imports local and re-exporting by declaring a name, as in `clamp :: core.math.clamp`.
decisions.gist: When `pub` goes away, how should a module re-export a name it imports?
decisions.lesson: Each file is a module: shapes.jet is `shapes`. A declaration is a named function, type or constant; `LIMIT :: 10` declares a constant. An import (`use`) lets one file use another module's names. A re-export makes an imported name part of your module, like `shapes.clamp`. The alias vote and the declaration-form vote come after this one.
decisions.story: Mia maintains a shapes library. Her code imports Core math to compute and a file helper to load sample data. Her users should get `shapes.clamp` but never `shapes.files`. When she later drops the file helper, nobody else's code should break.
decisions.detail:
Suite revision by BallotSuite1, 2026-10-07, repaired after the suite reader passes. Option B is restated in its strongest form, the one owner directive 21 leans toward. Its example now meets the story: both helper imports carry `priv use`, and a forgotten `priv` is shown as a labeled hazard. Its collision rules and its publish check are stated in full, including what the check does not catch.

Vote order and interplay. This ballot is first in its group, because the visibility cutover on card #4723 waits on it. D-ALIAS-BIND2 comes second and D-DECL-FORM2 third. Option A here makes a module-level `name :: dotted.path` an alias of a declaration, types included, under every option of D-DECL-FORM2. D-ALIAS-BIND2 then decides only whether a type expression such as `Rows :: [[String]]` gets the same keyword-free form. If B or C wins here, D-ALIAS-BIND2's first resolution step applies to types only, as its technical note already says.

Scope primer for readers. A loose file, with no package around it, is its own module and is imported by relative path, as `use "./shapes"`. A package is a folder of files that ship together and share one namespace. Its files see each other's top-level declarations without importing (spec.md:1772-1777), and other packages reach them with `use package.[names]`.

Reading the examples. `use core.math.[sqrt]` brings only `sqrt` from Core's math module; the brackets list the chosen names. `clamp(x, low, high)` returns x held inside low..high, so `clamp(15, 0, 10)` is 10.

Card #4723 rule 7 leaves re-export open. Rules 1 and 2 make every declaration public and remove `pub`; that is an owner directive, not a ballot. Until this vote, `pub use` (D-MOD4) is the last `pub` form. Owner directive 21 records the owner's lean toward option B and asks for research first. The surface names B's appeal and answers it in the B why-not.

Jet today, master 277033b7c, counted with git grep on 2026-10-07. There are 4,961 plain `use` lines in 4,016 `.jet` files. There are seven `pub use` lines. Five are in crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/core/prelude.jet:27-32, covering fourteen names. One is in Examples/features/modules/module_reexport/text/module.jet. One is in tests/ui/view_write_reexport/edit/module.jet.

These are indexed text matches, not users. They describe code written while imports were local by default, so they are a baseline, not a measure of how often libraries would publish imports under B.

Probe of option A's spelling with the shared release jet (dev-595e0dca3), `jet check` on a scratch file. Today a module-level `dbl :: util.twice` fails three ways. E0357 demands an ALL_CAPS constant name. E0622 demands a literal value (module values are literal-only, spec.md:235-242). `alias Pt :: util.Point` fails E0324, because `alias` is only for generic spellings. So A needs one new resolution rule, given in its technical note; nothing parses differently. Re-probed 2026-10-07 by OwnerNotes1: `alias Rows :: [[String]]` is still E0324, and `Grid :: [[Int]]` is E0357 plus E0622.

Odin (the model card #4723 adopts). Imports are file-scoped; the overview lists `@(private)` for all declarations except import statements, because imports never leave the file. Packages re-export by constant declaration: core/math/linalg/general.odin lines 81, 213 and 399-400 declare `transpose :: intrinsics.transpose` and similar. A uses the same pattern. It is not identical: Odin's `::` already declares any compile-time constant or procedure, while Jet's module-level `::` takes only literal values today.

Go. Imports are file-scoped and never re-exported. A package re-exports with declarations: `type T = other.T`, `const C = other.C`, `var F = other.F`, or a wrapper function. Type aliases came in Go 1.9 for moving APIs and splitting packages behind one exported API (golang/proposal design/18130-type-alias.md).

Adverse evidence from the same Go document: generalized aliases for every kind were rejected for Go 1.8. The reason given is that they overlap with and complicate other declaration forms, and cmd/vet and cmd/doc crashed on them. A answers this by limiting aliases to a bare path to a nameable declaration; every other right-hand side keeps today's constant rules. Documentation and API-record tests are part of A's acceptance list. That narrows the risk; it does not prove it away.

Zig. `@import` is an ordinary value, and re-export is `pub const x = other.x;`, a declaration. Zig 0.15 removed `usingnamespace`, which injected every name of another namespace. The release notes say it sent readers on a wild goose chase to find definitions and encouraged poor namespacing. This is a lesson about wholesale injection. Jet already rejects wildcard imports (E0612), so it does not rank A against B or C.

Rust. `use` is private by default and `pub use` re-exports, which is option C's shape and supports C directly. It keeps the publishing intent on the import line itself, a real readability strength. Glob re-exports cause collisions; rustc's warn-by-default lint `ambiguous_glob_reexports` covers them. Jet's wildcard ban makes that failure neutral across all three options.

Swift. SE-0409 (Swift 6.0) added access levels on imports. Imports are `public` by default in Swift 5 and 6 for source compatibility and become `internal` in a future language mode (flag `InternalImportsByDefault`). The motivation is dependency hygiene: dependencies leaked to clients by mistake, and clients had to load them. A public import does not re-export names; SE-0409 calls `@_exported` a step above `public import`. So Swift is evidence that imports should default to local, not a shipped example of option B.

TypeScript and JavaScript modules. `import` is module-local; re-export is a dedicated form, `export { x } from "./m"` or `export * from "./m"`, closer to C than to A. Conflicting star exports are error TS2308 in TypeScript v5.6.2 src/compiler/diagnosticMessages.json, re-checked on 2026-10-07. Its text asks the author to re-export explicitly: "Module {0} has already exported a member named '{1}'. Consider explicitly re-exporting to resolve the ambiguity." This covers star exports only; it is not cited for B's duplicate rules, which are Jet's own.

Barrel files. Re-export-only barrel files slow builds by loading large module graphs (Marvin Hagemeister, "The barrel file debacle", 8 October 2023). A facade under any Jet option builds the same graph, so this does not rank the options.

Python, option B's model in practice. Every import is a module attribute others can import at run time, so Python ships B's default, and large codebases live with it. mypy's `--no-implicit-reexport`, part of `--strict`, is a checker policy: it treats a plain import as not exported. Explicit forms are `from foo import bar as bar` or listing the name in `__all__`. Run-time behavior is unchanged.

Synthesis. Most surveyed statically checked module systems keep imports local by default (Odin, Go, Zig, Rust, TypeScript), and Swift is moving there. Python is the counterexample: every import is public at run time, as in B, and only checker policy narrows it.

The evidence then splits. Local-by-default evidence supports A and C equally against B. For the explicit form, Odin, Go and Zig declare a name (A), while Rust and TypeScript mark the import (C), which keeps intent on the import and adds no lookup rule.

The survey does not separate A from C. Directive 21 does: C keeps one `pub` after its removal, while A reuses the declaration form every module already has. A also works with card rule 3: a module keeps code in a `priv module` and publishes chosen names with aliases.

Migration. A rewrites seven `pub use` lines into fourteen alias lines. B's cutover can preserve behavior mechanically: plain `use` becomes `priv use` and `pub use` becomes `use`. The cost is that nearly every import then carries `priv`, and new imports default to public. C changes no re-export line.

Implementation module versus facade. In an implementation module, like Mia's, most imports are helpers: A and C write nothing extra for them, and B writes `priv use` on each.

In an intentional facade that gathers `clamp`, `lerp` and `sqrt`, B writes `use core.math.[clamp, lerp, sqrt]` and C writes `pub use core.math.[clamp, lerp, sqrt]`. A writes three lines, `clamp :: core.math.clamp` and so on. If the source module moves, B and C edit one path and A edits three; each stale A line is a build error, so none is missed.

Bulk exports. A facade exposing 100 names writes 100 alias lines under A and one 100-entry list under B or C. All three name every item, since wildcards are banned. A repeats the path on each line; that cost stays visible as A's second loss.

Design-away notes for A. The spelling `alias clamp :: core.math.clamp` was considered to avoid giving `::` a second meaning. It was rejected: the bare form matches Odin and the owner's own scratch note, "Remove alias keyword, just alias by assigning as a const/immutable declaration. myNewType :: myOldType". A grouped alias form was rejected because it would rebuild C's list under another name.

Relation to the owner's alias note. The note asks for every alias to be written `New :: Old` with no `alias` keyword. Option A is exactly that rule for the names a module re-exports: a bare path to a declaration. The note reaches further than this ballot. A type expression such as `Rows :: [[String]]` is not a bare path, and neither is a specialized generic. A leaves those on today's `alias` form, or E0324.

The companion ballot D-ALIAS-BIND2 asks whether to remove the `alias` keyword for those too. It also asks whether a module-level `::` whose value is a type simply names that type. A decides how imports become public names; D-ALIAS-BIND2 decides how far `New :: Old` reaches. If both pass, one rule remains: a module-level `::` names something known at build time. When that thing is a declaration or a type, the name is an alias of it. If D-ALIAS-BIND2 fails, A still stands on its own.

Earlier reader repairs. The first beginner pass found untaught terms, a duplicate-binding gap, mixed tenses and missing imports in client code; all were repaired on the surface. The first adversarial pass found the duplicate-binding contradiction, missing alias kinds and laws, an overstated Swift citation, a removable B migration cost, and an understated bulk-export cost. Each was repaired in the surface, technical notes or this detail. On 2026-10-07 OwnerNotes1 re-checked those findings and re-verified TS2308 at its source.

Suite pass repairs (SuiteBeginner and SuiteAdversary, 2026-10-07). B's example meets the story, with the forgotten-`priv` case as a labeled hazard, and A and C carry the same helper import. B's duplicate rules are stated in full as Jet's own rules. B's publish check is stated as a removal check at publish that must be extended to imports, not a guard against leaks.

The synthesis names Python as B's counterexample and separates evidence for local imports from evidence for alias declarations. A shows its parenthesized and in-function boundaries, its naming rule and its acceptance tests. The bulk-export cost is on the surface. C's example is valid, with the `pub fn` error as a separate probe. The examples define clamp, bracketed import lists and relative-file imports.

Shared work for every option. Update spec S18, D-MOD4 and the module reference. Rewrite the seven `pub use` lines with the card #4723 rewrite script. Give each removed form an error whose fix shows the new form, with UI snapshots.

Under every option, the public-API record must list each re-exported name with its target's signature: aliases under A, public imports under B, `pub use` names under C. `jet registry publish` compares that record between versions (syntax-decisions.md:5125-5133, Jetpack/Publication/Source/Diff.jet).

Separately, under public-by-default a directory module's child module is itself a public member. The D-MOD4 example re-exports a function `wrap` from a child module also named `wrap`, so that collision must be resolved in every option.

options.name: Local imports; re-export by declaration
options.detail: A `use` binds names for its own file or module body only, as today. To re-export, the module declares a second name for an existing declaration, such as `clamp :: core.math.clamp`. That alias is a declaration, so it is public by default and hidden inside a `priv module`, like any other. The module's own code uses it unqualified, like any of its declarations. A module-level `NAME :: value` with any other value stays a constant.
options.technical:
New resolution rule; nothing parses differently, but telling an alias from a constant needs name lookup, not spelling alone. At module level, `name :: P` declares an alias when P is a bare path to something a member import can name. P may be dotted (`core.math.clamp`) or a name brought in by `use` (`clamp`). Allowed targets are a function, type, enum, trait, tag, protocol, constant, or public module.

Anything else keeps today's constant rules (E0622, E0357): a call, an annotation, a generic instance, an enum case, or a parenthesized path. So `F :: (engine.f)` is a constant and fails E0622; the error's note says to drop the parentheses to declare an alias. Inside a function, `f :: other.f` stays a local binding, unchanged.

The alias name follows the target's case rule, so the lookup decides it. A function alias is cased like a function (`clamp`), a type alias like a type (`Path`), and a constant alias like a constant (`MAX :: limits.MAX`). Hover text and errors name the kind, as in "alias of fn core.math.clamp", so a reader never guesses.

An alias is the same declaration under a second name. Calls keep generics, defaults, named arguments, effects, and borrow and move rules. Constructors, patterns, methods, trait implementations, tags and type identity follow the original. An alias never moves the original's home module, so `priv` fields stay private to it and `impl` blocks still belong there.

Aliases resolve in any order and through chains of any length. A chain with no root, such as `a :: impl.b` beside `b :: impl.a`, is a new cycle error. An alias may publish a declaration from a `priv module` its author can see. Aliasing a `priv module` itself is an error whose fix lists its members instead.

A generic type made by a build-time recipe (D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1) is aliased by naming the recipe, `Parser :: impl.Parser`, which is a bare path. A specialized instance such as `impl.Parser(Token)` is a recipe call, not a bare path, so this rule does not alias it. The separate ballot D-ALIAS-BIND2 decides its spelling: `Tokens :: impl.Parser(Token)` under its option A, or `alias Tokens :: impl.Parser(Token)` under B.

A name both imported by `use` and declared as an alias is the ordinary duplicate-name error. Its fix says: delete `sqrt` from the `use` line; the alias already binds it here. After that, the module's own code still calls `sqrt(2.0)`, because the alias is one of its declarations. `pub use p.[a, b as c]` becomes an error whose fix writes `a :: p.a` and `c :: p.b`. A path resolves only names already in scope, so a loose-file dependency still needs a local `use "./engine"`.

Acceptance tests for A, each a UI snapshot. `shapes.Path` and `core.files.Path` are one type. A call through an alias keeps defaults, named arguments and effects. Reading a `priv` field through `shapes.Path` outside the home module still fails. A rootless chain reports the cycle error. `F :: (engine.f)` reports E0622 with the alias note. The documentation tool and the public-API record list each alias with its target; this answers Go's 1.8 lesson, where cmd/doc and cmd/vet crashed on generalized aliases.

Limits, stated plainly. Public function signatures may still mention imported types; A does not police that. Aliasing a public module publishes its future members too, exactly as a public import of that module does under B or `pub use` does under C.

options.name: Imports public; `priv use` keeps one local
options.detail:
Every `use` also makes its names members of the module, the same public default every declaration now has, and `priv use` keeps one import local, reusing the one visibility keyword. Re-exporting costs nothing to write, grouped lists work as they do today, and a facade module that gathers names from one source needs one line.

Collision rules, stated in full. These are Jet's own rules for this option, not borrowed from another language. Two imports that bind one name in one file are an error at the second import, naming both, whether or not either is `priv`; the fix renames one with `as`.

Other modules reach a public import through the module's name, as `shapes.clamp`. Inside a package it never joins the shared names sibling files see unqualified, so it never collides with their code. For other packages, though, a package's public imports are its members. Two public imports of the same declaration in two files are one member. Two of different declarations under one name are the duplicate-name error E0624 at the second, and so is a public import that shares a name with a declaration.

The publish check, stated plainly. When a package is published with `jet registry publish`, Jet compares its public names and signatures with the last published version. A removal on a minor or patch release is error E2601. The fix is a major version bump, restoring the name, or `--force`, which publishes with a warning banner.

B requires that this record list every public import, which it does not do today. The check runs only at publish and only once a version exists. It never stops a helper from becoming public; it only stops that helper's later removal from slipping out in a minor release.

The cost that remains: a library that wants a small public surface writes `priv use` on each helper import, and a forgotten `priv` publishes the helper with no warning.
options.technical:
`use` binds names for its file and as public members of the module; `priv use` binds them for the file or module body only. A public import is a qualified member only: `shapes.clamp` resolves from other modules, while the package's shared unqualified namespace (D-MOD-CYCLE1=A, spec.md:1772-1777) keeps holding declarations, not imports.

Duplicates. A second import of one name in one file is an error at that import, naming both. Across a package, public imports of the same declaration merge into one member. Public imports of different declarations under one name are E0624, as is a public import that clashes with a declaration. No ambiguous member is ever published.

Acceptance. The compiler's public-API record, consumed by Jetpack/Publication/Source/Diff.jet, gains one item per public import, with kind and signature taken from the target. `jet registry publish` then reports a removed public import as E2601 or E1218 (syntax-decisions.md:5125-5133). The cutover keeps behavior mechanically: plain `use` becomes `priv use` and `pub use` becomes `use`.

options.name: Keep `pub use`
options.detail: Re-export stays `pub use`, exactly as today, with grouped lists. Plain `use` stays local, and `::` keeps its single constant meaning, so no lookup-dependent rule is added. C draws a clear line: declarations are public, imports are local unless marked, and the mark sits on the import line where a reader looks first. The cost is that the `pub` keyword survives in this one position after being removed everywhere else; every other `pub` is an error.
options.technical: The parser keeps `pub` only before `use`; `pub` elsewhere is an error whose fix deletes it and says only `pub use` remains. Existing re-export lines are untouched. The wider visibility cutover still migrates declarations. Compared with A, C adds one keyword position learners must memorize; A adds one lookup rule that decides alias versus constant.

comparisons.note: Imports are file-scoped. A package re-exports with a constant declaration. Read 2026-10-07 from core/math/linalg/general.odin.
Imports are file-scoped; re-export is a declaration. Type aliases came in Go 1.9. Generalized aliases for every kind were rejected because they complicated other declarations.
comparisons.code:
type Reader = internalio.Reader
const MaxSize = internalio.MaxSize

comparisons.note: Re-export is a public constant. `usingnamespace`, which injected every name, was removed in 0.15 for hurting discoverability.
comparisons.code:
const other = @import("other.zig");
pub const parse = other.parse;

comparisons.note: Imports are private; `pub use` re-exports, as in option C. Glob re-export collisions get a default warning; Jet bans wildcards, so that is neutral here.
comparisons.code:
use std::fs;                // private
pub use crate::math::clamp; // re-export

comparisons.note: SE-0409: imports are public by default only for compatibility and become internal in a future mode. A public import does not re-export names; `@_exported` does.
comparisons.code:
internal import DatabaseAdapter
public import Geometry

comparisons.note: Imports are module-local; re-export is a dedicated form, closer to C. Conflicting `export *` lines are error TS2308.
comparisons.code:
import { sqrt } from "./math";   // local
export { clamp } from "./math";  // re-export

comparisons.note: Every import is a public module attribute at run time, so Python ships option B's default. mypy --strict adds --no-implicit-reexport, a checker policy; run-time behavior is unchanged.
comparisons.code:
from os import path          # shapes.path leaks
from os import path as path  # explicit re-export

recommendation.why: Imports are a file's private shortcuts; declarations are what a module offers. A keeps them apart, so nothing leaks by accident, and a re-export is just `New :: Old`, the alias form Odin uses.
gains: No import leaks into a module's public names.
Imports never need a marker.

losses.loss: `name :: path` gains a second meaning: another name for a declaration.
losses.mitigation: A plain path, dotted or imported, to a declaration is an alias; anything else stays a constant. Errors name which.

losses.loss: A facade repeats the source path on each published name.
losses.mitigation: Re-exports are rare today, seven lines in Jet. A moved source fails to build at each stale line, so none is missed.

whyNot.reason: B fits the public default and keeps grouped lists. But every import is public unless marked `priv`, and the publish check catches later removals, not the original leak.
C is coherent: declarations public, imports local unless marked. But it keeps one `pub` after `pub` was removed, a lone exception learners must memorize.

recommendation.tradeoff: One line per published name buys imports that never leak.

surface.gist: When `pub` goes away, how should a module re-export a name it imports?
surface.lesson: Each file is a module: shapes.jet is `shapes`. A declaration is a named function, type or constant; `LIMIT :: 10` declares a constant. An import (`use`) lets one file use another module's names. A re-export makes an imported name part of your module, like `shapes.clamp`. The alias vote and the declaration-form vote come after this one.

current.note: Jet is removing `pub`, so declarations become public. Today's re-export, `pub use`, is the one form still undecided.
current.code:
// shapes.jet
use core.math.[sqrt]           // only sqrt; this file only
use core.files                 // file helper; this file only
pub use core.math.[clamp]      // users see shapes.clamp
// app.jet
use "./shapes"                 // a file next to this one
print(shapes.clamp(15, 0, 10)) // 10: 15 held inside 0..10
