decisions.title: min, max and clamp with any number of values, available without an import
decisions.situation: Choosing the smaller or larger of some values, or keeping a value inside a range, is one of the most common small jobs in code. Today Jet has these helpers only inside its math library, they need an import line, and they accept exactly two whole numbers. The vote decides whether min, max and clamp become always-available helpers that take any number of values of any comparable type; we recommend yes.
decisions.gist: Should `min`, `max` and `clamp` work on any comparable values, with no import?
decisions.lesson: The prelude is the small set of names every file can use without `use`. Today `min`, `max` and `clamp` live in `core.math`, take exactly two whole numbers, and need an import. Whichever option wins, they become generic over anything comparable, with one rule for NaN.
decisions.story: Ana writes a small game and keeps the player on screen with `x = clamp(x, 0, width)`. Jet says the name does not exist, then that 2.5 is not an Int.
decisions.detail:
Source: owner scratch note, line 60: Odin has variadic min, max and clamp built in, with no import; ensure Jet has this.

Probe, shared release jet dev-595e0dca3, 2026-10-07. `print(min(3, 1))` is E0102, "Nothing named `min` exists here". `3.min(1)` and `12.clamp(0, 10)` are E0311. Core/math/math.jet lines 21-34 define min, max and clamp for two Int values only, with min_float, max_float and clamp_float beside them.

Ratified. D-TRAIT-OVERLOAD1 lets one `math.max` serve every number type through a `Numeric` trait. Card #4659 makes the two-argument forms generic over Comparable with the NaN rule from #2298: one NaN operand yields the other operand. The prelude is a closed list (D-CORE-PRELUDE1, D-PRELUDE-LAW1), so adding names needs this ballot.

Prelude tests from D-CORE-PRELUDE1. Frequency: min, max and clamp are among the most used numeric helpers in every surveyed language. Total and safe: yes, given at least one value. Names carry no hidden meaning. No better home: the math module stays as the qualified spelling. First-hour coverage: games and scripts need clamp early. Collision-conscious: user names still win, with lint L0510.

Technical. `min(first: T, rest: ...T) -> T` and `max` take one or more values of a Comparable T. `clamp(x: T, lo: T, hi: T) -> T` stops with a registered report when lo is greater than hi. Each call compiles per type, so there is no boxing. Floats use the #2298 NaN rule. `core.math.min` and friends are the same functions, not aliases. Lists keep `list.min()` and `list.max()`, which return an optional for an empty list.

In the wild. Odin provides min, max and clamp as built-in procedures over ordered types. Python's min and max are built-ins over iterables and arguments. Rust uses methods on Ord with two values, plus `clamp`. C++ has std::min with initializer lists.

Why B loses: it keeps an import for a helper beginners reach for in their first hour.

options.name: In the prelude, any count
options.detail: min, max and clamp join the prelude. min and max take one or more values of one comparable type; clamp takes a value and two bounds. The same functions stay reachable as core.math.min and so on.
options.technical: Signatures: `min(first: T, rest: ...T) -> T`, `max` likewise, `clamp(x: T, lo: T, hi: T) -> T`, T: Comparable. Generic and compiled per type. Floats follow the #2298 NaN rule. lo greater than hi is a registered stop. Adds three entries to the closed prelude list with the edition migration lint L2001.
options.code:
print(min(3, 1, 7))       // 1
print(max(2.5, 1.5))      // 2.5
print(clamp(12, 0, 10))   // 10
print(max("ant", "bee"))  // bee
print(clamp(5, 10, 0))    // stop: clamp bounds 10 > 0

options.name: Generic, but still imported
options.detail: The same generic functions, but they stay in core.math and need an import. The prelude does not grow.
options.technical: Same signatures as A inside core.math; the prelude list is unchanged.
options.code:
use core.math as math
print(math.min(3, 1, 7))     // 1
print(math.max(2.5, 1.5))    // 2.5
print(math.clamp(12, 0, 10)) // 10

comparisons.note: Built-in procedures over ordered types, no import.
Built-in functions over arguments or one iterable.
Methods on Ord, two values at a time.

recommendation.why: Picking the larger or smaller value is everyday code in games, graphics and scripts. A removes the import and the two-argument limit while keeping one function per job.
gains: Beginners write `max(a, b)` and it just works.
Experts get the same speed: each call compiles per type.

losses.loss: Three more names every file sees.
losses.mitigation: Your own `min` still wins, with the shadowing warning the prelude already gives.

whyNot.reason: It keeps an import for one of the most common helpers, which is exactly the friction the prelude exists to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three prelude names buy zero-import min, max and clamp for every type.

decisions.title: Free memory right after a value's last use, and guarantee tail calls
decisions.situation: When a Jet value stops being used, its memory is still held until the end of the block it lives in. A large value that dies early keeps its memory for the rest of the block. That pending cleanup also stops a recursive call at the very end of a function from reusing its stack space. The vote decides whether Jet frees plain memory right after the last use and promises those final calls never grow the stack; we recommend yes, keeping files and locks on today's rule.
decisions.gist: Should Jet free a value's memory right after its last use, and make tail calls never grow the stack?
decisions.lesson: Cleanup returns a value's memory, or closes its file. Today it runs at the end of the block, even when the value died earlier. A tail call is a call that is the last thing a function does. Whichever option wins, the rule is written down and tested on every engine.
decisions.story: Sam's log tool reads a 1 GB file, counts its lines, then spends a minute on the counts. The machine holds the whole file for that minute. His recursive directory walker also crashes on very deep trees.
decisions.detail:
Source: owner scratch note, line 77: RAII is not great; clean memory up earlier; tail recursion can keep memory alive because it is overwritten before it is cleaned up. Line 70 also asks to beat Rust with tail optimizations.

Jet today. Owned locals are cleaned up at the end of their scope under a drop flag. The header of Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Codegen/DropFlags.jet says execution order and drop timing are unchanged by its pass. D-FIELD-DROP-ORDER1 cleans fields last-first at scope exit. A last use already moves the value (D-COPY-DEFAULT1), and LastUse.jet computes last uses with one backward liveness pass. No decision mentions tail calls.

The problem. A value that is dead but not moved holds its memory until the scope ends. A call in tail position cannot reuse its frame while any cleanup is still owed after it, so a tail-recursive function grows the stack. This is why Rust cannot promise tail calls without its proposed `become` keyword (RFC 3407).

Evidence. Mojo destroys values as soon as possible after their last use and documents it as a core rule. Swift's ARC does not promise lifetime to the end of scope; `withExtendedLifetime` exists to ask for it. Scheme requires proper tail calls. Zig offers `@call(.always_tail, ...)` as an explicit request.

Option A, memory. A value has visible cleanup when its type has Close, #MustFinish, a lock or guard, or a defer registration. Any other value is freed right after its last use, counting uses through views and borrows, which LastUse.jet already counts. Values with visible cleanup keep the scope-end rule and D-FIELD-DROP-ORDER1.

Option A, tail calls. A call in tail position reuses the frame whenever no visible cleanup is pending after it. When one is pending, an advisory lint names the value that blocks the tail call. The same rule holds at O0, O1 and O2 and in comptime (I9).

Amends D-FIELD-DROP-ORDER1 only for memory-only values; field order among them stays last-first. No syntax changes.

Why B loses: it keeps memory alive after the compiler has proved it dead, and it leaves deep tail recursion able to crash.

options.name: Free at last use; tail calls kept flat
options.detail: Memory-only values are freed right after their last use. Files, locks and other values with visible cleanup still close at the end of their block. A call that is the last thing a function does reuses the frame when no visible cleanup is pending.
options.technical: Move the drop of each memory-only owned value to the point after its last use, as computed by the existing liveness pass, including view and borrow uses. Keep scope-end drops for types with Close, #MustFinish, guards or defer registrations. Emit tail calls as jumps when no visible drop is pending; otherwise report an advisory lint naming the blocker. Debug info records the free point.

options.name: Keep end-of-block cleanup
options.detail: Cleanup stays at the end of each block, as today. The optimizer may still turn some tail calls into jumps, but nothing is promised.
options.technical: No change to drop placement. Tail calls stay an optimizer choice at O1 and O2.

comparisons.note: As-soon-as-possible destruction after the last use.
comparisons.code: var n = len(big)   # big is destroyed here

comparisons.note: Drops at scope end; explicit tail calls are a proposed `become` keyword.
An explicit request for a tail call.

recommendation.why: Jet already knows each value's last use. Freeing memory there costs nothing to write, lowers peak memory, and removes the pending cleanup that blocks tail calls.
gains: Less memory held, with nothing new to learn.
Tail recursion becomes a safe loop.

losses.loss: A debugger shows a dead value as already freed.
losses.mitigation: The debugger names the line where it was freed, so nothing silently disappears.

losses.loss: Freeing order differs from Rust and C++ habits.
losses.mitigation: Values with visible cleanup, such as files and locks, still close at the block end.

whyNot.reason: It keeps memory alive after Jet knows it is dead, and leaves deep tail recursion able to crash.

recommendation.tradeoff: Memory-only values free early; anything with a visible effect keeps its written place.

decisions.title: Expert cache hints in core.mem: prefetch, streaming store, cache-line size
decisions.situation: Fast programs keep the data they need in the processor's small caches; a miss can cost a hundred times more than a hit. Jet already lets experts control memory layout, but it cannot ask for data early or write large results without flushing the cache. The vote decides whether core.mem gains three expert tools, a prefetch, a streaming store and the chip's cache-line size; we recommend yes, each proven by a measured test.
decisions.gist: Should experts get cache hints in `core.mem`: prefetch, a streaming store, and the cache-line size?
decisions.lesson: A CPU cache keeps recently used memory close to the processor; a miss waits for main memory. A prefetch asks for data before it is needed. A streaming store writes without filling the cache. Whichever option wins, the profiler work that shows misses per line goes ahead.
decisions.story: Lee's physics step walks a grid by columns. Each read misses the cache, and the profiler will soon show it, but Jet gives Lee no way to fetch the next column early.
decisions.detail:
Source: owner scratch note, line 17: cache hits are critical; give control over the L1, L2 and L3 caches, and show when code falls out of cache to RAM or disk.

Jet today. Layout control exists: `#Layout(c, align(N))` and target alignment (D-PLACE1, D-LAYOUT-ALIGN1). Byte sizes are facts (D-LAYOUT-SHOW1), and column storage is chosen per collection (D-SOA-SITE1). Proven kernels get cache blocking behind a measured gate (D-ACCEL1), and a hidden-cost view exists (D-COSTLAW1). No decision mentions prefetch, streaming stores or cache lines. The seeing half is card draft cards/cache-profiler.json, which needs no ballot.

Option A, technical. `mem.prefetch(place, .Read | .Write, level: .L1 | .L2 | .L3 = .L1)` takes a place or view, never faults, and is a no-op on targets without the instruction. `mem.stream_store(&dst, value)` writes with a non-temporal store where the chip has one and an ordinary store elsewhere. `$build.cpu.cache_line` is a build fact for the selected CPU, defaulting to 64 when the target is generic.

Safety and lowering. None of these needs #Unsafe, because none can read or write outside a checked place. They lower through D-CORE-BOUNDARY1 instruction entries whose plain bodies define the meaning.

Performance rule. AGENTS.md requires a surface added for performance to arrive with a paired two-program cell against the plain spelling, and ratification waits until it strictly beats the plain form. The cells are a strided grid walk with and without prefetch, a large copy with and without streaming stores, and contended counters with and without padding.

Evidence. Zig ships @prefetch. GCC and Clang ship __builtin_prefetch and streaming-store intrinsics. C++17 added hardware_destructive_interference_size for padding. Linux kernel code pads hot counters to cache lines to avoid false sharing.

Why B loses: a profiler that shows misses without a way to act on them leaves experts reaching for #Unsafe or inline assembly.

options.name: Expert hints in core.mem
options.detail: Three tools in core.mem: prefetch a place, store without filling the cache, and read the chip's cache-line size as a build fact. All are safe and need no #Unsafe.
options.technical: `mem.prefetch(place, .Read | .Write, level: = .L1)`, `mem.stream_store(&dst, value)`, `$build.cpu.cache_line` (default 64 on generic targets). Lowered through Core instruction entries; no-ops where unsupported. Each needs a paired gauntlet cell before ratification.

options.name: Compiler and profiler only
options.detail: No new API. The optimizer and D-ACCEL1 handle cache behavior, and the profiler shows misses.
options.technical: No change beyond the profiler card.

comparisons.note: Built-in prefetch.
GCC and Clang built-ins and intrinsics.
A named cache-line size for padding.

recommendation.why: Seeing cache misses is only useful if an expert can act on them. A adds three small tools that never break safety, and each must beat plain code on a measured test.
gains: Experts get the same cache control as C and Zig.
Beginners never meet it.

losses.loss: A wrong hint can make code slower.
losses.mitigation: The memory profiler shows misses before and after, and a paired test proves the gain.

losses.loss: Cache-line size differs between chips.
losses.mitigation: It is a build fact for the chip you target, with 64 bytes as the portable default.

whyNot.reason: It shows experts the problem and then gives them no way to fix it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three expert tools, each kept only when it beats the plain loop.

decisions.title: Choose a numbered enum's backing integer with #Layout(U8)
decisions.situation: An enum is a list of named cases, and a numbered enum gives each case a whole number so it can be stored in a file or sent over a network. Jet accepts the numbers but cannot say how many bytes the enum takes, and its conversions to and from numbers are not built yet. The vote decides how a program picks the backing integer; we recommend the existing layout marker, as in #Layout(U8).
decisions.gist: Should a numbered enum choose its backing integer type, such as one byte, with `#Layout(U8)`?
decisions.lesson: An enum lists named cases. A numbered enum gives each case a whole number, such as Read = 1. The backing type is the integer that stores the case in memory and in files. Whichever option wins, `Mode.from_int` and `mode.to_int()` get built.
decisions.story: Inez reads a device protocol whose mode field is one byte. She wants `Mode` to take exactly one byte inside her C-layout header and to reject unknown codes.
decisions.detail:
Source: owner scratch note, line 54: Odin lets an enum choose the integer that backs it and assign numbers; can Jet do this, even if only for simple enums?

Jet today. Numbered cases parse, and the numbers may be computed at build time (D-META-CONST1). A checked `Mode.from_int(n)` is ratified for enums whose cases all have explicit unique numbers (D-ENUM-INGRESS1). All values can be read as build-time data (D-ENUM-CASEVALUES1). Packed structs can store an enum field at a bit width (D-BITS1).

Probe, shared release jet dev-595e0dca3, 2026-10-07. `enum Mode { Read = 1  Write = 4 }` checks. `Mode.from_int(4)` is E0107, and `Mode.Write.to_int()` is E0304. No syntax chooses the backing integer.

Option A, technical. `#Layout(T)` on a payload-free enum, where T is a fixed-width integer such as U8 or I32. Every case number must fit T, or the case gets a range error. `#Layout(c)` structs store the enum as T. `Mode.from_int(n)` follows D-ENUM-INGRESS1, and `mode.to_int()` returns the number as Int. A payload enum with `#Layout(U8)` is an error that points to packed structs.

Without the marker, the compiler keeps choosing the representation, and the size stays a build fact (D-LAYOUT-SHOW1).

Evidence. Odin writes `enum u8`. Rust writes `#[repr(u8)]`, an attribute much like option A. C# and Swift write the type after the name. All of them use the choice mainly for files, protocols and foreign interfaces.

Why B loses: it adds a grammar form for something the existing layout marker already expresses.

options.name: `#Layout(U8)` on the enum
options.detail: The existing layout marker takes an integer type for payload-free enums. Case numbers must fit it. Conversions both ways are built.
options.technical: `#Layout(T)` with T a fixed-width integer, payload-free enums only. Out-of-range case numbers are range errors at the case. Storage in `#Layout(c)` and packed structs uses T. `from_int` per D-ENUM-INGRESS1; `to_int() -> Int`.
options.code:
#Layout(U8) enum Mode {
    Read = 1
    Write = 4
}
m :: Mode.from_int(4) ?? Mode.Read  // Write
print(m.to_int())                   // 4
SIZE :: prep { Mode.$layout.size }  // 1

options.name: Type after the name
options.detail: A new grammar form writes the backing type after the enum name, as Odin, C# and Swift do.
options.technical: Parser accepts `enum Name: T { … }`; same checks and conversions as A.

comparisons.note: Backing type after `enum`.
An attribute chooses the representation, like option A.
Backing type after the name, like option B.

recommendation.why: Jet already says how a type is stored with `#Layout`. Reusing it for enums adds one argument, not new grammar, and keeps every storage choice in one place.
gains: One home for every storage decision.
Checked conversions both ways.

losses.loss: The size sits on a marker line, not beside the name.
losses.mitigation: Hover and docs show `Mode (U8)`, the same place `#Layout(c)` already sits.

losses.loss: Only enums without payloads can choose an integer.
losses.mitigation: A payload enum gets an error naming packed structs as the tool for bit layouts.

whyNot.reason: It adds grammar for something the layout marker already says, and puts a type beside a name, which Jet avoids.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more `#Layout` argument buys exact enum sizes with no new grammar.

decisions.title: Number types with a fixed byte order, such as U32be and F64le
decisions.situation: Files, network packets and hardware registers store numbers with a fixed byte order, big-endian or little-endian, while each chip has its own. Jet handles byte order only when it reads or writes raw bytes, so a file header cannot be described as a plain struct and read in place. The vote decides whether Jet adds number types that carry their byte order, as Odin does; we recommend yes, with arithmetic still on ordinary numbers.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add number types with a fixed byte order, such as `U32be` and `F64le`, for files and protocols?
decisions.lesson: Byte order says whether a number's biggest byte comes first (big-endian) or last (little-endian). Files and networks fix the order, while chips differ. Today Jet chooses the order only when reading or writing bytes. Whichever option wins, arithmetic always happens on ordinary numbers.
decisions.story: Kai maps a 2 GB image file whose header and tile index are big-endian. He wants to describe the header once and read fields directly, without copying or converting each one.
decisions.detail:
Source: owner scratch note, line 33: include the primitive types Odin has, such as quaternions, endian types, complex numbers and floats with endian specialization.

Jet today. Byte order lives in codecs: Bytes has typed writes such as write_u32_le (D-CORE-IO-BUF1), the binary pack contract is checked (D-BINARY-CANONICAL1), and bit patterns read and write fields (D-BITS1). Number sizes come from one family definition each (D-CORE-NUMFAMILY1). Files can be mapped as byte views (D-FOUND-VIEW1). No decision adds a byte-order type.

Option A, technical. A byte-order parameter joins the integer and IEEE families, and the standard names are generated: U16le through U128be, I16le through I128be, F32le, F32be, F64le and F64be. They live in core.encoding.binary. They are storage types: reading converts to the native number, and assigning a native number converts back. They have no arithmetic of their own, so mixed-order sums cannot happen. They work in `#Layout(c)` and packed structs, in fixed arrays, and in mapped views.

Cost. On a chip with the other order a read is one swap instruction; with the same order it is a plain load.

Evidence. Odin ships u16le, u32be, f64be and similar. Rust users reach for crates such as zerocopy and byteorder for the same job. Zig and Go pick the order per read call instead.

Why B loses: one order per record cannot describe mixed-order formats or a typed array of big-endian numbers.

options.name: Byte-order number types
options.detail: Storage types with a fixed byte order, generated from the number families. Reading gives a normal number; writing a normal number converts it.
options.technical: Families gain an order parameter; names U16le…U128be, I16le…I128be, F32le/F32be, F64le/F64be in core.encoding.binary. No arithmetic; implicit read and write conversion; valid in C-layout and packed structs, fixed arrays and mapped views.
options.code:
use core.encoding.binary.[U32be, U32le]
#Layout(c) struct Header {
    magic: U32be
    length: U32le
}
fn body_end(h: Header) -> Int { h.length + 8 }  // a normal number
fn stamp(h: &Header) { h.length = 512 }          // stored little-endian

options.name: One order per record
options.detail: A `#Layout(c, order: .Big)` argument fixes the byte order for every number in a struct. No new types.
options.technical: New layout argument; every numeric field converts on read and write.

comparisons.note: Endian-specific basic types.
Byte-order types come from crates.
Order chosen per read.

recommendation.why: The order belongs to the stored number, not to the code that reads it. A lets any field, array or mapped file say its order once, then reads as ordinary numbers.
gains: File formats and protocols read in place, with no hand conversion.
Matches Odin's types one for one.

losses.loss: Many new type names.
losses.mitigation: They come from one family definition, live in one module, and beginners never import them.

losses.loss: A read costs a byte swap when orders differ.
losses.mitigation: It is one instruction, and no swap happens when the order matches the chip.

whyNot.reason: It cannot describe mixed-order records or a typed array of big-endian numbers, which real formats use.

recommendation.tradeoff: A family of storage types buys in-place reading of any binary format.

decisions.title: How Jet learns a target machine's hardware, and how a program can require it
decisions.situation: The owner wants an extensible way to feed target hardware information to Jet, like NixOS hardware description files, and let experts require a GPU or a memory minimum. Current build facts expose CPU information; the supplied records also describe compute capability checks, but no general target-description or requirement API. This vote recommends typed descriptions on the existing fact plane, extensible by packages rather than compiler releases, with requirements checked before ordinary execution.
decisions.gist: How should Jet learn a target machine's hardware, and how should a program require hardware it needs?
decisions.lesson: A hardware description is a Jet file listing a machine's hardware, such as its GPU and memory. A scan can write it, the way NixOS writes hardware-configuration.nix, or you can write it by hand. A requirement is a line saying a program needs some hardware; a machine without it refuses the program with the missing item named.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: no description or requirement is needed for an ordinary local program. The host supplies scanned facts and optional acceleration keeps a fallback. Mandatory requirements deliberately prevent running everywhere.

CPU is the general processor; GPU is a graphics/parallel processor; NPU is a neural-processing accelerator. Memory means main RAM; GPU.memory means device memory. GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes, not decimal GB. All options need any GPU plus 4GiB main RAM; tensor cores are optional matrix hardware. A 1GiB GPU with 64GiB RAM passes. GPU-memory requirements instead use GPU.memory_at_least(4GiB) under A and .GpuMemory(bytes: 4294967296) under B.

A proposes jet hardware scan --out hardware/workstation.jet, reusing the JetOS scan to write typed source. Import that module in package.jet. Set Target.hardware to workstation.WORKSTATION and SHIP.target to that Target. Cross builds consume the target description, not the build machine. The immutable target view is $build.hardware; $build.cpu is its CPU entry. Code shows this connection.

Requirements are mandatory; uses declares optimization interests, not powers. Shared pure predicates serve $build.hardware.has. Presence is GPU.any(), main-RAM minimum is Memory.at_least, and GPU.feature tests a feature. A conjunction within one GPU requirement must match one device, not combine different GPUs' capabilities.

Core proposes HardwareKind with fn satisfies(self, minimum: Self) -> Bool and fn coarse(self) -> Self. Reflected fields and package-qualified nominal identity supply schema/kind keys. Hardware.require(minimum) returns a HardwareRequirement with that type's checked comparison thunk. Core helpers GPU.any(), GPU.feature(), GPU.memory_at_least() and Memory.at_least() return the same requirement type. The compiler need not know NPU.

Hardware.has accepts that value. Missing kinds return false, not absent-record errors. NPU's example supplies comparison/projection methods and a separately trusted probe.

HardwareProbe carries name and run; run has signature fn(ScanContext) -> [HardwareKind]. The read_int(path) method returns Int? and reads only granted scan inputs. Missing files return None; malformed data is a scan error, never fabricated zero. The example path is an illustrative vendor sysfs contract, not universal NPU hardware.

Packages publish PROBES. The command jet hardware scan --probes vendor_npu names the grant before execution. Copy the full printed identity, review powers, then rescan. The displayed hash is illustrative. Probes never run during compilation or inside apps.

Native builds check the selected description. Startup rechecks actual host requirements before entry. False descriptions cannot authorize unsupported instructions: native CPU dispatch remains mandatory. Hardware-specific binaries refuse hosts incompatible with compiled assumptions; they do not gain portable recompilation.

Portable bundles check granted host facts at install and every launch. Changed code-relevant facts invalidate the copy and recompile before entry. Digests are content identities, not a hardware rescan in one comparison. Acquire a current snapshot first. Cache identity includes kind/probe package identities and privacy grants.

Unknown/withheld required facts refuse, naming the requirement and grant/removal remedy. Unknown optional facts select fallback. Coarse facts are safe lower bounds: memory rounded down to 4/8/16GiB without model/serial identifiers. Exact 6GiB can appear as 4GiB; it cannot satisfy 8GiB.

GPU facts grant no GPU handle. Jobs without that handle are denied by existing compute authority. Free GPU memory is never a build fact; check it before each GPU job, not merely at program launch.
decisions.story: Noor ships a matrix tool. It needs any GPU and at least 4GiB of main RAM. Tensor cores speed it up when present; otherwise its plain GPU path works. A customer adds an NPU unknown to the current compiler, and a package should be enough to describe and use that kind.
decisions.inWild:
# NixOS: generated hardware source feeds system configuration
{ imports = [ ./hardware-configuration.nix ]; }
# Android: required hardware narrows supported machines
<uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.camera" android:required="true" />
decisions.detail:
Owner question q2ufwwsv asks for target-tailored, future-proof hardware inputs and expert requirements. A answers directly: reusable scan, ordinary typed source, Target.hardware selection, extensible Core kinds, shared predicates and pre-entry checks. All newly named API fields, methods and commands below are proposals for this vote, not claims of implementation.

Letters: new A is extensible descriptions; B is the prior fixed-facts option; C is the prior runtime-query option. Their comparison now uses the same GPU-presence plus main-RAM requirement, not different memory resources.

Existing law reused: D-JOS-HARDWARE1 scans to hardware.<host> source and allows shared profiles; D-CONF-PLANE1/READ1/MERGE1/SPLIT1 give typed facts, $build reads, contribution priority and computed contributions in .jet/lock. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1 puts chip knowledge in typed library entries; A generalizes that to kinds. D-CPU-DISPATCH1 and D-CORE-FEATURE-FLOW1 keep CPU dispatch. D-FREESTAND-FACTS1's runtime-service menu stays closed: hardware descriptions do not add allocators, clocks or providers. Facts never grant powers (D-PORTABLE2), and D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1 handles transient resource checks before each GPU job.

Trust and provenance: selected descriptions retain writer/profile/Force provenance under the existing contribution law. Build-time source is an assertion about a target, not launch authority. At launch only host-observed, host-granted facts determine admission and cache validity. Changing a probe package, predicate comparison or privacy projection invalidates the corresponding facts and compiled specialization even if a physical device is unchanged. Denied scans never fall back to running a probe without a grant.

Open-kind transport: generated checked descriptors/thunks retain nominal identity, fields, comparison and projection when kinds are erased into Hardware's device list. A bundle carries the kind package needed for its requirements, while only the trusted host scan can supply observed values. Pure satisfies/coarse methods cannot probe the host. Requirements are evaluated on the actual granted device entries; no package can manufacture its own admission evidence.

B owns a fixed CPU/GPU/main-memory vocabulary and gets the same native and portable checks but requires a compiler release for new kinds. C's runtime record uses that fixed vocabulary too: absent GPU has has(...) == false, and RAM is bytes. It supports an explicit early program guard, not automatic pre-entry refusal; unknown NPU kinds need an API/compiler vocabulary change. All variants ship under C.

A retains more public vocabulary and a scan trust cost. It wins because B lacks package extensibility and C lacks the requested compiler input and declarative admission. No claim that an instruction format inherently cannot access accelerators is needed for this recommendation.

options.name: Extensible hardware descriptions with requirements
options.detail:
A target's hardware is a typed Jet description, written by a scan, by hand, or from a shared profile package, like NixOS's hardware file. It feeds build facts that code reads through $build.hardware. Outputs may list requires: and uses:. Packages can add new hardware kinds without a compiler release.

A native program checks its requirements at build and once at start-up; a portable bundle at install and at each launch, recompiling when hardware changed.
options.technical: Proposes Core Hardware, HardwareKind, HardwareRequirement, HardwareProbe and ScanContext as specified in the explainer. Hardware contains main memory, storage and typed device entries. Target gains hardware; every Output gains target, requires and uses. Package-defined kinds use pure type-owned satisfies/coarse methods; scan probes are separately trust-granted. $build.hardware shares D-CONF's typed fact plane and merge law; $build.cpu remains the CPU entry. Host observations, grants and kind/probe package identities determine launch admission/cache identity, never a producer's asserted facts. Free amounts are checked before each GPU job.

options.name: A fixed set of hardware facts
options.detail: The compiler owns a fixed list of hardware facts: $build.cpu and a new $build.gpu with features and fixed limits. Outputs may list requires: and uses: over that list. Missing requirements are refused before running, and each launch rechecks that the hardware still matches. A new kind of device needs a new Jet release.
options.technical: Fixed $build.cpu, $build.gpu and $build.memory; Output requires/uses over fixed enums. Native build/start-up and portable install/launch checks follow A, as do host-granted facts and privacy. No package-defined kind transport. Free GPU memory is checked before each GPU job.

options.name: Ask at run time
options.detail: A run-time call returns the host's capabilities, and the program branches on them while running. All variants are compiled in, and nothing is refused before the program runs.
options.technical: host.capabilities() returns a fixed CPU/GPU/main-RAM record at runtime. Absent GPU makes gpu.has(...) false; memory is main-RAM bytes. No package kind extension, declarative requirement or automatic pre-entry refusal. The program can guard at its start, then use existing host handles; queries grant no powers.

comparisons.note: A generated hardware file is imported by the system configuration; shared profiles cover known devices.
An app declares hardware it requires or merely uses; stores filter devices by it.

recommendation.why: A gives the compiler hardware knowledge the way NixOS does, from a typed description per target that packages can extend. Experts can require hardware, and it is checked before the program runs.
gains: New hardware kinds arrive as packages, with no compiler release.
One description per target, scanned, written or shared.
Requirements refuse a machine clearly before the program runs.

losses.loss: More to learn: a description type, kinds and requirement forms.
losses.mitigation: Beginners write nothing; the scan writes descriptions, and requires: is optional.

losses.loss: A package-supplied probe runs code on your machine during a scan.
losses.mitigation: Probes run only in the scan, under a jet trust grant, and write plain source you can review.

losses.loss: Hardware facts could help identify a machine.
losses.mitigation: The host grants which facts a bundle sees; by default only coarse classes.

whyNot.reason: B is simpler, but every new kind of device waits for a Jet release.
C ships every variant and checks through program code. An explicit entry guard can fail immediately, but this is not declarative pre-entry admission or compiler target input.

decisions.title: Remove the alias keyword: an alias is written New :: Old
decisions.situation: An alias is a second name for a type, such as Rows for a list of rows of text, and a function asking for Rows accepts the plain list too. Today the word alias works only for generic types, which take another type as input, and a ratified vote moves those to build-time recipes, leaving the word no job. Jet already writes a separate type as Usd :: distinct Decimal and a constant as LIMIT :: 10, so the keyword is the odd one out. This vote decides between Rows :: [[String]] with no keyword and keeping alias for every type; we recommend no keyword, and distinct still marks a type that must not mix.
decisions.gist: Should an alias be written `Rows :: [[String]]`, with the `alias` keyword removed?
decisions.lesson: A type is a kind of value, such as Int or a list of text. An alias is a second name for a type: a function asking for Rows takes a plain [[String]] too, with no warning. A distinct type is separate: a function asking for Usd refuses a plain Decimal. Either way, aliases outside functions become legal for every type, and the spec and errors change.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A type is a kind of value, such as Int, Decimal or [[String]], a list of lists of text. A generic type takes another type as input, as a list takes the type of its items. A build-time recipe is a `prep fn` that returns a type, such as `Parsed(Int)`. A constant is a fixed value outside any function, such as `LIMIT :: 10`. A re-export publishes another module's name from yours.

Beginner path: write `Rows :: [[String]]` outside a function under A, or `alias Rows :: [[String]]` under B. Then use Rows wherever [[String]] fits. Write `Usd :: distinct Decimal` when mixing must be an error.

Expert path: under A, Jet decides the kind from the right side in a fixed order. A bare path to a declaration comes first, then a type, then an unknown name, then a constant. The name's case is checked after the kind is known.

Shared by both options: an alias is the same type. `UserId :: Int` accepts any Int, including another Int alias such as OrderId, with no warning. Use `UserId :: distinct Int` to keep them apart.
decisions.story: Theo writes a CSV tool and wants to say `Rows` instead of `[[String]]` in ten function signatures. Jet refuses `alias Rows :: [[String]]` because aliases are only for generic types, and it reads `Rows :: [[String]]` as a badly named constant.
decisions.detail:
Source of the question: the owner's scratch note at Tools/tower/.tower/scratch/owner-scratch.md:58 asks to remove the alias keyword and alias by a constant-style declaration, myNewType :: myOldType.

Jet today. D-TYPEALIAS1 (ratified 2026-06-28) made `alias` a transparent alias for shortening generic spellings only, steering primitive newtypes to `distinct`. D-ALIAS-OP1=B moved it from `=` to `::`. Both are recorded at crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/core_surface.rs:423-426. `distinct` already uses `Name :: distinct Base` (D-DIST1, D-DIST3).

Why the keyword is now empty. D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A (ratified) makes generic types and aliases `prep fn` recipes called with parentheses and removes `<>`. Its own example is `prep fn Grid(T: Type) -> Type { [[T]] }`. After that cutover, `alias Name<T>` has no valid use, because its only allowed form became a recipe. This ballot decides whether plain aliases exist and how they are spelled.

What D-ALIAS-OP1 rejected, and what changed. Its option C, dropping the keyword, lost for two reasons. First, a reader could not tell an alias from a value binding at a glance. Second, the keyword fenced aliases away from general type programming. The second reason no longer holds, because D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 made type programming ordinary `prep fn` code. The first is A's real cost, reduced by the ordered rule and the case rules in A's technical note.

Probes, shared release jet dev-595e0dca3, 2026-10-07. `alias Rows :: [[String]]` is E0324, "A type alias needs type parameters" (OwnerNotes1/probe/alias.jet). `Grid :: [[Int]]` is E0357, constant must be ALL_CAPS, and E0622, a module binding's value must be a literal. `Grid :: Missing` gives the same two errors instead of an unknown-name error. Inside a function, `Rows :: [[String]]` is E0357, local must be snake_case, plus E0107 (AliasBallot/p).

More probes in $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/AliasBallot/p. `struct LIMIT` and `struct IO` compile, so type names may be all capitals. `N :: prep { 10 }` is a valid constant. `alias P<T> :: Point` cannot build a value: `P<Int>{x: 3}` is E0119, no type called P. Two aliases naming each other crash the compiler with a stack overflow (cycle.jet). That crash is a bug for a card under either option.

Usage. git grep finds seven `alias` declarations. Five are generic and move to `prep fn` recipes in the D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 cutover anyway. They are Examples/features/types/type_alias.jet, tests/ui/type_alias_ok.jet, optional_lift_nested.jet, parallel_function_worker_type.jet and the fuzz valid fixture. Two, tests/ui/type_alias_no_params.jet and its fuzz twin, expect a plain alias to fail, so they change under either option. D-CORE-NUMFAMILY1 plans `alias U8 :: Unsigned<8>`, which becomes `U8 :: Unsigned(8)` under A.

Other languages. Odin declares constants, procedures and types with `::`; `My_Int :: int` is an alias and `My_Int :: distinct int` a new type (odin-lang.org/docs/overview). Zig treats types as compile-time values, so `const Rows = [][]const u8;` names one (ziglang.org/documentation, comptime). Go writes `type A = B` for an alias, the same type, and `type A B` for a new type (go.dev/ref/spec, Type declarations).

Rust's `type Meters = f64;` names the same type. The Rust Reference notes that such an alias cannot name a tuple struct's constructor (doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/type-aliases.html); Jet's A keeps constructors. C11 section 6.7.8 says a typedef is only a synonym, not a new type. None of these sources measures user confusion. That the missing protection surprises people is an inference from the newtype pattern's existence, not a measured finding.

Relation to D-VIS-REEXPORT1. Its option A makes `clamp :: core.math.clamp` publish a declaration under a second name, by a bare path, with no keyword. This ballot's A adds type expressions and type-valued recipe calls to the same `New :: Old` form. If both pick A, every alias is `New :: Old`, decided by the ordered rule in A's technical note. If the re-export ballot picks A and this one picks B, `Path :: files.Path` needs no keyword while `alias Rows :: [[String]]` does.

Shared by both options. An alias is the same type, so values pass without any conversion or warning. Constructors, patterns, methods, trait implementations, `Type{value}` and the home module follow the original, the same law as D-VIS-REEXPORT1. Aliasing a distinct type keeps its protection. Errors and hovers show the name the source wrote, with one line expanding it once. Cycles get the alias-cycle error D-VIS-REEXPORT1 adds, listing the chain.

Shared work for either option. Update the spec's Core grammar, D-TYPEALIAS1's text, E0324's message, the two plain-alias tests and the UI snapshots. Fix the cycle crash and the alias constructor gap.

options.name: No keyword: `New :: Old`
options.detail: Outside a function, `Name :: R` names a type when R is a type, with no keyword. `Name :: distinct T` stays the separate type, and constants keep ALL_CAPS. Jet decides the kind from the right side in a fixed order, then checks the name. The `alias` keyword is removed, and `jet fix` deletes it from old alias lines.
options.technical:
Inside a function, `::` binds a local value as today. A type on the right is an error whose fix moves the line outside the function. At file or module level, Jet decides the kind from the right side first, in the order below, and then checks the name's case. Declaration order does not matter.

First, a bare path, a name or dotted name, that resolves to a declaration is an alias of it under D-VIS-REEXPORT1's law, if that ballot picks A. Otherwise this step applies only to types. The name follows the target's case rule. Examples: `Path :: core.files.Path`, and `Parser :: impl.Parser` for a recipe.

Second, a right side whose value is a type is a transparent type alias. That covers type syntax such as `[T]`, `[K:V]`, `T?`, `T E!`, `A | B`, `[T#N]` and function types. It also covers a recipe call that returns a type, such as `Parsed(String)` or `Unsigned(8)`. This refines D-VIS-REEXPORT1's rule that a call keeps constant rules. The name follows the type-name rule: it starts with a capital, so `U8` and `IO` are fine.

Third, a right side that names nothing gives the ordinary unknown-name error, E0107, alone. Fourth, anything else is a constant, as today: ALL_CAPS (E0357) and a literal or `prep { … }` value (E0622). A lowercase name with a type on the right, such as `rows :: [[String]]`, is E0357 with the fix `Rows`. It never suggests ALL_CAPS.

Identity. An alias is the same type, and no conversion runs. It works as a `Type{…}` head, in patterns and in signatures. Methods and trait implementations stay with the original. Aliasing `Usd`, a distinct type, gives another name for `Usd`, not for `Decimal`. Errors and hovers keep the written name, such as `U8`, and expand it once on a note line.

Cycles. `A :: B` beside `B :: A`, `A :: A` and `A :: [A]` are the alias-cycle error, listing the chain across files. Recursion through a struct, enum or distinct type stays legal.

Retirement. `alias` stops being a keyword, so names such as the field `alias` in Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/ForeignProviders.jet stay legal. Only the item form `alias Name :: R` at file or module level gets an error, whose machine-applicable fix deletes `alias`. Generic `alias Name<T> :: …` lines and their uses become `prep fn` recipes in D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1's cutover, not through this fix. Syntax.rs drops KW_ALIAS and registers the retirement under this decision.

options.name: Keep `alias`, allow every type
options.detail: `alias Name :: T` stays and works for any type, not only generic ones. Without the keyword, `Rows :: [[String]]` stays an error that suggests `alias`. `distinct` and constants are unchanged. Generic aliases still become `prep fn` recipes under D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1, so `alias` is used only for plain aliases and type-valued recipe calls.
options.technical: E0324's generic-only rule is removed. `alias Name :: R` accepts any type expression or type-valued recipe call, with the same identity, display and cycle rules as A. A bare `Name :: R` with a type on the right stays E0357 and E0622, with a new fix that adds `alias`. If D-VIS-REEXPORT1 picks A, a bare path such as `Path :: core.files.Path` is an alias without the keyword. The keyword then marks only type expressions and recipe calls.

comparisons.note: Types are named with `::`; `distinct` makes a separate type. odin-lang.org/docs/overview, Type alias and Distinct types.
Types are compile-time values, so a constant can name one, with no alias keyword. ziglang.org/documentation, comptime.
`=` makes an alias, the same type; no `=` makes a new type. go.dev/ref/spec, Type declarations.
`type` names the same type, and the Reference notes it cannot name a tuple struct's constructor. A newtype struct gives protection.
A typedef is only a synonym, not a new type (C11 section 6.7.8).

recommendation.why: D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 leaves `alias` with no job, and Jet already names constants and separate types with `Name :: …`. A spells an alias the same way, so the right side says what was named.
gains: One pattern for aliases, constants and separate types; the right side says which.
No keyword survives with nothing left to do.
If D-VIS-REEXPORT1 also picks A, re-exports and type aliases share one spelling.

losses.loss: The line no longer says alias, so a reader checks the right side to see that it names a type.
losses.mitigation: The type sits on the same line, and the editor tooltip says 'Rows: another name for [[String]]'.

losses.loss: `Name :: …` outside functions now means alias, constant or separate type.
losses.mitigation: Jet decides from the right side in a fixed order, and a wrong name case gets an error naming the kind.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a visible label, a real benefit. But it revives a word the generics vote emptied, and if the re-export vote picks A, some aliases need the word and others do not.

recommendation.tradeoff: No alias label on the line, for one `Name :: …` pattern beside constants and `distinct`.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: AliasBeginner. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass tested the complete ballot. Explain, predict and modify passed; undefined terms and the unshown old-spelling error failed derive, so the repair defines terms, shows migration errors, states the name rule and drops the re-export gain.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude. Adversarial model family: gpt. Fresh agent: AliasAdversary. The adversarial review attacked the recommendation. It found a rule clash with D-VIS-REEXPORT1, a generic shim and an overstated safety loss; repairs add an ordered rule, cut the shim, state identity, cycles and migration, and cite sources.

decisions.title: Is the wait from `jet run` to its answer part of Jet's speed rule?
decisions.situation: Jet's speed rule says Jet must beat every comparable language on every required benchmark, and no release ships while one loses. It does not say whether a quick run counts, where you type jet run and wait for the answer. People compare that wait with python3 and node, which answer a tiny script in about twenty to fifty milliseconds. The vote decides whether that wait is a required benchmark. We recommend yes, for script-sized programs, timed after an edit and on a repeat run.
decisions.gist: Should the wait from typing `jet run` to seeing the answer be a required speed benchmark?
decisions.lesson: The speed rule gates finished programs and build times against matched languages, and a losing required benchmark holds every release. A quick run includes checking, compiling and running, so its wait is a different number. Whichever option wins, the speed rule still gates release programs, and every measured loss stays on a card.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A benchmark cell is one workload and one measurement, such as run time of a log report, compared with the same program in other languages. Time to answer is the wall time from pressing Enter on `jet run app.jet` to the program finishing.

Two cache states are timed. After an edit: the script changed since its last run, and Jet's own libraries are prebuilt, as they ship. Repeat: nothing changed since the last run. A first run on a freshly installed machine with every cache empty is reported, not gated.

Beginner path: nothing to write. Under A, `jet run` is held to the same beat-the-peer rule as release programs.

Expert path: the cells name the exact commands, inputs and cache states, so an expert can reproduce each number.
decisions.story: Lena writes ten-line scripts to clean CSV files. Python answers before she lifts her finger; `jet run` takes seconds while it builds. Nothing in Jet's speed rule says that wait is a bug to fix.
decisions.inWild:
$ time python3 -c pass   # about 0.02-0.04 s on the reference machine
$ time node -e 0         # about 0.02-0.05 s
$ go run hello.go        # compiles, caches the binary, then runs
decisions.detail:
Source: RESEARCH.md revision 2 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ExecArch1), sections 3.4 and 5.4, and its owner decision 5. The adversarial audit (finding 1) warned the research not to treat quick-run evidence as release evidence. That makes the gate question explicit.

Revision by OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07. The posted A gated a warm and a cold cache without saying what cold meant. If cold meant every cache empty, Jet would also recompile its own libraries, which no peer does on a script run. A now names the two states users meet: after an edit, and a repeat run. The first run after install is reported only. The surface now states plainly that a losing required cell holds every release (AGENTS.md, performance gate).

Jet today. AGENTS.md's speed rule covers foundations including build time and run time, plus one real workload in each critical area, including CLI and scripts. It forbids substituting an easier tier, but it does not name `jet run`. A performance card, milestone or release gate stays open while any required cell fails.

D-EXEC2=A runs `jet run` through the build path until native in-memory O0 lands, with a target of about 1 to 5 seconds for small programs.

The gauntlet measures `runtime_first_stdout_seconds` and `runtime_wall_seconds` per cell (Tools/gauntlet/status.mjs). It has held an interpreter-tier `jet run --interpret` wall-time row (Tools/gauntlet/measurement-manifest.json).

Peer start-up was measured on the reference machine on 2026-10-07, at load 16 to 23, over three runs. `python3 -c pass` took 0.02 to 0.04 s. `node -e 0` took 0.02 to 0.05 s. A historical Jet receipt shows about 1.7 s of fixed start-up work for hello before any code generation (SpeedPlan1/HANDOFF.md).

Right ways elsewhere. Go's `go run` compiles to a cached binary and runs it; since Go 1.24 the linked program is cached too. Python and Node start an interpreter or JIT immediately. Every peer ships its own standard library ready to use, which is why the after-edit cell keeps Jet's prebuilt libraries. The cells under A compare against these exact commands.

options.name: Gate the time to answer
options.detail: Add required cells for `jet run` time to answer on the script and CLI workloads. Time it after an edit and on a repeat run, against `python3`, `node` and `go run` running the same program. Each cell follows the existing rule: Jet must be faster, every loss stays on a card, and releases wait while a cell loses. The first run after install is shown on the dashboard, not gated.
options.technical: Adds `run_time_to_answer_seconds` with `cache: edited|repeat` to the CLI-and-scripts critical area in the canonical manifest. `edited` touches the script before each sample; Jet's shipped libraries and each peer's standard library stay as installed. `repeat` reruns the unchanged script. A reported-only `cache: fresh_install` row empties every cache. Peers: CPython (`python3 main.py`), Node (`node main.js`), Go (`go run .`). Each cell records the same input, output check and process-start method as existing runtime cells. No change to release-program cells.

options.name: Report it, do not gate it
options.detail: Measure and show the time to answer next to each script cell, but do not count it in the speed rule. Only release programs and build times gate.
options.technical: Adds the same metric and cache states as reported-only columns. Gates and cards ignore them.

comparisons.note: Starts the interpreter and runs at once; about 0.02-0.04 s for an empty script on the reference machine.
`go run` compiles to a cached binary, then runs it.

recommendation.why: The quick-run wait is what script users feel first, and the speed rule only drives work it gates. Timing it after an edit and on a repeat run measures what users actually meet.
gains: Slow quick runs become tracked losses with owners.

losses.loss: Releases wait until quick runs beat Python, Node and Go.
losses.mitigation: Native in-memory quick runs are already the planned path (D-EXEC2); each losing cell is a card with its measured gap.

whyNot.reason: A number that never fails a gate does not get fixed.

decisions.title: Whether the portable sandbox's walls depend on the compiler being bug-free
decisions.situation: A Jet app file is one portable program that any machine checks, compiles and runs inside sealed walls, the way WebAssembly runs code. Today the plan trusts the machine's own compiler to build those walls correctly, so a compiler bug could let an app escape. Another engine's compiler had exactly such a bug, rated 9.9 out of 10. The vote decides whether a small checker inspects the final machine code before it runs; we recommend yes, so the walls hold even when the compiler is wrong.
decisions.gist: Should the host check an app's final machine code before running it, so compiler bugs cannot break the walls?
decisions.lesson: The walls, or isolation, keep an app inside its own memory and away from anything the host did not grant. The host already verifies the app file and grants each power. Whichever option wins, safety inside the app and the same answers as a native build still rest on Jet's compiler and its tests.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. An app file (`.jetapp`) holds checked portable Jet code. The host is the machine that runs it. The walls, or isolation, mean the app can touch only its own memory and the handles the host gave it. Machine code is what the host's compiler produces from the app file. A side channel is a way to leak secrets through chip timing, such as Spectre.

Beginner path: nothing changes. `jet run notes.jetapp` asks for powers and runs the app.

Expert path: hosts that run several untrusted apps in one process turn on side-channel hardening with one host setting; one app per process relies on the operating system's process walls.
decisions.story: Omar runs other people's plugins inside his note app. One plugin triggers a rare bug in the host's compiler. Under today's plan that bug can let the plugin read his notes; with a final-code check, the plugin is refused before it runs.
decisions.detail:
Source: RESEARCH.md revision 2 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ExecArch1), section 4.7, and owner decisions 7 to 9. The adversarial audit's blocking finding 10 showed that 'validation removes the optimizer from the trusted base' is true only for the walls. It does not hold for safety inside the app or for keeping the same answers.

Jet today. D-PORTABLE1=A ratified the Jet sandbox. The app file holds a versioned portable encoding of MIR. The host verifies structure, types, memory safety, control flow and host calls, and grants powers through unforgeable handles held in its own trust store.

D-PORTABLE1's trusted base names the verifier, the runtime and its broker, the native compiler and its cache. It explicitly does not promise protection from bugs in them, or from side channels such as Spectre. It starts a first run in an interpreter while native code compiles.

D-EXEC2=A later retired the interpreter once native in-memory O0 lands. So under both options here, the first run uses quick native code compiled on arrival. D-HOST-CAPS1 (open, proposed A) makes hardware such as tensor cores visible as build facts. A hardware fact never grants a power; only host handles do.

Evidence. Crocus (ASPLOS 2024) reproduced a 9.9 of 10 CVE in Cranelift's lowering rules, a real compiler bug that broke WebAssembly isolation. Native Client (2009) validated x86 code before running it, at under 5% (ARM) and 7% (x86-64) run-time cost for its fault-isolation scheme (Sehr et al. 2010).

VeriWasm (NDSS 2021) checks the native code Lucet produced, so the compiler leaves the isolation trusted base. Its disassembler and control-flow builder stay trusted. It does not check indirect-call types and allows some reads Wasm would not.

Swivel (USENIX Security 2021) shows that side-channel hardening costs depend strongly on the threat model. Process isolation is the common alternative.

What A requires. The compiler emits code in a checkable shape: memory accesses within the app's region or through checked handles, jumps only to known targets, and host calls only through the broker. A published checker validates each compiled function and refuses the app on any failure.

Checked code is cached by app hash, host, compiler, checker version and policy, as D-PORTABLE1 already keys its cache. Checker cost is unmeasured for Jet. A gauntlet cell for bundle start-up and steady speed measures it before ratification of the checker design.

Edge cases under both options. Hosts that forbid making code at run time, such as iOS apps, get a native copy built and signed ahead of time by the host's operator. Under A, the checker runs on that copy too. In browsers, apps still export to WebAssembly and WebGPU (D-WASISRV1, D-PORTABLE1) and inherit their limits.

options.name: Check the final machine code
options.detail: Before an app runs, the host checks the compiled machine code against the wall rules. Memory accesses stay in the app's region or go through handles, jumps go only to known places, and host calls go only through the broker. A compiler bug can then make the app wrong, but cannot let it out. Hosts that run several untrusted apps in one process turn on side-channel hardening.
options.technical:
Amends D-PORTABLE1's trusted base. For isolation, the trusted parts become the verifier, the machine-code checker, the runtime and broker, and the loader; the native compiler is untrusted. For memory safety inside the app and for same-answer behaviour, the compiler stays trusted and is covered by D-EXEC3's rule proofs, checkers and example runs.

Adds a host policy for side channels: `isolate: process` (default; one app per process) or `isolate: shared` with side-channel hardening. The checker spec, its admissible machine-code shape and its cost cells land before the checker is built.

decisions.title: How Jet's build levels share speed-ups, check them, and choose which examples rerun
decisions.situation: Jet builds a program at three levels: quick runs while you work, everyday builds, and the fastest release builds. They share one runtime and one checked program, but nothing says which speed-ups each level shares or how a level-only speed-up shows it keeps the meaning. Nothing says which examples a change must rerun either, so some changes merge without running a level at all. The vote sets those rules; we recommend shared speed-ups, proved or checked level-only ones, and rerunning exactly the examples whose build changed.
decisions.gist: How should Jet's build levels share speed-ups, check level-only ones, and choose which examples a change reruns?
decisions.lesson: A level is how hard the compiler works: O0 for quick runs, O1 for everyday builds, O2 for release. A golden example is a saved program with its expected output. Whichever option wins, every example still runs on every level before each milestone, and running out of stack or memory is a separate vote.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A level, or tier, is one way of building. O0 serves `jet run`, `jet dev` and compile-time code, O1 serves `jet build`, and O2 serves `jet build --release`. Compile-time code runs while the program is being built. The web is a level too, where a feature applies.

The runtime is the built-in library every program calls, such as `print` and lists. A speed-up, or optimization, rewrites the checked program so it does less work. A shared speed-up is one piece of compiler code that every level runs; a level-only speed-up runs on some levels.

A rewrite rule replaces one small pattern with an equal one, such as `x * 2` with `x + x`. A proof of a rule is a machine-checked argument that the rule never changes the answer. A checker is a small program that inspects one compiler result and refuses it when it is wrong. A golden example is a saved program with its expected output; passing examples is regression evidence, not proof.

A milestone is the point where finished work joins the released line, after one full test run of everything. In the example, `sum(1..=10)` adds the whole numbers 1 through 10, giving 55. `jet build --release sum.jet` makes a program file and `./sum` runs it.

Beginner path: nothing to write. With enough stack and memory, `jet run`, `jet build` and `jet build --release` print the same output.

Expert path: `-O0`, `-O1` and `-O2` still pick a level. `jet inspect passes` lists every speed-up with its levels and its evidence: proved, checked or tested. It also lists what each proof or checker covers and what it does not.
decisions.story: Priya adds a speed-up that only release builds use. She wants to know before merging whether it can change any program's output. She also wants her change to rerun only the examples it can affect, not every example at every level.
decisions.detail:
Source: the owner's execution requirements (a) to (f), relayed by Main on 2026-10-07. Tiers must not be able to differ, without running every test on every tier. Every tier must be as fast as possible. A hardware-agnostic optimizer is shared by all tiers, and release adds hardware-specific work.

Research: $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ExecArch1/RESEARCH.md revision 2, after two audits (AUDIT-adversary.md, AUDIT-Verifier.md). Fresh reviews of this ballot: review/D-EXEC3-ExecReaderBeginner.md and review/D-EXEC3-ExecReaderAdversary.md, repaired as listed in review/D-EXEC3-repairs.md. Section numbers below refer to RESEARCH.md.

Jet today. D-EXEC1=A ratified one runtime and one Jet code generator with O0, O1 and O2, with LLVM first for O2. D-EXEC2=A retired the Cranelift JIT; until native O0 lands, `jet run` and `jet dev` build and then run. D-TIER-FORM1=A and D-TIER-ONEIR1=A give every back end one checked MIR from one semantic lowering.

I5 requires every feature example to prove the same meaning on every applicable tier. I9 requires one executable meaning, compiled once into one runtime that code generators only call. AGENTS.md runs each card's narrow proof after integration and one composed sweep per milestone. No rule says which examples a change must rerun.

Already settled, so not on this ballot. D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1=B covers run-time re-optimization. D-SIMD3=B, D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A and D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1=D keep floating point bit-identical except under named recorded profiles. D-RTFAIL1=A and D-FAIL-BREACH1=A fix one report text and trace shape per failure on every tier. D-PORTABLE1=A fixes the portable form as MIR. D-BACKEND-OWN1 (open) decides whether Jet O2 replaces LLVM.

Not voted here. Which technology builds O0 (the Jet selector, a template baseline or copy-and-patch) is an implementation choice under D-EXEC1, measured on a real corpus. Copy-and-patch would need build-time clang or LLVM, which then needs its own ballot under the no-Rust directive. Running out of stack or memory is D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1; its I9 text starts with the same parity sentence as this one.

Finding 1, sharing (3.1). Sharing removes the duplication class of tier bugs: copied runtimes and per-engine lowering. CPython reports its JIT-only bugs were in the shared micro-op optimizer, not the copy-and-patch step (PEP 744). A shared bug agrees on every level, so differential runs cannot see it; golden outputs, as an independent oracle, can.

Finding 2, proof tools are bounded (3.1, 4.4). Alive2 (PLDI 2021) caught 29 of 36 known LLVM miscompilations. It checks one function at a time, had no function pointers and supported 21% of intrinsics. Crocus verified Cranelift AArch64 integer lowering rules and reproduced a 9.9 of 10 CVE, but trusts other passes and the runtime. regalloc2's checker validates register moves, not scheduling or calling conventions.

So proofs and checkers reduce risk without replacing whole-program runs. Every stage is therefore labelled proved, checked or tested, with its covered properties.

Finding 3, rerunning exactly what changed. A level's output for an example depends only on the example's checked program after shared speed-ups, that level's compiler, the runtime, the target and the build settings. If none of these changed and the build is reproducible, the result is the same program, so its earlier pass still stands. Reproducibility is already required for trusted cache outputs (D-JPK-REPROCACHE1=D); a rerun skip uses only such outputs.

A shared change that alters an example's checked program reruns that example on every level, which closes the gap a touched-files rule would leave (adversary 2). Milestone sweeps rebuild and rerun everything from scratch, which catches cache or reproducibility defects.

Finding 4, budgets (5.1). One optimizer output at every level would make the first quick run pay release cost, or cap release at quick-run cost. So levels share pass code and differ in budget. Running a shared pass longer at O2 is not a level-only speed-up.

Finding 5, the runtime boundary (4.1). Opaque runtime calls hide work from the optimizer. A adds an I9 clause letting levels inline runtime functions, but only from the runtime's own source and version. They must keep its allocation, traps, cleanup, captures and termination, and never rewrite its policy.

Finding 6, heavy search (4.5). Cranelift's e-graph pipeline gained about 2% run time for 7 to 8% more compile time, and keeping alternative forms gained about 0.1%. Superoptimizers search for seconds to hours per fragment. Under A they run offline to find rules, or at release within budgets counted in deterministic fuel, after a paired measurement shows a win.

Finding 7, optimality (3.2, 3.3). The claim that no faster organization exists cannot be computed (Rice) and is undefined without a hardware cost model. A promises a monotone reduction in named work counters. Each result is labelled completed or stopped by fuel. Removed drops are dead or redundant only; observable cleanup is preserved. Each gauntlet cell reports its measured fraction of a stated hardware bound, and matched peer cells stay the gate.

Scope of parity. It covers every applicable tier: O0, O1 and O2, and compile-time code, which uses the target's layout, not the host's. It also covers the web adapter where a feature applies, and portable apps compiled on arrival. Programs whose `#Unsafe` blocks break their stated obligations are not compared; sentries and hardened profiles report them under their own law.

Concurrent examples compare the output their contract fixes, not one interleaving. Foreign callbacks, task ordering, ownership and drop paths, and failures during cleanup each get named example families.

Costs of A. A level-only speed-up waits until its proof or checker exists. Proofs, models and checkers need upkeep when rules or targets change. The runtime keeps an inlining interface. The pass registry and the input-hash record must be maintained. Optimizing O0 can hide variables in the debugger, so O0 shared speed-ups must keep source stepping and variable visibility.

Right ways elsewhere. One instruction definition generates both interpreter and JIT (CPython, Deegen). Lowering rules are checked (ISLE with Crocus), and a checker runs after register allocation (regalloc2; CompCert validates allocation). Bazel reruns only actions whose inputs changed. Wrong ways: per-engine runtimes (Jet's old Cranelift engine, about 130,000 duplicated lines per D-EXEC1's text). Unchecked compiler facts: Rust disabled mutable-reference noalias from 2018 to 2021 after LLVM miscompilations.

options.name: Shared speed-ups, checked extras, rerun what changed
options.detail: Every level runs the same shared speed-ups, written once. A speed-up that only some levels run needs a proved rule or a checker on each result; an unproved rule never ships. A change reruns an example on a level exactly when that level's build of it changed, and keeps the earlier pass otherwise. Every milestone rebuilds and reruns every example on every level. Release picks hardware-specific code only among choices proved equal.
options.technical:
Amends I5: "Every feature has an example with golden-tested output. Each change reruns an example on each applicable tier whose build inputs for it changed. Those inputs are the checked program after shared passes, the tier's compiler, the runtime, the target and the settings. Every milestone and cutover rebuilds and reruns every example on every applicable tier."

Amends I9 by adding: "Programs run with enough stack and memory print identical output, exit status and reports on every applicable tier. Tiers share one checked MIR, one runtime and one implementation of each shared pass. A transform only some tiers run is a proved rule or passes a recorded checker. Any other stage is tested and labelled so."

"An unknown or timed-out proof keeps a rule out. A checker that cannot handle its input is a Jet defect, never a pass. Tiers may inline runtime functions only from the runtime's source and version, keeping its allocation, traps, cleanup, captures and termination." This replaces I9's call-only wording.

Jet-generated selectors (O0, O1 and any future Jet O2) come from shared lowering rules. Today's O2 emits LLVM IR from Jet rules; LLVM's own passes stay an external stage, tested by examples and by Alive2 runs in CI that are known to be bounded.

Adds one inspect view, `jet inspect passes`, beside the existing `jet inspect` views. Performance claims follow detail finding 7. Unchanged: D-EXEC2, D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1, D-SIMD3, D-RTFAIL1, D-PORTABLE1, D-BACKEND-OWN1, and the O0 technology choice.

$ jet run sum.jet                       # O0: shared speed-ups

$ jet build --release sum.jet && ./sum  # O2: shared + proved extras
55
// a change reruns this example only where its build changed

options.name: Keep the current plan
options.detail: Add no rule. I5 and I9 stay as written. Each card's proof picks its own examples, and the milestone sweep runs every example on every level. A level may add a speed-up that only examples check.
options.technical: No amendment to I5, I9 or D-EXEC1. Current cadence per AGENTS.md: a narrow proof per card after integration and one composed sweep per milestone. The O0 technology choice stays an implementation choice, as under A.

options.name: Check every compile instead of rerunning examples
options.detail: Every build checks each compiled function against its checked program with a sound checker. Anything the checker cannot handle fails the build. Examples run on every level only at milestones. How hard each level searches for speed-ups is a separate question, left as under A.
options.technical: Amends I5 to replace per-change example runs with per-build translation validation of every function, failing closed. Examples run on every applicable tier at milestones. Needs validators covering all of Jet's MIR, the runtime boundary, ABI, concurrency and the LLVM path before it can be switched on; until then builds of unsupported programs fail.
options.code:
fn run() { print(sum(1..=10)) }   // adds 1 through 10
$ jet build --release sum.jet
  check   every function shown equal to its checked program
$ ./sum
55
// a function the checker cannot handle: the build fails

comparisons.note: One instruction file generates the interpreter and the copy-and-patch JIT templates; PEP 744 reports JIT-only bugs were in the shared optimizer stages. Source: peps.python.org/pep-0744.

Lowering rules live in a rule language; Crocus proved a subset and found real bugs. Its e-graph optimizer avoids full saturation for compile time. Sources: cfallin.org/blog/2026/04/09/aegraph, doi:10.1145/3617232.3624862.
comparisons.code: (rule (lower (iadd x y)) (add x y))   ; simplified ISLE rule

comparisons.note: Bazel reruns a test only when an input it depends on changed, and otherwise reuses the recorded result. Source: bazel.build/docs/caching.

recommendation.why: Shared speed-ups remove the main cause of level mismatches. Level-only speed-ups are proved or checked before they ship, and each change reruns exactly the examples whose build changed.
gains: A level-only speed-up cannot ship unproved.
No change merges with an affected level left unrun.

losses.loss: A level-only speed-up waits until its proof or checker exists.
losses.mitigation: Shared speed-ups need no proof, and `jet inspect passes` shows which extras are waiting.

losses.loss: A change to shared code reruns examples on every level.
losses.mitigation: Only examples whose checked program actually changed rerun; the rest keep their recorded pass.

whyNot.reason: B lets a change merge without running an affected level, and lets level-only speed-ups ship unproved.
Today's checkers cover only parts of Jet, so C would fail many builds or need years first.

recommendation.tradeoff: Level-only speed-ups need proofs or checkers; changes rerun exactly what they affect.
