decisions.title: How deep recursion and running out of memory behave on each build level
decisions.situation: When a function calls itself, each waiting call holds a little memory called stack, and too many at once runs it out. Quick runs keep more in each call than release builds, which can even turn the calls into a loop. So one program can stop with a stack-overflow report in a quick run yet finish in a release build. Jet's rule that every level means the same thing says nothing about this. The vote decides how deep recursion behaves on each level; we recommend that a declared depth is exact everywhere and an undeclared one depends on the machine.
decisions.gist: How should deep recursion and running out of memory behave across quick runs and release builds?
decisions.lesson: The stack is the memory running function calls use; deep recursion fills it. Jet stops an overflow with a registered report. A ratified mark, `#MaxDepth(n)`, states how deep a function may recurse, but nothing yet says whether that limit is enforced. Whichever option wins, programs with enough memory give the same output on every level.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A call frame is the slice of stack one waiting call needs. Recursion means a function calls itself. In the example, `depth(n)` calls `depth(n - 1)` until n reaches 0, so `depth(2)` has three calls waiting at its deepest point: for 2, 1 and 0. A quick run (O0, used by `jet run`) keeps every value in its frame. A release build (O2, `jet build --release`) keeps values in registers, which are the processor's own small storage, and can turn recursion into a loop.

The heap is where lists and text live. Ambient memory is whatever the machine gives the program; a budget is a fixed amount the program sets itself, such as a fixed-size arena. A plain allocation that fails stops the program, as today. A `try_` allocation, such as `list.try_push(x)`, returns an error value the program can handle.

Beginner path: nothing to write. A program with enough stack and memory prints the same output on every level. When a quick run or everyday build runs out of stack, it stops with the stack-overflow report.

Expert path: write `#MaxDepth(n)` on a deep recursive function. It means at most n calls of that function wait at once, counting the first call. Under A, every level then reserves room for n calls and stops the call after n with the same report. `jet inspect memory app.jet` shows, per entry point and level, the stack needed, the stack requested and the stack actually granted.
decisions.story: Sam writes a recursive JSON walker. His tests pass in a release build, but `jet run` on a deeply nested file stops with a stack overflow. He cannot tell whether his program is wrong, or how deep it may safely go on every level.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: a configured recursion limit
import sys
sys.getrecursionlimit()   # 1000 by default
# deeper calls raise RecursionError
# docs: the safe maximum is platform-dependent
decisions.detail:
Source: RESEARCH.md revision 2 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ExecArch1), sections 3.1 and 6.3, and its owner decision 2. Fresh reviews: review/D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1-ExecReaderBeginner.md and review/D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1-ExecReaderAdversary.md, with repairs listed in review/D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1-repairs.md. This ballot and D-EXEC3 share one parity rule, quoted in both.

Probe. A C program with fully defined behavior was built with clang 21.1.8 and an 8 MiB stack. It overflowed at depth 74,446 at -O0. At -O2 it finished 50,000,000 levels with the correct value, because the compiler turned the recursion into a loop. A sanitizer build overflowed at 130,283. This shows that levels can differ; it is not a Jet limit or ratio. Receipts: ExecArch1/tierdiff.log.

Jet today, as implemented. E3012 is the registered runtime report `Stack overflow in {fn}` (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/DiagnosticRows.jet). `jet run` builds and then runs the program, until native in-memory O0 lands (D-EXEC2=A).

Jet today, ratified but not yet built. D-STACKBOUND1=A computes worst-case stack per entry point from each target's frame sizes and the sealed call graph. It enforces `!Mem.Stack(above: N)` and needs `#MaxDepth(n)` on recursion to compute that bound. It does not say how depth is counted or what happens past n; this ballot settles that. `#MaxDepth` is not yet registered in Syntax.rs, and this ballot adds no new spelling.

Other law this ballot keeps. D-RTFAIL1=A and D-REPORT-LAW1=A require one registered report with the same text and trace shape on every tier. S36 sends program stops through one report and cleanup boundary. D-ALLOCFAIL1=A keeps the hosted abort for plain allocation and makes `try_` allocation return an ordinary AllocError. D-FIXED-BACKING1 makes fixed-backing allocation fail atomically at its capacity, with no heap fallback.

The shared parity rule, quoted in D-EXEC3 and in A here. Programs run with enough stack and memory must print identical output, exit status and reports on every applicable level. A run that exhausts ambient stack or memory may stop at a different point on different levels. Its report code is the same, and everything it printed before stopping is a prefix of what the complete run prints.

The rule never excuses a wrong value, a different non-resource error, different output before the stop, or a changed budget failure. Goldens run with granted resources; exhaustion has its own fixtures, compared by report code and the prefix rule.

Runaway recursion. A release build may turn recursion into a loop, as clang did in the probe. Then a recursion that never ends does not overflow; it runs like an endless loop. Under A, only O2 may remove recursive calls, so `jet run`, `jet dev` and `jet build` always stop it with E3012. A marked function stops at n+1 on every level. Under B, the counter stops it at the limit on every level.

Stack sizing under A. Each level sizes stacks from its own frames, as it compiles, so a quick run never waits for a release build. A marked function's need is D-STACKBOUND1's worst case on that level's actual call graph, plus call, runtime and cleanup overhead. An unmarked program's quick run gets a larger default stack. That is a risk reduction, not a guarantee.

Where the room comes from. On hosted Linux, macOS and Windows, the runtime switches the entry point onto a larger stack on the same operating-system thread. Thread identity, thread-local data and main-thread-only APIs are unaffected; Windows also updates the thread's recorded stack bounds. Signals use their own alternate stack. Embedded and interrupt entries keep D-STACKBOUND1's static `!Mem.Stack` check and never grow.

Browsers and wasm engines own the stack: a marked depth beyond the engine's published minimum is refused at build time. Tasks get a stack sized from their own entry point. Room is reserved address space committed on use, so many tasks cost address space before memory.

Outcomes when room is short. If the platform cannot ever give the declared room, the build fails with a registered error naming the depth, the need and the limit. If the room cannot be reserved when the entry or task starts, a registered start-up stop fires before any of its code runs. If an admitted guarantee is still broken, that is a Jet defect, exit 101.

Foreign code. A marked recursion whose cycle passes through foreign code is refused at build time, because foreign frames are outside the sealed call graph. A marked function called from a foreign thread's callback keeps its limit check but has no room guarantee, and a lint says so. Raw C callback restrictions are unchanged. `#Unsafe` sentries and hardened profiles add their own frame needs, which are included when that profile is built. A memory-safety fault is never treated as exhaustion.

Heap under A. Ambient memory is the machine's. A plain allocation that fails keeps today's hosted abort. A `try_` allocation against ambient memory may fail on one level and not another, but only under real memory pressure; goldens never run under pressure. A level may remove an ambient allocation it proves unused, which removes its chance to fail.

Budgets are part of meaning on every level: arenas, `mem.Fixed` backings and allocator limits. Allocations against a budget are never removed or merged in a way that changes what the budget counts, so a budget failure happens at the same call everywhere.

Reports and cleanup. The overflow report renders from reserved emergency room without allocating. Its trace collapses repeated recursive frames into one line without a count, so the trace shape matches across levels. It never prints a reached depth, because optimized levels cannot know it.

S36's cleanup boundary then runs on that reserved room. If cleanup itself runs out of room or memory, the program ends with the first report; the first fault wins. Under A, the marked-depth stop is identical on every level, including function name and source location.

Right ways elsewhere. Python fixes a configured recursion limit, raising RecursionError when it is reached. Its docs warn that the safe maximum is platform-dependent and too high a limit can crash (docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html). Java and Go never turn recursion into loops, so runaway recursion always overflows. Rust and C release builds may turn it into a loop.

Costs, unmeasured. A adds a counter only inside marked functions, and per-level frame sizing during compiles. B adds an increment, check and decrement on every call inside a recursive cycle, and reserves room for the default depth in every program. Neither cost is measured; a gauntlet pair cell measures B's counter before ratification of an implementation.

options.name: Declared depth exact, undeclared depth depends on the machine
options.detail: A program with enough room prints the same output on every level. Without a mark, the point where it runs out of stack may differ, and only release builds may turn recursion into a loop. So quick runs and everyday builds always stop runaway recursion with the report. With `#MaxDepth(n)`, every level reserves room for n waiting calls and stops the call after n with the same report, or refuses the build and says why. Budgets fail at the same call everywhere.
options.technical:
Adds to I9: "Programs run with enough stack and memory print identical output, exit status and reports on every applicable tier. A run that exhausts ambient stack or memory may stop at a different point on different tiers. Its report code is the same, and everything it printed before the stop is a prefix of the complete run's output. Allocator budgets are part of meaning. Only O2 may remove recursive calls."

Defines D-STACKBOUND1's `#MaxDepth(n)`. At most n activations of the marked function are live at once on one thread, counting the outermost. Depth 0 is invalid. Mutual recursion counts activations of the marked function only. The (n+1)th activation stops with a new registered depth-limit report, identical on every tier. Room for n activations is computed per tier from that tier's frames and reserved at entry or task start.

Refusals: a build error when the platform can never supply the room; a registered start-up stop when reservation fails at launch. A marked cycle through foreign code is a build error. Stacks grow by switching stacks on the same OS thread; embedded and web entries do not grow. The details are in the long-form detail.
options.code:
#MaxDepth(1000001)
fn depth(n: Int) -> Int { if n == 0 -> 0 else -> 1 + depth(n - 1) }
fn run() { print(depth(1000000)) }
$ jet run deep.jet
1000000
$ jet build --release deep.jet && ./deep
1000000

options.name: One depth limit for every recursive call
options.detail: Every call inside a recursive cycle counts against one limit of 100,000 waiting calls per thread, on every level, even where a release build turns the calls into a loop. A runaway recursion stops at exactly the same call everywhere. `#MaxDepth(n)` raises or lowers the limit for one function. Every program reserves room for its limit. Heap behaves as in A.
options.technical:
Adds the same I9 text as A, except that the depth stop is part of meaning: "every tier stops at the same activation".

A per-thread logical counter is incremented on entry to, and decremented on return from, functions in recursive cycles and dynamic calls that may recurse. Non-recursive calls are not counted, and removed recursion keeps the counter in a register. Default limit 100,000; `#MaxDepth(n)` overrides it per function.

Each tier reserves physical room for the limit from its own frames at entry or task start, with the same refusals as A. A program whose room cannot be reserved is refused before running, so the logical stop is never pre-empted by a physical one. Raw C callbacks on foreign threads cannot update the counter; Jet code reached from them is refused unless it is non-recursive.

options.name: Keep the current plan
options.detail: No rule is added. `#MaxDepth(n)` stays an input to stack reports only. Where a program runs out of stack or memory, and whether that breaks the one-meaning rule, stays unstated. Golden examples must avoid running out.
options.technical: No amendment to I9, D-STACKBOUND1 or D-ALLOCFAIL1. D-EXEC3's parity rule still says resource-adequate runs must match; exhaustion has no comparison rule.

comparisons.note: A configured recursion limit; docs warn the safe maximum is platform-dependent and too high a limit can crash. Source: docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html.
One defined program overflowed at depth 74,446 unoptimized and finished 50,000,000 levels optimized, because the optimizer made it a loop (RESEARCH.md 6.3).
comparisons.code:
$ clang -O0 t.c && ./a.out   # stack overflow at depth 74446
$ clang -O2 t.c && ./a.out   # finishes

recommendation.why: Ordinary calls stay free and quick runs still catch runaway recursion. A program that needs depth declares it once and gets the same result on every level.
gains: A declared depth is exact on every level, or refused before running.

losses.loss: Undeclared deep recursion can stop earlier in a quick run than in a release build.
losses.mitigation: Quick runs get a larger stack, and the overflow report explains `#MaxDepth(n)` for code that needs depth.

losses.loss: In a release build, runaway recursion may run forever instead of stopping.
losses.mitigation: `jet run`, `jet dev` and `jet build` always stop it, and a marked function stops on every level.

whyNot.reason: B counts recursive calls in every program and reserves room for a depth most programs never use.
C leaves the one-meaning rule silent exactly where levels differ.

recommendation.tradeoff: Undeclared depth depends on the machine; declared depth is exact everywhere.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: ExecReaderBeginner. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass tested the complete ballot. Its runaway-recursion, #MaxDepth counting, B-limit, report-identity and cut-down-example failures are repaired with exact counting, a depth-3 example, complete snippets and a named B default.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude-opus. Adversarial model family: openai-gpt. Fresh agent: ExecReaderAdversary. The adversarial review attacked the recommendation. Repairs: one parity rule shared with D-EXEC3, O2-only recursion removal, exact #MaxDepth counting, same-thread per-level stack sizing, refusals, budget and first-fault rules, and option C.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Drafted by ExecArch1; revision 2 after the fresh reader passes. Validated offline with OwnerNotes1/validate.mjs only; no Tower write. It amends I9, so it uses the full two-reader profile.

Owner acceptance for A, once built. `#MaxDepth(3)` with `depth(2)` prints 2 on O0, O1 and O2. `depth(3)` gives the same depth-limit report, function and location on all three. A depth the platform can never supply gives a registered build error naming the need and the limit.

An unmarked runaway recursion stops with E3012 under `jet run` and `jet build`. A program printing three lines then overflowing shows those three lines first on every level, with the same report code. A `mem.Fixed` budget fails at the same `try_alloc` call on every level.

A marked recursion through a foreign call is refused at build time. A main-thread-only API still works after the quick-run stack switch. `jet inspect memory` shows needed, requested and granted stack per entry point and level.

decisions.title: Declaration form: keep struct Point, or name types first
decisions.situation: A declaration gives something a name, such as a type called Point or a function called double. Today a named struct, enum, trait or function starts with a word, as in struct Point { … } and fn double. A value or type written on the right is named first, as in LIMIT :: 10. You asked whether Jet should put the name first everywhere, as Odin and Jai do. Searching works about equally well either way, so we recommend, as a reading judgment, keeping the leading word that nearly every popular language uses.
decisions.gist: Should named types keep their leading word, struct Point, or be written name-first, Point :: struct, maybe functions too?
decisions.lesson: A struct is a type with named fields. Today named structs and functions start with their word: struct Point { … }, fn double(…). A value or type written on the right is named first with ::, as in LIMIT :: 10. B and C would also write every alias Rows :: [[String]].
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A type describes a kind of value. A struct is a type with named fields, such as Point with a field x. An enum is a type whose value is one of several named cases, such as Circle or Square. A trait lists methods that several types promise to provide. A function is named code, such as double; a method is a function inside a type, called with a dot. A constant is a name for one fixed value.

Name order. Name-first means the name comes before the kind word, as in Point :: struct { … }. Keyword-first means the kind word comes first, as in struct Point { … }. The two colons :: read as 'is'. Only the declaration line changes; what a struct, enum or function does stays the same under every option.

Three kinds of type name. Point :: struct { x: Int } makes a brand-new type; no other type is a Point. Rows :: [[String]] makes Rows another name for a list of lists of strings, so a plain [["a"]] is accepted where Rows is expected. UserID :: distinct Int makes a separate type, so a plain Int is refused where a UserID is expected.

How the example prints 42. Running a file calls its run function. Point{x: 21} builds a Point whose x is 21. Then .double() calls the method double, where self is that Point. The body self.x * 2 gives 42, because a body's last expression is its result. print shows 42. This trace is the same under A, B and C.

How it prints 16.0 and 2. area(.Square(4.0)) passes a Shape whose case is Square, with side 4.0. The table if s == { … } runs the arm whose case matches s, here .Square(side), which names that 4.0 side. side * side is 16.0, and return hands it back. [["a"], ["b"]] is a list holding two inner lists, and .len() counts the outer list's items: 2.

A type recipe is a prep fn that builds a type before the program runs. prep fn Pair(T: Type) -> Type { struct { first: T, second: T } } takes a type T and returns a struct whose two fields have that type. Pair(Int) is a pair of Ints, and IntPair :: Pair(Int) gives it a short name. The recipe itself is code, so it keeps prep fn under A and B.

How the search numbers read. Precision is the share of search hits that are real definitions. Recall is the share of definitions the search finds. Both come from rewriting Jet's own 7,468 files into each option's form with a text scanner, not the compiler, so read them to two digits. No study of people was run.

Reading a search pattern. In (struct|enum|trait) NAME, the bar | means 'or', the parentheses group the choices, and NAME stands for the name you look for. A ^ at the start of a pattern means 'at the start of a line'. Go-to-definition is an editor command: put the cursor on a name and jump to where it is defined. It ignores spelling style.

Beginner path under A. Every named struct, enum, trait and function starts with a word saying what it makes: struct Point { x: Int }, enum Shape { … }, fn double(…). A value or type written on the right is named first with ::: LIMIT :: 10, Usd :: distinct Decimal, IntPair :: Pair(Int), ROW :: prep { … }. Writing Point :: struct { … } gives an error showing struct Point { … }.

The rule is about named definitions. A recipe's result, struct { … } with no name, and a prep { … } block are bodies written on the right, so they never start a line with a kind word.

Expert path under A. Named items keep their kind word, and the same struct body appears unnamed only as a recipe result. Making Point generic moves the body into prep fn Point(T: Type) and drops the struct Point header. A plain-text search for a type of unknown kind lists the kind words: (struct|enum|trait|alias) NAME, or NAME ::, or prep fn NAME for recipes. The alias arm drops out if the alias vote drops the keyword.

Beginner path under B. You write LIMIT :: 10 for a constant, and a struct uses the same move: Point :: struct { x: Int }. A function still starts with fn, and a recipe with prep fn. If you write struct Point { … } out of habit, the error shows the new line and jet fix rewrites it.

Expert path under B. At file or module level, a struct, enum or trait on the right of :: makes a new type named by the binding. Any other type there is an alias, and distinct makes a separate type. Making a type generic moves its struct { … } body into a recipe, where only the fields that become generic change. Self-references and impl heads still change to Pair(T).

Beginner path under C. Nearly every named thing reads name :: kind, as in Point :: struct { … }, double :: fn(p: Point) -> Int { … } and arith :: module { … }. A field uses one colon, scale: fn(Int) -> Int, and a method uses two, double :: fn(self) -> Int { … }. Lowercase names are code; capitalized names are types.

C's exceptions. impl, use, #Test, derive, extern block headers, #UnitFamily and migration keep their word, and a trait's associated-type slot stays type Elem. Local helpers stay lambdas, so a helper moved from inside a function to module level changes spelling.

Expert path under C. A signature without a body is a trait slot when lowercase inside a trait, and a function type when capitalized. Inside a binding module it is a foreign function ending with its link string. Module instances resolve like aliases. Search by name works best as name :: fn, because locals also use ::.

Expert kinds. Markers, facts, effects, protocols, typestates and migrations are advanced declaration kinds. This ballot changes only where their name sits under C, never what they do; a beginner can skip them.
decisions.story: Maya joins a team whose Jet service has forty files. She reads each file top to bottom and wants every line to say what it makes. Later she must find where Order is defined without knowing whether it is a struct, an enum or an alias.
decisions.detail:
Suite revision by BallotSuite1, 2026-10-07, repaired by SuiteRepair1 after the suite reader passes. This ballot replaces D-DECL-FORM1 on the same card. Every letter in this ballot, including the research record below, is a current letter: A keeps the leading word, B names types first, C names everything first. D-DECL-FORM1 used the opposite letters for A and B; its numbers are restated here under current letters.

Why the recommendation changed. D-DECL-FORM1 recommended name-first types, now B, for consistency with recipes. Its own re-measurement found both type searches about 99% precise: 0.995 for B's NAME :: and 0.987 for today's alternation, with recall about 1.0 for both. These are scanner estimates, so they show a near tie, not that B gains nothing. No study measures learnability either way, and migration size does not rank options.

The judgment that decides. With search a near tie, the choice rests on reading. A keeps the kind word at the start of each named definition, where a reader scanning a file looks first. TypeScript and JavaScript, Python, Java, C#, Go, Rust, Swift and Kotlin share that shape; this is transfer from other languages, not evidence about beginners.

B's gains are real and are not answered by familiarity. Structs, enums, aliases and separate types share one naming shape, the one LIMIT :: 10 already has. One short query, NAME ::, finds a non-recipe type of any kind. The same struct { … } body serves a named type and a recipe result, and fn stays. Zig, Odin and Jai are the name-first family.

The owner's first reaction leaned against name-first types. The author's judgment agrees that a line starting with its kind word is worth more than one naming shape, and states that as a judgment, not a measurement. JavaScript already pairs class Point { } with class { } as a value, the same split option A uses for recipe results.

Order and interplay with the other declaration votes. Vote D-VIS-REEXPORT1 first, D-ALIAS-BIND2 second and this ballot third. D-VIS-REEXPORT1=A makes clamp :: core.math.clamp a re-export under A, B and C alike. D-ALIAS-BIND2=A, with no alias keyword, fits all three options here. D-ALIAS-BIND2=B, keeping alias, fits only A here. B and C would reverse it, because they name every type with ::.

So under A the alias vote alone decides alias spelling, and under B or C every alias is Name :: R. The visibility cutover on card #4723 is independent under A and B: priv sits on modules and fields only. C moves it to priv helpers :: module, an explicit spelling amendment with the same reach.

Placement of unnamed bodies, shared by every option. Jet has no unnamed struct, enum or trait types today; D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 lets a recipe return one and keeps types from reaching run time. All three options keep that. An unnamed body is an error as a field or parameter type, an argument, inside a prep { } block, or in a runtime function body, because none of those exist today.

B and C add one place, the whole right side of a module-level binding. This rule is written into this ballot, not inherited from a ratified text, so ratifying any option adopts it. Whether a recipe body may bind a helper aggregate before returning it is not decided here. It stays D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1's cutover question and reads the same under A, B and C.

Foreign bindings. #Bindgen and #Extern binding modules keep their casing exemption under every option. extern rust blocks appear in today's corpus, but directive 19 removes Rust, so no option converts them and no acceptance check depends on them.

The research record from D-DECL-FORM1 follows, restated in current letters.

Source. The owner asked whether Jet should adopt the Jai and Odin declaration style everywhere, with trade-offs measured rather than argued from elegance. The research report is $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/DeclStyle1/REPORT.md (agent DeclStyle1, 2026-10-07, Jet 277033b7c), with measure.mjs beside it. After the two reader reviews, DeclBallotRepair re-ran the Jet measurements with $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/DeclBallotRepair/measure2.mjs; results are in metrics2.json beside it.

Re-measurement. The corpus is pinned: the 7,468 tracked .jet files of 277033b7c, extracted with git archive. On it, the original method reproduces its inventory and its count-based 0.986 and 0.561 exactly. The new run scores a hit only when it lands on a definition line of the searched name. It rewrites only each option's own forms, and it rewrites commented-out headers too.

Jet today, name-first. Constants LIMIT :: 10 and NAME :: prep { … } (S2, D-PREP-SURFACE2=A). Distinct types Usd :: distinct Decimal (D-DIST1). Module instances module cache64 :: cache(String, 64) (D-GENMOD1/2). Locals and local lambdas.

Jet today, keyword-first. fn (S1, D-SIG-AFTER1=A), struct (S29), enum (S30), trait (S28), alias (D-TYPEALIAS1, D-ALIAS-OP1=B; generic-only, E0324) and module (U3). Also marker (D-MARKER-DECL1=A), fact (D-FACTDECL1=A), effect (D-EFFECT-DECL1=A), protocol, migration, derive, state, extern, #Test, impl and use. Associated types read type Elem in a trait and type Elem = Int in an impl (D-LIB2).

Parser homes. Item dispatch is crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Modules.rs:1086-1228 and Parser/Items/visibility_items.rs:3-90. The AST is crates/jet-foundation/src/AST/items.rs:9-85. Recovery syncs on a handful of reserved tokens at crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/mod.rs:909-925.

Ratified law, read precisely. D-SIG-AFTER1=A (2026-09-18) kept fn name(…) -> T { } and rejected named functions as const binds. It excluded fn(…) { … } expressions and kept local helpers as lambda binds. D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A (2026-10-02) made types build-time values that prep fn recipes return. It amended D-META-GATE1's refusal of type factories and kept recipe identity, bound checks and source-file recipes.

What each option amends. Generic functions can still be passed as values with an expected function type, and prep fn still runs build-time code. What stays refused is treating named functions as compile-time meta-objects. A amends no ratified header law. B keeps D-SIG-AFTER1, D-LIB2 and D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 and amends only the S28, S29 and S30 header spellings, plus the alias keyword through D-ALIAS-BIND2=A. C reverses D-SIG-AFTER1's named-function order and amends about a dozen more spellings, listed in its technical notes.

Corpus counts. The scanner found 29,522 functions, 3,249 methods, 99 trait slots, 23 extern functions and 11 external methods. It found 4,073 structs, 1,276 enums, 76 traits, 47 distinct types, 7 aliases (5 generic) and 2,235 module constants. It found 474 impl blocks, 25 associated-type fills, 1,988 tests, 4,946 use lines and 14,132 fields. Locals: 49,756 written name :: expr and 27,621 written name := expr.

Scanner limits. The reference is a comment- and string-aware, brace-scope-aware scanner, not the Jet parser. It misreads some one-line nested bodies and Jet code inside text blocks, and it does not parse string interpolation. The rewrites leave headers inside string literals unchanged. No stratified sample was checked against the parser, so read the numbers to two digits, not four.

Finding a type by name. Today the kind-unknown search is an alternation, (struct|enum|trait|alias) NAME or NAME ::, with precision 0.987 and recall 1.0 over 5,479 type definitions. A keeps that pattern and adds prep fn NAME for recipes after the recipe cutover; that added arm was not separately measured. Under B, NAME :: alone scores precision 0.995 and recall 0.999.

B's five misses are generic aliases, which become recipes found by prep fn NAME. For struct, enum and trait only, B scores 0.993 against today's 0.990. So B's gain is a simpler query at similar, high precision: about 99% for both at two-digit accuracy.

Finding a function by name. fn NAME scores 0.985 under today, A and B, with recall 1.0. Under C, name :: fn scores 0.999; that name-plus-kind query is the fair counterpart of fn NAME. Under C, bare name :: scores 0.559, because 49,756 locals also use ::. Still, 95.4% of function names have no stray hits; the noise sits on common names such as value, result and root.

Anchoring ^name :: lifts precision to 0.991 but finds only 70% of functions, since methods are indented.

Any kind, name unknown. Every option is weak here because locals share ::. Today's alternation scores 0.594, B's 0.599 and C's name :: 0.611, each with recall 0.994. Repeated names also matter: 289 type names are defined more than once, such as Point (74 times) and Shape (46). A hit on any of them counts as correct, yet the reader still has several places to look.

Censuses. No line in a function body starts with a PascalCase name and :: or :=. Three start with an ALL_CAPS name, all in invalid-input or text-block fixtures. No struct, enum or trait is declared inside a type body. Five scanner hits inside function bodies were Jet code in text blocks or a brace miscount. The literal search :: struct on B's rewrite finds every named struct, with 6 stray hits in 4,079.

Recovery is an expectation, not a measurement. Under A, recovery is today's. Under B, the parser can resync on fn and on a line-start capitalized name followed by ::, which no valid function body contains. Under C, about 41,300 declaration lines and 49,756 local lines begin name ::, so recovery must look further, at the kind word after ::. Neither new strategy was tested on malformed files; the acceptance probes check diagnostics instead.

Other corpora, scoped. Odin core, 1,288 files: NAME :: finds a procedure at 0.976. The plain pattern for procedures finds only 31%, because about 29,000 headers put a directive such as #force_inline between :: and proc. Zig std, 550 files: const NAME = scores 0.598 against a truth set of container aggregates only. Aliases, recipes and local Self bindings all count as noise there, so it is not comparable with B's figure. fn NAME scores 0.955.

Go: 33% of functions are methods, whose receiver sits between func and the name. Rust: doc-comment examples drop raw struct X precision to 0.847. GitHub code navigation covers Go, Rust, Swift and TypeScript but not Zig or Odin. Plain-text search matters while a language lacks hosted semantic navigation.

Zig's reversal, in context. Proposal #1717 would have made every function an anonymous expression bound by const. It was accepted in 2019 and rejected by Andrew Kelley on 2023-07-09. He cited symbol names in stack traces, profilers and debuggers, stack analysis, and a dislike of pervasive lambda style. A Jet name :: fn form could still derive the symbol from its binding, so C is feasible; Zig is a precedent, not proof.

Odin. Its designer tried keyword-first syntax twice for two weeks (gingerbill.org, 2018). He needed --- because 'a procedure without a body cannot be distinguished from a procedure type'. Odin's #type is a reader annotation that its compiler does not need. Jet's case rule removes most of that ambiguity, so C uses case and context instead of a mark.

Jai and others. Jai's payoff is moving code from lambda to global function with few edits. That needs one syntax for both, which Jet's ratified x -> … lambdas do not share. Google's TypeScript style guide prefers function declarations for named functions; that is a style preference, not a study. No controlled study compares name-first with keyword-first declarations, so learnability claims here are transfer arguments.

Migration is shared work and does not rank options, per the owner. On the pinned corpus, A rewrites no header. B rewrites 5,427 .jet header lines (5,425 aggregates and 2 plain aliases) in 1,698 files, adding 16 KB, plus 19 comment lines. The five generic aliases move in the recipe cutover instead. C rewrites 38,988 headers in 7,095 files, adding 117 KB, plus 489 comment lines and 25 associated-type fills.

Outside .jet files, migration.mjs counted on the live tree, for every header kind including fn. It found 500 Markdown fence lines in 47 files, 582 Markdown inline mentions, about 2,559 Rust string-literal lines in 309 files, and 446 snapshot lines in 284 files. B's share is a subset that was not counted separately. Tooling adds the tree-sitter grammar with its generated parser and tests, the TextMate grammar, Zed queries, the formatter and doc generators.

Corrections from review. The first draft said Point :: finds any type 98.6% of the time. That figure covered struct, enum and trait only, compared counts rather than locations, and came from a rewrite of every keyword. The draft also counted about 5,437 B headers by including five protocols that stay unchanged.

Suite pass repairs (SuiteBeginner and SuiteAdversary, 2026-10-07). The research record now uses current letters, and all acceptance is in this ballot. A's rule is scoped to named definitions, with recipe results and prep blocks shown beside it. B is credited with its one naming shape, short query and shared body, and the search figures read as a near tie.

C is compared on name plus kind, with its exceptions and its kept fn keyword stated. The unnamed-body placement rule is marked as new, and helper aggregates inside recipes are left to D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1. B's local-type move has stated limits, and Rust bindings are out of scope under directive 19. The examples trace 16.0 and 2, and search patterns are explained.

options.name: Keep the leading word
options.detail:
struct, enum, trait and fn keep their leading words. The rule has two parts. A named struct, enum, trait or function starts with the word for what it makes. A value or type written on the right is named first with ::. So constants (LIMIT :: 10), build-time constants (ROW :: prep { … }) and separate types (Usd :: distinct Decimal) use ::. So do aliases (Rows :: [[String]], if the alias vote drops its keyword), re-exports (clamp :: core.math.clamp) and recipe results (IntPair :: Pair(Int)).

The unnamed body struct { … } appears only as a type recipe's result, the way JavaScript writes class Point { } for a named class and class { } as a value. A body written on the right, such as that result or a prep { … } block, has no name of its own, so the rule does not apply to it. Point :: struct { … } at module level is refused with a fix to struct Point { … }.
options.technical:
Status-quo item grammar plus the shared placement rule in the detail, and one refusal. Point :: struct { … } at file or module level is an error whose jet fix writes struct Point { … }. That refusal mirrors B's retirement of struct Point: each option keeps one named form.

The rule, scoped. A named struct, enum, trait, function or module starts with its kind word. A binding that names a value or type written on the right starts with the name: LIMIT :: 10, ROW :: prep { … }, Usd :: distinct Decimal, IntPair :: Pair(Int). A body on the right, such as a recipe's struct { … } result or a prep { … } block, has no name of its own. A does not claim that every body starts with a word.

Alias spelling is coupled to D-ALIAS-BIND2, which stays open under A. If it picks A, aliases read Rows :: [[String]] and IntPair :: Pair(Int); if B, alias Rows :: [[String]]. Re-exports follow D-VIS-REEXPORT1. Associated types, privacy, markers, docs, casing and binding modules are unchanged. A amends no ratified law; the shared placement rule restates today's absence of unnamed aggregate types outside recipe results.

A's strongest case. Each named definition line starts with its kind, which helps a reader scanning a file and transfers from Rust, Swift, Kotlin and Go. The struct header and the recipe body are two contexts of one body grammar, not two semantic mechanisms. Its cost is naming: structs, enums and traits read struct Point, while aliases, separate types and recipe results read Name ::.

Finding a type of unknown kind. Editor go-to-definition and the language server's symbol search find any definition by name. The plain-text pattern is (struct|enum|trait|alias) NAME, or NAME ::, or prep fn NAME for recipes; drop alias if the alias vote drops the keyword. Without the prep fn arm, it scored precision 0.987 and recall 1.0 on today's corpus. The prep fn arm was not separately measured.

options.name: Types by name, code by keyword
options.detail:
At file or module level, every named non-recipe type and every fixed value is a binding. Examples: Point :: struct { … }, Shape :: enum { … }, Named :: trait { … }, Usd :: distinct Decimal, Rows :: [[String]], IntPair :: Pair(Int) and LIMIT :: 10. Recipes keep prep fn, so a generic type is still found by prep fn Pair. B changes only struct, enum and trait headers, plus alias spelling. Every other declaration keeps its word: fn, prep fn recipes, methods, trait slots, impl, module, marker, fact, effect, protocol, migration, derive, state, extern, #Test and use.

B's strongest case. Structs, enums, aliases and separate types share one naming shape, the shape LIMIT :: 10 already has. One short query, Point ::, finds a non-recipe type of any kind at about 99% precision. The same struct { … } body serves a named type and a recipe's result, so making a type generic moves the body unchanged. Functions keep fn. Its cost is that a type line starts with its name, not its kind word.

Trait and impl bodies do not change: a slot stays type Elem and an impl fill stays type Elem = Int. struct Name { }, enum Name { } and trait Name { } are retired with a jet fix edit. Ratifying B also settles D-ALIAS-BIND2 as its option A; if D-ALIAS-BIND2 already kept the alias keyword, B reverses that.
options.technical:
1. Scope. The binding form applies at file and module level only. Type, trait and impl bodies keep today's members and today's errors: fields, methods, impl blocks, slots type Elem and fills type Elem = Int. Nothing in the corpus declares a type inside a type body, and B adds no such form.

2. Resolution of a module-level Name :: R, in order. (a) R is struct { … }, enum { … } or trait { … }: a new nominal type named Name. (b) R is distinct T: a separate type. (c) R is a bare path to a declaration: an alias of it, by D-VIS-REEXPORT1 if that picks A, else for types only. (d) R's value is a type, including a recipe call: a transparent alias. (e) R names nothing: E0107. (f) Otherwise a constant, under E0357 and E0622.

Arm (a) is new and syntactic, so it is decided before name resolution. Arms (b) to (f) are D-ALIAS-BIND2=A's ordered rule unchanged. After the arm, the name-case check runs. Type arms need a leading capital, so IO and U8 are fine (S66); constants need ALL_CAPS; an alias of a function or module follows the target's case.

Immutable is not the same as build time. LIMIT :: 10 is an immutable module constant whose initializer must be a literal. ROW :: prep { … } is computed at build time, and IntPair :: Pair(Int) is a type the build fixes. LIMIT :: compute() stays E0622, and a prep { } right side stays a constant as D-ALIAS-BIND2 orders it; choosing a type belongs in a recipe.

3. Identity. Arm (a) mints exactly one type, with the constructors, patterns, methods, impl blocks and home module that struct Point has today. An alias is the same type: with Shape2 :: Shape, Shape2.Circle(3.0) builds a Shape and matches .Circle(r). IntPair :: Pair(Int) names the recipe's identity and never mints, so Again :: IntPair is still Pair(Int). Enum payloads, discriminants, groups and variant markers are unchanged.

4. Cycles. A :: B beside B :: A is the alias-cycle error. Recursion through an aggregate body stays legal, as today: Expr :: enum { Num(Int) Wrap(Expr) }. Recursive recipes keep D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1's reserved identity, so Tree(T) inside Tree's enum body means the type being built.

5. Where an aggregate expression may appear. Jet has no unnamed struct, enum or trait types today; D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 lets a recipe return one and keeps types from reaching run time. B admits the unnamed body in two places: as the whole right side of arm (a), and wherever that ballot lets a recipe produce its result, including branch results and return.

It is an error as a field or parameter type, an argument, inside a prep { } block, or in a runtime function body. The error says: name this type at module level, or make it its own recipe. Those places have no unnamed aggregate today, so the rule keeps today's behavior there. It is written into this ballot, not inherited from a ratified text. A has the same rule without arm (a), and C the same as B.

Not decided here: whether a recipe body may bind a helper aggregate before returning it. That stays D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1's cutover question, with type-valued local aliases inside recipes and markers on a recipe's result, and reads the same under A, B and C. If refused there, the workaround is a second recipe, prep fn Inner(T: Type) -> Type { struct { x: T } }, used as Inner(T), with that ballot's identity rule.

6. Inside a runtime fn body, Name :: <type> is an error (D-ALIAS-BIND2). A machine-applicable move above the function is offered only when three things hold. The right side uses no local name or prep parameter. The name is free at module level and in every enclosing module. No other function in the package declares a local type of that name.

The move is offered, never applied silently, and its message says the type becomes public like any declaration. The manual alternative it lists keeps the type hidden: move it into a priv module. Point := struct { … } gets 'a type is fixed; use ::'.

Otherwise the error gives manual steps only. For fn g(prep T: Type) { Items :: [T] }, the type uses T, so the message says to write prep fn Items(T: Type) -> Type { [T] } at module level and use Items(T). If two functions each declare Local, neither gets a move, and the message asks for two distinct names. D-ALIAS-BIND2's local-type fix should carry the same limits.

7. Names and foreign code. Type names start with a capital, as today. point :: struct { … } gets the name-case error naming the kind, with fix Point. Binding modules (#Bindgen, #Extern) stay exempt from casing (D-SHAPE-CASE2). Their foreign names and link strings are untouched; only a record header outside them changes, as in #Layout(c) HbFeature :: struct { … }. extern rust blocks exist today but are being removed under directive 19, so B does not convert them.

8. Markers, docs and privacy. /// doc comments and markers, including #[A, B] stacks and #Layout(c), sit where they sit above struct Point today and attach to the same type. Field and variant markers inside the body are unchanged. Generated docs list the type under its name, and diagnostic spans point at the name. A priv field still works: Secret :: struct { priv key: Bytes }. priv module and priv(package) module are unchanged; declaration-level priv or pub stays an error.

9. Layout and search. The formatter prints Name :: struct { on one line, with the kind word right after ::. A line break between :: and the kind word parses and is joined. So ':: struct' finds formatted named structs; it does not find recipe results. Search a recipe with prep fn Pair, not Pair ::.

10. Retirement and typos. struct Name { }, enum Name { } and trait Name { } at file or module level are errors with a machine-applicable jet fix; the parser keeps them only for recovery. Name :: strcut { … } parses as a typed construction, so B adds a did-you-mean. An unknown name within two edits of struct, enum or trait, followed by {, suggests the kind word.

11. Recipes are unchanged: prep fn Pair(T: Type) -> Type { struct { first: T, second: T } }. Making Pair generic moves its struct { … } body into the recipe, and only the fields that become generic change. Self-references become Pair(T), impl heads become impl Pair(T: Type), and callers write Pair(Int), all under D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1. generic.jet in B's code shows one conversion.

options.name: Name first everywhere
options.detail:
Nearly every named declaration is name :: kind …: functions, methods, external methods, trait slots, build-time functions, recipes, modules, markers, facts, effects, protocols and typestates as well as types. The exceptions, stated up front, are few. impl, use, #Test, derive, extern block headers and #UnitFamily stay as they are because they bind no new name. migration stays a keyword, a trait's associated-type slot stays type Elem, and local helpers stay lambdas.

C keeps the fn keyword and changes its order: fn double(…) becomes double :: fn(…). Private modules read priv helpers :: module, an explicit spelling amendment to card #4723 with the same reach. Amends D-SIG-AFTER1=A.

C's strongest case. Every named thing lines up at the left edge, and name :: fn finds a function at 0.999 precision, slightly above fn name at 0.985. Symbol names in stack traces come from the binding, so Zig's reason for rejecting #1717 does not apply. Bodiless signatures are told apart by case and context, without Odin's --- mark. Its costs fall on readers: a field and a method differ by one colon, a bare name :: search also hits locals, and a newcomer learns the case-and-context rules.
options.technical:
C's spellings, complete. Functions: double :: fn(p: Point) -> Int { … }. Methods in a type or impl body: double :: fn(self) -> Int { … }. External methods: Point.triple :: fn(self) -> Int { … }. Build-time functions: from_text :: prep fn(text: String) -> Int { … }. Recipes: Pair :: prep fn(T: Type) -> Type { struct { … } }. Types and constants read as under B.

Modules: arith :: module { … }, and a file module starts with math :: module. Private modules put priv before the name, where markers sit: priv helpers :: module { … } and priv(package) shared :: module { … }. This amends card #4723's spelling; the reach of priv and priv(package) is unchanged. Generic modules read cache :: module(prep K: Hash, capacity: Int) { … }. An instance reads cache64 :: cache(String, 64), recognised because cache resolves to a module template.

Markers and the rest: CardNumber :: marker { deny: [Log] }, Audit :: marker(topic: String) { … }, Exactness :: fact($holds: …), FS.Read :: effect, Chat :: protocol { … } and a typestate Open :: state { … }. Associated types: the slot stays type Elem, and an impl fills it with Elem :: Int. A fill naming no slot of the trait is an error.

Kept as keywords: impl, use, #Test, derive, extern block headers and #UnitFamily bind no new name. migration stays a keyword because User :: migration { … } would read as a second definition of the type User. Local helpers stay lambdas, as in helper :: n -> n * 2. fn(…) { … } is legal only as the whole right side of a file, module or type-body binding; inside a function it is an error suggesting a lambda.

Bodiless signatures are decided by case and context instead of a mark. Inside a trait, a lowercase name :: fn(…) -> T with no body is a slot. Anywhere, a capitalized Name :: fn(…) -> T is a function type. Inside binding modules, where casing is exempt, a foreign function ends with its link string: gzopen :: fn(path: String, mode: String) GzFile = "gzopen". A lowercase bodiless signature elsewhere is an error.

Binding modules keep their marker and take the same order: #Bindgen c.z.__bindgen__ :: module { … }. Foreign names, link strings and casing exemptions are unchanged. extern rust blocks exist today but are being removed under directive 19, so C does not convert them and no acceptance check depends on them. priv fields are unchanged.

Fields and methods. In a type body, scale: fn(Int) -> Int is a field holding a function, and double :: fn(self) -> Int { … } is a method. The tokens differ, so the parser is not confused; the risk is a reader's misread, which no study measured. Two diagnostics cover the slips: a bodiless :: member asks for a body or one colon, and a one-colon member with a body asks for ::. Novice slips and malformed-file recovery are hypotheses for C's acceptance probes, not observed failures.

Laws C amends beyond B's: D-SIG-AFTER1=A and D-CALLABLE-ONE1, for the named function spelling and a binding-only fn form. Also D-PREP-FN1, D-EXTMETH1, U3 and D-MOD2 for modules, D-GENMOD1/2 for instances, and D-MARKER-DECL1, D-FACTDECL1 and D-EFFECT-DECL1. Also D-PROTO1/2, D-STATE-DECL, S50 and S59 for binding-zone functions, D-LIB2 for impl fills, and card #4723's priv module spelling. This breadth is disclosure and acceptance work; it does not rank C.

C's strengths, credited. name :: fn finds a function at 0.999 precision, slightly above fn name at 0.985; name plus kind is the fair comparison on both sides. Every named thing lines up at the left edge. Its weaknesses are the kind-unknown query, bare name ::, at 0.559, the one-colon field versus two-colon method distinction, and the larger set of rules a newcomer must learn.

comparisons.note: Types by const binding, functions by fn. Proposal #1717 to make every function an anonymous const-bound expression was accepted in 2019 and rejected in 2023. github.com/ziglang/zig/issues/1717
comparisons.code:
const Point = struct { x: i64 };
fn double(p: Point) i64 { return p.x * 2; }

comparisons.note: Everything by ::. A foreign procedure without a body needs ---; #type is an optional reader annotation for a procedure type (odin-lang.org/docs/overview).
One function syntax at every scope, so code moves from lambda to global function with few edits (JaiPrimer).
Keyword, name, then kind; methods put the receiver between func and the name.
comparisons.code:
type Point struct { X int }
func (p Point) Double() int { return p.X * 2 }

comparisons.note: Keyword-first items; aliases use type.
Both forms exist for functions; Google's style guide prefers function declarations for named functions, as a style preference. Type aliases are binding-shaped.
comparisons.code:
type Point = { x: number };
function double(p: Point): number { return p.x * 2; }

recommendation.why: Search is a near tie, about 99% for both type queries, so this is a reading judgment. A keeps the kind word first on every named definition, as most popular languages do, and needs one scoped rule for Jet's two shapes.
gains: Readers see what a named definition makes before its name.
Learners from TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust and Swift meet familiar headers; this is transfer, not a study.
Named structs, enums, traits, functions and modules all start with their word.

losses.loss: Types use two shapes: struct Point, and Rows :: [[String]] for an alias.
losses.mitigation: One scoped rule: named structs, enums, traits and functions start with their word; :: names a value or type on the right.

losses.loss: An unknown-kind type search lists kind words, or NAME ::.
losses.mitigation: Go-to-definition finds any kind; the pattern found every definition, with about 99% of hits precise.

whyNot.reason: B's gains are real: one naming shape for every non-recipe type, a one-term type search at about 99%, and one struct body for declarations and recipes, with fn kept. It loses on judgment, not data: type lines no longer start with their kind word, which the author, like the owner's first reaction, values more.

C's double :: fn search is as precise as fn double, and every name lines up. But a bare double :: search also hits locals (56% definitions), a field and a method differ by one colon, and named functions change order against ratified law.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two shapes joined by one scoped rule, in exchange for familiar definitions that start with what they make.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: SuiteBeginner. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass tested the complete ballot. Repaired: one set of letters throughout, traces for 16.0 and 2, a scoped rule for A, explained search patterns, and every option's acceptance inside this ballot.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude-opus. Adversarial model family: gpt. Fresh agent: SuiteAdversary. The adversarial review attacked the recommendation. Repaired: B and C are credited fairly, search reads as a near tie, the placement rule is marked new, and the local-type move has stated limits.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Drafted by BallotSuite1 from D-DECL-FORM1 and its repair record ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ballots/review/D-DECL-FORM1-repairs.md). surface.gist: Should named types keep their leading word, struct Point, or be written name-first, Point :: struct, maybe functions too?
surface.lesson: A struct is a type with named fields. Today named structs and functions start with their word: struct Point { … }, fn double(…). A value or type written on the right is named first with ::, as in LIMIT :: 10. B and C would also write every alias Rows :: [[String]].

current.note: Values and separate types are named first; named structs and functions start with a word.
current.code:
LIMIT :: 10                     // a constant: name first
Usd :: distinct Decimal         // a separate type: name first
struct Point {                  // a struct: keyword first
    x: Int
}
fn double(p: Point) -> Int { p.x * 2 }   // a function: keyword first

wild.note: TypeScript starts a class with its word and also allows an unnamed class as a value; Zig names types like values.
wild.code:
class Point { x = 0 }              // TypeScript: named
const Pair = class { a = 0 }       // TypeScript: as a value
const Point = struct { x: i64 };   // Zig: a type is a value

options.name: Keep the leading word
options.gist: Named structs, enums, traits and functions start with their word; :: names values and types on the right.
gains: Each named definition says what it makes first.
Same shape as TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust, Swift and Kotlin.
losses: Structs read struct Point; aliases read Rows :: [[String]].
An unknown-kind type search lists kind words, or NAME ::.

options.name: Types by name, code by keyword
options.gist: Named types and fixed values read Name :: …; functions and recipes keep their word.
gains: Structs, enums, aliases and separate types share one naming shape.
Functions keep fn, the form Jet already settled on.
One short search, Point ::, finds a type of any kind.
losses: A type line no longer starts with its kind word.
Types and functions use two shapes.

options.name: Name first everywhere
options.gist: Nearly every named thing reads name :: kind, functions and modules included.
gains: One visual rule for nearly every named thing.
double :: fn finds functions as precisely as fn double.
losses: A bare double :: search also hits locals: 56% are definitions.
A field and a method differ by one colon.
Reorders the settled fn double and a dozen other spellings.

recommendation.why: Search is a near tie, so this is a reading judgment. A keeps each named definition's kind word first, as most languages do.
gains: Lines say what they make first.
Familiar to most learners.

losses.loss: Types use two shapes: struct Point, and Rows :: [[String]] for an alias.
losses.mitigation: One scoped rule: named structs, enums, traits and functions start with their word; :: names a value or type on the right.

losses.loss: An unknown-kind type search lists kind words, or NAME ::.
losses.mitigation: Go-to-definition finds any kind; the pattern found every definition, with about 99% of hits precise.

whyNot.reason: B's one shape and short search are real, but type lines lose their kind word.
Its double :: fn search is as precise, but bare names hit locals and fields differ from methods by one colon.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two shapes joined by one scoped rule, in exchange for familiar definitions that start with what they make.

designAway.loss: Types use two shapes.
attempts: Name every type with :: (option B); kept as the alternative.
State one rule for both shapes, shown in the error for Point :: struct; kept for A.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation.

designAway.loss: A kind-unknown type search needs an alternation.
attempts: Rely on go-to-definition and symbol search, which ignore spelling; kept.
Measure the plain-text pattern on today's corpus: recall 1.0, precision 0.987; the added prep fn arm is unmeasured.
designAway.result: Negligible with mitigation.

decisions.title: Web-style names: camelCase for functions, fields and variables
decisions.situation: Today Jet writes function, field and variable names in lowercase with underscores, such as fetch_user_profile and user_id. You asked for the most practical defaults across fields of work, leaning toward web development, where JavaScript, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift and Go write these names in camelCase. You already decided that type names keep capital acronyms, such as TaskID, and that camelCase JSON keys write acronyms as words, such as userId. This vote decides how values are spelled in code. We recommend camelCase with acronyms in capitals, userID, so every Jet name follows one acronym rule while web data still reads userId.
decisions.gist: Should Jet values use camelCase, and should acronyms inside them read userID or userId?
decisions.lesson: camelCase capitalizes each word after the first: fetchUserProfile. snake_case joins lowercase words with underscores: fetch_user_profile. An acronym is a word of initials, such as ID or URL. Types keep capital acronyms under every option: HTTPClient, TaskID. camelCase JSON keys write acronyms as words, userId, as you already decided. The choice is how values look in code.
decisions.explainer:
Every option shows the same small program: one record type, one choice type, one constant and two functions. Types, markers, effects and enum cases stay PascalCase with capital acronyms in every option, as already ratified. Constants stay in full capitals. Shared work for A or B: one casing section in the spec, compiler checks with automatic fixes, and one rename of Jet's own code.

Under A, an acronym looks the same in every Jet name: TaskID the type, taskID the field, parseURL the function. Only a leading acronym is lowercase, as in urlText and httpClient, the Swift and Go rule. Two touching acronyms take the underscore type names already use: parseHTTP_URL, like HTTP_API.

JSON keys are computed, not copied. Under A, the field userID sends and reads the key userId, the web's usual spelling, because you ratified word-cased acronyms in data keys. A key spelled userID gets an error naming userId, and jet inspect shapes prints every outside name.

Under B, acronyms in values are written as words: userId, avatarUrl, parseHttpUrl. A field then matches its JSON key letter for letter. But a value and its type spell the acronym differently, taskId: TaskID, which is a second acronym rule. It also reverses your ratified note that Jet code keeps userID.

Under C, values keep underscores, and JSON keys default to snake_case unless a package asks for camelCase.
decisions.story: Kai builds a web service in Jet and its browser front end in TypeScript. The same record travels between them as JSON. He wants Jet names that read like the rest of his web code, one acronym rule to learn, and JSON keys his front end already expects.
decisions.detail:
Revision, 2026-10-10, by BallotPolishA. The owner ratified D-WIRE-CASE1=A and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A at 2026-10-07T20:23, about two hours after this ballot was posted. D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A recommends "writing userId in data keys while Jet code keeps userID". Its option text says "Inside Jet code, acronyms stay fully capitalized." D-WIRE-CASE1=A's examples use camelCase fields with capital acronyms.

The posted A word-cased value acronyms and withdrew D-WIRE-ACRONYM1. That contradicts law ratified since, so the capital-acronym option now leads. Mapping: new A is the posted B; new B is the posted A; C is unchanged. Its detail now states that companion keys are computed under A, so A no longer carries the posted B's loss that a field "differs from common JSON keys" without a remedy.

Replaces D-CASE-LAW2 (OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07). D-CASE-LAW2's C, which also word-cased acronyms in types (HttpClient, Url), stays withdrawn: it reverses the owner's type rule.

Why A leads. D-ACRO-CASE1=A and the owner rule of 2026-09-30 (spec S66) put capital acronyms in every word of every type-like name. D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A then decided camelCase data keys word-case acronyms while Jet code keeps userID. A completes that pair: one acronym rule for every Jet name, and computed keys for web data. B would give values a second acronym rule and reverse the ratified note.

Irreducible part. Given the owner's type rule and the web's word-cased keys, some pair must differ: either field and key (A) or field and type (B). A keeps Jet code on one rule and lets the ratified projection convert the 1.9% of fields that hold an acronym. The projection is exact in both directions, and a near-miss key names the expected one.

DECISION BOUNDARY

Owner direction, 2026-10-05, given after D-CASE-LAW1=A was ratified the same day. The owner has personal style preferences but ranks pragmatism higher: the best defaults and rules for the most domains at the greatest criticality. The owner added that naming seems most important in web development, so Jet should likely lean toward web conventions. D-CASE-LAW1 is ratified and immutable, so the re-vote is a new decision. Choosing C re-affirms D-CASE-LAW1=A unchanged.

This ballot changes only the case of value-like names. PascalCase stays for types, traits, enum variants, markers including their library part (#Server.Get), effects, unit families and generic type parameters. SCREAMING_SNAKE stays for module-level immutable bindings and compile-time number parameters. The closed acronym lexicon (D-ACRO-LEX1=A) and full-capital acronyms in type-like names (D-ACRO-CASE1=A) stand under every option. Foreign names stay verbatim inside binding modules (D-SHAPE-CASE2=A), so browser names such as innerHTML keep their spelling.

COMPANIONS

D-PATH-CASE2=A, D-WIRE-CASE1=A and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A are ratified and work unchanged under A. The path word key already reads userID, user_id and userId alike. Under B, D-WIRE-ACRONYM1's note that Jet code keeps userID would need an amendment. Under C, keys default to snake_case words per D-WIRE-CASE1's detail.

WHAT OPTION A SPELLS

camelCase covers functions, methods, fields, parameters, locals, labels, lint names, import aliases and module path segments. Most module segments are one lowercase word, so core.text.fmt is unchanged. Manifest keys in package.jet are fields, so they become camelCase, as in npm's package.json (devDependencies). Acronyms follow the Swift and Go rule. Inside a name they are fully capitalized: userID, avatarURL, parseURL. At the start they are fully lowercase: urlText, httpClient. Two touching acronyms keep D-ACRO-CASE1's underscore: parseHTTP_URL. Jet's own code has 43 such functions.

WHAT OPTION B SPELLS

Every word of a value, an acronym included, is capitalized like a word: userId, avatarUrl, parseHttpUrl, httpClient, utf8Bytes. No acronym list is consulted for values, and touching acronyms need no underscore. A value and its type then differ: taskId: TaskID.

RESEARCH: WHAT EACH ECOSYSTEM WRITES

TypeScript and JavaScript use camelCase functions, variables, properties and parameters, and PascalCase classes, types and components. Acronyms are split. The browser platform writes innerHTML, URLSearchParams and toISOString, but also getElementById and XMLHttpRequest. Airbnb 23.9 says acronyms are all upper or all lower case. Google's TypeScript guide word-cases them (loadHttpUrl) unless a platform name says otherwise.

JSON keys are camelCase in Google's JSON style guide, JSON:API's recommendation, Microsoft Graph and protobuf's JSON mapping, and those sources write acronyms as words: userId, webUrl. GitHub's GraphQL API sends avatarUrl and databaseId. Stripe, GitHub REST and Slack use snake_case.

Swift and Go write capital acronyms in values: userSMTPServer, appID. Kotlin and Google Java style word-case them: newCustomerId. C# and .NET write Id and Url. Dart word-cases acronyms longer than two letters.

snake_case values: Python (PEP 8), Rust (RFC 430), Ruby, Elixir, the C standard library, SQL by habit, Odin and Jai. Python keeps capital acronyms in class names and lowercase words in values, the same split option A keeps.

Swift's API Design Guidelines say acronyms that are all capitals in English are "uniformly up- or down-cased according to case conventions": utf8Bytes, isRepresentableAsASCII, userSMTPServer. Go's code review comments ask for capital initialisms such as appID and ServeHTTP, and its linters (golint, staticcheck ST1003) report userId.

POPULATION

Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2024: JavaScript has been the most used language every year except 2013 and 2014. [INFERENCE: chart values recalled, not re-read] All respondents: JavaScript about 62%, Python 51%, SQL 51%, TypeScript 38%, Java 30%, C# 27%. Go and Rust are about 13% each, Kotlin 9%, Dart 6% and Swift 5%.

READING STUDIES

Binkley et al., ICPC 2009, 135 subjects: camelCase had 51.5% higher odds of a correct answer and took 13.5% longer. Sharif and Maletic, ICPC 2010, eye tracking, 15 subjects: no accuracy difference, and underscores about 20% faster. Binkley et al., Empirical Software Engineering 2013, 150 subjects: experience shrinks the effect. No study shows a large stable winner; practice dominates.

CENSUS, 7,409 tracked .jet files at 1e300d0af

22,276 function declarations have multi-word names. About 302,000 occurrences of 43,051 distinct snake_case spellings exist, counting call sites, fields, locals and comments. Fields: 13,571 declarations averaging 1.55 words, so most fields are one word and do not change. About 1.9% of fields contain an acronym. Type declarations: 5,396, unchanged under every option.

MIGRATION

Under A or B, one jet fix pass renames multi-word values and every use in one atomic commit between merge waves. A's rename reads each name's words with the shared splitter and lexicon that D-PATH-CASE2 and D-WIRE-CASE1 already use, so it is deterministic. An in-flight branch rebases and re-runs the same pass. The rename commit goes in a .git-blame-ignore-revs file, which git blame and GitHub both honor, so line history skips it.

options.name: camelCase values, acronyms in capitals
options.detail: Functions, methods, fields, parameters, variables and import names use camelCase, as in JavaScript, TypeScript, Swift and Go. An acronym is written in capitals in every Jet name: userID, avatarURL, parseURL, the same as in type names such as TaskID. A leading acronym is lowercase: urlText, httpClient. Two touching acronyms take the underscore type names already use: parseHTTP_URL. JSON keys come out userId, as already ratified. Compiler errors offer the exact fix.
options.technical:
Amends D-CASE-LAW1=A for value-like names only. Functions, methods, fields, parameters, locals, labels, lint names, import aliases, module path segments and manifest keys become lowerCamelCase. E0357 checks the new case. E0358 and the closed lexicon (D-ACRO-LEX1=A) extend from type-like names to values: lexicon acronyms in capitals inside a name, lowercase when leading. Touching acronyms keep D-ACRO-CASE1's underscore. Digits attach to the word before (utf8Bytes). Plural acronyms: userIDs, or urls when leading.

Data keys follow D-WIRE-CASE1=A and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A unchanged: userID encodes and decodes as userId, and a near miss names the expected key. Migration: one jet fix pass in one atomic commit, listed in .git-blame-ignore-revs. Foreign names in binding modules stay verbatim (D-SHAPE-CASE2=A).

options.name: camelCase values, acronyms written as words
options.detail: Values use camelCase as in A, but an acronym inside a value is an ordinary word: userId, avatarUrl, parseHttpUrl. Types keep capital acronyms, so a value and its type differ: taskId: TaskID. A field and its JSON key are always the same word. This reverses the ratified note that Jet code keeps userID.
options.technical: Amends D-CASE-LAW1=A for value-like names only, as in A. E0357 rejects a capital run in a value name with a fix (userID to userId). E0358 and the lexicon keep their role for type-like names only. Data keys then equal field names. Amends D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A's statement that acronyms stay fully capitalized inside Jet code. Migration as in A, without lexicon lookups.

options.name: Keep underscores for values
options.detail: Jet keeps the rule confirmed on 2026-10-05: functions, fields and variables in lowercase with underscores, like Python and Rust. Types, constants and acronyms in types are as in A. Nothing is renamed. Code shared with a JavaScript or Swift front end spells every multi-word field differently on each side, while outside names are still computed from words.
options.technical: D-CASE-LAW1=A stands unchanged. No migration. JSON keys copy snake_case field names unless a package or type asks for camelCase (D-WIRE-CASE1). Interop with Python, Rust and SQL needs no projection.

comparisons.note: camelCase values with acronyms uniformly upper or lower case by position. This is option A.

comparisons.lang: Protocol Buffers JSON and Google TypeScript style
comparisons.note: Acronyms written as words in camelCase. Jet's ratified JSON keys already do this under every option; option B also does it in code.
comparisons.code:
string user_id = 1;   // JSON key "userId"
function loadHttpUrl(userId: number) { ... }

comparisons.note: snake_case values, CapWords classes with capital acronyms. This is option C, and the same type and value split option A keeps.

recommendation.why: A spells values the way most web code does and uses your type acronym rule for every Jet name. JSON keys still come out userId, as you ratified, so web data needs no renames.
gains: One acronym rule for every Jet name: TaskID, taskID, parseURL.
Web JSON keys stay userId with nothing written.
Matches your ratified key vote and type rule.

losses.loss: Jet's own code is renamed once.
losses.mitigation: One deterministic jet fix pass in a single commit, which branches re-run after rebasing and git blame skips. Outside names do not move.

losses.loss: Acronyms stay capitals, unlike web keys: userID, parseHTTP_URL.
losses.mitigation: It is your type rule, so one rule covers every name, and Jet computes the userId key both ways.

whyNot.reason: B makes fields equal their keys, but gives values a second acronym rule, taskId: TaskID, against your ratified note that Jet code keeps userID.
C keeps fields spelled unlike the web code they meet, and its JSON keys default to snake_case.

recommendation.tradeoff: One rename, for camelCase names that follow one acronym rule while web data still reads userId.
