decisions.title: Every Jai build option as a Jet build option, and pinning options in fn build
decisions.situation: Jai lets a project control dozens of build settings from code, from the target processor to linker arguments and which runtime checks stay on. Jet's build profile has a handful of settings, and its rules say the command line always wins, so a project cannot fix a setting it depends on. Games, embedded programs and plugins therefore cannot be built the way their authors intend. The vote decides which settings Jet adds and whether build code may pin them; we recommend all of them, and pinning.
decisions.gist: Should Jet offer every Jai build setting, and may build code pin a setting the command line cannot change?
decisions.lesson: A build profile is a named group of settings, such as release, written in package.jet. `fn build` is Jet code that registers what to build. Pinning means build code fixes a setting so a command-line flag cannot change it. Today the command line always wins; option A reverses that where a project pins.
decisions.story: Sam ships a game to the web, a desktop build with a custom linker script, and a plugin library. He needs CPU features, linker arguments, a dynamic-library output and dead-code removal set from code, and he needs CI flags never to undo them.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

TODAY. The rules list five profile fields: optimize, debug_info, small, panic and settings (D-BUILDPROFILE1). THE CATALOG UNDER A AND B, with Jai names in brackets. Output: the output kind is chosen where it is today, by the package kind and by registration (`b.add_executable`, `b.add_library`). `b.add_library` gains `link: .Static` or `.Dynamic`, `b.add_object` is new, and check-only is `jet check` [output_type]. output_dir and work_dir [output_path, intermediate_path].

Entry name for freestanding targets is the target profile's entry fact [entry_point_name]. Target: os, arch, cpu (native or a name. The existing `--cpu` flag), cpu_features, min_os [os_target, cpu_target, machine_type, target_system_cpu, target_system_features, minimum_os_version]. Code generation: optimize keeps none, basic, full and size, and adds min_size [Optimization_Type]. Inline auto or never. Lto. Split_units. Function_sections. Frame_pointers. Red_zone.

Vectorize, unroll, tail_calls, merge_functions [llvm_options]. Emit ir, bitcode, asm or object [output_llvm_ir, output_bitcode]. Backend_args raw passthrough [llvm_options.command_line]. Fields apply per backend (Jet-native, Cranelift, rustc). A field a backend cannot honour is a registered error naming the backend, never silently ignored. Raw backend_args that make the backend reject the program remain an internal error under I2, and the receipt marks such builds.

Runtime checks: bounds, null and casts take fatal, report or off [array_bounds_check, null_pointer_check, cast_bounds_check]. `off` needs the unchecked_bounds, unchecked_null or unchecked_casts power. overflow sets the build default for `#Arithmetic` (D-WRAP-SCOPE1) and needs no power [math and arithmetic checks]. Per scope, `#Unchecked(bounds, casts, null)` removes named checks on one block or function (Jai #no_abc).

It is legal only inside an `#Unsafe("reason")` scope, the existing I1 gate, so it needs no power. The written reason is the audit record, `policy.unsafe` can deny or confine such scopes, and the build receipt lists each `#Unchecked` site. Today `#Unsafe` keeps bounds checks, and D-OOBPROOF1 elides only proven ones. Debug: debug_info none, lines or full (a Bool today). Debug_format. Stack_traces. Crash_backtrace. Debugger_names.

Step_into_expansions [emit_debug_info, stack_trace, backtrace_on_crash, use_natvis_compatible_types, -debug_for]. Size: dead_code all, packages or none [dead_code_elimination, -no_dce]. Type_info full, reachable or none [runtime_storageless_type_info, #type_info_none]. Max_instance_depth [maximum_polymorph_depth]. Link: link_args, libs, lib_paths [additional_linker_arguments]. Lazy_foreign [lazy_foreign_function_lookups]. A custom link step is D-JAI-EVENTS1's build.link.

Runtime: scratch_size [temporary_storage_size], only if D-JAI-CONTEXT1 adds scratch memory. Diagnostics: diagnostics human, msvc or json. Color. Short_paths. Timings. Quiet [use_visual_studio_message_format, shorten_filenames_in_error_messages, text_output_flags]. Data for build code: typed settings exist [user_data_*]. `jet build -- args` passes strings to fn build as `b.args` [compile_time_command_line].

COMMAND-LINE JAI FLAGS. -run maps to the existing `jet eval`. -add maps to `jet build --add 'decl'` under the raw_code power, if D-JAI-CODE1 passes. -debugger maps to card #5008, which debugs compile-time code. -very_debug maps to the existing hardened profile (D-HARDENED1) with full debug info. -no_jobs is the existing `--threads 1`. -randomize, -seed and -chaos map to `jet build --shuffle[=seed]`, the spelling `jet test` already uses. -report_poly maps to `--report instances` (#5000).

-no_cwd needs nothing. -import_dir maps to path and vendored dependencies, since Jet resolves packages by identity. PINNING (A only). `b.pin(setting, value)` in fn build makes a flag for that setting a registered error naming the pin. This reverses D-BUILDCTX-FLAGS1 ('command line always wins'), which the owner's 2026-10-07 notes digest restates, for pinned settings only, and adopts Blow's rule that program-set options win for reproducibility (OAIqCpqszVw 01:06:25).

INTERPLAY. D-JAI-EXPERT1 names the check powers. D-JAI-CONFIG1 reuses these fields for each profile, so if C wins, CONFIG1's os field comes from `--target` instead.

EVIDENCE. The Way to Jai book/30A, 30B and examples/30/30.4_build_options.jai:50-123. Focus first.jai:23-90. Infinite-pong first.jai:7-33. Cargo's typed profiles succeeded while RUSTFLAGS raw text is a long-standing pain. Zig's typed target query is the closest precedent.

decisions.title: Jai workspaces in Jet: may build settings change while an output compiles?
decisions.situation: Jai's build program makes workspaces, separate builds of one game with their own settings, and its message loop can change a few settings while compiling. In Jet each such build is an output, and in every option build code copies settings, shapes outputs and reads the build machine before compiling starts. The vote decides whether settings may change while an output compiles, for example adding a link library once a hook sees the program call Vulkan. We recommend letting compiler hooks change any setting until the first compiler stage that uses it, with every change recorded and only later steps re-run.
decisions.gist: May build settings change while an output compiles, and how?
decisions.lesson: In Jai, a workspace is one separate build; in Jet it is an output with its own settings, shaped by `fn build`. A compiler hook is a function marked `#On(stage)` that Jet calls at a named compiler step. The vote decides whether settings may still change while an output compiles. Hooks could change each one until Jet uses it, a Jai-style loop could, or nothing could.
decisions.story: Tomi's game calls a Vulkan wrapper only in some builds. Their old Jai build program watched compiler messages and added `-lvulkan` to the linker when it saw the call. Tomi wants the same in Jet without a special permission. CI must also show who added the flag and why only the link step re-ran.
decisions.detail:
Round 3, 2026-10-19. The owner wrote: "i dont like that we cant update build settings during a build like jai. why not?" This version answers that. A is new: settings may change until Jet uses them. B is Jai's pull loop, as before. C is the earlier recommendation, where nothing changes once compiling starts.

Rewritten 2026-10-19 on owner instruction: "ensure the ballots are cohesive and aligned, update or remove the jai config ballot accordingly". The update aligns it with card #5069's slate (Tower card c07glrub). The earlier full ballot, with recommendation A and two reader passes, was never ratified and is replaced. This version decides only the Jai-workspace parts the slate leaves open.

Moved to D-TARGET-ONE1: where outputs live, per-output `options:` in data or code, `b.output(name)`, `b.profile(name)`, picking an output by name, and `jet build` building every output. Moved to D-SETTING-ORDER1: whether a flag reaches an output with its own options. That ballot removes the old rule that such an output is built exactly as its code says. `b.pin(.optimize, .Size, output: game_web)` gives the exact build instead.

Moved to D-ENTRY-NAMES1: the name `BuildOptions` for the settings value. Moved to D-ENTRY-SHAPE1: `fn build(b: Build)` with no return value, sealing the plan when it returns, and `b.default(app)`. Words: output means a thing the project makes; target means only the platform, as in `#Target(Web)`.

Letters. The first version's option C let an output list profiles by name and build once per profile. It stays removed, because it contradicts D-TARGET-ONE1 option A and could not edit settings from code. The letter C now holds the earlier recommendation.

Order. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1, D-TARGET-ONE1, D-SETTING-ORDER1, D-ENTRY-NAMES1 and D-DEV-STATE1 are ratified with A, and this ballot uses their spellings. Show it beside D-DEV-SERVICES1 and D-SERVICE-WORD1.

Jai's model. A build program calls `compiler_create_workspace(name)`, edits `Build_Options` with `get_build_options` and `set_build_options`, and adds code with `add_build_file` and `add_build_string`. It then reads that workspace's compiler messages in a loop. Code does not cross workspaces unless done on purpose. Program-set options win over command-line flags (Blow OAIqCpqszVw 01:06:25).

Jai's mid-compile changes. Once compiling starts, `set_build_options_dc` changes only three fields: `do_output`, `write_added_strings` and `append_linker_arguments` (Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md:460, 586). Every other option must be set before compiling. The earlier reason for C, that a cache key would depend on compile order, is weak. A setting matters only to the stages that read it.

Shared, copying settings. `b.options()` returns the command's settings. The command picks its profile as D-BUILD-DEFAULT1=B and the profile row of D-SETTING-ORDER1 say. `b.profile(name)` returns a fresh copy of a package.jet profile; an unknown name is a registered error. An output without `options:` uses the command's settings. Settings values are data, while `b` and outputs are handles to the plan, so their methods take no write mark.

Shared, changing outputs. `b.add_source(out, path)` and `b.set_options(out, opts)` change an output until `fn build` returns. `b.generate(name, value, into: out)` is the typed form of D-BUILD-GENVALUE1=A, scoped to one output. The third argument of `b.add_*` stays the list of build steps the output needs (Core/build/declarations.jet:148); the outputs it depends on are the optional fourth argument (:153).

Precedence. This ballot adds no precedence order. Under A, a hook change sits in the entry-code layer. D-SETTING-ORDER1 gives the one order. Options written in package.jet are the package.jet layer, and options written in code are the entry-code layer. Under the ratified D-SETTING-ORDER1=A, a flag reaches every selected output unless a pin refuses it.

Files and commands, in every option. Today `jet build` names the default programmable output's file after it (`build_artifact_path`, Source/CmdCompile.rs:10302-10318); every other build uses the source-file stem (`bin_path`, :10291).

Every named output now goes to `.jet/build/<output>`, so two outputs built from one `run.jet` never collide. A project with no output list keeps its stem path, so zero-setup projects see no change. D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A's `output_dir` may move a path. `jet build` builds outputs in parallel, but events and reports arrive in output-name order. A program that cannot run on this machine, such as a web build, makes `jet run` fail with an error naming the output.

Shared, hooks per output. Compiler stages run once per output, and every stage payload gains `.output`. This is the Jet form of Jai's `if message.workspace != w continue`. Results that never read `.output` are shared when outputs share a compiled record.

Shared, build machine. `$build.host` sits beside the platform facts under `$build` (D-BUILD-FACT3=A). A read is a recorded input in the build record and cache key, so a result is never reused on another kind of machine by mistake. `jet inspect build` shows which host facts were read. The open D-META-HASH1 may respell `$` mechanically.

Option A, changing settings from a hook. In every stage payload, `.output` is the handle of the output being compiled. Its setting calls come from the option table, as on `Build`: `d.output.debug_info(.Full)`, `d.output.write(false)`. A list row adds with `d.output.add_link_args([...])`. Handle calls take no write mark, and the payload stays immutable. `d.output.options` reads the settings as they stood when the stage began. Jet collects setting calls as part of the hook's result, so hooks stay order-free (D-HOOK-STAGES1).

Option A, the rule. A setting may change until the first stage that reads it, and each option-table row records that stage. Fixed at a stage means hooks of that stage and every later stage see it read-only. A later change is a registered error naming the setting and the stage. `jet explain build.<setting>` shows the stage, extending the D-CONF-KEY1 explain form.

Option A, records and caching. Every change records the hook, the stage, and the old and new values. It joins the cache key of the stages after it, so only those re-run. A link-argument change re-links only. No expert permission is needed, because changing a setting is not unsafe. Turning a check `off` still needs the D-JAI-EXPERT1 power, from a hook or from `fn build`.

Option A, layers and tools. A hook change is in the entry-code layer of D-SETTING-ORDER1, and a pinned field cannot be changed by a hook.

A hook's list addition (`add_link_args`) is added after every layer merges, the flag included, as Jai's `append_linker_arguments` is; a pin on that row refuses it. When a flag replaces a hook's scalar change, Jet prints the D-SETTING-ORDER1 note naming the hook.

A dependency hook's grant names each settings group it may change as a result power (D-HOOK-STAGES1 grant identity). Dependency hooks may change code-generation fields and add library names; raw `link_args`, `link`, `write` and `output_dir` change only from main-package hooks, like link and write hooks (D-JAI-EVENTS1). `jet inspect build` marks every setting that attached hooks could still change; after a build it names who changed each.

Fixed-at stages, using the compiler's real order. The compiler moves through Parsed, Resolved, Typed, Prepared and Emitted (crates/jet-foundation/src/AST/metaprogramming.rs:29-35). D-HOOK-STAGES1 maps `compiler.parsed` to Parsed, `compiler.declared` to Resolved, `compiler.checked` to after Prepared, and `compiler.emitted` to Emitted. D-JAI-EVENTS1 adds `compiler.imported` per module, `compiler.settled` after `compiler.checked`, then `build.link`, `build.before_write`, `build.after_write` and `compiler.finished`.

Platform fields (`os`, `arch`, `cpu`, `cpu_features`, `min_os`) are fixed when compiling starts. Source markers such as `#Target(Web)` and `$build.os` folds are read while files are read and imports are chosen. So only `fn build`, package.jet or a flag can set them; no hook can.

Check fields (`bounds`, `null`, `casts`, `overflow`) are fixed when compiling starts. Compile-time code already runs during registration and generic-module expansion (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Registration/Items.rs:700; Sema/Bundle/GenericModules.rs:1085), so no hook stage is early enough.

Code generation fields (`optimize`, `inline`, `lto`, `debug_info`, `frame_pointers`, `vectorize` and the other backend fields) are fixed at `compiler.emitted`. Code generation runs after the last `compiler.settled` round, so hooks through `compiler.settled` may change them.

Link fields (`link_args`, libraries) are fixed at `build.link`, whose hook receives them as its link inputs. `link: .Static` or `.Dynamic` is the output kind, Jai's `output_type`, and is fixed when compiling starts. Write fields (`write`, `output_dir`) are fixed when the file is written, so a `build.before_write` hook may still turn writing off or move the file.

`write_generated` (Jai's `write_added_strings`) is fixed after the last `compiler.settled` round. Every field not named above is fixed when compiling starts; only a later decision may move a row later.

Fields readable through `$build` (target, profile, `settings:` values and stamps, D-BUILD-FACT3=A) are fixed when compiling starts, because `prep if` folds read them while files are read. So every row's fixed-at stage is static and `jet explain` shows it without compiling.

Improvements over Jai. Jai changes three settings mid-compile (`do_output`, `write_added_strings`, `append_linker_arguments`). A covers them as `write`, `write_generated` and `add_link_args`, and lets every other setting change until its stage. The plan is a value, so tools list every output and its planned settings without compiling. Order is fixed, while Jai's compilation order varied between runs (Blow KHIeP_-Kp00 01:28:00). Every change is recorded with its hook and stage, and outputs are typed, with no 0 for failure.

Not copied from Jai. Changing the platform or check fields mid-compile: files already read and folded for one platform would be wrong. Making workspaces from any compile-time code: only `fn build` makes outputs (D-BUILDENTRY1). Jai's pull loop becomes pushed hooks plus the read-only ordered `compiler.advanced.Session.stages()` (D-JAI-EVENTS1=A), unless B wins.

Option B restated in slate terms. Outputs come from the one list, and `fn build` reads each output's compiler messages in a loop with `b.messages(out)`. It may add code or change settings mid-compile. It needs the D-JAI-EXPERT1 metaprogramming permission. Settings are known only after compiling, so tools cannot list them, and results depend on message order.

Option C. This was the recommendation before round 3. `fn build` shapes every output, Jet seals the plan when it returns, and no setting changes while an output compiles. Hooks may still add code at `compiler.settled`. A library found during compiling can only be added by replacing linking with a `build.link` hook.

Research. Jai: The Way to Jai book/30A:27-67 and examples/30/30.13; Blow OHZwYYW9koI 00:02:01-00:03:01; host-imports workspace LPdMNsL5MgI 00:03:21. Zig's build.zig makes several artifacts, each with its own target and optimize mode. Cargo build scripts read HOST and TARGET as separate variables because scripts confused them. No adoption numbers were gathered.

Design away, loss one: new names. Calling outputs workspaces was rejected, because Jet's workspace already means a group of packages. Keeping file-stem folders was rejected, because two outputs from one source file collide. Result: a porting guide maps each Jai call, and `jet build` prints every output path. Negligible.

Design away, A loss: planned and final settings may differ. Showing only final settings was rejected, because tools must read the plan without compiling. Forbidding hook changes was rejected as option C's cost. Result: `jet inspect build` marks changeable settings and names the hooks, and the build record shows final values and who changed them. Negligible.

Design away, A loss: platform and check fields still fix before compiling. Letting hooks change them mid-compile was rejected, because code already read for one platform would be wrong. Re-running the whole compile after such a change was rejected, because it hides a second build and can loop. Result: Jai fixes them too, and `fn build` sets them from `$build.host`. Negligible.

Design away, host facts. No host facts was rejected, because cross-compiling build code must pick host tools. Result: host reads are recorded inputs, never silently shared across machines. No loss remains. `b.probe(name, "find_program", program)` already finds one host program, but it cannot tell build code the host OS or CPU to choose between tools or settings. `$build.host` covers that and is recorded like a probe.

Amendments in every option. Amends D-CTEFFECT1=A: host identity moves from ambient to a recorded input in its tier table. Amends D-BUILD-FACT3=A: `$build.host` joins the `$build` root. Amends D-HOOK-STAGES1=A: every stage payload gains `.output`, and results that read it are keyed per output. Amends D-BUILD-GENVALUE1=A: `b.generate` gains `into:`.

More amendments in every option. Amends D-BUILDTARGET1=A, beyond the D-TARGET-ONE1 changes: `b.options`, `b.add_source` and `b.set_options` are new. Amends D-JAI-EVENTS1=A: `build.link` runs once per output, and `compiler.settled` items go to the output being compiled.

Amendments if A wins. Amends D-HOOK-STAGES1=A: `.output` is a handle whose setting calls are a new result power beside findings and items, merged per output and field.

Amends D-JAI-EVENTS1=A: payloads stay immutable; only `.output` setting calls record changes, and `Session.stages()` sees `.output` read-only. Amends D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A: every option-table row gains a fixed-at stage. Amends D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A and D-TARGET-ONE1=A: the seal at `fn build` return fixes outputs, sources and generated values; each output's settings stay changeable by hooks until their fixed-at stage. `jet inspect build` and `core.build.graph` read planned values; the build record holds final ones.

Amends D-SETTING-ORDER1=A (if A wins): a hook's setting change sits in the entry-code layer. So a flag beats a scalar change (with the usual note naming the hook), and a pinned field cannot be changed by a hook (registered error naming the pin). A hook's list addition such as `add_link_args` is added after every layer merges, the flag included; a pin on that row refuses it.

If B wins: amends D-JAI-EVENTS1=A, which answered Jai's message loop with pushed hooks and a read-only ordered view. `b.messages(out)` adds a pull loop in `fn build` whose `b.add_code` and `b.set_options` change an output mid-compile. It needs the open D-JAI-EXPERT1 permission.

If C wins: no amendment beyond those in every option.

Not changed by this ballot: D-BUILD-DEFAULT1=B, which still picks the command's settings, and D-BUILD-INCLUDE1=A. D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A is amended by D-SETTING-ORDER1 and D-ENTRY-NAMES1; its fields reach each output through D-TARGET-ONE1's `options:`. D-BUILDENTRY1=B is amended by D-ENTRY-SHAPE1.

Prerequisites and names. `fn build` runs in the compile-time engine, so every part needs the native compile-time host (#5003). Register `b.options`, `b.add_source`, `b.set_options`, `into:`, `.output`, `$build.host`, `HostInfo`, the unknown-profile error, the shared-output-path error and the output-only module error (I7).

Under A also register the `.output` setting calls and the `add_<list row>` form. Register the new `write` and `write_generated` fields (Jai's `do_output` and `write_added_strings`), the fixed-at column, the fixed-setting error and the conflicting-change error. Cutover: `bin_path` names files by output, and `build_session_add_target` in Core/build/declarations.jet:133 takes `options:`.

Review: one fresh combined pass (beginner + adversarial), agent CohesionReview, Claude family, 2026-10-19, per owner directive for one review. Repaired: gist and shared parts, open-sibling wording, D-JAI-EVENTS1 amendment for B, amendment lists, per-output file visibility, `b.options()` timing, output paths, worked example, fourth argument, order. Round 3 (owner feedback): redesigned so settings may change until Jet uses them; review pending. Round 3 review: Round3Review, 2026-10-19; repaired handle calls, dependency-hook powers, seal amendment, static fixed-at stages, write_generated and link kind, list appends, merge identity.

options.name: Change a setting until Jet uses it
options.detail: Build code shapes outputs as in every option. In addition, compiler hooks may change the settings of the output being compiled, through the stage payload. A setting may change until the first stage that reads it, such as link arguments until linking. Every change is recorded with its hook and stage, and only the stages after it re-run.
options.technical:
Shared shaping, as in every option. `fn build` copies settings with `b.options()` or `b.profile(name)` and makes outputs. It changes them with `b.add_source(out, path)`, `b.set_options(out, opts)` and `b.generate(name, value, into: out)` until it returns. It reads `$build.host`. Every hook payload carries `.output`, and each output goes to `.jet/build/<output>`.

Changing settings from a hook. In every stage payload, `.output` is the handle of the output being compiled. Its setting calls come from the option table, as on `Build`: `d.output.debug_info(.Full)`, `d.output.write(false)`. A list row adds with `d.output.add_link_args([...])`. Handle calls take no write mark, and the payload stays immutable. `d.output.options` reads the settings as they stood when the stage began.

Jet collects the setting calls a hook made as part of its result, beside its findings and items. Changes apply when the stage ends, or at the end of each `compiler.settled` round.

The rule. A setting may change until the first stage that reads it. Fixed at a stage means hooks of that stage and every later stage see it read-only. Each row of the option table records that stage. Changing a setting after its stage is a registered error, for example `os is fixed when compiling starts for output game_web; set it in fn build`. `jet explain build.link_args` shows each layer and the stage where the setting is fixed.

Merging, as D-HOOK-STAGES1 already merges results. A scalar field is one merge identity per output for the whole build, across stages and `settled` rounds, so two different values from any hooks are a registered error naming both. A settings change adds no item, so it never starts another `settled` round. List additions, such as `add_link_args`, coexist in a fixed order by hook identity. Equal values deduplicate.

Records and caching. Every change records the hook, the stage, and the old and new values in the build record. The change joins the cache key of the stages after it, so a link-argument change re-links only. The hook result itself is cached as D-HOOK-STAGES1 already caches results.

Layers and authority. A hook change sits in the entry-code layer of D-SETTING-ORDER1. A pinned field cannot be changed by a hook; that is an error naming the pin.

A hook's list addition (`add_link_args`) is added after every layer merges, the flag included, as Jai's `append_linker_arguments` is; a pin on that row refuses it. When a flag replaces a hook's scalar change, Jet prints the D-SETTING-ORDER1 note naming the hook.

A dependency hook's grant names each settings group it may change as a result power (D-HOOK-STAGES1 grant identity). Dependency hooks may change code-generation fields and add library names; raw `link_args`, `link`, `write` and `output_dir` change only from main-package hooks, like link and write hooks (D-JAI-EVENTS1). Turning a check `off` needs the D-JAI-EXPERT1 power from a hook, exactly as from `fn build`.

Tools. `jet inspect build` lists planned values from `fn build` without compiling. It marks each setting that a stage with attached hooks could still change, and names those hooks. After a build it shows final values and who changed each.

Fixed-at stages, using the compiler's real order. The compiler moves through Parsed, Resolved, Typed, Prepared and Emitted (crates/jet-foundation/src/AST/metaprogramming.rs:29-35). D-HOOK-STAGES1 maps `compiler.parsed` to Parsed, `compiler.declared` to Resolved, `compiler.checked` to after Prepared, and `compiler.emitted` to Emitted. D-JAI-EVENTS1 adds `compiler.imported` per module, `compiler.settled` after `compiler.checked`, then `build.link`, `build.before_write`, `build.after_write` and `compiler.finished`.

Platform fields (`os`, `arch`, `cpu`, `cpu_features`, `min_os`) are fixed when compiling starts. Source markers such as `#Target(Web)` and `$build.os` folds are read while files are read and imports are chosen. So only `fn build`, package.jet or a flag can set them; no hook can.

Check fields (`bounds`, `null`, `casts`, `overflow`) are fixed when compiling starts. Compile-time code already runs during registration and generic-module expansion (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Registration/Items.rs:700; Sema/Bundle/GenericModules.rs:1085), so no hook stage is early enough.

Code generation fields (`optimize`, `inline`, `lto`, `debug_info`, `frame_pointers`, `vectorize` and the other backend fields) are fixed at `compiler.emitted`. Code generation runs after the last `compiler.settled` round, so hooks through `compiler.settled` may change them.

Link fields (`link_args`, libraries) are fixed at `build.link`, whose hook receives them as its link inputs. `link: .Static` or `.Dynamic` is the output kind, Jai's `output_type`, and is fixed when compiling starts. Write fields (`write`, `output_dir`) are fixed when the file is written, so a `build.before_write` hook may still turn writing off or move the file.

`write_generated` (Jai's `write_added_strings`) is fixed after the last `compiler.settled` round. Every field not named above is fixed when compiling starts; only a later decision may move a row later.

Fields readable through `$build` (target, profile, `settings:` values and stamps, D-BUILD-FACT3=A) are fixed when compiling starts, because `prep if` folds read them while files are read. So every row's fixed-at stage is static and `jet explain` shows it without compiling.

options.name: Jai's message loop
options.detail: A close copy of Jai. Build code makes outputs, then reads each output's compiler messages in a loop while it compiles. It may add code or change settings as messages arrive. The loop needs the expert metaprogramming permission, and the final settings exist only after compiling.
options.technical:
Shared shaping is as in A: `b.options()`, `b.profile(name)`, `b.add_source`, `b.set_options`, `into:`, `$build.host`, `.output` on hook payloads and `.jet/build/<output>`.

`b.messages(out)` pauses `fn build` while that output compiles and hands it each compiler message, in compile order, as D-JAI-EVENTS1 payloads. Inside the loop, `m.output` setting calls and `b.add_code(out, code)` may change the output mid-compile, like Jai's `set_build_options_dc`.

The loop needs the metaprogramming permission of the open D-JAI-EXPERT1. The final settings exist only after compiling, so the cache key includes what the loop did, and results depend on message order.

options.name: Fixed before compiling
options.detail: Build code copies settings, shapes every output and reads the build machine. When `fn build` returns, Jet seals the plan, and no setting changes while an output compiles. Hooks may still add code.
options.technical:
Shared shaping only. `fn build` copies settings with `b.options()` or `b.profile(name)`, makes outputs, and changes them with `b.add_source`, `b.set_options` and `b.generate(..., into:)` until it returns. Then Jet seals the plan, and no setting changes while an output compiles.

Hooks may still add code at `compiler.settled` and may replace linking at `build.link`. A hook that finds the program needs a library can only add it by replacing the whole link step.

comparisons.note: Each workspace has its own build options and files, made by the build program.
build.zig creates several artifacts, each with its own target and optimize mode.
HOST and TARGET are separate variables because build scripts confused them.

recommendation.why: A gives Jai's mid-compile changes and more, through ordinary hooks: a setting may change until Jet uses it. Every change is recorded, so builds stay repeatable and only later steps re-run.
gains: Adds link libraries or debug info after seeing the code.
Every setting Jet has not yet used may change, beyond Jai's three.
Each change is recorded with its hook and stage.
Only the stages after a change re-run.

losses.loss: Planned settings may differ from final ones.
losses.mitigation: `jet inspect build` marks settings hooks may change; the build record names who changed each.

losses.loss: Platform and check settings still fix before compiling.
losses.mitigation: Jai fixes them too; `fn build` sets them from `$build.host` before compiling.

whyNot.reason: It reopens the settled hook answer to Jai's message loop, tools cannot list settings without compiling, and a basic change needs an expert permission.
A hook that finds the program needs a library cannot add a link argument without replacing the whole link step.

recommendation.tradeoff: Settings may move during a build, for Jai's power with a record of each change.

decisions.title: Context parity: readable context, package-owned keys, scratch memory and an assertion handler
decisions.situation: Jai passes a hidden context into every function, holding the current allocator, logger, scratch memory and assertion handler. Jet has a block that sets the allocator, logger or deadline for a region, but code cannot read the context, packages cannot add entries, and there is no scratch memory. Jai games use the context for per-frame scratch memory, swappable logging and data passed through libraries without new parameters. The vote decides how far Jet's context goes; we recommend matching Jai with typed entries owned by packages.
decisions.gist: How far should Jet's context go to match Jai's context, push_context and temporary storage?
decisions.lesson: The context is a small set of values every function can see without parameters, such as the current allocator. `#Context(field: value) { }` changes it for a block. Scratch memory is fast memory cleared all at once, for example every frame. Reading the context is an effect, so it shows in a function's effect list.
decisions.story: Ines writes a game loop. Each frame builds hundreds of short strings and temporary lists, and she wants them all gone at the end of the frame. Her renderer library also needs the frame number for debug overlays, deep inside code that has no frame parameter.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

FIELDS UNDER A. allocator, logger, deadline (existing, now readable), scratch, on_assert, print (default formats, Jai print_style), thread (worker index) and trace (stack trace). The `#Context` block stays the only way to change them, restored on every exit (Jai push_context, push_allocator). E0761's field list grows, E0762 types the new fields, and E0760 stays.

KEYS. `#ContextKey pub frame_index: Int{0}` declares a typed key owned by its module (Jai #add_context). It resolves through imports like any name, so two packages' keys never clash (regret, SSVHWrYG974 00:40:00).

EFFECT. Every read of a context field or key adds a `Context` read effect to the function's row, so a function's dependence on context is static and listed. Pure `-[]>` functions and C callbacks, which have an empty row (D-CABI-CALLBACK1), cannot read context. That rule stands unchanged. Who set a value is dynamic and is not claimed.

PROPAGATION. The context belongs to the running task. Function values, generics and trait calls read the caller's current context with no signature change. A spawned task observes the context current when it is spawned (D-NETTASK1). Code entered from C through an exported function starts from the program's root context, which is fixed at load.

SCRATCH. `context.scratch` is an ordinary `mem.Arena`, not a second memory family (D-ALLOC1). A default per-task scratch arena of scratch_size bytes, 64 KiB unless set (D-JAI-BUILDOPT1), exists. `#Context(scratch: a)` swaps in another. Values from scratch are arena views: escape is E0631 and use after reset is E0632 where the arena binding is visible.

Elsewhere each view carries the arena's reset count, checked on every tier at the cost of one compare per read, so a stale read is a located stop, never a garbage read. When scratch is full, the arena's own rule applies (D-ALLOCFAIL1): try_ calls return an error and plain calls stop with a located error. Nothing grows silently. Scratch counts as a declared allocator for L0506.

An unannotated allocation uses context.allocator, which defaults to the program allocator, as today.

HANDLER. on_assert receives the location and message before a failed assertion stops. It may log or show a dialog but cannot resume.

PREP. In prep code, context reads see the build's root context with no scratch unless set. The meaning is the same on every tier (I9).

PREREQUISITE. Defect #5030 (allocator and logger ignored at run time) must be fixed first.

FROZEN CARD. #3502 (context extensions) was frozen when the owner asked what context adds. The owner's 2026-10-16 direction that every Jai feature be supported reopens it for this vote.

EVIDENCE. The Way to Jai book/25A:17-35 lists Context_Base fields. Blow ciGQCP6HgqI shows the context, logger and thread index. SSVHWrYG974 shows temporary storage and #add_context. FCbUV8oSDgI 00:29:00 explains context instead of thread-local storage. Wp9XD5FKZ2c 01:40:06-01:43:44 covers temporary storage. These timestamps come from the mining notes. Odin adopted Jai's context. Zig's explicit allocators are the option C model.

decisions.title: General defer: run any statement when a block ends
decisions.situation: Defer schedules work to run when the current block ends, so cleanup sits next to setup, such as logging the time right after a timer starts. Jai lets you defer any statement or block. Jet's rules allow only a deferred resource close, plus a library call, scope.guard, that runs a function at block end; the owner asked for defer when ratifying those rules. The vote decides whether `defer` takes any statement and replaces scope.guard; we recommend yes, keeping close as the one closing word.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's `defer` run any statement at block end, replacing scope.guard, like Jai's defer?
decisions.lesson: A block is code between braces. Defer runs a statement when its block ends, however it ends: normally, by return, by break, or by an error. Today only `defer close(^file)` works, `^` meaning the value is handed over; `scope.guard(() -> ...)` runs a function at block end. A and B reverse the rule against general defer.
decisions.story: Dev ports a Jai job system. Every worker marks a counter, logs its timing and restores a debug flag at the end of the block with defer. In Jet each of those needs a scope.guard value with a throwaway name and a closure.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling. A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

SEMANTICS UNDER A. `defer stmt` or `defer { block }` registers at that point and runs at every exit of its block: normal end, return, break or next, error exits and stops.

ORDER. Each block keeps one reverse-order list: a binding's automatic cleanup is registered at its declaration, and each defer where it is written. So `f := open(p); defer print(f.name)` prints before f closes.

VALUES. A return value is computed before deferred code runs: `n := 1; defer { n = 2 }; return n` returns 1. Deferred code sees variables as they are at exit.

SAFETY. Ownership is checked in run order: a deferred action may not use a value that an earlier-running action consumed. So `defer f.flush()` written before `defer close(^f)` is an error, because close runs first. A deferred body may not return, break, next or use `?`. A failing call inside must be handled there, so an exit never carries two errors. Each rule has a registered code (I4).

Deferred code's effects join the enclosing function's row, and unsafe operations inside still need `#Unsafe("reason")`.

TIERS AND STOPS. Defers run exactly where automatic cleanup runs, on every profile. Under `--small` (abort on panic), neither runs on a panic, as today, so defer adds no tier difference (I9). During cancellation, deferred code runs like cleanup, with wait points inside shielded. An explicit process stop runs active defers. A host kill does not.

PLACES. Defer is legal in any block, including expression and prep blocks, but not at module scope. Inside a macro (D-JAI-CODE1), a defer in the pasted code runs when that pasted block ends. Attaching work to the caller's block is not proposed.

RESOURCES. `defer close(^x)` stays the one closing word (S63). A lint flags `defer x.release()` on a resource and suggests `close(^x)`, so A does not revive the per-type closing verbs of D-SHAPE-RESOURCE2's rejected option C.

AMENDS. S63's rule 'There is no general deferred statement or block' (E0003) is reversed. scope.guard (`core.mem.scope`) retires in one cutover, with its examples moved to defer. The owner's comment when ratifying D-SHAPE-RESOURCE1 was 'But I want to support defer and have one consistent word for closing any type'.

WORK. A general Defer node replaces the close-only one through the AST, TIR and code generators, and about thirty sema walkers learn it.

EVIDENCE. Jai defer (The Way to Jai. Blow QX46eLqq1ps 00:23:40-00:28:30 and jjCfAg_gtDw 01:32:24, from the mining notes). Blow replaced destructors with defer and macros. Zig and Swift use block-scoped defer. Go's function-scoped defer is a known trap in loops.

decisions.title: Layout control: packed structs, overlapping fields and relative pointers
decisions.situation: Low-level programs sometimes need exact memory control: structs without padding, fields sharing the same bytes, or links stored as small offsets so a saved file loads without fixing addresses. Jai offers all three as language features. Jet offers C layout, alignment, column layout and a byte reader, but none of these three. The vote decides which Jet adds; we recommend all three, each checked so safe code never misreads memory.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add packed structs, overlapping fields and relative pointers, like Jai's #no_padding, #place and *~s32?
decisions.lesson: Padding is unused space the compiler adds so fields line up; packing removes it. Overlapping fields share the same bytes, as in a C union. A relative pointer stores the distance from itself to its target. So a block of data still works after it is moved or saved as one piece.
decisions.story: Yuki writes a save-game format and a network protocol. The protocol header must match the wire byte for byte, and the save file holds a linked list she wants to load with one read and no pointer fixing. Jai handles both; in Jet she writes byte code by hand.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

PACKED UNDER A. `#Layout(c, packed)` removes padding. Fields use unaligned loads and stores. Every borrow position takes a copy: reference, method receiver, view parameter and interpolation. Explicit `&` or `^` on a packed field is a registered error, as is a method that would change a packed field through a reference. Assign the field instead. Packed fields cost unaligned loads and stores on some processors. Atomic and Rel fields are not allowed in a packed struct.

With `align(N)`, the struct's alignment is N while fields stay unpadded (D-PLACE1's maximum rule, natural alignment 1). `Header.$layout.size` is 5.

OVERLAY. `#Layout(overlay)` starts every field at offset 0. Its size is the largest field plus trailing padding. Fields must be plain data: integers, floats, fixed byte lists and plain layouts, as `uninit` requires (E0423). Reading a field is safe when every bit pattern is valid for its type (integers, floats, byte lists). A field with invalid patterns, such as Bool or an enum, is read only inside `#Unsafe("reason")`.

Jai `#place` (partial overlap) maps to an overlay of a struct and a list: `#Layout(overlay) struct V { p: XYZ, xyz: [F32#3] }`. One mechanism covers both. No separate field marker is added.

RELATIVE POINTERS. `Rel<T, I32>` holds a signed offset from the field's own address. Zero means none, so a node cannot point to itself and `Rel<T, I32>?` costs no extra space. Rel is a field type, not a pointer: safe code follows it only through `mem.Image`, a loaded byte buffer. `follow` checks the target lies inside the image, is aligned and has room for T.

`img.link(from, to)` sets an offset, failing when the distance does not fit or a side is outside the image. A struct holding a Rel cannot be copied or moved out of an image (registered error), because its offset would point elsewhere. `follow` returns a view whose lifetime is the image's. `rel.get()` without an image needs `#Unsafe`, matching S58's pointer rules.

Image checks are bounds checks, so the unchecked_bounds power of D-JAI-EXPERT1 removes them like others. Layout types must use sized fields. Jet's Int is arbitrary precision and is refused under `#Layout(c)` (D-REPRC1). These forms follow S58's `use core.mem` discovery rule like `#Layout(c)` today. JAI. Source concepts map. Jai's relative-pointer encoding (zero null, high-bit XOR, Blow GQj8fzxpdrk 00:03:11) differs, so saved Jai bytes do not load unchanged.

Tsoding found built-in support catches type errors his hand-written C missed (_HGkhvpCbsk 01:46:44, mining notes). Column layout (Jai's user-level SOA) is already `#Layout(columnar)` (D-SOA1).

EVIDENCE. The Way to Jai Appendix C (#no_padding, #place). Blow Z0tsNFZLxSU and GQj8fzxpdrk (relative pointers, 2017). Rust made references to misaligned packed fields an error after years of undefined behaviour.

options.name: All three, checked
options.detail: `packed` removes padding. `overlay` starts every field at offset 0, for plain-data fields only. `Rel<T, I32>` stores an offset from its own address and is followed through `mem.Image`, which checks bounds, alignment and type.
options.technical: `#Layout(c, packed)`. `#Layout(overlay)` with plain-data fields. `Rel<T, I8|I16|I32|I64>` field type, zero meaning none. `mem.Image` wraps loaded bytes: `root<T>()` and `follow(rel)` return views into the image, `link(from, to)!` failing when out of range or outside the image. Raw `rel.get()` needs `#Unsafe`.
options.code:
#Layout(c, packed) struct Header { tag: U8, length: U32 }      // Header.$layout.size == 5
#Layout(overlay) struct Bits32 { f: F32, u: U32 }               // u reads f's bytes
#Layout(c) struct Node { next: Rel<Node, I32>?, value: I64 }
img :: mem.Image.load(bytes)?
first :: img.root<Node>()?
second :: img.follow(first.next)?          // checked; a view into img

options.name: Packed and overlapping only
options.detail: packed and overlay of A, with A's rules. Links in saved data are stored as indexes into a list.
options.technical: As A without Rel and mem.Image.

options.name: Byte reader and indexes
options.detail: The ratified byte reader and binary patterns decode packed formats today. Links are indexes into a list.
options.technical: No change.
options.code:
r :: Reader.over(bytes)
header :: Header{ tag: r.read_u8()?, length: r.read_u32_le()? }
f :: math.from_bits(r.read_u64_le()?)        // 64-bit bit view as Float
nodes: [Node]                                // links are indexes

comparisons.note: References to possibly misaligned packed fields are rejected; reading a union field needs unsafe.
comparisons.code:
#[repr(C, packed)] struct Header { tag: u8, length: u32 }
union Bits32 { f: f32, u: u32 }

comparisons.note: packed struct and extern union are explicit layout forms.
comparisons.code: const Header = packed struct { tag: u8, length: u32 };

comparisons.note: Unions and #pragma pack; misaligned access is undefined behaviour.
comparisons.code:
#pragma pack(push, 1)
struct Header { uint8_t tag; uint32_t length; };

recommendation.why: Games and file formats use these forms, and Jai builds them in. Checking every read keeps them safe.
gains: Jai's layout control with no unchecked reads.
Wire formats become plain structs.

losses.loss: Relative pointers work only inside a loaded image.
losses.mitigation: The image is the case they exist for; copying a Rel-holding struct out of it is a compile error.

losses.loss: Packed fields cannot be borrowed.
losses.mitigation: Every borrow position takes a copy automatically, and `&` on a packed field explains why.

whyNot.reason: B handles wire formats but leaves saved linked data to indexes, the case Jai's relative pointers solve.
C decodes formats well but gives no struct view of packed bytes and no way to write them as structs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three explicit layout forms with checked access, for Jai's memory control.

It found relative pointers unsafe after copies and an unchecked get; they are now followed only through a checked image, and overlays hold plain data only.

surface.lesson: Padding is unused space the compiler adds so fields line up; packing removes it. Overlapping fields share the same bytes, as in a C union. A relative pointer stores the distance from itself to its target. So a block of data still works after it is moved or saved as one piece.

current.note: Today Jet has C layout, alignment and column layout, and reads wire formats with a byte reader.

wild.note: #no_padding, #place and relative pointers (The Way to Jai Appendix C; Blow, 'Demo: Relative Pointers', 2017).

options.name: All three, checked
options.gist: Packed structs, overlapping plain-data fields and relative pointers read through a checked image.
gains: Binary formats map to structs exactly.
Saved linked data loads with one read.
Reads are checked unless an expert power removes checks.
losses: Relative pointers work only inside a loaded image.

#Layout(overlay) struct Bits32 { f: F32, u: U32 }               // u reads f's bytes
#Layout(c) struct Node { next: Rel<Node, I32>?, value: I64 }
img :: mem.Image.load(bytes)?
first :: img.root<Node>()?
second :: img.follow(first.next)?          // checked; a view into img

options.name: Packed and overlapping only
options.gist: Add packed structs and overlapping fields; no relative pointers.
gains: Covers wire formats and bit views.
losses: Saved linked data uses indexes or hand-written offsets.

options.name: Byte reader and indexes
options.gist: Keep today's layouts; read wire formats with the byte reader and store links as indexes.
gains: No new layout forms or unsafe surface.
losses: Writing a packed format needs hand-written byte code.
No struct view of packed bytes.

proposed.code:
r :: Reader.over(bytes)
header :: Header{ tag: r.read_u8()?, length: r.read_u32_le()? }
f :: math.from_bits(r.read_u64_le()?)        // 64-bit bit view as Float
nodes: [Node]                                // links are indexes

gains: Jai's layout control with no unchecked reads.
Wire formats become plain structs.

losses.loss: Relative pointers work only inside a loaded image.
losses.mitigation: The image is the case they exist for; copying a Rel-holding struct out of it is a compile error.

losses.loss: Packed fields cannot be borrowed.
losses.mitigation: Every borrow position takes a copy automatically, and `&` on a packed field explains why.

whyNot.reason: B handles wire formats but leaves saved linked data to indexes, the case Jai's relative pointers solve.
C decodes formats well but gives no struct view of packed bytes and no way to write them as structs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three explicit layout forms with checked access, for Jai's memory control.

decisions.title: Small Jai conveniences: flag sets, fall-through, member conversion and fixed enum values
decisions.situation: Jai has small conveniences Jet lacks: enums whose cases combine as bit flags, fall-through between switch cases, and structs that pass as one of their fields. It also has enums whose every value must be written. Other Jai conveniences, such as any-type arguments and stable arrays, already have Jet forms. The vote decides whether Jet adds the four missing ones; we recommend all four, each checked.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add Jai's flag enums, fall-through, member conversion and fixed enum values in checked forms?
decisions.lesson: Jai is a game language with many small shortcuts. A flag set stores several enum cases as bits in one number. Fall-through runs the next match arm's body too. Member conversion lets a struct pass where one of its fields' types is expected.
decisions.story: Joe ports a Jai tool of ten thousand lines. Most of it maps cleanly, but permission flags, fall-through switches, embedded structs and enums with fixed on-disk values each need a different workaround.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

THE ITEMS UNDER A. (1) Flag sets (Jai enum_flags): `Set<E>` over a fieldless enum of up to 64 cases is stored as a bit mask. Case i is bit i in declaration order. For C flags, a `#Specified` enum whose values are single bits maps each case to its own value. Any other value is a compile error. This changes Set's storage for small enums only. Its methods and printing are unchanged (amends D-COLLBREADTH1's storage note).

`.bits()` and fallible `Set<E>.from_bits(n)` cross C boundaries. No new enum kind is added. (2) `#Through` after a match arm (Jai #through) runs the next arm's body as well. That arm's bindings are not available, and the last arm cannot fall through. Or-patterns stay the tool for shared bodies. Fall-through is for 'do this, then also that'.

(3) `#As` on a struct field (Jai #as): the struct converts to that field's type where that type is expected. One #As per type, and the conversion is a view of the field, never a copy. (4) `#Specified enum` (Jai #specified): every case states its value, and changing one on a public type is flagged as a breaking change. ALREADY COVERED, NOT RE-PROPOSED. Jai ..Any maps to trait-bounded variadics `...Debug` (D-ANY-JAI1. No top type).

Jai xx maps to `U8.from_int(n)?` (D-SHAPE-CONVERT1). Bucket arrays map to `Pool<T>`/`Id<T>`, which give stable identities. Stable raw addresses stay behind `#Unsafe`, a deliberate difference from Jai. A custom entry symbol is the freestanding target profile's entry fact (D-TARGET-SURFACE1). C++ methods and non-POD returns are handled by the `cpp.*` binder (D-FFI-CPP1). Jai `#type,isa` maps to distinct types with an explicit conversion.

NOT PROPOSED. Identifier backslashes (public sources do not show their meaning) and textual #load (Jet modules use explicit names). Also #char (Jet has 'a'), #bytes (#FFI(asm) covers raw bytes), and #intrinsic and #runtime_support (compiler-internal in both languages).

EVIDENCE. The Way to Jai Appendix C rows. Blow 8tMq3QZyz8s 00:02:52 (enum_flags), from the mining notes. C# [Flags], Rust enum-set crates and Odin `using` fields are the precedents.

options.detail: Flag sets, `#Through` and `#Specified` from A. `#As` is left out.
options.technical: As A without `#As`.

options.name: Adopt none
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.

using on a struct field promotes its members, like Jai #as.

gains: The four remaining small Jai conveniences get a home.

losses.mitigation: Only one `#As` field per type, written on the struct, so each conversion has one visible source.

whyNot.reason: B avoids implicit member conversion but drops Jai's main composition tool.
C adds nothing and leaves every small porting gap open.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three markers and a set storage rule, for one-to-one Jai porting.

decisions.title: Changeable globals computed while compiling, of any storable type, with no startup copy
decisions.situation: A program often needs data worked out in advance, such as a table of opcodes or a list of names, that it later changes while running. Jai computes such data while compiling and stores it in the program file, ready to change. In Jet only an unchangeable value may be computed early, so the program must copy the data each time it starts. The earlier draft allowed only fixed-size number tables, because strings and growable lists live in memory the program later grows and frees. The vote decides how far the change goes. We recommend allowing any storable value, stored so the program can grow and free it like memory it made itself.
decisions.gist: May a changeable global start from any value computed while compiling, with no copy when the program starts?
decisions.lesson: A global is a variable declared outside functions; `fn run()` is where the program starts. `NAME :: value` is unchangeable and `name := value` is changeable. Heap memory is memory a running program asks for, grows and gives back; the allocator is the code that hands it out. Strings and growable lists keep their contents on the heap. Baked means computed while compiling and stored in the program file.
decisions.story: Ana's emulator works out an opcode table and a list of instruction names while compiling. At run time it patches table entries and adds names when a cartridge defines new instructions. Jet makes her copy both when the program starts. The earlier draft would have baked the table but still refused the list of names, because it holds strings.
decisions.detail:
Owner question q4tk0q5m asked for a design without the downside of the earlier recommendation, using full control of the compiler and runtime. No keyword is needed for the rule below; `comptime { }`, the ratified respelling of today's `prep { }`, appears only for file reads. Copies are spelled `x.copy()` (D-COPY-WORD1=A). Audit rows A10-A12 in Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md.

THE DOWNSIDE, PRECISELY. The earlier draft, now option B, accepted only fixed-size plain data: numbers, Bool, fixed-size lists and plain structs of those. Such data needs no heap; it is stored inline, as writable data. Strings, growable lists, maps and structs holding them were refused. Their contents live in heap blocks the allocator owns. Bytes in a program file are not allocator blocks today, so growing or freeing them would corrupt the heap.

The only alternative offered, rebuilding such values on the heap before `fn run`, brought back the copy the feature exists to remove.

THE DESIGN UNDER A: A BAKED HEAP. This is written against the native runtime's allocator (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Alloc.jet). Small blocks, up to 4096 bytes, live in 64 KiB slabs; larger blocks are their own page-aligned mappings. Each block has two header words; the slab header holds its links, its free list, its live count and a pointer to its size class's list.

The compiler lays out each baked heap value in exactly that format, in a writable, page-aligned section of the program file. Small blocks fill whole 64 KiB slabs that hold nothing else. Each large block gets its own whole pages, with the usual two header words. Executables load at a fixed address, so every pointer inside baked data is written as its final address at link time.

At start, before user code, the runtime's existing allocator setup does one more thing. It walks a table of baked slabs that the compiler emits, and writes one word into each: the address of that size class's list, which only exists at run time. Full slabs start unlinked with their real live count. A partly filled last slab per size class is also linked into its class's list, a few more stores. That is about one store per 64 KiB of baked data, about 16 stores per MiB.

From then on, baked blocks are ordinary heap blocks. Writing writes in place; growing moves the value to new heap memory and frees the old block; freeing returns the block for reuse. When a baked slab empties, the allocator keeps it as its spare slab or unmaps it, as it does today. Unmapping is safe because those pages hold only that slab.

The same is true for a freed large block's pages. So the free path is unchanged: no new branch, and the same lock as every other block.

Strings keep their two blocks, a 24-byte header and a data block, with capacity equal to length. An empty string is a real 24-byte header block whose data pointer is the runtime's shared empty value, 1, with capacity 0, as today. Baked blocks are not counted as allocations in the counting allocator mode; the counting mode gains a baked-bytes fact, and freeing one takes the same path as any untracked block.

WHAT IT COSTS. First, start time: one store per baked slab. That first write makes the operating system copy that slab's first 4 KiB page; other pages are copied only when the program first writes them. Second, file size: the program file holds the baked bytes. That is inherent to precomputed data in any language. Each build prints the bytes per baked global, extending D-COMPTIME-WORD1's line with the total bytes of early values.

Third, build time: each value is cached by key like every early value and recomputed only when its inputs change. The 10,000,000-step budget applies; `#StepLimit` is ratified, not yet built.

Fourth, scope. The baked heap is built for native executables on the Linux x86-64 runtime first. Other targets, shared libraries (which load at varying addresses) and the Rust tier until it is retired run the same program with the same meaning. They copy baked heap values into the heap before `fn run`, until their allocator gains the same setup step. The receipt names which path a build used.

THE RULE. A changeable file global's starting value is computed while compiling, with no keyword, under the same rule D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A gives file constants. A value that cannot be computed early is an error naming the reason, such as reading the clock; an exhausted budget is E0952, exactly as for file constants. Reading a file still needs `comptime { embed_file(...) }`, as for constants.

The value must be storable. D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A defines it: 'Storable means no tie to a running process and no identity. Handles, resources, borrowed views, live links, raw addresses, shared cells, Atomic<T> and anything holding them are not storable. Functions are storable because they name code in the program; closures are storable when everything they capture is.' A function value in a baked global is a link-time address too.

LIFETIME. Each launch starts from the baked value, and run-time changes are lost on exit. `#Persist` globals are unchanged. Under `jet dev --swap`, a global keeps its live value unless its starting value changed; then it resets, the new value is copied onto the live heap, and dev says so. Blocks from the original program file stay valid and are freed normally.

AMENDS. D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A has two sentences on this. One: 'Mutable and #Persist globals, which are storage the program changes, keep today's literal-only rule'. Two: 'Mutable and #Persist globals keep E0622'. Under A, both become: '#Persist globals keep the literal-only rule and E0622; changeable globals follow the file-constant rule'.

D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A also says 'Jet runs no hidden code before fn run().' A keeps that. The setup step and the fallback copy are runtime work with no user code and no initialization order. They sit beside the allocator setup that already runs before user code. Runtime work: a baked-heap writer in the backend and the slab setup step in Alloc.jet. Registered diagnostics with UI snapshots (I4).

WHY NOT B. B is simple for the runtime but refuses strings, growable lists and maps, the downside the owner asked to remove. WHY NOT C. C keeps today's rule and copies every computed value at each start.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT PATHS. A beginner writes `names := default_names()` at file level and it works. An expert reads the per-global byte line in the build output, and moves a huge, cheap-to-compute value into `fn run` when file size matters more than start time.

EVIDENCE. The Jai Primer shows `#run` initializers baked into the program; Blow notes compile-time heap data is duplicated into static storage (OHZwYYW9koI 00:18:04, 00:21:48). The Way to Jai Appendix C documents `#no_reset`. GraalVM Native Image ships build-time objects as an image heap in the executable.

options.name: Any storable value, baked as ready heap blocks
options.detail: A changeable file global's starting value is computed while compiling, like a file constant's. Any storable value works: numbers, strings, growable lists, maps and structs. The program file holds heap values in the allocator's own block format, so they grow and free like any heap memory, with no startup copy.
options.technical: Sema lifts E0622 for changeable file globals with storable, early-computable initializers. The backend writes baked slabs (whole 64 KiB, one size class each) and page-owned large blocks with final addresses; allocator setup stores one size-class address per baked slab. Free path unchanged. Native Linux x86-64 executables first; other outputs copy before `fn run`.

options.name: Fixed-size plain data only
options.detail: The earlier draft. A changeable global may start from a computed value only if it is plain fixed-size data, with no heap memory inside: numbers, Bool, fixed-size lists and plain structs of those. Strings, growable lists and maps are a build error.
options.technical: Sema accepts a computed initializer for plain fixed-size types only; anything else is a new registered error.

options.name: Keep today's rule
options.detail: A changeable global starts only from a number or Bool literal. Computed data is an unchangeable constant, copied at each start when it must change.
options.technical: No change.

comparisons.note: A #run initializer is stored in the program and stays writable; compile-time heap data is copied into static storage.
A var may start from a comptime value, but comptime values cannot hold heap memory the program later frees.
Objects built at build time ship in the executable as an image heap, mapped when the program starts.

recommendation.why: A lifts the limit to number tables and removes the startup copy for every storable type. Baked data is laid out as the allocator's own blocks, so the program grows and frees it like memory it made itself.
gains: Any storable value can start a changeable global.
No startup copy, and no extra cost per access or free.
Same rule as file constants, with no keyword.

losses.loss: Start does one store per 64 KiB of baked data.
losses.mitigation: About 16 stores per MiB, far cheaper than copying the data.

losses.loss: Some outputs still copy at start until their allocator catches up.
losses.mitigation: Same meaning everywhere; the receipt names the path, and each target gains the setup step.

whyNot.reason: B refuses strings, growable lists and maps, the downside this revision was asked to remove.
C copies every computed value each time the program starts.

recommendation.tradeoff: A baked-heap writer and one allocator setup step, for computed globals of any storable type with no startup copy.

The review found that slab headers need run-time addresses, that freeing could unmap the program image, and that large blocks and other targets were ignored. The design now uses whole slabs, page-owned large blocks, per-slab setup and a stated target scope.

decisions.title: Should Jet translate C source code into editable Jet?
decisions.situation: Many teams own large C programs and want to move them to a safer language a piece at a time. Today Jet can call C code through checked bindings, but it cannot turn C source into Jet source, so every line must be ported by hand. V offers a translator that converted the whole game DOOM, which is a strong reason people try V. The vote decides whether Jet gains a C translator; we recommend one that writes ordinary safe Jet and leaves anything it cannot prove safe in C.
decisions.gist: Should Jet translate C source into editable Jet, function by function?
decisions.lesson: A binding lets Jet call C code that stays in C. A translator rewrites C code as Jet code you then own. Jet already reads C headers with the Clang compiler to make bindings. Either way, C stays callable through bindings.
decisions.explainer: Jet already has source importers for Python, Java, C#, TypeScript, JavaScript and Go. They convert what they can prove and mark the rest with a JT0101 note. C was left out on purpose. The worry was that pointers, macros and undefined behavior would produce unreadable or unsafe Jet. Option A answers that worry by translating only the functions whose meaning Jet can prove. Every other function keeps running as C behind the same checked binding Jet uses today.
decisions.story: Priya maintains a 40,000-line C image library. She wants new code in Jet without a risky rewrite. With a translator she converts the arithmetic and parsing first, keeps the tricky pointer code in C, and replaces it later.
decisions.inWild:
$ v translate test.c        # V's c2v: writes test.v
$ v -translated test.v      # translated files relax V's safety rules
# https://github.com/vlang/c2v (README), vlang/v doc/docs.md 'Translating C to V'
decisions.detail:
Evidence. V's c2v (github.com/vlang/c2v, read 2026-10-16) reads Clang's JSON AST and writes V. It translated Chocolate Doom's game logic (github.com/vlang/doom) and the Doom 3 engine. V marks such files @[translated], which allows globals, pointer writes without unsafe, and C number conversions (vlang/v doc/docs.md:10990-11014).

The DOOM result still links Chocolate Doom's C platform objects. Its README lists broken sound effects and inlined #define constants.

Jet law today. Docs/spec/reference/migration-tier-map.md:28 makes C binding-only (D-ADOPT-TIER1=A). Importers obey D-MIGRATE-SRC1=A: editable output, JT0101 for omissions, a differential oracle, and byte-stable reruns. C headers are already read by one shared Clang extractor (D-CBIND-UPSTREAM1=A, D-CIMPORT1=A, card #4174).

Why V's relaxed-file model is not offered. It would let generated code use raw pointers outside an audited #Unsafe block. That is an I1 exception needing a full ballot, and it adds a second rule set against I8. Option A needs no invariant change, because a function that cannot be proved safe is not translated.

options.name: Safe translation, one function at a time
options.detail: jet import c converts each C function into ordinary Jet when every construct has a proven safe meaning: integer math, loops, structs, arrays with known lengths, pointers used as array views. A function using something it cannot prove stays in C and is called through the checked binding, with a JT0101 note naming the line and the reason. Translated code follows normal Jet rules; there is no relaxed file mode.
options.technical: Extend the shared Clang extractor (D-CBIND-UPSTREAM1=A) from declarations to bodies. Map pointer+length pairs to slices or views, tagged unions to enums, fixed arrays to [T#N]; fixed-width C arithmetic keeps wrapping semantics through explicit wrapping methods. Each translated function gets a differential fixture against the C original (D-MIGRATE-SRC1). The C row of the tier map changes from binder-only to source importer plus binder.

options.name: Keep C binding-only
options.detail: Keep today's rule. C stays C and Jet calls it through checked bindings. Teams port each function by hand behind the binding when they choose.
options.technical: No change to D-ADOPT-TIER1=A; #4174 continues to deepen header import only.
