{"capabilities":{...,"resources":{...}},
 "protocolVersion":"2025-11-25"}

wild.note: It speaks only LSP plus its own documented extension methods.
wild.code: rust-analyzer/expandMacro

options.name: Separate agent adapter
options.gist: An MCP adapter over the same session serves agents.
gains: Editor server speaks only LSP.
Agents keep the environment resource.
losses: Agents use a second endpoint.

options.name: Port as is
options.gist: Keep agent methods on the editor channel.
gains: No change for agents.
losses: Editor reply carries foreign fields.

proposed.code: {"capabilities":{...,"resources":{...}}}

options.name: Drop them
options.gist: No agent methods for now.
gains: Least work.
losses: Agents lose the environment resource.

proposed.code: // resources/read: no server offers it

recommendation.why: The editor channel stays pure LSP, and agents keep their resource through the surface built for them.
gains: Truthful editor capabilities.

losses.loss: Agents connect elsewhere.
losses.mitigation: The adapter uses the same session, so answers match.

whyNot.reason: Breaks the truthful-capability rule.
Removes a working feature.

recommendation.tradeoff: A second endpoint for agents, in exchange for a clean editor server.

decisions.title: Which processes may own the shared workspace session
decisions.situation: A workspace session is one warm Jet compiler that other commands in the same project can attach to, so they reuse its work. Today only `jet dev --serve` may open that shared endpoint. When an editor is open, its language server already holds a warm compiler for the same project. If it cannot share, the editor and `jet dev` check every edit twice with two caches. We recommend letting the language server own the endpoint too, when started with `jet self lsp --serve`.
decisions.gist: Which long-lived processes may open the one shared session endpoint for a workspace: `jet dev --serve` only, the language server too, or any session automatically?
decisions.lesson: A workspace has at most one shared session, guarded by a lock. Other commands attach to it and reuse its checked results. The ratified rule lets only `jet dev --serve` own it. The editor's language server is also a long-lived compiler session for the same files. This vote decides whether it may own the shared endpoint, so one warm brain serves the whole workspace.
decisions.story: Ken edits his game in VS Code, saves, then runs `jet build` in a terminal. The editor has already checked every file. He expects the build to reuse that work instead of checking everything again. When he also runs `jet dev --serve`, he expects the editor and the dev server to share one cache, not keep two.
decisions.inWild:
# TypeScript: the editor's tsserver and tsc --watch share the same Program model
tsc --watch
# Gradle: one build daemon per workspace serves the IDE and the terminal
./gradlew build
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 2.7 and section 5, ballot 3. Ratified: D-LSP1=C (one incremental compiler service, all tools are its clients), D-BUILD-SESSION1=A (only `jet dev --serve` opens a socket; `--session=auto|off|required`), D-JPK-NODAEMON1=A (no resident background daemon).

Under A, `jet self lsp --serve` is opt-in. The first owner holds the workspace lock; a later LSP attaches to it as a client. When the editor closes, the endpoint disappears and a CLI run falls back to a fresh process, saying why under --verbose. The editor-owned session is a foreground process, so D-JPK-NODAEMON1 still holds.

Endpoint security is as ratified: a 0700 per-user directory, symlinks rejected, peer credentials checked, a nonce from .jet/session, and one owner per workspace by lock.

Under C, an editor-started server would listen without any flag. That widens D-BUILD-SESSION1's opt-in rule.

options.name: `jet dev --serve` and `jet self lsp --serve`
options.detail: Either long-lived process may own the workspace endpoint when started with --serve. The first owner holds the lock and the other attaches as a client. A build after editing is faster while the editor is open, and every edit is checked once.
options.code:
# VS Code starts: jet self lsp --serve
$ jet build              # attaches to the editor's warm session
$ jet dev --serve        # lock held by the LSP: dev attaches as a client
# editor closes -> endpoint gone
$ jet build --verbose
note: no workspace session; running a fresh compiler

options.name: Only `jet dev --serve`, as ratified
options.detail: Keep today's rule. Without `jet dev --serve`, a build runs fresh even while the editor is open. With both running, the language server keeps its own engine beside `jet dev`, so there are two warm caches and every edit is checked twice.
options.code:
# VS Code runs jet self lsp (private engine)
$ jet build              # fresh compile; editor's work not reused
$ jet dev --serve        # second warm cache beside the editor's

options.name: Any long-lived session, automatically
options.detail: Every long-lived session opens the endpoint with no flag. Attaching is automatic, but an editor-started process would listen on a socket the user never asked for, which widens the ratified opt-in rule.
options.code:
# VS Code starts: jet self lsp   (listens automatically)
$ jet build              # attaches with no flag

comparisons.note: tsserver is the compiler, so editor and command-line checks come from one engine model.
One build daemon serves both the IDE and terminal builds, but it lives in the background, which Jet ruled out.

recommendation.why: One warm brain per workspace is the point of the ratified editor engine decision. Under B, an open editor and `jet dev` keep two caches and check every edit twice.
recommendation.tradeoff: The editor process may hold the workspace lock; `--session=off` always forces a fresh, independent compile.

whyNot.reason: It keeps two warm caches and checks every edit twice whenever the editor and `jet dev` both run.
It opens a socket without the user's opt-in, widening the ratified session rule.

losses.loss: A build may depend on the editor's session.
losses.mitigation: Attached and fresh builds must be byte-identical, and `--session=off` always forces a fresh compile.

surface.gist: Should the editor's language server, as well as `jet dev`, be allowed to own a workspace's shared session?
surface.lesson: A workspace has at most one shared session; other commands attach and reuse its work. Today only `jet dev --serve` may own it. The editor's language server is also a warm compiler for the same files. Letting it own the session means one warm cache per workspace.

current.note: Only `jet dev --serve` can share; the editor's work is never reused.
current.code:
# editor open, no jet dev running
$ jet build      # checks everything again from scratch

wild.note: The editor's tsserver is the compiler; one engine serves both.
wild.code: tsc --watch

options.name: Dev server or language server
options.gist: Either may own it when started with --serve.
gains: Builds reuse the editor's checked files.
Every edit is checked once.
losses: Builds may depend on the editor process.

proposed.code:
# VS Code: jet self lsp --serve
$ jet build    # attaches to the editor's session
# editor closes
$ jet build    # fresh compile

options.name: Dev server only
options.gist: Keep the ratified rule.
gains: No change.
losses: Two warm caches when both run.
Editor work is never reused.

proposed.code: $ jet build    # fresh, even with the editor open

options.name: Any session, automatically
options.gist: Every long-lived session shares with no flag.
gains: Attaching needs no setup.
losses: Opens a socket nobody asked for.

proposed.code: # VS Code: jet self lsp   (listens automatically)

recommendation.why: One warm brain per workspace is why Jet chose one compiler service for editors. B checks every edit twice when both run.
gains: One cache per workspace.
Faster builds while editing.

losses.loss: Builds may lean on the editor.
losses.mitigation: Attached and fresh builds must match byte for byte; `--session=off` forces fresh.

whyNot.reason: Two caches, double checking.
Sharing without opt-in.

recommendation.tradeoff: The editor may hold the lock, with an always-available fresh path.

decisions.title: The session protocol's wire format
decisions.situation: A compiler session is one running Jet compiler that several tools can talk to: the editor, a build in a terminal, and Jetpack. When a tool attaches from another process, the two sides need a shared message format on the wire. Jet's error reports and build events already have one ratified JSON shape, one object per line. This vote picks the wire format for everything else the session sends. We recommend newline-delimited JSON, so the wire reuses that shape and an attached build prints exactly what a fresh one prints.
decisions.gist: Which message format should Jet's compiler session use between processes: JSON lines, binary frames, or JSON-RPC with editor-protocol framing?
decisions.lesson: When `jet build` attaches to a running session, the two processes exchange requests, events and error reports. Reports and build events already have one ratified JSON form, one object per line. The wire carries no syntax trees or compiled files, only these control messages, so its speed matters little. The choice is mostly about reuse, debugging and keeping one shape per message.
decisions.story: Ken runs `jet dev --serve` for his game, then `jet build --session=required` in a second terminal. When the build fails, he wants the attached build to print exactly what a fresh build prints. When something goes wrong between the two processes, he wants to read the messages with a pipe and `jq`, not a decoder.
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 3 (transports) and section 5, ballot 1. Builds on D-BUILD-SESSION1=A (versioned protocol, request envelope), D-REPORT-MACHINE1=A (one JSON report per line) and D-BUILD-UI1=A (--json streams NDJSON events).

Under A, the first line is hello with the toolchain identity. A mismatch refuses the attach and the CLI falls back to a fresh process, saying why under --verbose. Jetpack reports E1227 as the engine handshake does. There is no negotiation and no compatibility branch.

Reports are the D-REPORT-MACHINE1 object unchanged, and build events are the D-BUILD-UI1 events unchanged. Artifacts never cross the wire; events carry store identities and paths. A line is capped at 1 MiB, as jet.devtools.v1 caps envelopes, and JSON escapes newlines inside reports.

Reuse: CompilerService.jet's tagged-value and CtValue codecs become the JSON codec, and its narrow diagnostic codec is replaced by the report writer. The proposal sets a revisit trigger: a paired measurement if protocol cost passes 5 percent of edit-to-result time on the corpus.

options.name: Newline-delimited JSON
options.detail: One JSON message per line, UTF-8. Reports and build events reuse their ratified shapes byte for byte. Any JSON tool can read the stream. Encoding JSON costs a little on a channel that carries only control messages.

options.name: Binary frames
options.detail: Each message is a fixed header with a tag, a length and a request number, then a binary body in Jet's record codec, as Zig's compiler server does. It is the cheapest to encode. Reports would need a second, binary encoding beside their JSON form, and reading the stream needs a decoder.

options.name: JSON-RPC 2.0 with the editor protocol's framing
options.detail: Each message has a Content-Length header and a JSON-RPC body, as LSP and BSP use. It reuses JSON-RPC ids and error codes. Events become notifications, and request ids reused after a cancel must be handled as in LSP.
options.code:
Content-Length: 88

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"build","params":{"targets":["game"]}}

comparisons.note: Zig's compiler server uses binary frames with a tag and a length, and checks only an exact version string.
comparisons.code: Header{tag: u32 LE, bytes_len: u32 LE} + body

comparisons.note: The Build Server Protocol used by IntelliJ and Metals is JSON-RPC 2.0 with LSP framing.

recommendation.why: Reports and build events already have one ratified JSON home, so A adds no second shape for them. The wire carries no syntax trees or artifact bytes, so binary frames would save little.
recommendation.tradeoff: JSON encoding costs a little; the proposal re-measures if protocol cost ever passes 5 percent of edit-to-result time.

whyNot.reason: It needs a second encoding of every report, and version skew becomes silent corruption unless separately checked.
It adds framing and request-id rules that a line-based stream does not need, for no gain on this channel.

losses.loss: JSON is slower to encode than binary frames.
losses.mitigation: Only control messages cross the wire; a paired measurement is required if cost passes 5 percent.

surface.gist: Which message format should Jet's compiler session use between processes?
surface.lesson: When a build attaches to a running session, the processes exchange requests, events and error reports. Reports and build events already have one ratified JSON form, one object per line. Only these small control messages cross the wire, so speed matters little. The choice is about reuse and debugging.

current.note: Error reports and build events already stream as JSON lines.

wild.note: Zig's compiler server sends binary frames: a tag, a length, then bytes.
wild.code: Header{tag: u32 LE, bytes_len: u32 LE} + body

options.name: JSON lines
options.gist: One JSON message per line, reusing the report shape.
gains: Attached output equals fresh output byte for byte.
Readable with any JSON tool.
losses: Slightly slower than binary.

options.name: Binary frames
options.gist: Tagged binary messages, like Zig's server.
gains: Cheapest to encode.
losses: A second encoding of every report.
Needs a decoder to debug.

proposed.code:
header {tag: u32, len: u32, request: u64}
body   binary record bytes

options.name: JSON-RPC with editor framing
options.gist: Content-Length headers and JSON-RPC bodies, like LSP.
gains: Reuses JSON-RPC ids and error codes.
losses: Extra framing and id rules for no gain here.

proposed.code:
Content-Length: 88

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"build",...}

recommendation.why: Reports and events already have one JSON form, so JSON lines add no second shape. The wire carries only small messages.
gains: One shape per message everywhere.

losses.loss: A little encoding cost.
losses.mitigation: Re-measure if it passes 5 percent of edit-to-result time.

whyNot.reason: It duplicates the report shape and hides version mistakes.
Its framing adds rules this channel does not need.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small encoding cost for one readable shape.

decisions.title: What an update request means for each command that serves the session on stdio
decisions.situation: A tool such as Jetpack or a third-party build tool can start a Jet command with --listen=- and talk to the compiler over standard input and output. The owner chose that every runnable command gets this flag: check, build, test, run and dev. Zig's build tool works the same way, and its main message, update, means do the work again on the newest files. Jet has not said what update means for each command, or whether a stdio session shares the warm compiler that an open editor already runs. The vote decides both. We recommend that update redoes the command's own work, and that a stdio session joins the workspace's running session when there is one.
decisions.gist: What should an update request do on each command started with --listen=-, and should it share a running session?
decisions.lesson: With `--listen=-`, a command reads requests from standard input and writes answers to standard output instead of to the terminal. `update` is the short request that says: do this command's work again on the newest files. A workspace session is a warm compiler run by `jet dev --serve` or `jet self lsp --serve`; other commands can join it.
decisions.story: Lena writes a build-tool plugin for her team's editor. It starts `jet build --listen=-`, sends update after each save and shows the errors. Her teammate's editor already runs `jet self lsp --serve`, a warm compiler for the same folder. Lena wants to know what update does for build, test and run, and whether her plugin checks every file a second time.
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, sections 2.4 and 2.7, and BallotFollowThrough's FOLLOWTHROUGH.md sections 4-9. Ratified: D-SESSION-ENTRY1=C (`--listen=-` on check, build, test, run and dev; each verb must define what an update means). Also D-SESSION-WIRE1=A (NDJSON), D-SESSION-OWNER1=A (`jet dev --serve` and `jet self lsp --serve` may own the workspace endpoint), D-BUILD-SESSION1=A (`--session=auto|off|required`).

WHAT EVERY OPTION SHARES. A `--listen=-` session first sends `hello` with the toolchain identity, then does nothing until asked. It accepts the full request set of section 2.4, such as `check`, `build`, `test`, `query` and `cancel`.

`exit`, or end of input, cancels in-flight work and exits with status 0. A malformed line gets an E2104 report line and the session continues. `--listen=<address>` with anything but `-` is refused with E2104, because sockets stay `--serve` only. `--listen=-` with `--watch` is refused, because `watch{}` is a request. `--listen=-` with `--serve` is refused: one process has one endpoint.

THE UPDATE TABLE (options A and B). `jet check --listen=-`: update is `check{selection}` on the newest revision, for the files or package named on the command line. It returns reports and writes no artifacts. `jet build --listen=-`: update is `build{targets, profile}` from the command line. It returns events and artifact paths; bytes never cross the wire.

`jet test --listen=-`: update is `test{filter}` from the command line. Test output is captured into `test.*` events. `jet run --listen=-`: update builds, then runs the target once with the program arguments. The program's output becomes `run.output` events and never reaches the terminal, and its standard input is empty. An update while the program runs cancels it and starts again.

`jet dev --listen=-`: update is `dev.update{mode: auto}`, a swap or restart under the D-LIVE1 rules. The first update builds and starts the program. Program output becomes `run.output` events.

JOINING A RUNNING SESSION. Under A, a stdio session for check, build, test or run follows the `--session=auto|off|required` rule of D-BUILD-SESSION1. `jet check` gains that flag for this purpose. With the default `auto`, it forwards its requests to the workspace session when one runs, so the editor and the tool share one warm compiler. `off` keeps a private compiler. `required` fails at start with no workspace session.

If the workspace session ends mid-stream, in-flight requests end with a cancelled response. Later requests run on a private compiler, and a `session.detached` note says so. `jet dev --listen=-` never joins, because dev itself may own a session; it keeps its own compiler.

Under B, `--listen=-` with any `--session` value is refused with E2102, and a stdio session always runs its own compiler. Jetpack still attaches to a `--serve` socket directly when one runs, as D-JETPACK-SERVICE1=A says.

OPTION C. There is no `update` request. The command word only sets the default selection, and a client always sends the typed request: `check{}`, `build{}`, `test{}`, `run{}` or `dev.update{}`.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT PATHS. Beginners never type `--listen=-`; tools do. A tool author sends update after each change, as with Zig. An expert sends typed requests with explicit selections, and chooses `--session=off` for an isolated compiler.

Why A over B: B gives a second warm compiler beside the editor's, so every edit is checked twice, which D-SESSION-OWNER1=A was ratified to avoid. Why A over C: C drops the one request D-SESSION-ENTRY1=C's option text assumed, and Zig-style tools would need per-verb logic.

New diagnostics and the `session.detached` event get registry rows with UI snapshots (I4). Implementation lands on #5050.

options.name: Update redoes the command's work; join a running session
options.detail: Update redoes each command's own work on the newest files, as in the table in the detail. Check, build, test and run started with --listen=- join the workspace session when one runs, under the same --session rule as the plain command. Dev keeps its own compiler.
options.technical: Per-verb update mapping as in the detail. `--session=auto` default forwards requests to the D-SESSION-OWNER1 endpoint; `off` keeps a private compiler; `required` fails at hello. Owner loss mid-stream: in-flight requests end `cancelled`, then a `session.detached` event, then local execution.

options.name: The same update table; a stdio session never joins
options.detail: The same update table as A. A --listen=- session always runs its own compiler, and --listen=- with --session is refused. This is the draft in the follow-through notes.
options.technical: As A for update. `--listen=-` plus any `--session=` value is E2102.
options.code:
$ jet build --listen=- --session=auto
error[E2102]: a --listen=- session runs its own compiler; drop --session
$ jet build --listen=-          # private compiler, even with the editor open

options.name: No update request; typed requests only
options.detail: There is no update request. The command word only sets the default selection, and a client always sends the typed request for the work it wants. Joining follows A.
options.technical: Remove `update` from the request set; the verb seeds default selection, targets, profile and filter for the typed requests.

comparisons.note: zig build --listen=- rebuilds on each update message and replies with an error bundle and output paths.
comparisons.code: $ zig build --listen=-   # client sends update after each change

comparisons.note: rust-analyzer runs cargo check as a separate process, so the editor and cargo keep two caches and check edits twice.

recommendation.why: Update means the obvious thing on every command, as tools expect from Zig, and joining the running session keeps one warm compiler per folder. That is the reason the editor session exists.
gains: One short request works on all five commands.
Tools and editors share one warm compiler.

losses.loss: If the editor closes mid-stream, some requests are cancelled.
losses.mitigation: The session says so with a detached note and continues on its own compiler.

whyNot.reason: B checks every edit twice while an editor session runs, the waste the shared session was ratified to remove.
C drops the request the ratified flag decision assumed, so Zig-style tools need per-command logic.

recommendation.tradeoff: One forwarding hop to the shared session, for one warm compiler per folder.

surface.gist: What should update do on each command started with --listen=-, and should it share a running session?
surface.lesson: With `--listen=-`, a command takes requests on standard input and answers on standard output. `update` is the short request that means: do this command's work again on the newest files. A workspace session is a warm compiler that an editor or `jet dev` runs for the folder.

current.note: The flag is approved, but update has no meaning yet on any command.

wild.note: zig build --listen=- rebuilds on each update message (Zig build-system protocol).
wild.code:
$ zig build --listen=-
// client: update -> server: error_bundle, emit_digest

options.name: Redo the work; join the session
options.gist: Update redoes the command's work; the tool joins the editor's warm compiler.
gains: Update works the same way on all five commands.
One warm compiler per folder.
losses: Editor closing cancels in-flight requests.

options.name: Redo the work; never join
options.gist: Same update meaning; each stdio session keeps its own compiler.
gains: Simplest: no forwarding.
losses: Edits are checked twice while an editor runs.

proposed.code:
$ jet build --listen=-    // private compiler
$ jet build --listen=- --session=auto
error[E2102]: drop --session

options.name: Typed requests only
options.gist: No update; clients always name the work they want.
gains: No command-specific meaning.
losses: Zig-style tools need per-command logic.

proposed.code: > {"kind":"request","id":1,"op":"test","filter":"physics"}

recommendation.why: Update means the obvious thing on every command, as Zig tools expect, and joining the running session keeps one warm compiler per folder.
gains: One request, one warm compiler.

losses.loss: Editor closing cancels in-flight requests.
losses.mitigation: A detached note says so, and later requests run on a private compiler.

whyNot.reason: Checks every edit twice while an editor runs.
Tools need per-command logic for basic work.

recommendation.tradeoff: One forwarding hop, for one warm compiler per folder.

decisions.title: What an entry function does when Jet calls it
decisions.situation: An entry function is code Jet calls for one command, such as `fn dev` for `jet dev` or `fn test` for `jet test`. Today a bare `fn dev()` replaces the program, and a test entry that forgets to start the tests still passes. The vote decides whether an entry only sets values, must take over the work, or sets values and takes over only when asked. We recommend the last, so `jet dev` always runs your program (`fn run`, or the entry of the output you picked) and the tests always run once.
decisions.gist: Should an entry function only set values, take over the work, or set values and take over when asked?
decisions.lesson: An entry function is code Jet calls for one command. Every option makes a bare `fn dev()` an error whose fix shows `fn dev(d: Dev)`. With no `fn dev`, `jet dev` serves an App or web build with live reload, or restarts the program on save. In A and B, `fn build(b: Build)` returns nothing and names its default with `b.default(app)`. C keeps returning a plan.
decisions.story: Mia builds a small web app. She types `jet dev`, clicks the link, and tests in the browser. Later she wants port 8080 every time, so she writes `fn dev(d: Dev) { d.port(8080); d.watch(true) }` in `@dev.jet` or any root file. Her teammate Noor needs golden files unpacked before the tests and a JUnit report written after them. Both needs should fit one entry shape, with no wrapper script and no way to skip the tests by mistake.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot decides the shape of an entry function and states what `jet dev` does with no `fn dev`. Sibling ballots on card c07glrub decide the rest. D-TARGET-ONE1 decides where outputs are declared. D-SETTING-ORDER1 decides setting rows, the one precedence order, and ports. D-ENTRY-NAMES1 decides type names. D-DEV-STATE1 decides kept values across restarts, and D-DEV-SERVICES1 decides local services.

No entry for run and check. `jet run` and `jet check` have no entry function. Their setting rows have two layers, package.jet and flag, which satisfies #4913 (no CLI-only or config-only options). The dev handle is the code form of the dev session's rows.

Settled by the owner on 2026-10-19, not voted. The handle types are `Build`, `Dev` and `Test`. `fn run` is the program, and `fn dev` always runs it. So in every option a bare `fn dev()` or `fn test()` without the handle is a registered error. Its fix shows `fn dev(d: Dev)` or `fn test(t: Test)`. There is no longer a way for dev to replace run.

Shared rule in every option. A direct call to the program's `fn run` inside `fn dev` or `fn test` is a registered error. It would run the program a second time. In option A the fix names `d.run()`.

Where entries run. `fn dev` and `fn test` are ordinary runtime code, compiled on the normal build path at O0, as `fn test(suite: TestSuite)` is today. `Dev` and `Test` are prelude-owned handles, and the session logic lives in the prelude and core library (I9). Only `fn build` runs at compile time. So no new compile-time effect rules apply to dev or test; this ballot does not change D-CTEFFECT1.

Process model. The one process model for the slate is in option A's technical note and holds for every option. D-DEV-STATE1 and D-DEV-SERVICES1 refer to it. Its core: the `jet` tool process holds the `#Persist` store and the local-service supervisor. The compiled `fn dev` session runs the program as its child, and editing program code restarts only the child.

Outputs. One `fn dev` configures the whole dev session for whichever output was picked. `d.output()` returns the picked output's name so code can branch. `t.run()` runs every selected check once. The word output means something a project makes; target means only the platform, as in `#Target(Web)`.

Build entry in options A and B. `fn build(b: Build)` returns nothing. A failing build entry writes `fn build(b: Build) !BuildError`. Jet seals the plan when the entry returns, and `jet inspect build` and `core.build.graph` read the sealed plan. `b.default(app)` names the default output and replaces `return b.plan(default: app)`. Package `defaults:` stays as the data form of the same setting, per D-TARGET-ONE1 and D-SETTING-ORDER1.

Root run first. A root `fn run` still runs first for bare `jet run` and `jet dev`; the default picks only when no root `fn run` exists. This is ratified D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1 and D-DX-ENTRY1, and this ballot does not change it.

Magic default with no `fn dev`, three rows checked in order. First, `fn run` returns `App`: Jet serves it with browser live reload and shows errors in the page. Second, the picked output's platform is web, resolved in the one settings order (`--target=web`, an output's `os: web` in code or data, package `target:`, `#Target(Web)`). Then Jet serves the wasm build with live reload. Third, anything else: Jet restarts the program on save.

Local services that are on in the dev environment start first, and Jet waits until they are ready.

The three rows match today's dispatch order after the `fn dev()` check. The App row is `entry_returns_app` at Source/main.rs:4216. The web row is Source/main.rs:4235, and the restart row is Source/main.rs:4250. So the magic default is today's stock behavior with the replace-the-program path removed.

First run and the ladder. The first `jet dev` prints one line, for example `run.jet returns App → serving http://127.0.0.1:8080 · live reload · customize: jet explain dev`. `jet explain dev` prints the effective `fn dev` for this project as Jet source, which a user can paste into `@dev.jet`. `--show-default` keeps its meaning: ignore the entry, run the stock default, and say so.

Reload boundary. Saving program code restarts the program only, as D-EXEC2=A requires. Saving `fn dev`, code it calls, or the env definition ends the session. Code after `d.run()` runs as cleanup, then Jet enters `fn dev` again. A second Ctrl-C during cleanup stops at once and names the cleanup it skipped.

Today in code. Source/main.rs:4191-4215 runs a top-level `fn dev()` first, and Source/CmdCompile.rs:4605-4612 compiles it as the program's real entry point. The `@dev.jet` template at Source/CmdCompile.rs:5526 says a `fn dev` replaces the stock default. The `@test.jet` template at Source/CmdCompile.rs:5530 writes `fn test(suite: TestSuite) { suite.run() }`. The suite value is crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CommandSuite.rs.

E1254 (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/DiagnosticRows.jet:12055-12068) says project `jet dev` runs `fn dev()` if present, else `fn run()`, and its fix suggests a bare `fn dev()`. Its meaning and fix text change: the fix names `fn run`, and `fn dev(d: Dev)` for settings.

Counts, by search for `^fn dev\s*\(` and `^fn test\s*\(` over tests, Examples and Core on 2026-10-19. There are 32 files with a top-level bare `fn dev()`. Most start `core.web.devserver` by hand or print a marker for a test. There are 6 files with `fn test(suite: TestSuite)`, including Examples/features/devloop/test_override.jet. These counts measure repository sites only, not users.

Amends D-CMD-OVERRIDE1=C: the test entry sets values by default and runs the suite at return unless it calls `t.run()`. A no-parameter override becomes an error instead of a full replacement. The recorded loss, an override that skips work and prints green, is removed because the suite always runs once. `--show-default` keeps its meaning. The handle name `Test` comes from D-ENTRY-NAMES1.

Amends D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1=D: `jet dev` still runs inside env(base + env.dev) and `jet env` still never runs project code. But `jet dev` now runs `fn dev(d: Dev)`, which sets values and wraps the program, and the fallback is the magic default above. E1254 text changes to match.

Under options A and B, amends D-BUILDENTRY1=B: the signature `fn build(b: BuildContext) -> BuildPlan ?` becomes `fn build(b: Build)`, optionally `!BuildError`, with the plan sealed at return. Under A and B, amends D-BUILDTARGET1=A: `return b.plan(default: app)` becomes `b.default(app)`, and `b.plan()` is removed. Option C keeps both as ratified, apart from the owner-settled handle name.

D-JAI-CONFIG1 (open) was rewritten on 2026-10-19 to the slate's terms (outputs, `BuildOptions`, `b.default`, no exact-options rule). Its change calls work until `fn build` returns, which is when every option here seals the plan.

Also amends the owner direction of 2026-07-01 recorded at Source/main.rs:4191, which made `fn dev()` the program's real entry point. Unchanged and relied on: D-EXEC2=A (restart only, no hot swap), D-RUN-WATCH1=A, D-WEBDEFAULT1=A (the web row uses its order), D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C, D-CLAIM-BENCH1=A. Also relied on: D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1 and D-DX-ENTRY1 for root `fn run` first (D-TARGET-ONE1 amends their default spelling and `defaults.dev`). D-DEVMODE1: amended by D-DEV-STATE1 if its option A wins; this ballot adds no further change to it.

Research, right ways. Go 1.15 removed the required `os.Exit` in `TestMain`: if it returns, Go exits with the result of `m.Run` (https://go.dev/doc/go1.15). The lesson is that the tool should finish a closing step users forget. Option A applies the same idea to the start step. pytest yield fixtures put cleanup after `yield`, which is the same split as code after `t.run()`.

Research, more right ways. Zig's `pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void` returns nothing, and the runner acts on the declared graph after it returns (https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/). That is the build shape of options A and B. Vite configures its dev server by values and sends everything else to plugin hooks (https://vite.dev/config/server-options). That is option B, and it needs a hook API for every new need.

Research, wrong ways. A full replacement entry lets dev run code that differs from run. Today's bare `fn dev()` does this, and owner direction now forbids it. A run-it-yourself entry with no default lets a forgotten call skip the work. D-CMD-OVERRIDE1 recorded this as its loss, and Go's pre-1.15 `os.Exit` rule had the same class of mistake. Fixed hook lists were rejected in D-CMD-OVERRIDE1 option D because new needs wait for new hooks.

Cutover. Migrate the 32 bare `fn dev()` files: web ones become `fn run() -> App` or the web platform row, and settings move to `fn dev(d: Dev)`. Migrate the 6 `fn test(suite: TestSuite)` files to `fn test(t: Test)`. Update the four `@*.jet` templates and the Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Host.jet templates. Update E1254 and E3501 text, run_dev_entry, has_dev_entry_fn, and the test override path. Update the spec and every `fn build(...) -> BuildPlan` site. Register new errors under I7.

options.name: Set values, take over when asked
options.detail:
The entry sets values on its handle. When the entry returns, Jet runs the work exactly once with those values. For `jet dev` the work is the dev session around your program. For `jet test` the work is every selected check.

An entry that needs code around the work calls `d.run()` or `t.run()` once. The work runs at that point instead of at return. A setting call after `run()` is an error. Code after `run()` runs when the work ends: after the suite for tests, and after the first Ctrl-C for a dev session.

Gains: the owner's two-line example works as written, setup and cleanup stay possible, and the suite can never be skipped. Loss: one entry has two shapes, which the error text and `jet explain dev` teach.
options.technical:
`Dev` and `Test` are prelude-owned handles. `fn dev` and `fn test` compile as ordinary runtime code on the normal build path, like `fn test(suite: TestSuite)` today. If no call to `run()` has happened when the entry returns, the runtime makes it. A second `run()` call and a setting call after `run()` stop with a registered error naming the call.

`fn dev` and the program compile into one O0 binary. The `jet` tool process holds the `#Persist` store and the local-service supervisor. It runs the compiled `fn dev` session, which runs the program as its child. Editing program code restarts only the child. Editing `fn dev` or the env definition ends the session and starts it again; the `jet` process stays, so kept values and running services survive. Ctrl-C ends everything.

`d.run()` returns when the session ends and gives no value. An entry that fails before `run()` stops `jet dev` with its error; the program never starts. `t.run()` runs every selected check once and returns the results, so a report can follow it.

One `fn dev` configures the whole dev session for whichever output was picked. `d.output()` returns the picked output's name so code can branch. `fn build(b: Build)` returns nothing, and Jet seals the build plan at return.

options.name: Set values only, with hooks
options.detail:
The entry only sets values, and Jet always runs the work after the entry returns. There is no `run()` call, so hooks are the only way to put code around the work. Option A may also have a `t.before` setting row, but it adds `run()` for code around the work. Setup and cleanup use named hooks that take functions: `t.before(unpack_golden)`, `t.after(remove_golden)`, and `d.before(seed_demo)`. An after-hook receives the results, so a report can be written there.

Gains: every entry reads as a short list of values, and Jet always controls the order. Losses: each new setup need waits for Jet to add a hook, and today's test entries must be rewritten as hooks.
options.technical: `Dev` and `Test` gain hook methods that store function references. The runtime calls before-hooks, runs the work, then calls after-hooks with the results. The hook list is fixed by Jet and grows only by new decisions. The handles still compile as ordinary runtime code, under the same process model as option A. `fn build(b: Build)` returns nothing, and Jet seals the build plan at return.

options.name: Entry takes over, `run()` required
options.detail:
The entry drives the work. It must call `d.run()` or `t.run()` exactly once on every path, and a missing call is an error. `fn build` keeps returning a plan with `return b.plan(default: app)`. This is today's test entry rule, made strict so a forgotten call cannot pass.

Gains: the order of every step is visible in code, and it matches Go's `TestMain`. Losses: the owner's example `fn dev(d: Dev) { d.port(8080); d.watch(true) }` is an error until `d.run()` is added, and every beginner entry carries that extra line.
options.technical: The checker requires exactly one `run()` call on every path through the entry, like a definite-assignment check. The build entry keeps the returned plan value and `return b.plan(default: app)`. `Dev` and `Test` are prelude-owned handles compiled as ordinary runtime code, under the same process model as option A.

comparisons.note: `TestMain` receives the test run as a value and wraps it. Go 1.15 stopped requiring the final `os.Exit` call: if `TestMain` returns, Go exits with the result of `m.Run`. The tool finishes the step users forget. Source: https://go.dev/doc/go1.15.

A yield fixture runs setup before `yield` and cleanup after it, when the tests end. It is the same split as code before and after `t.run()`. Source: https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/fixtures.html.

`build.zig` declares the graph and returns nothing. The build runner then runs the steps the command asked for. This is the shape of `fn build(b: Build)` in options A and B. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/.

The dev server takes plain values in a config file. Anything beyond those values goes through plugin hooks such as `configureServer`. This is the shape of option B. Source: https://vite.dev/config/server-options.

recommendation.why: Beginners write only values, and experts add one `run()` call for setup and cleanup. The work always runs once, so tests cannot be skipped.
gains: The owner's example and today's test setup both work.
A forgotten `run()` can no longer skip the tests.

losses.loss: One entry has two shapes: with and without `run()`.
losses.mitigation: A setting after `run()` is an error that states the rule. `jet explain dev` prints the short shape.

whyNot.reason: Each new setup need waits for Jet to add a hook.
It turns the owner's own two-line example into an error and adds a line every beginner must learn.

recommendation.tradeoff: Experts learn one rule about `run()`. Beginners never need it.

decisions.title: One list of what a project makes, written as data or code
decisions.situation: An output is one thing a project makes, such as a program, a server program, a library or a set of checks. Today Jet keeps two separate lists, one in the package file and one made by build code, so `jet run` and `jet build` see different outputs. Game teams porting from Jai, where build code makes each separate build with its own settings, cannot tell which list to use. The vote decides where outputs live, and we recommend one list that the package file and build code both add to, with every output picked by name.
decisions.gist: Where does a project declare what it makes, including Jai-style builds with their own settings?
decisions.lesson: An output is one thing a project makes: a program, server program, library or set of checks. Today the package file and build code keep two separate lists. A root `fn run` still runs first for bare `jet run` and `jet dev`; the default picks only when no root `fn run` exists. Each output can carry its own build settings, like a Jai workspace. A separate Jai-workspaces vote, shown after the settings-order and naming votes, decides how build code copies these settings and changes an output.
decisions.story: Mia keeps a small API and a command-line tool in one package. She lists both in the package file and types `jet dev api`. Her teammate Tomi adds a web build of their game from build code, with its own settings. Mia wants `jet dev game_web` to find it the same way. She also wants `jet run`, `jet dev` and `jet build` to see the same list.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot decides where outputs are declared and how commands pick one. Sibling ballots on card c07glrub decide the rest. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 decides entry shape, including `fn build(b: Build)` with no return value and `b.default(app)`. D-SETTING-ORDER1 decides the one settings order. D-ENTRY-NAMES1 decides type names. D-DEV-STATE1 and D-DEV-SERVICES1 decide dev state and services.

Words. Output means a thing the project makes: a program, a server program, a library or a set of checks. Target means only the platform, as in `#Target(Web)` and `--target=web`. Code uses the slate spellings `fn build(b: Build)` and `b.default(app)`. If those sibling ballots lose, only the spellings revert to `BuildContext`, `-> BuildPlan` and `b.plan(default: app)`.

Today, from the code. `jet build` names its artifact after the build plan's default entry, in `programmable_build_target_name` at Source/CmdCompile.rs:10295. `jet run` picks its entry from package `outputs:` through `select_output("run")` at crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Package/mod.rs:1089 and :1228. Neither reads the other. The Jet twin is `select_output` in Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Manifest/Compose.jet:30.

The spec documents both lists. `Output` values are at Docs/spec/spec.md:4063-4086, and `b.add_*` calls at :4369-4375. The default has two homes: `defaults:` checked by `validate_defaults` (mod.rs:1062), and `b.plan(default)` read by `default_target()`. The canvas fixture at tests/canvas_scenarios.rs:1308 lists seven outputs with `defaults: { run: cli }`. A grep on 2026-10-19 found 61 `.jet` files calling `b.add_executable(`.

Ratified law involved. D-ECO-OUTPUT1=A: one typed output collection that commands select from. D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A: nine closed kinds. D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1=A: an ordered selection rule, and adding a candidate never silently retargets automation. D-ECO-OUTPUT-PAYLOAD1=A: thin outputs. D-SHAPE-OUTPUT-CALLABLE1=A: `entry` is a checked function reference. D-DX-ENTRY1=C: bare command order, with a root `fn <cmd>` first.

More ratified law. D-BUILDTARGET1=A: `b.add_*` returns handles, and `b.plan(default: app)` names the default. D-BUILDENTRY1=B and D-CONF-ENTRY1=A: one `fn build` per package. D-ECO19=A: `pkgs.dep.name` accessors. D-BUILD-INCLUDE1=A: `b.include(pkg)` runs a dependency build in a sandbox. D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1=D: `jet env` never runs project functions. D-CLAIM-BENCH1=A: no bench output. D-JAI-CONFIG1 (open, rewritten 2026-10-19 to this slate's terms) decides how build code copies settings, changes an output and reads the build machine; per-output `options:` is decided here.

Option A design, one list. Each entry is an `Output` value. `outputs:` adds data entries, and each `b.add_*` call adds a code entry and returns it as an `Output`. Names are unique across both sources. A duplicate is a registered error naming both lines.

Option A kinds from code. `b.add_executable` makes an Executable, and the new `b.add_service` a Service. `b.add_library` makes a Library, and `b.add_test` a Check. `b.add_asset_bundle`, `b.add_doc` and `b.add_package` make a Bundle. `b.add_install` and `b.add_publish` stay steps on an output. No new kind is added. Environment, Image, System and Fleet stay data only, because `jet env` and deploy must read them without running project code.

Option A fields. A code-made output may pass `entry:`. Without it, the entry is `fn run` in its first source file, as today. Both forms accept `options:`, the output's own build settings, which is where Jai workspaces live. The data form writes `options: .{ os: web, optimize: size }`, the profile spelling of D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A with the type name elided. `b.output(name)` lets build code change a data-made output before the plan is sealed.

Option A zero setup and the default. With no runnable output, the root `fn run` is one implicit Executable named after the package. A root `fn run` still runs first for bare `jet run` and `jet dev`; the default picks only when no root `fn run` exists. So adding an output never retargets a bare command. The default row is `defaults: { run: cli }` in data, `b.default(cli)` in code, and `jet run cli` for one run, in the D-SETTING-ORDER1 order.

Option A default, continued. `jet dev` uses the `run` default, because dev always runs the program. Other command defaults, such as publish, keep their `defaults:` keys and take `b.default(t, command: .Publish)` in code. `jet inspect build` marks which output a bare command starts.

Option A names on the command line. A word naming a listed output selects it. A path with `/` or ending in `.jet` selects a file. A word naming both a file and an output whose entry is in that file selects that output. So in package `game` with `game.jet`, `jet run game` works. Only a word naming two different things is an error listing both.

Option A listing cost. Editors list code-made outputs from the last `jet inspect build`; data outputs need no build run. Option B pays that cost for every output, including the simplest two-program project.

Research, proven right ways. Cargo shows that one program needs no setup and that the default is one data line, `default-run`. SwiftPM evaluates Package.swift code into a plain manifest that tools read with `swift package dump-package`. Bazel macros make many targets, and `bazel query` lists them without building. Nix flakes keep programs, checks and dev shells in one typed `outputs` set, the model Jet's Output kinds already follow.

Research, known failures. Cargo's build.rs cannot add a program, so projects add helper crates such as the cargo-xtask pattern (github.com/matklad/cargo-xtask). Zig and Gradle make programs only in code, so editors must run build code to learn them. ZLS ships a build runner for this, and Gradle added a configuration cache to cut that cost (docs.gradle.org, configuration cache). No adoption numbers were gathered; these are documented designs, not measurements.

Design away, loss one: two ways to write one output. Attempt one was data only, option C. It was rejected because build code could no longer make builds in a loop. Attempt two was code only, option B. It was rejected because two programs would need build code and tools would have to run it. Result: one value type, one name space, a duplicate-name error, and the rule of data for fixed outputs and code for loops. Negligible.

Design away, loss two: other packages see only data outputs. The attempt to run every dependency build to list outputs was rejected, because it reverses the ratified rule that dependency builds are checked but not run. Result: `b.include(dep)` already reaches code-made outputs, and the error names both fixes. Reduced to one visible fix.

Amendments if A wins. Amends D-BUILDTARGET1=A: `b.add_*` calls add entries to the one output list and return `Output` instead of `BuildTarget`. `b.add_service`, `b.output(name)` and `b.profile(name)`, which returns a fresh copy of a package.jet profile, are new. The default's code spelling, `b.default(app)` or `b.plan(default: app)`, is decided by D-ENTRY-SHAPE1. Amends D-ECO-OUTPUT1=A: build code may add outputs of the compiled kinds, while Environment, Image, System and Fleet stay data.

Amends D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1=A: `b.default(t)` is the code form of the `defaults:` row, ordered by D-SETTING-ORDER1, and `jet dev` uses the `run` default. Its root `fn run` first rule is kept. Amends D-ECO-OUTPUT-PAYLOAD1=A: an output may carry `options:`, its own build settings; every other graph fact stays single-copy on the graph.

Amends D-SHAPE-OUTPUT-CALLABLE1=A only in wording: code-made outputs may pass `entry:`, and the spec drops the word legacy for `fn run`. Amends D-DX-ENTRY1=C: bare `jet dev` reads `defaults.run`; `defaults.dev` naming an Environment becomes an error pointing to `--env`.

D-JAI-CONFIG1 (open) was rewritten on 2026-10-19 to these terms (outputs, `BuildOptions`, `b.default`, seal at return, no exact-options rule) and takes per-output `options:` and `b.output(name)` from this ballot. Unchanged by this ballot: D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A, D-ECO19=A, D-BUILD-INCLUDE1=A and D-CONF-ENTRY1=A. D-BUILDENTRY1=B keeps one `fn build` per package here; D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 changes its signature.

Cutover. Join `programmable_build_target_name` and `select_output` over one list, in Rust and in the Jet twins. Rename the `BuildTarget` handle in Core/build/declarations.jet:175 and its Rust twin. Add `b.add_service` and `b.output`. Change the `dev` intent in `intent_accepts_kind` (mod.rs:1883), which selects an Environment today, to select like `run`. Environments stay selected by `--env` (D-ENVFLAG1=A).

Cutover, continued. Update spec sections Program commands and Output and Programmable builds. Register `b.add_service`, `b.output`, `b.profile`, the `command:` argument of `b.default` and `options:` on outputs (I7). Also register the output list in the existing `jet inspect build` (D-CLI-ONE1=A), the duplicate-name error and the name-clash error. The 61 existing `b.add_executable(` callers keep working unchanged.

Review: one fresh combined pass (beginner + adversarial), agent SlateReview, Claude family, 2026-10-19, per owner directive for one review. Repaired: root `fn run` rule, story, name-or-file rule, D-DX-ENTRY1 amendment, listing cost, `b.add_object`, code comments, output wording, mitigations, D-JAI-CONFIG1 note, length. Cohesion pass CohesionReview 2026-10-19 repaired: D-JAI-CONFIG1 references, inspect build, b.profile ownership, amendment lists, output wording.

options.name: One list, data or code
options.detail: The package has one output list. The package file adds plain entries, and `fn build` adds entries with `b.add_*`. Both make the same value with the same fields, so a command cannot tell them apart. `jet run name`, `jet dev name` and `jet build name` pick any output by name. Each output may carry its own build settings in data or in code, which is where Jai workspaces live.

options.name: Build code only
options.detail: Only `fn build` makes the outputs Jet compiles. The package file keeps no `outputs:` or `defaults:`, only machine setups such as environments, which `jet env` reads without running code. `b.default(cli)` is the only default. This is the Zig and Jai model.
options.technical: Retire `outputs:` entries of kinds Executable, Service, Library, Check and Bundle, and the `defaults:` block. Add `b.add_service`. With no `fn build`, the root `fn run` is still one implicit Executable. Editors, package tools and `pkgs.dep.name` accessors must run each package's `fn build` to learn any output. So dependency builds run whenever a consumer reads them, which reverses the ratified rule that they are checked but not run.
options.code:
fn build(b: Build) {   // build.jet: the only list
    cli :: b.add_executable("cli", ["cli.jet"], [])
    b.add_service("api", ["api.jet"], [])
    b.default(cli)
}
$ jet dev api

options.name: Package file only
options.detail: Only the package file lists outputs, and each entry may carry its own `options:`. `fn build` may change a listed output by adding sources, generated code or settings, but it cannot add one. This is the Cargo model with per-output settings added.
options.technical: Retire `b.add_executable` and the other `b.add_*` output calls, and `b.plan(default:)`. `b.output(name)` returns a listed output for the change calls of D-JAI-CONFIG1. The default is `defaults:` only. Settings in data can set fields but cannot be computed. Jai's `compiler_create_workspace` in a loop has no Jet form.

comparisons.note: Build code is the only way to make a workspace, and each workspace has its own options and files (The Way to Jai, chapter 30).
build.zig is code only. The Zig editor server ships a build runner so it can run build.zig and learn the modules.
comparisons.code:
const exe = b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "game", .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"), .target = target, .optimize = .ReleaseSmall });
b.installArtifact(exe);

comparisons.note: One src/main.rs needs no setup, `[[bin]]` lists more programs, and `default-run` picks the default. build.rs cannot add a program, so teams use helper crates such as cargo-xtask.
comparisons.code:
[package]
default-run = "cli"

[[bin]]
name = "server"
path = "src/server.rs"

$ cargo run --bin server

comparisons.note: Package.swift is Swift code, but SwiftPM turns it into a plain manifest that tools read (`swift package dump-package`).
One `outputs` set holds packages, apps, checks and dev shells, and `nix run .#name` picks one by name.
BUILD files declare targets, and macros can make many. `bazel query` lists them without building.

recommendation.why: One list gives one set of names and one way to pick. Data stays readable without running code, and code keeps Jai builds made in loops.
gains: `jet run name`, `jet dev name` and `jet build name` find every output.
Plain data for fixed outputs, and code for Jai-style loops.
Tools read data outputs without running code.
Jai-style builds keep their own settings, in data or code.

losses.loss: Two ways to write one output.
losses.mitigation: Use data for fixed outputs and code only for loops; `jet inspect build` lists both with their lines.

losses.loss: Other packages see only a dependency's data outputs.
losses.mitigation: The error names both fixes: list the output as data, or call `b.include(dep)` in build code.

whyNot.reason: Even two plain programs would need build code, and every output would need a build run before tools could list it.
Build code cannot make builds in a loop, which is the heart of Jai's workspaces.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two spellings of one value, for zero setup and the Jai model.
