decisions.title: In a cross build, which machine do build-time Core calls act on?
decisions.situation: Build code runs on the build machine, but the program it builds may run somewhere else. Today build code can only read the target, through $build.os, and nothing names the build machine. Core is also inconsistent. Most per-OS Core code asks the running machine, but one Core helper folds $build.os, so during a Windows build on Linux it would use Windows path rules on a Linux disk. We recommend one rule: Core calls act on the machine running them, $build always names the target, and $build.host names the build machine.
decisions.gist: When build code cross-compiles, do its Core calls act on the build machine or the target?
decisions.lesson: Build code runs on your machine, while the program it builds may run on another. A file read in build code can only read your disk. The question is whether Core calls in build code follow your machine, and how build code names each machine. Reading a fact never changes its meaning: $build.os always names the target.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: a normal build on one machine changes nothing. The question matters only when you build a program for another operating system.

If you build a Windows program on Linux, a preparation step that lists a directory must answer for one machine. Jet must say which one, every time, so the build is repeatable.
decisions.story: Theo builds a Windows installer on a Linux laptop. His build code lists the assets folder and checks that every file exists. The listing must use Linux path rules, because it reads his Linux disk. The installer itself still uses Windows rules.
decisions.inWild:
Cargo build scripts: cfg!(target_os) inside build.rs describes the build machine, and the target comes from CARGO_CFG_TARGET_OS. Cargo's docs warn about mixing them up. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-build-scripts

Zig: build.zig is compiled for the build machine; b.graph.host names it, and the target is a separate value. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/
decisions.detail:
WHAT EXISTS TODAY

Facts are served by Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/FactReads.jet:641-649. They are $package.name and version, $build.os and profile, the stamps and $build.cpu.cache_line. There is no host fact. Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:5268 says $build.os is the --target OS, or the host OS when no target is given.

Build code: Docs/spec/spec.md:4888-4935. jet build runs fn build(b: Build) natively at O0 on the build machine, and the spec example uses the FS and Exec effects directly.

Core already asks the running machine in most places. Core/Sys/Sys.jet:897 and Core/Ui/Host.jet:205 pick PathPlatform from core.files.__path_windows(). Core/Files/Files.jet:1105-1109 list_dir calls the runtime's __list_dir_raw, which can only read the disk it runs on.

The one outlier: Core/Service/Service.jet:1455-1465 StatePathPlatform.windows() folds $build.os. In a Linux-to-Windows cross build, a Service state path computed during build code would use Windows rules on the Linux disk.

CARD

Tower card c0rc40yf (Host facts for prep and build-time code) asks for host OS and architecture facts beside $build. It also asks for one stated rule for per-OS Core calls during preparation. Host reads must enter the cache key, and a policy must be able to reject them.

Related rulings: D-BUILD-FACT3=A puts build facts under $build. D-JAI-CONFIG1=A records every host read in the build record and cache key. D-HOST-CAPS1=A says target hardware facts follow the selected target, never the build machine.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. A Core call in build code answers for the build machine. Nothing that ships depends on that answer. Shipped names and paths come from b.add_executable, b.add_install and b.action outputs, which apply $build.os rules themselves. Build code that prints or branches on a target fact reads $build.os.

2. Builds reading the build machine. Every option has this, because build actions run on the build machine under all three. A records each $build.host read and host-touching Core call in the build record and cache key (D-JAI-CONFIG1=A). Equal inputs give equal outputs, and a package policy can deny host reads with a registered diagnostic.

No loss remains. Any output call that lacks a target rule today gains one as work owed under A.

WORK OWED UNDER A

Add $build.host.os and $build.host.arch to FactReads.jet and the syntax registry. Change Service.jet:1459 to ask the running machine, like Sys.jet:897. Add a cross-build golden example that prints both facts.

WHY NOT B OR C

B makes build code describe a machine it is not running on. A file listing cannot read the target's disk, so B must ban direct file and process calls in build code. Every read then becomes a declared action. C makes common calls in every cross build carry a side argument, which is noise when only one answer is possible.

options.name: Core calls act on the machine running them
options.detail: A Core call in build code acts on the build machine, the only one it can touch. $build.os always names the target. Build code reads the build machine through $build.host.os and $build.host.arch, and each read goes into the cache key. Everything that ships goes through Build calls such as b.add_executable and b.add_install, which apply the target's rules themselves.
options.technical: Add $build.host.os and $build.host.arch fact reads. Core per-OS code asks the running machine, as Sys.jet:897 already does; Service.jet:1459 moves to that form. Host reads join the build record, and a package policy can deny them. Build outputs (b.add_executable, b.add_install and b.action outputs) take target-relative paths and apply $build.os rules, such as the .exe suffix, with no host call.

options.name: Everything in build code answers for the target
options.detail: Pure Core calls in build code answer as the target would. Because build code cannot touch the target's disk, direct file and process calls in build code are refused, and each such step becomes a declared action.
options.technical: Build code loses the FS and Exec effects. Reads move to b.action steps, which run on the build machine. No host fact is added.

options.name: Refuse calls that do not name a side
options.detail: In a cross build, a per-OS Core call in build code is a compile error unless it names the machine it means.
options.technical: The checker rejects per-OS Core calls in build code under cross-compilation unless a .Host or .Target argument is given. Adds a side argument to those Core calls.

comparisons.note: In build.rs, cfg!(target_os) describes the build machine. The target comes from CARGO_CFG_TARGET_OS. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html
build.zig runs on the build machine. b.graph.host names it, and the target is chosen separately. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/
comparisons.code:
const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
const host = b.graph.host;

recommendation.why: A states one rule: a call acts on the machine running it. It is the only answer a file read can give. $build keeps one meaning, the target, and $build.host names the build machine.
gains: Build code reads its own disk with the right path rules.
$build.os means the target everywhere.
Host reads are recorded, so the cache stays correct.
Shipped files get the target's names and paths from the Build API.

whyNot.reason: B makes build code describe a machine it cannot touch, so every file read must become a declared action.
C adds a side argument to common calls in every cross build, though only one answer is possible.

recommendation.tradeoff: A acts on the running machine, and the Build API applies the target's rules to everything that ships.

surface.gist: When build code cross-compiles, do its Core calls act on the build machine or the target?
surface.lesson: Build code runs on your machine, while the program it builds may run on another. A file read in build code can only read your disk. The question is which machine Core calls follow, and how build code names each one.

current.note: Build code can read only the target. Nothing names the build machine.

wild.note: build.zig runs on the build machine and names both machines. Source: ziglang.org/learn/build-system

const host = b.graph.host;

options.gist: Core calls act on the build machine; $build.host names it.
gains: File reads use this disk's rules.
$build.os always means the target.
Shipped files follow the target's rules via the Build API.

options.name: Answer for the target
options.gist: Build code answers as the target would and cannot read files.
gains: Every call in build code means the target.
losses: Every file read becomes a declared action.

gains: Every call states its machine.

$build.os means the target everywhere.

C adds a side argument where only one answer is possible.

decisions.title: What the error says when a function can't be a C callback
decisions.situation: Jet lets you pass a function to a C library as a callback, but only a plain one. It must not capture locals, allocate, have effects, be generic, panic or schedule tasks. When a passed function breaks one of these rules, Jet points at the function correctly. The message is wrong, though: it says the callback type is not C-compatible, when the type is fine and the function is at fault. We recommend a dedicated error that names the broken rule.
decisions.gist: When a passed function can't be a C callback, which error should Jet give?
decisions.lesson: A callback type can be fine while the function you pass breaks a callback rule, for example by capturing a local. Those are two different mistakes. The error should name the one you made and the rule it broke, so the fix is obvious.
decisions.story: Omar passes a lambda that adds a local offset to a C library. Jet tells him the callback type is not C-compatible. He checks the type, finds nothing wrong, and is stuck. The real problem is that the lambda captures offset.
decisions.inWild: Rust: a capturing closure cannot be passed where a C function pointer is expected. The error says "closures can only be coerced to `fn` types if they do not capture any variables" and points at the capture. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/types/closure.html
decisions.detail:
TODAY (published base compiler, jet check on each fixture, 2026-11-05)

Six fixtures pass a function that breaks a callback rule: tests/ui/cffi_callback_capture, _allocation, _effect, _generic, _panic and _runtime_handle. Each reports E3203 jet.NonCAbiType at the passed function. The text blames the parameter type, for example "`fn(I32) -[]> I32` is not a C-compatible type". Its Why and Fix talk about stable C layout, which does not apply.

tests/ui/cffi_callback_bound_method reports the same misleading E3203 plus E0302.

tests/ui/cffi_callback_non_c_safe_signature declares cb: fn([Int]) -[]> Int. E3203 at the declaration is correct there, and stays.

The earlier draft said Jet gives E0102 and that the snapshots expect E3203 at the declaration. Both are stale: the snapshots point at the passed function, and E0102 no longer occurs.

CODE

Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Checking.jet:531-537 runs the callback check before the argument's type check. It reuses sema_checked_foreign_type_error (Registration/Checked.jet:944-949), which produces the type message. sema_call_c_callback_unsafe (Checking.jet:357-374) returns only a Bool, so the broken rule is lost.

E3216 jet.InvalidForeignBoundaryEvidence (Checked.jet:514-516, Items.jet:1991) covers incomplete provider and boundary metadata. It is not about the user's function. Ratified D-FFI-CALLBACK2=A limits callbacks to this plain subset, and D-FFI-CONTRACT1=A requires evidence per obligation. Neither names the diagnostic.

WORK UNDER A

sema_call_c_callback_unsafe returns the first broken rule with its span (the captured name, the allocating expression, the effect). A new registry row jet.UnsafeCCallback gets What/Why/Fix. The seven snapshots are regenerated in the same change. E3203 stays for declared types C cannot call.

WHY NOT B OR C

B keeps E3203. Its name, NonCAbiType, and its More page then cover two unrelated mistakes. C uses E3216, the reference compiler's choice. That code means missing provider metadata, which a user cannot fix in their own function.

options.name: A dedicated callback error that names the broken rule
options.detail: A new registered error points at the passed function and says which rule it broke: it captures offset, it allocates, it can panic. E3203 stays for callback types that C cannot call.
options.technical: Add jet.UnsafeCCallback with What/Why/Fix. The callback check returns the first broken rule and its span instead of a Bool. Regenerate the seven cffi_callback snapshots.
options.code:
Error [jet.UnsafeCCallback]: this lambda can't be a C callback: it captures `offset`
  --> app.jet:9:18
  9 |     print(c.call((x) -> x + offset, 40))
    |                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
 Why: C calls a callback as a bare function, with nowhere to keep `offset`.
 Fix: Read `offset` from a constant or a parameter instead.

options.name: Keep E3203, but name the broken rule
options.detail: The same E3203 code at the passed function, with its text rewritten for each broken rule.
options.technical: E3203 gains per-rule text. Its registry name stays NonCAbiType, and one More page covers both the type mistake and the function mistake.
options.code:
Error [jet.NonCAbiType]: this lambda can't be a C callback: it captures `offset`
  --> app.jet:9:18

options.name: Use the reference compiler's boundary-evidence error
options.detail: The call reports E3216, the error for missing foreign boundary evidence, as the old Rust compiler did.
options.technical: The callback check reports E3216 at the argument. E3216 also covers incomplete provider metadata.
options.code:
Error [jet.InvalidForeignBoundaryEvidence]: Foreign boundary evidence is invalid for managed callback
  --> app.jet:9:18

comparisons.note: A capturing closure passed as a function pointer gets a note naming the capture. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/types/closure.html
comparisons.code:
note: closures can only be coerced to `fn` types if they
      do not capture any variables
    |     move |x| x + offset
    |                  ------ `offset` captured here

recommendation.why: A says what went wrong and where: the function, the rule and the captured name. The type error keeps its one meaning, and each code's More page explains one mistake.
gains: The message names the rule the function broke.
E3203 keeps one meaning: a type C cannot call.

losses.loss: One more registered error code.
losses.mitigation: It replaces misleading text in seven existing snapshots, which are regenerated in the same change.

whyNot.reason: B fixes the text, but one code and one More page then cover two unrelated mistakes.
C's code means missing provider metadata, which a user cannot fix in their own function.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one code with a clear meaning. B keeps a code that means two things. C borrows an unrelated code.

decisions.title: Report every error by default
decisions.gist: Should check, build, run and test report every error they find, or stop at the first failing phase?
decisions.lesson: A compile can stop after the first phase that finds an error, so users fix errors one round at a time. A full report shows all of them at once. Run naively, later phases would also report errors caused by earlier ones; the recommended design hides those.
decisions.story: Ana runs jet build on a project with a type error in one file and a bad import in another. Under option A she sees both errors in one run and no output file is written. Under option B she sees the type error, fixes it, and only then learns about the import.

Rust: rustc reports every type error in one pass across a crate, then stops before code generation. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/

Go: go build reports up to ten errors per package, then stops. Source: https://go.dev/doc/
decisions.detail:
Owner ruling, 2026-10-09 (card #4914): every phase runs by default for check, build, run and test, with typed traps. No artifact is written when an error occurs. One canonical option is both a CLI flag and a build config setting.

Today the pipeline stops between phases at JetDriver Pipeline.jet:2220 and BodyComptime.jet:221. The full mode exists only behind the compiler-internal JET_KEEP_GOING=1 (Compiler/Bootstrap/Host/Entry.jet:10-128). The card plan keeps JET_KEEP_GOING_SKIP as a developer tool if needed.

No ratified decision found by keyword scan records this default.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version kept two losses: follow-on noise and a longer run. Both are designed away. A failed item is marked failed, and every later phase skips that item and anything whose meaning depends on it. A check that meets a failed type or name stays silent, as rustc does with its error type. So every printed error is a root error, and a later phase does less work, not more.

Follow-on errors are still recorded. The text summary counts them, and --json lists each one with the root it came from. This also settles the owner question about follow-on UI rows: they leave the default output.

options.name: Report every error by default
options.detail: check, build, run and test run every phase and report every root error they find. An error caused by an earlier one is hidden from the text output and counted in the summary. No output file is written when an error occurs. One option sets this in the CLI and in the build config.
options.technical: Remove the stop-between-phases gates at Pipeline.jet:2220 and BodyComptime.jet:221 for the default mode. A failed item carries an error mark; later phases skip it and its dependents, and checks that meet an error type or failed name emit nothing. Keep-going traps stay for lowering. Suppressed diagnostics are kept with a caused_by link for --json. The developer-only JET_KEEP_GOING=1 switch is replaced by the canonical option.

decisions.title: How the compiler and Jetpack reach Core operations that user programs must not call
decisions.situation:
Jetpack and the compiler need five Core operations that user programs must never call. Two exist today as `files.compiler_with_process_directory` and `files.compiler_link_held`. They are ordinary public functions, and a user program can call them: we checked one with the tree14 compiler and it passed. The other three are blocked because no rule lets the toolchain reach a private Core module.

We recommend one more qualifier in the existing `priv(…)` family, `priv(toolchain) module`. Only Core, the compiler and Jetpack may use such a module. User programs get E0605, as for any private module.
decisions.gist: Should Core operations meant only for the compiler and Jetpack live in a `priv(toolchain) module`, become public documented functions, or be reached through foreign-call glue?
decisions.lesson: Jet marks privacy on modules, not on functions. A `priv module` is usable only by its enclosing module, and a `priv(package) module` by its own package. Neither lets the compiler or Jetpack, which are separate packages, reach a private part of Core.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. The toolchain is the set of packages the Jet distribution ships: Core, the compiler packages and Jetpack, the package manager. A seam is a Core operation that only the toolchain needs, such as running a child process inside a folder that Jetpack already holds open.

A held folder is a `Directory` value that keeps the folder open. Work done through it cannot be redirected by renaming the folder's path.
decisions.story: Omar's app imports `core.files` and sees `compiler_link_held` in completion. He calls it inside an `#Unsafe` block, and the compiler accepts it, because the function is public. Next release the store changes the function's errno rules and his app breaks. Under A the function lives in `core.files.toolchain`, completion never offers it, and his call is E0605 from the start.
decisions.detail:
Source: card #4896 and its four added cases. Five seams need the same answer.

1. Run a child process inside a held folder. Jetpack's TreeHash.jet:562 calls `files.compiler_with_process_directory`.
2. Link an open file into a held folder. Jetpack's TreeHash.jet:738 calls `files.compiler_link_held`.
3. Pass a held lock to a child process, so a child keeps the same lock. Core has no such operation yet.
4. Lower the compiler's `sort_by` to one private Core kernel, so every tier shares one meaning.
5. Let the compiler's build-receipt producer read Core/build's private session.

Today. The double-underscore names were renamed to legal `compiler_` names, so the CLI source parses. But Sema has no caller check on Core calls (Sema core_call, traced by CoreReview5-2-2). A user file calling `files.compiler_with_process_directory` inside `#Unsafe` passes `jet check` on the tree14 compiler (probe ballot/xb/seam.jet). Seams 3 to 5 cannot be written, because a private module refuses every outside package.

The visibility law. Declarations carry no visibility marker; `priv` marks a module or a field. `priv(package) module` is the one qualified form, and any other qualifier is E0414 (syntax-decisions S18). The draft's `toolchain fn` mark broke that law, so A now uses a module qualifier instead.

What A adds. `priv(toolchain) module` is accepted only in a toolchain package; elsewhere it stays E0414. A use from any other package is E0605, the error every private module already gives. A package counts as toolchain when its source root lies inside the Jet distribution that supplied Core. Package names play no part, so a user package cannot claim the status.

Compiler-generated calls. When the compiler lowers `list.sort_by(f)` in a user program to the Core kernel, the call is the compiler's, so it passes. A call written in the user's source still gets E0605.

Safety. Seams 1 and 2 become typed functions that return `IOError`, with no raw errno tuple and no `#Unsafe` marker. Seam 1 has the same body as the public `Directory.pass_to`, which needs no gate. The `#Unsafe` blocks at Jetpack's two call sites go away.

A side question in the draft, whether diagnostics can read text without copying it, is not a privacy question. Borrowed text is ordinary public Jet, so it needs no seam.

options.name: One `priv(toolchain) module` in Core for all five seams
options.detail:
Core gathers the seams into private modules marked `priv(toolchain)`, such as `core.files.toolchain`. Core, the compiler and Jetpack may use them. Any other package gets E0605, and completion and the reference never list them.

The qualifier joins the existing `priv(…)` family and is accepted only inside a toolchain package. User code can never write it. Calls the compiler generates, such as the `sort_by` kernel, pass. The seams take typed arguments and return `IOError`, so their callers need no `#Unsafe` block.
options.technical:
Parser: `priv(toolchain)` is accepted before `module` when the file's package is a toolchain package, else E0414 as today. Sema: the E0605 check in Calls/Core.jet:354 and Expressions/Places.jet:790 admits a toolchain-private module in two cases. The caller's package root lies inside the distribution root that supplied Core, or the call is compiler-generated.

Core: move the two `compiler_` functions into `priv(toolchain) module toolchain` in Core/Files as `run_in` and `link_into`. Add `pass_lock`, the sort kernel and the build-session readers to toolchain modules beside their owners. Jetpack drops both `#Unsafe` blocks. Syntax-decisions S18 gains one line.

options.name: Make each seam a public, documented Core function
options.detail:
Each seam becomes a public function with documentation, such as `spec.run_in(folder)`, `reader.link_into(folder, name)` and `lock.pass_to(spec, at)`. The sort kernel and the build-session readers become public too.

Anyone may call them, and each becomes a promise Core must keep stable across releases.
options.technical: Rename the two `compiler_` functions to public methods and remove the `#Unsafe` markers. Add `AdvisoryLock.pass_to`. Export the sort kernel from core.collections and the build-session readers from core.build, which turns a read-only query surface into one with mutable session state.

options.name: Reach the runtime directly through foreign-call glue
options.detail:
Jetpack declares the runtime symbols itself with `#Import(c)` and calls them, as C code would. Core adds nothing.

Seams 4 and 5 are Jet functions, not runtime symbols, so glue cannot reach them and they stay blocked.
options.technical: Jetpack adds `#Import(c)` declarations for `jet_process_spec_with_directory_raw` and `jet_files_link_reader_at_raw`, and keeps their argument layouts in step with the runtime by hand. The Core checks in `process_directory` (slot range, closed folder, slot taken) are skipped.

comparisons.note: A module may export a package only to named modules. java.base exports `jdk.internal.misc` to a fixed list of JDK modules, and other code cannot use it. Source: JLS 7.7.2, qualified exports.

A package under `internal/` can be imported only by code rooted at its parent. Since Go 1.23 the linker also refuses new `go:linkname` pulls into the standard library. Source: go.dev/doc/go1.23, Linker.
comparisons.code: import "internal/poll"   // only the standard library may

comparisons.note: The standard library marks internal items unstable with no tracking issue, so stable user code cannot call them. The compiler's own crates opt in with `rustc_private`. Source: rustc-dev-guide, Stability attributes.

recommendation.why: A protects all five operations with the privacy rule Jet already has: one module qualifier and the existing E0605. User programs can no longer reach compiler-only operations, and the three blocked ones can be written.
gains: User programs cannot call compiler-only operations.
One rule for all five operations, with no new declaration marker.
Jetpack's two `#Unsafe` blocks go away.

losses.loss: A third-party package manager cannot use the operations Jetpack uses.
losses.mitigation: An operation useful to everyone moves out of the toolchain module into a public typed API, as `Directory.pass_to` did.

whyNot.reason: Every compiler-only operation becomes a public promise, and the build session gains public mutable state.
Glue skips Core's checks, any user can write it too, and two of the five seams stay blocked.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more `priv(…)` qualifier that only toolchain packages may write. In return, compiler-only operations are closed to user programs and all five seams have a home.

decisions.title: Games and apps share two independent subsystems: ray for visuals and input, audio for sound
decisions.situation: A Doom-style game must show its own pixel buffer, play raw sound samples and read every key press. Jet's game library cannot do these yet. You ruled that Jet talks to the display and sound system itself, with no C library. You also asked that games and desktop apps share one visual subsystem, our raylib, and one audio subsystem, our miniaudio. They should be independent parts, not one big platform. The web stays different. We recommend exactly that: ray and audio, each usable alone and together.
decisions.gist: Should games and apps share two independent subsystems, ray for visuals and audio for sound?
decisions.lesson: A subsystem is a library that owns one kind of hardware. ray owns windows, drawing and the keys and mouse of each window. audio owns speakers and sound mixing. Each works alone, and a program can open several of each. Games, apps and music players combine only the parts they need.
decisions.story: Ana ports a small Doom-style game. Every frame she draws 320 by 200 pixels with a 256-colour palette, queues a footstep sound and reads the arrow keys. Her friend writes a notes app with two windows, and another writes a music player with no window. All three want the same libraries, and tests that check pixels and sound without a screen.
decisions.inWild:
SDL: separate subsystems for video, audio and events, each started on its own with SDL_InitSubSystem. Source: https://wiki.libsdl.org/SDL3/SDL_InitSubSystem

raylib and miniaudio: raylib draws windows and reads input; its sound module is built on miniaudio, which can also be used alone. Source: https://miniaud.io/docs/manual/
decisions.detail:
WHAT CHANGED FROM THE LAST DRAFT

The last draft put window, sound and input into one game.Platform value. You asked for independent, modular systems shared with the app framework, with the web kept apart. Now ray is the visual subsystem and audio is the sound subsystem. Each stands alone; core.game and gui only combine them.

TODAY

Core/Game/Game.jet is a 19-line shell for scenes, input bindings and replays. Core/Game/Raylib.jet (2385 lines, core.game.raylib) opens a window, draws shapes and plays sound files. It cannot show a caller's own pixel buffer, queue raw sound samples, or hand over every input event.

Core/Ui holds app pieces such as dialogs, clipboard and drag and drop, but no window or drawing of its own.

RULINGS IT BUILDS ON

- D-RAYLIB-DRIVER-LOAD1=A: Jet speaks the display and sound protocols itself, and programs stay single static files. GPU drawing is a later opt-in.
- D-RAYLIB-FONT-HOME1=A: ray is Jet's own game library and font its font engine, used by ray and gui. raylib, the binding to C raylib, stays separate.
- D-RAY-API1=A: ray keeps raylib's names but draws through explicit window and frame values, so no state is global.

- Card c0776o2m: the Doom port is as much Jet as possible. The operating-system edge (Wayland or X11, ALSA or PipeWire) stays inside vetted #Unsafe Core code. Acceptance: a window shows a 320x200 indexed buffer at 35 Hz, plays a tone and logs key events on Linux. Headless checksums for pixels and sound match on every build level.

SHAPE UNDER A

ray, the visual subsystem. ray.open(width, height, title) opens a window, and a program may open several. win.frames(fps) yields one frame at a time. frame.events() lists that window's key, mouse and resize events in arrival order.

Each frame offers two levels of control. frame.present(pixels, palette) or frame.present(rgba) shows your own buffer. raylib-style calls such as frame.draw_rect draw for you. ray.gamepads() lists connected controllers, which belong to no window.

audio, the sound subsystem. audio.open(rate) opens an output device, and a program may open several. out.queue(samples) plays raw 16-bit sound at 11025 to 48000 Hz. audio.mixer(out) adds the miniaudio-style level: load sounds, play voices, set volume, and group voices into buses.

Composition. core.game keeps scenes, input bindings and replays. game.run(scene) opens a window and an audio device for you, or takes ones you opened. gui builds its widgets on ray windows and frames, with font for text. Neither holds device code of its own.

Tests. ray.headless(width, height) and audio.headless(rate) return the same types with no device. They record each frame and each block of sound as checksums for golden tests. Their events come from a script or a replay.

Web. core.web stays separate, as you said. Whether ray can also draw on a browser canvas is a later ballot.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Keeping picture and sound in step. They need no shared clock. The screen shows each frame when it is ready. The speakers play from a buffer at their own steady rate. out.queued() says how much sound is waiting, so a game keeps a few frames ahead; game.run does this for you.

2. More to open than one value. A game that uses game.run opens nothing itself. A program that opens its own parts writes one line per part, and only for parts it uses.

3. Tests need two fakes. Each headless call is one line, and game.run takes both, as the example shows.

4. Two ways to draw. present and the raylib-style calls draw into the same frame. A game may mix them, for example a pixel buffer under drawn text.

No loss remains.

EDGE CASES

- Closing one of several windows ends only its frame loop. Its events stop and its frames end.
- No audio device: audio.open returns a typed error, and game.run continues silent with a warning.
- A sound queue that runs dry plays silence and counts the gap, which the headless report shows.

- Two programs, or two outputs in one program, may share one device; the sound system mixes them.
- Keys are read per window, so the focused window gets them. A key press with no focused window reaches nobody.

AFTER A LANDS

core.game.raylib moves into ray, and its sound calls move into audio. The old module is deleted, and every example moves to the new names in the same change.

WHY NOT B OR C

B also splits input from ray. But keys and mouse belong to the focused window, so input has to point back at a window anyway, and a key would be asked about in two places. C keeps one platform value with window, sound and input. An app or music player then takes parts it does not want, and a program cannot have two windows or keep sound running when a window closes.

options.name: Two subsystems: ray and audio
options.detail:
ray is the visual subsystem: windows, frames, drawing, and each window's keys and mouse. audio is the sound subsystem: output devices, raw sample queues and a mixer. Each works alone, and a program can open several of each.

Games and desktop apps share both. core.game adds scenes and replays, gui adds widgets, and neither has device code of its own. Headless versions of both return the same types for tests. The web stays separate.
options.technical: ray.Window and audio.Output own their devices behind vetted #Unsafe Core code. win.frames(fps) paces on core.time's steady clock. audio.mixer(out) is a voice and bus graph over one Output. ray.headless and audio.headless open no device and record checksums. game.run takes an optional Window and Output.

options.name: Three subsystems: visual, input, audio
options.detail: Like A, but input is its own subsystem beside ray and audio. Keys and mouse still come from a focused window, so each input call names a window. A key can be asked about both through input and through the window's events.

A music player uses audio alone, with no window.

decisions.title: What an HTTP body value is once the Rust code is gone
decisions.situation: When a Jet program downloads something, the data arrives as an HTTP body. Jet's reader for that body was written in Rust, and that code is now deleted. Jet's own Body is a plain value that cannot hold a download still arriving, so Jet's package manager cannot download anything yet. The vote decides what a body is; we recommend a file-like reader, which keeps the large-download streaming you already approved.
decisions.gist: When a program receives an HTTP body, should it get a file-like reader, or a plain value?
decisions.lesson: A body is the data inside a web request or response, such as a downloaded file. Jet's body() reader used to live in deleted Rust code. Jet's own Body today is a plain value with three cases: empty, text or bytes. A plain value cannot hold a download that is still arriving. Whichever option wins, Jet's HTTP client must then be written in Jet.
decisions.story: Mia's build script downloads a 300 MiB package archive with Jet. She wants it streamed to disk under a size cap, not loaded into memory, and she wants the same body methods on her small server.
decisions.inWild:
resp, err := http.Get(url)
defer resp.Body.Close()
data, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
// https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Response
decisions.detail: Code: Core/http/http.jet:87 defines the Body enum with Empty, Text(String), and Bytes([U8]). A shared, one-shot native body cannot be held there. Option A makes Body opaque with a private shared carrier and constructors and inspection methods. Option B adds a hidden fourth case. Option C reads the whole body on access, which conflicts with the ratified streaming cap. The public carrier for the native body is decided in a separate card, which this ballot depends on.

options.name: A file-like Body
options.detail: Body becomes a closed Core type with private fields. Programs build one with Body.empty(), Body.text(s) or Body.bytes(b). They read one with text(limit), bytes(limit), json(limit), chunks() and copy_to(^writer), each a single pass. The size cap you approved in D-CORE-HTTPBODYLIMIT1 applies to every read. Client and server use the same type.
options.technical: Core/Http/Http.jet: Body becomes a struct with a private shared one-pass reader state (the connection, the remaining framing, a consumed flag) or an in-memory payload. body_as_text and body_as_bytes, the only matches on the cases today, move to the read methods. Calls/Http.jet keeps the same method names and results. No example matches on the cases.
options.code:
text :: resp.body().text(1024 * 1024) ?? panic("body")
resp.body(limit: 2.gib).copy_to(^file)
reply :: Body.text("ok")

options.name: Hidden fourth case
options.detail: Body keeps its Empty, Text and Bytes cases and gains a private Stream case that programs cannot name. Every match on Body then needs an else arm, which runs for streamed bodies.
options.technical: The enum gains a private variant carrying the shared reader state. The checker would need a new rule for a variant that is hidden from user matches.

options.name: Read it all on arrival
options.detail: The client reads the whole body into memory before it returns the response, so Body stays a finished three-case value. Streaming large downloads to disk is no longer possible.
options.technical: send() reads to the end of the framing and stores Body.Bytes. This contradicts D-CORE-HTTPBODYLIMIT1, which ratified a one-pass streamed body with its own cap.
options.code:
resp :: http.get(url) ?? panic("get")
text :: http.body_as_text(resp.body())

comparisons.note: net/http gives Response.Body as an io.ReadCloser that the program reads once: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Response.
reqwest reads the body through methods on the response (bytes, text, chunk), not through an enum: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.Response.html.

recommendation.why: Only a reader can stream a large download under a cap, and Go and Rust clients make the same choice.
gains: Keeps the approved streaming rule and one meaning for Body.

losses.loss: Code can no longer match on .Text or .Bytes cases.
losses.mitigation: Only Core's own helpers do this today, and they move to the read methods.

whyNot.reason: B makes every match carry an else arm that quietly mishandles streams.
C breaks the streaming you already approved and can exhaust memory on big downloads.

recommendation.tradeoff: Body loses pattern matching; reading it uses the same methods everywhere.

decisions.title: How each linked part is spelled, defaulted and reported
decisions.situation: Native Jet programs are fully static today. The GPU driver must load from the user's system, and a static process cannot load it. Each linked part needs its own linkage, because tools and graphics programs differ. We recommend per-part settings in the build function, with defaults that need no annotation in most programs. Tools stay one file.
decisions.gist: How should a program choose static or dynamic linking for each part it uses?
decisions.lesson: A program often mixes parts that must stay static with parts the system must load. One setting per program cannot serve both.
decisions.story: Eli builds a small command-line tool and a game. The tool should stay one file. The game must load the system's graphics driver at run time.
decisions.inWild: go build ./game   // static unless cgo uses a system library
decisions.detail:
Source: card #5088 log, 2026-10-21 owner amendment. Linkage is decided per linked item: Jet runtime and libc, system libraries such as libGL, bundled C libraries, and foreign closures. Defaults: pure Jet and bundled C static; OS driver and system libraries dynamic. CLI --linkage stays a whole-program override. Still open: exact spelling, the full defaults table, and per-item reporting in jet inspect. Ratified D-JPK-VARIANT1 (D) sets the axes.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version listed testing two linkage modes as a loss of A. It is shared work: any design where a graphics program runs needs dynamic loading, and any design where a tool stays one file needs static linking. B and C carry the same test work, so it is not a reason to choose between them.

The test matrix is generated from one list of cells, each run in its required mode. jet inspect shows each part with its linkage and why, so a wrong default is visible at once. A program that names no dynamic part stays one static file, exactly as today.

options.name: Per-part settings in the build function
options.detail: Each linked part has its own linkage. Defaults: pure Jet and bundled C static; OS driver and system libraries dynamic. The build function changes any part. jet inspect lists each part with its linkage and its source.
options.technical: The build function returns a per-item linkage map; the linker resolves each item separately and rejects impossible combinations as diagnostics.

options.name: One setting for the whole program
options.detail: The build command or manifest picks one linkage for everything.
options.technical: One linkage value passes to the linker; no per-item map.
options.code: jet build --linkage=dynamic game.jet

options.name: Separate link file
options.detail: Linked parts are listed in a linking file beside the package.
options.technical: A second input file is parsed and checked against the package's imports.
options.code: link.jet: gpu = dynamic

comparisons.note: Go builds static binaries and links dynamically only when a system library is needed.

recommendation.why: Each part gets the linkage its platform needs, from a default table, so most programs write nothing. Tools stay one static file and graphics programs load the system GPU driver.
gains: Static tools stay single-file.
Graphics programs work out of the box.
jet inspect shows each part’s linkage and its reason.

whyNot.reason: One setting cannot keep tools static and graphics programs working.
A second file adds a place to forget a setting.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining: testing both modes is shared work every option needs.

current.code: jet build game.jet   // one static file; the GPU driver cannot load

options.name: Per-part settings in the build function

gains: Pure Jet and bundled C stay static.
System drivers load from the OS.

options.name: One setting for the whole program
options.gist: Choose static or dynamic once in the build command or manifest.
gains: Simplest to explain.
losses: A static program cannot use the GPU, and a dynamic one loses single-file output.

proposed.code: jet build --linkage=dynamic game.jet

options.gist: List each linked part in a separate linking file next to the package.
gains: Build code and link settings stay apart.
losses: A second file must be kept in step with the package.

decisions.title: The language server runs on the one compiler session
decisions.situation: The language server answers your editor: errors as you type, hover text, go to definition. It used to live in the Rust host and checked code on its own path, so the editor could disagree with jet check. On 2026-10-17 you ruled that it is ported one-for-one to Jet and runs on the one compiler session that jet check and jet build use. The port now lives in the compiler tree, and the Rust server is gone. This records your ruling.
decisions.gist: Should the language server be ported to Jet and run on the one compiler session, or stay in the Rust command-line host?
decisions.lesson: A language server is the program an editor talks to for errors, hovers and jumps. If it checks code its own way, the editor and the command line can disagree. Running it on the same compiler session as jet check keeps their answers identical.
decisions.story: Chen edits a file in VS Code. The server is part of Jet and reads the same session as jet check, so the red underline in the editor is exactly the error jet check prints.
decisions.inWild:
Go: gopls is the language server, built on the same analysis packages the go tool uses. Source: https://go.dev/gopls/

Rust: rust-analyzer is the language server, built on the compiler's front-end crates. Source: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/
decisions.detail:
OWNER RULING

Owner ruling, 2026-10-17, recorded in the card #3410 log. It reads: “the LSP is 1:1 Rust-to-Jet parity work and is ported onto the one compiler session (D-LSP1=C)”. It adds: “the plan line keeping the LSP in the Rust host is superseded.” This ballot records it for one-click confirmation. The alternative is kept for the record.

D-LSP1 is not present in decisions.json; its ruling exists only in the card log. The same log records two amendments. D-INCR-PARK1=C (2026-10-17) keeps one compiler service, and editor answers recheck the whole package per edit, with no item-level reuse. D-SESSION-MCP1=A removes the port’s MCP methods and initialize fields, so the LSP speaks only LSP.

Related ratified decisions, all 2026-10-17: D-SESSION-WIRE1=A (NDJSON jet.session.v1), D-SESSION-ENTRY1=C (--listen=- on check, build, test, run and dev) and D-SESSION-OWNER1=A (jet dev --serve and jet self lsp --serve). D-LSP-BUILDSAVE1 is still open on this card.

TODAY

The port lives in Compiler/JetLSP, with 36 source files and 68 test files. The Rust server under Source/LSP is gone from the tree. positionEncoding negotiation is not yet in Compiler/JetLSP/Source, and the LSP 3.18 applicability inventory is still owed. The card is blocked on #3196.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

Parity work is not a cost of A. The Rust server is gone under every option, so any working editor support needs the Jet port to reach parity. A makes parity checkable: the LSP 3.18 inventory lists each item, and positionEncoding is one of them. No loss remains.

options.name: Port the LSP onto the one compiler session
options.detail: The language server is ported to Jet and runs on the one compiler session with jet check and jet build. The Rust server was retired once the port took over.
options.technical: Compiler/JetLSP on the one compiler session (jet self lsp --serve, jet dev --serve). It reaches 1:1 parity with the Rust server it replaced, including positionEncoding and the LSP 3.18 inventory. It speaks only LSP, per D-SESSION-MCP1=A.
options.code: $ jet self lsp --serve   # LSP and jet check share one session

options.name: Keep the LSP in the Rust host
options.detail: The language server stays in the Rust command-line host. It reads its own checks.
options.technical: Keep the Rust server on its own check path. Superseded by the ruling; the Rust server has since been removed.
options.code: $ jet lsp              # Rust server; separate check path

comparisons.note: gopls runs on the analysis packages that the go tool also uses. Source: https://go.dev/gopls/
rust-analyzer runs on the compiler's front-end crates. Source: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/

recommendation.why: You ruled this on 2026-10-17. One compiler session gives the editor the same answers as the command line.
gains: The editor and jet check report the same errors.
One session to maintain.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a second check path that can disagree with jet check.

recommendation.tradeoff: A finishes the port, and the editor and the command line share one checker.

decisions.title: Nixpkgs packages come in as native Jet packages, with no Nix
decisions.gist: Should Nixpkgs packages be translated into native Jet packages stored only in Hangar, with no Nix program or store at all?
decisions.lesson: Jetpack can use Nixpkgs packages, but today it can call an installed Nix as a fallback. Jetpack can instead read each Nixpkgs recipe itself and run its build steps inside Hangar, so every package installs with no Nix at all.
decisions.story: Ravi installs a tool that exists only in Nixpkgs. Under option A Jetpack translates its recipe into a native Jet package, and the install needs no Nix on his machine. Under option B Jetpack calls his installed Nix when the translation is missing, so the install depends on a Nix he never chose.
decisions.inWild:
Guix: a package manager with its own store and recipes, separate from Nix. Source: https://guix.gnu.org/manual/en/html_node/Invoking-guix-package.html

Nix: packages are built into /nix/store by the Nix daemon. Source: https://nixos.org/manual/nix/stable/
decisions.detail:
Owner requirement, 2026-09-13 (card #3402): ingest Nixpkgs through an adapter that translates definitions into the native Jet package model. Jetpack owns resolution, builds, installation, updates and removal. Hangar is the only store. No separately installed or bundled Nix package manager, daemon, profile or store is permitted, including hidden or mounted stores. Native Jet packages bypass the adapter. Jet and Jetpack code is MIT; the adapter must not depend on Nix executables, libraries, daemons, services or storage.

The card records that D-NIX-UPSTREAM1 was superseded unratified, so this requirement is not a ratified decision.

Conflict: ratified D-JPK-SNIXREUSE1 (2026-08-25, option A) keeps a local Nix import on a miss, and D-JPK-NIXSTORE1 (2026-07-10, option D) uses a projected Nix store. Both predate the 2026-09-13 requirement and conflict with it. The card's current state: crates/jetpack/src/NixFallbackPolicy.rs and Jetpack/Nix/Source/Fallback/FallbackPolicy.jet still call nix build.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version translated packages one by one, so an untranslated package failed until someone converted it. Now Jetpack translates at the level every package shares. NixEval, Jet’s own Nix-language evaluator, reads the recipe and yields its build plan: sources, dependencies, build script and environment.

Jetpack then fetches the sources by hash and runs that plan in its own sandbox, storing the result in Hangar under Jet’s own paths. That is generic, so any package Nixpkgs can build installs without per-package work, and no Nix program, daemon or store is used.

What can still fail is a recipe that uses a Nix language feature NixEval lacks. That failure names the feature, and one evaluator fix unblocks every package using it.

options.name: Build Nixpkgs recipes natively in Hangar
options.detail: Jetpack reads each Nixpkgs recipe with its own evaluator, fetches the sources by hash, and runs the recipe’s build steps in its sandbox. Hangar stores the result. The installed-Nix fallback is deleted. Native Jet packages skip this path.
options.technical: Delete the fallback files and the JETPACK_NIX_FALLBACK_POLICY variables. NixEval evaluates the attribute to its build plan; the realizer fetches fixed-output sources, runs the builder with the recorded environment in the Hangar sandbox, and rewrites output paths to Hangar paths. Upstream provenance is kept so updates re-evaluate. Unsupported evaluator features become named, tracked diagnostics.
options.code: $ jetpack install ripgrep-nix   # translated; stored in Hangar; no nix on PATH

options.name: Keep an installed-Nix fallback
options.detail: Native packages come first. When a Nixpkgs package has no translation, Jetpack calls an installed Nix.
options.technical: Keep Fallback/FallbackPolicy.jet and the nix build path behind the policy variable.
options.code: $ jetpack install postgres-nix   # falls back to installed nix build --json

comparisons.note: Guix keeps its own store and recipes, separate from Nix. Source: https://guix.gnu.org/manual/en/html_node/Invoking-guix-package.html
Packages are built into /nix/store by the Nix daemon. Source: https://nixos.org/manual/nix/stable/

recommendation.why: The owner required one native store and no Nix on the install path. Building recipes natively meets that for every package at once, instead of one translation at a time.
gains: One store, Hangar, for every package.
An ordinary install needs no Nix.
Any package Nixpkgs can build installs, with no per-package work.

whyNot.reason: B brings an installed Nix back as a dependency, which the owner requirement forbids.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining: every Nixpkgs package installs, and Nix is never installed.

surface.gist: Should Nixpkgs packages become native Jet packages stored only in Hangar, with no Nix at all?
surface.lesson: Today Jetpack can fall back to an installed Nix for Nixpkgs packages. Should it build those recipes itself, with no Nix at all?

current.note: A missing translation falls back to an installed Nix.
current.code: $ jetpack install postgres-nix   # calls nix build --json

wild.note: Guix keeps its own store and recipes, separate from Nix. Source: https://guix.gnu.org/manual/en/html_node/Invoking-guix-package.html
wild.code: guix install hello

gains: No Nix on any install path.

options.gist: Untranslated packages call the installed Nix.
gains: More packages install today.
losses: A Nix dependency remains on the install path.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining.

decisions.title: The optimizer report reads the slot IR optimizer
decisions.situation: The optimization report, jet inspect decisions, tells you what the optimizer did to your program and why it declined some steps. It was first written for the compiler’s old middle layers, which are now deleted. On 2026-10-22 you ruled that the report reads the new IR optimizer’s own records, with no translation layer from the old format. Module totals and declined-loop notes already come from it. This records your ruling.
decisions.gist: When the old middle layers are deleted, should the optimization report describe what the slot IR optimizer did, or be dropped?
decisions.lesson: An optimization report tells you which speed-ups the compiler applied and why it skipped others. It must read the optimizer that actually runs, or it describes code that no longer exists.
decisions.story: Dev wonders why a sum loop stayed scalar. jet inspect decisions prints the loop note from the IR optimizer, with the reason the vectorizing step declined.
decisions.inWild:
LLVM: optimization remarks report which passes fired or missed, per function. Source: https://llvm.org/docs/Remarks.html

Go: the -m flag prints inlining and escape decisions. Source: https://go.dev/wiki/CompilerOptimizations
decisions.detail:
OWNER RULING

Owner ruling, 2026-10-22, architecture cutover card log, quoted: “The optimizer ledger (jet inspect optimization, live report) is retargeted to the IR optimizer report, no shim.” This ballot records it for one-click confirmation. The alternative is kept for the record.

The same ruling ports the web emitter onto the slot IR and drops the old Rust-source emitter. Those parts are covered by the ratified one-IR architecture and the Rust removal scope ballot.

TODAY

The command is jet inspect decisions (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Inspect.jet:198). It prints the IR optimizer’s report for the checked program at the level jet build uses (InspectDecisions.jet:1-7).

The report is IROptReport (Compiler/JetIR/Source/Opt.jet:123-163). It holds module totals per pass: inlined calls, folds, fused compares, removed dead code and more. It also has one note per loop reduction or stepped index, vectorized or declined with the reason (OptReduce.jet:222-229, OptVersion.jet:194-197). Nothing translates old middle-layer records.

OWED UNDER A

Per-function outcomes for every pass, not only loop notes, so a user can ask about one function.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Recording cost. Per-function notes are recorded only when jet inspect decisions asks for them. A normal jet build passes no recorder, so it does no extra work and its output bytes are unchanged.

2. Per-function outcomes are owed work, not a cost to users. Each pass already decides per function; the note records that decision with its reason, as loop notes do today.

No loss remains.

options.name: Retarget the report to the slot IR optimizer
options.detail: The report lists what the IR optimizer did and why it declined steps, read straight from the optimizer that runs. Nothing translates the old format.
options.technical: jet inspect decisions reads IROptReport: module totals per pass plus per-loop notes. Per-function outcomes for every pass are added there. The old ledger code went with the old layers. Per-function notes are recorded only when jet inspect decisions asks; a normal build passes no recorder and pays nothing.
options.code:
$ jet inspect decisions app.jet
O1: instructions <before> -> <after>, inlined <n>, folded <n>, ...
sum reduction total: declined (<reason>)

options.name: Drop the report
options.detail: Delete the report with the old layers; bring it back later if wanted.
options.technical: Remove jet inspect decisions with the old layers.
options.code:
$ jet inspect decisions app.jet
# error: unknown inspect plane

comparisons.note: Optimization remarks per pass and function. Source: https://llvm.org/docs/Remarks.html
The compiler explains inlining and escape decisions. Source: https://go.dev/wiki/CompilerOptimizations

recommendation.why: You ruled this on 2026-10-22. Users keep one place to learn why code was or was not optimized, read from the optimizer that actually runs.
gains: The report describes the optimizer that actually runs.
No translation layer from the deleted middle layers.

whyNot.reason: B removes the only tool that explains optimization decisions.

recommendation.tradeoff: A reads the optimizer that runs and records notes only when asked, so builds pay nothing.

decisions.title: How a public Core type holds a native value that user code can neither name nor build
decisions.situation:
The ratified HTTP law wants one public `Body` type over a private native stream that reads the body lazily. Today `Body` is a plain enum that holds every byte in memory, so `chunks()` on a large download first buffers the whole body. The stream needs a native value that only Core may create, and Jet has no checked way to hide one.

We recommend that the native value's type live in a `priv module` inside core.http, and that `Body` hold it in a `priv` field. Both forms already exist in the visibility law. The checker then refuses any user code that names the type or builds a `Body` by hand.
decisions.gist: How should Core's `Body` hold a native stream that user code must never name or build?
decisions.lesson: Some Core values wrap a native resource, such as an open socket stream. If user code could build one with any contents, it could read from a resource it never opened. Jet already has `priv` modules and `priv` fields, which keep names and contents inside one module.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A facade is the public type users hold, here `Body`. A carrier is the native value inside it, here the stream that pulls the body's bytes from the connection. Forging means building a value by hand, with a struct literal, instead of getting it from the library.

A `priv module` is usable only by its enclosing module. A `priv` field can be read and written only by code in its type's own module.
decisions.story: Ines downloads a 2 GB file and reads it with `chunks()`. Today her program first holds all 2 GB in memory, because `Body` is a buffered enum. Under A the chunks arrive from the network one at a time. Her test builds a fake body with `http.body_text("…")`, and a typo that builds `Body{…}` by hand is a clear compile error.
decisions.detail:
Source: card #4903, which blocks the HTTP Body cutover and six HTTP goldens. The ratified HTTP law wants one public, source-owned `Body` over a private, lazy native transport.

Today. Core/Http/Http.jet:89 declares `enum Body { Empty, Text(String), Bytes([U8]) }`. `chunks()` (line 216) copies the whole body into a byte list first, so a large download is held in memory. A shared cell gives read-once behavior.

The forging gap, measured on the tree14 compiler (probes ballot/xb/carrier.jet and carrier2.jet). A user program that builds `files.Directory{path: "x", handle: 3}`, `files.FileWriter{path: "x"}` or a struct literal that sets another module's `priv` field passes `jet check`. Reading that `priv` field from another module also passes, and `jet run` prints it. The ui row import_private_field, which expects E0605, fails for the same reason.

So the draft's premise, a public carrier "with no public constructor", is not enforced for any Core carrier today.

The law already has the parts. Syntax-decisions S18 says a `priv` field is readable and writable only by its type's module. It says a `priv module` is usable only by its enclosing module. A only needs these enforced on struct literals and field reads, and the native-carrier registry to accept a carrier declared in a `priv module`.

What the registry holds. FileWriter is a known native carrier whose rows give its clone and drop behavior (core_types). The card notes that these rows are accepted only for public carriers today. A lifts that restriction: the carrier row names its module, and Sema applies ordinary privacy. No new attribute and no new IR kind are needed; the card's joint Core and native review found `Type.Named` sufficient.

Test bodies. User tests still build bodies with the public `http.body_text`, `body_bytes` and `body_empty` (Http.jet:734-741). These return a `Body` whose carrier is an in-memory stream.

Same rule for existing carriers. `Directory.handle` and `AdvisoryLock.handle` become `priv` fields, which closes the measured forging of a folder handle.

options.name: Carrier type in a `priv module`, held in a `priv` field
options.detail:
Core declares the native stream type inside a `priv module` of core.http, and `Body` becomes a struct that holds it in a `priv` field. User code cannot name the stream type and cannot build a `Body` by hand; both give E0605. Bodies come from responses, requests or the public `body_text`, `body_bytes` and `body_empty`.

The checker enforces the existing `priv` rules on struct literals and field reads, which also closes the forging of `Directory` and `FileWriter` measured today.
options.technical:
Sema: report E0605 when a struct literal or field read names a `priv` field outside its type's module. This is the rule S18 states, and it fixes the import_private_field ui row. Registry: a native carrier row may name a carrier declared in a `priv module`; its clone and drop entries match FileWriter's. A known native carrier's native part counts as a `priv` field, so `FileWriter{path: "x"}` outside Core is E0605 too.

Core/Http: `priv module transport { struct BodyStream }` over the runtime body kernel. `struct Body { priv stream: transport.BodyStream }`. `chunks()` pulls from the stream. Core/Files: `Directory.handle` and `AdvisoryLock.handle` become `priv`.

options.name: A new `#Carrier(native)` attribute checked for every wrapper
options.detail:
Core marks the facade with a new attribute that tells the checker it wraps a native value. The checker refuses literals of any marked type outside Core and tracks the native value's lifecycle.

The attribute is a second privacy spelling beside `priv`, and every carrier must adopt it.
options.technical: Add `#Carrier(native)` to the syntax tables, with a Sema rule refusing literals of marked types outside their module. Lifecycle rows key on the attribute rather than on the registry row. `Directory`, `FileWriter` and `AdvisoryLock` are re-marked.

options.name: Drop the facade; the native stream is the public `Body`
options.detail:
The native stream type itself becomes the public `Body`, registered as a known native type like FileWriter. There is no wrapper.

The type must stay literal-free by a special case in the registry, and its methods are native signatures rather than Jet source.
options.technical: Register `Body` as a known native carrier with native method signatures. The facade's Jet-source methods (`text`, `json`, `chunks`) move into the runtime. The forging gap on other carriers is untouched.

comparisons.note: A struct with a private field cannot be built outside its module, so `hyper::body::Incoming` comes only from the library. Source: Rust Reference, Visibility and privacy; hyper docs, body::Incoming.
comparisons.code: let b = Incoming { .. };   // error[E0451]: field is private

comparisons.note: `http.Response.Body` is an `io.ReadCloser` interface; the concrete type is unexported, so user code cannot build the library's body. Source: pkg.go.dev/net/http, Response.
comparisons.code: resp.Body.Read(buf)   // concrete body type is unexported

comparisons.note: `private` and `fileprivate` stored properties block memberwise initializers outside the file. Source: The Swift Programming Language, Access Control.
comparisons.code: struct Body { private let stream: Stream }

recommendation.why: A uses two forms the visibility law already has, a `priv module` and a `priv` field. User code cannot name or forge the stream, and the same rule closes the forging of Core's other carriers.
gains: Large bodies stream; memory stays at one chunk.
No new marker and no new public type.
Directory and FileWriter forging is closed too.

whyNot.reason: A second privacy spelling beside `priv`, which every carrier must adopt.
The body's methods move into the runtime, and a special case must refuse literals.

recommendation.tradeoff: The checker starts enforcing `priv` on struct literals and field reads, so Core code that relied on the gap must use the module's functions. In return no user code can forge a native value.

decisions.title: Graphical Jet programs speak the display and sound protocols directly and stay static
decisions.situation: Jet programs are single static files with no dynamic loader. Opening a window today seems to need C driver libraries that a static program cannot load, so games run only headless. But a desktop's display server and sound server are reached over local sockets, and the kernel exposes gamepads as plain files. This vote decides how `ray` reaches the screen, input and sound. We recommend speaking those protocols in Jet, keeping games static, and making GPU drivers a later opt-in.
decisions.gist: Should graphical Jet programs talk to the display and sound servers directly and stay single static files?
decisions.lesson: A window on Linux is a conversation over a local socket with the display server, X11 or Wayland. The program draws pixels into shared memory and tells the server to show them. Sound works the same way with the sound server. Only GPU acceleration needs the vendor's driver library.
decisions.story: Sam builds his Jet game and copies one file to a friend's laptop. It opens a window, reads the gamepad and plays sound with nothing installed. Later he switches on GPU drawing, and that build uses the laptop's own graphics driver.
decisions.detail:
Today. Jet executables are static musl programs, and musl's static dlopen does nothing. The raylib leaves take a no-library path (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/RouteAGame.jet:1-7), so `window_should_close` is always true natively. The old draft of this ballot recommended dynamic executables for all graphical programs, at the cost of the single-file deploy.

What A does for the screen. On Wayland, `ray` connects to the socket named by WAYLAND_DISPLAY and shares an RGBA buffer through a memfd. It opens the window with xdg-shell. On X11 it connects to the DISPLAY socket and presents with MIT-SHM, falling back to PutImage.

When a Wayland compositor offers no server-side title bar, as GNOME's does not, `ray` uses its X11 path through XWayland. A later stage can draw its own title bar instead.

Input. Keys and mouse arrive as display-server events. Key enums are physical key positions from the kernel key code, which both servers send. Typed-character input reads the XKB keymap the server hands over. Gamepads are read from /dev/input/event files, which logind grants to the seat user.

Sound. `ray` mixes in Jet and streams to the PulseAudio native socket. PipeWire serves that socket on current distros. With no sound server it writes to the kernel ALSA device through ioctl calls, as Android's tinyalsa does.

The operating-system doors. These need sockets with file-descriptor passing, memfd, mmap and ioctl. They sit in the Core platform module from card 5035 as audited calls, not as private runtime powers. Everything above them, including protocol encoding, is ordinary Jet.

GPU, a later stage. Mesa and NVIDIA drivers are glibc shared libraries and cannot load into a static musl process. A program that opts into GPU drawing builds as a dynamic executable that loads libvulkan.so.1 through the system loader. A GPU driver is always an installed shared library, so that build loses nothing a static file could give.

Why not a loader inside the runtime. Loading glibc-built drivers into a musl process mixes two C libraries, two allocators and two thread-local layouts. The glibc linker warns that a static program calling dlopen needs the exact glibc it was built with. Musl ships no static dlopen at all.

Peers. Rust's x11rb and wayland-client both have pure-Rust protocol backends. Go has jezek/xgb for X11 and jfreymuth/pulse for the PulseAudio protocol. Android ships tinyalsa for kernel sound. These show the protocols are stable and small enough to own.

Edge cases. With no DISPLAY or WAYLAND_DISPLAY, `ray.init_window` returns a typed error that names both variables. `ray.headless_window` always works. Programs that never open a window link none of this code.

decisions.title: Remove Rust: Jet's tools only, or every Rust file?
decisions.situation: Jet's compiler, package manager and other tools are now written in Jet. The repository still holds 64 Rust files, but none of them is part of Jet. Most are the Rust versions of speed tests that also exist in C, Go, Zig, Python and Node. The question is whether removing Rust means no Rust inside Jet's tools, or no Rust file anywhere. We recommend the first: Jet never needs rustc, a check enforces it, and Rust stays only where Rust is what we compare against or connect to.
decisions.gist: Does removing Rust mean no Rust in Jet's tools, or no Rust file anywhere in the repository?
decisions.lesson: You ruled that every Rust part of Jet's tools moves to Jet, with two exceptions: the Zed editor plugin, and Rust libraries users call from Jet. That port is nearly done. What is left is Rust speed tests that compare Jet with Rust, and a Rust-interop example. Eight Rust programs that check Jet's results, and two tool calls to rustc, get deleted whatever wins.
decisions.story: Mina installs Jet on a fresh laptop with no Rust installed. She runs jet check, jet run and jet test, and none of them looks for rustc. Separately, the speed board still shows how Jet's word-count program compares with the Rust, C and Go versions.
decisions.inWild:
Go: the toolchain is written in Go, yet its repository keeps C test programs for cgo, because C is what cgo connects to. Source: https://go.dev/src/cmd/cgo/internal/test/

The Computer Language Benchmarks Game keeps the same program in many languages side by side to compare them. Source: https://benchmarksgame-team.pages.debian.net/benchmarksgame/
decisions.detail:
OWNER RULINGS

2026-10-06 06:20 (card #4717): everything is ported to Jet so Rust can leave the toolchain. Jet-only native must contain no Rust remnants, not even policy-free provider leaves. Host and OS access goes through Jet FFI or syscalls inside vetted #Unsafe Core internals. 2026-10-22: keep user-facing extern rust FFI; remove --target=sandbox via rustc and the jet self doctor rustc checks.

D-ZED-EXT1 (2026-10-11) keeps the Zed extension in Rust. D-RUST-EMIT1's sandbox part is superseded by the 10-22 ruling. D-NATIVE-ANALYSIS-GAPS1 requires every missing native check to be ported before the Rust compiler is deleted.

The earlier draft asked 'port everything, or keep policy-free Rust leaves?'. The owner already answered that on 2026-10-06, so that option was a straw man. This revision asks the one question the rulings leave open.

WHAT IS LEFT TODAY (git ls-files '*.rs' on dev, 2026-11-05)

64 files, none in Compiler/, Core/ or Jetpack/. A keeps 56 and deletes 8.

Kept as speed peers, each beside a Jet version of the same program. Tools/gauntlet 31: 25 entries, 5 optimization fixtures, and the memory-safety fuzz axis (also in c, zig and jet). Tools/perf 19: function-boundary 14, build-time hello, runtime-library allocator, two domain-foundations baselines, and serde_peer. tests/compiled_workloads/adapters/peer 4.

Kept by ruling: Tools/editors/zed/wasm-src/src/lib.rs (D-ZED-EXT1) and Examples/ffi/projections/rust/host.rs (the extern rust example).

DELETED WHATEVER WINS

The 8 Tools/perf/selfhost/workloads/*/oracle.rs files use Rust as the oracle for Jet results, which the owner forbids. They are deleted. Their manifest.json and evidence.json rows switch to committed expected output that the Jet run must match.

Compiler/JetDebug/Source/Inferior.jet:615-624 runs rustc --print sysroot to load Rust pretty printers into lldb; Jet programs do not need them.

Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/ReceiptIdentity.jet:120 hashes the rustc and cargo binaries into every receipt identity. Both calls are Rust-era leftovers that the existing directive already covers.

KEPT USER-FACING RUST INTEROP

Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Doctor.jet:207-212 reports whether cargo is installed, only as a note for extern rust imports. Jetpack/Integrations/Source/Foreign/RustBridge builds the bridge crate for a user's extern rust import.

Compiler/JetBuildSession/Source/Declarations.jet:3-13 implements the build-script call b.legacy(kind, ...). It wraps an outside build tool (cmake, make, gradle, npm or cargo) as one declared action in the user's own build. It is not a Jet fallback path, and Jet runs it only when a user's build calls it. Renaming the method is outside this ballot.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Rust could creep back into the tools. A adds one gate check over tracked .rs files with an exact allow list.

- Tools/gauntlet/entries/*/rust/main.rs

- Tools/gauntlet/entries/nbody/rust-expert/main.rs

- Tools/gauntlet/axes/memory-safety-fuzz/rust/main.rs

- Tools/gauntlet/optimization/fixtures/*/peer-rust.rs

- Tools/perf/function-boundary/*/main.rs

- Tools/perf/build-time/hello.rs

- Tools/perf/runtime-library/allocator.rs

- Tools/perf/domain-foundations/prim-numerics-perf/rust_bench.rs

- Tools/perf/domain-foundations/prim-text/bench_rust.rs

- Tools/perf/enum_codec/serde_peer/src/main.rs

- tests/compiled_workloads/adapters/peer/*.rs

- tests/compiled_workloads/adapters/peer/candidates/*.rs

- Tools/editors/zed/wasm-src/src/lib.rs

- Examples/ffi/projections/rust/host.rs

Any other .rs file fails the gate. Card #4717 c3's process-tree proof shows jet check, run, test and build never start rustc or cargo unless the user's project uses extern rust or b.legacy("cargo").

2. The speed board needs rustc. Only the benchmark machine needs it, and the flake already provides the comparison toolchains (matrix.json: "zig+go rails added to flake"). A user machine never needs it.

WHY NOT B OR C

B deletes the Rust speed peers and the extern rust example. The strict performance gate then loses its strongest systems baseline, and the kept extern rust feature loses its only example. C moves them to another repository. Comparisons then drift from the Jet code they measure, and one commit can no longer update both.

A gate fails on any Rust file outside an exact list.

decisions.title: A built-in exit for expected failures
decisions.situation: Command-line scripts stop with a message when input is wrong. Today each script defines a four-line helper that prints to stderr and exits. The alternative returns an error from the entry function, which prints a framed report. We recommend a built-in fail that takes a message and an exit code. It prints the message, runs scope cleanup, and exits with no frame. Panic stays for program bugs.
decisions.gist: Should scripts get a built-in way to stop with a message and an exit code?
decisions.lesson: Scripts that stop on bad input need a four-line helper. A built-in call would print the message and exit with no frame.
decisions.story: Ana writes a tool that needs one file name. When the name is missing, she wants one line of usage text and exit code 64, not a crash report.
decisions.inWild: fn fail(message: String) -> Never { term.eprint(message); process.exit(1) }
decisions.detail: Source: card #5085, item B6. Four ported scripts each defined this helper. Ratified D-FAIL-EXIT1 makes errors report and exit 1, and keeps exit 101 for the compiler. Ratified D-PANICROOT1 places panic in the effect table. Ratified D-CORE-PRELUDE1 governs what the readable prelude may hold. The exit code parameter is a literal in the card's signature, so the type should be checked before ratification. Savings are per script.

options.name: Built-in fail with an exit code
options.detail: `fail(message, code)` writes the message and a newline to stderr, runs scope guards, and exits with the code. It prints no frame. `panic` remains for bugs.
options.technical: Prelude function returning Never. Uses the existing exit path, so guards run before exit as they do for a normal return.
options.code: fail("usage: tool FILE", 64)

options.name: Return an error from run
options.detail: The entry function returns an error value. The runtime reports it and exits. The report carries a frame.
options.technical: Uses the existing error-result path. No new surface.
options.code: return Err(UsageError("usage: tool FILE"))

comparisons.note: A script writes to stderr and exits with a status code.

recommendation.why: A usage error is expected, so it should exit with a message and no frame. A built-in call removes the helper each script repeats.
gains: Four fewer lines in each script.

losses.loss: A second way to stop with an error.
losses.mitigation: Built-in fail is for expected failures only. Bugs still use panic, and the docs place them side by side.

whyNot.reason: It prints a framed error report for a plain usage mistake, which reads as a crash.

recommendation.tradeoff: A new prelude name, in exchange for one call in place of a helper.
