decisions.title: A range in the `#` slot makes a capacity list: `[Contact#0..8]` holds up to eight items inline, with no heap
decisions.situation: Physics contacts, small paths and parser lookahead need lists with a known maximum. A `[T]` list allocates on the heap, which hot loops and embedded code avoid. A fixed array has no length of its own. Odin and Rust (arrayvec) have inline lists with a capacity. The vote decides how Jet spells one. We recommend a range in the fixed-array slot: `[T#0..8]` holds from zero to eight items, inline, with the same methods as a list.
decisions.gist: How should a list with a fixed maximum, stored inline with no heap, be written?
decisions.lesson: Sometimes you know a list will never hold more than, say, eight items. `[Contact#0..8]` stores up to eight inline, with no heap allocation, and has `push`, `pop`, `len` and loops like any list. Pushing a ninth stops like an out-of-range index; `try_push` returns an error instead.
decisions.story: Leo's collision code allocates a fresh list per object per frame. The game stutters every few seconds when the allocator compacts.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05gn07n (#6177); research card #6204. This is the capacity list question from the D-ARRAY1 package, asked alone. Ratified and not reopened: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A (`filled`, `from_fn`), D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A (bare place reads, `&place` writes, `~place` copies), D-OOBPROOF1 and the D-MATRIX family.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/arr. cap.jet: `[Int#0..8]{}` is E0003 "Expected `]` to close the list literal, found `#`". clear.jet runs option C's form today and prints 1.

Reads with D-ARRAY-ENUMTABLE1 and D-ARRAY-INDEX1: a count, an enum, an index type or a range in the slot all say how many items.

options.name: Range in the slot
options.detail:
A range in the slot means a length between its ends, stored inline with a length word. It has `push`, `pop`, `len`, indexing and loops, and passes to a `[T]` parameter as a window.

`push` past the end stops like an out-of-range index; `try_push` returns an error value. A nonzero start, as in `[T#2..8]`, keeps a minimum, and `pop` below it stops the same way.
options.technical: New slot kind (E0003 today). The checks follow the `bounds` setting, and D-OOBPROOF1 drops them where the fit is proven. Odin's `append` instead drops the item and returns a count.

options.name: Heap lists only

decisions.title: One column of a columnar list is a list place: `ps.x` reads it, `&ps.x` edits it in place
decisions.situation: A columnar list stores each struct field as its own column, so a loop over one field reads packed memory. Jet already has `#Layout(columnar)`, but a column can't be named: `ps.x` is refused, so a solver that wants all x values gets them one item at a time. Odin writes `v.x` for a column. The vote decides how code reaches one column. We recommend the field name: `ps.x` is the column as a `[Float]` place, read bare and edited with `&`.
decisions.gist: How should code reach one column of a columnar list, such as all the x values?
decisions.lesson: A columnar list keeps all the `x` values side by side, then all the `v` values. `ps.x` is that column, a `[Float]` you can pass to any list function. Pass `&ps.x` to let the function edit it in place, with no copy.
decisions.story: Max moves his particles to `#Layout(columnar)` for speed. His solver takes a `[Float]`, so he still copies every x into a new list each frame, and the speed-up vanishes.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05gn07n (#6177); research card #6204. This is the column question from the D-ARRAY1 package, asked alone. Ratified and not reopened: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A (`filled`, `from_fn`), D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A (bare place reads, `&place` writes, `~place` copies), D-OOBPROOF1 and the D-MATRIX family.

decisions.title: A fixed array passed to a `[T]` parameter is a read window, as a list is; `~a` still copies
decisions.situation: Under D-FIXARR1 a fixed array `[Int#4]` passed to a `[Int]` parameter is copied into a new list. A list passed the same way is a read window, with no copy, under D-SHAPE-PLACE1. We recommend it: every place reads the same, and `~a` copies when a copy is wanted.

options.detail:
A fixed array, like a list, is a place, so a bare argument is a read window under D-SHAPE-PLACE1. `&a` passes a write window to a `&[T]` parameter, and `~a` passes a copy.

The callee can't change the length through either window, since a fixed array has none to change.

Hot code converts once and keeps the list.

The bare call stays a copy, so the obvious spelling is the slow one.

decisions.title: `Mat3.inverse()` and `Mat4.inverse()` return `MatrixError!`, failing on a singular matrix as `Transform.inverse()` already does
decisions.situation: Core has `Mat3` and `Mat4` with products and `transpose()`, but no inverse. Cameras, physics and skinning need one. A singular matrix has no inverse: GLSL returns undefined cells, and Rust's nalgebra returns an Option. Jet's own `Transform.inverse()` already returns an error when the determinant is not finite or within 2.2e-16 of zero. The vote decides what `inverse()` returns for matrices. decisions.lesson: Some matrices, such as one that flattens space to a plane, have no inverse. Jet's `inverse()` returns an error in that case, so you handle it with `?` or `??`. A rotation can be undone with `transpose()`, which never fails.
decisions.story: Ana's camera matrix collapses when the zoom hits zero. The inverse fills with infinities, and every object on screen vanishes with no error.

decisions.title: Lane-wise comparisons are methods, `a.lanes_lt(b)` → `Lanes<Bool, N>`; `<` and `==` keep returning one Bool
decisions.situation: D-LANES1 ratified `Lanes<T, N>` for vector math. Clamping, masking and branch-free code need a comparison per lane: which lanes of `a` are below `b`. But `if a == b` must stay one Bool, or every equality test breaks. Rust's portable SIMD uses methods such as `simd_lt`; GLSL uses `lessThan`. The vote decides how a lane-wise comparison is written. We recommend methods, `lanes_lt` and siblings, returning a `Lanes<Bool, N>` mask.
decisions.gist: How should a comparison that gives one answer per lane be written?
decisions.lesson: `a < b` asks one question and gives one Bool. Vector code often wants an answer per lane instead. `a.lanes_lt(b)` gives a mask with one Bool per lane. `mask.select(a, b)` picks from `a` where the mask is true. `any()` and `all()` turn a mask back into one Bool.
decisions.story: Sam clamps a particle's four speeds with a loop and an `if` per lane. The loop blocks vectorizing, and the hot path runs four times slower than the C version.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05gn07n (#6177); research card #6204. This is the lane comparison question from the D-ARRAY1 package, asked alone. Ratified and not reopened: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A (`filled`, `from_fn`), D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A (bare place reads, `&place` writes, `~place` copies), D-OOBPROOF1 and the D-MATRIX family.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/arr. lanes.jet: `a + b` on two `[Float#4]` is E0109 today, since fixed-array arithmetic is still being built. eq.jet: `a == b` on the same arrays runs and prints false, the one-Bool answer A keeps. `Lanes` is ratified (D-LANES1=A) but has no Core type yet.

Reads with D-MATRIX-SOLVE1=B, which chose methods for matrix operations.

decisions.title: Core ships `Quaternion` beside `Vec3` and `Mat3`, built by the ratified literal and rotating a `Vec3` with `q * v`
decisions.situation: 3D games and robotics store rotations as quaternions: four numbers that blend smoothly and never lock up as angles do. Core has `Vec3`, `Mat3` and `Mat4`, and D-LITCARRIER1=D ratified the literal `1 + 2i + 3j + 4k`, but there is no type for it to build. The vote decides whether Core ships one. We recommend a `Quaternion` struct in Core math, with rotation methods, so the ratified literal has a home.
decisions.gist: Should Core ship a `Quaternion` type for 3D rotations?
decisions.lesson: A quaternion is four numbers that describe a 3D rotation. `Quaternion.angle_axis(0.5, up)` makes one, `q * v` rotates a vector, and `a.slerp(b, 0.5)` blends halfway between two rotations. Unlike three angles, blending never jumps or locks.
decisions.story: Ben stores his camera as three angles. Looking straight up, two angles line up, and the camera spins wildly when he nudges the mouse.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05gn07n (#6177); research card #6204. This is the quaternion question from the D-ARRAY1 package, asked alone. Ratified and not reopened: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A (`filled`, `from_fn`), D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A (bare place reads, `&place` writes, `~place` copies), D-OOBPROOF1 and the D-MATRIX family.

Probes. q/b4/arrp/today.jet runs `Vec3.new(1.0, 1.0, 1.0)` and `v.zyx.x`, printing 1.0. The package probe optA3.jet found `Quaternion` is E0107 today.

decisions.title: A lambda stored where no type is expected follows the declaration rule: it writes parameter and result types, as `fn square` would
decisions.situation: Most lambdas are passed to a call, which tells them their types. About 219 in Jet's code are stored in a local, where nothing does. Under D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=A a lambda is a function without its name. The vote decides what such a stored lambda must write. We recommend the rule a named function already follows: parameter types always, and the result type when the body gives a value, so adding a name never changes the meaning.
decisions.gist: When a lambda is stored with no expected type, must it write its result type?
decisions.lesson: When you pass a lambda to a call, the call tells it the types. When you store one in a local, nothing does. So you write them, as for a named function: `square :: fn(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }`. Forget the `-> Int` and Jet says the value is thrown away, as for `fn square`.
decisions.story: Rae stores `scale :: fn(x: Float) { x * 2.0 }` and later names it `fn scale(x: Float) { x * 2.0 }`. If the two rules differed, the lambda would return a Float and the named copy would fail to build.
decisions.inWild:
// Go: a stored function literal writes its full type.
square := func(n int) int { return n * n }
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0rqt0kq. This is the stored-lambda question from the D-LAMBDA-FN1 package, asked alone. It applies under D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=A; under B or C the arrow forms keep inferring results as today.

Data, from q/b4/lam/census.mjs: 219 lambdas are stored in a local with `::`, `:=` or `=`, and 150 of them have an expression body.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/b4/lamp, rerun on dev. p4.jet: `fn square(n: Int) { n * n }` is E0433 "This Int value is thrown away". p2.jet: `fn(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` as a value is E0003 today.

options.name: The declaration rule
options.detail:
With no expected type, a lambda is checked exactly as a declaration. Parameter types are required (E0801), and an omitted result means Unit, so a value body is E0433.

Where a type is expected, as in a call or a typed field, everything it gives may still be left out.
options.technical: Under D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=A the checker uses the declaration rules for a stored lambda. `jet fix` writes the result sema infers today for the 219 stored lambdas.

options.name: Infer the result
options.detail:
A stored lambda's result is the type of its last expression, as in Kotlin.

The same text then means different things with and without a name.
options.technical: Stored lambdas skip E0433 and infer the result.

comparisons.note: Results are inferred. Source: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/lambdas.html
Closure results are inferred; parameter types may be too, from first use. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/closure-expr.html

decisions.title: A method that changes its receiver is called as `c.bump()` on a changeable value; `grow(&c)` keeps its `&`
decisions.situation: In Jet, `c.n += 1` changes a field with no mark, but `c.bump()`, a method that changes `c`, must be written `&c.bump()`. The compiler already knows `bump` changes `c` from its declaration, and `c` already says it can change, with `:=` or a `&` parameter. Swift and Rust mark changes at arguments but not before the dot. The vote decides whether the mark before the dot is required. We recommend leaving it to the compiler, as for fields.
decisions.gist: Should calling a method that changes `c` need `&c.bump()`, or just `c.bump()`?
decisions.lesson: A value made with `:=` can change. Calling `c.bump()` on it may change it, just as `c.n += 1` does, and the editor shows a faint `&` there. Passing `c` to another function that changes it still takes `&c`, so changes that leave the line stay visible.
decisions.story: Jo's build file has `&runnable.push(member)` and `&entries.push(selected)` on every other line. Reviewers stop reading the marks, and the one that matters, `grow(&state)`, gets lost.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0meo2tr. This replaces the D-RECEIVER-INFER1 package; its option D, a rule only for locals, is dropped as a weaker A. Changes the method-call clause of D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2847) and extends D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A (:2867-2887). Reuses D-MARK-SCOPE1=A (:2540) for `writes: .Explicit`.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/recv. today.jet: unmarked `c.bump()` is E0224 "This call writes `c`, but `c` has no `&` mark", in `run` and on a `&` parameter. `c.n += 1` passes in both. marked.jet: with `&` on every call it passes, and `&k.bump()` on a `::` value is E0202, which A keeps.

Data: a text count over 17,440 .jet files found about 26,400 marks before a method call and 3,500 before a field. Typical: Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Entry.jet:1167-1169.

Reads with D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A: bare places read and `&place` writes in arguments, unchanged by A.

Other ballots' samples, such as `&ps.push(…)` in D-ARRAY-COLUMNS1, use today's spelling. If A wins, `jet fix` drops the receiver `&` and those samples follow the outcome.

options.name: No `&` before the dot
options.detail:
A method that changes its receiver may be called with no mark on a `:=` value or a `&` parameter. A `::` value still can't change, so `k.bump()` stays an error.

The editor shows the filled-in `&` as a hint. A team that wants it in text sets `writes: .Explicit`, beside the existing `copies: .Explicit`, and E0224 fires as today.
options.technical: Stops E0224 for unmarked receiver calls (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/Checks.jet:3732). Follows the owner's rule for marks on D-COPY-DEFAULT1: "Compiler chooses if unmarked, programmer can manually put sigils where desired for exact." `^` and `copies: .Explicit` already work this way (D-MARK-SCOPE1=A).

options.name: No `&` anywhere
options.detail:
As in Kotlin or Java, the callee's declaration alone says it changes the value.

A reader can't tell from the call which arguments change.
options.technical: Drops E0224 for both receivers and arguments; amends D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A.

options.name: Keep `&c.bump()`
options.detail:
A changing method call is marked like a changing argument.

Field writes such as `c.n += 1` stay unmarked, so the two forms differ.
options.technical: Today's D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D clause.

comparisons.note: Mutating methods are unmarked; inout arguments take `&`. Source: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/methods/
Receivers auto-borrow; arguments write `&mut`. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/method-call-expr.html
Inout receivers and arguments are both marked with `&`. Source: https://docs.hylo-lang.org/language-tour/functions-and-methods

whyNot.reason: B hides changes passed into other functions.
C keeps tens of thousands of marks that fields don't need.

recommendation.tradeoff: The receiver mark moves into the editor hint unless `writes: .Explicit` is set.

decisions.title: A lambda is the bound value without its name: `(n) { n > 2 }`, leaving out any part the call already fixes
decisions.situation:
A lambda is a small function passed to another function, such as the test in `nums.filter(…)`. Jet writes it today as `n -> n > 2`, a shape no named function uses.

D-DECL-BINDING1 proposes that a function is a binding, `square :: (n: Int) -> Int { n * n }`. This vote decides whether a lambda is exactly that value without the name, or also keeps a short arrow. We recommend one shape. Decide D-DECL-BINDING1 first; this vote holds under each of its outcomes.
decisions.gist: Should every lambda be written exactly as a function binding's value, `(n) { n > 2 }`, with no separate short arrow?
decisions.lesson: A lambda is a function without a name. Under this rule you write it as the value of a function binding: inputs in parentheses, then the body in braces. Types the call already knows may be left out, as in `nums.filter((n) { n > 2 })`.
decisions.explainer:
The two votes fit together. D-DECL-BINDING1 makes `square :: (n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` a function. Dropping `square ::` leaves a lambda, and dropping the types the call gives leaves `(n) { n * n }`.

The only question left is the short arrow. Most lambdas today have a one-expression body, and the arrow is a little shorter there.
decisions.story: Dev passes `n -> n > 2` to `filter`, then wants a log line in it. Today he turns it into `n -> { … }`. Under one shape he adds the line inside the braces he already has.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0rqt0kq. Version 1 proposed `fn(n) { n * n }` and is kept as D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1.v1.json. The owner asked that the shape align with the binding conversion, which D-DECL-BINDING1 now asks for. Under D-DECL-BINDING1=B both options here gain a leading `fn`. Under D-DECL-BINDING1=C, which keeps `fn name(…)`, the value form is `fn(n) { n > 2 }`, version 1's shape, so the choice here stays the same.

Data, from Main's census (q/b4/lam/census.mjs) rerun on a dev export. There are 4,812 lambdas in 1,197 files. Of these, 3,842 have an expression body and 970 a braced body; 888 have a bare parameter. 2,832 leave at least one parameter type to the call, and 220 are stored in a binding.

Size under A. A bare expression lambda grows by three characters, a parenthesized one by one, and a braced one shrinks by three. Over the corpus that adds 2,813 characters, 0.6 per lambda. Version 1's `fn(…)` form added 12,437. Only the 888 lambdas with a bare parameter and one expression grow by three, and a named function passes with no lambda at all.

Probes in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/probes/m-decl run at o0, o1 and o2. The program in today's spelling is d10_lambda_today.jet, and it prints the commented output on every tier. Main's probe q/b4/lamp/p5.jet shows `(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` running today as a typed value. With a `print` line added, p10.jet is E0399.

Known defect under both options: a `return` inside a braced lambda passed to `map` is checked against the enclosing function (q/b4/lamp/p12.jet, E0113). Under A a `return` leaves the lambda, as it leaves any function.

Reads with D-LAMBDA-STORED1=A, whose rule stays: a stored lambda with no expected type writes its parameter and result types. Only its spelling changes, from `fn(n: Int)` to `(n: Int)`.

options.name: Exactly the bound value
options.detail:
A lambda is `(params) arrow result failure { body }`, a function binding's value without the name. Parameter, result and failure types may be left out where the expected type gives them. The arrow appears only with a written result or an effect row, as in a named function.

Behavior changes. The arrow lambdas `n -> e` and `(n) -> { … }` are retired, and `jet fix` rewrites them. A `return` inside a lambda leaves the lambda. `(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` is a function, never a typed value.
options.technical: Parser: in value position, `(` followed by a parameter list and then `{`, `->`, `-[` or a failure rail reads a function, the D-DECL-BINDING1 rule. The arrow-lambda path in Expressions.jet:1152-1304 goes, and E0399 becomes the teaching error for the retired arrow. `jet fix` rewrites 4,812 lambdas, writing the inferred result for the 220 stored ones. Amends D-LAMBDA-IFACE2=A and replaces S46's form.

options.name: The bound value, plus a short arrow
options.detail:
The value form is used as in A. A lambda whose types the call gives, and whose body is one expression, may also be written `n -> n > 2` or `(a, b) -> a + b`.

After `->`, a type followed by `{` reads as a result type, as in a binding's value. So the 40 short lambdas whose body starts with a typed literal `Type{…}` need parentheses around it. Growing a short lambda to two lines changes its head.
options.technical: Keeps the expression arrow path in Expressions.jet:1152-1304 and adds A's value path. `jet fix` rewrites the 970 braced arrow lambdas and parenthesizes 40 typed-literal bodies. Two parse paths decide on the token after `->`.

options.name: The bound value, starting with fn
options.detail:
A lambda is exactly a function binding's value without its name, and like every function value it starts with `fn`: `fn(n) { n > 2 }`. It matches D-DECL-BINDING1 option B, `square :: fn(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }`.

The call still fixes the parameter types, so a passed lambda writes only the names. There is no separate short arrow.
options.technical: Lambda: `fn` `(` params `)` [`-[E]>` | `->` T] `{` body `}`. The params, effect row and result may be left out wherever the call fixes them. The parser sees `fn` and needs no tuple-or-function rule. `n -> e` retires; `jet fix` rewrites it to `fn(n) { e }`.

comparisons.note: One shape: a procedure literal passed inline is the bound value. Source: https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#procedures
comparisons.code: slice.sort_by(xs[:], proc(a, b: int) -> bool { return a < b })

comparisons.note: One shape: a function literal is a declaration without its name. Source: https://go.dev/ref/spec#Function_literals
comparisons.code: big := filter(nums, func(n int) bool { return n > 2 })

comparisons.note: The bound value, plus a short `=>` form. Source: Docs/research/jai-vs-jet-syntax-briefing-2026-09-16.html:234-238
comparisons.code:
square :: (x: float) -> float { return x * x; }
lam    :: (a, b) => a + b

comparisons.note: A lambda has its own braces-first shape, apart from `fun`. Source: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/lambdas.html

recommendation.why: C makes a lambda exactly a function value without its name, and `fn` marks every function, named or passed. It matches D-DECL-BINDING1 B, and dropping `fn` later stays a mechanical `jet fix` if it proves redundant.
gains: One shape for named and passed functions.
`fn` marks every function at a glance.
Growing a body keeps its head.
No tuple-or-function parsing rule.

whyNot.reason: A needs a rule to tell `(…)` lambdas from tuples, and adding `fn` back later is far harder than dropping it.
B keeps two spellings for one thing, and a growing body changes its head.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each lambda gains `fn`: two characters per lambda. `jet fix` rewrites every lambda once.

decisions.title: `#Pre` is checked while compiling whenever the values it reads are known; no new mark
decisions.situation: A function states a rule about its arguments with `#Pre(condition, "message")`, checked when the program runs. A call such as `simd_width(6, xs)` can never pass, yet it builds and stops later. The first draft added `##Pre`, a second mark that also made parameters compile-time without saying so. This revision adds nothing to learn. A `#Pre` is decided while compiling whenever the values it reads are known then, the rule you chose for `::` values.
decisions.gist: How should a rule on a function's arguments be checked while compiling, when the call's values are fixed?
decisions.lesson: `#Pre(lanes == 4, "need 4 lanes")` is a rule every call must keep. When a call passes fixed values, such as the number 6, the compiler can work out the answer itself. Under A it does, and a call that can never pass fails to build, on the caller's line, with the author's message.
decisions.story: Ivo calls a library's `simd_width(6, readings)`. Today it builds and ships, then stops on a customer's machine with "need 4 or 8 lanes", a rule the library stated all along. Under A, his build fails on that line with the same message. The library author wrote nothing new.
decisions.detail:
Why the draft was revised. `##Pre` added a second compile-time mark, although D-META-HASH1 A made `#` the one mark. It turned each parameter the rule reads into a compile-time one without a word at the parameter, so each distinct value built its own copy. A run-time value at a call then became an error. That is a hidden cost and behavior change (philosophy principle 8) and a new concept (principle 7).

The rule A uses already exists. D-COMPTIME-WORD1 A, which you ratified, computes every `::` value while compiling whenever it can and falls back to run time otherwise. `comptime` is the one word that requires it. A applies the same rule to `#Pre`: a pure condition over values known while compiling is worked out then. D-PREPOST1 already makes every `#Pre` pure.

What A does at each call. If every value the rule reads is known while compiling, such as a literal, a `::` constant or a `comptime` parameter, the compiler decides the rule. False is a build error on the caller's line, with the message and the values. True means that call carries no run-time check, as a proved check is erased (D-PROVE-SEM1). Otherwise the check runs when the program runs, as today.

If working out the rule runs past the compile-time step budget, the check stays at run time, as a `::` value does; it is never dropped. `#Post` needs nothing new: when a whole call is computed while compiling under D-COMPTIME-WORD1, its `#Post` is checked then too.

Requiring a fixed value. Some functions need the value fixed, for example to pick a vector width. The author writes `comptime lanes: Int`, the ratified spelling (D-COMPTIME-WORD1 A, D-CONSTGEN2 A). Every call then passes a fixed value, so every `#Pre` on it is decided while compiling. The first draft's option B is that case of A, not a separate rule.

Probes on dev, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-3/probes/pre, on o0, o1 and o2. pre.jet calls `width(6, …)` against `#Pre(lanes == 4, …)`: it builds, prints 6, then stops with E3001 on line 8. The first draft's internal compiler error no longer happens. In early.jet the same call sits in a file constant, `BAD :: width(6, …)`. `jet check` passes and the run stops at startup, so early `::` evaluation is not built yet either.

More probes. prepre.jet: `##Pre` is E0003. lead.jet: a `comptime` parameter is E0003, since it is ratified but not built. ctif2.jet: `comptime if` on a plain parameter is E0989. Census (probes/pre/census.mjs): 26 `#Pre` lines, 5 in Examples and 21 in tests; none in Core.

Overlap. Jet has one contract form, `#Pre` and `#Post` (D-PREPOST1); `#Require` was a placeholder name and was archived. Markers, `comptime` and generic recipes (D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1) keep their meaning. A adds no syntax, no error code beyond the build-time form of the existing contract failure, and no rule for parameters.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign-3 lane), revising the Main draft after the owner said he was not happy with it. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this revision.

options.name: `#Pre` is decided while compiling whenever it can be
options.detail:
At each call, if every value the rule reads is known while compiling, the compiler decides it. A call that can never pass is a build error on the caller's line, with the author's message. Other calls are checked when the program runs, as today. No new mark and no parameter changes.

Behavior change: a call with fixed values that breaks a `#Pre` fails to build instead of stopping at run time. A call decided true carries no run-time check.
options.technical: Sema, after argument substitution at each call: if the `#Pre` condition reads only literals, `::` constants and `comptime` parameters, evaluate it in the compile-time engine under the D-COMPTIME-WORD1 step budget. False: the contract-failure error at the call span, with message and values. True: drop that call's entry check, as D-PROVE-SEM1 erases proved checks. Budget exhausted or run-time inputs: keep the run-time check.

options.name: `##Pre` (the first draft)
options.detail:
A doubled mark, `##Pre`, runs the rule while compiling at each distinct call. Every parameter it reads becomes compile-time without a word at the parameter.

A call passing a run-time value is an error, and each distinct value builds its own copy of the function.
options.technical: Parser: `##Name(…)` before a declaration, a second marker form. Sema: the rule runs per distinct call, and the parameters it reads are specialized.

options.name: A check in the body

Hover and docs cannot show the rule, since it is code, not a declared condition.

decisions.title: A service worker is an ordinary function: its parameter type is the message type, and `tree.worker` returns `Endpoint<Email>`
decisions.situation: A task group runs `send_email(e)` for each email. Moving that work into a supervised service should keep the same function. Today the service API takes only a function with no parameters, and messages are text the worker reads back itself. The types fall off at exactly the step up from a group. D-SERVICE1 already promises typed workers. The vote decides their shape. We recommend the function itself: its parameter is the message.
decisions.gist: What shape should a typed service worker have?
decisions.lesson: A service runs work that keeps going and restarts when it fails. You write the work as a normal function, like `send_email(e: Email)`. `tree.worker` turns it into an endpoint that only accepts emails, and the service calls the function once for each one sent.
decisions.story: Pia moves `send_email` from a task group into a service so it restarts on failure. She has to rewrite it to take no parameters and parse a string from `tree.receive`.
decisions.inWild:

decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0mhdm27. This is the worker shape question from the D-SERVICE-TYPED1 package, asked alone. D-SERVICE1=D, reaffirmed by the owner on 2026-08-20, already promises typed builders that promote ordinary functions into workers. Hosts card #6048 (ladder audit L-10).

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/b4/sv/probe, on dev. p1.jet: `service.tree(…)` is E2104 "`service.tree` is not built yet", so no program runs a service today. p2.jet: a worker taking `Email` is E0108 "This needs fn(), but the value is fn(Email)"; messages are `String` today (Core/Service/Service.jet:1378, :1748). p3.jet: the rung below, `task.group` calling `send_email(e)`, runs and prints both lines.

p4.jet: the channel rung, a task looping over `Receiver<Email>`, prints "to ann@example.com" then "done". p6.jet: an enum `if` that misses a case is E0307 "This `if` doesn't cover every case — missing: Remove".

Reads with D-SERVICE-REPLY1, which decides how a worker answers, D-SERVICE-KEEP1, which decides how it keeps data between messages, and D-SERVICE-BATCH1, which decides how it takes many at once. The cutover rewrites the 61 files that call `.worker(`; no user program runs a service today.

options.name: The worker is its function
options.detail:
The runtime calls the function once per message, in order. `tree.send` takes only an `Email`; anything else is the ordinary E0112 argument error.

Several kinds of message are one enum, matched in the function, and a missed case is E0307. A worker with no parameter takes no messages and runs once under restarts.
options.technical: Core/Service/Service.jet: `worker` and `send` become generic over the handler's parameter; the String forms and `tree.receive` go. The runtime half is card #4957, which E2104 names.

options.name: A worker struct; each method is a message
options.detail:
Each method of a `#Worker` struct is one message. `tree.worker` returns a handle whose methods send.

Code moving up from a task group is rewritten into a struct.
options.technical: A new marker, and generated message types per method.

options.name: The worker loops over a typed channel
options.detail:
A worker takes a `Receiver<T>`; `tree.worker` returns the matching sender.

The worker may wait on other sources between messages, but every worker repeats the loop.
options.technical: Workers gain one `Receiver<T>` parameter; the runtime owns the channel across restarts.

decisions.title: A worker answers by returning a value; `tree.call(pricing, quote)` waits for it and returns `Int ServiceError!`
decisions.situation: Some workers answer: a pricing worker takes a quote and gives back a price. Today a service has no typed answers at all; the caller reads text back with `tree.receive`. Under D-SERVICE-WORKER1=A a worker is an ordinary function, so it already has a result type. The vote decides how a caller gets that result. We recommend `tree.call`, which sends, waits and returns the function's result, or a service error.
decisions.gist: How should a caller get a service worker's answer?
decisions.lesson: If a worker function returns a value, the service sends that value back. Use `tree.call(worker, message)` to send and wait for the answer, the way you would call the function directly. It can fail, for example if the worker crashes, so add `??` or `?`.

p5.jet: `price(Quote{sku: "A1", qty: 3})` as a plain function prints 750.

Reads with D-SERVICE-WORKER1, which makes the worker an ordinary function. A batched worker (D-SERVICE-BATCH1) can't reply; that error's fix removes the result or the batch.

`fn price(q: Quote) -> Int` gives `Endpoint<Quote, Int>`. `tree.call` returns `Int ServiceError!`. `tree.send` on a replying endpoint is an error whose fix is `call`, so no reply is dropped.

A call waits like any wait point, so `#Context(deadline: …)` bounds it. If the worker fails mid-message, the call returns `.Ambiguous`, never a silent retry.
options.technical: Adds `call` and a second type parameter to `Endpoint`. Uses D-SERVICE-DELIVERY1=D (`.Ambiguous`) and D-DEADLINE1. Sema refuses two workers that call each other, as D-SERVICE1=D refuses cycles.

decisions.title: A worker keeps data between messages as a `&` first parameter; `state:` on the worker line gives its starting value
decisions.situation: A cart worker must remember the cart between messages. Under D-SERVICE-WORKER1=A a worker is an ordinary function, called once per message, so the data needs a home. A plain function already changes data it is lent with `&`. The vote decides where a worker keeps its data. We recommend a `&` first parameter, with the starting value written on the worker line as `state:`. This is Gleam's actor and Elixir's GenServer shape.

decisions.lesson: A worker that remembers things takes them as its first parameter, with `&` because it changes them. You give the starting value when you add the worker. Each message then sees the data the last one left.

decisions.title: jet test mutates changed code on every run, and guided fuzzing finds the input each surviving mutant gets wrong
decisions.situation: A passing test suite can still be weak. Mutation testing checks it: the compiler makes small wrong versions of a function, and a test should fail for each. Fuzzing feeds tests generated inputs and keeps those that reach new branches. Jet has neither; Rust, Go, Java and JavaScript have both. Mutation is usually too slow to leave on, and some mutants cannot be caught. We recommend both, fast enough to run on every jet test.
decisions.gist: Should jet test mutate changed code on every run and hunt each survivor with guided fuzzing?
decisions.lesson: Coverage says a line ran. Mutation says a test would notice if that line were wrong. Guided fuzzing keeps inputs that reach new branches. Together they can show a weak test with the exact input it misses.
decisions.story: Sam edits clamp, and his test still passes. The same `jet test` reports a surviving mutant that returns `n` instead of `low`. It shows `clamp(-1, 0, 3)` as the input that tells them apart. Sam turns it into a property test, and the next run kills the mutant in milliseconds.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0fvnyiq (#6060), split from #6035 by owner answer Q4 (2026-10-28). Audit/drafts4/BEST-IN-CLASS.md rows Fuzzing and Mutation mark both LOSES. The owner rejected v1 because two losses stood: mutation runs are slow, and equivalent mutants survive. v2 removes both, so mutation can be on by default.

Why it is fast. Stock `mutate: changed` mutates only functions whose IR changed since the last stored run. Their kill results live in the #6035 store, keyed by function and test hashes, so unchanged code is never mutated again. All mutants of a package share one build with a switch, so there is one compile, not one per mutant.

Each mutant runs only the tests that reach its function (D-TEST-AFFECTED1), last killer first, and stops at the first failure. A mutant that loops is cut off at twice the test's normal time. The work grows with the edit, not the package.

Equivalent mutants. A mutant that does exactly what the original does can never be caught, so reporting it is noise. After the compiler folds constants and puts the code in canonical form, a mutant that matches the original is dropped unrun. A mutant that matches another mutant runs once. Research on this check found about 7% of mutants equivalent and 21% duplicates in C programs.

Survivors are then checked. For an effect-free function, the solver behind `jet prove` compares mutant and original. It either proves them equal, and the mutant is dropped as equivalent, or returns an input that tells them apart. Guided fuzzing searches for that input when the solver gives up. In clamp, `n >= high` for `n > high` is proved equivalent, and `return n` gets the witness -1.

What a survivor means. A survivor with a witness is a real gap, shown with the input a test should check. A survivor in effectful code, where neither the solver nor generated inputs may run, is reported as unchecked, not as a gap. Survivors are report rows, never test failures.

How it reads with other ballots. Rows follow the PLAN-6035 naming rule: `--mutate=all`, `mutate: all`. Under D-TEST-PROFILE1 A the profile is the package.jet line shown; under its B it is a `TestProfile` field in test.jet; under its C the flag goes in a CI script. D-CLAIM1=C owns `grade`, `time`, `iterations`, `seed` and `corpus`. Under D-TEST-READS1 mutant rows never reuse a pass.

Research. Trivial Compiler Equivalence (Papadakis and others, ICSE 2015) drops mutants whose compiled code matches. Mutant schemata (Untch, Offutt and Harrold, ISSTA 1993) build all mutants at once. Google runs mutation on every code review, only on changed lines (Petrovic and Ivankovic, ICSE-SEIP 2018). PIT's incremental analysis reuses kill results for unchanged code.

Probes on the dev jet are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/g11/mf. `jet check run.jet` is ok. `jet test` prints "clamps a big number: pass", "stays_in_range: pass" and "2 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped". `jet test --mutate=all` is E2102 and `--grade=generated` is E2104 today. Report lines marked new are proposed output.

Adversarial pass. Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotDesign (fresh pass). It found that `n <= low` is not equivalent when low is above high, so the example uses `n >= high`. A fresh clone records a baseline without mutating, CI sets `mutate: all`, and effectful survivors are reported as unchecked.

options.name: Both, on by default
options.detail:
Mutation: `mutate` is a row with three values, stock `changed`, plus `all` and `off`. The compiler makes mutants from typed IR: a flipped comparison, a swapped operator, a changed return, a dropped statement. Mutants equal to the original after folding are dropped unrun. A survivor in an effect-free function is proved equivalent, shown with an input that tells it apart, or marked unchecked.

Fuzzing: `grade: generated` (D-CLAIM1=C) steers generation by branch coverage. It keeps new-branch inputs and shrunk failures under `corpus`, stock testdata/fuzz/<test>/. Later runs replay them as ordinary rows.
options.technical:
Adds the `mutate` row to the PLAN-6035 table: changed (stock), all, off. A mutation pass after sema writes schemata: each site branches on a mutant id, in mutation test builds only. Mutant identity is (function IR hash, site, operator). The kill matrix (mutant, test hash) to verdict lives in the #6035 S4 store. A fresh store records hashes without mutating.

Pruning: canonical IR after constant folding equal to the original or to an earlier mutant. Survivors in -[]> functions go to the D-PROVE-LENS1 solver lens under a bounded budget, then to guided generation. Rows report KILLED, EQUIVALENT, SURVIVED with witness, UNCHECKED or TIMEOUT.

options.name: Mutation on by default, no guided fuzzing
options.detail:
Mutation as in A: changed code only, cached kill results, one build, and equivalent mutants dropped by folding and by the solver. Without guided fuzzing, a survivor gets a witness only when the solver finds one.

`grade: generated` keeps D-CLAIM1's fixed budget of 1,000 inputs per contract, drawn without feedback. Only a shrunk failure is stored and replayed.
options.technical: The `mutate` row, schemata, kill matrix and pruning as in A. No coverage probes in generated runs; no corpus writes beyond the shrunk-failure store.

options.name: Fuzzing only
options.detail: Guided fuzzing as in A. Test strength is judged only by coverage (`--coverage`, D-COV1), which counts lines run, not lines checked.
options.technical: Guided generation and the testdata/fuzz corpus as in A. No mutation pass.

comparisons.note: PIT runs only the tests that cover each mutant, and its incremental analysis reuses kill results for unchanged code. Source: https://pitest.org/quickstart/incremental_analysis/
Stryker builds all mutants into one bundle, switches between them at run time, and can reuse earlier results. Source: https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/stryker-js/incremental/
cargo-mutants builds each mutant separately and can limit a run to a diff. Source: https://mutants.rs/in-diff.html
go test runs coverage-guided fuzz targets and keeps new inputs in testdata/fuzz/. Source: https://go.dev/doc/security/fuzz/

recommendation.why: A is mutation testing fast and quiet enough to leave on. It mutates only changed code, reuses kill results, and drops proved-equivalent mutants. Each real survivor comes with the input a test should check.
gains: Every `jet test` measures the strength of the tests for the code just changed.
A survivor arrives with a witness input, ready to become a test.
Proved-equivalent mutants never reach the report.

whyNot.reason: B leaves generation blind, so fewer survivors get a witness and deep branches stay unreached.
C cannot tell a test that runs a line from one that checks it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each `jet test` after an edit also runs that edit's mutants: a few test runs per changed function.

decisions.title: A test that reads files or env vars, through Jet or through foreign code, is reused while what it read is unchanged
decisions.situation: jet test will keep each passing test row in a result store (#6035) and skip it on rerun while nothing it depends on changed. A test that reads a file or an env var always reruns, because the store cannot see those inputs. Go records the reads its own library makes, but not reads made by C code. The vote decides if Jet records reads, including foreign code's. We recommend yes, with no new flag.
decisions.gist: May a test that reads files or env vars, even through C code, be reused when what it read is unchanged?
decisions.lesson: A result is safe to reuse only if every input is unchanged. Jet's effect rows already say which tests can touch files or env vars. Test builds can note every read, whether Jet code or a C library makes it. The reused row then carries the exact list of what it read.
decisions.story: Ana's package has 300 tests that read fixtures from testdata/. Forty of them open a SQLite fixture through core.db, which is C code underneath. Every `jet test` reruns all 300, though she changed one file. With reads recorded, only the 4 tests that read that file rerun. The rest print `pass (cached)`.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0slmlyv (#6064), split from #6035 as open question Q7 (owner asked to card it, 2026-10-28). Audit/drafts4/BEST-IN-CLASS.md row Result caching marks file and env rows LOSES to Go. The owner rejected v1 because its loss stood: rows that call foreign code never reused. v2 records those reads too.

How foreign reads are seen. An extern whose declared row has no FS or Env reads nothing, so it reuses like pure code. That covers most foreign code, such as math, compression and hashing. For one that may read, the test build routes the C library's file calls through the recorder, as sanitizers intercept calls. So SQLite opening testdata/app.db is recorded like `files.read`.

Why it is sound. On Linux, a syscall filter checks where each file syscall comes from. A file syscall that bypasses the recorder marks the row unseen, and it reruns with the reason shown. On macOS and Windows the recorder sits in the lowest system library, libSystem or ntdll. Neither platform supports raw syscalls, which is why Go moved to libSystem. C code can read `environ` without a call, so an env read by foreign code keys on the whole environment.

What still reruns, and why. Rows with Net, Clock, Random or Process rerun. Their inputs are a server, the time, a seed or a child, none of which the store can hash. That is the meaning of those effects, not a gap in recording. A `.case` row starts processes, so it reruns, as in Go.

Cost. The recorder exists only in test builds; normal and release builds are unchanged. Jet's own reads are recorded at the Core route layer. Foreign reads cost one extra call per open or stat in tests. Hashing reads each recorded file once per run, the same work as Go's test cache.

How it reads with other ballots. `fresh` is an existing jet test flag that PLAN-6035 makes a row: `--fresh`, `fresh: true`, `.fresh(true)`. Under D-TEST-PROFILE1 A, `fresh: true` sits in a package.jet profile; under B it is a `TestProfile` field in test.jet; under C it is the flag. Under D-TEST-MUTFUZZ1, mutant and generated rows never reuse, since each run is new work.

Probes on the dev jet are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/rd2. `jet check run.jet` is ok, and `jet test` passes both tests, the second through core.db's SQLite. probe/rd2mk builds the fixture database. `jet test --fresh` prints the fresh-run note today. The `(cached)` lines and `--explain-reuse` are proposed; no store exists today (spec.md:3528).

Adversarial pass. Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotDesign (fresh pass). It attacked C code that reads `environ`, makes raw syscalls or maps a file. v2 keys on the whole environment, reruns rows Linux flags, and never stores a file changed mid-run.

options.name: Yes, always, foreign code included
options.detail:
A row whose effect row holds only FS and Env, beyond pure work, is eligible, whether the reads come from Jet or foreign code. While it runs, each read is recorded with a hash of what was returned, including a missing file. The next run reuses the stored pass when every recorded read still matches.

Rows with Net, Clock, Random or Process always rerun. `fresh` (flag, profile field, method) bypasses the store as today.
options.technical:
Adds a read log to the #6035 S4 store entry: (kind, path or name, content hash or absent). Jet reads are recorded in Core Files and Sys at the runtime route layer, under jet test only. Directory listings record a hash of the sorted names. A file that changes during the run is not stored. No new settings row.

Foreign reads: test builds link interceptors for the C library's open, openat, fopen, stat and opendir, as ASan does, at libSystem on macOS and ntdll on Windows. On Linux a seccomp filter compares each file syscall's instruction pointer to the recorder's own call sites; any other caller marks the row unseen. Env read by foreign code keys on the whole environment.

options.name: Opt in per profile
options.detail: The recorder and eligibility rules match A, foreign code included, but they switch on only under a profile, or a run, with `reuse_reads: true`. Stock is false, so a bare `jet test` reruns every file and env test.
options.technical: As A, plus one Bool row `reuse_reads` (`--reuse-reads`, `reuse_reads: true`, `.reuse_reads(true)`) in the PLAN-6035 settings table.

options.name: No, always rerun
options.detail: The #6035 store reuses a row only when its effect row holds none of FS, Env, Net, Clock, Random or Process. Fixture tests always run.
options.technical: No change to the #6035 S4 store.

comparisons.note: go test caches results and records the files and env vars read through package os; reads made by cgo code are not recorded. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Test_packages
Bazel reuses a test result when its declared inputs match; undeclared files are absent in the sandbox. Source: https://bazel.build/remote/caching
cargo test has no result cache; every test reruns. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-test.html

recommendation.why: A beats Go's test cache on safety and reach. Effect rows say which rows can read, and test builds record every read, foreign code included. A read the recorder cannot see makes its row rerun. `fresh` is the way out.
gains: Fixture-heavy suites rerun in seconds, including database and C-library tests.
No new setting; `fresh` already exists.

whyNot.reason: B adds a row nearly everyone sets, and the plain path stays slow.
C leaves fixture tests slower than Go's for good.

recommendation.tradeoff: A read recorder in test builds buys exact reuse for every file and env test.

decisions.title: Markers, effects, facts, derives and errors are ordinary types that implement a Core trait
decisions.situation: Jet has special declaration words for markers (the # rules above code), effects (what a function may do), compiler facts, derives and, as proposed, library errors. Each word has its own settings syntax, and none of them can be documented or inspected like an ordinary type. You asked whether they could be ordinary types that implement a Core trait, so one interface lists everything each one must define. The vote decides whether all of them become such types, whether effects and facts stay declared rows, or whether the special words stay.
decisions.gist: Should markers, effects, facts, derives and errors be ordinary types that implement a Core trait instead of special words?
decisions.lesson: Every Jet programmer already knows structs, enums and traits. Declarations written that way get docs, reflection and editor help for free. The trait is the checklist: it lists what each one must provide, and the compiler names anything missing.
decisions.story: Priya writes a storage package. She needs a Bucket effect, a Table marker, an Equatable-style derive and a MissingKey error. Today she learns effect rows, marker parameters with dollar settings, a derive link and a separate error form, and none of them can be inspected like her other types. With trait-backed types she writes structs and impls, and the compiler tells her exactly what each trait still needs.
decisions.inWild: C# attributes are classes; Java annotations are typed records; Scala 3 ties derivation to the type class; Rust error types carry fixed message templates with field holes.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. The owner asked in chat on 2026-10-30: "Should we just make effects & maybe markers types? Like structs as backing?" He wanted a trait for effects as one clear interface with more granularity. Tower question q066hpbq on D-MARKER-DIAG1 asked the same about library errors. His follow-up the same day asked to include facts and derives and do it all correctly the first time. Card #6039.

History. v1 covered markers, effects and library errors and passed one adversarial pass. v2 adds facts, derives and Jet's own diagnostic rows. It reconciles with D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A, D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 A and D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A, all ratified on 2026-10-30.

Today, markers (dev cbc43e0c5e). Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet declares 81 markers as marker Name(params, $sites: [...], ...). The $ parameters are fixed declaration settings: sites, repeatable, owns_menu, inherits, resolution, scopes and companion (Markers.jet:8-21). The repository holds 333 marker declarations in all.

Today, effects and facts. Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet declares 46 effect rows, such as effect FS.Write $irreversible. A root with leaves is closed (Effects.jet:8). Compiler/Prelude/Facts.jet declares compiler facts as fact Name($holds:, $safe:, $gates:, ...) rows under D-FACTDECL1 A. The repository holds 61 effect declarations.

Today, derives and diagnostics. Compiler/Prelude/Derives.jet writes derive T.Equatable { ... } template bodies. D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 A ratified the link marker Equatable($sites: [.Type]) derives Equatable. Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet holds 996 tab-separated diagnostic rows. Library refusals call reject(code:, what:, why:, fix:) and borrow Jet codes such as E0927. The repository has 100 reject calls.

What A changes. Core gains five traits: Marker, Derive, Effect, Fact and Diagnostic. A marker is a struct whose fields are its arguments. A derive is a trait that implements Derive. An effect is a struct or enum. A compiler fact is a field-less struct. An error is a struct.

What stays. The words marker, effect, fact and derive retire as declaration words. The diagnostic word proposed by D-MARKER-DIAG1 A is never added. Applying a marker, as in #web.Route("/orders") or #[Equatable], is unchanged. Writing an effect row, as in -[FS.Read]>, is unchanged.

The trait constant. This is the one new language capability. A trait may require a named compile-time constant, optionally with a default. An impl supplies it with name :: value. Rust associated consts and Swift static protocol requirements are the proven precedent. A trait constant is a member of its type, so it is snake_case like a field. The ALL_CAPS rule covers module-level constants only.

Settings become constants. Every $ setting becomes a trait constant whose value is a literal, an enum case or a list of them. Marker takes sites, repeatable, owns_menu, inherits, resolution, scopes and companion. Fact takes holds, safe, gates, name, identity and proved_by. Diagnostic takes code, severity and the registry columns. A diagnostic's what, why and fix are ordinary methods (rule 7).

Rule 1, cost. Applying a marker or naming an effect builds its value while compiling. That value costs nothing at run time unless code reads it through reflection. The types stay ordinary, so ordinary code may also construct them.

Rule 2, marker fields. Marker fields hold compile-time values. These are constants or the code-shaped kinds marker parameters take today: Value for an expression such as #Pre's condition, Ident for a name, and Type for a type. Policy's variadic ...PolicySetting becomes a trailing list field. The use site still writes its items as separate arguments.

Rule 2, effect fields. Effect fields must be constants. Effect checking therefore never depends on a run-time value or on code.

Rule 3, effect rows. An effect row names a type, an enum case, or a constant value written as an ordinary struct literal: -[Bucket{name: "photos"}]>. A bare type covers every value, and a case covers that case. A value covers only itself. So a function declared -[Bucket{name: "photos"}]> cannot call one that needs -[Bucket]>.

Rule 3, families. Enum cases are today's closed families. With enum FS { Read Write }, -[FS]> means any case and -[FS.Read]> means one case. Irreversibility is the trait method irreversible(self) -> Bool, default false. So FS.Write can be irreversible while FS.Read is not. Manifest grants and --allow/--deny name a type or case. A value narrows only in source rows.

Rule 4, effect powers. A library effect states the most it may do with #FX above its type, as D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A ratified: #FX(Net) struct Bucket. Its impl Bucket.Effect must sit in the same file as the type. A reader then sees the role next to the #FX.

Rule 4, one reading. #FX above any type means the most that work done in that type's name may do. For an effect type, that work is every function whose row names it. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1, still open, decides what #FX promises for an ordinary type's own methods. It must keep this one reading.

Rule 4, kernel effects. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 A holds as ratified. The machine powers are Core types the compiler recognizes by identity (rule 10). They are network, files, terminal, clock, randomness, environment, processes, foreign code, graphics card and browser host. Core declares DB, Log and Secret over them with #FX, like any package.

Rule 5, arguments. Marker arguments fill fields in declaration order or by name, as marker parameters do today. Field defaults use the struct form, name: Type{default}.

Rule 6, expand. The marker body becomes the trait method expand(self, target: Target), which runs while compiling. Unlike other methods, its body is a template, as today's marker and derive bodies are. Every declaration written in it is added at the marker's site, including fn and impl $name blocks. $name pastes a value. A helper that should not be pasted is an ordinary function outside the impl.

Rule 6, wrapping. Wrapping markers use the trait method wrap(self, call). Its default passes the call through.

Rule 7, error texts. A diagnostic's name is its package path, such as web.BadPath. Its what, why and fix are methods whose body must be one string literal. Their {self.field} holes may read only the value's own fields. The compiler names any other body. The texts are therefore fixed, so jet explain web.BadPath prints each literal with its holes. #Allow(web.BadPath) names one refusal when severity is .Warning.

Rule 8, reading a marker. Reading a marker returns its value. Inside expand, target.marker(Route) is Route?, and a repeatable marker gives [Route]. D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A's typed lookup is unchanged. The twin record it described is the marker struct itself.

Rule 9, derives. A trait becomes derivable by implementing the Core trait Derive. Derive's one requirement is fn expand(target: Target), a template with no self. Example: impl Equatable.Derive { fn expand(target: Target) { impl $target.Equatable { ... } } }. Writing #[Equatable] or #Equatable on a type applies it. Derive's sites are always types.

Rule 9, the impl head. In an impl head, the name before the dot is the trait itself. It is never the boxed value type that S48 gives a trait name in parameter, field and element positions. Derive is the only trait a trait may implement.

Rule 9, the link. The impl head is the explicit link D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 A required. The trait stays only its function contract, and no derive or derives word remains. A derive request carries no data, so it takes no arguments. target.marker(Equatable) answers Bool. Options are separate markers that expand reads. CLI(pack:) and Receipt(name:) stay struct markers that write impls.

Rule 10, Core's own. Core's own markers, effects and facts become Core and Prelude types that the compiler recognizes by identity. Examples are Unsafe, Policy, Net, FFI, Exactness and Rights. D-CORE-ROLE1 A already ratified this mechanism for library types with language meaning. Policy keeps its built-in tightening rule that way.

Rule 11, nesting. inherits and resolution keep today's meaning. .SiteBound and .Override need nothing more. A library marker that sets resolution to .Merge or .Tighten must also implement combine(self, inner: Self) -> Self. That method states how two nested writings join. The trait's checklist names it when missing.

Rule 12, facts. A compiler fact is a field-less struct that implements Fact, with its settings as trait constants. The holds and safe constants are the enum cases of today's rows. The name constant is a string, identity is a Bool, and proved_by is an enum case such as .Ownership.

Rule 12, gates. gates is a list of the Prelude enum Gate. Gate has one case per escape word: .Approx, .Rounded, .Raw, .Wrapping, .Saturating, .Checked, .Detach and .Drop. It also has .Marker(Type) for a marker type. Rights sets gates :: [.Marker(Unsafe), .Marker(Impure), .Marker(Grant)]. Every gate is therefore a checked value, not a bare word.

Rule 12, scope. Facts stay compiler vocabulary declared in the Prelude. A package does not add new facts in this step, because a fact needs a compiler rule that publishes and checks it. The rows' $decision fields are dropped in the cutover, as invariant I7 already requires.

Rule 13, Jet's own errors. Each of the 996 Prelude diagnostic rows becomes a struct that implements Diagnostic. The census is 845 active, 135 retired and 16 reserved rows, and 71 are lints. Jet's errors and library errors then share one shape for jet explain, #Allow and the editor.

Rule 13, row fields. Each hole in a row's texts becomes a String field. Meaning and detail are constant texts. Stage, moment, status and structured fix become enum constants with defaults. A typical row then sets only code, what, why and fix. A lint sets lint_name, which the compiler requires when severity is .Lint.

Rule 13, codes and reading. Codes stay E-numbers, set by code :: "E0927". The type gets a descriptive name, and jet explain accepts either name. Every constant and text is a literal (rule 7). So the foundation registry still reads these impls as source text without running them, as it reads the rows today.

Rule 13, cost. The cost is real. About 1000 one-line rows become about 1000 small struct-and-impl declarations, several thousand lines. jet fix must name each type. Retired and reserved rows convert too, so their codes stay explainable.

Rule 14, one role. A struct or enum implements at most one of Marker, Effect, Fact and Diagnostic. A trait may implement only Derive (rule 9). A type's role is therefore never ambiguous. Marker types are not generic in this step.

Rule 15, groups. A marker group is a struct with no fields whose Marker impl sets the constant group. Example: struct Fast {} with impl Fast.Marker { group :: #[Label("fixed"), Inline(.Always), Scalar] }. D-MARKER-GROUP1's law is unchanged. A group has two or more members and no parameters. Every member's gates and refusals apply at each use.

Folds in, open ballots. D-MARKER-DIAG1: A's Diagnostic trait is its option B plus one rule, that each text method is one string literal. That keeps the texts fixed and removes the reason B lost. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 (open): rule 4 fixes the one reading of #FX above a type that it must keep.

Folds in, ratified and kept. D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A keeps its lookup; the record is the marker, and a derive answers Bool. D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A keeps #FX above the effect type. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 A keeps its split, with kernel effects as recognized Core types. D-MARKER-GROUP1 keeps its law (rule 15). D-EXTEND-ARCH1 A already uses the impl Type.Trait shape, as in impl SQL.CheckedText.

Folds in, needing re-ruling. D-MARKER-DECL1 A chose one declaration word for everything applied with #. A keeps the one-form rule but replaces the word with struct plus impl Marker. D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 A's explicit link becomes the impl head, so only its spelling changes. D-FACTDECL1 A's fact word retires. D-META-HASH1: the $ settings disappear, which leaves $ only for template pastes.

Research, markers. C# attributes have been ordinary classes deriving System.Attribute since 2002, with [AttributeUsage] naming legal sites. The design is stable and widely used. Java annotations are typed records whose elements must be compile-time constants. That limit matches rule 2 and has not been a practical burden. Java lacked repeatable annotations until Java 8 and needed a wrapper type. A has a repeatable constant from the start.

Research, derives. Kotlin declares annotation class, and Scala annotations extend scala.annotation.Annotation. Rust derive macros are separate items linked to their trait only by name, so a derive and a trait can drift apart. Haskell's DeriveAnyClass and Scala 3's derives clause tie derivation to the type class itself. Rule 9 takes that shape.

Research, errors. Rust's thiserror and miette give errors fixed message templates whose {field} holes name struct fields. rustc's own diagnostics are structs with fixed message slugs. Swift macro diagnostics are structs conforming to the DiagnosticMessage protocol. That is the shape A gives Diagnostic.

Research, effects. Effekt declares effects as interfaces. OCaml 5 effects are constructors of the extensible type Effect.t. Both are ordinary type-system declarations. Koka and Unison use dedicated effect and ability words, which is option C's shape. The known failure to avoid is C# attribute constructors running arbitrary code during reflection at run time. A runs marker code only while compiling.

Migration. One cutover converts everything, and no old spelling remains. jet fix rewrites every marker, effect, fact and derive declaration and every reject(code: ...) call. The Prelude's 81 markers, 46 effects, fact rows, derive bodies and 996 diagnostic rows move to types. The compiler registries read the trait impls instead of the rows.

options.name: Types with Core traits, for all of them
options.detail: A marker is a struct whose fields are its arguments and which implements Marker. A derive is a trait that implements Derive and writes its impl. An effect is a struct or enum that implements Effect, and may carry constant data, so a function can name one bucket known while compiling. A compiler fact is a field-less struct that implements Fact. Every error, Jet's own and a library's, implements Diagnostic with fixed texts. The trait lists what each must provide.
options.technical: Adds the Core traits Marker, Derive, Effect, Fact and Diagnostic, plus the trait constant (name :: value in an impl). Retires the marker, effect, fact and derive words and every $ setting. Marker bodies become expand(self, target), a template. Effect rows accept a type, a case or a constant struct literal. Diagnostic texts are one-literal methods, and Jet's 996 rows become Diagnostic types.

options.name: Types for markers, derives and errors; effects and facts stay rows
options.detail: Markers, derives and errors become trait-backed types as in A. Effects and facts keep their declaration words, so they carry no data and cannot be read as values.
options.technical: Same Marker and Diagnostic traits, derives and trait constants as A. Effects keep the effect word with #FX above it (D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A) and carry no data; facts keep the fact word (D-FACTDECL1 A).

options.name: Keep special declaration words
options.detail: Markers, effects, facts and derives keep their declaration words with $ settings, and library errors get a new diagnostic word.
options.technical: Keeps marker, effect, fact and derive declaration words with the ratified derives link (D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 A), and adds diagnostic (D-MARKER-DIAG1 A).

comparisons.note: Attributes are ordinary classes; AttributeUsage names legal sites. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/reflection-and-attributes/creating-custom-attributes
A type class provides derived, and a type asks for it with derives. Source: https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/reference/contextual/derivation.html
thiserror error types carry fixed message templates whose holes name fields. Source: https://docs.rs/thiserror
Effects are declared as interfaces, an ordinary type form. Source: https://effekt-lang.org/tour/effects

recommendation.why: A gives every compiler-meaningful declaration one familiar form. The trait is the checklist, so a missing setting is an ordinary compile error. Markers become typed values other code can read, and a derive is tied to its trait by its impl head. Effects can carry constant data, so a function can name one bucket instead of all network access. Errors keep fixed texts, so their help pages still work.
gains: Four declaration words and the $ settings syntax retire.
Docs, visibility and reflection work as for any type.
Effects can be as narrow as one named bucket or host.

losses.loss: Declaring a marker takes three lines instead of one.
losses.mitigation: Only package authors declare markers; users still write #web.Route("/orders"), and jet fix converts every existing declaration.

losses.loss: Jet's own 996 error rows become 996 small types, several thousand lines.
losses.mitigation: jet fix converts them in one pass, and a typical one sets only its code and three texts.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two more declaration forms, so effects and facts carry no data and cannot be read as values.
C keeps five special words with their own settings syntax, and markers still need a twin record to be read.

recommendation.tradeoff: Package authors write a struct and an impl where they wrote one line; in return every declaration is an ordinary type with one checklist, and users' code does not change.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotDesign. Two passes against the dev Prelude, S48, the casing law and I7 fixed 12 v1 defects, replaced an unsound trait-as-marker with a Derive trait, and made fact gates enum values. They also stated the 996-row diagnostic cost as a mitigated loss.

decisions.title: Show, per source line, whether a program's data came from cache, RAM or disk
decisions.situation: You asked how to see when code falls out of the cache and waits on RAM or disk. Linux already lets a normal user count this per source line, and a probe on this machine points straight at the slow line. Jet has no command for it: `jet perf` is registered but not ported. This vote decides how the memory view is asked for and where it is drawn. We recommend a `memory` lens in `jet perf run`, shown in the terminal and in the Canvas code map.
decisions.gist: How should a Jet user ask for, and see, which source lines wait on RAM or disk?
decisions.lesson: A load that misses the small fast caches waits on a slower one, then RAM, and after a page fault, the disk. The chip counts where each load was served. Sampling those counts and mapping them to source lines shows which line waits on what. A lens is what `jet perf run` observes, such as cpu or alloc. A method is how it collects evidence, sampling or counting.
decisions.story: Ana's simulation slows down when the grid gets big. She runs `jet perf run sim.jet --lens=cpu,memory`. The top row is `sim.jet:48  64% time, 51% from RAM`. Line 48 walks the grid column by column. She swaps the loops, runs it again, and the row drops to 3% from RAM.
decisions.detail:
Before and after. Today `jet perf run walk.jet` prints that `jet perf` is not ported (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Front.jet:1601). The old Rust command never read hardware counters either. Under A the same command with `--lens=cpu,memory` prints a table of source lines. Each row shows time, where its loads were served, and its page faults.

Evidence. On this machine, a normal user sampled the chip's fill-source events for `walk.jet`, built at o2 with line tables. Line 12, the strided loop, took 58% of all refills from L2. The sequential loop took 0.09%. Page-fault counts put list growth on line 21. Disk waits show as major faults: a probe that reads a dropped file counts 16 of them.

What A says. `memory` joins the lens list that D-PERFSESSION1 D ratified (`--lens=cpu,alloc,memory`). It records rows per source range, as D-PROFILE-DETAIL1 A requires, with the source level named: L2, L3, another core's cache, RAM, and disk. dTLB misses and minor faults ride along. `jet perf view` prints the same table from a saved trace.

The code map. D-CODEMAP-VIEW1 A put run-time hotness out of the Canvas code map. A amends that in one narrow way. When the user opens a saved `.jtrace`, the map gains a Memory metric that shades each line by where its data came from. Without a trace, the map is unchanged.

When counters are missing. Some kernels refuse counters to normal users, and virtual machines often hide them. Then the lens prints `unavailable` and the reason, and records no rows. It never prints zeros, retries with other settings or asks for root, as D-PROFILE-METHOD1 A requires. A chip missing from Jet's event table is not this case. Jet's table is generated from the Linux kernel's per-CPU event lists, and an unlisted chip gets the kernel's generic RAM, disk and fault events, with the missing levels named.

Limits stated in the output. Samples can land a few instructions late, and some land in the kernel's page-fault code; those count as outside Jet code. One major fault can bring in many pages through readahead, so it counts waits, not bytes. L1 hits are too frequent to sample and are not shown. Runtime code such as list growth is charged to the Jet line that called it.

Option B. Card #4727 proposed a third method, `--profile-method=memory`. Methods are exclusive under D-PROFILE-METHOD1 A, so one run gives memory rows or time rows, not both. A user who wants to know whether the slow line is the RAM line needs two runs, and the two runs differ.

Option C. The lens as in A, but the code map stays compile-time only. The terminal table and the trace carry everything; nothing changes in Canvas. It is less work, but the map is where a user sees a whole program at once.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-cache-control-and-visibility.md, sections 4 and 5, has the probes and counts. Linux `perf mem`, Intel VTune and AMD uProf all show load sources per line. Cachegrind simulates caches on any host, but runs 20 to 100 times slower and shows a model, not the chip.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

options.name: A memory lens, in the terminal and the code map
options.detail:
`jet perf run app.jet --lens=memory` records, per source line, where loads were served: L2, L3, another core's cache, RAM or disk. It combines with `cpu` in one run. `jet perf view` prints the table.

Opening the saved trace in `jet dev --canvas` adds a Memory metric to the code map. Missing counters print `unavailable` and the reason, never zeros.
options.technical: Adds `memory` to D-PERFSESSION1's lens list. Linux first: perf_event_open, per thread, user mode, inherited by spawned threads. It samples the CPU model's fill-source events and the page-fault software events. Rows follow D-PROFILE-DETAIL1: source range, lens, level, weight; totals are derived. The trace stores the CPU model and event names. The code-map metric reads only an opened .jtrace (amends D-CODEMAP-VIEW1).

options.name: A third profile method
options.detail:
`jet perf run app.jet --profile-method=memory` replaces sampling by time with sampling by memory events. The table and the code map are as in A.

Methods are exclusive, so time rows need a second run.
options.technical: Extends D-PROFILE-METHOD1's method list to sample|count|memory. Same collection and rows as A, but the method excludes the cpu lens. Comparing time with memory means joining two traces from two runs.

options.name: A memory lens, terminal and trace only
options.detail:
The lens is as in A. The code map stays compile-time only, as D-CODEMAP-VIEW1 A says today.

Users read the terminal table or export the trace to other tools.
options.technical: Same lens and rows as A. No Canvas change; D-CODEMAP-VIEW1 stands unamended.

recommendation.why: A answers your question in one run and shows the whole program at once. It reuses the ratified lens list, rows and unavailable rule. The probe proves it works on default Linux without root.
gains: Time and memory rows from one run.
A whole-program picture in the code map.
Honest `unavailable` with a reason.

whyNot.reason: B makes the user run twice to see whether the slow line is the RAM line.
C keeps the answer in a table when the map is where a user scans a program.

recommendation.tradeoff: None for the user. Jet's event table follows the Linux kernel's per-CPU lists. An unlisted chip still gets RAM, disk and page-fault rows.
