decisions.title: A script run again with `jet run` gets the optimized program, not the quick unoptimized one
decisions.situation: `jet run`, `jet dev` and `jet test` compile with optimization `none`, so the first run starts fast (D-BUILD-DEFAULT1=B). `jet run` keeps the built program and reuses it while the source is unchanged. So a script you run every day keeps running unoptimized code, 1.25x to 1.83x slower than its `--release` build on the measured scripts. The vote decides whether a kept script program should become the optimized one.
decisions.gist: Should `jet run` rebuild a script it keeps reusing at full optimization, so repeat runs are as fast as `--release`?
decisions.lesson: A first run should start quickly, but a script you run again and again should not stay slow. Jet already keeps the program between runs. The choice is whether the kept program stays the quick unoptimized build, or is replaced once by the optimized build with the same meaning.
decisions.explainer: Every optimization level of Jet has one meaning (I9): the same output, errors and exit codes, from the same runtime. Only speed and size change. So swapping the kept program for an optimized build cannot change what the script does.
decisions.story: Ada runs `jet run tidy.jet` on her logs every morning. The first run compiles in a second and works. A month later it still takes 1.4x as long as the binary her teammate built with `jet build --release`, because `jet run` keeps reusing its quick build. Under option B, her second run starts the optimized build in the background, and from her third run on she gets the optimized program with no flag to remember.
decisions.inWild:
# Node and Bun: one command; hot code is recompiled with optimizations while it runs (tiered JIT)
node tidy.js

# Go: `go run` always compiles with optimizations and caches the build
go run tidy.go

# Rust: `cargo run` is unoptimized until you ask
cargo run --release
decisions.detail:
Today `jet run file.jet` compiles at `none`. That is the `stock_run` value of the `optimize` row in BuildOptions.jet. It keeps the image in the script cache (ScriptCache.jet) and reuses it while the source, runtime pack and jet executable are unchanged. The cache key includes every build option, the optimize level among them.

Measured warm wall time, `jet run` against the built `--release` binary, comes from ScriptBench on 2026-10-28. w03 18,572 / 14,790 ms (1.26x), w05 2,747 / 1,976 ms (1.39x), w06 12,223 / 9,785 ms (1.25x), w14 135.7 / 74.1 ms (1.83x).

Those ratios mix two costs: unoptimized code, and a fixed launch cost of `jet run` itself. A sleep-only script took 3,127 ms under `jet run` against 3,007 ms built, so about 120 ms per launch is not code speed. B removes most of the gap on w03, w05 and w06, but little of the short w14.

B's costs are estimates: one `full` build per script source, about as long as `jet build --release` on it. The cold first run is unchanged in every option. `jet dev` and `jet test` rebuild on every edit, so they keep `none` in every option.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first B left three losses: a background build per script, a build that could outlive the script, and a level-specific bug first showing on a later run. Two rules remove them.

Payback: the `full` build starts only when the previous run of that source lasted longer than one second. A full build of a script costs about as much, so it only starts where it repays itself. Short scripts never start one, and they would gain only milliseconds.

Owned by the run: the build runs beside the next run, as its child at idle priority, and stops when that run ends. Nothing outlives `jet run`, in CI or a container. An unfinished build leaves the `none` program in use and is tried again on the next long run.

A level-specific bug is not a cost of B. Every example and test already runs at every level, so such a bug would break `jet build --release` too, and it fails the level gate before release. `jet run --verbose` still names the kept level.

options.name: `jet run` builds at `basic` by default
options.detail: Every `jet run` compiles at `basic` (O1) instead of `none`. Warm and cold runs both get basic optimization. `jet run --release` stays `full`. D-BUILD-DEFAULT1 is amended for `jet run` only.
options.technical: The run command and the script cache key change their default level. Every first run compiles slower: the compiler itself took 54.7 s at basic against 19.9 s at none. Small scripts differ less. Repeat runs are faster than today, but slower than `full`.
options.code:
$ jet run tidy.jet        # compiles at basic, every time the source changes
$ jet run tidy.jet        # reuses the basic build
$ jet run --release tidy.jet   # full, as today

options.name: First run at `none`; a reused script is rebuilt once at `full`
options.detail: The first `jet run` of a source is unchanged: it compiles at `none` and runs. If a run of that source lasts longer than one second, the next run builds the `full` program beside it, as its child, and keeps it when done. From then on Jet reuses the `full` program. Output, errors and exit code are the same at every level (I9), so only speed changes.
options.technical: The kept program is keyed on the build options minus the level, and the record names its level and the last run time. A run whose recorded previous run exceeded one second starts one idle-priority `full` build as a child. The build takes the cache lock and swaps in by atomic rename; it is stopped when the run ends, leaving `none` in use. A failed build leaves a marker, so it is not retried for that source.
options.code:
$ jet run tidy.jet        # 1st run: quick none build, runs 4 s
$ jet run tidy.jet        # builds full beside this run
$ jet run tidy.jet        # every later run: the optimized program

options.name: Keep today's rule: `jet run` stays `none`; ask for speed with `--release`
options.detail: Nothing changes. A script you run often stays at `none` unless you write `jet run --release` or build it with `jet build --release`.
options.technical: No code change. The `jet run` script cells keep their 1.25x to 1.83x gap to the built binary.
options.code:
$ jet run tidy.jet             # none, every time
$ jet run --release tidy.jet   # full, when you remember

comparisons.note: Tiered JIT: code starts in a quick tier, and hot code is recompiled optimized while it runs. No flag. Closest to B.
`go run` compiles with full optimizations and caches the build; there is no quick tier. Closest to always-full.
`cargo run` builds the unoptimized debug profile until you pass `--release`. Same as C.
Caches bytecode (.pyc) between runs; the interpreter has no optimization tiers.

recommendation.why: B keeps the quick first run that D-BUILD-DEFAULT1 chose, and gives scripts you run again the `--release` code with no flag. Every level has one meaning, so only speed changes.
gains: The first and second runs start as fast as today.
Later runs of a long script execute optimized code with no flag.
Nothing runs after `jet run` exits, and short scripts never build twice.

whyNot.reason: A slows every first run and every edit-and-run cycle, and repeat runs stay at `basic`.
C leaves long scripts you run daily up to 1.39x slower unless you remember a flag.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining: a build happens only where it repays itself, and only while a run is going.

It also scaled the gains down to exclude the fixed launch cost, and added losses for leftover background builds and history-dependent machine code.

decisions.title: What hand-written reference sets the ceiling for the two web cells
decisions.gist: For the web benchmark cells, should the hand-written ceiling be WebAssembly written by hand, run by the same browser loader?
decisions.lesson: Every required benchmark cell needs a hand-written, best-possible reference that Jet must match. Native cells use x86 assembly. Web cells run in a browser engine, so x86 assembly cannot run there.
decisions.story: Lena ships a small widget built with Jet to the web. The gate compares her wasm file with the best program a person could write by hand for the same widget. If the reference is native assembly, the comparison measures a different machine and tells her nothing about her page.
decisions.inWild:
WebAssembly text format: a hand-writable form of wasm modules. Source: https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/text/index.html

Binaryen wasm-opt: the common size and speed optimizer for wasm. Source: https://github.com/WebAssembly/binaryen
decisions.detail:
AGENTS.md requires an asm-parity reference for every required cell, in cycles and bytes. Two required cells, webfront.widget and webfront.app, measure first stdout, wall time, binary bytes, artifact bytes and wasm bytes in a browser engine (node or a headless browser). Tools/perf/asm-parity has native x86-64 references only, so both web cells report uncovered and fail the gate.

Under A, each web cell gets a WebAssembly module plus the smallest JavaScript loader that runs it. The harness assembles it with wat2wasm and runs it in the same engine as Jet's output. Bytes are wasm plus loader bytes; time is the same engine's wall time and first output.

Two costs are engineered out. wabt joins binutils in jet-env, which already supplies `as` for the native references, so nobody installs anything. The first module is produced by the best tool, then tuned by hand; a better module later replaces it, as the policy already allows.

Under B, the reference is hand-written JavaScript only.

Under C, the web cells use the native x86 reference of the same workload.

The harness assembles with wat2wasm, runs node (or the headless browser the cell names), and records wasm bytes, loader bytes, wall time and first output. Output must equal Jet's.
options.code: (module (func (export "run") ...))   ;; ref.wat, assembled to ref.wasm

options.name: Hand-written JavaScript
options.detail: Each web cell gets a hand-tuned JavaScript program as its reference.
options.technical: Tools/perf/asm-parity/<cell>/ref.js; bytes are the JS source bytes.
options.code: export function run() { /* hand-tuned JS */ }

options.detail: The web cells are compared with the x86 reference of the same workload.
options.technical: cells.json maps webfront.* to an existing native cell.
options.code: "webfront.widget": "taskfile"   // native ref.S

comparisons.note: The text format is written by hand and assembled one-to-one into wasm. Source: https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/text/index.html
comparisons.code: (module (func $add (param i32 i32) (result i32) local.get 0 local.get 1 i32.add))

comparisons.note: C compiled to wasm with a JavaScript loader. Source: https://emscripten.org/docs/compiling/WebAssembly.html

recommendation.why: It is the web version of hand-written assembly: the lowest code the browser engine runs, measured in the same engine as Jet.
gains: Both web cells get a real ceiling, so the gate can pass.
Bytes and time are measured the same way as Jet's web output.
No new install: wabt arrives through jet-env, like `as` for the native cells.

whyNot.reason: JavaScript is not machine-level code, so it would set a lower bar than the policy asks.
C measures a different machine, so it says nothing about web bytes or browser time.

recommendation.tradeoff: None left for users or contributors: the tool comes with jet-env, and the two modules start from tool output.

decisions.title: How a `use` block imports several names from one module
decisions.situation: You chose import blocks with `alias :: path` rows, and answered that member lists become alias rows. That answer rested on a wrong count: Main reported 2 lists. The step-2 tree has 2,772 lists of the form `use pkg.[A, B]`, importing 16,498 names, mostly in the compiler and Jetpack. The cutover in flight keeps lists as rows, so choosing B or C adds a second mechanical rewrite. This ballot asks again with the real numbers, and we recommend keeping lists as rows.
decisions.gist: Inside a `use` block, how do you take many names from one module?
decisions.lesson: Big programs pull dozens of names from one module. One row per name is uniform but long.
decisions.story: Mia adds a parser file to the compiler. It needs nine names from jet_foundation; she writes nine path rows or one list, and `jet fmt` prints one list row. Her teammate Leo, new to Jet, needs one name: he writes `core.math.max`, and it stays that way.
decisions.inWild: use std::{env, path::PathBuf};
decisions.detail:
Today the compiler imports names like this: `use jet_foundation.[BuildOptions, CORE_SOURCE_OWNED_ROWS, build_options_key]`. Counted on the step-2 tree: 2,772 lists, 16,498 names, largest 111. Large lists are already one name per line, so the lists take 10,527 lines now.

Under A, a list is one row of a block: `jet_foundation.[BuildOptions, build_options_key]`. It is the ordinary path row with its last segment grouped. Each entry is a path under that prefix, so a dotted entry such as `m.[a.b, c]` stays legal.

A bare path row such as `core.math.max` already binds `max` today. `jet fmt` groups two or more path rows that share a prefix into one list row; a single row stays a bare path. It rewrites an identity alias row such as `term :: core.term` into the bare path `core.term`.

A one-line `use x` is the block form holding one row, not a second spelling. `jet fmt` folds a file's one-line uses into one block once there are two. Brace groups such as `use m.{x}` stay the existing E0003 error.

The cutover moves plain lists unchanged. An `x as y` entry, found in at least 73 one-line lists, becomes the alias row `y :: m.x`. `pub use` re-export lists and foreign-language lists such as `use c.[…]` follow the same row rules.

`jet fmt` sorts list names. It puts one name per line once the row passes the line width. Importing one name twice is the existing E0105 error, "defined twice".

Under B, lists are removed and each name is its own path row: `jet_foundation.BuildOptions`. The module prefix repeats on every row, and the tree grows by about 6,000 lines.

Under C, the module is imported once and code writes `jet_foundation.BuildOptions` at each use. The rewrite is mechanical but touches most compiler lines. It matches Go, which qualifies every use.

The `use` block itself, `alias :: path` and the removal of `as` are unchanged by this vote.

options.name: A member list is a row
options.detail: A row may be `module.[A, B]`: the path row with its last segment grouped. It brings in those names, unrenamed. Rename a name with an alias row. `as` is gone everywhere.
options.technical: Plain lists move into blocks unchanged; `x as y` entries split into `y :: m.x` alias rows, including `pub use` and foreign-language lists. Dotted entries stay. `jet fmt` groups two or more same-prefix path rows, rewrites identity alias rows to bare paths and folds one-line uses into a block. Duplicates are E0105.

options.name: One path row per name
options.detail: Member lists are removed. Each imported name is its own bare path row, `module.Name`, with the module prefix repeated.
options.technical: A second codemod turns each listed name into its own path row: about 6,000 more lines, with the module prefix repeated on each.

options.name: Qualify at each use
options.detail: Member lists are removed. Code imports the module and writes `module.Name` where it uses a name.
options.technical: A second codemod qualifies every use site of the 16,498 names; mechanical, but it touches most compiler lines. This is how Go reads.
options.code:
use jet_foundation

fn f(options: jet_foundation.BuildOptions) { … }

comparisons.note: No member lists: code qualifies every use (fmt.Println).
A use tree brings in several names from one path.

recommendation.why: It keeps a 111-name import one row long, and each import has one canonical spelling, which `jet fmt` prints.
gains: No 6,000-line growth, and no module prefix repeated per name.
A beginner can write one path per name, as today, and `jet fmt` groups them.
`as` is still gone and aliases still read `name :: path`.

losses.loss: `jet fmt` reshapes what the writer typed: two path rows from one module become a list.
losses.mitigation: It is the same canonical printing `jet fmt` already does; a single row is never changed.

losses.loss: Two branches that add names to the same short list conflict on that line.
losses.mitigation: Long lists are one name per line, so conflicts stay on small lists and resolve by keeping both names.

whyNot.reason: The module prefix repeats on every row, and the compiler imports grow by about 6,000 lines.
It rewrites every use site of 16,498 names and makes long qualified names the norm.

recommendation.tradeoff: Formatter reshaping and rare one-line merge conflicts, for short imports with one canonical spelling.

decisions.title: What `comptime use` imports, and where its names can be used
decisions.situation: Imports now use Go-style `use` blocks, and a file may hold several of them. You mentioned `comptime use` for custom linking logic in single-file programs, and the #6542 step-1 criterion names it, but no meaning exists yet. Today every import is an ordinary import, so build-only helpers sit beside the program code they configure. This ballot decides whether `comptime use` exists and what it means. We recommend a `comptime use` form whose names only compile-time code can see, so the helpers never ship.
decisions.gist: Should `comptime use { … }` import modules that only compile-time code can see, so they never ship in the program?
decisions.lesson: Some code runs only while building, for example choosing link libraries. Its imports should not become part of the program that ships.
decisions.story: Ana writes one file that builds a small tool and links a system library only on Linux. She imports the build helpers with `comptime use`. The helpers run while building, the tool links the library, and the shipped binary contains none of the helper code. If she calls a helper from `main`, the compiler stops her with a clear error.
decisions.inWild:
Zig: build logic lives in build.zig, a separate file that imports std.Build. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/

Rust: build-only dependencies go in [build-dependencies] and are visible only to build.rs. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html#build-dependencies
decisions.detail:
`comptime` is already a registered keyword, used by comptime blocks, functions and loops. The `link` and `build` helper names in the examples are proposed API. They do not exist in Core today; the vote is about the import form.

Under A, `comptime use` takes the same rows as `use`, as a block or as one line. Its names work only in compile-time positions: a `comptime { }` block, a `comptime fn` body, a comptime argument, and a constant computed while building. In that last case the value ships, but the helper does not.

A use in a runtime body, a runtime type or a `#Test` body is a sema error. It has its own registered code, what/why/fix text and UI snapshot. The fix offers both ways out: move the call into compile-time code, or switch to plain `use`, which ships the helper.

Plain `use` stays visible to compile-time code too. Importing one name both ways is the existing E0105 error, "defined twice". A `comptime { }` block inside a `#Test` body is a compile-time position, so tests reach build helpers through it.

A module reached only from compile-time code is built for the comptime child and left out of the runtime link set, whichever form imported it. So a beginner who writes plain `use` ships no build helper either. `comptime use` is the expert opt-in that turns a runtime call into an error. Jetpack still resolves and locks the package like any dependency. Target-dependent linking is an ordinary `if` inside the comptime block, so imports are never conditional.

Under B, there is no new form. Plain `use` works in comptime code, a lint warns when a module is used only from comptime code, and the linker drops unreached modules.

Under C, build logic lives only in a separate build file.

A build-time constant whose type comes from a `comptime use` module cannot ship, because that type is not linked. Using one in runtime code raises the same new error, and the fix is to import that module plainly.

Under A and B alike, a module used only from compile-time code is never linked. A adds an enforced boundary: a runtime call to an opted-in helper is an error, not a lint.

options.name: A comptime-only import block
options.detail: `comptime use { … }` takes the same rows as `use`. Its names work only in compile-time code. Any module used only by compile-time code, however imported, is never linked into the program.
options.technical: Parser: `comptime use` block and one-line form, registered in the syntax registry. Sema: comptime-only bindings; a runtime, type-position, shipped-constant-type or #Test-body reference raises a new registered diagnostic with a UI snapshot and a two-way fix. Driver: modules used only from compile-time code stay out of the runtime link set. The helper API shown is proposed.

options.name: Plain `use` plus a lint
options.detail: No new form. Compile-time code imports with ordinary `use`; a lint warns when a module is used only from comptime code; the linker drops unreached code.
options.technical: No grammar change; a new lint; relies on linker reachability for size.
options.code:
use link :: core.build.link

comptime { link.system("z") }

options.name: Build logic only in a build file
options.detail: Link and build logic must live in a separate build file; program files import only runtime modules.
options.technical: No grammar change; the single-file case needs a second file.

comparisons.note: Build-only dependencies are visible only to build.rs. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html#build-dependencies
Build logic is a separate build.zig file. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/
comparisons.code:
const std = @import("std");
pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void { ... }

recommendation.why: It keeps build logic in the same file, as you asked, and lets a writer make a runtime call to a build helper a compile error.
gains: One file can hold its own link logic.
An opted-in build helper can never be called from runtime code: it is an error, not a warning.
Beginners keep plain `use`, which links nothing that only compile-time code uses.

losses.loss: Two spellings import a build-only helper: plain `use` and `comptime use`.
losses.mitigation: They differ in meaning: plain `use` is the default, and `comptime use` is the expert opt-in that adds the error.

losses.loss: Compiler work: one grammar form, one sema binding class and one new diagnostic with its snapshot.
losses.mitigation: Comptime blocks already carry compile-time-only checks that the binding class reuses.

whyNot.reason: B never makes a runtime call to a build helper an error; the boundary stays advice.
C needs a second file, which defeats the single-file setups you asked for.

recommendation.tradeoff: One opt-in import form, for single-file link logic with an enforced compile-time boundary.

decisions.title: Whether Jet executables pack code and data into shared file pages, with linker-checked gadget-free edges
decisions.gist: Should Jet executables drop all page padding by sharing file pages between code and data, with the linker proving that no shared byte can start or end a new gadget?
decisions.lesson: Linux maps an ELF program in whole 4 KiB pages, so data sharing a page with code is also mapped executable. Padding avoids that but costs up to 4 KiB per file. Linker checks can make the shared data inert instead.
decisions.story: Kim builds hello with jet build --release. The hand-written assembly version is 504 B. With padded pages her file stays above 4 KiB. With checked packing it can come within 1.20x of 504 B.
decisions.inWild: LLVM lld shares file pages by default, without checks. GNU ld 2.31 and later pads code pages, like B. The hand-written asm references map headers, constants and code in one executable segment.
decisions.detail:
Measured on 12 asm-parity cells in default and release builds (24 images). With padding, every file is at least 4096 B plus code, above every 1.20x byte budget. Under the gadget check, a measurement over today’s images frees the pad in only 4 of 24 images, saving about 9.8 KB.

Today every constant shares one data section with pointers, whose bytes fail the check. Emitting each constant in its own section, with pointer data on its own page, lets clean constants fill the shared page. That is part of option A’s work.

Checked packing keeps one invariant: no non-code byte in an executable view can start an instruction sequence that transfers control. Code comes last in the file, so only its first page is shared. A 16-byte int3 guard stops fall-through into code.

Shared bytes hold no opcode that begins a return, jump, call, interrupt or system call. ASCII text is always clean. No page is writable and executable. #6328 c5 forbids per-program flags, so the chosen layout applies to every executable.

Code-only pages are not gadget-free: the code bytes themselves contain gadgets. Under A, the linker proves the shared bytes add none, so the executable pages hold exactly the gadgets of the code, as under B. A file smaller than a page plus its code must place some non-code bytes in an executable page, because the kernel maps whole pages. No layout can remove the remaining audit note.

options.name: Packed pages with gadget-free edges
options.detail: File order: ELF header, program headers, R data, RW initial data, unmapped notes and section headers, a 16-byte int3 guard, then code to the end of the file. Only the code first page is shared, and its non-code bytes are scan-clean.
options.technical: Each segment address is congruent to its file offset modulo 4 KiB. Shared bytes may not contain C2, C3, CA, CB, CF, CD, FF, 0F, E8, E9 or C7. Within 128 bytes of code, EB, 70-7F and E0-E3 are also excluded. Item order and zero fill keep them clean. Jet's own image audit changes in the same cutover: an executable page may hold code or bytes the linker proved inert, and the audit re-runs that proof.
options.code:
$ readelf -lW hello
  LOAD 0x000000 0x400000 R
  LOAD 0x000240 0x402240 RW
  LOAD 0x0003a0 0x4043a0 R E (int3 guard, then code to EOF)
$ wc -c hello   # headers + data + code, no pad

options.name: Padded code pages (DT-32 layout)
options.detail: File order: ELF header, program headers, R data, RW initial data, section names and headers, zero pad to 4 KiB, then code to the end of the file. R and RW share one non-executable page. The code mapping holds only code and int3 fill.
options.technical: The DT-32 layout, in wave 32. Minimum file is 4096 B plus code. No executable mapping contains data bytes.
options.code:
$ readelf -lW hello
  LOAD 0x000000 0x400000 R   (headers, constants)
  LOAD 0x001000 0x401000 R E (code only, to EOF)
  LOAD 0x000400 0x403400 RW
$ wc -c hello   # at least 4096 + code

comparisons.note: Defaults to -z noseparate-code: segments share file pages, without any gadget check.
Defaults to -z separate-code since binutils 2.31: code on its own padded pages, like B.

recommendation.why: Only packing lets small programs reach the 1.20x byte target. The linker check removes the gadget risk of plain packing. No page is ever writable and executable.
gains: Small programs drop below 4 KiB, so every asm-parity cell can reach its 1.20x byte budget.
Executable pages hold exactly the code's own gadgets, as with code-only pages.
Once constants get their own sections (#6501), every image also drops its last page pad, with no further layout change.

losses.loss: A checker that requires code-only executable pages would note the shared first code page.
losses.mitigation: lld's default output shares pages the same way, and Jet's own audit re-checks the linker's proof that the shared bytes add no gadget.

whyNot.reason: B keeps every executable at least 4 KiB plus code, so no cell can reach its 1.20x byte budget.

recommendation.tradeoff: Inert, linker-checked data shares code pages so small programs reach hand-written size.

surface.gist: Should code share file pages with data, checked so the shared data cannot form gadgets, letting small programs fit under 4 KiB?
surface.lesson: Linux maps files in 4 KiB pages, so data sharing a page with code becomes executable. Padding avoids that at up to 4 KiB per file; linker checks make shared data inert instead.

current.note: Code on its own padded pages (DT-32), which is option B.
current.code: LOAD 0x001000 R E (code only)   # file >= 4096 + code

wild.note: Defaults to -z noseparate-code: shared file pages.
wild.code: ld.lld -z noseparate-code

options.gist: No padding; shared data holds no control-transfer bytes, behind an int3 guard.
gains: Small programs can reach hand-written size, with no new gadgets.
losses: An outside code-only scanner would flag the inert shared bytes.

proposed.code: LOAD 0x000180 0x401180 R E   # no pad

options.name: Padded code pages
options.gist: Code alone on its pages; every file at least 4 KiB plus code.
gains: No executable mapping holds data.
losses: No cell can reach its 1.20x byte budget.

proposed.code: LOAD 0x001000 0x401000 R E   # code only

recommendation.why: Only packing meets the 1.20x byte target, and the linker check removes its gadget risk.
gains: Every cell can reach its byte budget, with no new gadgets.

losses.loss: A code-only-page checker notes the shared first page.
losses.mitigation: lld's default does the same; Jet's audit re-checks inertness.

whyNot.reason: Every file stays at least 4 KiB plus code, so no cell meets its byte budget.

recommendation.tradeoff: Inert, checked data shares code pages so small programs reach hand-written size.

decisions.title: Whether the fatal-signal report handler is linked only into programs that can fault
decisions.gist: Should a program that provably cannot fault leave out the 5.1 KB fatal-signal report handler, so tiny programs can reach hand-written size?
decisions.lesson: Every Jet executable installs a handler that turns a crash signal into a readable report. Some programs cannot crash by construction, so for them the handler is dead weight that only a runtime bug could ever reach.
decisions.story: Kim builds hello. The hand-written assembly is 504 B, and her budget is 605 B. The fault handler alone is 5.1 KB, and even a shrunk always-on handler would be about 1.5 KB.
decisions.inWild: C and Rust programs install no crash-report handler by default; a fault ends the process with the signal and the shell prints it. Go always installs its handler and prints a goroutine trace.
decisions.detail:
Docs/spec/diagnostics.md says every native fatal signal is reported, with E3012 and exit 70 for a stack overflow. Today the handler costs about 5.1 KB in every image, against budgets of 547 B to 5288 B.

An image can fault when it has a call cycle, a dynamically sized stack frame, mapped files, or calls a runtime routine marked as able to fault. The compiler computes this from the call graph. No user marker or flag is involved.

A fault report is a Jet feature, so it is never cut to save bytes; its cost is made as small as possible instead. The ceiling for a Jet program is the best hand-written code that delivers the same features. Each asm-parity reference therefore gains the same smallest report, and Jet must still match or beat it. The tightest report without an address measured 113 B; the address costs 35 B more.

options.name: Full report where a fault is possible; a small address report elsewhere
options.detail: Programs that can fault keep today's report exactly. Programs proven unable to fault carry a small report instead: on a fatal signal it prints `Jet defect at 0x…` with the faulting address, then exits 70. Every program reports every fault.
options.technical: The compiler decides from call-graph facts, the same way on every tier. The small report installs one handler for SIGILL, SIGBUS, SIGFPE and SIGSEGV. A hand-assembled version is 148 B of file (132 B of code, 16 B of text); it is assembled, not yet run. Each asm-parity reference gains the same report, because the ceiling must do the same observable work as the Jet program. Builds are reproducible, so the address names one instruction in the build's symbols.
options.code:
fn run() { print("hi") }   // small report: a fault prints Jet defect at 0x… and exits 70
fn walk(n: Int) Int { walk(n + 1) }   // cycle: full handler, overflow reports E3012

options.name: Always link a shrunk handler
options.detail: Every program keeps the full report. The handler is rewritten to about 1.5 KB.
options.technical: No spec change. Every image carries at least the shrunk handler.
options.code: fn run() { print("hi") }   // still links the ~1.5 KB handler

comparisons.note: Links no crash reporter by default; only stack overflow prints a short message through a small guard handler.
Always installs its signal handler and prints a full trace.
comparisons.code: panic: runtime error: invalid memory address

recommendation.why: Every program reports every fault with exit 70, and tiny programs still meet a budget that compares equal work.
gains: Proven-safe programs drop about 5 KB of handler.
Every fatal signal is still reported, with exit code 70, on every tier.
A defect report names the exact faulting instruction of a reproducible build.

whyNot.reason: B keeps about 1.5 KB in every program, many times hello's whole budget.

recommendation.tradeoff: Full reports where faults are possible; address reports where only a Jet defect can fault.

surface.gist: Should programs that provably cannot fault leave out the 5.1 KB crash-report handler?
surface.lesson: Every Jet executable carries a crash-report handler. Programs that cannot crash by construction only need it if Jet itself has a bug.

current.note: Every program links the 5.1 KB handler.
current.code: fn run() { print("hi") }   // 5.1 KB handler linked

wild.note: Links no crash reporter by default.
wild.code: Segmentation fault (core dumped)

options.name: Full where possible, small elsewhere
options.gist: Proven-safe programs print the faulting address and exit 70.
gains: Every fault reported; tiny programs drop about 5 KB.

proposed.code: fn run() { print("hi") }   // 148 B address report

options.name: Always, shrunk
options.gist: Every program keeps a 1.5 KB handler.
gains: Every fault is always reported.
losses: Hello cannot reach its 605 B budget.

proposed.code: fn run() { print("hi") }   // 1.5 KB handler

recommendation.why: Every fault reported, and tiny programs meet their budget.

decisions.title: Whether an explicit para_map limit may exceed host parallelism
decisions.gist: When a program writes `para_map(f, limit: 32)`, should Jet run up to 32 items at once even on a machine with fewer cores?
decisions.lesson: A parallel map runs several items at the same time. The limit says how many. For waiting-heavy work such as web requests, more items in flight than cores is faster.
decisions.story: Ana fetches 100 web pages with `urls.para_map(http.get, limit: 32)`. Her laptop has 8 cores, so only 8 requests run at once, and each waits on the network. Bun keeps 32 in flight and finishes 1.46 times faster.
decisions.inWild: Bun, Node and Python's thread pools let the caller set any concurrency. Rayon caps at the core count, because it targets compute work.
decisions.detail:
spec.md:2715-2716 says the worker count never exceeds available host parallelism, so an explicit limit above the core count is silently lowered. Compute-heavy work gains nothing from more workers than cores. Waiting-heavy work, such as network calls, does.

Without a limit, nothing changes under either option.

Memory grows with the written limit under every design that keeps n items in flight; Bun keeps the same per-item state. A waiting item costs only the stack pages it touched.

options.name: The limit bounds items in flight; waiting items hold no thread
options.detail: A written `limit: n` lets up to n items be in progress at once. An item that waits on the network, a sleep, a child process or a file read parks its own small stack and frees its worker for another item. Workers never exceed the cores, and waiting items hold no thread.
options.technical: spec.md:2716 changes: workers stay bounded by host parallelism, and an explicit limit bounds items in flight. The runtime runs each item on its own stack. A host wait submits the operation to io_uring and switches to another item. Where io_uring is unavailable, network and timer waits use epoll, timerfd and pidfd, and regular-file reads go to one shared I/O helper thread. Nothing in the language changes, and the same runtime serves every tier. Chunk boundaries stay stable, so results and order are unchanged.
options.code:
pages :: urls.para_map(http.get, limit: 32)   // 32 in flight on any machine
sums :: rows.para_map(score)   // no limit: at most one worker per core

options.name: Keep the core-count cap
options.detail: The limit can only lower the worker count below the core count. Waiting-heavy work stays bounded by cores until an asynchronous I/O path exists.
options.technical: No spec change. ScriptBench w11 keeps losing to Bun on wall and CPU.
options.code: pages :: urls.para_map(http.get, limit: 32)   // 8 in flight on an 8-core machine

comparisons.note: The caller sets any concurrency.
The pool is capped at the core count.

recommendation.why: The program gets the concurrency it wrote, computing work never oversubscribes the cores, and waiting costs no threads.
gains: Network maps keep up to the written limit in flight, as Bun does.
Compute maps never run more workers than cores, so a large limit is harmless.
A waiting item holds no thread, only the stack pages it used.

whyNot.reason: B silently ignores what the program wrote and keeps waiting-heavy maps slower than peers.

recommendation.tradeoff: Running work stays within the cores; waiting work reaches the written limit.

surface.gist: Should `para_map(f, limit: 32)` run 32 items at once even on a machine with fewer cores?
surface.lesson: A parallel map runs several items at once. For waiting-heavy work, more items in flight than cores is faster.

current.note: The limit is silently lowered to the core count.
current.code: urls.para_map(http.get, limit: 32)   // 8 in flight on 8 cores

wild.note: The caller sets any concurrency.
wild.code: await pMap(urls, fetch, {concurrency: 32})

options.name: Limit counts items in flight
options.gist: Waiting items park their stack; workers never exceed the cores.
gains: Network maps match peers.

proposed.code: urls.para_map(http.get, limit: 32)   // 32 in flight

options.name: Keep the core cap
options.gist: A limit can only lower the worker count.
gains: No spec change.
losses: Network maps stay slower than Bun.

proposed.code: urls.para_map(http.get, limit: 32)   // 8 in flight

recommendation.why: Waiting work reaches the limit with no extra threads.
gains: Network maps match Bun; compute stays core-bounded.

whyNot.reason: It silently ignores the written limit.

recommendation.tradeoff: Compute within the cores; waiting up to the limit.

decisions.title: One overflow rule for every fixed-width operation, conversions included
decisions.situation: Fixed-width overflow in Jet has grown five spellings. Gates such as wrapping(a + b) cover one operator, receiver methods such as a.wrapping_add(b) repeat them, and #Arithmetic covers a block. Conversions sit outside all three. U8{x} stops, U8.from_int(x) returns a Result, and nothing keeps the low bits. Int{b} and Int.from_u8(b) are two spellings of one widening. The owner asked for one beautiful, cohesive rule. The vote picks it.
decisions.gist: Should every fixed-width operation, conversions included, follow one overflow rule with one spelling each?
decisions.lesson: A fixed-width integer such as U8 or U32 holds a limited range. When a result does not fit, Jet stops the program unless the code chose another outcome. The outcomes are wrap around, clamp to the range, or give no value.
decisions.story: Dana writes a 32-bit hash. Its loop keeps a U64 state, mixes in bytes and stores the result in a U32. She wants to say "wrap here" once, the same way for the multiply and for the conversion.
decisions.inWild:
Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Iter.jet:696 state = wrapping(wrapping(state * U64{6364136223846793005}) + U64{1}) nests gates, because each gate covers one operator.
Examples/features/lowlevel/fixed_overflow_modes.jet:30-38 the gates and the #Arithmetic block side by side.
Core/Data/Sketch.jet:102 hash = (hash.bit_xor(U64.from_u8(byte))).wrapping_mul(U64{1099511628211}) mixes a receiver method with a widening method.
Census of this tree: 2,622 integer from_* conversion calls (2,195 are Int.from_u8) and 365 receiver overflow methods.
Swift: UInt32(x) traps, UInt32(truncatingIfNeeded: x) wraps, UInt32(clamping: x) clamps; &+ wraps one operator.
decisions.detail:
THE RULE UNDER A

A fixed-width operation is +, -, *, unary -, pow, / and a conversion T{x}. Plain, each one stops the program when its result does not fit. Three words choose another outcome, and they mean the same thing everywhere.

wrapping(e) keeps the low bits. saturating(e) clamps to the range. checked(e) gives T?, which is None when anything inside would have stopped. A word covers every fixed-width operation inside its parentheses, up to a function call, so one word is enough per expression.

#Overflow(.Wrapping), #Overflow(.Saturating) and #Overflow(.Stop) set the same outcome for a function, method or block. A word is that block rule at expression scope, so the two never disagree. The innermost one wins, and neither crosses a call.

ONE SPELLING EACH

T{x} is the only integer conversion. Widening, such as Int{b}, never stops. Narrowing follows the rule above. The integer from_* methods retire, so U8.from_int(x) becomes checked(U8{x}) and Int.from_u8(b) becomes Int{b}. jet fix rewrites all 2,622 calls.

The receiver methods retire too, such as a.wrapping_add(b) and a.checked_div(b). jet fix writes wrapping(a + b) and checked(a / b). #Arithmetic is renamed #Overflow, because it now covers conversions, which are not arithmetic.

Its explicit default .Checked becomes .Stop. Today .Checked means "stop", while checked(e) means "give None". After the change, each word has one meaning.

WHAT STAYS

Exact Int arithmetic never overflows. Named conversions that are not about range keep their names: Float rounding methods, from_bits, Char.from_u32 and parse. Shifts, indexing and bounds keep their rules. No new keyword or name is added except the .Stop case.

EDGE CASES

A word or block around an operation that cannot overflow, such as a widening, is refused, as a gate around such an operation is today. A written literal that does not fit is refused even inside a word, and the fix names the value it would become: wrapping(I8{200}) says to write I8{-56}.

Division by zero is not overflow. It still stops under wrapping and saturating, and checked(a / b) gives None, as checked_div does today. Sign changes count as narrowing: wrapping(U64{i}) keeps the two`s-complement bits. A negative v makes saturating(U8{v}) zero.

Existing gates change meaning only where an inner operation would have stopped the program: wrapping(a * b + c) now wraps the multiply too. jet fix flattens nested gates such as wrapping(wrapping(x * k) + 1) into one word.

RESEARCH

Swift traps on a plain conversion and names truncating and clamping variants. It renamed truncatingBitPattern after readers misread it (SE-0104). Zig separates the checked @intCast from @truncate. Rust`s silent as is the known mistake, which Clippy lints. Rust`s Wrapping<T> wraps every operation on a value, which is the scoped behavior A gives a word.

COST

Sema treats a conversion as one more fixed-width operation and lets a word cover its whole operand. The marker and its enum are renamed, and the lexical policy gains conversions and division. jet fix gains the conversion, method and nested-gate rewrites. Every caller migrates in one cutover, with the E3010 and E0930 texts updated.

options.name: One overflow rule, one spelling each
options.detail: Plain stops. wrapping, saturating and checked cover everything inside their parentheses, and #Overflow covers a block, for arithmetic and conversions alike. T{x} is the only integer conversion, and the receiver methods and from_* methods retire.
options.technical: Sema gives conversions and division the fixed-width overflow policy, and a word sets the policy for its operand up to a call. #Arithmetic becomes #Overflow with modes Stop, Wrapping and Saturating. jet fix rewrites the retired spellings.

options.name: Conversions join the gates only
options.detail: wrapping, saturating and checked also accept a conversion as their operand. Gates still cover one operator. The receiver methods, the from_* methods and #Arithmetic stay as they are.
options.technical: Sema lets a gate hold a conversion. No retirement and no rename.

options.name: A low_bits method
options.detail: Each fixed-width type gains low_bits(x), which keeps the low bits. Clamping uses clamp. Everything else stays as it is.
options.technical: One static method per fixed-width type, lowering to the truncating cast.

recommendation.why: A turns five overlapping spellings into one rule. Plain stops, a word picks another outcome for an expression, and #Overflow picks it for a block, the same for arithmetic and conversions. Every outcome then has exactly one spelling, and each word has one meaning.
gains: One overflow rule for arithmetic and conversions, with one spelling each.
One word covers a whole expression, so gates no longer nest.

losses.loss: About 3,000 call sites move to the new spellings.
losses.mitigation: jet fix rewrites every one mechanically in the same cutover, and the meaning of each call stays the same.

losses.loss: A word now covers inner operations that stopped before.
losses.mitigation: That changes only paths that crashed, and the word now means what readers already assumed.

whyNot.reason: B keeps five spellings and the nested gates, and adds conversions to only one of them.
C adds a new name and leaves every existing overlap in place.

recommendation.tradeoff: A one-time migration of about 3,000 calls, in exchange for one overflow rule with one spelling each.

decisions.title: The name of Jet's web framework
decisions.situation: Jet ships its own web framework: the built-in modules for routing, data loading, forms, tables, long lists and app state. It has no name of its own, so guides call it Jet's web library. Its sample app sits in a placeholder folder after dropping a borrowed JavaScript framework's name. The owner picks the name for docs, the website and that sample; code does not change, and we recommend Contrail.
decisions.gist: What should Jet's web framework be called?
decisions.lesson: A framework name is what people search for, write in job posts and say in talks. It should be short, easy to say, tied to Jet, and not already used by another web framework, so searches and packages are not confused.
decisions.explainer: Under every option the code stays the same: `use core.web as web` and `web.app(...)`. The name changes the docs title, the website section, the reference app folder and the noun used in guides. The rename lands in one cutover across the repository.
decisions.story: Ana tells a colleague she built her shop in Jet. The colleague asks which framework. With a name she answers in one word that a search finds; with "Jet Web" she must add that it is the one built into Jet.
decisions.inWild: First-party: Microsoft names its C# web framework ASP.NET Core. Community: Rust has Axum and Leptos, Elixir has Phoenix, Ruby has Rails. Go ships net/http unnamed; Gin, Echo and Fiber grew to add routing it lacked.
decisions.detail:
Collision checks ran on 2026-11-01 and 2026-11-03 against npm names and search, crates.io, PyPI, RubyGems, Hex, GitHub repository names and trademark notices.

Contrail: Juniper's Contrail® networking software (contrail-controller, 436 stars, plus the contrail-web-core and contrail-web-controller UI repos). VibeIQ's Contrail Platform owns the @contrail npm scope (@contrail/sdk, about 17,000 downloads a month).

flo-bit/contrail (57 stars, npm @atmo-dev/contrail) is a pre-alpha Bluesky backend with HTTP endpoints. Also: the Contrails Bluesky feed tool (80 stars), a backtracking crate, an OpenContrail Ruby gem, a PyPI price tracker and an empty npm placeholder. No general web framework uses it. The GitHub user name contrail and contrail.dev and contrail.io are taken.

Jetstream: Laravel Jetstream (about 4,000 stars) is a web starter kit. NATS JetStream (built into nats-server, about 21,000 stars), Bluesky's Jetstream service, Google's JetStream inference engine, a Rust RPC crate and Uber's npm sync framework also use it.

Dropped: Slipstream, best known as the NAT Slipstreaming attack (samyk/slipstream, about 2,000 stars) and DNS covert-channel tunnels. Taxiway is free on every registry checked, but it fits any plane and reads as cabs.

decisions.title: How is a value tag declared once the tag word retires?
decisions.situation: D-MARKER-DECL1 A retired the tag word, and D-DECL-TYPES1 A made every marker a struct implementing Marker. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 A then let any type write `#FX(!Net)` above itself to forbid an effect in everything done in its name. A tag`s deny list says the same thing about the tagged data, so a separate deny setting would be a second way to forbid an effect. The vote decides how a tag is spelled as a type and where its denials live.
decisions.gist: How is a value tag declared as a type, and where do its denials live?
decisions.lesson: A value tag, such as #PII String, marks data that must not reach some effects. The compiler tracks the mark through every value computed from it, and #Scrub(PII) on a function is the one way to remove it. A tag`s from list names sources whose results carry the tag automatically, such as from: [Store.read]. Jet`s built-in tags are Input, PII, Secret and Credential.
decisions.story: Dana`s payment package must keep card numbers out of logs and the network. She declares a CardNumber tag, marks the card parameter, and writes one #Scrub function that returns the last four digits.
decisions.inWild:
Examples/features/types/value_tag_type.jet:4 tag Raw { deny: [DB] }
Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Taint.jet:304-311 the built-in tags: Input, PII and Secret deny [DB, Exec, Net]; Credential also denies Log.
D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 A, ratified: #FX(!Net, !FS) above struct Parser bounds all work done in Parser`s name.
Java Checker Framework: @Tainted and @Untainted are annotations declared like every other annotation.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED
D-MARKER-DECL1 A: tag retires as a word, and a tag declares a value label with its denials and an optional from list.

D-DECL-TYPES1 A: a marker is a struct implementing Marker, and its $ settings become trait constants. Rule 9 gives derives their own trait, Derive.

D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 A: #FX above a type bounds everything done in that type`s name, with the same row syntax as a function arrow. `!Net` is a denial that also reaches through calls.

Owner direction: a type contains its own impls, so the impl is written inside the struct body. This amends the spelling of D-DECL-TYPES1`s examples.

THE PROBLEM WITH A SEPARATE DENY
Both a type row and a tag deny list name effects that must never happen. If a tag kept its own deny setting, Jet would have two spellings for one meaning, against I8. A reader would also have to learn which one applies where.

HOW A AND B UNIFY THEM
A tag has no fields and no methods, so the only work done in its name is work done on tagged data. Its #FX row therefore bounds every operation a tagged value reaches. For an ordinary type the same row bounds its methods. The row syntax, the denial meaning and the codes (E0749) are shared. Only the place the check looks differs: methods for an ordinary type, data flow for a tag.

WHAT EVERY OPTION KEEPS
The use sites do not change: #PII String in a parameter, field or return type, a tagged expression, and #Scrub(PII). Site gains a .TypeUse case for value positions.

.Type stays the declaration site, so #CardNumber struct Point is still refused as E0731. A tag has no fields, expand, wrap or methods; any of those is refused as E0732 is today. from stays a tag setting, written from :: [Store.read], because no other rule has it.

REFUSALS UNDER A AND B
A tag with no denial is refused, as E0734 is today. A ceiling entry in a tag`s row, such as #FX(Log), is refused for now. Tagged text passes through allocation and other plain work, so an allow-list would refuse ordinary string handling. The fix says to write denials.

The tag is the struct, so a second declaration with that name is an ordinary E0105. A package struct named Input, PII, Secret or Credential is refused as E0106, redefining a built-in. Nine test fixtures that redeclare a built-in tag are renamed.

COST
Every option converts the 36 tag declarations and declares the four built-in tags in the Prelude. It also removes the copies of their names and laws: EffectsSurface.jet:95, Taint.jet:304-317 and :644, and the TaintKind enum (CoreEnumRows.jet:26). The texts of E0733 and E0734 (Diagnostics.jet:449-450) are rewritten.

Under A and B, a tag`s row needs #FX on types, which c09kjhit builds. The compiler`s internal origin rows also deny the sinks SQL.raw, HTML.raw and Sh.raw, which are functions, not effects. No written tag denies a sink. Those rows stay internal until the library-effect step on c09kjhit makes the sinks effects.

EDGE CASES
The tag Secret and the effect Secret (Effects.jet:54) are both Prelude names. A later step of D-DECL-TYPES1 that turns effects into types must rename one. A tag cannot also be a group, an effect or a fact (rule 14).

decisions.title: Should compiler fact planes become markers, or keep their own Fact trait?
decisions.situation: Under D-DECL-TYPES1 A, a marker becomes a struct that implements Marker. A compiler fact plane becomes a field-less struct that implements Fact. You asked whether facts should merge into markers to remove a duplicate concept. The vote decides whether the Fact trait stays, or whether planes become markers that nobody writes with #.
decisions.gist: Do compiler fact planes become markers?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a rule you write above code with #, such as #Unsafe("reason") or #web.Route("/orders"). A fact plane is something the compiler tracks, such as whether a number is exact or which rights a scope has. Each plane lists the escape words that can weaken it, such as wrapping or #Unsafe. Only the Prelude, Jet`s built-in library, declares planes; there are 49.
decisions.story: Dana reads the Prelude to learn how #Unsafe works. She finds Unsafe declared as a marker, and Rights declared as a fact plane whose gates name Unsafe. She wants to know whether these are one kind of thing or two.
decisions.inWild:
Compiler/Prelude/Facts.jet:19 fact Exactness($holds: .Value, $safe: .Gain, $gates: [approx, rounded, raw, wrapping, saturating, checked], …)
Compiler/Prelude/Facts.jet:23 fact Rights($holds: .Scope, $safe: .Shrink, $gates: [Unsafe, Impure, Grant], …)
Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet:27 marker Unsafe(reason: String, obligations: ObligationMode{.None}, $sites: [.Function, .Method, .Block, .Operation])
Java: @Override and @FunctionalInterface are annotations javac checks; the facts javac tracks, such as definite assignment, are not annotations.
Rust: lang items are marked with the built-in #[lang] attribute, but the facts rustc tracks, such as borrow state, are not attributes.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED
D-DECL-TYPES1 A: a marker is a struct that implements Marker. Its fields are its arguments. Its $ settings become trait constants: sites, repeatable, owns_menu, inherits, resolution, scopes and companion. Rule 15 adds group. A fact plane is a field-less struct that implements Fact. Fact`s settings are holds, safe, gates, name, identity and proved_by. Planes stay Prelude-only (rule 12). A type has one role (rule 14). Owner direction: a type contains its own impls, so the impl is written inside the struct body.

D-TAG-MARKER1, on the board beside this one, decides how a tag is declared. The tag in the code below shows its recommended option.

WHY THIS IS ASKED AGAIN
Folding facts into markers lost twice. D-FACTDECL1 option C lost because calling a knowledge plane a marker breaks the one word a beginner already learned. D-MARKER-DECL1 option C lost because fact is written only in the Prelude, so folding it helps no learner. D-DECL-TYPES1 has since made both kinds ordinary types with traits. A merge now means one trait instead of two, not one keyword instead of two.

THE STRONGEST CASE FOR B
Picking a role with a setting is already ratified: rule 15 makes a group a marker that sets group. D-FACTDECL1 says markers and facts differ only in what they attach to, in one registration table. Tags are facts on the Taint plane that people write with #, so the line between written and tracked is already blurry. A merge removes one Core trait from the docs.

OPTION B IN DETAIL
Marker gains one optional constant, plane: Plane?, defaulting to None. Plane is a Prelude struct holding the six fact settings. Setting plane makes sites default to [], and any other sites is refused. Only the Prelude may set plane, so rule 12 is stated on one constant. Reflection: target.marker(Exactness) is a compile error naming the plane, because a plane is never written at a site. Plane facts keep their $ reads, such as value.$origin.

OPTION C IN DETAIL
As B, but the six plane settings sit directly on Marker with defaults, and a marker that sets holds is a plane. Every marker`s checklist then lists six settings that only planes use.

COST
Every option converts the same 49 Prelude fact rows in the same cutover. Under every option, the Gate enum first needs cases for 20 rows it cannot express yet. Rights and PackagePolicy name the retired Grant, BuildSettings names Force, three Structure rows use strings, and fourteen Target rows name a provider and digest. B and C also add three refusals: a package marker that sets plane (or holds), a plane with non-empty sites, and a reflection read of a plane.

EDGE CASES
A type that is both a plane and a written marker is refused under every option. Under A, rule 14 refuses it. Under B and C it is refused because a plane`s sites must be empty. Build facts such as Build.OS and Target.Memory are planes under every option. Under B, a marker that sets both plane and deny is refused.

options.name: Keep Fact as its own trait
options.detail: D-DECL-TYPES1 as ratified. Markers implement Marker, and the 49 Prelude planes implement Fact. A marker and a plane meet only through the plane`s gates list.
options.technical: No change to D-DECL-TYPES1 rules 12 and 14.

options.name: Planes become markers with one plane setting
options.detail: One trait for markers and planes. A plane is a marker that nobody writes: it sets one plane setting that holds the fact law, and its sites are empty. Only the Prelude may set it.
options.technical: Marker gains plane: Plane? (default None), where Plane{holds, safe, gates, name, identity, proved_by}. Setting plane makes sites default to [], and any other sites is refused. The Fact trait is never added. Refusals: plane outside the Prelude, and target.marker(P) on a plane P.

options.name: Planes become markers, settings flat
options.detail: One trait, as in B, but holds, safe, gates, name, identity and proved_by are ordinary Marker settings with defaults. A marker that sets holds is a plane.
options.technical: Marker gains six constants with defaults. The Fact trait is never added. The same refusals as B, keyed on holds.

recommendation.why: Groups, and tags under D-TAG-MARKER1 A, pick their role with a Marker setting, but they are still written with # at sites. A plane is never written and uses none of Marker`s members: not sites, repeatable, resolution, expand or wrap. Keeping Fact separate means no Marker member needs a refusal to keep planes out.
gains: Each trait lists only members its role uses.
No marker can declare a plane by accident, so nothing extra is refused.

losses.loss: Core keeps two traits where one could do.
losses.mitigation: Only the Prelude implements Fact for now (rule 12). Users see it only in the Core trait docs.

whyNot.reason: Groups, and tags under D-TAG-MARKER1 A, pick their role with a Marker constant but are still written with #. A plane would use none of Marker`s members, so sites and reflection need refusals to keep it out.
C adds six plane-only settings to every marker`s checklist, for 49 Prelude rows.

recommendation.tradeoff: One extra Prelude-only trait, in exchange for Marker holding only things written with #.

decisions.title: Can a type write its markers inside its body?
decisions.situation: Markers such as #FX, #Layout and #Deprecated set facts on a declaration, and today they can only be written above it. A type with many markers gets a long line or a stack of lines before its name. The owner asked for a formal form inside the body that sets the same facts, so the marker above is only a shorthand for it. The vote decides whether that form exists and how it is spelled. Either way it must stay one mechanism with one meaning (I8).
decisions.gist: Should a type be able to write its markers as lines inside its body?
decisions.lesson: A marker like #Layout(c) sets a fact on the declaration below it. Markers on a type today sit above the struct line. Fields and methods already carry their own markers inside the body. In Jet, # always means a marker and $ means a compiler read or a template paste.
decisions.story: Ravi`s Point type needs a C layout, an effect limit and a deprecation notice. Three markers above the struct push the name off the first screen line. He wants them inside the struct, as a header above the fields.

Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Syntax/Spellings.jet:13 every __ name is classed Reserved; Core`s __show and __debug are hooks the compiler reads (CoreModules.jet:324).
Rust: inner attributes go inside modules, functions and impl blocks, but not struct or enum bodies.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

D-DECL-TYPES1 A: a marker is a struct implementing Marker, a type contains its own impls, and $ settings retired so that $ means reads and pastes. D-NAME-SPLICE1 B: a template pastes a binding with $name. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 A: #FX above a type bounds everything done in its name.

THE RULE UNDER A

The line inside is the formal declaration, and #X(args) above is the shorthand that writes the same entry. Moving a marker inside is one swap: #X(args) becomes #X :: (args) at the top of the body. The # keeps the marker sigil, and :: reads as "this declaration`s X is".

The value after :: has four shapes. true applies a marker with its defaults, as #MustUse :: true. false refuses one, as #Debug :: false for #!Debug, and only where #!X is allowed. One name, string or number needs no parentheses, as #Layout :: c. Any other argument list is written in parentheses, exactly as above.

So #MustUse :: true and #MustUse mean the same, and no empty () exists. A Bool argument is always written in parentheses, as #X :: (true), so true alone never means two things. jet fmt drops parentheses around one simple argument, so each line has one printed form.

The arguments use the marker argument grammar, so every marker accepts exactly what it accepts above. Library markers work the same way, as in #orm.Table :: "users". No marker opts in, and nothing is translated.

ONE MECHANISM

Both spellings fill the same marker list on the declaration. Checks, templates and reflection read that list and cannot tell which form was used. target.markers sees the same entries either way. No new name is declared, so there is no Point.$FX to read.

ONE PLACE PER TYPE

A declaration writes its own markers either all above or all inside. Mixing them is refused, so a reader never searches two places. jet fix offers to move all of them inside, or all of them above. Markers that tools or templates add go wherever the declaration`s markers already are, and above when it has none.

The # lines come first in the body, before fields, constants and impls. A later one is refused, and jet fix moves it up. A repeated marker gets the error it gets above today.

WHERE IT APPLIES

Inside every braced declaration body: struct, enum, trait, impl block, inline module, function and method. A function body is code, but no statement starts with #X ::, so the header lines never look like code. The function`s effect row stays in its arrow, because #FX`s sites do not include functions.

A marker whose sites exclude the declaration gets the site error it gets above, so #Redact :: true in a struct body fails like #Redact struct X. Blocks, lambdas and tests already carry their marker at their own head, as #FX(IO) { … }, so there is nothing to move.

NO CLASHES

A module body binds Name :: path, a trait or marker body has constants such as sites :: [.Function], and a function body has statements. A # line differs from all three by its first character. Template pastes and environment reads use $, so they never meet a # line.

COST

The parser reads the leading # lines right after the opening brace, then applies them where it applies markers above today. Layout, derives, SingleUse and MustUse therefore still take effect before the members are parsed.

The formatter prints the form the author chose. jet fix gains the two whole-type moves. No existing code changes, and no marker is converted. #FX on a type also needs D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 A`s site change, which is not built yet. The other markers work as soon as this lands.

WHY NOT __

B uses __, which matches the idea of an internal field the marker sets. Core already has __show and __debug, which the compiler reads. But D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 A rejects every __ name written in user code as E0067, with no escape. D-NAME-SIGIL1 A says two underscores are machine space with no user meaning.

B would open one user-written slice of that space, so a reader can no longer assume a __ name is generated. Debuggers and suggestion menus hide __ names, so they also hide these lines. A needs no amendment and keeps # as the only marker sigil.

WHY NOT $

$ stays the template paste and the compiler read. The sigil law says programs never declare a $ name. $Layout :: c would also read like a fact member, inviting Point.$Layout, and a bare $MustUse line in a template has the same shape as a pasted enum variant.

options.name: #X :: value lines at the top of a body
options.detail: Any marker on a declaration with a braced body can be written at the top of that body as #X :: value. It means exactly what #X(args) above means. A declaration puts its own markers all above or all inside.
options.technical: Leading body members # Path :: value, read right after the opening brace and added to the declaration`s marker list before its members. Values are true, false, one name, string or number, or a marker argument list in parentheses.

options.name: __X :: (args) lines in the body
options.detail: As A, but each line starts with __ instead of #. It reads as an internal field the compiler sets, which is what the marker above fills in. This amends D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 and D-NAME-SIGIL1, which reserve every __ name for the compiler.
options.technical: As A with __Path. User code may write a __ name only as one of these leading lines, and only for a marker in scope. Every other __ name stays refused as E0067.

options.name: Markers stay above
options.detail: No new form. A long list becomes a named group written once, then applied with one marker above each type.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.why: A gives every marker on a braced declaration a formal line inside it, with one swap rule and no per-marker work. It keeps # as the only marker sigil, declares no new name and amends no ratified rule. Both spellings fill one marker list, so there is still one mechanism.
gains: Every braced declaration can declare its markers as a header inside it.
One swap rule covers every marker, including library markers.

losses.loss: Readers meet one more line shape.
losses.mitigation: It is the marker itself with :: before its value, and editor hover names the shorthand it equals.

losses.loss: A declaration cannot split its markers between above and inside.
losses.mitigation: That keeps them in one place to read, and jet fix moves the whole set either way.

whyNot.reason: B amends two ratified decisions to let user code write __ names, which tools treat as generated and hide.
C leaves no formal in-body declaration, which is what the owner asked for.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two spellings for one marker list, in exchange for a formal header inside the type.

decisions.title: How does a package declare its own kind of an existing effect, such as an audit kind of Log?
decisions.situation: D-DECL-TYPES1 A already ratified that an effect is a struct or enum that implements the Effect trait, the same shape as a marker. One case is still open. Today a package can add its own kind of an existing effect with `effect Log.Audit`. A function marked -[Log.Audit]> may log, and a caller allowed -[Log]> may call it. Families with fixed kinds, such as FS with FS.Read and FS.Write, are closed today and become enums. Log has no fixed kinds, so packages may extend it. This ballot picks how the struct form says "Audit is a kind of Log". The only use in the repository is Examples/features/effects/effect_declarations.jet, plus about 12 tests.
decisions.gist: A package effect is a struct; how does it say it is a kind of Log?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a struct that implements Effect, like a marker implements Marker. The open question is only how a package effect joins an existing one.
decisions.story: Mia writes an audit package. Its functions record audit events, which is a kind of logging. Apps that already allow logging should be able to call them, and an app that denies logging must also deny auditing.

decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY DECIDED

D-DECL-TYPES1 A: an effect is a struct or enum that implements Effect. Settings are trait constants written name :: value inside the impl, like sites :: [.Function] in impl Marker. Effects with fixed kinds are enums, such as enum FS { Read Write }. D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A: package effects carry their package path, as in audit.Audit.

WHAT A ADDS

The Effect trait gains one optional setting, parent. Writing parent :: Log makes Audit a kind of Log. Allowing Log allows Audit, denying Log denies Audit, and Audit may do at most what Log does. No #FX line is needed, because the parent is the limit. A function may still allow only the audit part with -[audit.Audit]>.

RULES UNDER A

The parent must be an effect struct. An enum family such as FS or DB stays closed, as today, and naming one as a parent is an error with a fix. Chains are allowed: a kind of Audit is also a kind of Log. A cycle is an error. Irreversibility defaults to the parent's. A #FX line may narrow the limit further, never widen it.

SAFETY

Joining Log grants nothing new. A kind of Log can do only what Log does, so an app that allows Log gains no power. Two packages cannot clash, because each kind carries its package path: audit.Audit and billing.Audit are different.

MIGRATION

jet fix rewrites each `effect Log.Audit` into the struct with parent :: Log. It also rewrites each -[Log.Audit]> row to -[Audit]> inside the package and to -[audit.Audit]> outside. No caller that allowed Log changes.

options.name: A struct with parent :: Log
options.detail: A package effect is a struct that implements Effect and names its parent: parent :: Log. Allowing Log allows it, denying Log denies it, and it may do at most what Log does. Callers that allowed Log change nothing. A caller may also allow only the narrow kind, as audit.Audit.
options.technical: Effect gains an optional trait constant parent (default none). Sema walks the parent chain for coverage, denial and the limit. A parent must be an effect struct, not an enum family. Cycles are refused. The dotted effect Log.Audit form retires, and jet fix rewrites declarations and rows.

options.name: A separate effect with its own limit
options.detail: A package effect is its own struct with #FX(Log) above it, giving its limit. It is not a kind of Log, so allowing Log does not allow it. Every caller names it, as audit.Audit. Denying Log still denies it, because its limit is Log.
options.technical: No new setting. Uses the #FX limit from D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A. jet fix rewrites declarations and adds audit.Audit to every caller row the check would refuse.

options.name: No package kinds; Log carries a topic

decisions.title: What does a derive with no trait become when the derive word retires?
decisions.situation: D-DECL-TYPES1 A makes a derive a trait that implements Derive: impl Equatable.Derive { fn expand(target: Target) { ... } }. But every user derive in the repository today is a provider with no trait at all. For example, derive T.DebugText adds a debug_string method, derive T.FieldNames adds one method per field, and derive T.LayoutFacts adds only constants. There are 40 such declarations in 37 files: 8 examples, 3 perf constructs, and the rest tests. None of them names a trait, so impl X.Derive has nothing to attach to.
decisions.gist: Should a derive that has no trait become a marker that writes the code?
decisions.lesson: A derive writes code onto a type when you mark it, as in #DebugText struct Point. Under D-DECL-TYPES1 A, a derive belongs to a trait. A marker can also write code onto the item it marks, through its expand template (rule 6).
decisions.story: Lee's package has derive T.FieldNames, which writes field_x and field_y methods onto any struct marked #FieldNames. The method names depend on the fields, so no fixed trait can describe them. When the derive word retires, Lee needs a form that still writes those methods.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

D-DECL-TYPES1 A rule 9: a trait becomes derivable by implementing Derive, whose one requirement is fn expand(target: Target). The derive and derives words retire. Rule 6: a marker's expand(self, target: Target) is a template, and every declaration in it, including impl $name blocks, is added at the marker's site. Rule 9 also keeps CLI(pack:) and Receipt(name:) as struct markers that write impls.

WHAT IS OPEN

No rule says what jet fix writes for a derive with no trait. The Prelude's two derives, Equatable and Comparable, are compiler-known traits and are not affected.

CENSUS

At dev 2d8aea4762: 40 user derive declarations in 37 files, all trait-less. Some write a fixed method (DebugText), some write methods with pasted names (FieldNames), and some write only constants (LayoutFacts).

options.name: A marker struct that writes the code
options.detail: A derive with no trait becomes a marker: a field-less struct with impl Marker { sites :: [.Type] } and an expand template that writes impl $target { ... }. Writing #DebugText on a type is unchanged. A derive whose name is a trait becomes impl X.Derive, as rule 9 says. jet fix picks the form by checking whether a trait of that name exists.
options.technical: Uses only ratified forms (rule 6 markers, rule 9 derives). The derive orphan rule (E2711) and the derive collision checks apply to the trait form only; a provider that becomes a marker follows the marker rules. Their UI snapshots change wording.

options.name: jet fix writes a trait for it
options.detail: jet fix writes a new trait from the methods the derive adds (trait DebugText { fn debug_string(self) -> String }) and turns the derive into impl DebugText.Derive. A derive whose methods depend on the fields (FieldNames) or that adds only constants (LayoutFacts) has no fixed method list, so it still becomes a marker as in A.
options.technical: Adds a trait per provider with a fixed method list. Two forms remain for user code that writes methods onto a type, and jet fix must decide which one applies to each provider.

options.name: Keep a trait-less derive form
options.detail: A provider keeps a derive form without a trait, such as impl Derive for a field-less struct named after the request. Derive then has two shapes, one with a trait and one without.
options.technical: Needs a new rule for Derive on a struct, against rule 14 (a struct implements at most one of the four roles, and Derive is the trait-only role).

recommendation.why: A uses only forms that are already ratified. A derive stays tied to a trait, and code that just writes methods onto a type is a marker, which rule 6 already lets write impl blocks.
gains: No new trait or new rule.
One mechanical fix, chosen by whether a trait of that name exists.

losses.loss: Derive-only checks (the orphan rule E2711 and the derive collision checks) no longer apply to these 40 providers.
losses.mitigation: The marker rules cover the same sites, and expand output is checked like any other code.

whyNot.reason: B invents traits nobody asked for, and still needs A for providers with pasted names or only constants.
C gives Derive a second shape and breaks rule 14.

recommendation.tradeoff: Derive-only checks stop applying to trait-less providers, in exchange for using only ratified forms.
