decisions.title: Comment glyph: keep // or move comments to ##
decisions.situation: Jet starts a comment with two slashes, and a doc comment, which tools show as help, with three. The owner asked whether two hash signs would be better, since that frees the slash and the hash already marks compile-time work. Nothing planned needs the double slash, but Python's 7 // 2 compiles today and silently keeps 7, while two hashes would sit beside markers and rewrite every comment. We recommend keeping two slashes and adding a warning that catches the Python habit.
decisions.gist: Should Jet comments start with ## instead of //?
decisions.lesson: A comment is text the compiler skips. Jet starts one with //, and a doc comment, shown as help, with ///. A single # marks places where the compiler acts, such as #Inline. The vote: move comments to ##, freeing //, or keep //.
decisions.story: Mia learned Python first. She writes half :: 7 // 2, the program runs, and half is 7 instead of 3. Ben came from Rust and types // and /// without thinking. The owner wants # to feel like Jet's meta mark. This vote decides which glyph comments use, and how Mia is protected.
decisions.inWild:
// Odin, Swift, Rust, C, C# and Jai mark compiler work with # and keep // for comments.
share :: #force_inline proc(total, people: int) -> int { return total / people } // Odin
print(#file, #line) // Swift
# Python, shell, Ruby, Nim and Nix use # for comments and nothing else.
half = 7 // 2  # Python: // is floor division, so half is 3
## Nim: a doc comment. In C macros, a ## b pastes two tokens.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY DECIDED

S5 makes // the line comment and nested /* */ the block comment (ratified 2026-06-15). S49 makes /// the doc comment, which jet doc shows and jet test --docs runs. The registry rows are COMMENT_PREFIX and BLOCK_COMMENT_OPEN and BLOCK_COMMENT_CLOSE in Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/CoreSurface.jet:188-195.

D-META-HASH1 A (2026-10-30) defines # as the one compile-time mark: markers such as #Inline, site values such as #line, and pastes such as #{x}. Its stated meaning is that the compiler acts here. D-PRE-COMPILE1 A (2026-10-31) rejected a doubled-hash form, ##Pre. Whole-number division was ratified as /% on 2026-08-05.

TODAY

Probes ran on the admitted compiler at commit 1f70b8d4. Probe c14 is the ballot program; it runs, prints 333 and passes jet fmt --check. Probe c11, half :: 7 // 2, prints 7 with no diagnostic. Probes c02 and c12 show that ## is an error today (E0003), so the glyph is free. Probe c04 shows a #! line after byte 0 is E0042.

WHAT THE SLASH WOULD FREE

The single / is never a comment, so division and the positional-only parameter zone already use it (probe c08). Only // and /* are taken. Python's floor division is the one strong rival meaning for //, and Jet already spells it /% (1,057 uses). Regex is the typed literal Regex{"..."}, and paths are typed native values. No ratified or open decision needs //, /* or slash literals.

CENSUS

Tracked .jet files under Compiler, Core, Examples, tests and Jetpack hold 94,746 comment tokens in 7,815 of 17,255 files. That is 90,855 full-line comments, 1,140 trailing comments and 2,698 doc lines. There are 17 block comments and 14,325 # tokens in code. 829 comments begin with #, mostly card references such as // #4828, and 28 are commented-out markers.

EDGE CASES

A commented-out marker stays readable either way: // #Inline or ## #Inline. A #{x} or #line inside a comment is plain text in both options (probe c13). The shebang rule does not change. Under B, a doc line that holds a markdown heading reads ### ## Examples; the corpus has none today. Nim's #[ ]# block form would collide with the #[A, B] marker list, so B drops block comments; only 17 exist.

BEGINNER PATH

A newcomer writes // for a note and /// above a function to document it, as in Rust, Swift, C# and Zig. A Python habit such as 7 // 2 gets a warning with the /% fix under A, or an error under B.

EXPERT PATH

Experts keep nested /* */ to fence off a region under A, or use the editor's toggle-comment key under B. Machine-read comments such as doctest // => lines keep working under A. Under B they are renamed to ## =>.

NOT ON THE BALLOT

Single # comments, as in Python and shell, would need every marker, [T#N], pkg#1.2.0 and #!Name moved to another glyph. That reverses the owner's own # rulings, so the research note studies it but the ballot does not offer it. Spending a freed // on floor division would reopen /% and belongs to a later ballot if B wins.

Research note: Docs/research/2026-11-04-comment-sigil.md (drafted at $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Research/comments/).

options.name: Keep //, and warn on Python's //
options.detail: Comments stay as they are: // for a line, /// for a doc comment and nested /* */ for a block. One new warning catches the Python habit. It fires when the code before // ends a number expression and the comment text is itself a number expression whose names exist here. The fix shows /%.
options.technical:
Lexer, parser, registry and editors are unchanged. The warning lives where types and scope are known, after type checking. It needs three things on one line. A number-typed expression ends right before a line comment. The comment text parses as an expression of number type. Every name in it resolves in scope. The structured fix replaces // with /%.

Lexical rules are not enough. The census in floor-warn-census.mjs flags 367, 146 or 61 corpus lines under three lexical rules. All 61 lines under the tightest rule are labels, such as return false // WB3. Each fails the typed rule, because it ends in a Bool or a unit call, or because it names something not in scope.

options.name: Two hashes
options.detail: A comment starts with ## and a space, and a doc comment with ### and a space. Four or more hashes make a plain divider comment. Block comments are removed, as in Python and Zig. A ## followed by a letter is an error, so ##Inline cannot silently drop a marker. // and /* become teaching errors, and a // b points to /%.
options.technical:
Lexer: ## followed by a space, a tab or the line end is a line comment. ### followed by the same is a doc comment. Four or more # make a plain comment. ## followed by anything else is a new error saying a marker uses one #. # stays one token everywhere else, so markers, [T#N], pkg#1.2.0, #line and #{x} keep working. The byte-zero shebang rule stays, and the config-file exception for :// is deleted.

Registry: COMMENT_PREFIX becomes ##, a doc row ### is added, and the block rows are removed. One lexer-driven jet fix rewrites 94,746 comment tokens in 7,815 files, 17 block comments and about 630 lines in 40 Markdown files.

The same cutover updates about 30 hand-written comment scanners, five machine-read comment forms, both TextMate grammars, the tree-sitter grammar, Zed and VS Code settings, and the self-host fixtures.
options.code:
### Splits a bill evenly.
#Inline fn share(total: Int, people: Int) -> Int {
    ## whole-number division drops the cents
    total /% people  ## #4828: round up later
}

fn run() {
    half :: 7 // 2
    print(share(1000, 3))
}

## jet check:
##   Error: Jet comments start with "##", not "//"
##     --> run.jet:8:15
##   Fix: whole-number division is "/%": half :: 7 /% 2
##   (a "##Inline" with no space is also an error: a marker uses one "#")

comparisons.note: Odin marks compiler directives with # and keeps // and nested /* */ for comments. Source: odin-lang.org/docs/overview.
Swift uses # for compiler-supplied values and macros, and // and /// for comments.
Rust attributes start with #, and comments use // and ///. Its lexer must tell a #! shebang from a #![ attribute on the first line.
Nim comments use #, doc comments ##, and nested blocks #[ ]#. Pragmas in {. .}, not #, mark compiler work. Source: nim-lang.org/docs/manual.html.
comparisons.code:
proc share*(total, people: int): int {.inline.} =
  ## Splits a bill evenly.
  # whole-number division drops the cents
  total div people

comparisons.note: In C macros, a doubled ## pastes two tokens. C readers know ## as paste, which Jet spells #{x}.
comparisons.code:
#define FIELD(name) int field_ ## name;  // ## pastes tokens
FIELD(total)  // expands to: int field_total;

comparisons.note: Both use # for comments. That frees // for floor division in Python and for merging records in Nix. Neither uses # for anything else.
comparisons.code:
half = 7 // 2              # Python: half is 3
defaults // { port = 8080; }  # Nix: merge two records

recommendation.why: Nothing planned needs //, because whole-number division is already /%. Keeping // matches every language that uses # for compiler work, and # keeps meaning that the compiler acts here.
gains: No rewrite, and every editor already knows //.
Comments never look like markers.

losses.loss: Python's 7 // 2 compiles and keeps only 7.
losses.mitigation: A new warning fires when a number is followed by // and a number expression, and shows /%.

losses.loss: On German and Nordic keyboards, / needs Shift.
losses.mitigation: Most of those keyboards need Shift or AltGr for # too, and editors toggle comments with one shortcut.

whyNot.reason: Two hashes put comments beside markers and rewrite 95,000 lines to free a glyph nothing needs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep the familiar comment and one meaning for #, and give up the thematic fit of ##.

decisions.title: One rule for foreign words and retired Jet spellings
decisions.situation: Jet's compiler can spot another language's word, such as `fun`, or an old Jet spelling, such as `#Suppress`, and name the current form. In June the owner paused these teaching messages, but the port of the compiler to Jet brought most of them back. Today `fun add(...)` gets an error that points the wrong way, while `length()` teaches. Nine tests fail on missing teaching text, and 27 pass while pinning teaching the pause removed. The recommendation keeps the pause everywhere, with generic errors that name the legal Jet forms.
decisions.gist: When code uses another language's word or a retired Jet spelling, should Jet name the replacement, and what happens to the tests that pin it?
decisions.lesson: Jet paused its teaching messages in June, but the port to Jet brought 29 of them back. Nine tests fail because their teaching text is gone, while 27 others pass and pin teaching that the pause removed. One rule has to decide which messages Jet prints.
decisions.story: Maya comes from Kotlin and writes `fun add(left: Int, right: Int) -> Int`. Jet tells her the line computes a value she does not use, so she wraps it in `print` and gets a stranger error. A minute later she writes `sizes.length()`, and Jet says `length` is another language's name for `len`. The two answers follow two different rules, and the first one sent her the wrong way.
decisions.detail:
Five owner rulings disagree. The June pause, confirmed in July, removes teaching for foreign words and retired spellings until after the FFI epoch. The owner added that retired spellings leave the tests too. The August retirement rule makes a retirement that changes meaning a hard error with a fix line, and checks that the old form is gone from the repo. The August foreign-keyword rule teaches each known foreign keyword. The October foreign-teaching ballot kept the pause and asked only for better generic errors.

Measured at commit 125e2e8f89, 29 teaching rows still print, and three of them are already marked Retired in the registry. The 27 tests that pin them pass. Method lookup also still says `length` is another language's name for `len`. Nine tests fail. Three are foreign cases: `fun` and friends, `jet install`, and a list of foreign method names. Six are old Jet spellings: `tasks.channel<Int>()`, `Ability`, `#Suppress`, `.origin()` on a tracked value, a bare `?`, and the old HTTP response literal.

The bare `?` test also expects the `Int E!` suffix to be retired. That suffix is current syntax, and the compiler itself uses it, so that half of the test is stale under every option. The test keeps its bare `?` error and is re-recorded from real output. The `semaphore_teaching` test fails only on a trailing blank line, and it follows the same rule as the other teaching tests.

Two codes mean several things at once, and this is not a teaching question. E1206 is registered as a lint-selector error but is also printed for package file, allocator, path and lock errors. E0128 is registered as a zip length error but is also printed for distinct types, so `Meters{a + b}` says a `Meters` cannot be used where a `Meters` is expected. Under every option each meaning gets its own registered code.

Some codes are never printed today. E0983 and nine lint codes are checks the Jet compiler has not built yet, so each keeps its test and gets a real check on the package and lint cards. E0043 (`jet install`) and E0037 (a print macro) are teaching codes and follow this ruling.

Nothing is deleted outright. A test that leaves the suite is moved to the held archive with a log row, and git history keeps it. A registry row that stops printing stays with status Retired, so `jet explain` still answers for old logs. About 115 tests have retired, foreign, teach, legacy, migration or deprecated in their path, and 92 of them pass. Each is checked once during the change.

options.name: Pause everywhere, with generic errors that name the legal forms
options.detail:
Jet stops recognizing foreign words and retired spellings, including the foreign method-name hints. Every unknown word, method, type or rule gets one generic error built from Jet's own grammar and library. It lists the legal forms at that spot and suggests current names by spelling and by signature. An unknown rule no longer stops the check, so the code inside it is still checked in the same run.

Tests that pin only teaching leave the suite. Tests that pin a current rule keep that rule but use an invented word instead of an old spelling.
options.technical:
Remove the recognizers behind the 29 printing teaching rows and the foreign branch of method lookup. Mark those rows, E0037 and E0043 Retired. The parser and checker still reject every form; before the tests leave, one recorded run shows each program still fails.

Add a check that no active registry row is named Foreign or Retired, apart from the FFI rows that describe calls into C. This replaces the fix-line half of the August retirement rule and the August foreign-keyword rule. The check that a retired form appears nowhere in the repo stays.

options.name: Pause foreign words, teach retired Jet spellings
options.detail: Foreign words get the same generic errors as in A. A retired Jet spelling gets a hard error that names its replacement, from one retirement table. The six retired-spelling tests are fixed by restoring their messages, and the three foreign tests leave the suite.
options.technical: Retire the foreign rows as in A. Keep the retired-spelling rows and port the six missing messages into one table of old form, new form and fix line. Pure renames get a machine fix, as the August retirement rule says. The retired spellings stay in the tests, which the June owner comment ruled out.

options.name: Teach both from one table
options.detail: Jet names the replacement for both foreign words and retired Jet spellings. All 29 printing rows stay, the nine failing tests are fixed by restoring their messages, and one table holds every taught word. This reopens the October ruling that kept the pause.
options.technical: Move the 29 recognizers and the method-name hints into one table. Port the nine missing messages, including `fun`, `def` and `var` and `jet install`. Re-record `semaphore_teaching` without its trailing blank line. Someone must keep the table current for every language it covers.

comparisons.note: Python suggests near names by spelling only, and keeps no table of other languages' words.
comparisons.code:
[].apend(1)
# AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'apend'. Did you mean: 'append'?

recommendation.why: Two owner rulings say pause, and the latest one, in October, kept it. One rule ends today's mix, where `length` teaches and `fun` misleads. Generic errors that list legal forms help every unknown word, including typos, not only the words someone thought to list.
gains: One rule for every unknown word, method, type and rule.
No retired or foreign spellings left in the tests, as the owner asked in June.
Generic errors stop pointing the wrong way, which helps typos as well as habits from other languages.
An unknown rule no longer hides the errors inside it.

losses.loss: A form whose meaning moved, such as `#Suppress`, gets no direct pointer to its replacement. This is irreducible: without a table of old forms, no rule can know what the old form meant.
losses.mitigation: Checking continues past the unknown form, so the next error in the same run names the current form, as `.drop("reason")` does here.

losses.loss: The change touches 29 recognizers and about 115 tests in one pass.
losses.mitigation: It lands as one change with the full test suite run before and after, and every removed test is kept in the held archive.

whyNot.reason: It keeps retired spellings in the tests, which the owner ruled out in June, and it still leaves two rules for unknown words.
It reverses the October ruling, and it needs a table of other languages' words that someone must keep current.

recommendation.tradeoff: Clear, uniform errors for every unknown word, at the cost of no direct pointer for the few forms whose meaning moved.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Main, reviewing the Prep-2 draft under the four-agent cap. Findings were that the October claim checks out (D-FOREIGN-TEACH1 chose Keep the pause), and the code splits apply under every option, so they do not tilt the vote.

surface.lesson: Jet paused its teaching messages in June, but 29 came back when the compiler moved to Jet. Today `length()` teaches while `fun` gets a misleading error. Nine tests fail on missing teaching. One rule should decide what Jet says for every unknown word.

current.note: Today one foreign word misleads and another teaches.

losses: Old spellings stay in the tests.

losses: Reverses the October ruling.

Generic errors stop pointing the wrong way.

losses.mitigation: Checking continues past the unknown form, so the next error names the current form.

It reverses the October ruling and needs a table of other languages.

decisions.title: How are the ui and cases corpus suites named, and how does a code suite report its rows?
decisions.situation: D-TEST-PROFILE1=A made test profiles data in package.jet. Its example names one stock suite field, golden_corpus, and says code suites register with Test.suite(name, value) in fn test, without saying what value is. Jet's own ui and cases corpora need field names, and the jetpack, selfhost and perf suites need a signature. Today only golden_corpus is ratified, so the testkit package declares only golden, and ui, cases, jetpack, selfhost and perf are left out. This vote names the two corpus fields and fixes how a code suite reports its rows.
decisions.gist: What are the ui and cases corpus fields called, and does a code suite return rows or report each one?
decisions.lesson: A suite is a named set of rows that `jet test --profile` runs and compares. A stock suite is a folder of test files, written as data. A code suite is a function that checks something no folder describes, such as a binary-size budget, and reports one row per check.
decisions.story: Sam adds a size budget to CI. Today it is a Node script that prints its own format. With a code suite he writes one Jet function that reports a row per program. `jet test --profile perf` then shows those rows beside the golden rows, compares them with the last run, and fails when a row that passed now fails.
decisions.inWild:
Cargo: [[test]] harness = false points at a binary that prints its own results.
Go: a TestMain or t.Run(name, fn) reports each subtest as it runs.
Vitest: projects in config name test folders; each test reports as it finishes.
pytest: a plugin's pytest_collect_file turns any file type into reported items.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS DECIDED ALREADY

D-TEST-PROFILE1=A (2026-10-30) made profiles `test:` records in package.jet, such as `quick: TestProfile{ suites: [tests], time_limit: 60s }`. The suite `tests`, every #Test, is built in. Stock suites are `suites:` data. The ratified example names one field: `golden: TestSuite{ golden_corpus: "tests/golden" }`. Code suites register in test.jet's fn test with Test.suite(name, value).

WHAT IS OPEN

1. Field names for the other two corpora Jet runs: the ui corpus (tests/ui, a source file with its expected stdout and stderr) and the cases corpus (tests/cases, step files).

2. What value is in Test.suite(name, value). Today Test has one method, t.run(), which runs the stock suite and returns its exit code (sema THandleOp.TestSuiteRun). There is no Test.suite.

TODAY (dev b032d40638)

- `ui_corpus:` or `cases_corpus:` in package.jet is E1206 "unknown Package field" (Jetpack PackageModel apply_field), as `test:` was before D-TEST-PROFILE1.
- The testkit package's ui and cases runners exist (Tools/testkit, Jet). Moving them under `jet test` is #6035 c3, which needs these names.
- The perf, selfhost and jetpack checks are shell and Node scripts today (Tools/perf/ci-perf-check.sh, Tools/agent/s5, the Jetpack tests), outside `jet test`.

THE OPTIONS

A and B both add ui_corpus and cases_corpus beside golden_corpus, and differ only in the code-suite value. C replaces the three corpus fields with one `corpus:` field plus `kind:`. That rewrites the ratified example, and C uses B's code-suite value.

A: the value is a function that receives a row sink, fn(rows: TestRows). It calls rows.pass(id), rows.fail(id, detail) or rows.skip(id, reason) as each check finishes.

B: the value is a function that returns its rows, fn() -> [TestRow]. TestRow is a plain struct: id, outcome (.Pass, .Fail(detail), .Skip(reason)).

C: `TestSuite{ corpus: "tests/ui", kind: ui }`, with kind one of golden, ui, cases; code suites as in B.

EDGE CASES (the same under every option unless noted)

- A suite name in both `suites:` and a Test.suite call is an error that names both places.

- Test.suite names are string literals, so `jet check` and `--profile` list every suite without running code. A computed name is an error with a fix to write the name.

- A profile that names an unknown suite is the D-TEST-PROFILE1 error listing the known suites, code suites included.

- Two rows with one id in a suite: the second is a failing row "duplicate row id".

- A code suite that panics: under A, rows reported before the panic stay and one failing row "stopped: <message>" is added. Under B and C every row of that suite is lost and the suite is one failing row.

- time_limit bounds each corpus row, and each code-suite call as a whole. Under A the rows reported before the limit stay.

- -u rewrites a ui row's expected streams. A code suite has no snapshots; -u accepts its new rows as the stored last result.

- cases_corpus reads .case files only while they exist. When D-TESTKIT1=A's migration moves them to #Test, they join `tests` and the field retires with the corpus.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

Beginner: nothing changes. `jet test` runs every #Test, with no package.jet fields and no test.jet. Expert: package.jet names the corpora and the profiles, and test.jet registers code suites. `jet test --profile full` runs them all in the c4 pool and prints one row stream.

ADVERSARIAL

- Three corpus fields grow by one per new corpus kind; C's one field with a kind never grows the vocabulary.

- C rewrites a ratified example six days after ratification, for a naming gain only.

- B loses every row of a suite when one check panics, which is the failure case suites exist to show.

- A adds a second handle type, TestRows, beside Test, so beginners meet two handle types instead of one.

- Literal-only suite names forbid generating one suite per target in a loop.

- cases_corpus names a format D-TESTKIT1=A already plans to retire.

decisions.title: Ask whether a Pool id still names a live entry: pool.has(id)
decisions.situation: A Pool is Jet's box for game objects such as monsters. Adding a monster gives you an id, a small ticket for its spot in the box. A monster can remember its target by id. When the target dies and is removed, reading through that old id stops the program, and today there is no way to ask first. We recommend pool.has(id): it answers yes or no, copies nothing, and the read after it still checks, so an old id can never reach the wrong monster.
decisions.gist: Should Pool answer whether an id still names a live entry?
decisions.lesson: An id holds a spot number and a count. Removing an entry bumps the spot's count, so an old id never reaches a new monster that reuses the spot. Reading through an old id stops the program. A yes-or-no check lets a chasing monster forget a dead target instead.
decisions.story: Ana's imp chases a target it holds by id. Between two game ticks the target dies and is removed. On the next tick the imp must hit the target if it still exists, or else forget it. Every option runs the same program and prints 90, then true. No option may hit a new monster that took over the old spot.
decisions.inWild:
Rust's slotmap crate, a widely used generational arena, offers contains_key(id) -> bool beside indexing. Source: https://docs.rs/slotmap/latest/slotmap/struct.SlotMap.html#method.contains_key

In C the same check is written by hand: the spot number is in range and the spot's count matches the id's count.
decisions.detail:
RATIFIED RULES

Docs/spec/spec.md:1569-1576 and Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2848-2856 (D-POOLID-API1) give Pool add, indexing, ids and remove. Ids are copyable and comparable. Indexing a stale id stops the program; remove returns an optional value. add, remove and pool[id] = v need a writable pool: a := binding or a & parameter. D-HAS-VERB1=A makes has the membership word for lists, sets and map keys. 

D-FNVAL-WRITE1=A lets a function type carry & and ^ input marks, which makes option B's write callback legal. D-WRITE-TAKE1=A gives replace(&place, value) and swap on any place, including pool[id].

WHAT THE CODE DOES TODAY

Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildPools.jet:111-129 (ir_pool_find) computes one live bit: the spot number is below the pool length and the spot's count equals the id's count. remove (:133-155) and indexing (:192-217) both use that bit. Indexing stops with 'this ID no longer refers to a live value — its pool slot was removed' (:207). Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/SharedOwner.jet:378-429 checks add, remove and ids; has is unknown, E0102.

Probes, rechecked on 2559996f at O0 and O2: opus_pool_today prints 60, then stops with E3001 after removal. opus_pool_has_today fails with E0102. opus_pool_reuse shows a stale id still stops after a new entry takes the spot, and removing it again returns None. opus_pool_shape runs every line of option A except has and prints 90, then true.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

The earlier draft listed two losses for A and a third caveat. Each now has a concrete answer.

1. Two checks (has, then index). has returns the same live bit that indexing computes, so the extra cost is one length compare and one count compare on a spot just read. It never reads or copies the monster. Code that already knows an id is live indexes directly.

2. The answer could go stale before the read. Only code that holds the pool for writing can remove an entry (spec.md:1574-1576). So between has and the read, only code written on that path can remove it. If it does, the read still checks and stops. It never reaches a newer monster in the same spot.

3. Ids carry no pool identity. In review61_edges an id from one pool read 300 from another. This is true of indexing and remove today and of every option. It is shared, not a cost of A. A pool stamp in ids would fix it for all options and needs its own card.

WHY B CHANGED

The earlier B returned a copy. A copy cannot write the target back, costs a full copy and does not work for entries that cannot be copied. With D-FNVAL-WRITE1=A, the honest alternative is a write callback, which removes A's two-step gap. So B is now that design.

KNOWN DEFECTS, NOT VOTES

review61_id_eq fails with E0312 even for id == id, against the comparable-id rule; option C needs it fixed. review61_edges removes an entry through a read-only Pool parameter, against spec E0202. That defect weakens A's staleness argument until fixed and needs a defect card whatever the vote.

STALE IDS AND REUSE

has(id) is false exactly when remove(id) would return None: spot out of range or count mismatch. Reusing a spot never makes an old id live again. The count is a 64-bit number, so wraparound needs 2^63 removals of one spot.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

Beginners call has right before indexing. Experts who know an id is live index directly and keep the safety check. Proposed examples use the ratified name-first declaration spelling (D-DECL-BINDING1=B); probes use the current spelling.

options.technical: has returns the live bit that indexing already computes: spot in range and matching count. It is false exactly when remove(id) would return None. It neither reads nor copies the entry. Sema gains one Pool method beside add, remove and ids; the lowering reuses ir_pool_find.

options.name: pool.edit(id, action) -> Bool
options.detail: Run an action on the entry if it is live, and return whether it ran. Check and write happen in one step. While the action runs, the pool is busy, so the action cannot touch other monsters in it.
options.technical: action has type fn(&T), allowed by D-FNVAL-WRITE1=A. edit checks once, lends the entry to the action and returns true, or returns false for a stale id. The pool is borrowed for writing during the call, so a lambda that also uses the pool is refused. It adds a second way to write an entry beside indexing.

C needs no new method, but every check builds and scans a list of all monsters each tick.

decisions.title: Preserve write and move parameters in stored function types
decisions.situation: A function value is a function kept in a variable or table, like the action in each Doom monster state. Today a stored function may only read its inputs. A function that changes its input, such as chase spending a monster tic, cannot be stored. So a Doom-style action table cannot hold its actions directly. Programs must return a changed copy of the monster, or store an enum and switch on it. You are deciding whether stored functions may keep write and move inputs, which changes an earlier ruling. We recommend A: a function type uses the same input marks as a declaration.
decisions.gist: May a stored function change or take over its input, as a directly called function can?
decisions.lesson: A function value lets a table pick which code runs. A plain input is read-only: it is lent, not copied. An input marked & is lent so the function can change it in place. An input marked ^ is handed over for good.
decisions.story: Ana has a monster table with two states, Look and Chase, each holding an action. Look heals the monster by 1, and Chase spends one tic. Three steps from state 0 must print 62 7 1. Every option runs this same program. It is a small model of the Doom table, not a line-for-line port.
decisions.inWild: C stores a function pointer taking a monster pointer. Rust stores fn(&mut Mobj), which preserves exclusive write access in the pointer's type. These are comparisons of parameter passing, not claims that Jet has C's pointer layout or Rust's callable representation.
decisions.detail:
RATIFIED RULES

S47 in syntax-decisions.md:467-483, with spec.md:881-887 and 927-930, governs function values; D-MEM-PARAM1 defines parameter marks. The spec records D-CALLVALUE1=B for .call; Tower ratifies D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=C and D-DECL-BINDING1=B. A and D amend S47 on purpose. They do not treat the current rejection as a bug.

WHAT CHANGES IN S47

S47 has three parts. Part 1: fn(T1, T2) -> R, where an unmarked parameter is read-only. Every option keeps it. Part 2: a named function becomes a value only when every parameter is read-only. One with & or ^ stays direct-call-only, and a callback that must change a value returns the new value instead. Part 3: capture rules, closure copying and the invocation lock. Every option keeps it.

A replaces part 2. Function types may mark parameters with & or ^, and a function becomes a value when its marks match the type. Returning a new value becomes one choice, not the rule. D replaces part 2 for & only; a function with a ^ parameter stays direct-call-only. B and C leave S47 unchanged. Under A or D, spec.md:881-887 and 927-930 and the syntax-surface.jet:444-446 comment change too.

CHECKED TODAY

Written against 0ccdff27 and rechecked on 2559996f at O0 and O2. opus_fnval_return and opus_fnval_enum each print 62 7 1. opus_fnval_ref fails with E0003 at fn(&Mobj), and opus_fnval_move fails with E0003 at fn(^Mobj). review61_return_read shows that returning an unmarked m unchanged is E0120; m.copy() works. Parser/Types.jet:424-470 parses parameter types without marks.

DEFECTS FOUND, NOT VOTES

opus_fnval_coerce stores chase, which takes &Mobj, in a fn(Mobj) slot. Sema accepts it, then the backend fails with an internal compiler error at O0 and O2. S47 requires a user diagnostic there. That needs a defect card whatever the vote. Lambdas also cannot spell a marked parameter today: (m: &Mobj) -> is E0003 in opus_lambda_write.

THE PROPOSAL

A accepts fn(&T) and fn(^T), mixed with unmarked parameters. The requirement survives assignment, fields, lists, generics and returned function values. A function needing & never fits fn(T). A move slot consumes its argument as a direct call does; using it afterward is an ownership error. D permits only the & part. Effects, labels, parameter zones and returned-view contracts remain obligations.

LAMBDAS

Under A and D a lambda takes marks like a named function: (m: &Mobj) -> { m.tics -= 1 }. Where the slot fixes the type, m -> { m.tics -= 1 } takes its mark from the slot. The caller still writes .call(&m), so no write happens without the caller mark.

ALIASING

A stored call must enforce the same exclusivity as a direct call. Two write arguments must not overlap, including paths through Pool ids or shared links. Known overlap is rejected; uncertain linked overlap follows the D-MEMREF-EXCL1=A runtime checks. A captured write path that overlaps an explicit argument is a conflict too. A function value cannot erase those checks.

CAPTURES

Passing &m lasts for the call; it does not authorize storing a writer to m in an escaping closure. The S47 capture ownership and lifetime checks still apply. Mutable closure environments keep the S47 invocation lock. That lock protects the environment, not explicit arguments or another closure captures. Move parameters transfer arguments on each call; they do not make every function value a one-shot callable.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

Beginners keep plain parameters until they need to change an input. A stored writer uses the same & at declaration, type and call. Experts can pass ownership with ^ under A. No action-table speedup, unchanged call layout or allocation saving has been measured. The proposal avoids rebuilding Mobj in source, not every cost of function values.

EXAMPLES AND I8

Full options use ratified name-first bindings, which 2559996f does not build yet. B and C were run after translating only declaration heads to the current spelling. A and D reuse parameter marks and the existing .call mechanism; they add no special action-table or mutable-callback type. Changing S47 needs this explicit owner amendment.

options.name: Function types preserve both & and ^ parameters
options.detail: A function type may mark inputs with & (write) or ^ (move), the same marks a declaration uses. A function or lambda fits only when its marks match. Calls write the same mark: .call(&m). Read-only types and calls do not change.
options.technical: Access mode is part of the callable contract at every storage boundary. Reuse direct-call ownership checks and preserve effects, labels, zones and view provenance. Do not assume that the existing call representation already carries addresses correctly: lowering must implement marked arguments without copying the lent T.

options.name: Keep S47: return the updated monster
options.detail: Actions read the original and return an owned replacement. The caller assigns the result. This is useful when actions are deliberately value transformations, not just a workaround.
options.technical: Read access does not copy the input. Each call builds a new Mobj, and the caller assigns it back. Whether the optimizer removes that work is unmeasured. Forgetting to assign the result drops the update.

options.name: Keep S47: store an enum and call actions directly
options.detail: The table stores an Action case. One dispatcher makes direct calls with &. It is a good fit when the application controls a fixed set of actions.
options.technical: No replacement Mobj is required. The enum and dispatcher must be edited when an action is added; a new module cannot register an arbitrary function without changing that set. This can make the action list easy to audit. Dispatch speed is unmeasured and may be optimized differently from an indirect call.

options.name: Add write parameters only: fn(&T)
options.detail: Permit fn(&T), but keep functions with move parameters direct-call-only. This solves the action-table example with a smaller amendment. It does not authorize fn(^T).
options.technical: Write-argument alias and capture checks are exactly those required by A. Keeping ^ out reduces this ballot's ownership-transfer scope, but leaves function values unable to preserve one existing parameter mode. It creates no separate writer-callback mechanism.

comparisons.note: A small state-table model changes the monster through a function pointer; not a quotation from Doom.
The pointer type preserves exclusive write access to the argument.

recommendation.why: A uses one rule: a function type carries the same input marks as a declaration. There is no second kind of callback and no exception to explain. D also fixes this program, but keeps move inputs as a special case that stays direct-call-only.
gains: In-place actions without reconstructing Mobj.
Write and move obligations survive storage.
One set of parameter access rules.

losses.loss: This reverses part of an earlier ratified ruling on function types and adds ownership checks at stored calls.
losses.mitigation: Approve the amendment explicitly; require overlapping-argument, capture, move-after-call and nested-storage proofs before implementation is accepted.

losses.loss: The vote includes move callbacks beyond this monster example.
losses.mitigation: D is an explicit write-only choice if the owner wants the narrower scope.

whyNot.reason: A fair design when actions really are transformations. For an in-place edit, every action must rebuild the whole monster, and forgetting to assign the result loses the change.
A strong choice for a closed game. It does not allow independently supplied action functions without editing the dispatcher.
Solves the demonstrated need with less scope, but keeps one parameter mode unavailable in function values, an exception users must learn.

recommendation.tradeoff: A preserves all access modes; D adds only writing; B and C keep the current callable restriction and change application design.

decisions.title: Check downloaded libraries once, not on every run?
decisions.situation: Your project uses libraries, such as a geometry library called geo. Today Jet reads and checks every library from scratch on every run, even one you downloaded and never touch. You already ruled that your own code always compiles fresh and that Core ships already checked. The question is whether a downloaded library may also be checked once and then reused, the way Core is. We recommend yes for downloaded libraries only; any library in a folder you can edit still compiles fresh every time.
decisions.gist: May Jet check a downloaded library once and reuse that result, like Core?
decisions.lesson: A library you download at a fixed version, like geo#2.1.0, never changes. Jet still checks it from scratch on every run today. Core will ship already checked. A saved check holds a library's checked types and compiled code for one exact compiler and setup. Whatever wins, your own code is checked fresh, and so is library code used with your types.
decisions.story: Ana's game has 3 files and uses geo#2.1.0, a downloaded library with 40 files. She runs jet run ten times an hour. Today Jet checks all 43 files each time, though only her 3 change. Her teammate Ben keeps his own copy of geo in a folder and edits it. The examples show proposed behavior; installing libraries by version is not built yet.
decisions.inWild:
Cargo (Rust) compiles each downloaded crate once and keeps the result in the target folder. Later builds reuse it and recompile only your own crate. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/build-cache.html

Go keeps a build cache keyed by source, compiler and flags. Its documentation warns that changes in outside C libraries are not noticed automatically. Source: https://go.dev/cmd/go/ , 'Build and test caching'.

Nix downloads prebuilt results only from builders whose signing keys you trust, and builds locally otherwise. Source: https://nix.dev/manual/nix/latest/command-ref/conf-file.html#conf-trusted-public-keys
decisions.detail:
WHAT THE OWNER ALREADY RULED

2026-10-30 (#2517): no incremental compilation, period. 2026-11-05 (#5910 log): jet run, dev and test link Core and the runtime as pieces built once with the compiler. Only the user program compiles fresh. Main noted on #5910 that the Core piece must carry checked types, not only machine code.

D-EXEC1=A ratifies shared compiled Prelude/Core. Older law: D-LIB-REUSE1=B (sealed dependency outputs tied to exact inputs), D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1=A (saved checks only when every input is covered), D-INCR-PARK1=C (no reuse of single functions). The latest ruling wins, so A and C each need an explicit exception. B needs none.

WHAT JET DOES TODAY (checked)

A two-package program with a folder dependency printed 42 on two runs. Both traces show geo parsed and checked again (geo parse at trace line 23, its check at line 53). Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/Pipeline.jet:3319-3322 loads source, :3481-3504 registers it, and :3542-3544 and :3642 check the whole graph.

Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/Identity.jet:932 defines jet_driver_package_check_key, which nothing calls yet. jet update exits 2 with E2104, not built yet (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Front.jet:1938, :367). The spec spelling for a versioned dependency is deps: { textkit: textkit#1.2.0 } (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:5603-5606). The admitted runtime lists 340 source files and none under Core/, so the checked Core piece is not built yet either.

The Jetpack store already verifies and restores signed results from trusted builders. It checks revocation and reproducibility. Unsigned, mismatched, corrupt and revoked results are refused. Sources: Jetpack/Store/Source/Hangar/RealizeVerified.jet:642-687 and Jetpack/Store/Source/Cache/CachePublication.jet:279-301. Tests: Jetpack/Store/Tests/EngineCachePublication.jet:102-141. D-BUILD-STORE1=E gives the store its size cap, free-space reserve and leases that protect entries in use.

HOW A REMOVES ITS DOWNSIDES

The earlier draft listed four costs for A. Each is now designed out or made negligible.

1. Trusting an outside builder. A accepts a downloaded saved check only from a builder you already trust for your compiler. By default that is the Jet release builder that made the compiler itself, which could already change your compiler, so the default adds no new party to trust. A team may add its own builder to the store's trust list; that is an explicit choice to trust one more party, and nothing is added without it.

Every read checks the signature, the exact inputs and the revocation list. The existing rebuild-from-source-and-compare contract (D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1) stays available.

2. Disk space. Saved checks live in the existing store, which already has a size cap and evicts the oldest unused entries (D-BUILD-STORE1=E). No new cache folder and no cleanup command.

3. Exception to the no-incremental rule. A reuses only what can never change: an exact downloaded version. Nothing you can edit is ever reused, so the rule's purpose holds: your code always compiles fresh. This mirrors the Core exception the owner already granted.

4. A missing saved check after a compiler upgrade. Jet downloads the matching one if the release builder published it; otherwise it checks the library once, which costs what B pays on every run.

The former option D (build saved checks only on this machine) is folded into A. A's only outside builder is the one that already made the compiler D runs, so D gave no extra safety and made every new machine pay a first build.

WHAT EVERY OPTION KEEPS

One format and one reader serve Core and library saved checks (I8). A saved check holds checked types, checked bodies, diagnostics with source spans, and compiled code. Its key covers compiler build, package, locked source digest, dependency results, features, profile, CPU, OS and target. It also covers settings, embedded and generated files, foreign sources and toolchains. A wrong key is refused before linking.

Generic code is specialized where it is used. Checks that depend on the caller still run per program: authority grants, effects, ownership and unsafe gates. Consumer-dependent compile-time code stays in checked bodies and runs per program. Reading a saved check never runs package code. There is no second checker and no second language meaning.

WHAT THIS VOTE CHANGES

A exempts exact downloaded versions (registry or a git tag pinned in the lock) from the no-incremental rule. Folder dependencies and workspace members compile fresh even when unchanged. C also exempts unchanged folder libraries. B keeps every library fresh. No option allows reuse of single functions or a stable cross-compiler format.

options.name: Check downloaded libraries once
options.detail: A downloaded library at an exact version is checked once and the result is saved. Later runs reuse it. If the Jet release builder already published that result, Jet downloads it instead of checking. Libraries in your own folders compile fresh every run, like your code.
options.technical: Exact downloaded versions get the same treatment as Core. Saved checks go in the existing Jetpack store and use its signature, revocation and size-cap rules. Downloads are accepted only from builders already trusted for the compiler. A compiler upgrade or setting change needs a different saved check, downloaded or built once.
options.code:
# package.jet
deps: { geo: geo#2.1.0 }

$ jet run   # first time: check geo once and save it; check Ana's code
$ jet run   # reuse saved geo; check Ana's code fresh

# Ben's copy in a folder:
deps: { geo: ../geo }
$ jet run   # geo is checked fresh on every run, as today

options.name: Check every library on every run
options.detail: Keep today's behavior. Only Core and the runtime come already checked. Every library, downloaded or not, is read and checked again on each run.
options.technical: Keeps the no-incremental ruling with no exception. The store still holds downloaded source and other outputs. Each run repeats parsing and checking for every library. Core's saved check and faster cold compiles still help, but library cost grows with library size.
options.code:
# package.jet
deps: { geo: geo#2.1.0 }

$ jet run   # check geo's 40 files and Ana's 3
$ jet run   # check all 43 files again

options.name: Also reuse unchanged folder libraries
options.detail: Do everything A does. Also save checks for libraries in folders you can edit, and reuse them while their files are unchanged. An edit rechecks that whole library.
options.technical: This is library-level incremental compilation. It reverses the no-incremental ruling for code people edit. It needs file-change tracking and must confirm every input on each reuse. It stores more versions and uses the same store as A.
options.code:
# Ben's copy in a folder:
deps: { geo: ../geo }

$ jet run   # check geo once and save it
$ jet run   # geo unchanged: reuse it
# Ben edits geo/shape.jet
$ jet run   # recheck all of geo, then save again

comparisons.note: Cargo compiles each downloaded crate once per setup and reuses it. Your own crate is recompiled. It never downloads prebuilt crates. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/build-cache.html
comparisons.code:
$ cargo build   # compiles serde once, then your crate
$ cargo build   # reuses serde; rebuilds only your crate if it changed

comparisons.note: Nix downloads a prebuilt result only when it is signed by a key you trust, and builds it locally otherwise. Source: https://nix.dev/manual/nix/latest/command-ref/conf-file.html#conf-trusted-public-keys

recommendation.why: A downloaded library never changes, so checking it again on every run is wasted work. A saves that work, trusts only the builder that already made your compiler, and still compiles everything you can edit fresh.
gains: Runs stop rechecking libraries that cannot change.
A new machine can download checks instead of building them.
Core and libraries share one saved format and one reader.

losses.loss: After a compiler upgrade, each library is checked once more.
losses.mitigation: The release builder publishes matching checks; otherwise one check costs what option B pays on every single run.

losses.loss: A downloaded check is only as honest as its builder.
losses.mitigation: Only the builder that made your compiler, or one your team added, is accepted. Signatures and revocation are checked on every read.

whyNot.reason: B rechecks libraries that never change on every run, and that cost grows with every library Ana adds.
C reuses code people edit, which is the incremental compilation you ruled out, and needs change tracking to stay correct.

recommendation.tradeoff: A treats downloaded libraries like Core and keeps editable code fresh. B keeps everything fresh at a growing cost. C also reuses editable code.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT Sol. Fresh agent: PacksSol. Checked active and archived decisions, driver and store sources, runtime provenance, and two native dependency runs plus the update refusal. Reframed this as an explicit installed-pack exception, corrected identity and trust claims, and added the existing verified-store alternative.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Today's proof: admitted compiler 66c2a661a6 ran a folder-dependency program twice, printing 42 both times, and both traces show geo parsed and checked. jet update geo returned E2104, exit 2. These do not measure speed or prove registry installs.

Acceptance for A: a saved check is refused when the compiler, target, features, flags or any embedded, generated, foreign or dependency input differs. Forged, unsigned and revoked checks are refused. Two independent builds of the same inputs give identical bytes. A folder dependency is checked fresh on every run. Diagnostics from a saved check match a fresh check. Eviction never removes an entry in use. Results match on every execution level.

decisions.title: Every jet test flag is also a setting: shard, list, levels, results, compiler and the rest
decisions.situation: Some test runs need choices that change each time. A release check splits the golden tests across eight processes. A census first lists the tests, then runs one build level and saves the verdicts to a file. An A/B check runs the same tests under an older compiler. Today these scripts call a separate test-kit program with its own flags. You ruled that every command-line flag must also be a setting. We recommend that each jet test flag is also a test-profile field and an fn test call, with the same name.
decisions.gist: Should every jet test flag also be a profile field and an fn test call, with one name?
decisions.lesson: A choice can be written in three places: a test profile in package.jet, code in test.jet's fn test, or a flag on one command. Each place uses the same name. Later places win: the profile, then fn test, then the flag. Build settings already work this way.
decisions.story: Ana's release script checks a new compiler on the golden tests. It starts eight processes, each told to take one eighth of the tests, then merges the eight verdict files. Her census lists the tests first, then runs only the jet run level. She wants plain jet test commands, and the same choices written in her package when they never change.
decisions.inWild:
cargo nextest: --partition count:2/8 runs one of eight slices, and the same choice can live in a profile in .config/nextest.toml. Source: https://nexte.st/docs/configuration/

pytest: every flag can also be written in the addopts setting of pytest.ini. Source: https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/reference/customize.html
decisions.detail:
WHAT CHANGED FROM THE LAST DRAFT You ruled that any flag must also be a setting. The last draft added flags only, and only with --profile. Now every jet test flag, old and new, is also a test-profile field and a call on t in fn test. The flags work on every jet test, not only with --profile. TODAY Test profiles live in package.jet (D-TEST-PROFILE1=A). A profile already has suites, baseline, jobs, memory, filter, shard, opt_in, optimize and time_limit fields. fn test in test.jet declares code suites with t.suite and has no settings calls (Compiler/test.jet:26-31). Build settings already come in three layers (D-SETTING-ORDER1=A): the profile in package.jet, a call in fn build such as b.optimize(.Full), then the flag. jet test instead refuses --optimize when the profile sets optimize:, with E2104 (TestProfile.jet:96-100). Most jet test flags have no setting at all: --serial, --shuffle, --coverage, --capture, --fresh, --seed, --iterations and the browser flags, among others (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CLICommands.jet:901-953). Scripts that need per-run choices call the separate Tools/testkit program. They are release-compiler.mjs (--shard, --results), goldens-census.mjs (--list, --tier, --shard, --results), compiler-registries.mjs (--opt-in, --results), and suite.sh A/B runs (--jet for another compiler). SHAPE UNDER A 1. One rule. Every jet test flag has a profile field and a t call with the same name, dashes becoming underscores. --shuffle=7 is shuffle: 7 in a profile and t.shuffle(7) in fn test. A bare flag such as --serial is serial: true and t.serial(). 2. One order. The profile applies first, then fn test, then the flag, exactly as build settings do. jet test runs fn test once to collect its settings and suites before any test runs, as jet build runs fn build. The E2104 refusal for --optimize becomes an override. 3. Four new choices, each in all three places. shard runs the I-th of N slices, the same tests for the same slice and tree. list prints the selected test names after filter and shard, runs nothing and exits 0. results writes every selected test's verdict as JSON, with the same writer and row format as JET_CI_EVIDENCE_DIR. compiler builds and runs the tests with another jet, while slicing, baseline and verdicts stay with the running jet, so an A/B run differs only in the compiler. 4. optimize takes a list of levels, so a census needs no --tier word. none is jet run, basic is jet build, and full is the release build. 5. Settings that are not choices. --profile selects a profile, so its setting is the existing defaults: { test: ... }. --help, --show-default and --browser-scaffold are actions, not run choices, so they have no setting. HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY 1. Many new names. Every name is a flag that exists today. One registry row per flag produces the flag, the profile field and the t call, so the three can never drift apart. jet help test shows all three spellings on each line. 2. A setting that should be one-off, such as -u or list, written into a profile by mistake. Such a profile says so in its name, and jet test prints the settings it used and where each came from. 3. Shards overwriting the baseline. A sharded run compares with the baseline but never writes it. -u with shard stays refused with E2104. 4. Two verdict formats. results and JET_CI_EVIDENCE_DIR share one writer and one row format. No loss remains. EDGE CASES - list with -u is refused with E2104, since listing runs nothing to record. - shard 0/8, 9/8 or a malformed value is refused with E2104, naming the valid range. - results to an unwritable path fails before any test runs. - Parallel shards share no scratch files; each run gets its own temporary directory. - A settings call after t.run() is refused with E2104, since the run has already started. AFTER A LANDS The four scripts switch to jet test /Compiler --profile

with these flags, and the Tools/testkit command is deleted. Its engine stays as the library jet test calls. WHY NOT B OR C B keeps the test-kit command as a second front door with its own words, so every new choice lands twice. C adds the flags but no settings, which breaks your rule, so a fixed choice can only be typed again on every command.

options.name: Every flag is also a setting
options.detail:
Every jet test flag, old and new, is also a field of a test profile in package.jet and a call on t in fn test, with the same name. The profile applies first, then fn test, then the flag, as build settings already do.

Four new choices arrive in all three places: shard, list, results and compiler. optimize takes a list of levels. The separate test-kit command is deleted once its scripts move.
options.technical: One registry row per jet test flag generates the flag, the TestProfile field and the Test method. jet test runs fn test in a plan step to collect settings and suites before any row runs. Layering follows D-SETTING-ORDER1=A. --results shares the evidence writer. A sharded run never writes the baseline.

options.name: Keep the test-kit command too
options.detail: Profiles stay as they are. Scripts that need per-run choices keep calling the separate test-kit command, which has its own flag words, over the same engine.
options.technical: Tools/testkit/run.jet stays a permanent command with --shard, --list, --tier, --results, --jet and --scratch. jet test gains no flags or settings.
options.code: $ testkit all --jet ./jet --tier o0 --shard 3/8 --results shard3.json

options.name: Flags only
options.detail: jet test gains --shard, --list, --results and --compiler, and --optimize takes a list. They have no profile field and no fn test call, so a choice that never changes must be typed on every command.
options.technical: The flags parse in the profile plan and override the run for one command. TestProfile and Test gain nothing.
options.code:
$ jet test Compiler --profile golden --shard=3/8 --results=shard3.json
$ jet test Compiler --profile golden --list --optimize=none

comparisons.note: A slice per process on the command line, or the same settings in a named profile. Source: https://nexte.st/docs/configuration/
Any flag can also be written in the config file. Source: https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/reference/customize.html

recommendation.why: It follows your rule: any choice can be written once in the package or in fn test, or typed for one run, always with the same name. Scripts and people use one test command, and the test-kit command goes.
gains: Every jet test flag can also be written in a profile or in fn test.
One name per choice in all three places, generated from one table.
Release and census scripts call plain jet test.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a second test command with its own words, so every new choice lands twice.
C breaks your rule: choices that never change must be typed on every command.

recommendation.tradeoff: A gives every choice three places with one name. B keeps two commands. C has flags only.

$ testkit all --tier o0 --shard 3/8 --results r.json

decisions.title: jet cc ships its own C toolchain with jet, like zig cc: no Nix, no index, no key
decisions.situation: jet cc compiles C code, for example a C library a Jet package wraps. Today it downloads a C compiler from the Nix package collection, found through a package index signed by Jet's own key. That key and index were never published, so on a fresh machine jet cc fails. You said the end shape is not the best of any language, and that Zig just works. Zig ships its C compiler and every C library it needs with zig itself. We recommend the same for Jet.
decisions.gist: Should jet cc ship its own C toolchain with jet, the way zig cc does?
decisions.lesson: To compile C, you need a C compiler, a linker and the C library for the machine you build for. Zig ships all of these with zig, so zig cc works on any machine and can build for any other, with nothing else installed. Jet can do the same: the toolchain comes with jet, checked against a hash built into jet.
decisions.story: Ana installs jet on a new laptop with nothing else on it, and runs jet build on a package that wraps a small C library. It just builds. Then she builds the same package for an ARM board with --target and it builds too, with no Nix, no package index and no second install.
decisions.inWild:
Zig: zig cc is a C compiler shipped inside the zig download, with C library sources for every target, so cross-compiling needs nothing installed. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/overview/#zig-is-also-a-c-compiler

Go: cgo uses the C compiler already installed on the machine, so it fails where none is. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/cgo
decisions.detail:
WHAT CHANGED FROM THE LAST DRAFT

The last draft kept the Nix route and only asked how to trust it before the key exists. You said the end shape itself was not the best, and that Zig just works. The new A drops Nix, the index and the key from jet cc entirely. It ships the toolchain with jet, as Zig does.

TODAY

jet cc looks for a verified C toolchain already in the Hangar, Jet's local store. If none is there, it fetches one through the Nix package index (Jetpack/CLI/Source/CcDriver/DriverInvocation.jet:256-282). The index needs a public key and an address that were never published, so it fails with E1348 (Jetpack/Provider/Source/Core/Realized.jet:188-201).

The owner ordered that every proven compiler be published as a GitHub release with its checksums (card #6564 c4), and that repo tools run with no Nix once jet exists (#6564 c6).

SHAPE UNDER A

1. The toolchain pack. Each jet release publishes one more file beside jet: a C toolchain pack. It holds a static clang and lld, and the source of the musl C library. It also holds the headers and link stubs for each glibc version, as Zig makes them. Today it covers the Linux targets; other systems join when Jet supports them.

2. Trust by hash. The pack's SHA-256 is written into jet itself when the release is built. jet accepts only a pack with that exact hash, so no key, index or signature server is needed. A new pack comes only with a new jet.

3. Just works. The first jet cc, or a jet build that compiles C, downloads the pack from the same release as jet, checks its hash, and keeps it in the Hangar. Later runs use it at once. jet env fetch-toolchain downloads it ahead of time, for a machine that will be offline.

4. Any target. The C library for each target is built from the pack's sources the first time it is needed, and cached, exactly as Zig does. So --target builds for another machine with nothing else installed.

5. Building the pack. The release tool builds it from pinned LLVM and musl sources, so anyone can rebuild it and compare the hash. Nix may help build it on the release machine, but no user ever needs Nix.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Size. A static clang and lld are about 60 MB packed, like Zig's download. The pack is a separate file, fetched only when C is first compiled, so a pure-Jet program never downloads it.

2. Offline first use. jet env fetch-toolchain fetches it ahead of time, and the release also offers one archive with jet and the pack together. A missing pack offline gives one error naming both fixes.

3. Trusting an outside build of clang. The release tool rebuilds the pack from pinned sources and fails if the hash differs. The hash inside jet then guards every download, with no key to lose.

4. Two ways to get C tools. Nix leaves jet cc completely. The Nix index work for jet cc is deleted, and Jetpack's Nix support stays only for system packages a project asks for by name.

No loss remains.

EDGE CASES

- A machine that already has the pack in its Hangar never touches the network.
- A pack with the wrong hash is refused and deleted, with an error naming the expected hash.
- jet cc --target for a system the pack does not cover yet gives a typed error naming the covered targets.

- A C program that needs a library beyond libc, such as zlib, declares it as a package dependency, as today.
- Updating jet updates the pack with it, since the hash lives in jet.

WHY NOT B OR C

B keeps the Nix route but publishes the signed index first. jet cc then depends on Nix's package servers, a signing key and an index host, and still cannot cross-compile out of the box. C uses the C compiler already on the machine, as Go does. That fails on a clean machine, differs from machine to machine, and cannot build for other targets.

options.name: Ship the toolchain with jet, like Zig
options.detail: Each jet release ships a C toolchain pack: clang, lld and C library sources for every supported target. jet checks the pack against a hash built into jet, fetches it the first time C is compiled, and keeps it. jet cc then works on any machine and builds for any supported target, with no Nix, no index and no key.
options.technical: release-compiler.mjs builds the pack reproducibly from pinned LLVM and musl sources and embeds its SHA-256 in jet's IDENTITY. jet cc resolves the pack from the Hangar, else fetches it from the release, verifies the hash, and builds per-target libc lazily into a cache. The Nix index path leaves CcDriver.

options.name: Keep Nix, publish the signed index
options.detail: jet cc keeps fetching clang from Nix's package servers, through an index signed with Jet's key. The key and index must be published first. Building for another target needs a matching toolchain from Nix.
options.technical: Key ceremony, publish.sh with the signer, DNS and TLS for index.jet-lang.dev. Until then a reviewed local list in the repo stands in, as the last draft proposed.
options.code:
$ jet cc -c hello.c
// toolchain: clang from the signed Nix index

options.name: Use the machine's C compiler
options.detail: jet cc runs the cc already installed, as Go's cgo does. A clean machine has none, results differ between machines, and building for another target needs a separate cross compiler.
options.technical: CcDriver resolves cc or clang on PATH and records its version in receipts. No pack, no index.
options.code:
$ jet cc -c hello.c
error: no C compiler found on PATH
  fix: install clang or gcc

comparisons.note: zig cc ships clang and C library sources with zig, so it works and cross-compiles with nothing installed. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/overview/#zig-is-also-a-c-compiler
comparisons.code:
zig cc -o hello hello.c
zig cc -target aarch64-linux-musl -o hello hello.c

comparisons.note: cgo uses the installed C compiler, so it fails where there is none. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/cgo
comparisons.code:
CGO_ENABLED=1 go build ./...
# needs gcc or clang on PATH

recommendation.why: It is the Zig shape you named: jet cc works on a clean machine and builds for any supported target. It needs no Nix, no index and no signing key, because the hash inside jet guards the one download.
gains: jet cc works on a clean machine with nothing else installed.
Building C for another target works out of the box.
No Nix, no package index and no signing key.
Pure-Jet programs never download the C toolchain.

whyNot.reason: B depends on Nix servers, a signing key and an index host, and still cannot cross-compile out of the box.
C fails on a clean machine, differs between machines, and cannot build for other targets.

recommendation.tradeoff: A ships the toolchain with jet. B fetches it from Nix through a signed index. C relies on the machine.

decisions.title: Reset the Core untested-function list to the honest count, by function
decisions.situation: Every public function in the Core library should have a test that runs it and proves it works. A check in hosted CI counts the public Core functions that no test, example or doc example runs yet. It fails when that count rises above a stored ceiling. The ceiling, 37, came from a broken count; the true count is 4639 of 7395. Nothing is removed or judged useless: an untested function is work owed, a missing test. We recommend recording today's untested functions by name, so the list only shrinks as tests are written.
decisions.gist: The untested-function ceiling came from a broken count. Reset it to the true list, or stay red?
decisions.lesson: A public function is tested when some test, example or doc example runs it. Untested does not mean unused or unwanted: it means nothing proves the function works yet. The check stops the number of untested functions from growing. It only works if the stored starting point was counted correctly.
decisions.story: Ana adds a function to the Core text module, with a test. Hosted CI still fails: the check says 4639 Core functions are untested, against a ceiling of 37. Hers is tested. The 4602 extra were always untested; the old count simply missed them.
decisions.inWild: Detekt (Kotlin): detekt --create-baseline records existing findings, so only new findings fail the build, and the baseline shrinks as findings are fixed. Source: https://detekt.dev/docs/introduction/baseline/
decisions.detail:
WHAT CHANGED FROM THE LAST DRAFT

The last draft said uncovered and talked about functions gaining a use. That read as if a function nobody in this repo calls were unwanted. It never meant that, and nothing in any option removes a Core function. The check asks one thing: does a test prove this function works? The ballot now says untested.

TODAY

Tools/agent/core-coverage-census.mjs lists each public Core function, methods included. It marks one tested when a test, example or doc example in the repo calls it (:2-6). It reads calls in source; it does not run anything.

--check fails when the untested count rises above the number in Tools/agent/core-coverage-ratchet.json. --write can lower that number but never raise it (:9-10, :355-359). Hosted CI runs --check (.github/workflows/ci.yml:27-30).

The stored number is 37. It was written in a checkpoint commit on 2026-10-02 (7bc7cc9d19), not by a decision.

Commit 73e720ed17 fixed the census. It used to crash on repeated names, and its module names never matched any call, so it missed most functions. The honest run on 2026-11-05 finds 7395 public functions, 4639 of them untested, over 128 modules. For example, core.files has 92 of 226 untested, core.text 68 of 108 and core.time 129 of 343.

SHAPE UNDER A

The stored file lists each module's untested functions by name and signature, instead of one number. The reset writes today's list once, in a commit that cites this decision.

--check fails when an untested function is not on the list. So a new function must arrive with a test, and a tested function that loses its last test fails too. --write only removes names, as tests are written. The message names the module and function and says to add a test, example or doc example that runs it.

Writing the missing tests becomes tracked work on this ballot's card, module by module. Each test removes its function from the list.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. The stored size jumps from 37 to 4639. Under A no count is stored at all. The file names each untested function, so it guards each one, which no count can.

2. A count would let new untested functions in whenever old ones gain tests. The name list stops that.

3. A reset by hand could become a habit. --write can only remove names. Adding one needs a hand edit citing an owner decision, and the check's message says so.

4. Moving or renaming. A moved untested function keeps its entry, matched by name and signature, so a move needs no test it did not already need.

No loss remains.

EDGE CASES

- Deleting a module removes its list on the next --write. An entry for a function that no longer exists is ignored by --check.
- If a later census fix finds more untested functions, it needs the same owner reset; --write cannot add them.

WHY NOT B OR C

B keeps hosted CI red until 4602 functions gain tests, which takes weeks. A check that is always red hides real regressions, because nobody reads it. C deletes the check and tracks the gap on a card. Then nothing stops new untested Core functions.

options.name: Reset to today's untested list
options.detail: You reset the check once to today's true list of untested functions, by module and name. After that the list can only shrink. A new function needs a test, example or doc example that runs it, and a tested function stays tested. No function is removed.
options.technical: core-coverage-ratchet.json version 2 lists untested functions per module by name and signature. --check fails on any untested function not listed; a moved function keeps its entry. --write removes names and never adds one.

options.name: Stay red until 37
options.detail: The ceiling stays at 37. Hosted CI fails on every push until 4602 more functions have tests.
options.technical: No change. --check fails with 4639 > 37 on every push.
options.code:
$ node Tools/agent/core-coverage-census.mjs --check
Core untested functions: 4639 > ceiling 37

options.name: Drop the check
options.detail: Remove the check from hosted CI and track untested Core functions on a card instead.
options.technical: Delete the CI step and the ceiling file. The census stays as a report.
options.code:
$ node Tools/agent/core-coverage-census.mjs
total: 7395 public functions; 4639 untested

comparisons.note: A baseline records existing findings; only new ones fail, and fixing one shrinks it. Source: https://detekt.dev/docs/introduction/baseline/

recommendation.why: No work can meet a ceiling taken from a broken count. One reset to the true list, by name, keeps the check honest, keeps every function, and makes sure each new one arrives with a test.
gains: Hosted CI goes green and stays meaningful.
Every new Core function arrives with a test.
A tested function can never quietly lose its last test.

whyNot.reason: B keeps CI red for weeks, and an always-red check hides real regressions.
C loses the guard that stops new untested Core functions.

recommendation.tradeoff: A records today's untested functions by name and lets the list only shrink. B waits red. C stops checking.

surface.gist: The untested-function ceiling came from a broken count. Reset it to the true list, or stay red?
surface.lesson: A Core function is tested when some test, example or doc example runs it. Untested does not mean unwanted; it means nothing proves it works yet. The check stops untested functions from growing. The old starting number was miscounted.

Nothing stops new untested Core functions.
