decisions.title: How Jet reads Arrow IPC (Feather) files
decisions.situation: Arrow IPC files, also called Feather files, are how pandas, Polars, DuckDB and Spark hand tables to each other. Jet can read Parquet with its own reader in Core, and it can take an Arrow table that another program already holds in memory. It cannot read an Arrow file from disk. Asking for one fails with a typed error today. We recommend a Jet-owned Arrow IPC reader in Core next to the Parquet reader, checked against pinned test files.
decisions.gist: Should Core read Arrow IPC files with its own reader, through a native library, or not at all?
decisions.lesson: Arrow has two contracts. The C data interface hands a table that is already in memory from one program to another, and Jet already has a checked owner for that. An IPC file is a format on disk: a small schema header, then record batches of raw column buffers, with an optional footer that indexes them. Reading a file means checking that header and every buffer offset before any column is used.
decisions.story: Mia gets a sales.arrow file from a Polars notebook. She wants it as typed Sale rows in Jet, the same way she already loads sales.parquet. Every option runs the same program. It prints the row count, then the total cents, or a typed error that says why the file was not read.
decisions.inWild: Polars, Arrow JS (TypeScript), Arrow Go and Arrow Java each read IPC files in their own language. pyarrow and R arrow use Arrow C++. DuckDB reads them through its arrow extension, which is built on the nanoarrow C library. Format: https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html#serialization-and-interprocess-communication-ipc
decisions.detail:
RATIFIED RULES

D-DATA-READER2=A: Jet reads Parquet with its own reader in Core. Core/Data/Parquet.jet (1,129 lines) is that reader. It reads flat columns, v1 pages, PLAIN, dictionary and RLE encodings, and SNAPPY. Examples/features/tooling/data_loader prints its Parquet line on o0, o1 and o2.

D-COLUMNAR-BOUNDARY1=A: a table that another program already holds in memory arrives through the Arrow C data interface as one checked owner (Core/Data/Arrow.jet, DataArrowBatch<T>). That ruling says, in its own words: do not treat Arrow C as Arrow IPC or Parquet support, and new external format or runtime libraries need their own ballots.

D-DATA-READER1 (the earlier Rust-reader ruling, since replaced for Parquet by D-DATA-READER2) also says it selects the Parquet decoder only, not the separate Arrow IPC file format.

TODAY

Core/Data/Data.jet maps the format names ARROW, ARROW-IPC and FEATHER to DataFormat.Arrow. Loading one returns DataErrorKind.Bridge: "Arrow IPC has a separate provider boundary; Parquet is the registered reader" (Data.jet:3039-3041). No code in Core, Compiler or Jetpack decodes an IPC file. Card #6419 c7 asks for an Arrow IPC file loaded into a typed frame on o0, o1 and o2, faster than pyarrow and Polars. That criterion cannot start until this is settled.

THE FORMAT

An IPC stream is a sequence of messages. Each message has a FlatBuffers header (Schema, DictionaryBatch or RecordBatch) and a body of column buffers padded to 8 bytes. The file format, which Feather v2 is, wraps a stream between ARROW1 magic bytes and adds a footer that indexes every batch. Buffers may be compressed per batch with LZ4 frame or Zstandard. Core already has a Jet Zstandard decoder (Core/Archive/Zstd.jet, 1,012 lines). D-DATA-READER2=A already commits Core to a Jet LZ4 decoder.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Another reader in Core. The new code is a bounded FlatBuffers header reader and message framing. Column batches, validity bitmaps, limits, error kinds and the Zstandard decoder are the Parquet path's, reused. Arrow's format is frozen at metadata version 5 under its 1.0 stability promise, so the reader does not chase a moving target.

2. Fewer column types. The first version reads every column type the Arrow C owner in Core/Data/Arrow.jet accepts, the types a typed frame can hold. Any other type returns Unsupported naming it, under every option.

3. Speed against pyarrow and Polars. An uncompressed file is mapped once and its column buffers are shared, not copied, so the read is the metadata checks pyarrow also does. Compressed buffers decode in parallel, one per buffer. The c7 cell gets an asm-parity ceiling like every gate cell.

No loss remains.

WHAT EACH OPTION OWES

Every option keeps the same Jet code: data.file<[T]>(path, "arrow", limits) and the same typed DataError kinds. Every option checks schema-to-type matching the way the Parquet path does: a nullable column never becomes a required field without an explicit conversion. Limits on bytes, rows, nesting and allocation follow the existing DataLimits. The arrow-testing integration files are pinned as fixtures. pyarrow is a development-only oracle and never a runtime dependency. A timed read against pyarrow and Polars is published, and any loss becomes a card.

Review. Author: BallotLead. Adversarial pass and loss redesign by Main. The code samples now use the real loader API from Examples/features/tooling/data_loader.jet. They print the typed error instead of returning silently. The speed risk for c7 is now a stated loss.

options.name: A Jet-owned IPC reader in Core
options.detail: Core reads Arrow IPC stream and file formats in Jet code, beside the Parquet reader. It checks the FlatBuffers headers and every buffer offset and length against the file before it makes a column. It decodes LZ4 frame and Zstandard bodies with Jet decoders. The checked buffers become the same column batches the Parquet path and the Arrow C owner use.
options.technical: A bounded FlatBuffers table reader for Schema.fbs, Message.fbs and File.fbs (verifier rules: offsets in range, vtables in range, depth limit). Message framing with the 0xFFFFFFFF continuation marker and the legacy 4-byte form. Primitive, boolean, string, binary, list, struct, dictionary and null columns, with validity bitmaps. Endianness other than little is refused with Unsupported. Buffers alias the loaded file bytes where alignment allows, else copy, and the shared or copied result is reported as D-COLUMNAR-BOUNDARY1 requires. Same o0/o1/o2 and web byte-source meaning as the Parquet path.

options.name: A native reader behind the C data interface
options.detail: A pinned native library reads the file, for example nanoarrow's IPC reader or Arrow C++. It hands Jet each batch through the Arrow C data interface, and Jet takes it with the existing checked owner. Jet does not decode the file itself.
options.technical: Vendored under the dependency rule with its license, provenance and per-target build: Linux, macOS, Windows and WebAssembly each need one. The foreign reader validates the file. Jet checks only the schema it receives and the C release contract. Typed errors come from mapping the library's error codes. The runtime gains a native dependency that Core does not have today.

options.name: No Arrow IPC files: Parquet only
options.detail: Jet reads Parquet files and takes in-memory Arrow tables, but it does not read Arrow IPC files. Asking for one keeps returning a typed error that says to save the table as Parquet. The IPC half of card #6419 c7 is withdrawn.
options.technical: No new code. The Bridge error becomes an Unsupported error whose fix text names Parquet. Every caller that has an IPC file converts it outside Jet first, which costs a full rewrite of the file.

comparisons.note: pyarrow reads IPC files through Arrow C++. Source: https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/ipc.html
comparisons.code:
import pyarrow as pa
with pa.memory_map("sales.arrow") as source:
    table = pa.ipc.open_file(source).read_all()
print(table.num_rows, pa.compute.sum(table["cents"]))

comparisons.note: Polars reads IPC files with its own Rust reader. Source: https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/api/polars.read_ipc.html

recommendation.why: A matches how the owner ruled for Parquet. IPC is a much smaller format than Parquet: a header and raw column buffers, with no page encodings. Core already owns the one codec it needs, and the other is already promised. A keeps Core free of native libraries and works the same on every tier and on the web.
gains: Arrow files load with the same call and errors as Parquet.
No native library to build for each target, including WebAssembly.
Every buffer offset is checked by Jet code before use.
Uncompressed columns are shared with the file, not copied.

whyNot.reason: B adds Core's first native data library, with a build for every target, and the file's checks run in foreign code.
C leaves out the format that pandas, Polars and DuckDB use to hand tables to each other, and makes users rewrite files as Parquet.

recommendation.tradeoff: A writes a small reader on a frozen format and keeps Core native-free. B builds a native library per target. C drops the format.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude. Adversarial model family: claude. Fresh agent: Main. The pass replaced invented loader calls with the real data_loader API, made each sample print its typed error, and added the c7 speed risk as a stated loss.

decisions.title: Path dependencies run outside the project environment
decisions.gist: Should a path dependency need the project's declared environment before `jet run --no-prepare`, `jet dev` or `jet test` can use it?
decisions.lesson: A project can declare an environment in env.jet. Outside it, `jet run --no-prepare`, `jet dev` and `jet test` stop with E1355 when the code imports a package that needs it. A registry package comes from the hangar, so it needs the environment. A path dependency is source in the tree. Jet exempts it today, but no spec line says so.
decisions.story: Ana splits her app into `app` and a local `helper` package and runs `jet test` from a plain shell. With A it runs. With B it stops with E1355 until she enters env.dev, which provides nothing her tests use.
decisions.inWild:
[dependencies]
helper = { path = "helper" }   # read from disk
serde = "1"                    # needs the registry or its cache
// Cargo builds path dependencies from the tree. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html#specifying-path-dependencies.
decisions.detail:
HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

Reading path manifests. The check runs on the package graph the loader already builds for the run, so it opens no extra file. It stops at the first non-path import. No loss remains.

options.name: Exempt path dependencies
options.detail: Imports that resolve to a registry or other non-path dependency need the declared environment, and so do such imports inside a path dependency. The path dependency's own source does not. Spec line, added to Docs/spec/spec.md after line 2462: "Outside a declared environment, `jet run --no-prepare`, `jet dev` and `jet test` refuse with E1355 for a non-path package import. That includes one reached through a path dependency. A path dependency itself, and a toolchain-only program, need no environment (D-ENV-PATHDEP1=A)."
options.technical: Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/EnvBoundary.jet skips a `path:` dependency today, but does not look inside it. A path package that imports a registry package therefore runs past E1355 and fails later. Under A the walk follows each path dependency's own package.jet dependencies and refuses on the first non-path one. Cases cover a path import that runs, a path import whose package imports a registry package (E1355), a registry import (E1355), and a toolchain-only program (runs).

options.name: Require the environment for every package import
options.detail: Any package import needs the declared environment. Spec line, added after line 2462: "Outside a declared environment, `jet run --no-prepare`, `jet dev` and `jet test` refuse with E1355 when the target imports any package (D-ENV-PATHDEP1=B)."
options.technical: EnvBoundary.jet drops the path-dependency skip; a cases row for a path import outside the environment expects E1355.
options.code: use helper      // error[E1355]: This project declares env.dev; ...

comparisons.note: Path dependencies build from disk; registry crates need the registry or its cache. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html#specifying-path-dependencies
A flake's devShell supplies tools; local sources in the tree build without entering it. https://nix.dev/manual/nix/stable/command-ref/new-cli/nix3-develop
comparisons.code: nix develop   # enter the dev shell for its tools

recommendation.why: The environment exists to supply realized packages and tools. A path dependency needs neither: it is source the compiler reads from the tree.

whyNot.reason: B makes every local multi-package project enter the environment even when it uses nothing from it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Path packages run anywhere; only packages that come from the hangar need the environment.

surface.gist: Should a path dependency need the project's declared environment before `jet run --no-prepare`, `jet dev` or `jet test` can use it?
surface.lesson: A project can declare an environment in env.jet. Outside it, `jet run --no-prepare`, `jet dev` and `jet test` stop with E1355 when the code imports a package that needs it. A registry package comes from the hangar, so it needs the environment. A path dependency is source in the tree. Jet exempts it today, but no spec line says so.

current.note: 3d2ad15865 and the Rust driver: only non-path package imports need the environment.

wild.note: Cargo builds a path dependency from the tree. Registry crates need the registry or a filled cache. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html.
wild.code:

helper = { path = "helper" }   # read from disk

options.name: Exempt path dependencies
options.gist: Only registry and other non-path package imports need the declared environment.
gains: Local packages run with `jet test` outside the environment.
A registry import inside a path package still stops at E1355.

options.name: Require the environment for every package import

gains: One simple rule: a project with an environment runs its packages inside it.
losses: Local multi-package projects must enter the environment even when nothing in it is used.
Changes today's behavior for path packages.

recommendation.why: The environment exists to supply realized packages and tools. A path dependency needs neither: it is source the compiler reads from the tree.

decisions.title: How a test asks to be rerun with its tasks taking turns differently each time
decisions.situation: Some bugs only happen when two tasks take turns in one unlucky order. For example, both tasks read a counter before either writes it back, so one increase is lost. Today jet test runs such a test once, so it passes almost every time and the bug ships. This vote picks how a test asks to be rerun many times, with the tasks taking turns differently each time. We recommend writing reruns: 100 on the test line.
decisions.gist: How should a test ask to be rerun many times, with its tasks taking turns differently each time?
decisions.lesson: When two tasks run at once, their steps can interleave in many orders. A bug may appear in only one order. Rerunning the test many times, in a different order each time, finds it. Every rerun must pass, and Jet never retries a failure. Each order has a number, so a failing order can be replayed exactly.
decisions.story: Priya writes a counter that two tasks increase. Her test passes every time on her laptop. In production one increase is lost once a week, and nobody can make it happen again. She wants jet test to find the bad order for her and print a command that replays it.
decisions.inWild:
Shuttle (Rust) reruns a test body 100 times in random task orders, in its README example: shuttle::check_random(|| { ... }, 100). Source: https://github.com/awslabs/shuttle

Loom (Rust) reruns a test in every possible task order: loom::model(|| { ... }). Source: https://github.com/tokio-rs/loom
decisions.detail:
WHAT CHANGED FROM THE LAST DRAFT

The word is now reruns, as you suggested, and the ballot is rewritten in plain words. Schedules named the machinery, not what you see. Following your rule that every flag is also a setting, the count can also be set in a test profile and in fn test.

TODAY

A test that starts two tasks runs once, in whatever order the machine picks. Jet already records task order so a run can be replayed (D-REPLAY-ORDER1=A). That recorder must move into the Jet runtime under every option.

Card #6012 asks for: a rerun count, a report per order, two planted bugs found within the guide's count, and replay of a failing order three times in a row.

PRECEDENTS

- expected_fail: true is already an argument on the #Test line (D-TEST-XFAIL1=A).
- Counts and seeds are plain whole numbers (D-TEST-COUNT1=A).
- jet test already takes --seed=<n> (Docs/spec/reference/cli.md:215).

WHY THE WORD RERUNS

Some tools use rerun to mean trying a failed test again until it passes, such as pytest-rerunfailures. That hides bugs. Jet has no such retry: here every rerun must pass, and the report says so. B and C use the same word, so the vote is only about where it is written.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Time. Reruns are independent, so they run side by side on the profile's workers. Sleeps and timers use simulated time during reruns. A small test stops after its few possible orders. A passing test whose inputs did not change is reused from the test cache (D-TEST-READS1=A).

2. Missing a bad order by chance. A small test is rerun in every possible order, so its bug cannot slip through. A large test samples orders, and a deep run raises the count.

3. A hidden default. The count is always written, as D-TEST-COUNT1 asks of counts. The guide's first example writes reruns: 100, the same number as Shuttle's README.

EDGE CASES

- A test that never starts a second task runs once and says so: 1 run (no tasks take turns).
- expected_fail: true with reruns: expects some rerun to fail. If all pass, that is an unexpected pass.
- A property test, which already runs many generated inputs, cannot also take reruns:. The error's fix moves the task part into a plain #Test, so the two counts never multiply silently.

- A blocking file read or a child process counts as one step that no other task can interrupt.
- The profile's time_limit applies to each rerun.
- --reruns=<n>, reruns: and t.reruns(n) change the count only for tests that already ask for reruns. They never turn reruns on for other tests.

WHY 100 IN THE GUIDE

For the two-task lost update, about half of all orders fail, so 100 random reruns miss it with odds near 2^-100. A two-lock deadlock fails in about one order in four, so 100 reruns miss it with odds below 10^-12. Both planted bugs also have few enough orders to be checked completely. These are estimates, not measurements.

WHY NOT B OR C

B reruns only when someone passes a flag, so a plain jet test on your machine still hides the bug, and the code never says which tests need it. C reruns only a block inside the test. Values made before the block carry over from one rerun to the next and cause failures that are not real bugs.

options.name: reruns: on the test line
options.detail:
Write reruns: 100 on the #Test line, beside expected_fail:. The value is a whole number of at least 1. Without it, a test runs once, as today. A value below 1 is a compile error with a registered code and a UI snapshot.

What happens. jet test runs the test 100 times, and each time the tasks take turns in a different order. The order is chosen wherever a task can pause. Those points are starting or joining a task, a lock, a channel send or receive, a shared read or write, and yielding.

Small tests. If a test has fewer possible orders than its count, Jet runs each possible order once and stops. The report then says all 6 orders, so a small test is checked completely, not by chance.

Report. A pass prints one line, such as pass counter keeps every increment (100 reruns). A failure prints which rerun failed, its order number, each step in order with its source line, and the command that replays it. A deadlock, where every task waits on another, names who holds what and who waits.

Replay. jet test FILE "name" --seed=<n> replays exactly that order. --seed is a flag jet test already has.

Deep runs. The count is also a setting, as every flag must be. reruns: in a test profile and t.reruns(n) in fn test set it for a whole run. --reruns=<n> sets it for one command. They apply in that order, as build settings do.

Beginner path: add reruns: 100, run jet test, and copy the printed replay command. Expert path: pick a count per test, raise every count in a deep profile, and replay one order under jet debug.
options.technical: The typed #Test argument path parses reruns:, and sema checks the count. The generated test entry loops reruns and hands them to the profile's workers. The runtime gains a seeded one-worker scheduler whose choice points are the replay recorder's switch points. A depth-first walk over the same choices covers small tests completely. TestProfile and the Test value of fn test gain reruns, layered profile, then fn test, then the flag.

options.name: A flag only
options.detail: jet test --reruns=<n> reruns every test that starts a second task, n times each. The code does not change. A plain jet test runs each test once, so reruns happen only where someone passes the flag, usually on the build server. The code never shows which tests need reruns, and every such test pays the same count. Replay uses --seed=<n>, as in A.
options.technical: The flag and its matching profile and fn test settings set the count for the harness. Whether a test starts a second task is found while it runs. The scheduler is the same as A's.

options.name: A block inside the test
options.detail: reruns(100) { ... } inside a test reruns only that block. Code before the block runs once, so every rerun shares its values. A change made in one rerun carries into the next and causes failures that are not real bugs. jet test learns about the reruns only while the test runs, so it cannot list them first. It also adds a second place for test options beside the #Test line.
options.technical: Needs a rerun boundary inside the harness and a new Core testing call. The scheduler is the same as A's.

comparisons.note: Reruns the body in random task orders; its README example uses 100. A failure replays exactly. Source: https://github.com/awslabs/shuttle
Reruns the body in every possible task order. Source: https://github.com/tokio-rs/loom

recommendation.why: The test itself says it needs reruns, every plain jet test does them, and a failure prints the command that replays it. It is written like expected_fail:, which people already know.
gains: These bugs are found on every plain jet test, not only in special runs.
Small tests are checked in every possible order.
A failure prints the order number and the exact replay command.

losses.loss: A test with reruns takes longer than one run.
losses.mitigation: Reruns run side by side on simulated time, small tests stop early, and unchanged passing tests are reused.

whyNot.reason: A flag nobody passes on their own machine leaves the bug hidden, and the code never says which tests need it.
Values made before the block carry between reruns and cause false failures, and it adds a second place for test options.

recommendation.tradeoff: A spends a little test time, spread across cores, to find these bugs on every plain run.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude (TestProfiles, rewritten by Main). Adversarial model family: claude. Fresh agent: Main. The pass kept the count a plain Int, added complete checking of small tests, and made the flag also a setting.

surface.gist: How should a test ask to be rerun many times, with its tasks taking turns differently each time?
surface.lesson: Two tasks running at once can interleave their steps in many orders. A bug may appear in only one. Rerunning the test in a different order each time finds it. Every rerun must pass; Jet never retries a failure. A printed number replays the failing order.

current.note: Today a test with two tasks runs once. It passes almost every time, so the lost increase hides.

wild.note: Shuttle reruns the body in random task orders, 100 times in its README (github.com/awslabs/shuttle).

options.name: reruns: on the test line
options.gist: Write reruns: 100 on the #Test line; --seed replays a failing order.
gains: The test itself says it needs reruns.
A plain jet test always does them.
Small tests are checked in every order.
losses: A test with reruns takes longer than one run.

options.name: A flag only
options.gist: jet test --reruns=100 reruns every test that starts tasks.
gains: No change to test code.
losses: A plain jet test never reruns, so the bug hides.
The code never says which tests need it.

proposed.code:
#Test("counter keeps every increment") { ... }
// jet test --reruns=100

options.name: A block inside the test
options.gist: Wrap the task part in reruns(100) { ... } inside the test.
gains: Code before the block runs only once.
losses: Values carry between reruns and cause false failures.
A second place for test options.

recommendation.why: The test says it needs reruns, every plain run does them, and a failure prints its replay command.
gains: Bugs found on every plain jet test.
A failure prints the exact replay command.

losses.loss: Reruns take longer than one run.
losses.mitigation: They run side by side, and small tests stop early.

whyNot.reason: Nobody passes the flag locally, so the bug hides.
Values carry between reruns and cause false failures.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little test time, spread across cores, finds these bugs on every run.

decisions.title: Memory marks live in signatures only; calls carry no & or ^
decisions.situation: Today a Jet call repeats what the called function's signature already says. An argument the function edits carries &, so you write grow(&c). A method that edits its receiver was ratified to need no mark, but the compiler still demands &values.push(3). A take carries ^ in four special cases and not at a last use. You said marks at every call are ugly, tedious and distracting, and that the split rule is hard to teach. We recommend one rule: the signature says what happens, and calls carry no marks.
decisions.gist: Should & and ^ appear only in function signatures, so every call is written plainly?
decisions.lesson: A function's signature already says whether it edits or takes each input. Writing the same mark again at every call repeats that fact about 105,000 times in Jet's code. Under this rule the signature carries the mark, calls look like reads, and the editor shows the marks as faint hints.
decisions.story: Mia writes scores.push(10) and bump(score), with no marks, exactly as she would in Python. Her editor shows a faint & before score. When she declares score :: 0 by mistake, the error says bump edits its input and score is fixed, and offers score := 0.
decisions.inWild:
Mojo: a parameter says mut or owned in the signature, and the call is plain. Source: https://docs.modular.com/mojo/manual/values/ownership

Kotlin, Java, Python and C++ references: calls carry no edit marks. Rust and Swift mark changed arguments but not receivers. Source: Docs/research/2026-10-29-write-sigil-at-call-sites.md
decisions.detail:
WHAT YOU ASKED

On 2026-11-06 you said marks belong in declarations, that marks at every call are ugly, tedious and distracting, and that a split rule is hard to teach. The full proposal, with counts and examples, is Docs/proposals/2026-11-06-memory-marks-in-signatures.md.

TODAY

D-CALLSITE-MARK1=A keeps & on edited arguments and drops ^ at a last use, except for four kinds of take. D-RECEIVER-MARK1=A drops & on receivers, but that is not built: the compiler still reports E0224. D-COPY-MOVE-SPELL1=A spells an early move x.move(), also not built.

Counts on dev b486d6c09a: 69,758 & marks on arguments, about 29,800 on receivers, 4,222 ^ on arguments, about 1,230 ^ in value positions. Signatures hold 14,246 & and 3,147 ^ marks.

THE RULE UNDER A

A signature says what a function does to each input: fn bump(c: &Counter), fn seal(^self). Every call is plain: bump(score), items.push(3), buf.seal(). A mark stays only where no signature decides. Those places are a write window bound to a name (edit :: &values[2..3]), a match that writes into its subject (if &shape == { … }), and a task that takes a name.

An early move is x.move(), as already ratified, and the ^x value form retires. A part of a list passed to a writing parameter becomes a write window by itself.

WHAT STAYS CHECKED

Safety never depended on the call mark. A call that edits a value needs a changeable value, declared := or received as a & parameter. Two overlapping inputs, one edited, stay an error. A value used after a call took it is an error that names the call, with the fix x.copy() or a reorder. A call never copies on its own.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Seeing changes in plain text. The editor shows & and ^ as faint hints at each call, and the language server underlines a changed argument. In the terminal, jet audit writes lists every call that edits or takes a named value, as jet audit copies lists copies.

2. Teams that want marks in text. #Policy(writes: .Explicit), already ratified for receivers, extends to arguments. It requires the marks everywhere, with a Safe fix that inserts them. No new mechanism is added.

3. A value with cleanup closing at a plain call. The take is in the signature and shown as a hint, and any later use is an error naming the closing call.

4. Errors losing the mark they pointed at. Each memory error quotes the signature line that causes it.

5. The cutover. The compiler knows every mark, so jet fix removes about 105,000 in one commit, with grammars, spec, examples and snapshots.

No loss remains.

EDGE CASES

- values.push(values.len()) stays legal: the length is read before the push writes.
- A function value keeps its marks in its type, fn(&Map), and is called plainly.
- A foreign function keeps its marks in its signature.

WHY NOT B OR C

B keeps today's split, which you called messy: arguments marked, receivers not, and four take cases marked. C marks every call again, which is the 105,000 repeated marks you called tedious.

options.name: Signatures only
options.detail: Marks appear in signatures and on the few places no signature decides: a named write window, a writing match, a task that takes a name. Every call is plain. The editor shows marks as hints, and #Policy(writes: .Explicit) restores them for teams that want them.
options.technical: Sema already resolves each argument's convention from the callee. E0202 (missing write mark) and E0224 (missing receiver mark) retire; the changeability checks they guarded quote the parameter instead. jet fix strips call marks from the parse tree. jet audit gains writes.

options.name: Keep today's split
options.detail: Edited arguments keep &, receivers are plain, a last-use take is plain, and four kinds of take keep ^. This is D-CALLSITE-MARK1 with D-RECEIVER-MARK1, once built.
options.technical: Build D-RECEIVER-MARK1's receiver change; argument checks stay as they are.

options.name: Mark every call
options.detail: Every argument and receiver that a call edits or takes carries & or ^, as D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D first ratified. Nothing is inferred at calls.
options.technical: Revert D-RECEIVER-MARK1 and D-CALLSITE-MARK1's last-use rule; keep E0224 and E0202.

comparisons.note: Signatures say mut or owned; calls are plain. Source: https://docs.modular.com/mojo/manual/values/ownership
Changed arguments carry &mut, receivers do not. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-02-references-and-borrowing.html

recommendation.why: It is one rule, the one you asked for: the signature says what happens, and calls read plainly. Safety is unchanged because every check reads the signature, not the call mark.
gains: One rule for arguments and receivers.
About 105,000 repeated marks leave the code.
Calls read like Python or Kotlin.

losses.loss: Plain text does not show which call changes a value.
losses.mitigation: Editor hints, an underline, and jet audit writes show every change; a package may require marks by policy.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the split you called messy and hard to teach.
C repeats the signature at about 105,000 calls, the tedium you named.

recommendation.tradeoff: A trades marks in plain text for one rule and plain calls, with hints and a policy for readers who want the marks.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude (Main). Adversarial model family: claude. Fresh agent: Main. The pass added the resource-close and error-quoting fixes and kept named write windows marked. It found no case where removing a call mark weakens a check.

surface.gist: Should & and ^ appear only in function signatures, so every call is written plainly?
surface.lesson: A function's signature already says whether it edits or takes each input. Repeating that mark at every call adds about 105,000 marks to Jet's code. Under A, only signatures carry marks. Calls look like reads, and the editor shows the marks as hints.

current.note: Today edited arguments and receivers carry marks at every call.

wild.note: Mojo puts mut in the signature; the call is plain.
wild.code:
fn grow(mut list: List[Int]): ...
grow(xs)
xs.append(4)

options.name: Signatures only
options.gist: Marks live in signatures; calls are plain; the editor shows hints.
gains: One rule for arguments and receivers.
Calls read like Python.
losses: Plain text hides which call changes a value.

options.name: Keep today's split
options.gist: Arguments keep &, receivers are plain, some takes keep ^.
gains: Edited arguments stay visible in text.
losses: Two rules for the same act.
Four special take cases to learn.

proposed.code:
grow(&xs, more)
xs.push(4)

options.name: Mark every call
options.gist: Every edited or taken argument and receiver carries a mark.
gains: Every change is visible in plain text.
losses: About 105,000 repeated marks.
push and pop need marks.

proposed.code:
grow(&xs, ^more)
&xs.push(4)

recommendation.why: One rule: the signature says what happens and calls read plainly. Every safety check reads the signature, so nothing becomes unsafe.
gains: One rule to teach.
About 105,000 marks leave the code.

losses.loss: Plain text hides which call changes a value.
losses.mitigation: Editor hints, jet audit writes, and an opt-in policy show the marks.

whyNot.reason: Keeps the split rule you called messy.
Repeats every signature mark at every call.

recommendation.tradeoff: Marks in plain text, for one rule and plain calls.

decisions.title: && marks an input a function takes, and ^ becomes free
decisions.situation: A signature marks an input the function edits with & and one it takes for good with ^. You asked us to study && for taking instead, which would free ^. If marks move to signatures only, the take mark appears about 3,150 times in signatures and in tasks that take a name. Value positions already use x.move(). We recommend &&, because it pairs with &, matches C++'s move parameter, and avoids a dead key.
decisions.gist: Should a signature mark an input it takes with && instead of ^, freeing ^?
decisions.lesson: A function can borrow an input to change it, or take it for good. Jet marks the first with &. Marking the second with && makes the pair one family: & changes it, && keeps it. C++ already writes its move parameter as T&&.
decisions.story: Ravi reads fn close(file: &&GzFile) and guesses right away that close keeps the file, because && looks like a stronger &. On his German keyboard he no longer types ^ followed by a space.
decisions.inWild:
C++: a move parameter is written T&&, an rvalue reference that std::move hands over. Source: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/reference

Swift writes consuming, Mojo owned and Hylo sink for the same idea. Source: https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0377-parameter-ownership-modifiers.md
decisions.detail:
WHAT YOU ASKED

On 2026-11-06 you asked us to investigate & for editing and && for moving as prefix marks, judged on frequency, readability and intuitiveness. The full study is section 5 of Docs/proposals/2026-11-06-memory-marks-in-signatures.md.

FREQUENCY

On dev b486d6c09a, signatures hold 14,246 & marks and 3,147 ^ marks, so takes are 18% of signature marks. The rarer mark gets the longer symbol, which matches how often each is typed and read.

CLASHES

&& is also logical and, used 23,545 times. Under D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A the take mark appears only in a parameter type, before self, and after the word task. Logical and always sits between two values. No && appears in any type today, so the parser and the reader never meet both meanings in one place.

If calls keep marks (D-CALLSITE-MARK2 B or C), f(&&x) becomes possible beside a && b. In that case && is a weaker choice, and B or C on this ballot fits better.

READABILITY AND INTUITION

& reads as this function changes it, and && as more than that: it keeps it. C++ programmers already link && with moving. In Rust &&T is a reference to a reference, but Jet has no reference types, so that reading has nothing to attach to. Hover text says takes the value.

TYPING

^ is a dead key on German, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Swiss and Nordic keyboards: it waits for the next key, so ^self needs an extra space. && is one key pressed twice on every common layout.

FREEING ^

With && for takes and x.move() in value positions, ^ has no meaning left. Under D-SIGIL-FREED2 a freed symbol stays an error until a new ballot gives it a job.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Two meanings of &&. Kept apart by position, and the editor colours them differently. A take mark can never start an expression, so a b &&c typo still means and.

2. Two keystrokes. Takes are 18% of marks, and ^ already costs two keystrokes on most non-US keyboards.

3. Rust's double reference. Jet has no storable reference type, so there is nothing to confuse it with.

No loss remains.

EDGE CASES

- task &&job { … } takes job into the task.
- fn(&&Map) is a function type that takes its input.
- A foreign function writes file: &&GzFile, as it writes file: ^GzFile today.
- An early move inside an expression stays x.move().

options.name: && for take
options.detail: A taken input is written &&: fn seal(&&self), file: &&GzFile, task &&job { … }. Value positions use x.move(). ^ has no meaning left and stays free.
options.technical: The lexer already has the && token; the parameter, self and task-capture parsers accept it where they accept ^ today. The syntax registry renames SIGIL_MOVE to &&. jet fix rewrites ^ marks.

options.name: The word move
options.detail: A taken input is written with a word: fn seal(move self), file: move GzFile, task move job { … }. Clearest for a beginner, five letters per use, and one more keyword.
options.technical: A contextual keyword in parameter, self and task-capture position. ^ is freed.
options.code:
fn seal(move self) { … }
fn gzclose(file: move GzFile) -> Int = "gzclose"

options.name: Keep ^
options.detail: Nothing changes: fn seal(^self), file: ^GzFile. ^ stays taken, and stays a dead key on many keyboards.
options.technical: No change.
options.code:
fn seal(^self) { … }
fn gzclose(file: ^GzFile) -> Int = "gzclose"

comparisons.note: A move parameter is T&&. Source: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/reference
A taken parameter is marked consuming. Source: SE-0377

recommendation.why: & and && read as one family, change and keep. C++ already writes moves as &&, the symbol never meets logical and once calls are plain, and ^ is freed.
gains: One family of marks: & changes, && keeps.
Frees ^ for a later use.
No dead key on European keyboards.

losses.loss: && also means logical and.
losses.mitigation: The take mark only appears in signatures and after task, never between two values.

whyNot.reason: A word is clearest but adds a keyword and five letters to every take.
C keeps ^ taken and keeps the dead key on many keyboards.

recommendation.tradeoff: A reuses a symbol that means and elsewhere, kept apart by position, for a short paired mark and a free ^.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude (Main). Adversarial model family: claude. Fresh agent: Main. The pass found that && is weak if calls keep marks, so the ballot states that dependency. It confirmed no && appears in any type today.

surface.gist: Should a signature mark an input it takes with && instead of ^, freeing ^?
surface.lesson: A function can borrow an input to change it, or take it for good. Jet marks the first with &. Under A the second is &&, so the pair reads as one family. C++ already writes its move parameter as T&&.

current.note: Today a taken input is marked ^.
current.code:
fn seal(^self) { … }
fn gzclose(file: ^GzFile) -> Int = "gzclose"

wild.note: C++ writes its move parameter with &&.
wild.code:
void close(File&& file);
close(std::move(f));

options.name: && for take
options.gist: & changes an input, && keeps it; ^ becomes free.
gains: One family of marks.
Frees ^.
No dead key on European keyboards.
losses: && also means logical and elsewhere.

options.name: The word move
options.gist: Write move before a taken input.
gains: Clearest for a beginner.
losses: A new keyword.
Five letters on every take.

proposed.code:
fn seal(move self) { … }
fn gzclose(file: move GzFile) -> Int = "gzclose"

options.name: Keep ^
options.gist: Nothing changes.
gains: No cutover.
losses: ^ stays taken.
A dead key on many keyboards.

proposed.code: fn seal(^self) { … }

recommendation.why: & changes and && keeps read as one family, C++ already uses && for moves, and ^ is freed.
gains: One family of marks.
Frees ^.

losses.loss: && also means logical and.
losses.mitigation: The take mark appears only in signatures and after task.

whyNot.reason: Adds a keyword and five letters per take.
Keeps ^ taken and the dead key.

recommendation.tradeoff: A shared symbol, kept apart by position, for a paired mark and a free ^.

decisions.title: Every declaration is written name: value
decisions.situation: Jet writes a constant as limit :: 100, a function as fn area(…), and a type as struct Point { … }. Package files, struct literals, named arguments and fields already write name: value. You asked for name: value everywhere: fewer characters, a feel closer to Python, a natural configuration language like Lua or Nix, and one shape for every declaration. We recommend writing every declaration that way, with := still marking a value you may change.
decisions.gist: Should every declaration, from constants to functions, types and modules, be written name: value?

CUE and Jsonnet write name: value for data and definitions alike. Source: https://cuelang.org/docs/tour/basics/

JavaScript objects and JSON write name: value. Nix and Lua write name = value for settings and functions alike. Source: https://nix.dev/manual/nix/2.24/language/
decisions.detail:
WHAT YOU ASKED

On 2026-11-06 you asked for name: value instead of name :: value, for constants, functions and modules, with example files and every downside designed away. The full proposal with five complete example files is Docs/proposals/2026-11-06-colon-declarations.md.

THE RULE UNDER A

Everything that introduces a name is written name: value; a value you may change is name := value. limit: 100. area: fn(r: Float) -> Float { … }. Point: struct { x: Int, y: Int }. Mode: enum { Fast, Safe }. Shape: trait { area: fn(self) -> Float }. math: module { … }. int_cache: cache<Int>(32). use process: core.process. package: { name: "x" }.

Kind parameters go on the kind word, never on the name: first: fn<T>(xs: [T]) -> T?, Box: struct<T> { value: T }, cache: module<K>(capacity: Int).

Inside the braces after struct, trait, enum or a foreign #Import module, name: Type describes what each value holds. Everywhere else, name: thing makes name that thing. The word before the brace always says which.

WHY

Package files, struct literals, named arguments and fields already write name: value, so source and settings become one language. :: came from Jai's x : Type : value; typed bindings are retired, so the type slot between the colons is gone.

Each of 141,892 :: bindings loses two characters. fn name(…) and name :: fn(…) are two ways to write a function today (891 uses of the second), and A makes them one.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Readers from TypeScript, Python or Rust read x: T as a type. In Jet a declaration has no separate type, so name: thing always declares. Where thing is a type, the familiar reading is right. Where it is a value, limit: 100, a type reading is impossible, so nobody misreads it silently.

2. { a: 1 } as block or record. A brace group whose entries are all name: value is a record. A block that only binds names produces nothing, so no meaningful program changes.

3. x: Int at file level makes an alias, as x :: Int does today. Using it as a number gets a registered error with the fix x: Int{0}.

4. Foreign functions have no body. Inside a foreign module every entry is a signature with its symbol, as today. At file level a bodiless fn(…) is a function type, as on the right of :: today.

5. Searching for a definition. fn area becomes area:, still one search; outlines and go-to-definition read the parser.

6. Headers grow by one character: fn run() is 8, run: fn() is 9. Bindings save two characters each and outnumber headers, and every name starts at the left margin.

7. The cutover. About 225,000 declaration lines change. jet fix rewrites them from the parse tree in one commit, with grammars, registry, spec, examples and snapshots. Meaning does not change, so the run-time tests prove the rewrite.

EDGE CASES

- impl blocks and #Test blocks introduce no name and keep their form.
- An associated type is Output: type in a trait and Output: T in an impl.
- A name: fn binding may call itself, at file level and inside a function.
- String interpolation such as {x:Debug} is unchanged.

WHY NOT B OR C

B changes only constants, so functions and types still read differently and the two function forms stay. C keeps the :: that no longer has a job.

decisions.title: A drag that leaves with no action
decisions.gist: When a drag leaves a window without dropping, what action should Jet report?
decisions.lesson: While you drag something over a window, the browser says what a drop would do: copy, move or link. When the drag leaves, it says none. Jet's drag event always holds one of three actions, so every web leave event is an error today. Whichever option wins, leave events must arrive without an error.
decisions.story: Maya builds a web to-do list where people drag notes between columns. When a note leaves a column, she clears the column's highlight. Today her program gets an error on every leave, so highlights stick.

options.name: Optional action
options.detail: UIDragEvent.operation becomes UIDragOperation?. Enter and over carry the browser's action, or none when the target refuses the drop. Leave and cancel carry none. A drop always carries an action.
options.technical: Core/Ui/Host/DragDrop.jet: drag_operation maps "none" to None. A drop record whose effect is none becomes phase Cancel, so Drop implies Val. The provider record format is unchanged. Native providers send the same five fields.
options.code:
if event.operation == .Val(op) -> show_hint(op)
else -> clear_highlight()

options.name: None case
options.detail: UIDragOperation gains a None case. Every event carries an action value, and None means nothing would happen.
options.technical: Core/Ui/Host/DragDrop.jet: the enum gains None; drag_operation maps "none" to .None. Exhaustive matches on UIDragOperation everywhere gain an arm.

comparisons.note: The browser models dropEffect as a string that includes none. MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/DataTransfer/dropEffect.
winit reports a file hover as a separate event, and a cancelled hover as HoveredFileCancelled with no action. See https://docs.rs/winit/latest/winit/event/enum.WindowEvent.html.

recommendation.why: Jet already spells "may be missing" with optional values. One spelling of nothing keeps the drag type honest, and drops keep a guaranteed action.
gains: Leave events work on the web with no new enum case.

losses.loss: Code that reads the action on hover checks for none first.
losses.mitigation: Core guarantees drops carry an action; a browser drop with none becomes a Cancel event.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second way to say nothing and forces a None arm into every drop handler.

recommendation.tradeoff: Hover and leave code checks for a missing action; drop code never does.

decisions.title: Keyboard shortcuts in web pages
decisions.gist: How should a web page hand key presses to Jet's shortcut table?
decisions.lesson: Jet keeps a table of shortcuts, such as Ctrl+S for save. A program registers a key and an action, and Core decides which key matches. A Jet web page never forwards key presses, so a registered shortcut never fires. Ctrl+S opens the browser's own save page instead. Whichever option wins, Core keeps deciding matches.
decisions.story: Sam writes a small web notes app in Jet and binds Ctrl+S to save. On the desktop it saves. In the browser, Ctrl+S opens the browser's save page, and the app never hears the key.

options.name: Key queue
options.detail: Registering a shortcut also tells the page which key to claim. The page blocks the browser's default for claimed keys only and queues each press. shortcuts.poll takes the next press, matches it in Core's table, and returns Dispatched or Unhandled.
options.technical: Core/Ui/Host/Shortcuts.jet gains poll() over provider queue 2 (capability 4), the same provider record and overflow mark as ime.poll and drag_drop.poll. register() also calls one new raw host primitive that passes the normalized key and modifier bits to the provider. The default web provider (JetWeb Host.jet) listens for keydown, compares against claimed keys, calls preventDefault, and enqueues target, key and modifier bits. Desktop providers enqueue the same record.

options.name: UI key events
options.detail: Key presses arrive through core.ui as key events that now carry modifiers. The core.ui event loop asks the shortcut table before the program's own handler.
options.technical: core.ui InputEvent.Key gains a modifiers field; DomRuntime.js forwards keydown into the node tree; the UI loop calls shortcuts.dispatch. Programs that use core.ui.host without core.ui nodes see no key source.

options.name: Desktop only
options.detail: The web provider reports the Shortcuts capability as unavailable, so register and dispatch fail with CapabilityUnavailable on the web.
options.technical: JetWeb Host.jet capability() returns false for code 4.
options.code:
shortcuts.register(save)?
// web: Err(CapabilityUnavailable{capability: "Shortcuts"})

comparisons.note: Pages own shortcuts by listening for keydown and calling preventDefault. MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/keydown_event.
egui reads queued key events each frame and checks shortcuts against them. See https://docs.rs/egui/latest/egui/struct.InputState.html#method.consume_shortcut.

recommendation.why: Drag and drop and typing composition already arrive through page queues and poll. Keys joining the same path keeps one mechanism, and Core still owns every match.
gains: Web shortcuts work with the same code as desktop.

losses.loss: A program that stops polling misses presses after the queue fills.
losses.mitigation: A full queue reports QueueFull on the next poll, like drag and drop, so nothing is lost silently.

whyNot.reason: B leaves host-only programs without shortcuts and changes a public event type.
C makes the same program behave differently on the web.

recommendation.tradeoff: Programs poll shortcuts like other host events; a stalled program learns it missed presses.

decisions.title: Finish G1 and G2 sooner by moving the feature backlogs to the goals that own them
decisions.situation: G1 has 18 open cards and G2 has 9. The backlog cards are #6418 unbuilt CLI commands (12/141), #6419 unbuilt Core APIs (27/52) and #5454 failing ported Rust tests (1/92). They also include test-toolkit features #6012, #6015, #6060 and #6064, and in G2 #6425 silent checker families (0/7). With only three agents running, these backlogs would keep both goals open for a long time after the hand-off work itself is done.
decisions.gist: Should the feature-backlog cards leave G1 and G2, with every row they block kept as a tracked known failure?
decisions.lesson: G1 is hand-off and durability, and G2 is finishing Rust removal. Both still hold cards that are really feature backlogs, such as unbuilt CLI commands and unbuilt Core APIs. G1 also says every golden, ui and cases row must pass. About 1,100 rows are known-failing today, and almost all of them wait on a feature from one of those backlogs. So G1 and G2 cannot finish until those features are built.
decisions.story: The hand-off work is nearly done: #6564 is at 20 of 23 criteria and test.jet is at 60 of 66. G1 still shows 18 open cards. Most of the remaining criteria sit in #6418 with 141 criteria and #5454 with 92.

Rust's release trains ship when the train leaves. Unfinished features stay behind their own tracking issues instead of holding the release.

decisions.title: Enum declarations write each case with its leading dot, as values and patterns already do
decisions.situation: Enum declarations write case names bare, while values and case patterns use dots. A dotted declaration is refused by the current compiler, so copying a case into its declaration needs an edit. This vote decides whether declared cases also start with a dot. We recommend dots for labelled cases, leaving bare type names available if the separate shared-case vote passes.
decisions.gist: Should enum declarations write each case with a leading dot, like values and patterns?
decisions.lesson: An enum lists possible cases. Today declarations use bare names on separate lines; values and case patterns use a leading dot. This vote changes only case declarations, not comma layout or type identity.
decisions.story: Dmitri copies .Paused from a match arm into an enum declaration. The compiler refuses the dot even though his value and case pattern use it.
decisions.inWild: Swift declares cases with case and uses contextual dotted values or patterns. Its manual illustrates enum CompassPoint and switch directionToHead with .south. Source: https://docs.swift.org/latest/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/enumerations/
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS DECIDES

Add a dot to labelled case declarations, including payload cases and nested groups. Methods, marker lines and type cases are not labelled declarations.

CHECKED TODAY

SolBallotReview's enum_dot.jet gives E0003 at .Fast; enum_comma.jet gives E0003 at the comma. These are independent parser limitations. Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Patterns.jet:597-607 reports E0367 for a bare payload constructor such as Circle(n), not every uppercase name. A bare unit name can parse as a comparison expression; the earlier claim that Fast -> always gets E0367 was false.

DEPENDENCIES

D-DECL-COLON1=A illustrated bare enum cases; A amends that spelling. D-BRACE-LAYOUT1 decides one-line comma bodies independently. Without it, dotted declarations use separate lines. D-ALT-CASES1 depends on this vote for enum type cases: Int denotes a type case, .Int a labelled case. A alone adds neither type cases nor encoding changes.

Migration adds dots from parsed case declarations, never method names. Preserve comments and nested groups. A missing dot receives a registered diagnostic and edit. B is cohesive and familiar but needs two contextual spellings.

gains: One spelling per case.

Bare names stay free for type cases.

losses.loss: One more character per case line.
losses.mitigation: jet fix adds every dot; a missing dot gets an error whose fix adds it.

whyNot.reason: A case keeps two spellings, and copying it between a match and its declaration fails.

recommendation.tradeoff: One character per case line, in exchange for one spelling of every case.

decisions.title: One accessibility provider contract, using AccessKit on supported desktops
decisions.situation: Drawn controls need an accessibility description so assistive tools can find and operate them. Jet has four view roles, but its native host provider reports accessibility unavailable. This vote chooses whether to reuse desktop adapters or write every adapter in Jet. We recommend AccessKit behind the existing provider contract on supported desktops, with Jet providers for phones and semantic elements on the web.
decisions.gist: Should Jet reuse AccessKit's desktop adapters behind one accessibility provider contract?
decisions.lesson: A provider translates one logical view tree into a system's accessibility interface. Different platform adapters are implementations of that contract, not different state or view models. Both choices still need complete roles, focus, actions and manual assistive-tool acceptance.
decisions.story: Hana needs a Pay button that a keyboard user and a screen-reader user can both find and activate. The same action must run whichever adapter exposes it.
decisions.inWild: AccessKit describes itself as accessibility infrastructure for custom-drawn toolkits. Its published adapters cover macOS, Unix and Windows, and it offers C bindings and prebuilt libraries. Source: https://accesskit.dev/
decisions.detail:
OWNER GATE

A approves a pinned AccessKit desktop dependency and its C bridge. This is a new dependency choice, not a second accessibility mechanism. D-CORE-PROVIDER1=A supplies one replaceable provider contract; D-UI-HOME1 keeps system services in core.ui.host and views in the ui package. D-UI-VIEW1's ui.app/state model stays unchanged.

CHECKED TODAY

Core/Ui/Ui.jet:39-44 lists Button, Container, Label and TextInput. Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/gui/gui.jet:542-548 wraps accessibility metadata. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/UiHostProvider.jet:17-25 reports every native capability absent. SolBallotReview compiled and ran ui_values.jet for view construction and ui_gtk_clean.jet for the unavailable GTK result. These checks do not establish browser screen-reader behavior.

RESEARCH AND CORRECTION

https://accesskit.dev/ lists macOS, Unix and Windows adapters, C/Python bindings, prebuilt C libraries, and users including egui and Slint. That page does not list phone adapters; A does not assume they exist. The earlier claim that binding AccessKit needs every user's machine to build Rust was false: prebuilt C-interface libraries are available. Local source rebuilds still require the upstream toolchain. An upstream project can be pinned or patched; fixes need not wait indefinitely for a release.

BRIDGE AND AUTHORITY

D-FFI-RUST1=A currently authorizes static user helpers only on x86_64 Linux. A explicitly extends that scope for this first-party desktop accessibility provider, not arbitrary Rust helpers. Approve the I6 bridge here: pinned source/version and license, reproducible per-target C-interface artifacts, signed distribution, typed ownership and callback lifetimes, no extra user toolchain, and normal provider availability diagnostics. Do not claim this bridge has been implemented or verified. Linux packaging must meet the existing static deployment contract or return for a separate linking decision; no hidden dynamic-loader exception.

ONE CONTRACT

One logical tree owns identity, role, label, state, reading order, focus and actions. A desktop provider forwards it through AccessKit; phone providers marshal it directly; web uses semantic elements under D-ONEAPP-WEBOUT1. A target selects one provider, never two competing trees. Provider callbacks invoke the same checked actions.

SHARED ACCEPTANCE

Compare normalized semantic projections, not byte-identical platform trees or exact speech strings. Require focus traversal, action dispatch, live updates, editable text, virtualized lists and manual checks with platform assistive tools. D-A11YGATE1=B keeps optional accessibility linting separate from runtime correctness. Test gates do not magically remove adapter bugs; that obligation is shared by A and B.

B avoids an outside dependency and gives Jet all adapter code, but copying role tables alone cannot make five exports a negligible maintenance cost. A reuses maintained desktop adapters without pretending they cover phones.

decisions.title: Use the graphics chip on phones only after a measured win; keep desktop software defaults
decisions.situation: An app can paint with its main processor or its graphics chip. The approved Linux plan uses the main processor so a graphical app can remain one static file, without loading graphics drivers. The seed refuses phone runs, so this vote sets a future default rather than claiming a working phone renderer. We recommend graphics drawing on phones only after measurement, with automatic software fallback and explicit overrides.
decisions.gist: Should phones use the graphics chip after a measured win, while desktops keep software drawing?
decisions.lesson: The graphics chip is hardware for drawing. A uses it on phones only after Jet measures a win for the same app. Otherwise software drawing stays the default. Experts can choose either path explicitly. All options keep the same screen and actions; phone work still waits for Linux and web.
decisions.story: Jun wants his reading app to scroll well on a phone without learning graphics drivers or losing its portable Linux build.
decisions.inWild: Flutter documents Impeller as the default on iOS and Android API 29+. Android without Vulkan uses the older OpenGL renderer, not software drawing. This is precedent for hardware drawing, not evidence of a Jet speed or battery win. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/perf/impeller
decisions.detail:
SCOPE

D-RAYLIB-DRIVER-LOAD1=A chooses static Linux display and sound clients, with dynamically linked GPU builds as an expert opt-in. It does not establish a software default for every desktop and phone. A sets the phone policy and leaves existing desktop defaults alone. Browser acceleration remains the browser's choice. D-MOBILE-UNDEFER1=B puts phone work after Linux and web, with no pilot.

A'S CONTRACT

Both drawing paths consume the same scene, layout and shaped text. Required acceptance compares clipping, fractional positions, antialiasing, color and actions; these checks are future obligations, not proof that every device produces identical pixels. If graphics startup fails or the graphics device is lost, rebuild the drawing resources in software without losing app state. If neither path can present a window, report the actual failure; fallback is not a promise that a screen can never fail.

The paired phone workload must keep the app, fonts, resolution, refresh rate and scroll trace fixed. Record frame time, energy, cycles and bytes, and apply AGENTS.md:189-192 and the full performance gate. A switches only on a passing result before phone release; otherwise the default remains software. No phone renderer or benchmark was exercised in this review.

EXPERT CONTROL

The proposed package setting drawing: .Software forces software; drawing: .Gpu explicitly requests graphics drawing on a supported target. Forced graphics reports an unavailable driver instead of silently ignoring the request. Automatic fallback belongs to the default policy, not the forced setting. This setting controls the same renderer, not another view model.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES

B retains software as the default even if a GPU option measures better for a phone workload. It still offers GPU opt-in, so it does not have only one renderer to test. C extends measured hardware defaults to macOS and Windows too; those platforms need their own evidence. Neither Flutter's adoption nor the absence of Jet measurements proves a desktop loss.

EVIDENCE

The seed's jet run club.jet --target=ios returned E2104. The approved Linux rule and phone sequencing were read directly from their ratified options. No build, phone run or battery measurement ran.

ONE COST REMAINS

Hardware and software rendering can differ slightly on real devices. Shared inputs, comparison checks and an explicit software override reduce that risk; they do not prove universal pixel identity.

decisions.title: View literals become typed messages; an opt-in package supplies translation
decisions.situation: Translation shows an app's words in the reader's language, including different forms for counts. The seed has an English plural helper, but a plain string cannot become a checked message just because a parameter expects one. This vote chooses automatic view messages, explicit markers, or named keys in resource files. We recommend automatic messages with translation in an opt-in package, while keeping author review for text built elsewhere.
decisions.gist: Should text in views be translatable automatically, with translation itself in an opt-in package?
decisions.lesson: A turns view literals into typed messages automatically, extending Jet's literal capability to text. An opt-in package later collects and translates catalogs. English-only apps need no catalogs or language data. Runtime data uses ui.verbatim(value), not a translation key. One cost remains: authors must review helpers, runtime text and phrases needing context.
decisions.story: Ana's booking app starts in English. A year later a Brazilian club wants it in Portuguese. She wants that to be a translator's job, not a rewrite of every screen.
decisions.inWild: SwiftUI interprets a literal passed to Text as a localization key, but displays a String variable without localization. Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/text. This is precedent for A, including its helper boundary, not evidence that Jet already supports it.
decisions.detail:
WHAT VOTING A INCLUDES

An opt-in first-party i18n package uses public CheckedText parts-and-holes metaprogramming under D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1=A and D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A. The small ui.Text message carrier belongs in ui; the separately ratified kit package uses it too. There is no second interpolation mechanism.

A ALSO EXTENDS LITERALS

D-FOUND-LITERAL1=A ratified numeric literal capabilities, not text literals. A explicitly extends that contextual construction mechanism to checked text. View text parameters take ui.Text only, giving a literal one expected type and retaining its fixed parts and typed holes. Runtime data uses ui.verbatim(value: String), returning the same ui.Text carrier without translation. This avoids an ambiguous ui.Text-or-String overload and prevents database values becoming catalog keys. Translatable helpers return ui.Text. Other checked kinds do not silently opt in.

PACKAGE OR METAPROGRAMMING?

Both: the optional package uses public metaprogramming for extraction and catalogs, supplying locale selection, plural rules and number/date formatting. The proposed jet i18n command is a jet-i18n PATH helper, not a private compiler subsystem. View literals need no later wrappers, making this useful for apps that may translate. No measured zero-overhead result is claimed; artifact checks must prove unused catalogs and language data are absent.

SAME MESSAGE AND FAIR ALTERNATIVES

All options show 1 booking today or 3 bookings today. A and B give the English one: form; C's source catalog gives one and other. Translation catalogs preserve hole names/types and supply each language's required forms. Missing translations fall back to source text; wording changes need review. B explicitly marks phrases. C uses stable keys that survive wording edits. English-only apps may delay either conversion until they translate, so neither charges every app up front.

ONE COST REMAINS

Authors must review helpers, runtime text and ambiguous phrases. Use ui.Text helpers, ui.verbatim for data, and context: for different meanings. Extraction can report explicit verbatim inputs and repeated phrases, but cannot list every runtime phrase or infer human meaning.

CHECKED TODAY

Core/Text/Fmt.jet:31-34 selects singular when abs(n) is 1. fmt.jet printed 1 booking and 2 bookings. msg_explicit.jet printed 3 bookings today from an explicit Msg head; msg_plain.jet failed E0112 for String passed to Msg. No proposed ui.Text, ui.verbatim, extractor or catalog ran.

WHAT A APPROVES

A approves contextual checked-text literal construction plus the public ui.Text/ui.verbatim API. It does not add a compiler rule recognizing ui by name or change other checked text kinds without their opt-in.

decisions.title: Rows, columns and grids have defaults; experts can override them or write layouts
decisions.situation: Screens need to place views side by side, in columns, or in grids that adapt to the available space. The seed's box stacks children, while the approved constraint model describes relationships between their sizes and positions. This vote chooses the everyday layout model without removing custom layouts or the solver. We recommend simple containers with defaults and explicit expert settings, including a choice of narrow-screen behavior.
decisions.gist: Should layout have useful defaults, with advanced settings and custom layouts available by explicit opt-in?
decisions.lesson: A two-column signup grid fits labels to their text and gives inputs the remaining width. Below 600 logical pixels of container width it becomes one column, regardless of device. Experts override gaps, tracks, wrapping and that breakpoint. Containers use one layout contract; custom layout functions and the constraint solver remain opt-in. Browser layout follows the companion web-output vote.
decisions.story: Ana's signup form should look tidy on a laptop and stack neatly on a phone, without her learning layout rules. Rui needs exact column sizes and a custom layout for a dashboard.
decisions.inWild:
SwiftUI stacks and grids apply default spacing and alignment when none is given; modifiers override them. Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/grid

Flutter separates the box model from HTML and lets experts write custom layouts. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/layout/constraints
decisions.detail:
SCOPE

A amends D-LAYOUT1=A's default surface, not its expert constraint power. Containers and custom layouts implement one measure-and-place protocol in ui under D-UI-HOME1. The solver implements that protocol as a library, not a second state/view system. D-VIEW-SET1=C keeps composed controls in kit.

DEFAULTS AND OVERRIDES

row, column, grid, stack and scroll need no optional settings. Gaps default to 8 logical pixels and padding to 0, with theme overrides. Start alignment follows reading direction. A grid with columns: N uses content-sized tracks followed by one remaining-space track.

Below 600 logical pixels of container width, the default grid becomes one column in child order. A phone is not itself the trigger. responsive: false keeps the columns; collapse_below: changes the threshold. Explicit track lists follow the same responsive rule unless overridden. Rows wrap when needed; wrap: false opts out.

A single oversized or unbreakable child can still overflow. scroll contains it, and preview checks report observed clipping. No finite preview proves every runtime state.

EXPERT PATH

Expose every supported flex/grid property, not every CSS feature: gap, padding, alignment, wrapping, grow/shrink, tracks and spans. Unsupported properties are errors. Custom functions measure and place children. The approved solver uses that same contract and retains its constraint authoring; this vote does not invent Layout{...} as another syntax.

WEB DEPENDENCY

Under D-ONEAPP-WEBOUT1=A, standard containers map to CSS under its named layout/text exception. Custom functions run Jet code inside their container, without browser-side copies of app policy. With web-output B or C, shared Jet layout computes geometry. Neither vote promises identical wrapping on every engine.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES

B gives beginners the same presets, implemented through constraints, and experts direct relationships. It does not start beginners with equations. C includes a first-party default stylesheet and responsive rules, not an unstyled screen. Its selectors and cascade change how styles interact; it need not contain an entire browser engine.

CHECKED TODAY

ui_values_fixed.jet printed 15.0 x 2.0. Core/Ui/Ui.jet:132-146 computes maximum width and summed child heights, with text measured in display cells. That proves this example, not every layout API's absence. SwiftUI Grid documentation confirms default spacing/alignment and overrides.

NO REMAINING DEFAULT-LOCK-IN COST

Every default is overridable, with custom layouts and the solver still available. Implementation and acceptance remain shared obligations, not completed tests.

decisions.title: Phone apps follow Linux and web, with an early one-phone pilot of native contracts
decisions.situation: Phone platform work remains deferred, and current phone runs are refused. A shared app needs an explicit condition for restarting that work, not an implied delivery date. We recommend full phone bring-up after Linux and web app acceptance, within the approved compiler-target order. A bounded pilot on one phone tests native text input, lifecycle, safe areas and screen readers before the shared view contracts freeze.
decisions.gist: Should phone apps follow Linux and web, with an early one-phone pilot that tests native input and lifecycle?
decisions.lesson: A restart gate is not a release promise. Linux and web prove shared behavior, not native phone lifecycle or input. The approved compiler-target order remains binding. Browser access cannot erase later native validation.
decisions.story: Tomas leads a small team. He wants Jet on phones, but he would rather have a working Linux window and web page first than three half-finished targets at once.
decisions.inWild: JetBrains announced Compose Multiplatform for iOS stable in version 1.8.0 in May 2025, including accessibility, navigation and native text-editing integration. Source: https://blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2025/05/compose-multiplatform-1-8-0-released-compose-multiplatform-for-ios-is-stable-and-production-ready/
decisions.detail:
OWNER GATE

Amend D-VERDICT-480-1's mobile-native deferral with a measurable restart condition. D-NATIVEUI3 retains phone support, signing and store upload. D-TARGET-ORDER1=A specifically orders wasm32-wasip2, then aarch64, then embedded bring-up; a browser page alone is not proof that the entire WebAssembly target obligation passed.

CHECKED TODAY

SolBallotReview checked union.jet for ios/android successfully, but its phone runs gave E2104. Checking source is not an executable target proof. No phone build ran during this review.

A'S CONDITION

One booking app must pass state, navigation, input, normalized accessibility and golden-view acceptance as a real Linux window and a browser app. Use the renderer and web presentation actually approved by their ballots; neither a drawn renderer nor DOM may be assumed if its vote loses. Compiler WebAssembly and ARM64 prerequisites retain their ratified order. This condition authorizes beginning native phone integration, not shipping phone targets before their own complete acceptance.

Validate portable app logic and phone-sized responsive fixtures while building the shared base. Do not claim these prove native IME, lifecycle restoration, safe areas, permissions or store delivery. Before accepting architecture choices that affect those contracts, review concrete phone requirements rather than waiting until the end to discover them.

A'S EARLY PILOT

As soon as the ratified ARM64 target exists, one phone runs a bounded native pilot. It covers text input and composition, lifecycle restore, safe areas and the screen reader. It runs before the shared view and input contracts freeze, so native risks surface early. It ships no store build.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES AND LOSS

B is the same milestone without the pilot, so native risks surface only at bring-up. C keeps the deferral until another owner vote. A's residual cost is the pilot's bounded effort before Linux and web are done.
