decisions.title: One first-party app package serves the web, the desktop and phones
decisions.situation: Jet currently exposes web app builders and a separate UI tree. Ratified rulings already put their higher-level code in shipped packages, with system services remaining in Core. This vote asks whether the web package becomes the shared app layer for web, desktop and phones. We recommend one app package over the existing UI model, without moving authentication or system services back into Core.
decisions.gist: Should one first-party app package serve web, desktop and phone apps, replacing separate web and window libraries?
decisions.lesson: The app layer adds screens, navigation, forms and server calls above views. Jet currently has a web builder and a separate UI tree, not two proven complete app frameworks. This vote extends the shipped web package across targets while retaining the approved UI and authentication package homes.
decisions.story: Dana runs a tutoring business. She wants a booking site for parents, a desktop tool for her staff and a phone app for tutors. She would rather learn one way to write screens, forms and sign-in than three.
decisions.inWild: Expo Router uses the same file-based routes across Android, iOS and web, while allowing platform-specific APIs. Source: https://docs.expo.dev/router/introduction/
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS DECIDES

Rename the first-party web package to app and extend its app graph across targets. Amend D-WEB-HOME1's package name and scope, D-WEB-NAME1=C's framework name, D-ROUTE-ONE1's builder name, and D-GAME-PLATFORM1's web/app separation. D-UI-HOME1 and D-DB-AUTH-HOME1 retain their homes: ui is a package, core.ui.host stays Core, and auth remains its own package.

CHECKED TODAY

Core/Web/Web.jet:188 defines web.app; :291-360 holds routing and serving methods. Core/Ui/Ui.jet:195-209 supplies backends. SolBallotReview's ui_missing.jet gives E1004 for ui.application, despite D-UI-WINDOW-LIFE1's approved API. web_value.jet checked and ran web.app().facts_json(). The gui editor uses core.ui at Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/gui/gui.jet:460-475. This does not prove a complete desktop app model exists.

A'S BOUNDARY

app.new is the routed-app wrapper over D-UI-VIEW1's ui.app(view, state:). It creates no second mount, diff, state or window mechanism. ui.app is the smallest one-screen entry; app adds routes, navigation and shared form/data policy. The same route identity drives URLs and device deep links. Server handler rows remain server-only; unsupported effects are refused rather than ignored.

Core keeps HTTP and networking. app depends on auth without copying or re-exporting another authentication implementation. The gui editor may consume ui; independent editor helpers are not deleted merely to rename widgets. Standard controls use ui under D-VIEW-SET1. This adjusts D-GAME-PLATFORM1's gui composition while preserving independent video and audio packages.

C can share form and auth primitives without an I8 breach; its cost is separate top-level navigation models. B explicitly reverses the Core-home ruling; changing that ruling is not itself evidence B is technically unsound.

CUTOVER

Migrate existing core.web and first-party web callers together; do not assume no web package callers exist. Preserve server-only APIs. Prove unused target code is excluded rather than asserting this already happens. One booking example must preserve route state, browser Back and device deep links across web, desktop and phones.

decisions.title: Jet draws every control itself by default; an opt-in native library swaps in the system's real control where an expert wants it
decisions.situation: A screen can use Jet-drawn controls, each system's real controls, or a browser view inside the app. The seed's GTK example reports that its runtime is unavailable, rather than opening a window. This vote sets the default drawing model; it does not prove that any future phone renderer already works. We recommend Jet-drawn controls with explicit system-control replacements, subject to the companion vote allowing those controls inside a Jet screen.
decisions.gist: Should Jet draw every control itself by default, with system controls as an opt-in library for experts?
decisions.lesson: A draws the booking screen with Jet's styling; system typing, screen readers and expected platform behavior remain. Experts replace one picker with native.date_picker(day). Inline replacements require the companion system-view option A too. A theme only changes drawn styling; it does not turn a Jet control into a real system control.
decisions.story: Ana builds a booking app and wants it to look the same on every phone and computer without learning five toolkits. Her colleague Rui wants the iPhone build to show Apple's own date wheel.
decisions.inWild:
Flutter draws its widgets itself, while each platform embedder supplies the system keyboard, accessibility bridge and windows. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/resources/architectural-overview

Flutter embeds a real system view when an app needs one, through platform views. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/ios/platform-views
decisions.detail:
SCOPE

A amends the default-widget clauses of D-NATIVEUI3=A and D-NATIVEUI-ANDROID1=C, retaining approved interop and the single view/state model. D-ONEAPP-WEBOUT1 chooses browser presentation. D-VIEW-SET1=C puts standard composed views in kit, not ui. The owner's no-ship instruction applies independently of this drawing choice.

ONE MODEL, DIFFERENT PRESENTATIONS

Jet draws ordinary ui primitives and kit controls. Layout, state and actions remain shared; typography, accessibility settings and platform conventions can change appearance and interaction details. Do not promise one pixel image or identical scroll physics on all systems. Core host services still provide text input and composition; Jet-written adapters export accessibility under D-A11Y-EXPORT1=B. System sheets and permission prompts stay system-owned. Release acceptance must cover typing, selection, input-method composition, focus, screen readers and system navigation. Those are obligations, not measured successes.

THE SHARED NATIVE PACKAGE

The native package is the same one used in D-THEME2 and D-PLATFORM-OVERRIDE1. native.theme() supplies system-like styling for drawn controls; it is not another control implementation. native.date_picker(day) instead uses the one host-view embedding contract to return a ui.Node backed by a real system control. Where no equivalent exists, it falls back to the kit control without changing state or actions. The date state in the examples is core.time.LocalDate. A target-specific native.view(handle) cannot silently fall back and needs a supported target branch.

DEPENDENCY, NOT A SILENT FALLBACK DESIGN

A's inline native-control promise requires D-PLATFORM-OVERRIDE1=A. If the owner chooses that ballot's B or C, this A must be reconciled before implementation; it must not silently turn an inline date picker into a full-screen interaction. The surface states this dependency. Theme styling remains possible without inline embedding.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES

B maps the same Jet views to native toolkits. Authors still use one API, not five APIs; differences arise in toolkit behavior and available controls. The seed's static GTK refusal is an implementation fact, not proof that a future native Linux toolkit cannot work. C uses the system's browser view, which can reuse an installed engine rather than bundle one; it adds browser integration and resource costs that require measurement, not a fabricated startup number.

ONE COST REMAINS

Default controls look like Jet rather than exactly like the host. Explicit native replacements reduce that cost where supported, but inherit the composition limits and work described in the companion vote. A does not promise every imaginable system control in one line.

CHECKED TODAY

ui_gtk.jet with --allow=Browser printed UI_UNSUPPORTED[gtk.runtime]. ui_values_fixed.jet printed 15.0 x 2.0. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/UiBackends.jet:13-16 documents the current static GTK path. These do not establish that GTK is the only possible desktop renderer. Flutter's architecture and platform-view documentation provide precedent, not a Jet prototype.

decisions.title: Use real browser elements and server HTML; allow browser layout without promising identical line breaks
decisions.situation: Jet's browser host positions elements using pixel coordinates supplied by Jet. Real browser layout would let text and controls adapt naturally to zoom, translation and the available width, but cannot guarantee native-identical line breaks. This vote chooses browser elements or Jet-computed drawing and positioning, keeping server rendering and resumable handlers in every option. We recommend browser elements, explicitly allowing browser layout and text shaping rather than pretending tests make the engines identical.

decisions.lesson: Every option shows the same order screen and keeps server HTML and resumable handlers. A uses real text and buttons with browser layout. Shared fonts and comparison checks reduce differences, but cannot guarantee identical wrapping. Voting A also permits a web-only exception: browser layout and text shaping replace Jet's implementation there.
decisions.story: Ana wants her order screen to use browser zoom and translation well, without clipped content when its lines wrap differently from her phone app.
decisions.inWild: Qwik resumes server-rendered HTML and lazily loads handlers without replaying the initial component render: https://qwik.dev/docs/concepts/resumable/. Taffy implements CSS block, flex and grid layout outside browsers; its repository has a Chrome-based fixture generator. It does not implement text layout, so its layout tests do not prove identical line breaks: https://github.com/DioxusLabs/taffy.
decisions.detail:
ONE CHOICE AND ITS NECESSARY EXCEPTION

D-UI-HOME1 and D-UI-VIEW1 retain the ui package and shared state/view model. D-RESUME1 keeps server HTML, serialized state and lazy handlers. D-WEBBACKEND1 and D-WASM1 keep effect-checked placement. A permits one named I9 exception, for browser layout and text shaping of page elements on the web tier only. App rules, validation, state and action meaning remain shared Jet code; the exception does not authorize browser-side copies of those rules.

WHAT A CAN AND CANNOT GUARANTEE

Serve the same bundled fonts where the reader allows them, agree on supported layout and line-breaking rules, and compare native geometry with fixtures from Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. Tests must cover zoom, long translations, right-to-left text, missing glyphs, font loading and user font overrides. Mismatches outside the accepted rounding range block release. This is future acceptance, not an existing browser suite.

The same font file does not guarantee identical glyph metrics or wrapping: shaping, fallback fonts, engine rounding and user settings can differ. Unicode line-breaking rules permit choices and tailoring. Tests reduce known differences; they cannot prove every line break on every browser version. Do not exclude every disagreement and then claim all expert features work identically. Supported features and limits must be explicit, with readable overflow behavior.

SERVER OUTPUT

Send semantic elements with serialized state and handler references. Static content can appear before app code runs; network, server and font delays still exist. A simple text node is not automatically a heading. The logical tree determines roles and reading order under D-A11Y-EXPORT1=B; page-element order already follows tree order in the current host.

EXPERT DRAWING

A canvas view for charts or games remains opt-in under D-GAME-PLATFORM1. It uses shared drawing geometry and an accessibility projection, not a second app model. It does not make all displays pixel-identical or give canvas text automatic browser find and translation.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES

B paints the same screen after server HTML, using shared Jet geometry and a synchronized accessible tree. Canvas can zoom as pixels; automatic text find, translation and reflow require additional integration. C uses semantic elements with shared Jet-computed positions and recomputes them on size or text-metric changes. Absolute positioning does not inherently prevent responsive layout; C's cost is having Jet maintain that reflow integration rather than using browser flow. Both retain server output and resume.

CHECKED EVIDENCE

Compiler/JetWeb/Source/Web/Host.jet:479-491 creates real elements, sets absolute position and pixel boxes, then appends them in tree order. SolReworkReview read that code but ran no web build or browser. The native ui_values_fixed.jet probe printed 15.0 x 2.0. No claim of current browser failure beyond the source's positioning strategy is made.

ONE COST REMAINS

Text can wrap differently from native even with shared fonts. Allow flexible heights and reflow; check clipping and focus at varied widths, zoom and translations. The owner is accepting that remaining presentation difference, not being promised it away.

decisions.title: Jet builds signed phone upload files; developers upload and stores deliver, with no ship command
decisions.situation: Earlier phone rulings included a command for uploading apps, but the owner has ruled that Jet is not a distribution platform. That boundary is settled: Jet has no ship command and does not deliver updates. This vote asks whether a release build produces a locally signed upload file or leaves signing and packaging to platform tools. We recommend signed files, with the developer supplying app details and managing signing credentials.
decisions.gist: Should release builds produce signed upload files, or leave signing and packaging to platform tools?
decisions.lesson: A builds a signed .ipa for Apple's upload tool or .aab for Google Play. The developer supplies icons, app details and signing credentials; the store still handles review and delivery. Jet never signs into a store. One cost remains: Apple signing files need manual setup and renewal, not just one download forever.
decisions.story: Dana finished her club app. She wants one command that produces exactly what Apple and Google ask for, then she will upload it the way every store developer does.
decisions.inWild: Flutter documents flutter build ipa producing an archive and .ipa, followed by a separate upload using Transporter, altool or Xcode: https://docs.flutter.dev/deployment/ios. Android App Bundles use an upload key, while Play App Signing manages the key used on delivered APKs; lost upload keys can be reset: https://developer.android.com/studio/publish/app-signing. Apple describes expiry and revocation of distribution certificates: https://developer.apple.com/help/account/certificates/certificates-overview/.
decisions.detail:
SETTLED BOUNDARY

The owner's no-distribution instruction overrides the jet ship/upload clauses in D-NATIVEUI3=A and D-RUN-DEVICE1=A, regardless of this vote. No option restores uploads, store login or an update engine. Apps may fetch ordinary content from their server. D-MOBILE-UNDEFER1=B keeps phones after Linux and web, without a pilot.

THE REMAINING CHOICE

A keeps first-party local signing from D-NATIVEUI3 and folds it into release builds. B emits unsigned output for platform tools to finish. Both produce the same club app, with the same metadata and permissions; neither rewrites the UI. This is an output boundary, not another distribution vote.

A'S OUTPUT

A configured iOS build produces a signed .ipa for App Store Connect; Android produces a signed .aab for Play Console. Use approved toolchains, including the Mac-hosted Apple SDK. Developers supply identifiers, versions, artwork, privacy declarations, entitlements and signing inputs. Jet packages them and diagnoses missing or invalid inputs. It cannot invent privacy practices or guarantee review acceptance. Store listings, screenshots, enrollment and uploading remain outside Jet in both options.

SIGNING

Keep private keys local. Apple signing needs the private key matching the distribution certificate, not merely a certificate/profile download. Never put secrets in ordinary source settings or logs. Jet never signs into a store account. Errors name missing or expired assets and link the issuing page. Apple certificates/profiles require replacement after expiry, revocation or relevant app changes.

Android can create an upload keystore locally: reuse and back it up, never silently replace a configured key. Google Play supports upload-key reset; loss does not necessarily prevent future updates forever.

FAIR B

B supports vendor command-line tools or Xcode/Android Studio, including automatic signing. It need not force a GUI on every release. Its advantage is vendor signing workflows; its cost is a separate release step. Device development still needs signing support under D-RUN-DEVICE1.

ONE COST REMAINS

A leaves Apple signing setup and renewal to the developer. Missing/expired-asset messages guide that work, not remove it.

CHECKED TODAY

SolReworkReview observed E2104 from jet run club.jet --target=ios. No build, signing or upload ran. Release output examples are proposed, not existing output.

decisions.title: A Jet screen can show a real system view, such as Apple Maps, inline through the opt-in native library
decisions.situation: Some screens need a real system view, such as Apple Maps or a camera preview, beside ordinary Jet content. Choosing code for each target is already settled, but the seed's core.ui has no native embedding item. This vote chooses inline embedding, a separate system screen, or drawn substitutes and external apps. We recommend explicit inline embedding through the shared native package, with its drawing limits and extra work stated rather than hidden.
decisions.gist: How should a Jet screen include a real system view, such as Apple Maps?
decisions.lesson: A puts Apple's real map inside the route screen using native.view(...). Jet controls its size and joins focus and accessibility; the host still owns the map's pixels and gestures. Basic fades, movement and clipping are supported. One cost remains: mixed screens do extra composition work and cannot apply Jet pixel filters to that live view.
decisions.story: Ana's booking app shows the route to the venue. On iPhone she wants Apple Maps with its familiar gestures, inside her screen, not as a separate app.
decisions.inWild:
Flutter checks the platform and embeds a real iOS or Android view inside its drawn screen with platform views. Its docs list the composition costs and limits. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/ios/platform-views

React Native wraps system views as components that sit in its layout. Source: https://reactnative.dev/docs/legacy/native-components-ios
decisions.detail:
SETTLED TARGET SELECTION

D-BUILD-FACT3=A supplies target facts; D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A and D-META-HASH1=A give comptime and build.target.os. The seed still accepts $build.os instead. That mismatch is not another target-selection choice, and this greenfield vote adds no old-spelling diagnostic or rewrite.

ONE HOST-VIEW CONTRACT

native.view(handle) consumes a typed target-specific system view and returns ui.Node. The first-party native package is shared with D-ONEAPP-RENDER1 and D-THEME2 and uses the public ui provider contract. The mapkit example denotes bindings through the ratified D-FFI-SWIFT1 bridge. The rest of the route screen and route data stay the same in all options.

Mounting owns the handle; unmounting disconnects callbacks and releases it exactly once on the system UI thread. Size, hit testing, tab order, focus and the accessibility subtree are joined once, not copied as competing Jet controls. D-A11Y-EXPORT1=B requires Jet-written system adapters. Callbacks after unmount must not access released state. These are acceptance obligations, not a working embedding claim.

A portable wrapper such as native.date_picker uses this same contract and falls back to kit where no host equivalent exists. A target-specific native.view(handle) instead requires a supported reachable compile-time branch; it cannot substitute an unrelated view silently. Native theme presets only style drawn controls and do not instantiate host views.

COMPOSITION

Require basic opacity, movement, rotation, rectangular clipping and Jet overlays by composing layers above and below the live host view. Do not claim arbitrary shaders, masks or 3D effects work. A does not expose host pixels to Jet filters; blur/color-filter operations that require those pixels are unsupported by this contract, not physically impossible in all toolkits. Flutter supports some backdrop blur, so a blanket claim that Flutter cannot blur native views would be false.

Static construction may diagnose a known unsupported combination early. For data-driven trees, the same support check must run when the scene is constructed at runtime and report a registered error before presentation. Preview-only checks cannot guarantee runtime safety. The application can choose a drawn substitute for effects requiring pixel access. Never silently ignore an effect.

ONE COST REMAINS

Mixing live system views into a drawn screen adds composition work and limits pixel filters. Keep host-view regions small, avoid unnecessary layer crossings during animation, and use drawn views where filters matter. Only mixed screens incur that additional work; no universal small-cost or zero-overhead result was measured.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES

B shows the same route in a separate system map screen, avoiding mixed composition but losing the inline form. C shows the same route with a drawn map; opening the Maps app remains an ordinary external action. It gives up the exact system map, not the route information.

CHECKED TODAY

os.jet printed linux using $build.os; os_plain.jet failed OsDispatchSubjectMismatch using build.target.os. ui_native.jet failed E1004 for core.ui.native. These probes prove the specific seed boundaries, not that every package in the world lacks embedding. Flutter's iOS platform-view documentation confirms transforms, clips, opacity and composition trade-offs. No Jet system view was embedded.

decisions.title: One --target flag names the platform for run, dev, test and build, and --device picks a phone
decisions.situation: Jet's command help exposes target and operating-system flags, while the current seed refuses web and phone runs. Earlier rulings already chose target names for phone builds and development. This vote extends one target selector across commands and adds an unambiguous device selector. We recommend retaining those names, retiring duplicate operating-system selection and refusing ambiguous device choices without starting a server or choosing a phone silently.
decisions.gist: Should one --target flag name the platform for every command, with --device picking a phone?
decisions.lesson: A platform is where an app runs: Linux, macOS, Windows, iOS, Android or the web. A device is one machine of that platform, such as your phone or a simulator. Earlier rulings spelled phone builds as jet build --target=ios and store upload as jet ship ios. Today the target flag mostly takes machine triples, and a second flag names the operating system.
decisions.story: Priya edits her habit app on a laptop. She wants to see it on her own iPhone, then in a browser, then run its tests on Android, without learning a triple like aarch64-linux-android.
decisions.inWild: Flutter's command-line guide exposes devices and emulators through one tool and uses a device selector on device-oriented commands. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/reference/flutter-cli
decisions.detail:
OWNER GATE

Extend D-NATIVEUI3's build target names and D-NATIVEUI-DEV1's development target names to run/test, with --device selecting a concrete execution destination. D-HOTSTATE1 retains state migration semantics; this vote does not redefine hot reload. D-GAME-PLATFORM1's headless twins prove device-free execution of that API, not universal UI accessibility testing already built today.

CHECKED TODAY

SolBallotReview ran run/dev/build --help: --target is documented for triples, boards or database targets; --os lists linux, macos, windows, web and freestanding. Running union.jet with --os=web gave E2104, Linux x86-64 ELF images only. ios/android runs gave E2104 and ship gave E2101. No build or test suite ran. Checking ios/android source succeeded, which does not establish device execution.

A'S SELECTION RULE

--target accepts platform shorthands, exact triples, board.<name> and existing named targets. A platform shorthand resolves a documented default architecture/profile and prints the resolved target; an incompatible --device is an error, not an implicit target rewrite. build needs no device. run/dev/test select exactly one matching device or browser. With none, report discovery/install guidance. With multiple matches, stop and list stable IDs; repeated friendly names never select arbitrarily. Noninteractive runs receive the same error, not a prompt or hang.

Retire --os entirely, including freestanding. Boards and complete freestanding triples already belong in --target; keeping a special --os=freestanding would leave two selectors for one target fact. Source profiles use the same target value. Teach the old flag with an exact replacement, and migrate checked-in source profiles and launch scripts. Do not promise jet fix rewrites arbitrary shell command text.

A web target launches the app host for that target; a browser selection chooses which browser receives it. Port/bind authority remains the approved development/server policy, not permission to expose a server publicly. Device tests use the same state/action acceptance, with physical input/accessibility checks when relevant. Existing jet ship ios remains; update publication belongs to the separately proposed ship update form.

FAIR OPTIONS

B makes individual jobs read naturally but introduces unrelated selector names. C groups device operations and can be clear for device administration; its cost is a second execution command family, not inherent unsafety. A changes existing --os callers, so the claim that no spelling changes was false.

decisions.title: A #Server mark on a function makes it run on the server, called from any screen like a plain function
decisions.situation: Jet web apps register action handlers by name, and screens need typed calls to those actions across the network. A function marker could derive registration and client stubs while preserving one route table. The vote chooses that declaration style, not whether network effects or authorization disappear. We recommend the marker with checked transport errors, shared form handling and narrowly eligible optimistic previews.
decisions.gist: Should a #Server mark on a function make it run on the server, callable from any screen?
decisions.lesson: Remote calls require serializable data, authorization and typed network failures. Both options generate typed clients from one action graph. A moves registration onto the function; eligible optimistic previews still obey the existing state-only rule.
decisions.story: Lena's club app has an invite button. The invite must run on the server, where the mail key lives. She wants to write the function once and call it from the web page and the phone app the same way.
decisions.inWild: React's use server marks remotely callable server functions, requires serializable arguments and warns authors to authorize every mutation. It also supports module-level placement. Source: https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-server
decisions.detail:
OWNER GATE

A adds a new bare #Server function marker, replaces action registration, and derives one action row and typed client stub. D-ROUTE-ONE1 keeps the single route table; D-SECRETEDGE1 checks client sinks. D-ROUTE-FILES2 introduced #Server.Get, but the later D-ROUTE-ONE1 text fixes route spelling to #server.Get. Examples still use the older uppercase route spelling. Do not present bare #Server as an already working route form.

CHECKED TODAY

Examples/features/web/app_hello.jet:15-16 and web/jet_web/run.jet:244 register actions. Core/Web/Web.jet:50-52 describes POST /actions/<name>; :472-508 checks Origin, and :503 accepts missing Origin. SolBallotReview checked and ran web_value.jet to inspect the app graph. That is not an end-to-end server-call or CSRF test. D-DX-SERVERFN1 also described typed action clients, but decision show reports it archived; do not silently treat its old awaiting syntax as current law.

EXACT A CONTRACT

A server-only effectful body stays server-side. Client projections carry Net plus structured transport, cancellation and uncertain-completion errors; normal server calls retain the body's own type. Higher-order references must preserve that distinction. Argument/result/error types must be serializable; secrets, handles and closures cannot cross. A transport failure after dispatch does not mean the mutation did not happen. No automatic retry of a possibly completed mutation is implied.

D-OPTIMISTIC1 allows safe state-only action previews in clients. A therefore cannot promise that every marked body is absent from the client. Only bodies satisfying that existing eligibility rule may supply a preview, with server authority retained; anything reading secrets or having other effects stays server-only. #Server(optimistic: false) explicitly disables that preview. This is one action body and one route row, not a second hand-written client policy.

Every endpoint authorizes its caller using the auth package and validates untrusted arguments. Origin checking alone is not complete authentication or CSRF protection, especially when missing Origin passes. Keep checked request context, token/same-site protection for cookie-authenticated mutations and the same handler for scripted and progressive form POSTs. Server-only module placement is not an implicit authentication boundary.

FAIR B

Registration can derive a typed client such as site.client(.invite); it need not force untyped string calls or late typo failures. B's cost is registration separated from its declaration, not absence of type safety. A replaces that registration rather than claiming it impossible.

SURFACE

One new marker form must be counted under D-SURFACE-BUDGET1. Removing a library method does not cancel a marker count. D-CALLSITE-MARK2 concerns ownership marks; it does not prove that every possible network operator is forbidden.

decisions.title: App data lives in typed local collections that work offline and sync with the server
decisions.situation: Apps can lose their network while users are editing records. Jet's current sync API accepts display text, while the approved merge types do not yet provide a typed persistent collection. This vote chooses typed local collections over the same merge and transport mechanism, not a second sync engine. We recommend local persistence with explicit pending, rejected and conflicting states, preserving concurrent edits rather than silently replacing them.
decisions.gist: Should app data live in typed local collections that work offline and sync when online?
decisions.lesson: Local-first means the app saves changes on the device first, then sends them to the server when it can. A merge rule decides what happens when two devices change the same record. Jet already has merge types for shared text, lists and counters. Today an app has no typed offline store.
decisions.story: Rui's crew-scheduling app is used in tunnels with no signal. Crews mark shifts done underground, and the office must see every change when they surface, with nothing lost.
decisions.inWild: Replicache persists a browser-side local copy, queues offline changes and reconciles with server authority. It is now in maintenance mode; its site directs new work toward Zero. Source: https://replicache.dev/
decisions.detail:
OWNER GATE

Add typed persistent collections as a wrapper over D-SYNC1's merge documents and transport. D-INVALIDATE1 supplies read/write footprints; D-REACT-REF1 supplies notifications; D-OPTIMISTIC1 supplies pending/rejected reconciliation. Keep typed app.sync as the expert primitive. Replacing display-text shims is owed; replacing the ratified typed app.sync API with an unrelated collection engine is not a mere defect fix.

CHECKED TODAY

Core/App/App.jet:126 accepts doc_show and over as String. The public import is app, not core.app: SolBallotReview's app_sync.jet checked and ran, printing SyncError(invalid session) and x:y from core.web.sync. Core/Web/Web.jet:1336-1365 stores live results in a process registry; :1406-1408 concatenates sync strings. The failed core.app import is not evidence that the public app module is absent.

A'S CONTRACT

A collection has stable record IDs and durable per-user storage. Writes through collection.edit(id, fn(record) { ... }) operate on tracked persistent records; changing an arbitrary copied Shift does not secretly persist it. Local commit updates readers and marks a pending operation. Server authorization remains authoritative. Server queries expose read-only projections through the same observation API, not a promise that arbitrary remote queries become writable local tables.

Use D-SYNC1 merge semantics for text, lists, maps and counters. Plain fields use causal versioned registers: sequential writes replace their predecessor; concurrent alternatives are retained until resolved. A deterministic display choice does not mean chronologically latest. Order causal versions and break concurrent ties by stable actor/op identity; do not claim a hybrid logical clock is immune to wall-clock skew. Retain losing concurrent values and surface a standard conflict state with a default resolution view. The author may select a merge type for domain-specific intent.

REJECTION AND PRIVACY

Apply authorized server state, then rebase still-pending local operations; never undo a later edit by restoring an old snapshot. Deletes carry tombstones with causal versions so offline edits cannot silently resurrect deleted records. Access filters run on the server. Partition caches by account; logout removes that account's local credentials and cache. Offline revocation cannot erase copies already held by a disconnected device, and no option promises that.

PERSISTENCE

Write schema versions into shipped manifests and stored data. check can compare a declared release baseline, not infer all historical schemas from current source. Require migrations for incompatible changes; test upgrades with old data and pending edits. Quota, corruption and unavailable storage return typed errors; a failed durable write must not be shown as saved. No browser or device database implementation was exercised here.

decisions.title: One Jet theme by default; experts can choose system-like presets or real host controls
decisions.situation: Drawn controls need colors, fonts and spacing even when an app author supplies no styling. The seed's node_color call accepts a fixed color, not an app-wide theme. This vote chooses one Jet design, system-like designs by default, or minimal styling that authors complete themselves. We recommend one useful default with typed overrides and an optional system-like preset, without claiming a preset is an exact system control.
decisions.gist: Should apps use one Jet theme by default, with system-like styling as an expert opt-in?
decisions.lesson: A gives an app a default theme; one accent color brands it. Appearance follows light, dark and accessibility settings. Experts override individual values or choose native.theme(), a system-like preset for drawn controls. That preset is not a real system control. Exact host controls use the companion native embedding path instead.
decisions.story: Ana wants her booking app in her club's green, on every phone and computer, from one line. Rui wants his notes app to look like a Mac app on a Mac and an Android app on Android.
decisions.inWild:
Flutter apps commonly use one Material theme on every system, seeded from one color, with typed theme values and local overrides. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/cookbook/design/themes

Flutter also offers Cupertino widgets as a separate library for apps that want the iOS look. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/widgets/cupertino
decisions.detail:
SCOPE AND DEPENDENCIES

This chooses visual direction, not final mockups. Under D-ONEAPP-RENDER1=A, ui primitives and separate kit controls share a typed theme. D-UI-HOME1 keeps it in ui; D-ONEAPP-MODEL1=A keeps app as the higher-level wrapper. app.new(..., theme:) forwards the same value to ui.app, without another theme engine. If the renderer vote chooses a different model, reconcile this drawn-theme contract before implementation.

BEGINNER DEFAULT AND EXPERT CONTROL

No theme argument gives a neutral finished design. ui.theme supplies typed accent, typography, radius, spacing and density overrides. All values can change app-wide or locally through the same theme mechanism; nearer overrides inherit unspecified values. Honor live light/dark changes, high contrast, forced web colors, text scaling and reduced motion. Those reader settings deliberately affect colors and sizes, so one design does not mean identical pixels. Diagnostics and visual acceptance remain necessary; contrast checks alone cannot prove accessibility.

THE SHARED NATIVE PACKAGE

native.theme() returns the same theme type. It uses available host font, accent and appearance values, maintained shape/spacing presets, and documented Jet fallbacks. This is proposed behavior, not proof every host exposes every value. Presets approximate system styling and may lag redesigns; they never instantiate host widgets. Exact controls use native.date_picker through D-PLATFORM-OVERRIDE1=A's native.view contract, with its composition limits. Theme-only use does not require embedding approval.

PLATFORM BEHAVIOR

Back commands, window chrome and input/scroll conventions belong to host integration, not theme values. They remain shared requirements for every option and never change action meaning.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES

B defaults to per-system drawn presets, while still allowing an explicit common brand theme. A maintains those presets for opt-in users too, so 'B triples the work' is unfair. The difference is the beginner default. C deliberately starts minimally styled and still honors explicit accent and radius values. Every option styles the same booking screen.

OWNER ACCEPTANCE

Approve actual palette, typography, spacing and focus appearance from native/web mockups in light/dark/high contrast and large text. Seed output does not prove visual taste or delegate that final approval.

ONE COST REMAINS

An exact host look is not automatic: system-like presets are opt-in approximations. Experts can tune values and use supported real host controls, inheriting the companion embedding costs.

CHECKED TODAY

ui_values_fixed.jet printed 20.0 for node_color. Core/Ui/Ui.jet:222-224 accepts a custom-node color. That proves this call, not every theme API's absence. Flutter's theme guide documents app-wide defaults and local overrides.

decisions.title: Jet ships a full standard set of about forty views, built only from public primitives
decisions.situation: Jet's current view tree has five node kinds, while complete apps also need pickers, lists and overlays. A shipped control set can save beginners from selecting an outside kit. This vote chooses that first-party set and its package home, not another view or state system. We recommend standard controls in ui, built from public view, layout, text and host-service primitives.
decisions.gist: Should Jet ship about forty standard views, built only from public primitives, instead of only the basics?
decisions.lesson: Foundations compose into standard controls. All options retain one state-driven view model. A ships the set with ui; C ships it separately; B leaves kit selection to users. Five node kinds do not limit the number of composed views.
decisions.story: Kofi writes a clinic booking app. He needs a date picker, a time picker, a list with search, tabs and a confirmation dialog. He wants all of them from Jet, matching each other, on every target.
decisions.inWild: Compose Material 3 provides DatePicker, DatePickerDialog and DateRangePicker over typed picker state. Source: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/components/datepickers
decisions.detail:
OWNER GATE AND HOMES

D-UI-HOME1=A already puts the node tree in the ui package; D-UI-VIEW1=A already chooses ui.app, ui.Node and state-driven views. A adds a shipped standard control set in that package, not a Core framework or rival gui tree. D-GAME-PLATFORM1's gui controls consume this set; independent editor helpers remain consumers. app is an optional routed wrapper, not required for one date picker. All alternatives keep the same view/state protocol.

CHECKED TODAY

Core/Ui/Ui.jet:46-52 lists Custom, Text, Box, Button and TextInput. Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/gui/gui.jet:424-475 contains editor-specific views, with host wrappers at :492-548. SolBallotReview's ui_values.jet checked and ran text/button/box construction. Five node kinds do not prove that only five public view constructors exist.

A'S SET

Public foundations: text, box, button, image, canvas, text_input, row, column, grid, stack and scroll. Controls: link, text_area, checkbox, switch, radio_group, slider, stepper, select and search_field. Pickers/status: date_picker, time_picker, progress_bar, spinner, badge and avatar. Structure: list, table, tabs, toolbar, sidebar, split_view, card, divider and spacer. Overlays: sheet, dialog, alert, menu, context_menu, tooltip and toast. This is about forty views including foundations, not forty additional node kinds. Layout details depend on D-LAYOUT2; theme direction is D-THEME2.

Every standard view uses public composition and host-service APIs, never compiler privileges. Native system dialogs may be providers beneath public host primitives; do not pretend all services can be built from six visual nodes. Reorderable rows have stable keys under D-UI-VIEW1. Shared acceptance includes keyboard navigation, focus restoration for overlays, accessibility roles/actions, long text, locale-aware dates, text scaling, right-to-left layout and virtualization without losing focus.

D-API-COMPOSE1 requires documented primitives and typed options rather than policy-only sibling names. Customize through theme values and composition first. Copying source remains an expert path, not a magic removal of maintenance: copied variants must adopt relevant upstream fixes.

FAIR PACKAGING AND COUNTS

C can keep versioned UI-independent kit dependencies separate; this is a real organization benefit even if linker reachability removes unused code. A chooses one shipped dependency for the beginner. Artifact-size equivalence must be proved, not asserted here. D-SURFACE-BUDGET1 counts library APIs without gating their count; no keyword/marker ceiling rises merely because a control function is added.

Research: Compose Material 3 documents DatePicker with DatePickerState at https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/components/datepickers. No toolkit requires every app to use every control.

decisions.title: A generic alias writes its type parameters on its name: Grid<T>: [[T]]
decisions.situation: A generic alias gives one name to an existing shape, such as rows of any element type. The compiler accepts parameters on that name, while the declaration ruling puts parameters on a kind word such as struct. An alias has no kind word, leaving that rule incomplete. We recommend stating the exception explicitly: generic alias parameters go on the alias name, without introducing a keyword.
decisions.gist: Should a generic alias write its type parameters on its name, since it has no kind word?
decisions.lesson: A type parameter, such as T, stands for any type the user picks. A struct writes it on its kind word: Box: struct<T> { value: T }. A function writes it on fn. An alias has no kind word, because it only renames a type. Today the compiler accepts Pair<T>: (first: T, second: T).
decisions.story: Ravi writes many functions over [[Float]] and [[String]] grids. He wants one name, Grid<T>, that means a list of rows of T and stays the same type as [[T]].
decisions.inWild: TypeScript places generic parameters after the declared type name; its generic types preserve the selected element type. Source: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/generics.html
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS DECIDES

Where a generic alias writes its type parameters, given that an alias has no kind word.

TODAY

A scratch file with Pair<T>: (first: T, second: T) and swap: fn(p: Pair<Int>) -> Pair<Int> passed jet check and ran. Another with Grid<T>: [[T]] and total(g: Grid<Float>) accepted a plain list of Float rows and printed 6.0. The parser takes parameters on the alias name (Declarations/Types.jet:51-57).

D-DECL-COLON1=A says kind parameters go on the kind word, never on the name. Its table writes an alias as Meters: Int, with no keyword. That replaces the alias keyword D-ALIAS-BIND2=B had kept, so an alias has no kind word.

D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A had made generic types and aliases into recipe functions and removed <>. It was archived on 2026-10-29, and D-DECL-COLON1's struct<T> and fn<T> use <> again.

A separate lag: a plain alias such as Key: Int | String gave E0324 in a scratch run, an alias needs type parameters. D-DECL-COLON1 ratified plain aliases, so that refusal is a defect to fix under any option.

OPTION A IN DETAIL

The law becomes: type parameters go on the kind word; an alias has no kind word, so its parameters go on its name. Grid<T>: [[T]] is the same type as [[T]] for each T. Writing <T> anywhere else on an alias gets an error with the fix.

options.technical: Amends D-DECL-COLON1's sentence with one stated case; matches Declarations/Types.jet:51-57.

run: fn() { total(Grid{rows: [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0]]}) }

options.name: An alias kind word

options.technical: Revives the alias word D-ALIAS-BIND2=B kept, for generic aliases only; plain aliases stay Meters: Int.

total: fn(g: Grid<Float>) -> Float { … }

recommendation.why: An alias has no kind word, so its name is a clear place for parameters. This preserves transparent generic aliases without adding a keyword.
gains: Familiar from peer languages.
No new keyword.
No code changes.

losses.loss: One stated case beside the kind-word rule.
losses.mitigation: The rule reads: on the kind word, or on an alias's name; <T> elsewhere gets an error with the fix.

whyNot.reason: A plain [[Float]] no longer passes, and every caller wraps its value.
A keyword only generic aliases use, so plain and generic aliases look different.

recommendation.tradeoff: One stated case in the parameter rule, in exchange for familiar generic aliases with no new keyword.

decisions.title: May a field list named cases such as Celsius(Float) inline, written exactly as inside an enum?
decisions.situation: A union lists types a value may hold, while an enum lists named cases such as Celsius and Fahrenheit, each holding a Float. The seed accepts a separate Temp enum but rejects those case declarations written directly in a field's union. This vote chooses inline structural cases, a separately named enum, or an inline anonymous enum. We recommend inline structural cases with the existing dot-free declaration spelling, keeping bare names unambiguously types.
decisions.gist: May a union list named cases like Celsius(Float), written exactly as inside an enum?
decisions.lesson: Every option stores Celsius or Fahrenheit in the same field. A writes cases directly there; fields listing the same cases share a type. Bare names still mean types. A named empty state such as Off needs a declared enum; ? means absence only. C instead writes an enum body in the field, making a separate type for each declaration.
decisions.story: Yuki stores a thermostat temperature in a settings record. Only that one field uses Celsius or Fahrenheit, yet today she must declare and name an enum first. She wants to write the two cases in the field itself.
decisions.inWild: OCaml polymorphic variants allow named alternatives without a declared type, with structural type checking: https://ocaml.org/manual/5.2/polyvariant.html. Its manual also warns about weaker typo discipline in open inferred variant sets. Jet's proposed inline sets remain explicitly closed and exhaustive; this vote does not add OCaml's open-row inference.
decisions.detail:
THE CHOICE

A permits Name(T) as a named structural union case. Bare Name stays a type, preserving Int | String. Named cases may mix with type cases but cannot reuse a type-case name in the same union. Sets are closed, flattened and duplicate-free; one name with two payload types is an error. Construct and match .Celsius(value); plain Floats never guess a scale.

RATIFIED BOUNDARIES

D-ENUM-DOT1=B keeps declarations dot-free. A extends D-UNIONTYPE1's existing sum mechanism, not a competing enum runtime. D-ALT-SUBSET1=A widens exact subsets by value, not mutable references or containers. Named cases match by exact name/payload. Declared enums remain nominal, requiring explicit outward conversion; transparent aliases remain structural. Earlier type cases inside enums are dropped because bare enum names declare cases.

EMPTY CASES

A requires a declared enum for a named empty state such as Off. Optional ? means absence, not any business state. This is A's restriction, not proof that unambiguous alternatives are impossible. C supports empty cases without lookup-dependent meaning.

STRONG C

C permits an anonymous enum type in a field, using the existing enum body spelling. Each expression introduces a nominal type fixed by its enclosing field. Context builds .Celsius(21.5) in that type. An alias can name the same type; an independently declared enum is different.

C can include an ordinary empty Off case, but does not mix structural type alternatives or gain structural subset widening. Comma layout belongs to the separate brace vote.

SERIALIZATION

Do not promise every inline/named wire format is identical: enum markers can change tagging and names. This ballot adds no serialization options. Extend existing sum encoding where derivation is requested and reject ambiguous tagged/untagged mixes. SerdeItems.jet:1047-1089 contains the encoding choices; the old 988-1031 citation did not establish them. No serialization probe ran, so no existing wire result is claimed.

ONE COST REMAINS

Named empty cases cannot appear directly in A's union form. Use a declared enum for Off, and ? for absence only. No teaching diagnostics or retired-spelling rewrites are added.

CHECKED TODAY

temp_enum.jet printed 21.5 C. temp_union.jet failed E0003 at the case parenthesis. enum_comma.jet failed E0003 at the comma; enum_empty.jet showed Off() also fails E0003 in today's enum grammar. A and C's new type-position forms are proposed, not working syntax.

decisions.title: A value of a smaller union passes where a larger union holding all its cases is expected
decisions.situation: A plain Int passes to Int or String, but an Int-or-String value is refused by a helper accepting Int, String or Bool. Authors must match and rebuild values that already fit. The vote decides whether whole structural unions widen automatically, without widening mutable references or containers. We recommend exact subset widening; transparent aliases remain structural, while declared enums retain their outward conversion boundary.
decisions.gist: Should a value of a smaller union pass where a larger union with all its cases is expected?
decisions.lesson: A union type such as Int | String says a value is one of those types. Widening means a value fits a broader type with no conversion code. Today a plain Int widens into Int | String. A whole Int | String value does not widen into Int | String | Bool.
decisions.story: Omar's parser returns Int | String for a cell. His table stores Int | String | Bool. Every cell needs a two-arm match that rebuilds the same value, just to satisfy the types.
decisions.inWild: TypeScript accepts any member of a union and restricts operations to those valid for the possible members. Source: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#union-types
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS DECIDES

Extend D-UNIONTYPE1=A's member conversion to structural subset values. SolBallotReview's union.jet passed check and run with 7; subset.jet gave E0112 at store(x).

EXACT RULE

At value bindings, arguments, returns and failure propagation, every source case must occur unchanged in the target. Matching uses resolved type identity, not printed names. Preserve the active case and payload; remap its discriminant if necessary. Normal payload ownership costs remain; no hidden container-wide copy or allocation is permitted.

A transparent alias is the same structural union on either side. A declared enum remains nominal and never widens outward into another type. Entry into an enum is allowed only if D-ALT-CASES1=A separately permits it; this vote alone does not amend D-UNIONTYPE1's explicit enum boundary. Exact labelled cases compare by label and payload type, never payload alone.

LIMITS

No widening through editable or retained references, including & and &&. Otherwise a callee could write a Bool into storage declared Int | String. No recursive conversion inside lists, maps, records or function signatures. A collection must explicitly map its elements when a larger element type is needed. Exhaustive matching still covers every target case.

Changing a transparent alias changes nothing; introducing enum creates nominal identity. Neither ballot promises that adding enum is behavior-free.

options.name: Widen automatically
options.detail: A smaller unnamed union widens into a larger alternative at the places plain values already widen. Not through & parameters or inside lists.
options.technical: Exact subset value conversion; no recursive variance or reference widening. Enum entry depends on D-ALT-CASES1; enum exit remains explicit.

options.name: Rebuild by hand
options.detail: A smaller union never widens; the author matches each case.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.why: Every value of the smaller union already fits the larger one, so the rebuild match adds nothing. Plain values already widen the same way.
gains: No rebuild matches.
Same rule as plain values.
Declared enums stay separate.

losses.loss: A list of a smaller union does not widen into a larger list.
losses.mitigation: The error shows a one-line map that widens each element, so the copy stays visible.

whyNot.reason: Every call needs a match that rebuilds the same value.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more implicit widening, in exchange for no rebuild code.

Reproduced subset refusal and ordinary member widening; aligned enum entry with the case ballot and removed unconditional constant-time claims.

decisions.title: Commas separate data members; method declarations with bodies take no comma
decisions.situation: The seed accepts commas between struct fields, but its formatter removes them from declarations and enum commas are rejected. Values use comma-separated entries, while method declarations already end at their own body brace. This vote chooses one separator rule for brace data lists without adding commas after methods. We recommend commas between data members, with a trailing comma when the formatter wraps a list.
decisions.gist: Should commas separate data members, while method declarations with bodies take none?
decisions.lesson: A uses commas between fields, enum cases and value entries. A trailing comma is accepted on either line layout; the formatter writes it only across lines. A method declaration with a body takes no comma. A field containing a closure or record is still data and needs a separator. All options show the same enum, fields and method.
decisions.story: Hana wants her Server fields and values to use one list rule, without a comma after its url method.
decisions.inWild: Rust separates struct fields with commas and permits a trailing comma: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/structs.html. Its methods are separate associated items rather than comma-list fields. This is precedent for separating data from code declarations, not proof that every language requires a comma on every multiline field.
decisions.detail:
A'S PRECISE RULE

Require commas between data members in brace member/value lists: struct fields, enum cases, record entries, typed collection elements and map entries. A final comma is optional in source on either line layout. The formatter writes it for multiline lists and removes it for compact one-line lists, following D-TRAILCOMMA1=A. Line wrapping does not change which member is data.

ONLY METHOD DECLARATIONS ARE EXEMPT

A declared method or other declared code-body member ends at its closing brace, with no comma. A data field whose initializer happens to end in a record literal, closure or code block still takes its list separator. A function requirement with no body is a data-like member and takes a comma. Associated types and constants follow that member-list rule in trait and impl bodies. Module/file bodies, ordinary statements and control blocks are unchanged. No comma goes after an ordinary function body just because it is inside braces.

RATIFIED BOUNDARIES

D-ENUM-DOT1=B settles dots, not enum comma parsing; commas remain this vote. D-RECORD-BRACE1=A makes {min, max} a punned record. A keeps commas when the formatter wraps it, so its special formatter clause retaining an explicit member can be dropped. Parenthesis and bracket list semantics do not change. Greenfield cutover updates repository callers together; no compatibility parser, teaching diagnostic or old-spelling rewrite ships. Greenfield does not prove that no user code exists.

SAME PROGRAM

Each option declares Mode and Server, constructs the same server and prints 8080. B retains formatter-style declaration lines and comma-separated values. C makes newlines separators only in multiline brace lists; it must account for ambiguous wrapped punned records. Neither alternative adds commas after methods.

ONE COST REMAINS

Multiline data declarations gain visible commas under A's formatter. It writes them during wrapping; authors do not put commas after methods. This is a visible syntax cost, not a cost removed by mentioning a formatter.

CHECKED TODAY

brace_today.jet ran and printed 8080. Formatting that scratch copy expanded the enum and removed struct-field commas, keeping the method comma-free. brace_mixed.jet ran with comma-separated fields and a comma-free method, printing 3. enum_comma.jet failed E0003. These establish the shown grammar and formatter behavior; A's unified rule is proposed.

decisions.title: Every record uses braces: {x: 1} is an unnamed struct, and paren tuples retire
decisions.situation: Unnamed records use parentheses today, while context-typed struct values use braces. One-member parenthesized records fail, and turning a record into a struct requires changing brackets. The vote decides which brackets hold named members and how records differ from code blocks. We recommend braces, with an explicit rule preserving function bodies, empty blocks and punned fields.
decisions.gist: Should every group of named values use braces, so {x: 1} reads as a struct without its name?
decisions.lesson: A record is a group of named values, like a struct with no declared name. Today one record has two spellings. One is (x: 1, y: 2) in parentheses. The other is {x: 1, y: 2} in braces, where a type is expected. Struct literals use braces: Point{x: 1, y: 2}. Parentheses also hold arguments and grouping.
decisions.story: Kemal returns (min: lo, max: hi) from a helper. Later he wants a method on it, so he declares a struct. He must change every parenthesis to a brace, and he learns that (n: 3) alone is an error.
decisions.inWild: TypeScript describes object types in braces and accepts matching object values in braces; object properties can be named directly or through a type alias. Source: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS DECIDES

Move unnamed record types, values and destructuring from parentheses to braces. D-LIT-DOT1=B already chose braces for struct and named-payload values; removing the surviving named-parenthesis payload is owed independently. Amend S73, S74, D-TUPLE-DESTRUCT1 and D-PAT-NAMED-NEST1 where their parentheses change.

CHECKED TODAY

SolBallotReview's record_clean.jet passed check and run: tuple destructuring printed 1 9, and move_to({x: 3, y: 4}) printed 3. one.jet gives E0003 for (x: 1). record_arm.jet and payload_statement.jet fail at a comma. map.jet returned [ana: 3]. Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Expressions.jet:1036-1074 rejects one-member tuples; :1974-2054 parses record fields and both payload forms. Parser/Statements.jet:844-863 treats dispatch-arm braces as blocks.

A'S BRACE RULE

Braces after a function signature, control head or block marker hold code. Braces after struct, enum, trait, module or impl hold members. Elsewhere a group is a record when all entries are fields or puns and at least one field has a colon or a comma separates puns. Quoted keys select map grammar. Empty {} remains a block; typed empty maps remain [String: Int]{}.

Thus {x} yields x as code, {x, y} is a record, and {x: x} is a one-member record. In multiline punned records the formatter retains one explicit field, rather than removing every comma and turning the result into code. A one-member pun canonicalizes to {x: x}. This also binds D-BRACE-LAYOUT1.

Function bodies always hold code. Returning a record needs inner braces, even for one member. Missing braces get a result-type diagnostic; do not promise an error at a comma when no comma exists. No blanket claim that every changed brace reading is harmless substitutes for migration tests.

A statement-start brace pattern followed by : or := is destructuring through bounded lookahead. Partial patterns keep .. under D-DESTRUCT1. Migrate parenthesized records in one parser-based cutover preserving evaluation order. Prove record/block classification, control-header literals, nested maps, interpolation, singleton puns and multiline puns.

decisions.title: Record member order becomes part of the type and determines comparison
decisions.situation: A record groups named values, such as a guest's last and first names. The seed sorts record members alphabetically, so that guest list compares first names even when last is written first. Written-order comparison requires preserving member order in the record type, not merely changing the sorting function. We recommend that change, with explicit sort keys for other orders and the resulting type and display consequences stated openly.
decisions.gist: Should member order belong to a record's type and determine its default comparison?
decisions.lesson: Python tuples and ordered dataclasses compare in written order; dicts support equality but not <. A preserves member order in record types, comparison, display and encoding. Reordered members therefore form a different type. All options add multi-key sort_by for explicit orders. B instead removes default ordering, including use as ordered map or set keys.
decisions.story: Ines sorts a guest list written {last: "Zed", first: "Amy"} and {last: "Abe", first: "Bob"}. She expects Abe first. Jet puts Zed first, because first sorts before last alphabetically.
decisions.inWild: Python dataclass(order=True) compares fields in definition order, and requires identical classes for the generated comparison: https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html. Tuples and named tuples compare by position; dicts compare for equality but reject ordering. Custom sorts can use several keys with attrgetter: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html. Rust derived Ord follows struct declaration order: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cmp/trait.Ord.html#derivable. Neither fact establishes that every comparable record in every language follows written order.
decisions.detail:
THE OWNER'S PYTHON QUESTION

Python tuples and named tuples compare by position. dataclass(order=True) opts into field-order comparison; plain dataclasses do not order by default. Dicts preserve insertion order but reject < and related ordering operations, while equality remains available and ignores insertion order. Executed Python probes confirmed ordered guests put Abe first, custom first/last keys put Amy first, tuples/named tuples compare positionally, dict equality succeeds and dict < raises TypeError. These are distinct data models, not a blanket 'Python records compare in written order' rule.

WHY WRITTEN ORDER

Alphabetical ordering is coherent for label-sorted type identity and insensitive to source reordering; that is C's genuine strength. It can nevertheless surprise users: year/month/day compares day first, and min/max compares max first. The old draft's major/minor/patch example was wrong because that written order is already alphabetical. No claim about all mainstream languages is needed.

A CHANGES TYPE IDENTITY

D-TUPLE-ORDER1=A and S73 currently use label-sorted identity. A amends both: an ordered sequence of names and member types defines the record type. Its comparison, printing and encoded field order use that sequence. Moving a member changes those outcomes and type identity. An initializer with an expected record type evaluates expressions in source order, then arranges matching named fields in the expected type's order. The same named fields may convert by value at bindings, arguments and returns; this is not mutable-reference or container covariance.

An untyped list takes its record order from the first entry and converts later matching entries to that element type. Comparing independently typed records with different orders requires a common explicit target type first; do not silently pick the left operand's order, which could break comparison symmetry. Equality, ordering and ordered-key behavior all use the same resulting type, without a private second order for maps or sets. Wrong member types still fail rather than being repaired by reorder conversion.

SHARED KEY API

All options add sort_by and sort_by_desc with one or more key functions, applied in the written key order. The existing two-argument comparator form remains. .member is the ratified shorthand under D-SUBJECT-CALL1=A, not a second key mechanism. The examples propose guests.sort_by(.first, .last); extra arguments are not implemented by the seed. They do not require another sorting algorithm or hidden per-value order metadata.

FAIR B AND C

B retains label-sorted record identity and equality but removes default ordering. It also removes records as ordered map/set keys rather than keeping an invisible alphabetical order for those APIs. Use an explicitly ordered named key type when that is needed. C retains the coherent label-sorted identity and comparison. Every option supports explicit multi-key sorting.

CUTOVER AND ACCEPTANCE

D-RECORD-BRACE1=A moves the proposed record spelling to braces; seed probes use today's parentheses only as evidence. Migrate all affected repository callers, synthesized signatures, nested records, printing/encoding expectations and ordered keys in one cutover. Do not defer Core signature changes to later edits or promise retired-spelling rewrites. Require comparisons with reversed field orders, operand-swap consistency, expected-type conversion, first-list-item inference and effectful initializer order.

ONE COST REMAINS

Member order becomes significant for type identity, sort order and output order. Name explicit sort keys where ordering must not change, and use a fixed declared record type at stable boundaries.

CHECKED TODAY

order.jet printed Zed, the label-sorted first/last record, a 2024 date chosen by day, Abe after sort_by(.last), and Bob after sort_by_desc(.first). order_keys.jet failed E0104 and E0107 for two keys. S73 is at Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1171-1176 in the reviewed checkout. No proposed order-sensitive type or multi-key API ran.

decisions.title: Run normal exit cleanup before process replacement, with an explicit skip setting
decisions.situation: Process replacement hands the running program over to another one, like a shell's exec. The approved call skips cleanup, and the seed does not implement that call yet. Running cleanup first would finish logs and restore the terminal, but cleanup cannot be undone if startup fails or deletes an input file. We recommend normal cleanup by default with an explicit skip setting, while stating that irreversible cost without calling it rare.
decisions.gist: Should process replacement run normal cleanup first, with an explicit opt-out for resource-sensitive handoffs?
decisions.lesson: Every option hands the same launcher to sh, which exits 3. A prepares the command, then runs normal exit cleanup before handing over. Checks can catch errors early, but cannot guarantee startup. One cost remains: cleanup is irreversible, including deleted temporary inputs. Use explicit kept handles or .cleanup(.Skip) when the target needs those resources.
decisions.story: Priya's launcher records a tool choice and leaves a full-screen picker before handing over. She wants its log finished and terminal restored without writing a second cleanup path.
decisions.inWild:
# POSIX shell; source and exercised results are in detail.
exec sh -c 'exit 3'
# Same process, exit 3; the old shell's EXIT trap does not run.
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS AMENDS

D-CORE-PROCREPLACE1=A ratified spec.replace_process(), skip-cleanup and a Windows waiting stand-in. A changes default cleanup and post-cleanup errors; B keeps that approval. Retain -[Exec, Time.Wait]> Never IOError!, admitting Exec before preparation or cleanup. D-JAI-DEFER1=A supplies one reverse-order cleanup list; D-TERM-COMMANDS1=A supplies terminal restoration. Reuse the ordinary exit boundary, not a second cleanup mechanism.

PREPARE, THEN COMMIT

Reject ratified incompatible settings before side effects: Capture/Stream, terminal, detached, timeout, output_limit and under. Retain cwd, environment, supported limits and explicit keep_open ownership under D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1=A. Unset stdin stays closed. Pin launch data and kept handles outside frames cleanup destroys. Resolve using the spec's PATH/cwd and check what can be validated without changing the caller. Preparation failure returns IOError without exit cleanup.

After preparation, A commits to normal cleanup and terminal restoration. Launch data and kept handles survive; flush writers without closing transferred handles. Start only after cleanup succeeds. A reported startup failure after commitment prints once and exits 127 for missing program/interpreter, otherwise 126, without repeated cleanup. Cleanup failure follows existing exit-failure policy and never starts the target. Cleanup can remove files or cancel work; it cannot be rolled back.

NO AUTOMATIC TEMPORARY RETENTION

The prior draft scanned argument strings and cancelled temporary-path deletion. That misses --input=path, script/config dependencies, environment references, symlink aliases and arbitrary deferred deletes. It also changes ownership and can leave unowned files. Remove that mechanism: temporary owners keep normal deletion semantics.

Targets needing temporary content use existing explicit keep_open ownership and an open-handle path where supported, or .Skip when the original pathname must survive. No new file-lifetime API is hidden here.

PREFLIGHT IS NOT A PROOF

Opening an executable protects that file against replacement/unlinking, not its interpreter, loader, libraries or later permission/resource checks. Path-based starts and scripts have different constraints. Do not substitute a script interpreter manually and claim unchanged semantics. Linux execveat of a script with a close-on-exec descriptor can fail ENOENT; inheriting it can leak a descriptor. Use the approved launch and kept-handle contracts, not a prescribed syscall trick. No Jet measurement establishes failure frequency.

SKIP AND FAIR B

spec.cleanup(.Skip).replace_process() keeps skip-cleanup behavior: no defers, resource cleanup or exit handlers; output still flushes. This suits deliberate terminal/resource inheritance. A defaults to .Run. The setting applies to replacement, not run/spawn.

B keeps skip as the sole contract. Callers can finish resource scopes and restore the terminal explicitly; not every launcher needs to duplicate all cleanup. Ordinary reported launch errors return as approved. Neither option can recover from kernel failure after the old image is already destroyed.

ONE COST REMAINS

Cleanup is irreversible: late startup failure ends the launcher, and cleanup may delete inputs the target needs. Use explicit kept handles where suitable or .Skip for resource-sensitive handoffs. This is not engineered away or proven negligible for every launcher.

WINDOWS AND TIERS

Keep Windows start/wait/exit with the child's status. A cleans once before start; B skips. Add no descendant-killing policy. One runtime contract covers O0/O1/O2, memory execution and file fallback under D-EXEC-RELAUNCH1=A and D-EXEC-NOEXEC1=A. Web refuses Exec before cleanup.

Future acceptance covers rejected settings, normal cleanup/defer order, terminal restoration, kept writers/handles, temporary-path deletion, scripts, missing interpreter/loader, cleanup failure, late startup failure, signals and the Windows stand-in. These are not completed checks.

CHECKED EVIDENCE

exec_now.jet ran a child and exited 3; exec_replace.jet failed E0102. HostProcess.jet:72-85 uses a root stop for cleanup. RouteAFiles.jet:694-698 describes last-owner temporary-file deletion. ProcessExecutionPrepare.jet:192-278 contains relaunch and argv/env preparation, not the old draft's complete preflight. Shell probes skipped EXIT traps on successful exec (3) and missing executable (127).

PRIMARY SOURCES

Linux execve documents permission, interpreter, I/O, resource and format failures, including failure after image teardown: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execve.2.html. execveat documents script-descriptor limitations: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execveat.2.html. No proposed replacement implementation or late-failure rate was exercised.
