sections.body:
# Project, package and config files today: a map and what confuses people

Status: research, for card #6368. Written 2026-10-30 against dev `e784bb1ffe`.
Companion proposal: `Docs/proposals/project-package-config-2026-10-30.md`.

## Summary

Jet has no single answer to "where does this setting go?" today. The same fact can be written in two to six places, the same word means three or four different things, and several ratified rulings disagree with each other and with the code.

- **Files.** Twelve file names carry configuration or command code: `package.jet`, `pkg.jet` (retired but still read), `workspace.jet`, `env.jet`, `config.jet`, `build.jet`, `test.jet`, `dev.jet`, `bench.jet`, `run.jet`, `.jet/lock` and the ratified-but-unbuilt `jet.lock`. On top of those come an inline `package { }` block and freely named `configs:` files. `fn build` can sit in any file of a package, including `tools/build_entry.jet` and `workspace.jet`.
- **Fields.** `package.jet` accepts 25 top-level fields. They mix four kinds of fact: what the package *is* (name, version), what it *needs* (deps, effects), what it *makes* (outputs), and how *this checkout* works (profiles, members, environments, toolchain, policy ceilings). Nothing in the file tells you which kind a field is.
- **Words.** "Workspace" means the monorepo root (`workspace.jet`), the editor window (Canvas), and, in Jai, one compilation with its own options. The owner has ruled that it moves to "project". "Profile", "target", "build" and "package" are each overloaded too.
- **Rulings.** Three rulings named the root differently (Package, Jetspace, workspace). Two rulings place `fn build` differently. Two rulings order settings layers differently. Today's D-MANIFEST-ONE1 folds `workspace.jet` and `env.jet` into `package.jet`, which makes one file mean both "a package" and "a group of packages".
- **A real bug from that overlap.** A root `package.jet` with a `name:`, its own `run.jet` and `members:` silently skips its own code: `jet check` passes with a broken root `run.jet`, and `jet run` runs a member's program instead (probe P3 below).
- **Peers.** Every peer that scales well separates "what a package is" from "how this checkout builds" (Cargo by root-only profiles, Go by `go.work`, pnpm by `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, Gradle by `settings.gradle`, Bazel by `MODULE.bazel` + `BUILD` + `.bazelrc`). Zig, SwiftPM, Gradle and Nix all let real code drive the build, but keep one fixed file for it. Bazel retired its `WORKSPACE` file in Bazel 8.

Section 8 turns these findings into eight requirements that the proposal answers.

## 1. Every file that carries configuration

Counts are `git ls-files` at `e784bb1ffe`. "Read by" names the code that gives the file meaning.

| File | What it holds today | Count | Read by | Ruling state |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `package.jet` | identity, deps, outputs, profiles, settings, policy, members, and more (section 2) | 2310 | `Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Manifest/PackageParse.jet` (one parser, 521 lines) | D-CONF-PLANE1, D-MANIFEST-ONE1 |
| inline `package { }` block | the same fields, inside a source file (all of `Core/` uses it, e.g. `Core/Build/Build.jet:1-10`) | 604 files | same parser | D-ECO-INLINEPACKAGE1; may not coexist with `package.jet` |
| `pkg.jet` | retired name for `package.jet`, still a project marker | 5 | `JetCli/Source/Cli/Request.jet:232`, `Entry.jet:74` | retired, still recognised |
| `workspace.jet` | `module workspace { members: … }`, overlays, sometimes `fn build` or even `fn run` | 22 | `JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/JetpackConfig.jet:484`, `Entry.jet:70` | D-WORKSPACE1=B said "no workspace file"; D-MANIFEST-ONE1=A folds it into `package.jet` (not built) |
| `env.jet` | `module env.<name> { sources: … packages: … prompt: … }`: dev tools and source aliases | 159 | `JetpackConfig.jet:469` | D-MANIFEST-ONE1=A folds it into `package.jet environments:` (not built) |
| `config.jet` and `configs:` files | `NAME :: Config{ … }` records: deps, environments, even `outputs:` (`Examples/features/tooling/compiler_api_package/config/release.jet`) | 30 + 2 users of `configs:` | `PackageParse.jet` (E: ConfigMembers forbids members, build, settings) | D-MANIFEST-ONE1 keeps `configs:` for env-only files |
| `build.jet` | `fn build(b: Build)`; `jet new` writes a commented stub | 27 | `JetCli/Source/Cli/Entry.jet:72`, `Loader.jet:2613` | D-CONF-ENTRY1: one per package, any file |
| `test.jet` | `fn test(t: Test)` | 8 | same | D-TEST-PROFILE1: only for code suites |
| `dev.jet` | `fn dev(d: Dev)` | 6 | same | D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 |
| `bench.jet` | old bench entry | 3 | none (Bench handle retired, D-ENTRY-NAMES1) | stale |
| `run.jet` | the stock program entry, `fn run()` | 1695 | `Entry.jet:77` | D-ECO14 |
| `.jet/lock` | toolchain pin, build stamp, dependency graph | 22 committed; `jet new` writes and git-ignores it | `Host.jet:1607,1618`, `InspectProvenance.jet:308` | D-LOCKFILE1=A moved it to a committed root `jet.lock` (not built) |
| `jet.lock` | the ratified lock | 0 | none yet | D-LOCKFILE1=A |
| `.jet/` | build output, cache, generated code, last-run records | 6 committed `.jet/last-run/*` files in `Examples/features/tooling/build_entry_discovery` | everything | D-WORKSPACE-CMD1: one `.jet/` at the root, disposable |
| `project.jet` | one stray fixture | 1 | none | none |

The command code that `fn build` holds can live in any file of a package. A census of top-level `fn build|test|dev(` declarations finds them in `main.jet` (55 files), `run.jet` (36), `build.jet` (25), `workspace.jet` (3), `package.jet` (3) and others, such as `tools/build_entry.jet`.

`JetCli/Source/Cli/Entry.jet:72-74` reserves nine names that user code cannot use as module files: `run.jet`, `build.jet`, `dev.jet`, `test.jet`, `package.jet`, `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, `config.jet` and `workspace.jet`.

## 2. Every field of `package.jet`

The parser's switch (`PackageParse.jet:160-215`) accepts these fields. The census column counts `package.jet` files (not inline blocks) that use the field. The last column sorts each field by the question it answers. That sorting is this document's own, and it drives the proposal.

| Field | Meaning | Files | Kind of fact |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name`, `version` | identity | 2305, 2265 | what the package **is** |
| `edition`, `jet`, `source` | language edition, toolchain requirement, source root | 389, 92, few | is |
| `description`, `license`, `repository` | publishing metadata | 114, 109, 95 | is |
| `deps` | dependencies | 177 | what it **needs** |
| `authority` | effects the package may use, grants to its deps, trust | 1494 | needs |
| `boundaries` | which modules may import which | 7 | needs (code rules) |
| `policy` | lints and code rules (`lints: { deny: [auto_derive] }`, `check_removal: .Forbid`, `sentries`) | 47 | needs (code rules) |
| `allocator`, `runtime` | program allocator and runtime flavour | 5, 12 | what it **makes** |
| `outputs` | the things the package makes (nine kinds, D-TARGET-ONE1) | 94 | makes |
| `packages` | an older map of output kinds (`packages: { backend: library }`) | 80 | makes (second home) |
| `targets` | platform profiles (`targets: { machine: { profile: "hosted" } }`) | 6 | makes (and a third meaning of "target") |
| `settings` | typed knobs the package declares | 8 | makes |
| `build` | named build profiles, plus `allow:` for build-time effects | 35 | how **we work** |
| `defaults` | which output `jet run` uses; which profile bare commands use | 18 | how we work |
| `dev`, `services` | dev-loop policy, local services | 0, 0 | how we work |
| `environments` | dev tools and shells | 1 | how we work |
| `members` | the packages this root groups | 5 | how we work |
| `configs` | extra files holding `Config{}` records | 2 | how we work |
| `test`, `suites` | ratified by D-TEST-PROFILE1, not accepted yet (E1206) | 0 | how we work |
| `dev_deps`, `patch`, `workspace` | reserved; must be empty | 0 | — |
| `grants` | retired, moved under `authority:` | 0 | — |

One more spelling sits beside these: a `package.jet` may also declare the package's single `fn build`, and an inline `NAME :: Config{ … }` record.

The fourth kind ("how we work") is the trouble. None of these fields describe the package to someone who depends on it. They describe one checkout, one team or one machine. Cargo reached the same split and enforces it by ignoring a dependency's profiles (section 7).

## 3. Every concept and word

| Word | Meanings in use today | Where |
|---|---|---|
| package | (1) the unit with a `package.jet`; (2) the root noun for a group of packages (D-ECO-ROOTNAME1=I); (3) the old `packages:` output map; (4) env.jet `packages:`, which means tools | ratified rulings, `PackageParse.jet:186`, `env.jet` files |
| workspace | (1) the monorepo root and `workspace.jet` (D-WORKSPACE-CMD1, D-BUILD-REUSESET1, spec "Workspace overlays" §2360); (2) the Canvas editor window (`Docs/spec/reference/canvas-workspace-architecture.md`); (3) in Jai, one compilation with its own build options (`compiler_create_workspace`) | owner ruling on #6368: rename (1) to project |
| Jetspace | the whole checked graph (D-ECO-ROOTNAME2=D) | ratified, never used in code |
| project | the folder the CLI and Canvas call "the project" (`project-navigation.js`, `Request.jet:232 JET_CLI_PROJECT_MARKERS`) | used informally everywhere, defined nowhere |
| member | a package listed by a root | `members:` in `package.jet` or in `module workspace` |
| output | a thing a package makes (D-TARGET-ONE1) | `outputs:`, `b.add_*`, `b.output(name)` |
| target | (1) the platform (D-TARGET-ONE1); (2) the `targets:` platform-profile field; (3) old meaning "a thing to build", still in `Core/Build/Build.jet` `BuildGraphTarget`; (4) the field name `target`, which is an error | parser, Core, flags |
| profile | (1) a named bundle of build options (D-CONF-WORD1); (2) a test profile (D-TEST-PROFILE1, same namespace); (3) a target platform profile (`targets: { … profile: "hosted" }`); (4) env presets (renamed by D-CONF-WORD1) | `build:`, `test:`, `targets:` |
| build | (1) the `build:` profiles field; (2) `Build{ … }`, the profile constructor (until `BuildOptions` lands, D-ENTRY-NAMES1); (3) `Build`, the handle in `fn build(b: Build)`; (4) `build.jet`; (5) `jet build`; (6) the `build.*` hook stages | `Examples/features/tooling/build_link_inputs` uses (1), (2), (3) and (4) together |
| config | (1) `Config{}` records; (2) `config.jet`; (3) `configs:` | parser |
| settings / options | (1) `settings:`, knobs a package declares; (2) build options (`BuildOptions`, D-SETTING-ORDER1's one option table) | spec, rulings |
| policy / authority / grants / boundaries | four blocks about what is allowed: code rules, effects, effect grants, import rules | `package.jet` |
| environment | dev tools and shells: `env.jet`, `environments:`, `Config{ environments: }` | three homes |
| lock | `.jet/lock` (code, git-ignored by `jet new`) and `jet.lock` (ratified, committed) | two homes |

## 4. The rulings in force, and where they disagree

| Ruling | Says | Conflicts with |
|---|---|---|
| D-WORKSPACE1=B (06-25) | Reuse the package file; no workspace manifest | 22 `workspace.jet` files, spec §3905 ("`workspace.jet` supplies workspace membership") |
| D-ECO-ROOTNAME1=I | The root noun is "Package" | D-ECO-ROOTNAME2=D ("Jetspace"), D-WORKSPACE-CMD1 and D-BUILD-REUSESET1 ("workspace"), the owner's "project" |
| D-BUILDSCOPE1=A (07-19) | `fn build` lives in the unit's existing definition file at every rung (single file, `pkg.jet`, `workspace.jet`) | D-CONF-ENTRY1=A: any file of the package; `jet new` writes `build.jet` |
| D-CONF-SPLIT1=A | Facts in text, actions in `fn build` | D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A: `fn dev` sets facts in code (`d.port(8080)`); D-TARGET-ONE1=A: outputs from data and from code |
| D-CONF-MERGE1=A | declaration < profile < workspace < environment < system < fleet < CLI | D-SETTING-ORDER1=A: stock < source marker < `package.jet` < entry code < flag; D-BUILD-REUSESET1=A adds a root layer between stock and each member |
| D-SETTING-ORDER1=A, owner directive #4913 | every option row has a flag, a package field and a handle method | D-OPTFLAG1=A removed `--optimize`, `--opt-level` and `--inline` in favour of profiles |
| D-TEST-PROFILE1=A | named test runs are data in `package.jet` (`test:`), code suites in `test.jet` | the parser rejects `test:` (probe P1); `jet new`'s `test.jet` stub still says "replace the stock default" |
| D-LOCKFILE1=A | `<root>/jet.lock`, committed | `jet new` writes `.jet/lock` and git-ignores it (probe P4) |
| D-MANIFEST-ONE1=A (10-30) | `package.jet` is the one project file; a root without `name:` is a virtual root | makes a `package.jet` mean "a package" or "a group" depending on one missing field; keeps `configs:` files |
| D-ENTRY-NAMES1=A | `Build` is the handle; the profile record is `BuildOptions` | 35 `package.jet` files still use `Build{ … }` as the profile record |

## 5. The confusions, with examples

Each confusion names a real file or probe. They are ordered by how often a newcomer meets them.

**C1. One project, many homes.** `Examples/features/tooling/build_entry_discovery` is one small project spread over seven configuration places: `package.jet` (identity, authority), `workspace.jet` (members, and also `fn run`), `tools/build_entry.jet` (the root's `fn build`, found "package-wide" per its `tools/README.md`), `packages/foundation/tools/build.jet` (a member's `fn build`), two member `package.jet` files, and six committed `.jet/last-run/*` files. Nothing in `package.jet` points at any of the others. A reader must know the discovery rules to find the build.

**C2. A root is both a package and a group.** `Compiler/package.jet` has `name: "compiler"`, a version and 13 `members:`. Its comment says `jet build Compiler/` runs `build.jet`, which builds an executable from the JetCli member. So is `compiler` a package with code, a group, or both? Probe P3 shows the cost: a named root with `members:` and its own `run.jet` is silently skipped by `jet check` and `jet run` (bug B1).

**C3. One fact, several homes.**
- Members: `members:` in `package.jet`, or `module workspace { members: }` in `workspace.jet`. Probe P3 accepts both at once, listing the same member twice, with no warning.
- Environments: `env.jet` `module env.<name>`, `Config{ environments: }` in a `configs:` file (`Examples/jetpack/epoch5/config/dev.jet`), or `environments:` in `package.jet`.
- Outputs: `outputs:`, the older `packages:` map, `Config{ outputs: }` in a configs file, or `b.add_*` in `fn build`.
- The entry function: any file of the package. The census found `fn build`, `fn test` or `fn dev` in `main.jet`, `run.jet`, `build.jet`, `workspace.jet`, `package.jet` and `tools/build_entry.jet` (section 1).
- The lock: `.jet/lock` or `jet.lock`.

**C4. Three syntaxes for one kind of data.** Top-level `field: value` (`package.jet`), `module workspace { field: value }` (`workspace.jet`, `env.jet`), and `NAME :: Config{ field: value }` (`config.jet`). A fourth, the inline `package { }` block, holds the first syntax inside a source file. The output constructor is spelled `.Executable{ … }` in `package.jet` and `Executable{ … }` in a configs file.

**C5. "Workspace" collides with Jai.** In Jai a workspace is one compilation with its own build options, created by `compiler_create_workspace` ([The Way to Jai, ch. 30](https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai); `Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md` §D). Jet's equivalent of that is one output with its options (D-JAI-CONFIG1). Jet uses the same word for the monorepo root, and Canvas uses it for the editor window. A user reading Jai material and Jet material at once meets two meanings for the word.

**C6. "Build" names six things.** `Examples/features/tooling/build_link_inputs/package.jet` writes `build: { vendored: Build{ optimize: none, link_args: ["-Lvendor"], os: linux } }`. Its `build.jet` writes `fn build(b: Build)`. Here `build:` is a profile map, `Build{}` is a profile record, `Build` is a handle and `build.jet` is a file, all in one example.

**C7. "Target" and "profile" are overloaded.** `targets: { machine: { profile: "hosted" } }` uses both words in a third and a fourth sense. A field named `target` is an unknown-field error. Test profiles and build profiles share one namespace (D-TEST-PROFILE1) but live under different fields.

**C8. Facts and code overlap without a rule.** D-CONF-SPLIT1 says "facts in text, actions in code". Yet the default output is `defaults: { run: cli }` or `b.default(x)`, a profile is `build: { … }` or `b.profile(…)`, an option is a field or a handle call, and a test suite is `suites:` data or `t.suite(…)`. Each pair is ratified. No rule says which to pick, so two teams write the same project two ways.

**C9. The settings order has two versions and a hidden layer.** D-CONF-MERGE1 lists seven layers, D-SETTING-ORDER1 lists five, and D-BUILD-REUSESET1 adds the root's `package.jet` as a layer under each member. A member's effective `optimize` depends on which ruling the implementation follows.

**C10. Inheritance has three different rules.** Members inherit `version`, `edition` and `license` from the root (D-CORE-HEADER1), build settings from the root (D-BUILD-REUSESET1), and policy ceilings through the grant chain (D-BUILDSCOPE1). They do not inherit deps, lints or outputs. A member cannot tell what it inherits without reading three rulings.

**C11. What publishes and what does not is unstated.** A library's `build:` profiles, `environments:`, `members:` and `defaults:` mean nothing to a consumer, but they sit beside `name:` and `deps:` in the file that gets published. Nothing says whether a consumer's build honours them. Cargo answers this explicitly ("Profile settings defined in dependencies will be ignored", [Cargo profiles](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html)).

**C12. Command files are named by convention only, and their stubs are stale.** `jet new --template overrides` writes `build.jet`, `dev.jet` and `test.jet` stubs that say "Uncomment one `fn build` to replace the stock default" (`Host.jet:1514-1516`). D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 says entries set values and never replace the stock work. Nine file names are reserved (section 1), so a module cannot be called `test.jet` or `config.jet`.

**C13. Four blocks say what is allowed.** `policy:` (lints, code rules), `authority:` (effects, grants, trust), `boundaries:` (imports) and `build: { allow: }` (build-time effects, parsed inside the profiles map by `BuildProfiles.jet:310`). The project's ceiling ("this team never allows `unchecked`") has no home of its own; it sits in the root's `package.jet` beside the package's own needs.

**C14. Errors point the wrong way.** Probe P1's E1206 for `test:` says "Identity is bare `name:` and `version:` at the top level — there is no `identity:` or `payload:` wrapper", which has nothing to do with `test:` (bug B2). Probe P5's duplicate `fn build` is E0105 "Imported names share the module namespace" from `jet check` but E3520 "Two build entries" from `jet build` (bug B3).

## 6. Probes

Run with `JET_COMPILER_IDENTITY="jet@0.1.0#probe" JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT=<export of e784bb1ffe> $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/base/latest/jet`.

| Probe | Input | Result |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | `package.jet` with `test: { quick: TestProfile{ suites: [tests], time_limit: 60s } }` | `E1206 Unknown field test:`; the "Why" line talks about identity wrappers |
| P2 | `build: { small: .{ optimize: size } }` | `E1206 … remove the dot before {` |
| P3 | root `package.jet` with `name: "p3"`, `members: ["a"]`, an `outputs:` app and a `run.jet` containing an undefined name; `workspace.jet` also listing `a`; member `a` prints "hi" | `jet check .` and bare `jet check`: "ok: …/a/run.jet has no problems". `jet run`: prints `hi` (the member's program). `jet check run.jet`: E0107 for the root file. Removing `workspace.jet` changes nothing. |
| P4 | `jet new demo` | writes `demo/.jet/lock` and a `.gitignore` containing `.jet/lock` |
| P5 | `build.jet` and `tools/build.jet` both declaring `fn build` | `jet check .`: E0105 at `build.jet:1:4`; `jet build`: E3520 |

## 7. How peers draw the lines

| System | Package data | Build code | Multi-package root | Profiles and flags | Lock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cargo | `Cargo.toml` `[package]`, `[dependencies]` | `build.rs`, one fixed file per package | `[workspace]` in the root `Cargo.toml`; a root without `[package]` is a "virtual manifest" | `[profile.*]` honoured only at the workspace root; `.cargo/config.toml` per machine or repo | `Cargo.lock` at the root |
| Go | `go.mod` | none; `go generate` runs by hand and its output is committed | `go.work`, a separate file, "generally inadvisable to commit" | build tags and flags only | `go.sum` |
| Zig | `build.zig.zon`, "metadata specifically pertaining to build.zig" | `build.zig`, real Zig code that builds a step graph | none; a package is the unit | `b.standardOptimizeOption` and `-D` flags declared in `build.zig` | hashes inside `build.zig.zon` |
| SwiftPM | `Package.swift`: Swift code that builds one declarative `Package` value | plugins (build-tool and command plugins), separate packages | none (Xcode workspaces are an IDE concept) | `swift build -c release`; `swiftSettings` per target | `Package.resolved` |
| Bazel | `MODULE.bazel` (identity and deps) | `BUILD` files (Starlark, restricted) and `.bzl` rules | the repository root marked by `MODULE.bazel`; the `WORKSPACE` file was disabled by default in Bazel 8 | `.bazelrc` named configs (`--config=release`) | `MODULE.bazel.lock` |
| Buck2 | `BUCK` files | Starlark rules | cells in `.buckconfig` | `.buckconfig`, modifiers | — |
| Nix flakes | `flake.nix` `inputs` | `flake.nix` `outputs`, a function of the inputs | none; one flake per repo is the norm | outputs per system | `flake.lock` |
| npm | `package.json` | `scripts` strings | `"workspaces"` globs inside the root `package.json` | none | `package-lock.json` |
| pnpm | `package.json` | `scripts` | `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, a separate file that also holds shared version "catalogs" | `.npmrc` | `pnpm-lock.yaml` |
| Gradle | `build.gradle(.kts)` per project | the same file, real Kotlin or Groovy; shared logic in convention plugins (`build-logic`) | `settings.gradle(.kts)`, a separate file that lists included projects | `gradle.properties`; version catalog `libs.versions.toml` | dependency locking, opt-in |
| Jai | none | the metaprogram (`first.jai` / `build.jai`), real Jai code run by the compiler | none | `Build_Options` per workspace | none |

What each teaches Jet:

- **Cargo** proves the split between package facts and checkout facts is real. It enforces it silently ("Cargo only looks at the profile settings in the `Cargo.toml` manifest at the root of the workspace. Profile settings defined in dependencies will be ignored", [profiles](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html)). It also shows the cost of one file for two roles: a root `Cargo.toml` can be a package, a workspace or both, and its docs need a "root package" vs "virtual manifest" section to explain the difference ([workspaces](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html)). `[workspace.package]` and `[workspace.dependencies]` add opt-in inheritance (`version.workspace = true`): explicit, per field. `build.rs` has one fixed name ([build scripts](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html)).
- **Go** keeps the module file free of checkout concerns and puts multi-module work in `go.work` ([Go modules reference, Workspaces](https://go.dev/ref/mod#workspaces)). It is the cleanest split, but it gives up build code entirely, which Jet will not do.
- **Zig** uses a data file for identity and dependencies and a code file for the build graph, and names the data file after the code file to show they belong together ([build.zig.zon](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/doc/build.zig.zon.md), [Zig build system](https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/)). Options are declared in code (`b.option`), then set by `-D` flags: one mechanism.
- **SwiftPM** writes the manifest as code that builds one declarative value ([PackageDescription](https://docs.swift.org/swiftpm/documentation/packagedescription)). This is close to Jet's "data file is Jet values" design. Plugins extend the build without making the manifest imperative ([Plugins](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-package-manager/blob/main/Documentation/Plugins.md)).
- **Bazel** splits three concerns into three file kinds: identity and deps (`MODULE.bazel`, [modules](https://bazel.build/external/module)), targets (`BUILD`, [BUILD files](https://bazel.build/concepts/build-files)) and invocation flags (`.bazelrc`, [bazelrc](https://bazel.build/run/bazelrc)). It replaced its `WORKSPACE` file because of its "shortcomings"; "the WORKSPACE file is already disabled in Bazel 8" ([Bzlmod migration](https://bazel.build/versions/8.1.1/external/migration)). Bazel's lesson for Jet is the cost of a word and file that grew several jobs.
- **Buck2** names the multi-repo root a "cell" in `.buckconfig` and keeps targets in `BUCK` files ([Buck2 docs](https://buck2.build/docs/)).
- **Nix flakes** put inputs and outputs in one file, outputs as a function of inputs, with a committed lock ([nix flake](https://nix.dev/manual/nix/latest/command-ref/new-cli/nix3-flake)). One file is clear when it holds one project; it does not attempt multi-package grouping.
- **npm** puts `"workspaces"` inside the root `package.json` ([npm workspaces](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/using-npm/workspaces)); **pnpm** moved it to its own `pnpm-workspace.yaml` ([pnpm workspaces](https://pnpm.io/workspaces)) and added "catalogs", "a workspace feature for defining dependency version ranges as reusable constants" ([catalogs](https://pnpm.io/catalogs)).
- **Gradle** has a separate settings file for the build as a whole and a build file per project ([multi-project builds](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/multi_project_builds_intermediate.html), [organizing projects](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/organizing_gradle_projects.html)). Shared logic moves into convention plugins, and shared versions into a catalog ([version catalogs](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/version_catalogs.html)). Note the naming trap: Gradle calls each sub-unit a "project", which is Jet's package. Jet's docs must define the word once and keep it.
- **Jai** has no package or project file. One metaprogram creates workspaces, sets each one's options and drives the compiler ([The Way to Jai](https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai) ch. 30; `focus` [`first.jai`](https://github.com/focus-editor/focus/blob/main/first.jai)). It is the strongest primitive layer of any peer and has no wrappers at all, so every project re-writes the same message loop (`jai-parity-2026-10-16.md` line 91).

The pattern across peers:

1. The ones that scale keep "what this package is and needs" apart from "how this checkout builds it": Cargo by a root-only rule, Go, pnpm and Gradle by a separate root file, Bazel by three file kinds.
2. Where build code exists, it has one fixed home: `build.rs`, `build.zig`, `build.gradle.kts`, `BUILD`, `first.jai`.
3. The data file and the code file meet through shared value types, not by repeating facts: Zig's `b.dependency("x")` reads `.zon`; SwiftPM's manifest is a value.
4. Shared versions and options across many packages are an explicit, opt-in feature of the root (Cargo `workspace = true`, pnpm catalogs, Gradle catalogs), not silent inheritance.

## 8. What a cleaner system must do

These requirements come from sections 4–7 and from `Docs/spec/philosophy.md` (ladders, not cliffs; one mechanism; enterprise auditability; the language is a library). The proposal answers each one.

- **R1. Two nouns, two files, no overlap.** One noun and one file for the unit others depend on (package). One noun and one file for the folder people work in (project). No file means both.
- **R2. One home per fact.** Every field has exactly one file it may appear in. A beginner can sort any fact with one question.
- **R3. One home per entry function.** `fn build`, `fn test` and `fn dev` each have one fixed file name, found without discovery rules.
- **R4. One settings order.** One list of layers, with pins and policy forbids stated on the same list.
- **R5. Explicit inheritance.** A package states what it takes from its project, or the project states what it gives. No hidden layer.
- **R6. Composition.** Data files and entry code build the same Core values. The primitive (`b.add(output)`, a typed action) can express everything; the wrappers (`outputs:` entries, `b.add_executable`) cover the common cases and expand to the primitive.
- **R7. One meaning per word.** "Workspace" leaves the package system; "build", "target" and "profile" each keep one meaning.
- **R8. A mechanical migration.** `jet fix` moves every file and field, and a leftover old spelling is an error that names the fix.

sections.title: A greenfield FFI design, and what Jet should adopt
sections.body:
# A greenfield FFI design, and what Jet should adopt

Card #6366. Status: proposal. Owner choices are in the ballots listed in §9.
They are not decided here.

## Plain summary

- **The idea.** Every foreign boundary is described once, as a *boundary
  contract*. That is a typed list of functions and types, plus the facts a C
  header cannot say: who owns memory, how long a view lives, how errors come
  back, which thread may call, and whether a call is async.
- **Readers and writers.** A reader package builds the contract from whatever
  the other side has (a C header, a Rust crate, a `.d.ts`, a WIT file, a JVM
  class, Windows metadata, a GPU shader). A writer package turns the same
  contract into bindings for whoever calls *us*. Both directions share one
  model, so N languages cost N readers plus N writers, not N×N bridges.
- **Two layers.** A small, complete, unsafe *primitives* layer can express
  every boundary: layout, symbols, calls, memory, callbacks, errors, threads,
  async, isolation. Pareto *wrappers* sit on top: `use "png.h" as png`,
  `#Export`, and typed imports for Rust, Python and JS. Every wrapper
  expands into primitives that you can inspect, so the expert path is a ladder,
  not a cliff.
- **Safe by default.** A call is safe when its facts are checked, vouched for
  in a named `#Unsafe("reason")`, or *isolated*. Isolated means the same import
  runs in a wasm sandbox or a separate process, with no source changes.
- **Zero cost.** A crossing whose types already match costs one direct call.
  When the foreign source is visible, the optimizer can inline across the
  boundary.
- **For Jet.** Most of this is already ratified: header import, C source import,
  binder packages, ownership sigils at the border, vouches, both embedding
  artifacts, and the hardened profile. The new pieces are a public primitives
  layer, isolation as a placement option, and rich exports. Each is one ballot.
  Inline C stays, and becomes a thin wrapper over C-source import, which
  removes the "two ways to bring in C" loss that D-FFI-ONE1 recorded.

This builds on, and does not replace, the boundary audit
[`Docs/audits/ffi-owned-source-and-boundaries.md`](../audits/ffi-owned-source-and-boundaries.md)
(#2933), which covers project arrangements and workflows. This document is the
mechanism underneath them.

---

## 1. What "perfect" means: ten testable goals

| # | Goal | Test |
|---|------|------|
| G1 | **Any to any.** Call out to, and be called from, C, C++, Rust, Zig, Swift, Objective‑C, Java/Kotlin, C#, Python, JS/wasm, GPU kernels and OS ABIs. | Every language has a reader and a writer, or a documented reason why not. |
| G2 | **Zero cost when shapes match.** | A blittable call compiles to the same machine code as a C-to-C call. |
| G3 | **Safe by default, total control when asked.** | No safe code can corrupt memory through a binding. Every unchecked fact is a named, auditable vouch. |
| G4 | **No hand-written glue for the common case.** | One line binds a library. Zero lines of marshalling. |
| G5 | **No cliff.** | Every wrapper is a documented composition of public primitives (philosophy: *Ladders, Not Cliffs*). |
| G6 | **Facts, not guesses.** | Each fact (ownership, length, nullability, error style) carries its provenance. Unknown facts get the conservative projection, never a guessed one. |
| G7 | **One meaning everywhere.** | The same import behaves the same at every tier, on the web, and in compile-time code (I9). |
| G8 | **Versioned.** | A library upgrade that breaks the contract fails at build time or at load time, with a diff. It never shows up as a crash. |
| G9 | **Debuggable.** | Mixed-language backtraces, boundary tracing, and hardened checks at the edges. |
| G10 | **Placement independent.** | The same import can run in-process, in a wasm sandbox, or in another process. Only one option changes. |

No shipping system meets more than four of these goals today (§2).

## 2. State of the art

Each row lists the idea worth taking and the gap that stops it being the
answer. Sources are in §10.

| System | Model | Best idea | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Zig** `@cImport` / translate‑c | Compile-time header translation with a bundled Clang | The compiler is also a C compiler, so C and Zig cross-compile and link with no extra toolchain. | C only. No ownership or length facts. `@cImport` is moving to the build system (0.16 notes) because compile-time import tied the language to Clang's life cycle [Z1,Z2]. |
| **Rust bindgen / cxx / UniFFI / PyO3 / Diplomat** | Build step (bindgen), bridge macros (cxx), IDL or proc-macro (UniFFI, Diplomat), per-host crate (PyO3) | cxx: a safe *bridge* language that is checked on both sides. UniFFI and Diplomat: **one description, many host languages**. Rust 2024 `unsafe extern` lets each item be marked `safe` [R1–R6]. | Five tools with five models. Outward bindings come from Rust only. The stable ABI (`crabi`) is still experimental [R7]. |
| **Swift ↔ C/C++/ObjC** | Clang importer in the compiler | Imports headers directly. Clang *API notes* refine imported facts without editing the header. Non-escapable types and lifetime annotations make C++ views safe [S1–S3]. | Safety rests on annotations that most libraries lack. Template and virtual-class support is partial [S4]. |
| **Kotlin/Native cinterop, Swift export** | `.def` file plus a build-time tool | A declarative definition file that holds options, headers and filters. Direct Swift export without ObjC headers [K1–K3]. | Build step only. ObjC import is still Beta. |
| **.NET P/Invoke → `LibraryImport`** | Source generator at compile time | Marshalling code is *generated and visible*, works with AOT, and is extensible through custom marshallers [N1,N2]. `UnmanagedCallersOnly` handles the reverse direction. | One direction at a time. No lifetime facts. |
| **Java FFM (Panama)** | Runtime linker API plus `jextract` | A complete *primitives* API (Linker, FunctionDescriptor, MemoryLayout, Arena) with jextract as the wrapper. `captureCallState` reads errno. Confined arenas bound lifetimes [J1–J3]. | Verbose without jextract. Safety is a runtime check, not a type. |
| **LuaJIT FFI** | Parse C declarations at run time | The JIT compiles FFI calls inline. Close to zero overhead from a dynamic language [L1]. | No safety at all. C only. |
| **Python cffi / ctypes** | ABI mode (dlopen) or API mode (compile a shim) | Offers *both* modes behind one declaration language [P1,P2]. | Copies by default. No ownership model. |
| **Nim** `importc` / `importcpp` | Pragmas on declarations | Pattern strings for C++ calls (`#.method(@)`) reach templates without a shim [M1]. | Nothing is checked. A wrong pattern means undefined behaviour. |
| **Odin** `foreign` blocks / **Jai** `#foreign` | Declarations in the source, link by name | The shortest syntax there is. Calling convention and library on the block [O1,JA1]. | Hand-written. Nothing is read from headers. |
| **D** ImportC / `extern(C++)` | Compiler compiles C directly | `import foo;` on a `.c` file. Matches C++ mangling and vtables for single inheritance [D1,D2]. | C++ templates must be mirrored by hand. |
| **Carbon** | `import Cpp library "x.h"` | C++ interop is a *design mandate*. Bidirectional, with no wrapper layer [C1,C2]. | Experimental. |
| **Mojo** | Python objects in Mojo, plus `PythonModuleBuilder` for exports | Both directions with a single builder [MO1]. | CPython only. Exports are built by hand. |
| **GraalVM polyglot** | Shared VM, interop protocol | One object protocol across JS, Python, Ruby, Java and LLVM bitcode [G1]. | Needs the Graal VM. Not a native ABI. |
| **wasm Component Model / WIT** | IDL plus canonical ABI | **A language-neutral contract with resources (owned handles), results, and since WASI 0.3, async `future`/`stream`** [W1–W3]. Isolation comes free. | Copies across the boundary. Sandboxed only. |
| **WinRT / win32metadata** | Machine-readable metadata, then projections | Windows APIs described once, projected into C#, C++ and Rust [WM1]. | Windows only. |
| **RLBox** (Firefox) | Compile C libraries to wasm, then back to native | *Isolation without rewriting*: the same library is sandboxed, with "tainted" types at the edge [RB1]. | C++ only. Annotations by hand. |
| **Arrow C Data / DLPack** | ABI-stable structs for columns and tensors | Zero-copy data exchange across every runtime [A1,A2]. | Data only, no calls. |
| **Clang `-fbounds-safety`** | `counted_by` / `sized_by` annotations | Length facts live in the C header itself, so any reader can use them [B1]. | Only as good as adoption. |

**The pattern:** the best systems separate a *contract* (WIT, winmd, UniFFI
UDL, cxx bridge) from *projections*. The best ergonomics come from reading
sources the user already has (Zig, Swift, D, Carbon). The best expert control
comes from a public primitives API (Java FFM). Nobody combines all three, and
nobody makes placement (in-process versus sandbox) a single option.

## 3. The design in one picture

```
 foreign sources          readers (packages)        contract           writers (packages)        callers
 C/C++/ObjC headers ─┐                          ┌─ functions, types ─┐  C header ─────────────┐
 C/C++ source        ├─► c, cpp, objc ──────────┤  + facts with      ├─► C++ RAII header        │
 Rust crate (rustdoc)├─► rust                   │    provenance:     ├─► Swift package          │
 Swift .swiftinterface► swift                   │  ownership, life-  ├─► Kotlin/JVM (FFM, JNI)  ├─► any host
 JVM class / .NET md ├─► jvm, dotnet            │  time, length,     ├─► C# LibraryImport       │
 .pyi / .d.ts / WIT  ├─► python, js, wit        │  errors, threads,  ├─► Python ext (abi3)      │
 winmd / SDK .tbd    ├─► os                     │  async, effects,   ├─► Node-API / JS + WIT    │
 SPIR-V / PTX / WGSL ┘─► gpu                    └─ version, purity ──┘  Rust crate, WIT world ──┘
                                     ▲                     │
                                     │        lowered by the primitives layer
                       overlays (API-notes style)          ▼
                                            layout · symbol · call · memory · thunk ·
                                            error capture · thread attach · async bridge ·
                                            marshal · isolate
```

There are four layers. Each one is written only in terms of the layer below.

1. **Primitives (L0).** The complete, unsafe vocabulary (§4).
2. **Contract (L1).** Plain data: the rows and their facts. Readers produce it,
   overlays refine it, writers and the lowering pass consume it (§5).
3. **Readers and writers (L2).** Ordinary packages that run at compile time.
   They are sandboxed and have pinned tool versions (§6).
4. **Wrappers (L3).** The pareto one-liners (§7).

## 4. Layer 0: the primitives (complete set)

Every primitive is public. The ones that can break memory safety are callable
only inside `#Unsafe("reason")`. The comptime-only ones are safe. Together they
must express every boundary in G1. If a reader needs something they cannot
express, that is a bug in L0, not a reason for a private hook.

| Primitive | Purpose | Safe? |
|---|---|---|
| `layout<T>(target:)` → `Layout` (size, align, field offsets, bitfields, padding) | Ask the exact per-target layout. Pick a layout with `#Layout(.C | .Packed(n) | .Explicit | .Std430 | .Scalar)`. | yes (comptime) |
| `abi(target:)` → `CallConv` classifier (SysV x86‑64, Win64, AAPCS64, Apple arm64, RISC‑V, wasm32, Swift, Rust‑C, `.Vectorcall`, …) | Shows how each argument is passed (register, stack, sret, split). Used for the Apple arm64 rule that variadic arguments always go on the stack [AP1]. | yes (comptime) |
| `symbol<Sig>(name, from:)` (static), `Library.open(path)` and `lib.symbol<Sig>(name)` (dynamic) | Get the address of a foreign function or global. Weak or optional symbols return `T?`. | link: yes; dynamic: `#Unsafe` |
| `FnPtr<Sig>` call; `call_variadic(fp, fixed, extra: ...CArg)` | Direct call through a typed signature. C default argument promotions are applied by the compiler. `va_list` is a type. | `#Unsafe` unless the row is checked |
| Raw memory: `Ptr<T>`, offset, cast, `alloc_raw` / `free_raw`, `view(ptr, count)` | The memory model, with provenance kept. | `#Unsafe` |
| `thunk(f, conv:)` → `Callback<Sig>` (code pointer + context + owned registration) | Pass closures to C as a (function, user data) pair. `trampoline(f)` covers APIs that take no user data, using a fixed pool. | creating: yes; handing over a raw pointer: `#Unsafe` |
| `capture: [.Errno, .LastError, .NSError, .HResult]` on a call | Read thread-local error state atomically with the call (as in Java `captureCallState`). | yes |
| `unwind: .Abort | .Catch(.Cpp) | .Catch(.RustPanic) | .Propagate` | What happens when a foreign exception reaches the edge. The default is `.Abort`, because unwinding through frames that do not expect it is undefined behaviour (Rust `C-unwind` [R8]). | yes |
| `attach()` and `affinity(.Any | .Main | .Creator)` | Foreign threads enter the runtime automatically through thunks. Affinity is checked when a call is made. | yes |
| `completion<T>()` → (token, Future) and `poll_bridge(handle)` | Turn callback-style or poll-style foreign async into Jet tasks, and the reverse. | yes |
| `Marshal<F>` trait: `lower`, `lift`, `release`, and `BLITTABLE: Bool` | User-extensible conversion. Every built-in projection is a `Marshal` impl. | impl: yes; raw parts: `#Unsafe` |
| `Contract` values: `read`, `merge(overlay)`, `verify(lib)`, `hash` | The L1 data, available at compile time to every package. | yes |
| `isolate(contract, placement: .InProcess | .Wasm | .Process)` | Run the same contract behind a sandbox. Arguments are copied or shared according to their facts. | yes |

Why this set is complete: a boundary needs (a) a shape (layout and ABI),
(b) a target (symbol), (c) a transfer (call, memory, marshal), (d) the reverse
transfer (thunk, attach), (e) the out-of-band channels (error capture, unwind,
async), and (f) a trust decision (contract, isolate). Each primitive covers
exactly one of these.

## 5. Layer 1: the boundary contract

A contract is a list of rows: functions, types, constants and globals. Each
row has a signature plus **facts**. Every fact records where it came from:

| Provenance | Meaning | Callable from safe code? |
|---|---|---|
| `Read` | Stated by the source: a `counted_by`, `_Nonnull`, a Rust `&`, a WIT `own<T>`, Java `@NonNull`, or a `.d.ts` type. | yes |
| `Proved` | Checked by analysis. The C source is visible and the fact holds. | yes |
| `Vouched` | Written by a person inside `#Unsafe("reason") { … }`. Listed by `jet audit`. | yes, at the vouch |
| `Observed` | Asserted at run time by the hardened profile (D-HARDENED1). | adds checks only |
| `Unknown` | Nothing is known. | **only through the conservative projection** (copy in, copy out, opaque handle, `T?`) or isolation |

Fact kinds, one vocabulary for every language:

- **Ownership.** Lend for this call (`&`), give away (`^`), returns owned (with
  a `#Close(fn)` release), returns borrowed from parameter *p*, shared
  (refcounted: ObjC ARC, COM, `Arc`, `shared_ptr`).
- **Lifetime.** A view is valid while *p* lives, until the next call on *p*, or
  only for this call. This is the Swift `@lifetime` and non-escapable model [S2].
- **Length and termination.** `counted_by(n)`, `sized_by(n)`,
  NUL-terminated, sentinel-terminated.
- **Nullability and encoding.** Nullable or not. UTF-8, UTF-16, Latin-1,
  OS-native path, or raw bytes.
- **Errors.** Return code with a success set, status plus out-parameter, errno,
  `GetLastError`, `NSError**`, `HRESULT`, C++ exception, Rust panic, JS throw,
  Python exception. Each maps to a typed `T E!` result.
- **Threads.** Thread-safe, main-thread only, same thread as the creator,
  reentrant or not.
- **Async.** Completion callback (which argument, called how many times),
  promise or future, stream.
- **Effects and purity.** The Jet effects the call performs (`Net`, `FS`, …).
  `pure` allows compile-time evaluation and common-subexpression elimination.
- **Version.** Introduced in, deprecated in, optional symbol.

**Overlays** are the Clang API-notes idea generalised [S5]. A user module can
add or correct facts and rename rows without touching the foreign source. The
overlay wins, and a fact the overlay changes from `Read` to `Vouched` becomes
an audit entry. (In Jet this is `#Import module c.png { … }`, D-FFI-CMAP1 and
D-FFI-VOUCH1.)

**The conservative projection** is what makes "safe by default" real without
blocking work:

| Unknown fact | Safe projection |
|---|---|
| Pointer with no length | Opaque `Handle` (no indexing) |
| Pointer that might be null | `T?` |
| `char*` with no encoding | `Bytes` (copied) |
| Returned pointer with no owner | Borrowed for this call only. It is copied out before the call returns. |
| Callback with no thread fact | Delivered on the caller's executor through a queue |
| Error style unknown | Plain return value, with an audit note |

## 6. Layer 2: readers and writers

Readers and writers are ordinary packages written with comptime and the L0/L1
API. The compiler has no private hooks for them; this is philosophy's *The
Language Is A Library*. They run sandboxed with pinned tool versions, and their
output is cached by content (reader version, inputs, target). The same reader
runs as a build step (`jet bind`) when a team wants to commit or vendor the
result. **One mechanism serves both compile-time import and build-step
generation**, which answers the problem behind Zig's move of `@cImport` into
the build system [Z1].

| Language | Reader input | How a call crosses | Writer output (being called) |
|---|---|---|---|
| C | Headers and source, through a pinned Clang. Constant macros are evaluated. Function-like macros are instantiated as tiny typed C shims. | Direct C ABI | `.h`, plus `counted_by` and nullability annotations |
| C++ | Clang AST. Templates are instantiated on demand in a generated shim. Overloads are folded by label. Virtual classes can be subclassed through vtable thunks. | C ABI shim. Exceptions are caught in the shim. Inlined at O2 when the source is visible. | A C++ header of RAII classes over the C ABI (the cxx/Diplomat pattern [R2,R5]) |
| Objective‑C | Clang plus nullability, `NS_SWIFT_NAME`, ARC rules | Typed `objc_msgSend` per selector. Blocks are thunks. Retain and release map to ownership. | An ObjC header with `NS_*` annotations |
| Swift | `.swiftinterface`, using library-evolution layout rules [SW1] | The Swift calling convention on Apple targets, or `@_cdecl` shims elsewhere | A Swift package (C module plus a Swift overlay) |
| Rust | rustdoc JSON, plus a generated `extern "C"` shim crate. `crabi` when it is stable [R7]. | C ABI. Panics are caught in the shim (`C-unwind`). | A crate with an `unsafe extern` block whose items are marked `safe` [R6], plus safe wrappers |
| Zig | Exported C-ABI declarations | Direct C ABI | A `.h` (Zig consumes C headers) |
| Java/Kotlin | Class files and Kotlin metadata | An embedded JVM through JNI invocation, or a JVM sidecar | FFM bindings (jextract-shaped) on desktop and server, JNI on Android |
| C# / .NET | ECMA‑335 metadata | Hosting through `hostfxr`, or NativeAOT exports | A `LibraryImport` partial class with generated marshallers |
| Python | `.pyi` plus the C-API, HPy, or a supervised worker | In-process (CPython stable ABI), or isolated | A stable-ABI (`abi3`) extension module |
| JS / TS | `.d.ts` | Browser: direct imports. Native: an embedded engine in a wasm component. | Node-API addon, ES module plus wasm, a WIT world for jco |
| wasm components | WIT | Canonical ABI. Async uses WASI 0.3 `future`/`stream` [W2]. | A WIT world and a component |
| GPU | SPIR-V reflection, PTX, WGSL, Metal libraries | Launch descriptors and buffer-binding layouts (std430/scalar). DLPack or Arrow for zero-copy tensors and columns [A1,A2]. | SPIR-V/PTX modules with generated host bindings |
| OS ABIs | Linux syscall tables. winmd (Win32/WinRT/COM) [WM1]. Apple SDK headers and `.tbd` files. | Raw syscalls on Linux only, where that ABI is stable. Otherwise libc, ntdll or libSystem. COM vtables with refcounts mapped to ownership. | Not applicable |

**Embedding when we are called.** The writer emits an `init(capabilities)`
entry and lazy per-thread attach. The capability list comes from one contract,
for both a native library and a component (Jet already ratified this as
D-EMBED2=C).

**Garbage-collected hosts (JVM, CLR, JS, Python).** Foreign references become
owned handles with a `#Close` that releases a global reference. Nothing
collects cycles across two heaps. The writer documents weak handles for back
references, and the hardened profile reports leaked handles.

## 7. Layer 3: the pareto wrappers

| Need (most common first) | Wrapper | Expands to |
|---|---|---|
| Use a C library | `use "png.h" as png` | C reader → contract → lowering. Safe rows are callable, the rest need a vouch or isolation. |
| A few lines of C | an inline foreign body on a `fn` | An anonymous C source unit read by the **same** C reader. The prototype comes from the Jet signature. |
| Fix or rename imported rows | `#Import module c.png { … }` | An L1 overlay |
| Vouch for an unchecked row | `#Unsafe("reason") { fn … = "sym" }` | A `Vouched` fact plus an audit entry |
| Use a Rust, Python, JS or C++ package | `#Import module rust.serde_json`, `use py.numpy`, … | A reader package, a contract, and a placement |
| Sandbox an untrusted library | `use "libxml2.h" as xml, isolate: .Wasm` | `isolate(contract, .Wasm)`. No call site changes. |
| Be called from another language | `#Export` plus `bindings: [c, python, swift]` | Writer packages over the same contract |
| Share tensors or columns | `Tensor.from_dlpack(x)` / `.to_arrow()` | `Marshal` impls over DLPack and Arrow |

Every wrapper shows its expansion through `jet inspect bind <name>`. That
command prints the row, each fact and its provenance, the projection used, and
the primitives it lowered to.

## 8. Cross-cutting rules

**Zero cost (G2).** A crossing whose `Marshal` impls are all `BLITTABLE` is
one call instruction, with no prologue and no runtime transition. Jet has no GC
and no safepoints, so the JDK `critical` and .NET `SuppressGCTransition`
tricks are not needed [J4,N3]. Only thunks entered by foreign threads pay for
an attach check, which is one thread-local load. When C or C++ source is
visible, the pinned Clang emits LLVM IR into the optimizing tier's module, so
the optimizer can inline across languages (the Rust linker-plugin LTO
precedent [R9]). Inlining is an optimization, never a change of meaning (I9).

**Strings and buffers.** A lend (`&`) of `String` or `[T]` passes
pointer plus length with no copy. A NUL-terminated parameter gets a stack copy
only when the Jet value is not already terminated. Returned views are
zero-copy when a lifetime fact links them to a living owner, and copied
otherwise.

**C variadics.** Typed per call site. The compiler applies default promotions
and the ABI's variadic rule; on Apple arm64 every variadic argument goes on the
stack [AP1]. `printf`-style rows with a `format` attribute are format-checked
at compile time.

**Macros.** Constant macros are evaluated by Clang. A function-like macro
becomes a typed shim, `static inline T name(params) { return MACRO(params); }`,
compiled by the same Clang. Its parameter types come from an overlay, or are
inferred when the macro body is a single call. A statement macro that cannot
be typed is reported, not guessed.

**C++.** Classes are owned handles whose destructor runs as `close`. Movable
types map to `^`. Templates are instantiated on demand in a shim; explicit
`instantiate:` is for libraries with no visible use. Overloads fold into labels,
and ambiguity is a compile error. `std::string_view` and `std::span` become
lifetime-bound views. `unique_ptr` maps to an owned value, `shared_ptr` to a
shared one. Exceptions become `T CppError!`.

**Callbacks.** A closure lowers to a (code, context) pair. Registration returns
an owned token, and dropping the token unregisters it. A callback that a C API
keeps beyond the call needs a `retained` fact: either `Read` (with a matching
unregister) or `Vouched`.

**Threads.** Main-thread-only APIs (UIKit, AppKit, most GUI toolkits) carry
`affinity(.Main)`, and calling them off the main thread is a compile error
where it can be proved and a checked trap otherwise. Foreign threads that enter
Jet are attached on first entry and detached at thread exit.

**Async.** Callback-style APIs turn into `async` functions through
`completion<T>()`. A Jet `async` export becomes the host's native form: a JS
Promise, a Swift `async` function, a Kotlin `suspend` function, a .NET `Task`,
or a WIT `future<T>` [W2].

**Versioning.** Every contract has a hash, and the bound library is verified
at link or load time (symbols present, interface hash equal). `jet build`
diffs the contract against the last frozen one (`api: stable`) and reports
breaking changes. Foreign structs whose size can change between versions are
accessed through generated accessors, so an upgrade cannot shift field offsets
under compiled code (Swift library evolution [SW1]). Optional symbols are `T?`.

**Debugging.** Every tier emits DWARF, so backtraces mix languages. `--trace-ffi=png.*`
logs each crossing with its lowered arguments and results.
The hardened profile checks vouched facts at the edges. An isolated placement
turns the boundary into a message boundary, which can be recorded and replayed.

## 9. Adoption analysis: the design mapped onto Jet

The verdicts are: **Fits** (already ratified, or implementation under a ratified
rule), **Extends** (new capability that is consistent with ratified rules), and
**Replaces** (changes a ratified rule; needs an owner ballot).

| Idea | Jet today | Verdict | Migration | Owner ballot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contract plus readers as packages | D-FFI-UNIFY1, D-FFI-BINDER1 (23 readers, about 22.8k lines), D-CIMPORT1 (pinned Clang), the `jet-ffi-descriptor-v1` stamp | Fits; the descriptor grows into the full fact vocabulary | Medium: descriptor schema v2, readers fill in more facts | none (implementation) |
| Facts with provenance; conservative projection | D-FFI-CMAP1 (nullable → `T?`, `counted_by` → lists), D-FFI-VOUCH1 (vouch blocks, `jet audit`), D-HARDENED1 | Fits; `Proved` and `Observed` become explicit labels | Small | none |
| Ownership across the border | D-FFI-CAP1 (`&`, `^`, `#Close` at the border) | Fits exactly | none | none |
| Public primitives layer (§4) | D-RAWPTR2 raw pointers; `jet_builtins` (D-CORE-BUILTINS1); readers use `foreign.read`; layout and ABI queries, dynamic symbols, thunks, error capture and `Marshal` are compiler-private or missing | **Extends** | Medium: about 12 primitives, most of them already exist internally | **D-FFI-PRIMS1** |
| Inline C as a wrapper over C-source import | D-FFI-ONE1=A keeps inline `#FFI(c)` bodies with the prototype written from the Jet signature. Its recorded loss is "two ways to bring in C". | Fits. The inline body is lowered as an anonymous unit through the D-FFI-CINPUT1 reader, so there is one mechanism and the recorded loss goes away. Syntax is unchanged. | Small, compiler-internal | none: implementation under I8 |
| `#Unsafe` and I1 | The only escape hatch. Vouches name a reason. | Fits. Isolation adds a third safe route that needs no vouch. | none | (see the next row) |
| Isolation as a placement option | Python and JS already run in supervised workers or JS-on-wasm (D-FFI-JS1). Plugins are sandboxed components (D-PLUGIN*). C libraries are in-process only. | **Extends** | Medium: a wasm-compiled C path through the pinned Clang (`wasm32-wasip2`), plus a process host | **D-FFI-ISOLATE1** |
| One meaning across tiers (I9; D-EXEC1, amended by D-EXEC3) | The comptime evaluator refuses foreign calls by name | Extends. `pure` rows run at compile time through the wasm placement, so they are deterministic and sandboxed. The web tier compiles the same C to wasm32. | Comes with the isolation work | covered by D-FFI-ISOLATE1 |
| Wasm and web | D-PORTABLE-WEB1, D-WASISRV1, WIT for plugins, D-EMBED2=C | Fits. WIT becomes one reader and one writer of the contract. WASI 0.3 async maps onto `completion`. | Small | none |
| Rich exports (being called) | `#Export(c)` allows C primitives only (spec, Embedding artifacts). D-EMBED2=C lists `bindings: [c, python]`. | **Extends**: records, lists, strings, errors, callbacks, handles and async, projected per language by writer packages | Medium to large: one writer per language, C first | **D-FFI-EXPORT2** |
| Zero-cost and cross-language inlining | O2 goes through LLVM. D-EXEC3 limits runtime-function inlining to the runtime's own source. | Fits. Visible C and C++ source is lowered to LLVM IR in the O2 module. | Small to medium | none |
| GPU | D-ACCEL-LIB1 (devices as libraries with CPU reference), D-GPU-COMPUTE-LAUNCH1, D-GPU-DEVICE-OPS1 | Fits. Adds std430/scalar layouts to `layout`, a SPIR-V/PTX reflection reader, and DLPack/Arrow `Marshal` impls. | Medium | none now |
| C++ depth | D-FFI-CPP1 (opaque classes, `CppError`, on-demand templates) | Fits. Adds lifetime-bound views and vtable subclassing. | Medium | none |
| Versioning | `api: stable` (D-CAP4), descriptor stamp, E3208 | Fits. Adds load-time verification and resilient accessors. | Small | none |
| Debugging | `jet inspect bind`, D-HARDENED1 | Fits. Adds `--trace-ffi` and mixed DWARF backtraces. | Small | none |

**Net effect on ratified decisions.** Nothing ratified is reversed. D-FFI-ONE1's
recorded loss goes away through implementation. Three ballots add capability:
D-FFI-PRIMS1, D-FFI-ISOLATE1 and D-FFI-EXPORT2. The ballot JSON files are in the
lane's `ballot/` directory.
