  under A; the file form `module math;` stays.
- D-TUPLE-DESTRUCT1=A: tuples have named members, `(x: 1, y: 2)`. This is the
  value a function head must be told apart from.
- D-DOTCTOR3=A: `Type{ body }` is a typed literal. It is why
  `(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` runs today as a typed value.
- D-CALLVALUE1=B and D-MARKER-DECL1=A: unchanged; markers stay above the
  binding.

## 2. What happens today

Probes live in `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/probes/m-decl`. Each ran
with the dev jet at `--optimize=none` and `full`, and d8 and d10 also at
`basic`.

- `d1_lambda_today.jet`: `square :: (n: Int) -> n * n`, `n -> n * 2` and
  `(n) -> { n + 1 }` all run.
- `d2_tuple.jet`: `p :: (x: 1, y: 2)` is a tuple and prints 3.
- `d3_bind_fn.jet`: a module-level `square :: (n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` is
  E0357, "Constant `square` must be ALL_CAPS".
- `d4_point_struct_bind.jet`: `Point :: struct { x: Int }` is E0003.
- `d5_fn_value.jet`: a `:=` lambda can be reassigned and prints 3.
- `d6_local_recur.jet`: a local lambda calling itself is E0804.
- `d7_fn_literal.jet`: `fn(n) { n * n }` as a value is E0003.
- `d8_program_today.jet`: the D-DECL-BINDING1 program in today's spelling,
  minus the generic parts, prints 7, 4.0, [1, 4, 9], [1, 4, 9], 2, 120 and 7.
- `d10_lambda_today.jet`: the D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1 program in today's spelling
  prints [3, 4], [10, 20, 30, 40], [9, 16], `> done` and [3, 5, 7, 9].

Writing the program surfaced two checks worth knowing. `#Inline(Always)` on a
function that is also passed as a value is E0918. An error enum named in a
failure rail needs `#Error`, or the result is E2417.

## 3. The design

Every named thing is `name :: value`. A function value is
`(params) arrow result failure { body }`: today's head without `fn` and the
name. A type is `struct { … }`, `enum { … }`, `trait { … }` or another type on
the right. A lambda is the same value without a name, leaving out what the
call gives: `nums.map((n) { n * n })`.

A parenthesized list is a function only when `{`, `->`, `-[` or a failure rail
follows its `)`. So `origin :: (x: 0, y: 0)` stays a tuple, and
`Pt :: (x: Int, y: Int)` stays a tuple type. In `if` and `loop` heads the test
is off, as Rust does for struct literals. A scan of every `.jet` file found no
`if (name) {` or `loop (name) {` head in Jet code.

Inside a type body, `x: Int` is a field and `norm1 :: (self) -> Int { … }` a
method. `Shape.area :: (self) -> Float { … }` adds one outside, replacing
`fn Shape.area`. `impl Type { … }` keeps its head, because it names nothing
new. `::` binds a fixed function that may call itself; `:=` binds a changeable
function value that may not. `fn` remains only in function types.

D-DECL-BINDING1 also shows Odin's form, `square :: fn(n: Int) -> Int { … }`,
and keeping the words. D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1 v2 shows keeping a short arrow beside
the value form. Ballots: `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/ballot/`
`D-DECL-BINDING1.json` and `D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1.json`.

## 4. Size of the change

`$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/b2/census-decl.mjs` over a dev export of 17,636 `.jet` files counted:

| site | count | under A |
|---|---|---|
| `fn name(` heads | 62,347 | `name :: (` |
| of those, indented members | 49,924 | `name :: (` inside the body |
| `struct Name` heads | 7,168 | `Name :: struct` |
| `enum Name` heads | 1,889 | `Name :: enum` |
| `trait Name` heads | 183 | `Name :: trait` |
| inline `module name {` | 576 | `name :: module {` |
| `impl` blocks | 1,612 | unchanged |
| `fn(` function types | 773 | unchanged |
| markers before a function | 4,808 | unchanged, above the binding |

Main's lambda census (`$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/b4/lam/census.mjs`), rerun
on the same export, counts 4,812 lambdas in 1,197 files. Of these, 3,842 have
an expression body, 888 a bare parameter, and 220 are stored in a binding.
Version 1's `fn(…) { … }` form adds 12,437 characters. The bound-value form
adds 2,813, or 0.6 per lambda, because braced lambdas shrink.

## 5. Sources

- Jai: Docs/research/jai-vs-jet-syntax-briefing-2026-09-16.html:234-238 and
  https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai
- Odin: https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#procedures
- Zig, RFC to bind functions with `const`: https://github.com/ziglang/zig/issues/1717
- JavaScript arrow functions:
  https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Functions/Arrow_functions
- Kotlin lambdas: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/lambdas.html
- Earlier Jet review: Docs/research/jai-vs-jet-fable-brief-2026-09-16.md:106

sections.title: Working back from the speed of light (card #6343)
sections.body:
# Working back from the speed of light (card #6343)

Date: 2026-10-30. Lane: SurfaceDesign-2. Dev: 4e514f96e1.

The owner asked us to work backwards from the machine's physical limits to
what Jet must support and generate, and to be faster than Rust, tail calls
included. This note takes each hardware limit in turn. For each it says what
the hardware allows, what Jet does today, what Rust, Zig, C, Mojo and Odin
guarantee, and what Jet must guarantee.

Most answers are compiler work, not language surface. Those become numbered
criteria in section 5, for codegen cards. One answer needs an owner choice:
whether tail calls are jumps on every build level. Ballot D-TAIL-CALL1
carries it.

## 1. Method

The probe machine is an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D (Zen 4, 16 cores, 32 threads,
AVX-512). Its load average ran from 40 to 95 during the runs, so wall time
was useless. Every kernel ran three times under `perf stat -e
cycles:u,instructions:u`, and the tables keep the minimum of each.
Instruction counts are exact; cycle counts still carry some noise from the
shared caches.

- Jet kernels: `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/probes/k6343/*.jet`,
  built at `--optimize=none`, `basic` and `full` (O0, O1, O2) with the dev
  compiler, toolchain root an export of 4e514f96e1.
- Rust peers: `probes/r6343/kernels.rs`, one binary, the kernel picked by
  argument. Built with rustc 1.97.1 at opt-level 0, at opt-level 3, and at
  opt-level 3 with `-C overflow-checks=on`. Inputs pass through `black_box`.
- Harness: `probes/pstat.sh`. Raw table: `probes/pstat6343.tsv`.

Hardware figures come from AMD's Software Optimization Guide for Zen 4,
publication 57647 revision 1.01 (cited below as SOG).

## 2. Measured kernels

Each cell is millions of user cycles / millions of user instructions. The last
two columns divide Jet O2 by Rust O3. The AGENTS.md gate (AGENTS.md:149-154)
is a Jet/Rust ratio at or below 1.05. Every finished kernel printed the same
output in Jet and Rust. `tail2` stops in Jet, so its ratio columns say
"stops". Each figure is the lowest of three runs, taken with `perf stat`
on a loaded 32-core machine.

| kernel | Jet O0 | Jet O1 | Jet O2 | Rust O0 | Rust O3 | Rust O3 + overflow checks | cycles O2/O3 | instructions O2/O3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `loop_int` | 5,652 / 31,110 | 6,418 / 28,310 | 2,707 / 16,402 | 14,438 / 30,400 | 1,853 / 5,200 | 1,850 / 7,600 | 1.46 | 3.15 |
| `loop_i64` | 6,682 / 27,110 | 5,906 / 23,910 | 3,558 / 18,310 | 8,014 / 30,400 | 1,415 / 5,200 | 1,472 / 7,600 | 2.51 | 3.52 |
| `sum_index` | 2,009 / 13,472 | 1,759 / 12,132 | 2,182 / 11,542 | 6,892 / 20,040 | 236 / 500 | 442 / 1,350 | 9.25 | 23.08 |
| `sum_iter` | 1,562 / 8,712 | 1,135 / 7,132 | 1,035 / 6,572 | 2,412 / 9,240 | 270 / 500 | 293 / 1,350 | 3.83 | 13.14 |
| `axpy` | 4,524 / 27,008 | 3,630 / 20,572 | 2,758 / 16,992 | 5,284 / 16,356 | 505 / 750 | 542 / 750 | 5.46 | 22.66 |
| `inline_small` | 4,471 / 30,202 | 3,038 / 18,885 | 1,660 / 10,519 | 5,622 / 20,742 | 873 / 2,788 | 620 / 3,259 | 1.90 | 3.77 |
| `struct_ret` | 2,528 / 14,226 | 2,078 / 12,676 | 2,018 / 11,827 | 1,203 / 4,400 | 473 / 1,275 | 473 / 1,275 | 4.27 | 9.28 |
| `option_ret` | 942 / 5,885 | 837 / 4,902 | 537 / 3,319 | 1,490 / 5,450 | 201 / 784 | 212 / 900 | 2.67 | 4.23 |
| `fib` | 362 / 1,809 | 266 / 1,495 | 269 / 1,495 | 198 / 672 | 75 / 302 | 152 / 433 | 3.59 | 4.95 |
| `dispatch` | 5,351 / 16,620 | 3,161 / 14,932 | 2,778 / 9,440 | 4,065 / 14,638 | 925 / 3,175 | 776 / 3,488 | 3.00 | 2.97 |
| `matmul` | 1,101 / 6,056 | 833 / 5,157 | 490 / 2,337 | 2,133 / 5,457 | 20 / 102 | 25 / 102 | 24.50 | 22.91 |
| `byte_count` | 4,174 / 23,900 | 3,098 / 15,041 | 3,006 / 11,622 | 7,617 / 30,410 | 1,084 / 3,364 | 1,114 / 4,872 | 2.77 | 3.45 |
| `closure_map` | 1,876 / 9,818 | 2,837 / 9,124 | 2,076 / 8,776 | 5,191 / 11,019 | 188 / 553 | 184 / 603 | 11.04 | 15.87 |
| `tail2` | 645 / 1,353 | 464 / 1,110 | 504 / 1,110 | 310 / 527 | 6 / 25 | 62 / 185 | stops | stops |

Reading the table:

- No kernel meets the 1.05 gate at O2. The closest in cycles are `loop_int`
  (1.46) and `inline_small` (1.90). In instructions every kernel needs at
  least three times Rust's count.
- The worst gaps are loops over lists: `matmul`, `sum_index`, `axpy`,
  `sum_iter` and `closure_map`, at 13 to 23 times Rust's instructions. Each
  step pays a bounds check, `Int` tests and scalar code, where Rust
  vectorizes and removes the checks.
- Quick runs already beat Rust's debug builds on most kernels. Jet O0 used
  fewer cycles than Rust O0 on 10 of the 13 finished kernels. Rust O0 won on
  `struct_ret`, `fib` and `dispatch`.
- O2 adds nothing over O1 on `fib` and `tail2`: the instruction counts are
  identical.
- Rust with overflow checks on is the fair peer for checked arithmetic. It
  costs 1.46 times plain Rust's instructions on `loop_int` and 2.7 times on
  `sum_index`; Jet costs 3.15 and 23.08 times.
- `tail2` is not a finished run in Jet. It prints the first result, then
  stops with E3012 in `is_even(10000000)` on every level. Rust O3 finishes in
  25 million instructions because LLVM turned both recursions into loops.
  Rust O0 overflows its stack.
- Cycle counts carry noise from the loaded machine; for example Jet O2
  `sum_index` shows more cycles than O1 with fewer instructions.
- The first `dispatch` peer used Rust's truncating `%`, and printed a
  different total. Jet's `%` on `Int` is the floor modulo (`-7 % 3` is 2), so
  the peer now uses `rem_euclid`, and both print 967383. The `dispatch` row
  comes from that rerun (probe `probes/m6343/mod.jet` prints 2 and -4).

## 3. The limits, one by one

### 3.1 Instruction throughput

**Hardware.** Zen 4 dispatches up to 6 macro ops per cycle and keeps up to
320 in flight (SOG sections 2.9.8 and 2.10.3). A loop's speed is set by how many
instructions each step needs, and by the longest chain of dependent ones.

**Jet today.** `loop_int` needs 3.15 times Rust's instructions at O2, and
`inline_small` 3.77 times. Every `Int` operation carries a small-or-big test
(D-INTBIG1=A: "arithmetic carries a small-versus-big check"). The O2 code of
`axpy` holds about seven `add`/`jo` pairs per step. The fixed-width `I64` loop
is slower than the `Int` loop (18,310 against 16,402 million instructions),
because each `I64{i}` conversion and each `I64` operation is checked too.

**Peers.** Rust release builds turn overflow checks off by default, so `+`
wraps silently (Cargo book, profiles: `overflow-checks` defaults to false in
release). C makes signed overflow undefined, so the compiler assumes it never
happens. Zig checks overflow in Debug and ReleaseSafe and assumes it away in
ReleaseFast (ziglang.org/documentation/0.15.2, Build Mode). This note did not
check Odin's or Mojo's overflow rules.

**What Jet must guarantee.** Exact `Int` and checked fixed widths stay; they
are ratified safety. The compiler must then remove the checks it can prove
away, so a counted loop costs what Rust's costs. Rust with overflow checks on
is the honest peer for checked arithmetic: `loop_int` costs 7,600 million
instructions there, against Jet's 16,402. Range analysis (P-RANGE in
Docs/research/ir-optimization-inventory-2026-10-21.md:257-259) is the
missing pass.

### 3.2 Memory bandwidth and latency

**Hardware.** The L1 data cache serves three memory operations per cycle, at
most two of them 256-bit loads (SOG section 2.6.2). A main-memory miss costs
hundreds of cycles, so a stream must be sequential and prefetchable.

**Jet today.** `byte_count` scans a 64 MB list of `U8`. `sum_iter` and
`sum_index` scan 80 MB of `Int`. Even so, their instruction ratios (table
above) show the loop body, not memory, is the limit today. Two layout costs
show up as well: optionals and small records returned from functions
(`option_ret`, `struct_ret`).

**Peers.** Rust, Zig and C store plain values inline and return small structs
in registers under the platform C ABI. Rust's `Option<i64>` is two words with
no heap use.

**What Jet must guarantee.** Values in lists, optionals, results and records
are stored inline (D-MEM-UNBOX1=A). Layout control for experts is ratified
(D-JAI-LAYOUT1=A), and so are cache hints (D-CACHE-CONTROL1=A). The compiler
criteria are box elimination for optionals (P-BOX, inventory:270-271) and
register returns for small records (G2, inventory:246).

### 3.3 Caches

**Hardware.** 32 KB of L1 data, 1 MB of L2 per core, and 96 MB of L3 on this
part (SOG sections 2.6.2 to 2.6.4; `lscpu` on the probe machine). Each cache line is 64
bytes.

**Jet today.** A fresh `String` is two allocations: a 32-byte header and the
bytes (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Text.jet:54-63, 74-77). That doubles
allocator traffic and splits each text over two lines. `matmul` keeps three
300 by 300 `Float` lists, 2.2 MB in all, so they spill out of L2 into L3. Rust
runs the same layout in 20 million cycles, so Jet's gap there is in the loop
body, not the cache.

**What Jet must guarantee.** Nothing new at the surface. Note #6342
(Docs/research/2026-10-30-fixed-text-and-buffer.md) lists the text layout
criteria.

### 3.4 Branch prediction

**Hardware.** A mispredicted branch costs 11 to 18 cycles, 13 in the common
case (SOG section 2.8). A predictable branch costs almost nothing, so checks
that never fail are cheap if they sit off the hot path.

**Jet today.** `if op == { … }` on an enum compiles to a chain of compares,
one arm per `If` (Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildExpr.jet:3552-3553). Jet has no
jump table. `dispatch` measures the cost. Bounds and overflow stops in `axpy`
are inline in the loop body, each behind a forward branch.

**Peers.** Rust, C (Clang), Zig and Odin compile through LLVM, which lowers a
dense `match` or `switch` to a jump table when that is cheaper than compares.

**What Jet must guarantee.** Nothing at the surface: `if x == { … }` already
says everything a jump table needs. The criteria are a jump table for dense
enum and integer matches, and stop paths moved out of line.

### 3.5 SIMD width

**Hardware.** Zen 4 runs AVX-512 by issuing each 512-bit operation over two
cycles on 256-bit paths, so peak FLOPS match 256-bit code (SOG section 2.11).
Four `Float`s per operation per pipe is the floor a loop should reach.

**Jet today.** Jet has no vectorizer (P-VEC, inventory:281). `axpy` at O2
uses scalar `movsd`, `mulsd` and `addsd`. It needs 22.66 times Rust's
instructions. Before the loop it copies `dst` when the list might be shared:
a uniqueness test, then `jet_rt_alloc_8` and `jet_rt_mem_move`.

**Peers.** Rust and C vectorize through LLVM, helped by `&mut` being
`noalias` in Rust and by `restrict` in C. Zig has `@Vector`, Mojo makes
`SIMD[type, width]` its base numeric type, and Odin has `#simd`.

**What Jet must guarantee.** Already ratified: auto-vectorization by default
with an opt-out (D-SIMD3=B), one lane type family (D-LANES1=A) and checked
native intrinsics (D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A). Jet's `&` is exclusive
(D-MEMREF-EXCL1=A), and plain parameters cannot be written (D-PARAM-CONST1=A).
So Jet can promise the "no alias" fact that Rust gets from `&mut`, on every
call, with no annotation. The vectorizer must use it.

Float reductions are the one trap. Adding Floats in a different order changes
the result, and I9 (AGENTS.md:135-147) forbids a result that depends on the
build level. A vectorized Float sum must keep the source order, or the
program must ask for lanes. Integer sums can be reordered freely.

### 3.6 Call overhead

**Hardware.** A call and return cost a few cycles plus any registers saved,
restored or spilled around them. Inlining removes all of it and opens the
callee to the caller's optimizations.

**Jet today.** `fib(35)` needs 4.95 times Rust's instructions and 3.96 times
its cycles at O2. Each call and return also costs a fetch bubble (SOG
section 2.8.1.3.3). Jet's inliner skips any callee over 40 IR
instructions at O1 and 60 at O2 (inventory:198), and does not honour
`#Inline(Always)` (P-IA, inventory:272). Every `Int` argument carries a drop
after the call, because an `Int` may own heap digits.

**Tail calls.** A call that is the last thing a function does can reuse the
caller's frame. D-DROP-ASAP1=A promised this: "Emit tail calls as jumps when
no visible drop is pending". D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A says "Only O2 may remove
recursive calls". Today no level does it. `walk(10000000, 0)` and
`is_even(10000000)` stop with E3012 on O0, O1 and O2. The O2 code of `walk`
is `call tail2_walk` followed by `call jet_rt_int_drop`. The drop is the
pending work that blocks the jump.

Rust has no stable guarantee. `become` is nightly only and "incomplete"
(doc.rust-lang.org/std/keyword.become.html). Rust O3 turns `walk` into a loop
by choice, but Rust O0 overflows. Clang's `[[clang::musttail]]` and GCC 15's
same attribute guarantee the jump or refuse to compile: a GCC 15.3 build at
`-O0` ran `walk(10000000, 0)` to completion (`probes/c6343/mt.c`). Zig has
`@call(.always_tail, f, args)`. Scheme requires proper tail calls of every
implementation (R7RS section 3.5).

Guaranteed tail calls are a place where Jet can beat stable Rust. Interpreters
and parsers written as small functions that jump to each other keep their
state in registers. The upb protobuf parser reached over 2 GB/s that way
(blog.reverberate.org, 2021-04-21, "Parsing Protobuf at 2+GB/s").

**What Jet must guarantee.** Ballot D-TAIL-CALL1 recommends that every tail
call is a jump on every level, with a lint naming any call that cannot jump.
With ASAP drop, an `Int` argument's digits are freed before the jump, so the
drop no longer blocks it.

### 3.7 Code size

**Hardware.** The op cache holds 6.75 K macro ops and the L1 instruction
cache 32 KB (SOG section 2.9.1). Hot code that fits runs from the op cache at
up to 9 ops per cycle.

**Jet today.** Inline overflow and bounds stops bloat hot loops. The
inventory records O1 code 4.5 percent and O2 code 9.6 percent larger than O0
over 280 programs (inventory:216-221).

**What Jet must guarantee.** Nothing at the surface. The criterion is that
stop paths and cold calls move out of the loop body, so hot loops fit in the
op cache.

## 4. Peer guarantees

| guarantee | Rust | Zig | C | Mojo | Odin | Jet (ratified) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| integer overflow | wraps in release, panics in debug | checked except ReleaseFast | signed is undefined | not checked | not checked | exact `Int` (D-INTBIG1); fixed widths trap |
| bounds checks | always, optimizer removes | except ReleaseFast | none | not checked | default on, `#no_bounds_check` per block | always; proofs remove (D-OOBPROOF1) |
| no-alias facts | `&mut` is noalias | `noalias` keyword | `restrict` | not checked | not checked | `&` exclusive (D-MEMREF-EXCL1) |
| guaranteed tail calls | nightly `become` only | `.always_tail` | Clang and GCC 15 `musttail` | not checked | not checked | promised (D-DROP-ASAP1), not built |
| SIMD | auto plus `std::arch` | `@Vector` | auto plus intrinsics | `SIMD` type | `#simd` arrays | auto plus lanes (D-SIMD3, D-LANES1) |
| destruction | end of scope | manual, `defer` | manual | at last use | manual, `defer` | at last use (D-DROP-ASAP1) |
| forced inlining | `#[inline(always)]` | `inline fn` | `always_inline` | `@always_inline` | `#force_inline` | `#Inline(Always)` (D-INLINE-PARAM1), not honoured |

Sources: Cargo book profiles (doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html);
Zig 0.15.2 documentation, Build Mode and `@call`; Clang AttributeReference,
`musttail`; Mojo manual, "Value destruction" (mojolang.org/docs/manual/lifecycle/death);
Odin overview and directives (odin-lang.org/docs/overview, /docs/directives).

## 5. Compiler criteria (no owner choice)

Each criterion is a codegen card's acceptance list. Each names the kernel
that proves it; a criterion is met when that kernel's Jet O2 / Rust O3
instruction ratio is at or below 1.05.

1. **Range facts on `Int`** (P-RANGE). A loop counter with known bounds, and
   arithmetic on it that provably stays in range, compile to plain machine
   arithmetic with no small-or-big test and no drop. Kernels: `loop_int`,
   `inline_small`, `sum_index`.
2. **Checked `I64` costs one test.** A fixed-width operation compiles to the
   machine operation plus one overflow branch, and `I64{i}` from an in-range
   `Int` counter costs nothing. Kernel: `loop_i64`, against Rust with
   overflow checks on.
3. **Bounds-check removal** (P-BCE). An index proven below the list length
   needs no check, and the length is loaded once per loop when the list
   cannot change. Kernels: `sum_index`, `axpy`, `matmul`.
4. **Hoisting** (P-LICM). Loop-invariant loads, such as a list's data pointer
   and length, move before the loop. Kernels: `axpy`, `matmul`.
5. **Vectorizer** (P-VEC, D-SIMD3=B). Inner loops over `Int` and `Float`
   lists use AVX2 or AVX-512 lanes. Exclusive `&` and read-only parameters
   are the no-alias proof. Float sums keep source order unless lanes are
   written. Kernels: `axpy`, `sum_iter`, `byte_count`, `matmul`.
6. **No copy on write when unique.** A `&` list parameter is unique by
   construction, so the uniqueness test and copy at function entry go.
   Kernel: `axpy`.
7. **Small records and optionals in registers** (P-BOX, G2, G3). A record of
   up to four words, and an optional of one word, return in registers with no
   heap box. Kernels: `struct_ret`, `option_ret`.
8. **Inliner** (P-IA, D-OPT-INLINE1, D-INLINE-PARAM1). `#Inline(Always)` is
   honoured at every level that inlines. Leaf calls in hot loops are inlined
   past the 40/60 budget when the caller's loop is hot. Kernels:
   `inline_small`, `fib`.
9. **Jump tables.** A match on an enum or a dense integer range with five or
   more arms becomes one indexed jump. Kernel: `dispatch`.
10. **Tail calls** (D-DROP-ASAP1, ballot D-TAIL-CALL1). Under D-TAIL-CALL1 A
    every tail call is a jump on every tier, compile-time evaluation
    included. Kernels: `tail1`, `tail2`, `tail3`.
11. **Cold stop paths.** Bounds, overflow and division stops sit after the
    function's hot code, reached by a forward branch that falls through on
    success. Kernels: all loops.
12. **Closures.** `map` and `filter` with a literal lambda inline the lambda
    and fuse into one pass with one result allocation. Kernel: `closure_map`.
13. **Debug info for jumps.** Release builds record tail calls in DWARF
    (`DW_TAG_call_site` with `DW_AT_call_tail_call`, DWARF 5 section 3.4).
    Quick runs keep the last 16 tail calls per thread for stop reports.

## 6. Paired perf cells against Rust

Each row is one cell for Tools/perf/native-cells: a Jet program, a Rust peer
and a metric. The gate is AGENTS.md:149-154: Jet/Rust at or below 1.05 in
cycles. The sources exist already in `probes/k6343` and `probes/r6343`.

| cell | Jet program | Rust peer | criteria | today (O2/O3 instructions) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `numerics/int_loop` | `k6343/loop_int.jet` | `kernels.rs loop_int` | 1, 11 | 3.15 |
| `numerics/i64_loop` | `k6343/loop_i64.jet` | `kernels.rs loop_i64` | 2, 11 (peer: Rust O3 with overflow checks) | 3.52 |
| `collections/sum_index` | `k6343/sum_index.jet` | `kernels.rs sum_index` | 1, 3, 4, 5 | 23.08 |
| `collections/sum_iter` | `k6343/sum_iter.jet` | `kernels.rs sum_iter` | 5 | 13.14 |
| `numerics/axpy` | `k6343/axpy.jet` | `kernels.rs axpy` | 3, 4, 5, 6 | 22.66 |
| `numerics/inline_small` | `k6343/inline_small.jet` | `kernels.rs inline_small` | 1, 8 | 3.77 |
| `numerics/struct_ret` | `k6343/struct_ret.jet` | `kernels.rs struct_ret` | 7 | 9.28 |
| `numerics/option_ret` | `k6343/option_ret.jet` | `kernels.rs option_ret` | 7 | 4.23 |
| `numerics/fib` (exists) | `k6343/fib.jet` | `kernels.rs fib` | 8, 1 | 4.95 |
| `numerics/dispatch` | `k6343/dispatch.jet` | `kernels.rs dispatch` | 9 | 2.97 |
| `numerics/matmul` | `k6343/matmul.jet` | `kernels.rs matmul` | 3, 4, 5 | 22.91 |
| `text/byte_scan` (exists) | `k6343/byte_count.jet` | `kernels.rs byte_count` | 5 | 3.45 |
| `closures/map_filter_collect` (exists) | `k6343/closure_map.jet` | `kernels.rs closure_map` | 12 | 15.87 |
| `numerics/tail_walk` | `k6343/tail2.jet` | `kernels.rs tail2` | 10 | Jet stops with E3012 |

Two cells pair a surface with its plain spelling, as AGENTS.md:171-174
requires for a surface added for performance:

- `numerics/tail_walk`: `walk(n - 1, acc + n)` as a tail call against the
  same sum written with `loop`. D-TAIL-CALL1 A passes when the tail form costs
  no more than the loop form, on every level.
- `numerics/tail_interp`: a 16-opcode bytecode interpreter written as
  handlers that tail-call the next handler, against the same interpreter as a
  `loop` around a match. The peer is the Rust `loop` plus `match` version,
  because stable Rust cannot promise the tail form.

## 7. Bugs found

1. Tail calls are not jumps on any level, against D-DROP-ASAP1=A. Repro:
   `probes/k6343/tail1.jet` stops with E3012 on O0, O1 and O2. `tail2.jet`
   stops in `is_even(10000000)`, and `tail3.jet` stops at depth 1,000,000.
2. `#Inline(Always)` is not honoured (already tracked as P-IA,
   inventory:272).
3. The fixed-width `I64` loop needs more instructions than the `Int` loop
   (`probes/k6343/loop_i64.jet` against `loop_int.jet`).
4. A `&` list parameter is tested for uniqueness and may be copied on entry,
   though `&` is exclusive. Repro: disassemble `axpy_axpy` in a full build of
   `probes/k6343/axpy.jet`.

## 8. Decisions consulted

D-DROP-ASAP1=A, D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A, D-TAIL-RETURN1=A, D-TASK-SLICE1=A,
D-DEADLINE-ONE1=A, D-STACKBOUND1=A, D-INTBIG1=A, D-OOBPROOF1=A,
D-UB-BOUNDARY1 (open, owned by MemDesign), D-SIMD3=B, D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A,
D-SIMD-COMPILER1=A, D-LANES1=A, D-OPT-INLINE1=A, D-CODEGEN-HINTS1=A,
D-INLINE-PARAM1=A, D-MEMREF-EXCL1=A, D-PARAM-CONST1=A, D-MEM-UNBOX1=A,
D-CABI-PLATFORM1=A, D-CACHE-CONTROL1=A, D-JAI-LAYOUT1=A, D-ARRAY-CAPACITY1=A,
D-ARRAY-INDEX1=A, D-OPTFLAG1=A, D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1=B, D-EXEC3=A,
D-SCRIPT-SLOTADD1 (open: compound update of a list slot).

sections.title: GPU work in Jet: one way in, one meaning on every device
sections.body:
# GPU work in Jet: one way in, one meaning on every device

Date: 2026-10-30. Card #6344, criteria 1 to 3. Author: MemDesign-2 lane
(design only). Probes live in `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-2/probes/`
(`g/` for GPU and facts, `perf/` for the timing cell) and ran with
`$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/base/latest/jet` (commit 4e514f96e1) against a
`git archive` export of dev 4e514f96e1. Every probe ran with `jet run
--optimize=none|basic|full` (o0, o1, o2) through `probes/tiers.sh`; outputs are
in `probes/out/<name>.<tier>.{out,err,rc}`. Unless a row says otherwise, all
three levels gave the same result.

The owner asked four things: how Jet can split one program into CPU and GPU
parts as Mojo does, whether Jet can have a portable GPU kernel library, how a
user pushes code to the GPU without a large barrier, and how math such as sine
stays portable and accurate. This note answers each from ratified law, from
what the compiler does today, and from peer languages. It raises one owner
choice, filed as the ballot `D-GPU-DEVICE-OPS1`; everything else is
implementation under law that already exists.

## Ratified and open decisions

Tower decisions (read with `node Tools/tower/tower.mjs decision show <ID>`):

| Decision | Status | What it settles for this card |
|---|---|---|
| D-GPU-COMPUTE-LAUNCH1 | ratified A, 2026-09-11 | `compute.launch(kernel, inputs: …)` launches a checked `#Kernel`; a real GPU, never an implicit CPU substitute. |
| D-GPU-SHADER-SURFACE1 | ratified B, 2026-09-11 | Graphics functions use `#Shader`; `#Kernel` stays for compute. |
| D-GPU-F32-STORAGE1 | ratified A, 2026-09-12 | A typed `[F32]` list becomes a Tensor without widening. |
| D-GPU-INDEXED-RESOURCE1 | ratified A, 2026-10-05 | One GPU calculation returns one answer, or places several through indexed writes. |
| D-ACCEL-LIB1 | ratified A, 2026-10-28 | GPUs and accelerators are libraries over a public, versioned kernel IR, each checked against the CPU result. |
| D-CORE-BOUNDARY1 | ratified A, 2026-10-05 | Chip knowledge lives in the library as typed instruction entries with a plain Jet body. |
| D-CORE-FEATURE-FLOW1 | ratified A, 2026-10-05 | Chip features are automatic by default with explicit expert control. |
| D-HOST-CAPS1 | ratified A, 2026-10-07 | Typed hardware facts through `$build.hardware`, `requires:` and `uses:`. |
| D-AUTOPIN1 | ratified A, 2026-09-28 | Every automatic choice (including placement) can be seen and locked. |
| D-EXEC3 | ratified A, 2026-10-07 | Build levels share speed-ups and are checked against each other. |
| D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 | ratified A, 2026-10-30 | The compiler builds in machine powers; Core declares the rest. |
| D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1 | ratified A, 2026-10-30 | Each build's effect limit comes from its target profile. |
| D-COMPUTE-AUTODIFF-SCOPE1 | ratified B, 2026-10-17 | Scope of automatic differentiation in `core.compute`. |
| D-ARRAY-LANESCMP1 | ratified C, 2026-10-30 | Lane-wise comparisons are methods returning `Lanes<Bool, N>`. |
| D-LANES1, D-CPU-DISPATCH1 | ratified A | CPU vector lanes and automatic CPU chip copies. |
| D-MATH-BITS1 | open, recommendation A | `core.math` returns the same correctly rounded bits on every platform, level and at compile time. |

Decisions kept in `Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md` (not in Tower):

- D-COMPUTE1=D, one Core compute family (`syntax-decisions.md:6892-6896`).
- D-COMPUTE-TYPE1=D, `Tensor<T>` owner and unified `View` (`:6898-6903`).
- D-COMPUTE-PLACE1=D, `.Auto` placement with receipts; a fallback "cannot
  change precision, effects, failure shape, or observable results"
  (`:6905-6910`).
- D-COMPUTE-KERNEL1=D, proved safe kernels plus an audited raw tier
  (`:6912-6917`).
- D-COMPUTE-KERNEL-SURFACE1=B, the `#Kernel(.parallel)` marker. "This epoch
  ships the conservative read-only, effect-free expression subset; indexed
  writes, loops, captures, and opaque/provider calls remain rejected until
  their proof facts exist" (`:6919-6925`).
- D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1=D, default F32Strict plus Reproducible; "Fast math,
  reassociation, and nondeterministic reductions require named recorded
  policies"; every backend conforms to the CPU oracle (`:6953-6959`).
- D-COMPUTE-RAWBOUNDARY1=A, raw device code only inside `#Unsafe` with a
  provider-issued contract (`:6961-6967`).
- D-SIMD3=B (`:3762`), D-EXEC2=A (`:3773`), D-DET1 (`:3303`), D-FLOATW1
  (`:1082`).
- Table rows: D-GPU-HELPER-SCOPE1=A (`:9124`), D-GPU-PACKAGING1=A (`:9126`),
  D-ACCEL1=A (`:8458`), D-TIER-FORM1=A (`:9735`).

The drafts D-GPU-GROUP1, D-GPU-SUBGROUP1, D-GPU-ATOMIC1, D-GPU-TILE1,
D-GPU-U321 and D-GPU-RANKED-SCOPE1 were written but never ratified; they are
gated on performance evidence (`Docs/research/mine-for-jet-2026-09-12.md:3082-3088`).

## What runs today

| Probe | Program | Result on o0, o1, o2 |
|---|---|---|
| g1, g15 | `#Kernel(.parallel) fn axpy(a: Float, x: Float, y: Float) -> Float { a * x + y }`, called on the CPU | Prints `cpu:5.0` and `axpy:7.0`. The marker parses and sema accepts the kernel. |
| g2b | `compute.launch(add, inputs: (left: xs, right: ys))` | E1004 "`core.compute` has no item `launch`". |
| g2c | the ratified example's positional `inputs: (xs, ys)` | E0048 "Jet tuples name every member". |
| g8 | `compute.from_list` of an `[F32]` list | E0112 "wants [Float] … but this is [F32]" (D-GPU-F32-STORAGE1 unbuilt). |
| g3, g4 | `compute.from_list`, `compute.add`, device values | ICE 101, "ir.build unlowered … runtime route jet_compute_from_list" and "argument type ComputeDevice … unlowered". |
| tm4k | gauntlet `Tools/gauntlet/entries/tensor-map-4k/jet/run.jet` | ICE 101, "runtime route jet_compute_full". |
| g5 | `#Shader` | E0927, unknown marker. |
| g6, g7 | `print` or `math.sin` inside a kernel | E1102 "cannot prove no reachable effects or opaque calls". |
| g11 | a kernel calling a pure helper `fn sq(x: F32) -> F32 { x * x }` | E1102, same obligation (D-GPU-HELPER-SCOPE1 unbuilt). |
| g12, g13 | `math.sqrt`, `math.abs` in a kernel | E1102 "audited Core compute calls only". |
| g10 | a mutable local in a kernel | E1102 "immutable scalar locals". |
| g9 | an `Invocation` parameter | E1102, not sendable. |

The marker is declared at `Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Policy/PreludeMarkers.jet:43`
and its mode and proof record at `Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/AST/Items.jet:704-722`.
The kernel obligations quoted above are raised in
`Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Kernel.jet:93`, `:132` and `:146`. `Core/Compute/Compute.jet`
is 18 lines of opaque carriers, and the `jet_compute_*` routes exist only as
call rows (`Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CoreCallRows.jet:662-723`), which is
why tensor operations reach the IR builder unlowered. These ICEs are the known
family tracked by #5454 (`Tools/testkit/known-failing.tsv:33-37`, `:290-291`). In the browser
prelude, `.Auto` placement maps to the CPU
(`Compiler/Prelude/Web/Core/ComputeWebGpu.js:525`), against
D-GPU-COMPUTE-LAUNCH1's "never an implicit CPU substitute".

Core math is C libm: `Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/CompilerNeededMath.jet:3-4`
says "Import that same C operation, never approximate transcendental
functions", and `:28` imports `sin`. Probe h5 prints
`math.sin(36.844070105782698)` as `-0.754598304262754` and
`math.cos(1.0e22)` as `0.523214785395139`, the same digits on every level.

The test machine has an AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (RADV NAVI31, Vulkan 1.4, seen
with `vulkaninfo`), so a real device exists for the cells below. What blocks
them is the compiler, not hardware.

## How peers do it

**Mojo.** A kernel is an ordinary function launched from the host with
`ctx.enqueue_function[vector_addition](…, grid_dim=1, block_dim=…)` and indexes
its data with `thread_idx.x`
(`Mojo/docs/site/code/tools/notebooks/vector_addition.mojo:28-81`, corpus
commit 85356f6562ed). The compiler builds the same source once for the host and
once per GPU target. Inside a kernel, `comptime if` on compile-target
predicates such as `is_nvidia_gpu()` is evaluated for the kernel's target,
while host-side `std.sys.info` checks describe the host
(docs.modular.com/mojo/manual/gpu/fundamentals; `stdlib/std/sys/info.mojo:1081`,
`:1111`, `:1839-1845`). Mojo's `sin` uses that split: on NVIDIA F32 it calls
the PTX instruction `sin.approx.ftz.f32`, on Apple GPUs `llvm.air.sin`, and
elsewhere `llvm.sin` (`stdlib/std/math/math.mojo:1749-1788`). Its `exp` uses
`exp2(x * log2e)` on GPUs for F16 and F32 and a Mojo polynomial on CPUs
(`math.mojo:609-658`). So Mojo's sine is portable in the sense that it compiles
everywhere, not in the sense that it gives the same digits everywhere.

**CUDA.** `sinf` is accurate to 2 ULP; the intrinsic `__sinf` has absolute
error 2^-21.41 on [-π, π] and is larger outside; `--use_fast_math` silently
replaces `sinf` with `__sinf`. NVIDIA states that functions outside IEEE 754
"may differ across different platforms, including between host, device, and
different device architectures", and that contraction is on by default (CUDA
Programming Guide v13.4.2, section 5.5, "Mathematical Functions").

**Metal.** The Metal Shading Language 4.1 specification sets
`-fmetal-math-fp32-functions` and `-fmetal-math-mode` both to `fast` by
default; `fast` allows reassociation and assumes no NaNs or infinities
(section 1.6.3, pages 15-16).

**WebGPU and WGSL.** WGSL states accuracy per built-in: F32 `sin` has
"absolute error at most 2^-11" on [-π, π], `exp` is 3 + 2·|x| ULP, division
2.5 ULP, and implementations may reassociate and fuse (W3C WGSL, sections
15.7.4 and 15.7.5).

**OpenCL C 3.0.** `sin` is within 4 ULP; `native_sin` is implementation
defined (Khronos OpenCL C 3.0 specification, section 7.4, "Relative Error as
ULPs").

**Triton.** `tl.dot` uses tensor cores in TF32 by default on NVIDIA, and the
documentation warns that F32 inputs "may be truncated to TF32 format (19-bit
floating point) without rounding" (triton-lang.org, `triton.language.dot`).

**SYCL 2020.** One C++ source holds host and device code ("single-source");
implementations compile it either with separate host and device passes (SMCP)
or one pass (SSCP) (Khronos SYCL 2020, sections 3.12.1-3.12.2).

**Halide.** The algorithm and its schedule are separate; the schedule picks
tiling, vectorizing and placement without changing the result
(halide-lang.org; Ragan-Kelley et al., PLDI 2013).

**Futhark.** Parallel work is written with second-order array combinators such
as `map` and `reduce`, which the compiler flattens for the GPU (Futhark
language reference, section 3.14.1).

**Correctly rounded math.** CORE-MATH provides correctly rounded functions and
checks univariate binary32 functions exhaustively
(core-math.gitlabpages.inria.fr). Float matrix units do not promise a plain
loop's rounding (Fasi, Higham, Mikaitis and Pranesh, "Numerical behavior of
NVIDIA tensor cores", PeerJ Computer Science 7:e330, 2021).

The pattern across peers: every vendor path lets the chip change the digits by
default (CUDA contraction, Metal fast math, Mojo per-target sine, Triton TF32).
Jet's ratified law already refuses that: D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1 makes strict and
reproducible the default and checks every device against the CPU oracle. That
is the one place Jet can clearly beat Mojo.

## One way to push code to the GPU

Ratified law already gives one mechanism with three depths. Nothing below adds
syntax beyond the one ballot.

**Beginner: tensor operations, no kernel.** The smallest GPU program uses
`core.compute` operations on tensors, with `.Auto` placement:

```jet
xs :: compute.from_list([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) ?? panic("xs")
ys :: compute.from_list([4.0, 5.0, 6.0]) ?? panic("ys")
print(compute.to_list(compute.add(xs, ys)))
```

Placement picks a GPU when one is present and emits a receipt
(D-COMPUTE-PLACE1, D-AUTOPIN1); a CPU fallback must be named and "cannot
change … observable results". Today this program stops with ICE 101 (probe g3).

**Next step: a marked kernel and a launch.** The user marks an ordinary
function and launches it by name:

```jet
#Kernel(.parallel)
fn add(left: F32, right: F32) -> F32 { left + right }

out :: compute.launch(add, inputs: (left: xs, right: ys)) ?? panic("launch")
```

The same function stays callable on the CPU (probe g15), so a user can test it
with ordinary code first. Jet tuples name every member (S73, probe g2c), so the
inputs are named after the kernel's parameters. The ratified example in
D-GPU-COMPUTE-LAUNCH1 writes a positional `(xs, ys)`, which E0048 rejects; the
decision's example text needs the named form when `launch` lands. This is a
spelling fix under two ratified rules, not a new choice.

**Expert: indexed kernels, memory spaces, matrix units, raw tier.**

- Indexed writes and per-thread positions through `Invocation`
  (D-GPU-INDEXED-RESOURCE1); today E1102 (probe g9).
- Workgroup-shared memory, subgroups, atomics and tiles are the unratified
  D-GPU-GROUP/SUBGROUP/ATOMIC/TILE drafts and #3026 criteria 11-16. Each needs
  its own proof fact before sema admits it.
- Matrix units (tensor cores) are the one open owner choice, ballot
  `D-GPU-DEVICE-OPS1`. The recommendation: matrix units are library operations
  such as a tile multiply-add, each with a plain Jet body that defines its
  answer. Device libraries lower them to the unit when the chip has one and
  the precision profile allows it. Kernel code reads `$build.hardware` facts,
  which are the same for the CPU reference and every device build, but never
  asks which device is compiling it. Under the default strict profile, float
  matrix units are not used, because they round differently from the plain
  loop; a kernel opts in with a named profile recorded in the receipt.
  Integer units that sum 8-bit products into 32 bits are exact while the sums
  fit, which the tile shape bounds, so they can be used by default.
- Raw vendor code stays in `#Unsafe` with a provider contract
  (D-COMPUTE-RAWBOUNDARY1).

## Split compilation

Mojo compiles one source twice. Jet's ratified pieces already describe the same
split with a stronger check:

1. Sema proves a `#Kernel` and attaches one proof record before the IR is built
   (D-COMPUTE-KERNEL-SURFACE1).
2. The kernel lowers once to the public, versioned kernel IR (D-ACCEL-LIB1).
   The host part compiles through the ordinary pipeline at o0, o1 or o2; the
   build level changes only the host code, never the kernel IR, which keeps I9.
3. The CPU reference is always compiled from the same kernel IR. Device
   libraries (Vulkan, Metal, CUDA, and WebGPU in the browser,
   D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1) lower the IR at build time when the device is named, or
   at install or first launch when placement is `.Auto`. The cache key holds
   the kernel IR hash, the library version, the hardware facts used and the
   precision profile (D-HOST-CAPS1 "Cache identity includes kind/probe package
   identities").
4. Conformance compares each device with the CPU reference: bit-equal under
   the default profile, within the stated bound under a named looser one.

The difference from Mojo is in step 3: under the recommended option of
`D-GPU-DEVICE-OPS1`, the CPU reference compiles the very code each device runs,
so a test on any machine covers every device's branch.

## A portable kernel library

#4731 asks for elementwise maps, reductions, scan, radix sort, tiled matmul,
convolution, softmax and attention, written in Jet with CPU-oracle and vendor
gauntlet cells and no new syntax. Under the law above, each library entry is an
ordinary Jet `#Kernel` (or a Core instruction entry with a plain body). Two
design points follow from Reproducible being the default:

- A reduction's combine order must be fixed by the library, not by each
  device's workgroup size. A fixed-shape pairwise tree, with block size chosen
  by the library and mapped onto workgroups by each device library, gives the
  same bits on every device. Faster, reordered reductions need a named policy
  (D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1).
- Tile sizes come from `$build.hardware` facts as compile-time parameters; they
  change speed, not results, because the fixed combine order is part of the
  plain body.

This makes the library portable in the strong sense: same answers, with speed
tuned per chip.

## Portable math

Today `math.sin` is a C libm call (`CompilerNeededMath.jet:28`), so it cannot be
proved inside a kernel (probe g7, E1102) and its bits depend on the host's libm.
D-MATH-BITS1 (open, recommendation A) makes `core.math` Jet code returning
correctly rounded results on every platform, level and at compile time, with
F32 versions "once they exist". Under it, `math.sin` becomes a pure Jet helper.
D-GPU-HELPER-SCOPE1=A then admits it into kernels, and the GPU, the CPU and
compile-time evaluation return the same bits. That answers the owner's request
for "custom declarations … more portable and accurate" better than Mojo, whose
GPU sine is the vendor approximation (above).

Two findings for the D-MATH-BITS1 author before it is ratified:

- **Wording conflict.** D-MATH-BITS1 says no option or flag switches the math
  library. D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1 allows fast math under named recorded policies,
  and #4732 says faster versions come only through a named compute precision
  profile. The two must agree on whether a profile may change what `math.sin`
  returns, or whether a fast sine is a separately named function with a stated
  bound. Either reading keeps one meaning per name; mixing them does not.
- **GPU cost.** Correctly rounded F32 functions are usually built with F64
  internals (the CORE-MATH binary32 approach). Consumer GPUs run F64 far
  slower than F32, so the F32 kernels need float-float internals or a paired
  cell that shows the cost (cell G2 below).

## Paired performance cells

AGENTS.md requires performance claims to come as two programs measured side by
side. These cells are specified now and blocked until #5454 (tensor ICEs),
#3026 (launch and indexed kernels) and #5964 (device library) land.

**G1: beginner against expert, same answer.** Workload: `y = a * x + y` over
16,777,216 F32 values, 100 passes, then a checksum.

| Side | Program |
|---|---|
| Beginner | `compute.add(compute.mul(a, xs), ys)` with `.Auto` placement. |
| Expert | an indexed `#Kernel` with `Invocation`, launched with a pinned Vulkan device. |
| Reference | the CPU oracle for the same kernel. |
| Peer | the same loop as a hand-written GLSL compute shader through Vulkan on the RX 7900 XTX. |

Report kernel time and end-to-end time separately (#3028 criteria 8 and 11),
and assert equal checksums. The gate: the beginner path within 2x of the
expert path end to end, and the expert path within 1.25x of the GLSL peer for
kernel time.

**G2: portable sine.** Workload: `math.sin` over 16,777,216 F32 inputs spread
over [-1000, 1000], on the same device.

| Side | Program |
|---|---|
| Jet | a `#Kernel` calling `math.sin` (correctly rounded, D-MATH-BITS1=A). |
| Peer | GLSL `sin` on the same device, and the CPU reference. |

Report time and the largest ULP error of each against the correctly rounded
result. The gate: Jet's answers equal the CPU reference on every input, and the
cost against the vendor sine is published, not hidden.

A CPU-only paired cell was measured for #6345 and is in
`Docs/research/2026-10-30-portable-target-capabilities.md`; it shows the scalar
F32 loop that kernels lower from is today 29x slower than C at o2.

## Criteria and cards this note feeds

- #3026 criteria 10 and 17: `compute.launch` with named inputs, and helper
  calls in kernels (probes g2b, g11).
- #4731: the fixed-order reduction rule above, and cells G1 and G2.
- #4732 and D-MATH-BITS1: the wording conflict and the F32 GPU cost.
- #5454: the tensor operation ICEs (probes g3, g4, tm4k).
- The browser `.Auto` mapping to the CPU (`ComputeWebGpu.js:525`) needs a card
  if none exists.

## Ballot

- `D-GPU-DEVICE-OPS1`: how expert kernels reach a chip's matrix units with one
  meaning. Options: A, library operations with a plain meaning (recommended);
  B, kernels branch on the device being compiled, as Mojo does; C, raw vendor
  code only. Builder and JSON in `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-2/ballot/`.

sections.title: A portable Jet target better than WebAssembly, and what it may learn about the host
sections.body:
# A portable Jet target better than WebAssembly, and what it may learn about the host

Date: 2026-10-30. Card #6345, criteria 1 to 3. Author: MemDesign-2 lane
(design only). Probes live in `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-2/probes/`
(`g/` for facts, `w/` for targets, `perf/` for the timing cell) and ran with
`$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/base/latest/jet` (commit 4e514f96e1) against a
`git archive` export of dev 4e514f96e1, at o0, o1 and o2 through
`probes/tiers.sh`. Unless a row says otherwise, all three levels gave the same
result.

The owner asked for a portable target that replaces WebAssembly without being
a lowest common denominator: portable code should reach tensor cores, wide
vector units and GPUs through some metadata the sandbox host exposes. Most of
that is already ratified. This note shows what is ratified, what runs, how the
pieces fit, where the security boundary sits, and what the paired cells
measure. It raises two owner choices, filed as `D-HOST-FACTS-VIEW1` and
`D-PORTABLE-WEB1`.

## Ratified and open decisions

Tower decisions:

| Decision | Status | What it settles for this card |
|---|---|---|
| D-PORTABLE1 | ratified A, 2026-10-02 | The portable file holds verified Jet code; the host checks it, grants each power and compiles it locally. Technical: a "versioned portable encoding of D-TIER-FORM1 MIR; host verifier; brokered unforgeable handles; interpreter then local native cache". Browsers need a separate adapter. |
| D-PORTABLE2 | ratified A, 2026-10-07 | The host checks the final machine code against the wall rules, so a compiler bug "can then make the app wrong, but cannot let it out". |
| D-HOST-CAPS1 | ratified A, 2026-10-07 | Typed hardware descriptions read through `$build.hardware`; outputs list `requires:` and `uses:`; packages add hardware kinds with `satisfies` and `coarse` methods; "host observations, grants and kind/probe package identities determine launch admission/cache identity, never a producer's asserted facts". |
| D-CPU-DISPATCH1 | ratified A, 2026-10-02 | `#Multiversion(levels...)` builds one copy per CPU level; `$build.cpu` describes the level inside each copy. |
| D-LANES1 | ratified A, 2026-10-02 | `Lanes<T, N>` exact widths and `Lanes<T>` native width; "Fixed reduction order is part of the Core definition". |
| D-CORE-BOUNDARY1 | ratified A, 2026-10-05 | Chip instructions are library entries with a plain Jet body. |
| D-CORE-FEATURE-FLOW1 | ratified A, 2026-10-05 | Chip features are automatic by default with explicit expert control. |
| D-ACCEL-LIB1 | ratified A, 2026-10-28 | Accelerators are libraries over a public kernel IR, checked against the CPU result. |
| D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1 | ratified B, 2026-10-05 | Recorded runs plus an opt-in in-program optimizer, refused for browsers and WebAssembly. |
| D-EXEC3 | ratified A, 2026-10-07 | Build levels share speed-ups and are checked against each other. |
| D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 | ratified A, 2026-10-30 | The compiler builds in machine powers; Core declares the rest. |
| D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1 | ratified A, 2026-10-30 | A build's effect limit is read from its target profile. |
| D-CORE-PLUGINLIMITS1 | ratified A, 2026-09-28 | A host sets a sandbox component's fuel, memory and time limits. |
| D-WASISRV1 | ratified A, 2026-08-12 | wasm32-wasip2 is a full server target. |
| D-LEARN-WEB1 | ratified A, 2026-10-07 | Jet's checker and runner compile to WebAssembly and run in a static page. |
| D-TARGET-ORDER1 | ratified A, 2026-10-28 | Targets return in the order wasm32-wasip2, then aarch64, then embedded. |
| D-AUTOPIN1 | ratified A, 2026-09-28 | Every automatic choice can be seen and locked. |
| D-COMPTIME-WORD1 | ratified A, 2026-10-17 | `comptime` forces compile-time work; with D-PREP-SURFACE2=A, `prep` is retired. |
| D-MATH-BITS1 | open, recommendation A | `core.math` returns the same correctly rounded bits everywhere. |

Decisions kept in `Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md`: D-TIER-FORM1=A (`:9735`),
D-FREESTAND-FACTS1=A (`:9098`), D-DEP-WASM1=A (`:8843`), D-SIMD3=B (`:3762`),
D-EXEC2=A, JIT retired (`:3773`), D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1=D (`:6953-6959`). The
glossary row for `comptime` records that `prep` is retired
(`syntax-decisions.md:35`).

## What runs today

| Probe | Program | Result on o0, o1, o2 |
|---|---|---|
| w/hello | `jet build --target=portable`, `web`, `wasm32-wasip2`, `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `sandbox` | E2104 "is not built yet" for each. |
| h6b | `print($build.os)`, `print($build.profile)` | `Linux`, `dev`. |
| h1, h2, h6 | `$build.cpu`, `$build.hardware`, `$build.arch` | E0107 "Nothing named `$build` exists here". |
| h3 | `#Multiversion` | E0927, unknown marker. |
| h4 | `Lanes<F32, 4>` | E0003. |
| h8 | `F32x4(1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0)` added to itself | `F32x4 { lanes: [2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0] }`. |

No `.jetapp` code exists in `Compiler/` or `Core/` (a search for `jetapp`
finds nothing). The target table knows the wasm triples
(`Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Target/TargetMachine.jet:573`, `:594`, `:615`)
and maps `wasm32-unknown-unknown` to the browser profile (`:527`).
`Compiler/JetWasm/Source/Wasm/` holds a decoder, validator, text form and
component model (`Bytes.jet`, `Component.jet`, `Decode.jet`, `Module.jet`,
`Opcodes.jet`, `Text.jet`, `Validate.jet`): Jet reads WebAssembly, it does not
yet write it.

One naming hazard: `core.hardware` already exists as the embedded-board
capability `Target.Hardware` (`TargetMachine.jet:666`, `:714`), available only
when the target has register blocks or interrupts (`:827`). D-HOST-CAPS1's
Core `Hardware` description is a different thing with the same word. The
implementing card should keep them apart.

## What WebAssembly gives and lacks

- **Fixed-width vectors.** WebAssembly SIMD has one vector type, the 128-bit
  `v128` (WebAssembly Core Specification 2.0, vector types). A machine with
  AVX-512 or SVE gets four F32 lanes at most.
- **Relaxed SIMD trades determinism for speed.** "This proposal introduces
  non-deterministic instructions"; the same instruction may give different
  results on different engines (WebAssembly relaxed-simd Overview,
  "Consistency").
- **Threads** need shared memory imported or defined by the host
  (WebAssembly threads proposal Overview, "Shared Linear Memory"); creating
  threads is left to the embedder.
- **No GPU outside the browser.** In browsers, GPU access is WebGPU through
  JavaScript. For WASI, WebGPU is a Phase 2 proposal, not a standard
  interface (WebAssembly/WASI `docs/Proposals.md:33-43`).
- **Walls from the engine.** The engine validates and bounds-checks; the
  compiler that made the module is untrusted.

## What peers do

- **Mojo.** A precompiled `.mojoc` package "contains non-elaborated code, so
  you can share it across systems"; it becomes machine code only when imported
  into a program built with `mojo build`, and it "is tied to the exact version
  of the compiler that produced it"
  (`Mojo/docs/site/manual/packages.md:150-157`, corpus commit 85356f6562ed).
  It is a portable compile input, not a sandbox format.
- **SPIR-V.** A module declares every capability it uses with `OpCapability`;
  "A client API is allowed to reject modules declaring capabilities it does
  not support" (Khronos SPIR-V specification, section 2.1). This is the model
  for `requires:`.
- **JVM and .NET tiered compilation.** .NET starts on quick JIT or
  precompiled ReadyToRun code and recompiles hot methods with full
  optimization (learn.microsoft.com, "Tiered compilation"). Jet's portable
  host does the same in two steps: interpreter, then a cached native build
  (D-PORTABLE1 technical).
- **Capability APIs.** Java's Vector API has `FloatVector.SPECIES_PREFERRED`
  and promises "graceful degradation" where vectors are missing (JEP 529).
  .NET has `Vector.IsHardwareAccelerated`. Both are open to any code.
- **eBPF.** The kernel's verifier checks a program in two steps, a control
  flow check and then a walk of every path, before it may load
  (docs.kernel.org, "eBPF verifier"). Jet's host verifier plus machine-code
  checker is the same idea for whole applications.
- **WebGPU.** "A user agent must not reveal more than 32 distinguishable
  configurations or buckets"; limits may be binned; adapter identifiers stay
  broad unless the user consents; timing fingerprinting is
  "low-signal and relatively intractable" to prevent (W3C WebGPU editor's
  draft of 27 October 2026, sections 2.2, 2.2.1, 2.2.3 and 2.2.6).

## The form Jet ships

The owner's three candidates were an IR, a bytecode, or ahead-of-time code per
host. Ratified law already picks a combination, with one encoding:

1. **The file is IR.** A `.jetapp` is the versioned, content-hashed encoding of
   Jet's mid-level IR (D-PORTABLE1, D-TIER-FORM1). There is no separate
   bytecode; the MIR encoding plays that role, which keeps I8.
2. **GPU parts travel inside it** as the public kernel IR (D-ACCEL-LIB1), so
   the host's device library lowers them for the GPU it has.
3. **The host compiles it ahead of time, locally.** The host verifies the file,
   starts it in the interpreter, and caches a native build compiled for this
   machine (D-PORTABLE1). Before native code runs, the machine-code checker
   proves it stays inside the walls (D-PORTABLE2).

Local compilation is what beats WebAssembly. At local compile time the host
knows the real machine, so `Lanes<T>` lowers to the widest register the CPU has
(D-LANES1), Core's chip copies are built for this CPU only rather than for a
list of levels (D-CPU-DISPATCH1), and kernels lower to the GPU that is present.
Every one of those paths has a plain Jet meaning tested equal
(D-CORE-BOUNDARY1), and lane reductions have a fixed order (D-LANES1). So
unlike relaxed SIMD, the faster path never changes the answer, and I9 holds
across the interpreter, the cached build and every machine.

## Hardware facts as typed facts

Under D-HOST-CAPS1 a program reads hardware facts the same way on every target.

- **Admission.** `requires:` lists what the app cannot run without. The host
  checks it at install and at each launch, like SPIR-V's `OpCapability`, and
  refuses with the missing fact named.
- **Specialization.** `uses:` lists what the app can use when present. The app
  branches with `comptime if $build.hardware.has(…)`; the branch folds at
  local compile, so the built code contains no run-time query.
- **Cache identity.** The answers join the cache key. When the hardware
  changes, the host recompiles.
- **Coarse facts.** Facts are lower bounds; "a coarse projection never
  overstates capability" (D-HOST-CAPS1 explainer).

The ratified examples in D-HOST-CAPS1 and D-CPU-DISPATCH1 spell the branch
`prep if`, which is retired (`syntax-decisions.md:35`); the current spelling is
`comptime if`, which works today for `$build.os` (probe h6b and
`Examples/features/comptime/fact_plane.jet:3-11`).

## The security boundary

What a portable app can learn about its host, under ratified law plus the
recommended option of `D-HOST-FACTS-VIEW1`:

1. **Declared answers only.** In a portable bundle, code may ask
   `$build.hardware.has(q)` only for a question listed in `uses:`. The host
   answers each from facts it observed and granted, as one bit. Reading a
   hardware value in a portable bundle is a build error.
2. **A budget.** By default an app gets at most five answers, so it can tell
   apart at most 32 kinds of machine, matching WebGPU's limit. The user may
   raise it for one app.
3. **A host may answer no.** Because every chip path has one meaning, a "no"
   costs speed, not correctness.
4. **Package rounding is not trusted.** The package that defines a hardware
   kind also writes its `coarse` method and could return precise values. Under
   option A only one bit per question reaches the app, whatever `coarse` does.
5. **Same answers everywhere.** Under I9 and D-MATH-BITS1=A, results do not
   differ by machine, so arithmetic itself does not reveal the chip. Relaxed
   SIMD does.
6. **Facts never grant powers.** Powers come from the host's grants
   (D-PORTABLE1); a hardware answer cannot open a file or a socket.
7. **Native programs are trusted** and keep every fact.

Limits that remain, under every option:

- **Timing.** An app can time a loop and guess the chip. WebGPU reaches the same
  conclusion (section 2.2.3). Separate processes per app, the side-channel
  hardening D-PORTABLE2 requires when untrusted apps share a process, and
  coarse timers are host policy.
- **Resource failures.** D-HOST-CAPS1 checks free GPU memory before each job.
  A refused job tells the app something about free memory. The implementing
  card should report such refusals in coarse buckets.

## The browser

D-PORTABLE1 says a browser needs a separate adapter. Ballot `D-PORTABLE-WEB1`
asks whether that adapter should be an in-page Jet host that runs the same
`.jetapp`: verified, then translated to WebAssembly in the page with the same
back end as the web export (#5201), with an optional ready-made WebAssembly
copy keyed by the app's hash. D-LEARN-WEB1 already puts Jet's checker in the
page, so the in-page host extends ratified work.

## Paired performance cells

**P1, measured: one loop, native against WebAssembly.** `y = 0.999 * x + y`
over 1,048,576 F32 values, 400 passes, then a Float checksum. Sources:
`probes/perf/saxpy.c` and `probes/perf/saxpy.jet`. Every build printed checksum
629040256. The machine was shared and loaded (load average about 92 on 28
cores), so these are indicative; the table shows the minimum of five runs
unless marked.

| Build | Command | Time (s) |
|---|---|---|
| C native, `-march=native` | gcc 15.3 `-O2 -ffp-contract=off -march=native` | 0.044 |
| C native, baseline | gcc 15.3 `-O2 -ffp-contract=off` | 0.059 |
| C to WebAssembly, SIMD | zig 0.15.2 `cc -target wasm32-wasi -O2 -msimd128`, Wasmtime 48 `run -C cache=n` | 0.122 |
| C to WebAssembly, scalar | the same without `-msimd128` | 0.324 |
| Jet native, o2 | `jet build --optimize=full` | 1.72 (single runs 1.7 to 3.4) |
| Jet native, o1 | `jet build --optimize=basic` | 2.50 |
| Jet native, o0 | `jet build --optimize=none` | 7.08 (one run) |
| Jet portable | `jet build --target=portable` | E2104, not built |

Two findings. First, WebAssembly costs about 2x to 2.8x against native C here,
including Wasmtime's compile at load; that is the gap a locally compiled
`.jetapp` should close. Second, Jet's own native scalar F32 loop is 29x slower
than baseline C at o2. That gap belongs to native code generation (#6205,
#2414) and must close before any portable cell can show Jet beating
WebAssembly.

**P2, specified: the portable file against native and WebAssembly.** The same
workload as a `.jetapp`, run three ways on one machine: Jet native at the same
level, the `.jetapp` after local compile (cold and cached reported
separately), and the C WebAssembly SIMD build above. Gates: the cached
`.jetapp` within 5% of Jet native; the `.jetapp` faster than WebAssembly SIMD
on a CPU wider than 128 bits, through `Lanes<F32>`; equal checksums
everywhere.

**P3, specified: one meaning under specialization.** A matmul app with
`uses: [GPU.feature(.TensorCores)]`, run once with the host answering yes and
once with it answering no. Gate: equal checksums under the default profile,
with both times reported. This cell proves that a "no" answer costs only speed.

## Criteria and cards this note feeds

- #4195 criteria 1 to 3 (portable app, two hosts, hardware requirements) and
  #6126 (per-target facts): `$build.cpu` and `$build.hardware` are E0107 today.
- #1914 and D-TARGET-ORDER1: every wasm target is E2104 today.
- #5201: the web back end that the in-page host would reuse.
- #6205 and #2414: the 29x scalar F32 gap in cell P1.
- The `core.hardware` naming overlap and the resource-failure bucket above.
- The retired `prep if` spelling in the D-HOST-CAPS1 and D-CPU-DISPATCH1
  examples.

## Ballots

- `D-HOST-FACTS-VIEW1`: what a sandboxed app may learn about the machine.
  Options: A, declared yes-or-no questions within a budget of five (recommended);
  B, coarse descriptions of every device, as ratified; C, no facts in portable
  apps.
- `D-PORTABLE-WEB1`: whether the same `.jetapp` also runs in a browser.
  Options: A, an in-page Jet host translates it to WebAssembly (recommended);
  B, a separate web build, as ratified.

Builders and JSON are in `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-2/ballot/`.

sections.title: Hello-world binary size: what the runtime keeps alive, 2026-10-30
sections.body:
# Hello-world binary size: what the runtime keeps alive, 2026-10-30

Card #6328 C1. This audit breaks down the size of `jet build` of hello world:
every runtime function and data object over 1 KB, and the root that keeps it
in the binary. It is a read-only audit; nothing here changes behavior.

The program is `fn run() { print("hello") }`. The compiler is `82d3369757`
plus #6106 C1 and C2 (per-function runtime sections, section gc, and the
vault split). The runtime sources are unchanged from there through dev
`abc19f121d`. The target is x86-64 Linux (musl), static.

## Totals

All five builds are byte-identical at 437,416 B: `jet build`,
`--optimize=none`, `--optimize=basic`, `--optimize=full` and `--release`.
Hello's own code is `main_run` (105 B). It makes one runtime call, so there is
nothing for the optimizer to change. Everything else is runtime.

The optimization levels do work on real code. A loop-and-format probe's
`main_sum` is 572 B at o0 and 484 B at o2. That probe's o2 binary is still
64 B larger than its o0 binary, 458,208 B against 458,144 B.

| section | bytes | share |
|---|---:|---:|
| `.text` | 387,880 | 88.7% |
| `.eh_frame` | 29,148 | 6.7% |
| `.symtab` + `.strtab` + `.shstrtab` | 9,938 | 2.3% |
| `.data` | 3,816 | 0.9% |
| `.debug_*` | 482 | 0.1% |
| `.rodata` | 352 | 0.1% |
| `.init_array` / `.fini_array` | 304 / 16 | 0.1% |
| `.bss` (no file bytes) | 2,044 | |

Program code is 310 B: `main` (36), `main_run` (105) and `jet_ir_stop_poll`
(169). The runtime pack contributes 749 live sections:

- 384,671 B of text;
- 3,747 B of data;
- 1,956 B of bss;
- 313 B of rodata.

Peer hello worlds built on the same machine:

| peer | bytes |
|---|---:|
| Zig `ReleaseSmall`, stripped | 10,720 |
| C, musl static, `-Os`, stripped | 17,696 |
| Rust, `opt-level=z`, stripped | 394,032 |

## Method

Section liveness was recomputed over `jet_runtime.pack.o` with the static
link's own rules (StaticLink.jet `link_collect`).

The roots are:

- `_start`;
- every `.init_array`, `.fini_array` and `SHF_GNU_RETAIN` section;
- the CIE personality routines;
- the program's references.

The program's references were recovered from the binary. They are the call
and RIP-relative operands of the program's functions that land on runtime
symbols. There are seven:

- `jet_rt_main`
- `jet_rt_host_arguments`
- `jet_rt_host_program_start`
- `jet_rt_process_entry_return`
- `jet_rt_session_propagate`
- `jet_rt_stdout_flush`
- `jet_term_write_stdout_line`

An FDE's LSDA edges follow the function's section.

The recomputed live set matches the binary exactly: 749 sections. Their
bytes, plus program code and alignment, equal `.text`.

The pack strips the names of private functions. They were recovered by
matching section bytes against `jet_runtime_jet.o`.

**Held** is the number of bytes that leave the binary if that one section is
never reached. It is computed by removing the section and recomputing
reachability. A cut's **freed alone** figure is the same measure applied to
one edge of the graph.

## Root causes

Cuts overlap, so the freed-alone figures do not sum. The cumulative table
below is the additive view.

1. **Runtime-gated features are linked unconditionally. Observe is kept
   alive by an environment read: 107,301 B.**
   - `jet_rt_main` always calls `jet_rt_observe_runtime_start_from_env`.
     It checks `JET_OBSERVE` at run time.
   - That check is a branch. Liveness cannot prune a branch, so the writer
     thread, the snapshot and JSON publishers and thread spawn are all
     linked.
2. **A shared-state read links the whole scheduler: 72,224 B, inside cause
   1.**
   - The environment read takes `shared_acquire`.
   - Its contention path calls `scheduler_blocking_wait_enter`, which makes
     up for the blocked worker by starting another one. That chain is:
     1. `scheduler_get`
     2. `scheduler_worker_count`
     3. `cpu_available_parallelism`
     4. the cgroup v1 and v2 quota parsers and the mountinfo search
     5. `jet_rt_scheduler_worker`
     6. `task_run`
   - So reading one variable keeps the task scheduler, worker threads and
     cgroup parsing alive in a program that never spawns a task.
3. **The fault handler is always installed: 50,111 B.**
   - `jet_rt_main` calls `fault_start`, which takes the address of
     `jet_rt_fault_signal`.
   - The handler carries an in-process DWARF reader to print crash
     locations. Its largest parts are:

     | function | bytes |
     |---|---:|
     | `fault_line` | 6,115 |
     | `fault_file` | 5,523 |
     | `fault_sections` | 4,715 |
     | `fault_unit` | 4,424 |
     | `fault_source` | 4,137 |
     | `fault_form` | 3,949 |
     | `fault_abbrevs` | 3,829 |
4. **EH frame registration is decided when the pack is built: 22,047 B, plus
   29,148 B of `.eh_frame`.**
   - The pack defines the unwinder. So `link_eh_shims` writes
     `__jet_eh_startup` as `jmp __register_frame_info`, and every program's
     `_start` reaches:
     - libgcc's FDE code, which is one 13,371 B `.text` that is not split
       into function sections;
     - musl `malloc`;
     - `pthread_cond_timedwait`.
   - The Jet runtime never unwinds; stops travel by stop edges. The tables
     and the unwinder serve only foreign code, and hello has none.
5. **Every runtime stop fans out into comptime serving and test
   publication: 18,287 B for the serve protocol alone.**
   - `trap_simple`, `jet_rt_fixed_shift_stop` and the other stop routines
     first call `comptime_serve_stop`. It checks `comptime_serving()` at run
     time, but statically links the whole protocol:
     - `comptime_serve_loop`
     - `comptime_serve_value`
     - `jet_rt_int_from_static`
     - big-int packing
   - The stop routines then go through `rt_task_panic_publish` to
     `test_scope_record_coded_stop` and text formatting.
   - The runtime's own checked arithmetic reaches these stops from
     `jet_rt_alloc_init`.
6. **38 unconditional static constructors.** Every runtime module with
   global state registers an `.init_array` entry, and init arrays are gc
   roots. Hello keeps all 38, including:
   - `alloc`, `task_exit`, `layout` (`layout_literals_init` alone is
     4,893 B) and `test_capture`;
   - `thread`, `codec_text_cells`, `journey`, `session`, `log_state` and
     `fault_allocation`;
   - `net_poller`, `observe`, `crypto_entropy`, `comptime`, `sentry`,
     `test_suite`, `fs_held` and `stm`.

   After the cuts in the next section, the constructors still hold
   108,890 B.
7. **The exit path always reports parked tasks: 12,856 B through
   `main_exit_cleanup`.** It runs `jet_rt_task_exit_handlers` and
   `jet_rt_observe_parked_tasks_report` with its detail and cancel paths.
   This happens even when no task or exit handler exists.
8. **Print goes through test capture: 5,947 B.** It is held by the
   constructor and by `jet_term_write_stdout_line` calling
   `jet_rt_test_capture_print` on every line.

## Cumulative cuts

The pack has 390,687 live bytes. Each row cuts one more edge.

| cut | freed alone | freed cumulative | remaining |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| fault handler | 50,111 | 50,111 | 340,576 |
| observe start (includes shared → scheduler) | 107,301 | 157,412 | 233,275 |
| EH registration shim | 22,047 | 181,635 | 209,052 |
| stop → comptime serve | 18,287 | 199,922 | 190,765 |
| parked-task report | 10,751 | 241,907 | 148,780 |
| test capture (init + print) | 5,947 | 247,854 | 142,833 |
| layout literals init | 5,442 | 253,296 | 137,391 |
| task exit handlers | 1,577 | 254,873 | 135,814 |
| root stop take | 4,877 | 260,759 | 129,928 |

The remaining 130 KB is mostly the 38 constructors (108,890 B). The rest,
about 16 KB, is `jet_rt_main`, host arguments and environment seeding. So the
size is set by the design: unconditional startup, unconditional exit, and
gates that are checked at run time. Removing individual symbols cannot fix
it.

## Data objects

No runtime data object reaches 1 KB. The largest is musl's
`__malloc_context`, 928 B of bss, which is reached only through the EH
unwinder's `malloc` (cause 4). The next largest are two bss blocks of 336 B
and 232 B and a 197 B `.data` table.

briefings.title: Two lanes on speed, three on cleanup; hello-world numbers
briefings.body:
## Where things stand (early afternoon, 24 Oct)

**Lanes now follow your rule: two on speed, three on the other goals.**
- Speed: O0Speed-3 works on the code generator and runtime fast paths. RustOut-4 works on the type checker's hot spots.
- Rust removal: O0Comptime-3. The old Rust bridge is already unused, so the database, HTTP, email and vault features fail on native today (31 goldens). The lane is replacing them with Jet code plus vendored C: SQLite first, then mbedTLS for TLS.
- MIR/TIR/LIR cleanup: O0Image-3. It found 2,669 files that mention the old layers and is landing deletions and renames in five batches.
- Goldens and the bug backlog: O0Load-3. It sorted 382 bad goldens by cause; 133 are "native can't build this yet". It is fixing a crash first: the compiler did not require a `match` on the dynamic JSON value type to cover every case.

**Landed since noon:** a faster `String.bytes()`, and four cuts to compile-time evaluation. In a like-for-like comparison, self-compile went from 13.6 s to 12.4 s, and compile-time evaluation from 2.45 s to 1.43 s.

**Hello world today** (minimum times, busy machine):
- Run as a script: `jet run` takes 35 ms, against LuaJIT 1 ms, Bun 6 ms, Python 10 ms, Node 19 ms and `go run` 40 ms.
- Build from scratch: 51 ms. That beats gcc (87–89 ms), clang (108 ms) and rustc (139 ms); Go takes 42 ms using its cached standard library.
- Binary run time: 0.7 ms, the same as Rust and 0.2 ms behind C. The binary is 4.9 MB.
- Bug #5926: a warm cache makes Jet slower (80–1,700 ms). No lane owns it yet.

**Your rulings, recorded:**
- Unboxed `Option<Int>` is approved (#5894).
- The Zed extension is exempt from Rust removal.
- The Rust FFI host example and the Cargo test fixtures stay.

briefings.title: Afternoon status 2026-10-24: 4 leaks fixed, -2.4 GB, code generator is the speed limit
briefings.body:
# Status, 2026-10-24 afternoon

## Landed since 10:00 (dev, not yet pushed)

| Commit | What it does |
|---|---|
| 277c996280 | Parse claim queue (R5a). Load wall 0.97 → 0.78 s; neutral overall. |
| 94d81c7d95 | Closures are freed at their last owner (#5909). A test of 16 closure patterns peaks at 4 MB instead of 4.9 GB. |
| 4ee52a723d | A direct call names its callee by declaration ID (L2b-1). Neutral; enables later layers. |
| f5300bffdc | Front-end M2. `jet check Compiler` 2.2 s → 0.25 s. |
| 3153454982 | Fallible transaction hooks no longer leak (#5918). |
| d51932e30f | `map`/`filter_map` with an optional callback typed correctly (#5920; it printed garbage or crashed), plus L2b-2a. |
| 2f7aafe191 | A process that cannot start returns a typed error instead of crashing (#5921). |
| ba69799c71 | Front-end M3. Load 0.77 → 0.68 s. |
| 803195f620 | Authority follow-ups (#5070). `jet fix --all` no longer hangs. |
| 7574d49abe | Recursive-type structs no longer leak (#5917). Self-compile peak memory −1.37 GB. |
| 5217eca4cc | Symbol keys are 64-bit hashes (keyhash v2). About 2 s less CPU. |

Cards closed: #5909, #5917, #5918, #5920, #5921 and #5889 (#5889's cost was entirely the #5917 leak).

## Where speed stands

- Self-compile: about 12–13 s of wall time.
- Self-compile peak memory: about 6.5 GB, down from about 8.9 GB this morning.
- Target: 2.5 s and less than 1 GB.

## What we learned

- **Generated code is the main limit.** A plain byte loop costs 14–24 instructions per byte, where about 1–5 is ideal. A small accessor call costs about 35–45 instructions. Building the compiler at the release level does not fix this. Front-end source changes can reach about −23%, not the 64× needed. The code-generator fixes are now P0 card #5925.
- **Measurement fix.** The shared baseline compilers are built by the seed, one generation behind lane builds, so comparisons against them were not like for like. The parse claim queue's "−4.4%" was that artefact. Every comparison now builds both sides the same way in one run. Some gains reported this morning could not be re-measured and are marked unverified.

## In progress

| Lane | Work |
|---|---|
| O0Load-3 | #5910, memory under 1 GB (free each phase's data, arenas) |
| O0Comptime-3 | #5912, compile-time evaluation from 1.65 s to about 0.7–0.85 s cold |
| RustOut-4 | #5911, single-threaded stretches; about −1.0 to −1.3 s projected |
| O0Speed-3 | #5925, code generator: cancellation checks, register use, integer checks |
| O0Image-3 | #5914, parser token cursor and lexer name interning |

## Owner items

- The D-MEM votes on #5894. UNBOX1 gates the Option<Int> patch: it passes its proof, and the back-end phases are 3.4% faster.
- Ballot #3595; votes on #5831–#5834; the #5838 temp-allocator ballot; coredump configuration.

## New cards

- #5919: closures copy captured structs unnecessarily.
- #5922: runtime witnesses cannot see frees inside the runtime.
- #5923: 24 authority test cases fail.
- #5924: memory test cases: 4 fail, 1 internal compiler error, 3 refused.
- #5925: code generator quality.

# Status at 10:00, 2026-10-24

## Speed (goal #1)
- Self-compile is not at 2.5 s. The cleanest number today is a 3-round same-run median of 11.85 s at default threads (09:44, base 8d2082ea63). It was about 14.4 s under load yesterday evening.
- Landed today: name numbering on a fast hash (R3a, −5.1% instructions), a diagnostic-scan fix (−2.6%), the first and second type-table slices (−3.3%, −0.5%) and a word-wise string compare. Together they cut compiler work by about 7.6% (0.828 → 0.766 trillion instructions).
- Also landed: the IR build work queue (8a26534c9f). It cuts the ir.build phase from 1.63 to 1.27 s (−22%); the whole build gains only −0.6% (11.85 → 11.78 s) in the same-run A/B. An earlier −1.2 s figure came from runs under different load and is withdrawn.
- dev HEAD is c324db24be. Nothing is pushed to origin yet.
- Direction change (owner, 08:00): the data-oriented core is the plan, and it is the same work as the TIR/MIR/LIR removal. Design: lanes/RustOut/tp/s3-design.md and lanes/O0Speed/flat-ir.md. Layers L0-L7 each land as a complete cutover. Estimates: names, declarations and types as numbers −15-20% CPU; side tables, flat tree and IR from the tree another −10% CPU and −2 GB RSS. 2.5 s needs the whole core, which is days of work, not hours.

- TIR removal landed in five steps today (s4c2a, s4-literals, s4-constref, dead walkers, program_body), each with byte-identical compiler output.

briefings.title: Memory model review (overnight 2026-10-23)
briefings.body:
## Memory model review (you asked before bed)

The full report is on master: **Docs/audits/2026-10-23-memory-model-review.md** (commit 55246c13f2). It was a read-only review by a separate Opus agent; nothing was built or run, so the speed points rest on code and card evidence.

**In short:** the foundations hold up. Ownership is read / `&` write / `^` take; sharing is reference counting plus copy-on-write; there is one allocator, and comptime runs on the same runtime, so the meaning is the same on every tier. The big problems:

- **Promised features that can't be built:** arenas and pools, raw pointers, stack sentries, `#Context(...)` and `#Policy(gc)` have no native lowering, but the spec describes them as working.
- **Possible use-after-free:** `jet_rt_secret_from_bytes` takes over a list buffer without checking that nothing else shares it (#5888, P1).
- **Close may run while a buffer is still shared:** Close glue closes every List/Map element even when the buffer is shared (#5889, P1, needs a check).
- **Two Secret mechanisms:** the crypto one wipes less and is skipped on crash. This breaks I8 (#5891).
- **Biggest speed gap:** every Option, Result and enum with a payload is a separate heap box with an atomic count. On top of that, the allocator wastes nearly 2x (24-byte header plus power-of-two sizes), and counts are atomic even in single-threaded code.
- **Small waste:** the inlined release ignores the exit flag, so drop walks still run at exit (#5890).

**Cards filed:** #5888, #5889, #5890, #5891, #5892 (spec says working), #5893 (stale comments).

**Needs your rulings: #5894** (9 questions). Build the expert tier or mark it unbuilt; the `@` link cutover; GC: build or retire; `#Context`: build or remove; stop boxing Option/Result; non-atomic counts by default; Secret page locking; long-lived host heap; ballot #4935.
